        Gert Smith

How does one even begin to tell the history of the community called Beulah,
North Dakota? Statistics, facts and dates will verify events and give census
counts, but they do not reflect the nature of the people. Photographs give a
memorable image of an event, but they do not tell a complete story.

No writer could ever find the words to tell the history of a town. It is the
people themselves who must tell their story. They must tell of their hopes and
dreams and their difficulties and defeats. They must tell of their beginnings,
their progress and their failures. Only after their story is told can the
history of our people be understood.

In these pages, we have attempted to let the people tell their own story of the
birth, growth and expansion of the community we call home. They have told a
story of a townsite that grew into a village, expanded into a town and later
became a focal point of a massive energy development that was far beyond the
dreams of any of our early ancestors.

Their stories show how they laughed, played, toiled and sorrowed in their
day-to-day lives over the past 75 years, and we believe the individual
collective spirit of these people tells more about their nature than any
writer's words could ever describe.

It is true that each person and experience encountered in the life of an
individual subtly shapes the soul and spirit. Thus a study of our history gives
us the beginnings of wisdom to understand who we are, where we have been and
where we are going.

In the course of researching, compiling and writing this 75th anniversary book
for the city of Beulah, we have seen how blessed our community has been
throughout its 75-year history. We have recognized the many family, community
and political leaders who have helped to shape our destiny. We have appreciated
the qualities of our citizens which enabled them to endure through years of
drought, depression, war and weather conditions.

The story told by the people in this book is a story of a people always in
transition, yet always holding firmly to the values of the past. It is the
unique unmatchable story of the people of Beulah, North Dakota.

We hope you, as residents and friends, enjoy reading this book as much as we
have enjoyed compiling it from the lives of those who, over the last 75 years,
have created it.

Sincerely,

Nancy Northrup          Jo Ann Miller

The Ballad to Dakota

I thought some last night
Of the cowboys I've known,
Some I just heard of;
Of the tribute we've shown.
And the more I remembered,
The more that I smiled,
For their stories are colorful,
Some are just wild!
I'll start with the one
I could say I knew best,
A fellow, a farm lad,
With a dream like the rest,
He found he could ride
The broncs in the corral,
So he figured he'd give
The rodeo world hell!
Well, Del and his buddy
Started putting on miles,
They rode 'em and raked 'em,
They had many trials;
But finally one day,
After many miles and months passed,
An old cowhand spoke up:
"Did you know you must mark that bronc?"
Was the question he asked!
Well, after he was given
This clue to success,
Del rode with a style
That made him one of the best!

Then there's the story of Kenny S.
His is a story that I will confess
Brings tears to your eyes,
A youthful love gone wrong;
His was a life that would fit
Some old cowboy's song.
He was one real hand
With the broncs, they say,
One especially, a big rangy bay
That no one else ever rode,
Is the story they tell,
But Kenny broke him and tamed him,
Left his spirit intact.
That was one cowboy
Who never lacked
In hoss sense and savvy;
He was the best!
But he became ill
With a dread disease
It brought that cowboy
To his bended knees.
He wasn't so old, but he trembled and shook,
While he saddled the bay
Who stood and just took
Whate'er Ken did to mount him. Then
He walked away; he was one horse in ten!
Wild in spirit, but tamed by a man
Who ended his life by his own hand;
Left his saddle, his hoss,
To his sister, Ann,
When life became more
Than he could stand.

There's also the story
Of the Indian brothers, three,
Immanuel, Emerson, and Joe,
Most stories agree
They were riders and ropers,
All tough and so proud,
Which one was the best?
Well, I've heard it allowed,
'Twas Immanuel who could ride a bronc
Till that ten-second whistle blew,
Just spurring and digging
Till blood he drew,
Then haul up that horse
By the halter rope,
Strong as a bull!
The bronc hadn't a hope!
He rode with the best
Even matched Casey Tibbs,
Matched 'em and beat 'em,
If only he'd lived!
His story so mournful,
A cowboy gone bad;
The booze is what did it,
Such talent he had!
A cowboy once told me
That Joe would have been the best,
Might have won the world title
If Immanuel had lived
Like the rest.
"But why?" we all asked.
"Was he the more fit?
Joe wasn't the better;
Why would he make it?"
Well, when he blew a bronc,
Is the story I'm told,
His brother would whale him,
He didn't take time to scold!
That man was so tough,
So hard and so strong,
It's sad that his life
Just had to go wrong
They say that he died
In Ft. Worth one dark night,
Probably after a drunk
And a barroom fight.
We never will know
Where he might have gone,
But he is remembered,
His story lives on.

Women in history
Also have their appeal
Women like the rugged
Maggie Goodall were real.
She trailed cattle
Over North Dakota range,
She drove a team of six horses,
Never once thought it strange;
Rode shotgun, they say
In those days past,
When women stayed home and cooked
With no questions asked.
She could hold her own
With all of the men,
But dance and flirt like a lady
On the rare occasions when
A celebration was held.
She raised a family too,
Became known on the plains,
Maggie, stouthearted and true!

Those were also the days
Of the relay race,
When you could put money
On the team of your choice;
Three horses that pranced,
When they saw the race track,
Old Tarzan and Copper
You could scarcely hold back!
There were people with horses
They thought were the best,
But Glen's horses always
Stood up to the test!
It began when he was
A very young lad;
Some fellows were sitting
And making a bet
On some fancy horseflesh they had
When old Charley they met;
He stuck out his hand
With a twenty-dollar bill,
"I'll bet it right now
That my boy Glen will
Beat you and your horses!
They're all sorry nags!"
Well, Glen heard his daddy
And his heart really raced
As he rode that relay
Not a second did he waste!
He heard a man say
When 'twas all said and done
"That's a tough hand to beat,
A man and his son!"

And then there were folks
Like my Ma and Pa
Who came to this land,
They liked what they saw.
Some, like my dad,
Crossed an ocean wide,
Crossed mountains and plains
TilI they came to abide
Here, where the prairie
Stretched wide and free;
'Twas a land so rich
With opporturuty.
But my mother was born
In the Manning buttes
This country was hers,
it gave her roots;
She knew what it was
To ride from dawn until dusk,
She knew how to shock
Wheat, oats, or corn on the husk.
She grew up riding
Green horses as well
As any cowhand;
Many stories she'd tell,
Of those years of work
How the barbwire came.
Of the man that she married,
Of their struggle on the plains.
They survived it all,
Prairie fires and drought,
Raised eight kids,
Knew what hardship's all about.
Folks like mine
Helped settle this land,
Gave us our beginnings
And helped me understand
What it means to love and cherish
The blue skies above
The coyotes howling nightly
Dakota hills and prairie that I love!

Colorful characters,
Their legends live on,
Though some in real life
Have now long since gone.
They're all part of the history
Of Dakota land,
And the part they played
Helps the legend to stand.
There were bronc busters
And sod busters,
And numerous others,
There were cowthieves and cowpokes,
There were the Barker brothers.
Their stories as rich
As the buffalo grass
That still waves in the wind
Where now only
The Whitetails pass.
A few of these people I'm proud to have known.
Some others were gone
Before I was grown.
But I'm glad
To have heard
And it behooves me
To tell
Of these folks and their lives;
Of what they did
So well.

Fran Erickson

        Glenn Murray on the left horse, raced in the annual Cowboys' Reunion
        Relay Race, which was quite an event in Beulah's early days.

        July 4, 1914 - the year the railroad came to Beulah, North Dakota.
        Townspeople all came out to see and celebrate that landmark event,
        which heralded the birth of a new town.

The beginnings of a townsite

In 1915, the editor of the Beulah Independent, Peter W. Reese, wrote this about
his town: "A town is very much like an individual. To be flourishing, it must
have energy and enterprise."

The 1915 townsite of Beulah had both. Speculation concerning the westward push
of the Northern Pacific Railroad created the townsite, and the railroad's
progress sustained it and caused it to grow. By 1915, editor Reese determined
that Beulah had grown more than any other town along the railroad line that
extended west to Killdeer.

A 1915 census showed that 300 people were living in the townsite, and the
business community was growing by leaps and bounds. The tremendous increase in
business since the train had been stopping in Beulah caused H.C. Warrington to
enlarge the dining room of his hotel in order to take care of the added
patrons.

The transfer and dray lines were flourishing, and during September and October
of 1915, 30 new businesses or residences were built or were under construction.
Reese remarked that Beulah has experienced "sure and steady growth" with four
mercantile stores and two more under construction, two hardware stores, and
three grain elevators.

The Northern Pacific Railroad was responsible for the development and expansion
of Beulah. It was the only major means of communication for the citizens of the
townsite, and the train brought the mail, the goods for the businesses and the
potential businessmen who were interested in checking out the town for a future
business. Hardly a week passed when the Independent did not note the visit of a
businessman from Expansion, Bismarck or Minnesota who came to seek his fortune
in this new townsite of Beulah. The Northern Pacific sold landseeker excursion
tickets from St. Paul-Minneapolis to points in North Dakota for $12 for the
round trip, and there were many who found this a good opportunity to visit the
Beulah area. The frequent usage of the Northern Pacific is illustrated by these
figures from the year 1914: 111 passengers were injured that year, 740
employees, 41 trespassers and 50 people categorized as "non-trespassers" all
met with accidents of more or less serious nature. Undoubtedly, the train
system had its disadvantages; the service was irregular and uncertain, high
water washed out the bridges and stopped the train service, and mail service
via the train was considered unsatisfactory compared to the stage service; yet,
all things considered, the "iron horse" was still the single most important
factor in the settlement of the early Beulah townsite.

And, as the Northern Pacific pushed its way westward, there were persistent
rumors in 1915 that the train would soon be running a line from Werner up the
Knife River via Manning and Fayette to Sidney, Mont. Train engineers were
speculating that extending the Killdeer line throughout the Badlands would cost
many millions because of the tunnels necessary to obtain good grade.

Many of the farming settlers of the early townsite were German-Russian
immigrants, who came to America searching for a chance to raise their families
in a land free from government intervention and persecution. They were fiercely
protective of their political and personal views, and they held their family
business to be a very private affair.

In 1914-1915, many of the citizens of Beulah spoke only German, some
advertisements in the local paper were worded in German and English, and the
legal notices were all printed in German. The Bismarck Tribune was incorporated
in 1915, and the articles of incorporation state that the paper was "to uphold
and promote the interests of German-speaking citizens of the state, and be
independent in politics." The Beulah Independent also stated its policy on the
front page of every edition: "Our policy: men before party, strictly
independent."

In the days before television, radio and telephone, a weekly newspaper was a
vital element in a townsite such as Beulah. Except for word of mouth, the
newspaper was the only means of communication between the farmers and the
businesspeople in town, and the only way for local people to receive news from
the rest of the country. In 1914-1915, Beulah was fortunate to have Peter W.
Reese as the editor and manager of the Beulah Independent. He was a man who
believed very strongly in "boosting" the advantages of Beulah, and he did just
that at every opportunity.

        Left to right, Stevens and son, Philip E. Joos, Carl Johnson and
        Lorenz Joos, who owned the Joos Hardware Store at this location.
        The building is now occupied by the Coast to Coast Hardware Store.

        Philip Hausauer, Sr. and his wife, Rosina, had a shoe repair shop on
        Beulah's Main Street in the early days of the town's life.

"Look at the advantages of your home town," he said, "and think how they could
be utilized successfully. Agitate clean streets, yards and alleys, and good
roads and public institutions, a city park and things that make a town look
like it's wide awake. Let the people know the great opportunity your town
offers, and they will sit up and take notice."

        The first service station on the corner, a Standard station, was just
        north of the railroad tracks on Main Street. Current Magi-Touch
        occupies the building which later went up.

Reese wore many hats in his position at the paper. In addition to "boosting"
Beulah's advantages, he also promoted another cause he felt essential to the
progress of Beulah - good roads. It was his theme and he advocated good roads
over and over again.

"We should have better roads going into Beulah, to the east and to the north,
and a bridge across Spring Creek straight west of Beulah, and a bridge at the
Keogh place, for farmers living southwest, on account of the rough country
there," he wrote in 1915. "Nothing is gained by waiting and a good many things
can be gained by push and aggressiveness"

The road situation was indeed a problem for everyone. Until 1915, few roads
were laid on section lines, and people were in the habit of taking the easiest
and the shortest route to their destination. Most farmers had fenced their
land, preventing travelers from taking short cuts. Owing to the increase of
6,000 automobiles in North Dakota from 1914 to 1915, there was a constant cry
for better roads.

Secretary of State Thomas Hall announced that during the year 1914, the sum of
$50,345.77 was distributed to the "good roads" funds of the state's 52
counties, being divided according to the number of automobiles and motorcycles
registered in each county. In 1915, the total number of automobiles registered
in North Dakota was 17,347. The total number of motorcycles was 1,255.

Reese also showed his concern over the impact caused by the many new citizens.
He implored the people of Beulah to "plant some trees, and show everyone you're
not just living here temporarily." As the number of citizens grew, so did the
amount of garbage and refuse within the townsite, and this presented a problem
since there was yet no method of organized garbage collection. Said Reese, "It
is the duty of every good citizen to see that his accumulation of garage and
winter refuse is disposed of."

He also implored honest and economical men to build more houses that could be
rented cheaply, and he reported on services and methods of benefit to area
farmers, thus fulfilling the role that a county agent might serve in later
years.

It is also interesting to note that Reese recognized the importance of the
lignite coal in the Beulah area, and was fond of speculating about the impact
it might have upon the town in later years. At that time, Beulah had two coal
mines, both within two blocks of the train depot, but neither mine was working
at full capacity. It was expected that when they were running full blast they
would employ about 50 men.

Reese noted, "It is safe to say that the average North Dakotan does not realize
that the state has such vast coal beds and that North Dakota has the
distinction of having more coal deposits than any other state in the nation.
The demand for our excellent coal will increase."

        E.A. Kees, in the Ford on the left, was an early Beulah real estate
        and insurance salesman, operating such an office for many years.

It might be thought that in the early townsite of Beulah, there would not be
many opportunities for enjoyment or community development. Such was not the
case. Early in 1915, Beulah was organizing a baseball team, and that sport
proved to be very  popular with spectators and participants alike. A basket
social was held to raise money for the fledgling team of 20 players. Although
the "Beulah boys," as they were called, lost their first game to Golden Valley
with a score of 12-9, the game was full of "brilliant and spectacular plays,"
according to the local newspaper, and the loss did little to dampen their
enthusiasm. In May of 1915, the Beulah boys won a doubleheader against Golden
Valley and also defeated Hazen, 5-3. Even back in 1915, it seems there was a
spirit of rivalry between the Beulah and Hazen athletic teams, prompting Reese
to comment in the next edition of his paper, "The rivalry that sometimes exists
between small towns in the same county is a shortsighted policy."

The popularity of the sport increased, and a baseball tournament held in Hazen
in 1915 was attended by more than 2,000 people, a rousing tribute to the
acceptance of the game. The tournaments were apt to last several days, and also
featured activities such as boxing, wrestling and tennis matches, parades, a
band concert, bronco busting, continuous minstrel shows and a bowery dance.
Thus the sport of baseball afforded the citizens of Beulah and the surrounding
area many moments of enjoyment in those early years.

The Beulah Commercial Club organized in 1915, and the officers they elected
were president, C.B. Heinemeyer; vice president, W.C. Kees; secretary, Peter W.
Reese; and treasurer, W.A. Johnson. They held a banquet and dance in March of
1915 and quickly determined some goals for their townsite to achieve, including
good roads and streets within the town. They sponsored a street carnival during
the summer and by the end of 1915, a movement was afoot to incorporate Beulah
as a village. In September of 1915, the first annual Mercer County Fair was
organized by the Beulah Commercial Club, sometimes referred to as the
"boosters." They were an active, progressive group, and they were the
beginnings of a community involvement that later became the Chamber of Commerce
and is still present in Beulah.

Although the eighteenth amendment approving Prohibition had not yet been
ratified on the national level, the North Dakota state Legislature had approved
Prohibition, and the townsite of Beulah sold soft drinks in its pool halls.
Except for an occasional "sample of rowdyism caused by drinking too much
squirrel whiskey," the prohibition of alcohol remained in force and was
endorsed by the community leaders.

The Beulah Band was organized in 1915, offering an opportunity for musically
inclined individuals to show their community spirit. About 20 musical
instruments made up the band and they performed at many area functions.

An interesting social activity of 1915 was the Dust Cap Social, a variation of
the basket social, held at the Rose Hill Schoolhouse. The ladies were invited
to bring lunches for two, and to include a bow to match each dust cap in the
lunch box.

The business community underwent many changes in management and places of
business in those early years. Some of the Beulah businesses that operated
during 1915 were Evans and Evans, selling dry goods and food; Johnson Hardware
Store, E.L. Kuhl; The New Hardware, W. A. Johnson; The First State Bank, N.P.
McGregor pres.; Pool Parlor, John Lang, Jr.; The Chris Henry Hotel; Occident
Elevator, W.S. Remund; City Meat Market, Blankenberg and Carter and The Osman
Store. C.B. Heinemeyer corn shellers, feed mills, gasoline engines; Beulah
Transfer Line, D.A. Grant; East Side Livery and Feed Barn, Lew Carter; Powers
Elevator Company, R.G. Stuhr; Well Drilling, Karlin and Sandau; A.P. Westlin,
carpenter and contractor and Frank's Barber Shop.

Other notable events of 1915 include the following: Woodrow Wilson was U.S.
President and L.B. Hanna was governor of North Dakota. The 640-acre Homestead
Act was passed and a complete telephone circuit from New York to Denver was
completed, with the cost of a three-minute call estimated at $21. Although the
war in Europe was in its second year, it did not have a drastic effect upon the
town or its citizens. Beulah's first doctor, Hugo Nukemp from Fessenden,
arrived in town and there was talk among the area farmers of securing a rural
route mail delivery. The first Beulah school was completed and 26 pupils
attended school on the first day. The opening of the Standing Rock Indian
Reservation had been approved by President Wilson and an electric light plant
run by Oulmonn and Luthander would soon be erected in Beulah in a two-story
cement building that would be 48 x 70 feet.

        Early Beulah residents Joseph and Susana Goldade with children
        Florence and Steve posed on the undeveloped prairie near Beulah.

        The Iron Horse, the railroad, was the reason for existence of many
        of North Dakota's rural towns. 1t brought connections with
        civilization and shortened travel time.

When 1915 drew to a close, the townsite of Beulah, which would soon become a
village, was two years old. It was an energetic, enterprising town, but it was
nevertheless a town without good roads for the farmers or city streets and
crossings of any kind. It was a town without electricity or garbage collection
services, and a town without a fire department. Prairie fires caused the ruin
of many acres of crops, farm buildings, and often human lives, because the
"bucket brigade" was simply not effective in coping with the fury of a fire
raging on the open prairie. The school bell at the new school was used as a
fire alarm, except when partygoers rang it for fun--thus it became difficult to
tell when there really was a fire.

There was still much to accomplish in this new town on the prairie. What the
town lacked in services, it more than accounted for in human and natural
resources. Many of the community leaders had strong, progressive personalities,
and they would be a major factor in shaping the town. The railroad would
continue to be a determining force in the area for many years to come, until
its decline in the 1930s due to the advancement of the automobile and aircraft.

The farmland and natural resources and the strong people it took to make them
fruitful were also blessings to the town's future. According to a Wall Street
publication of 1914, one-sixth of all the improved farm property in the U.S. in
1914 was in North Dakota, 112 percent more than any other state in the union.
In 1914, North Dakota marketed five times as many hogs as in 1912 and corn
production doubled, and this accounted for the "Hogs and Hominy" theme of the
'20s and '30s in the Beulah area. The average North Dakota farm was 582 acres
in 1914, and the Wall Street publication stated that "business conditions are
excellent and the real estate and loan agents report that the loan business is
very slow this season owing to the splendid financial condition of the
farmers."

And, of course, the lignite that remained virtually untapped beneath the
prairie surface would prove to be a mainstay of the community far beyond even
the wildest dreams of editor Peter Reese.

The cornerstones of the foundation for the townsite of Beulah were laid in
these years. The next decades would be years of building upon those
cornerstones and nurturing the town that was like a baby who had yet to crawl
and walk. There was much to learn and much to look forward to, and it was just
beginning.

        six-year-old Carl, sitting on the fence in the back, watched.

Our Pioneers - Beulah's German-Russians

In the year 1989 the city of Beulah is composed of several ethnic groups and
individual citizens who have come from all over America to work at the
gasification plant. Yet it can be safely said that no ethnic group has
influenced the shaping of Beulah more than the German-Russians.

They were a people who had endured the hardship of migration to Russia from
Germany and, worse yet, the events that led them to migrate from their adopted
motherland. During the 1800s, living conditions in Germany were very difficult.
The state treasuries were empty, the manner of justice and management was
deceitful and the business of begging flourished all over.

The public officials were not always the ones with the most experience and
talent, because the normal practice was to bid for such positions. The
individual who could pay the most money was often the one who was given the
power of the office. The whole bureaucracy was corrupt. A characteristic
symptom of the conditions of the times was the practice of selling the services
of young men as soldiers to a foreign power to support the wild and extravagant
lives of the princes who ruled the country.

The common people simply had no choice in the matter. Public meetings were
forbidden, assemblies were monitored and the participating subjects were
pointed out to officials. The entire population was under heavy oppression. The
high taxes and military burdens were a difficult load for the people to bear.

By the year 1816 the poverty had become unbearable . Never had there been such
a famine. The people were compelled to sell whatever goods they had at
ridiculously low prices and in turn buy food at very high prices.

At the same time, while the country was in the midst of economic disaster and
political impropriety, a religious crisis had found its way into the church.
Reason and logical evidence were substituted in the place of the testimonies of
the Bible. These kinds of sermons could not be accepted by a searching people
and it was the great tragedy of the time that the hard-pressed people, who had
to struggle to keep body and soul together, could not even find comfort in
their own church.

At the same time, Russia concerned itself with German immigrants. A new
immigration wave to Bessarabia, Russia, began in 1814. Russia wrested
Bessarabia from Turkey in 1812 and resolved to settle people in this area after
the war with Napoleon. The plan was to bring as many people as possible, who
were to serve as models for later settlers. Since Czar Alexander I already had
favorable experience with Germans in other settlements, he was in favor of
inviting Germans to settle in Bessarabia also . He released a manifesto on Nov.
29, 1813, inviting volunteer immigrants to Russia with the following terms:

1. The Russian government will place the colonists from the Dukedom of Warsaw
under its special protection and guarantee them every right and convenience,
which are enjoyed by the natives.

2. The colonists will be required that they involve themselves in the pursuit
of the advancement of farming (arable land) garden, wine and silk industries.

3. They are free of all fees and land taxes for 10 years apart from a small
number of Bessarabian land leasers (renters).

4. Each family will receive 270 rubles Banko from the Crown over a period of 10
years; the other (families) will receive as much as they need to establish
their first household.

5. Each family will receive 60 dessjatine land for their personal and
hereditary real property.

6. Moreover, all those who have no provisions will, from the day of their
arrival in Russia, receive five kopecks per soul until the first corn harvest.

7. The immigrants as well as their descendants are once and for all free of
conscription draft, likewise from military quartering, except those times when
a
military troop marches through the area.

8. The colonists are free to build suitable churches for their religious
purposes, maintain clergy, and to practice their religion as they desire.

9. After a period of 10 years, another 10 years will be allotted in which the
colonists can pay back to the Crown the monetary support they received
initially.

The invitation was directed to the Germans who lived in the Dukedom of Warsaw
after settling there in the time of the Prussian colonization under Frederick
the Great and Friedrich Wilhelm III, primarily as land renters and farm
laborers on Polish estates.  They lived in great poverty and they responded to
the call of the Czar. The first ones arrived in Bessarabia in 1814, followed by
others from time to time. They founded the communities of Alt-Elft, Arzis,
Beresina, Borodino, Brienne, Dennewitz, Friedenstal, Katzbach, Klostitz,
Krasna, Kulm, Leipzig, Neu-Arzis, Neu-Elft, Paris, Plotzk, Posttal, Tarutino
and Wittenberg.

Political and economic factors played an important part in the emigrations to
Russia from 1803-1807. Religious reasons were vital in the 1816 migrations. The
German people did not move from the homeland with a light heart. They tore
themselves away only when spiritual and physical duress were too great to
endure. The emigrants always suffered severe pangs of homesickness and never
would have left had there not been greater opportunities awaiting them.

In 1842 the Russian government halted further immigration to its empire and
German immigration to that country came to an end.

The trip made by immigrants took up to three months in travel time alone. When
they got to the Russian border, they had to spend anywhere from one to eight
weeks in quarantine. Since up to 10,000 people immigrated each year, there
weren't always enough quarantine buildings, food, clothing or officials to look
after the dying people. Many of the immigrants died of fever or dysentery, and
some families died on the roadside while praying to God for mercy.

The families who did make it to Russia had to live in sod houses or houses made
from clay until lumber arrived from Odessa - and even then there were only 20
pieces of wood per house. The clay houses they lived in were called
"semeljanka" and were used until houses of stone were built. The land that was
given to the immigrants was usually spread over a five-mile radius and their
house was built on the largest piece of land in one spot.

The trek of German immigrants to Russia from 1803-1804 had been halted by
Napoleon and his "reign of terror," which lasted three years in Europe. He
didn't allow churches to function, put priests into prisons and inducted the
young men into the army.

In 1807, after France had conquered the Russians and the Austrians at
Austerlitz, the treaty of Tilsit was signed, making Russia an ally of France.
Only after the treaty was signed was immigration again allowed to start.

In 1808 the German-speaking people of Alsace immigrated to the Black Sea area
of Russia. These people helped form the original 40 villages of Odessa. Some of
the larger villages were Liebental, Kutschurgan and Beresan districts.

Most of the immigrants had a difficult time learning to adapt to the different
times of planting and harvesting crops. Eventually they built windmills to
grind their wheat into flour and planted trees to beautify their towns. They
worked hard at farming and soon farming methods, implements and homes were
improved. They were able to put money aside to buy more land.

The next generation became accustomed to the land and the way to farm it. They
married young and had large families. By the third and fourth generation there
wasn't enough land for the new families. Uncultivated land was cheap but far
away. They purchased this land and soon daughter villages were formed. Within
40 years the cost of land rose from 35 to 90 rubles. This expansion continued
until 1914.

        Playing on the tracks has always been a favorite pastime of little
        fellas, and this early Beulah boy was no exception.

In 1855 Nicholas I died and Alexander II became Czar of Russia. He abolished
the manifesto that had been issued to the German colonists by Catherine II and
Alexander I. The German people were angry and felt they were being treated as
foreigners without any thought being given to the advancement they had worked
for on their farming lands and towns. In the schools, their children had to
learn Russian rather than their native German.

Their Russian neighbors were jealous of their prosperity so they started to
steal cattle and horses from them. When the Germans caught and arrested the
thieves, they brought them to court only to see them spend one night in jail or
to be set free entirely. Colonists obtained vicious dogs to protect themselves.

In 1874 the Russian government passed a law that all men had to serve six years
in the Russian Army and thousands of young men were drafted at the age of 21.
Colonists were good soldiers but never received any promotions. Men were beaten
for the slightest infraction of the rules and given almost nothing to eat.

In 1892 there was a severe famine in Russia and the Russian people demanded
that all the property owned by the Germans be revoked and all the inhabitants
sent to Siberia.

The Black Sea Germans began to immigrate to America in 1872 and others soon
followed. It is not known how many came to America because of the lure of free
land and how many came because they were afraid of what the Russians would do
to them if they stayed, but by 1914 thousands of Germans had left for America.

The generation of German people who left Russia for America was not the same
generation that had migrated to Russia from Germany, but the move had many
similarities. They left under duress, with few possessions, headed for an
unknown land which at that point bore only the promise of freedom.

Yet the land they were leaving now had never been their homeland. Even though
they occupied the Russian soil for almost a century, they had never become
Russians. They were still Germans, with German religions, language, customs and
ways. They only rarely intermarried with the Russians and tended to live in
their own communities. Thus, they had developed a sense of community belonging
that would serve them well when they arrived in America.

The hardships and political oppression they had endured throughout the
generations had developed some special qualities within the German-Russians.
They had learned to work hard and to get by with few provisions. They had
learned the strength of their Lutheran, Catholic and Mennonite religions and
the importance of faith and endurance. But most of all, the Germans from Russia
had sustained a longing for freedom.

Our pioneers

The passports for the trip to America were expensive and the trip was not an
easy one. Many families made the long journey only to arrive in America and
have one or more members of the family rejected for health reasons. These
individuals had to return to Russia, save enough money for the ticket and make
another journey. Some families left loved ones behind, never to see them again.

Many Germans made the trip by first traveling to Hamburg, Germany, and then
waiting to board a ship to America. The journey took about three weeks and most
immigrants traveled fourth class. Food was limited but since many people were
seasick, there seemed to be enough food for everyone.

Nicholus Unruh, his wife, Rosina, and six children, Christ, Ludwig, John,
Rosina, Jake and Katie, were one of the many families who came to America in
this manner. In 1905 they set sail for America on the ship Kaiser Wilhelm and
eventually docked in New York. A train took the Unruhs to the Dakotas, an area
where homestead land was still available. In New York before beginning travel,
each family received a bag of food containing a supply of bread, different
types of sausage, and dried foods to carry them through to their first stop,
which was Chicago. On the train, each family carried its own tea kettle to boil
water for tea.

        The Scheid homestead, where all the Scheid children were born, was
        like many other sod houses which sprouted on the prairie during the
        early days when the settlers came.

After a two-day stop in Chicago, the Unruh family traveled to Glen Ullin, where
they obtained their homestead consisting of one quarter of land in Mercer
County.

Each homesteader received 160 acres which was free, although there was a $10
filing fee for the land. The homesteaders had to improve the land by building a
dwelling and tilling 30 acres per year.

With money left over from traveling, Nicholus Unruh bought three milk cows and
a few chickens which, for a long while, were the family's only source of food.
When the older members of the family were breaking the land, they received one
egg for a meal. The younger ones who spent their time in the house received
only half an egg. Food and money in the first years of homesteading were
carefully budgeted.

Most early pioneers had furniture made of crates and the only "store bought"
furniture most of them had was a stove. Only the most necessary furniture was
obtained and it was built by the homesteaders themselves.

Usually the first project facing the pioneer family when they arrived at their
homestead was building a sod house. Their ancestors had learned this skill when
they immigrated to Russia almost a century ago, and it was useful knowledge on
the Dakota prairies. The sod house was a one-room house with a dirt floor with
openings for windows and doors. In the evening a blanket was hung over the door
of the Unruh soddy to keep the animals out of the house.

A house made from sod usually lasted only about three years. A plow was used to
cut the sod in square blocks which were piled on top of each other to form the
walls of the house. The house then had to be plastered inside and out with a
mud-and-straw coating which had to be renewed yearly. Some of the homesteaders
added additional rooms later, or a root cellar to store their produce and
supplies.

The children's clothing in the Nicholus Unruh family consisted of two sets of
apparel--both made from flour sacks. One set of clothing was for Sunday and
one was for everyday.

        Osman's General Merchandise was one of the stores in Beulah during
        its first decade, when the progressive town already had sidewalks.

Trips to Glen Ullin for supplies were very seldom made as it took one day to
travel 18 miles. The journey was usually a two-day affair.

Winters were long and hard. Many times the snowstorms lasted for weeks and the
snowdrifts piled up higher than the sod houses.

In the first few years the grain from the harvest was all planted and harvested
by hand. The grain was threshed by letting the horses trample on piles of cut
grain until the grain was loosened from the heads. Then the older members of
the family used forks to lift the straw and allow the wind to clean the grain.
Later the horse-powered threshing machines were used, which were pulled by
teams of horses pulling in a continuous circle, allowing the grain to be
threshed and cleaned at the same time.

In 1910, the homesteaders in the area where the Unruhs lived built a sod
schoolhouse, which was three miles from the homestead. The students were varied
in age; some were as old as 20 and just beginning their education in this
country. All students packed lunches containing sandwiches made of pumpkin
jelly, made by cooking pumpkin in sugar and vinegar and mashing it for the
sandwich.

Many of the early pioneers, like Joseph and Katherina Boeshans, homesteaded
land that still remains in the family several generations later. Joseph and
Katherina came to America in 1893 and settled on their homestead north of
Beulah. They had four sons. Ludwig died in infancy, and Heinrich, Johannes, and
Friedrich grew to manhood.

Fred Boeshans remembers that the prairie fires were a terrible menace to the
early pioneer homesteaders. Once a fire got started, even a gentle breeze could
turn it into a raging inferno and it was almost impossible to control a prairie
fire. He remembers one prairie fire that burned the original homestead, taking
the haystacks and the machinery stored between them. Another in 1915 came from
the west, roaring across 110 acres of flax and killing the cattle in the
pastures, burning everything as far east as Krem.

There were even women pioneers who crossed the ocean alone and homesteaded the
prairie with their children, like Rosina (Heine) Raszler, whose husband Jacob
died while serving in the Russian Army. She brought her four sons, Gottfreid,
Adolph, John and David to America and "hired out" for some years to raise the
money to start her homestead east of Beulah, near Otter Creek.

What gave these early pioneers the courage and endurance to withstand the
prairie fires, harsh winters and poverty? Their schools were made from sod, yet
they were free to teach whatever they wished in their schools. They had no
churches in those early years, yet they held services in their homes when a
traveling minister could come and otherwise the scriptures would be read and
the Sabbath observed as best as the cycle of planting and harvest would allow.
The prairie needed to be plowed and planted, but the land they tilled belonged
to them; they were not merely the tenants. After more than a century of
political oppression, their longing for freedom had been fulfilled and their
prayers answered. At last, the Germans from Russia had found a home.

Early recollections

On the 4th of July in 1910 was when I first saw Beulah, a farm house was there.
The rest was prairie. It (farm house) was located by the east bridge and called
Troy.

In the fall of 1913 we drove 10 miles from our home in a lumber wagon to see
rails for the railroad being laid. Now they had a store, post office and eating
place.

The next time I saw Beulah was on the 4th of July in 1914. The railroad was
here and with it came new business, Boeckel's grocery.

Mr. Joos was the first hardware man. The upstairs of his store had the first
recreation hall, they would also have church services there when a preacher
would come.

Bill Johnson built a hardware store where the present Ben Franklin store is.
Powers Elevator was also here.

Neucamp was the doctor and Art Smith was the first real estate man. L.F. Temme
worked for Mr. Smith and Mr. Neidermeyer built our first shoe store. In about a
year a restaurant was built. A.D. Brown was our first newspaper editor.

Mrs. Tyrell had our first and only millinery (she was the mother of Abbey
Tyrell). She came in 1914. At about this time a theatre was built.

A couple of years later it burned, along with several other buildings.

Notes taken from a letter written in 1943 by Gladys Scheidt's mother, Mrs.
Arthur Erickson (Anna Sevallius).

        The Morris Frank store in the middle was part of the town of
        Expansion, which contributed to Beulah's early history

Sisch Schun Hun'ad Joha, 1884-1984

Uf Nord Dakota kummen se na
Un fangen ganz vun fa'na a'.

Sin Deitscha-Russa vum Zareland
Sie ziechen wida in e fremdes Land.

In vierenachzig kummen d'erschda;
Ehra Mud da wa' vum greeschda.

Hun'ad joha sin schun va'ganga;
Hen viel durch gemachd; "Des sed jeds langa."

Am A'fang sin se arrig arm
Sie hoffen as sich Gott erbarm.

"D'zeida sin ha'd", hee'd ma se sacha,
'Greidz isch gross, ma muss awa dracha."

Sie nehmen Land uf; sisch ehja Dram
Un zaggerens va' de Uncle Sam.

Im neija Land gehds frieh un spohd
As ihna Gott helfd in de Nod.

Sie bauen Stad un d'Farmerei
Un unnanehmen allelei.

Sie bleiwen Deitsch, meja wissen doch,
Va'zehlen heid noch d'Muddasproch.

Awa d'Junga redden nimmi Deitsch;
Kamma nid emol zwinga mid de beitsch;

Un bleiwen nimmi uf em Land;
Studierren anstad allehand

Fiehren G'schada gla un gross;
Gelachenheida hods; ma suchds se bloss.

Va'lossen d'Hamed wie ehja Leid;
Suchen imma ma Freiheid

De Vada schaffd deham ellanig;
Hilf vun Seina' hod a'wenig.

Speeda naus nod kummen d'Cara;
sWa'd uhna Geil de Weg aus g'fahra.

Do hods Maschiena gross un gla;
Sie kaffen imma ma un ma.

sWa'd bequam as nochera wed
Nod zaggerns Land noch uhna Geil.

Awa mancha hen zu viel gekaud;
Va'lieren alles, d'hooa un d'Haud

E gross Va'meecha hen schun mancha
Beino zu gross ischs, zum va'han'la.

De Vada grengd sich, sisch bal' Zeid
Va' sLand va'dala uhna Streid

sGehd als schlechd un sgehd als gud
Awa sie finnen imma frischa Mud

Meja hoffen as eich Gott bedengd
Un snegst Joha-hu'ad a' noch schengd

It's Already One Hundred Years, 1884-1984

To North Dakota plains they came
To start their life all over again.

German-Russians from the land of Tsars
They came here with belongings sparse.

In eighty-four the first ones came
With spirits high; they were so game.

A century has already passed
Endured a lot; they should have rest.

To start with they were very poor
But with God 's help they did endure.

"Times are hard" - we hear them say
"Must bear the load without dismay."

Their dream it was, to own some land;
To plow their fields for Uncle Sam.

They work early; they work late
That God may help their needs abate.

They built farms and cities too
And undertake so much that's new.

They remain German all along
And Still employ their Mothertongue.

But young folks cease to speak in German;
Force or whip will not exhort them.

In due time, too, they leave the land;
They seek their knowledge to expand.

Excelling in work of every kind;
Opportunities are there to find.

Like their parents they leave their home;
Ever in search of freedom, they will roam.

Dad works hard, alone, at home;
Not much help comes from 'his own'.

Later on, come cars, and folks are lucky;
Drive down the road, in horseless buggy.

Machinery too, both big and small
Tendency to overbuy, judged, all in all.

It becomes so handy, in due course
To plow the fields without a horse.

Many tried to 'chew' too much;
They lost their 'hide and hair', and such.

To great heights of wealth some rose;
Often became difficult to dispose.

To hold down strife, Dad must decide
To divide the land and do it right.

It's good and bad through many a year;
They always come through with good cheer.

We hope that God remembers you;
Bequeaths his next new century. too.

        John England, grandfather of Phillip, Ellen and Larry Joos, operated
        a dray line in Beulah. This photo, taken in 1910, was at Aplin.

Busy beginnings

When we moved onto my mother's homestead in 1903, Glen Ullin was our closest
town. All traveling was done by wagon, horseback or on foot. There was nothing
but prairie as far as you could see, with a few herds of broncos or cattle
grazing on it.

Our closest neighbors were Tom Keogh, Charles Herman and Bernie Evans, about
five miles from us. Other ranchers we heard about were Buchlis, Jim Keogh and
Farringtons.

That first winter we lived on bread, tea and beef - nothing else.

Once, when we hadn't been to Glen Ullin for several months, we had a flour sack
full of mail, and took a week off to read it.

Land was worth from 75 cents to $1.50 per acre.

From 1903 - 1905 the country was settled by homesteaders and soon there were
sod shanties or small wooden shacks everywhere, and people were breaking up the
prairie.

In 1910 the present site of Beulah, Sec. 25, Twp. 144 Rge. 88, was just another
piece of land under cultivation. It was being farmed by Aleck Tweet and John
Hogan, who were running their stock in this neighborhood.

Stanton was the closest railroad town. Tom Farrington had a little country
store and post office about one mile east of here, just north of what is still
called the Farrington bridge. The house Mrs. Chilson lives in is the former
Carrington residence.

About three miles west, Jim Bowdish had a post office and general store on
Spring Creek.

There was quite a settlement at Spring Creek. There were families with
children, John Henersons, John Wetzels, Carl Johnsons, Fischers, Fergusons and
bachelors too numerous to mention. Spring Creek School District No. 13 had been
organized and a little school house was built. May Wagner was the first teacher
and the Spring Creek Telephone Co. had built a rural line with their exchange
at Henersons. After Beulah was established, they built the Beulah exchange and
still later sold out to the present owners.

In 1911 Dr. Vreedenborg bought Sec. 25 from Alex Tweet, plotted it and called
it Troy. Hanke built an Implement Store, which is the first building erected
(it was also the Joos Hardware store).

On July 4, 1911, Beulah, then Troy, had its first celebration. There was a
large crowd and there were ball games, horse races, fire works, and a dance
upstairs in the new store in the evening.

In 1912 the railroad grade was built and was often used as a highway when there
were no railroad officials around. It was so much nicer to travel on than the
prairie trails which ran in any old direction and of course were not graded.

In 1913 the rails were laid from Stanton to Killdeer. People came from far and
near to watch the rails being laid and the big pile drivers at the railroad
bridges.

Soon the train was running. It was both passenger and freight. It went west to
Killdeer in the morning and returned in the afternoon. At first the freight was
unloaded on the platform but soon the depot was built.

By 1914 Troy had been sold to the Tuttle Land Co. and named Beulah. Joe Evans
was appointed the first postmaster and the Sardotz building was the first post
office and general store in Beulah. Jacob Bacal's store was the second and I
think Osmans (the old R.C.U. Store) was the third general store. Nyhus had the
first lumber yard and I think the first Ford car in Beulah. Dr. Neukamp was the
first doctor and had a hospital. And Kuhl had the first drug store in the same
location as it is now.

Church services and entertainments were held upstairs over the Joos Hardware
store. Walter Kees was cashier of the First State Bank now occupied by the
Variety Store. Spring Creek School Dist. 13 built the first school houses where
the Legion Hall and Scout Hall are located. A little later Beulah separated
from District 13 and became District No. 10.

In 1916 A. D. Brown bought the Beulah Independent and opened his printing
office in a building between the present Variety Store and Mrs. Voegele's
Coffee Shop, and the Independent was printed by the Brown Family until about a
year ago, when Dally bought the paper.

Mrs. Husom is the oldest living resident of Beulah. Other long time residents
are Jacob Bacal, Niedermeyer father and son shoe store; hardware store, Max
Martell and son; Mrs. Helvik, boarding house, Mrs. Tyrell, millinery store.

Karl Semmler opened the coal mine with Jesse Crowe as manager.

Beulah has had several large fires. The first one burned Dale Sovereign's
Theatre, Mrs. Sovereign's candy store and a garage (all on south side of main
street). Another theatre was burned where the V.F.W. Hall is now located and
the Mine Tipple burned about nine years ago (1937).

Quite a few rodeos have been successfully put on at Beulah.

The County Agent's Office, the Triple A Office, The O.P.A. and the Selective
Service Office are now located at Beulah, and since it is the center of Mercer
County it ought to be the county seat. There are three large grain elevators
and the Knife River Coal Mine is the largest underground lignite mine in the
world. The power from the Light Plant extends over North Dakota, South Dakota
and Montana.

There is a modern school building that is supposed to hold 500 children and is
often crowded. There is a theater, at least seven churches, many beautiful
residences, trees, a park and grandstand south of town. The following
organizations are active: American Legion, Legion Auxiliary, Ladies Aid,
Women's Club, Homemakers Clubs, Boy Scouts and Girl Scouts.

Although Beulah is only 23 years old, it has gone places and done things.

Written by Agnes Johnson in 1947 on file in the Mercer County Historical
Society Museum.

        Push cars were used by the railroad workers to go from one place to
        another more rapidly; and it looks like children were just as
        fascinated then as they would be now.

Early settlers had to have determination

It's easy to romanticize the simplicity of earlier days, longing for times when
schedules weren't so hectic and life was less complicated.

But it's also easy to laugh at the cold from a well-heated house. Most times
the only simple thing about those days was the sophistication of the equipment
with which people had to accomplish the same jobs that must be done today.

Take, for instance, the romantic sod house; a poignant reminder, as one sees
crumbling remains jarring the horizon on an occasional field, that early
pioneers didn't have much in the way of construction equipment or materials.
They made do with what they had, and that wasn't much.

Soddies were built by hand from bricks of turf, cut from the virgin prairie sod
using a one-bottom plow. Primitive as they seem, they were a great improvement
to the overturned wagons in which some pioneers spent their first Dakota
winters and to the temporary small wood shacks often thrown up, just to keep
the rain out, while the sod was broken and seeds planted.

Take, for instance, this brief but poignant description of the early days of
one Beulah area couple, Mag and Ezra Emig:

The ride was a long and bumpy one, and as Mag sat on the hard, uncomfortable
wagon seat, she couldn't help thinking that she and Ezra must have completely
lost their minds to have left their beloved state of Missouri.

Ezra had always dreamed of having a piece of land of his own. The 160 acres of
homestead land that had enticed them to make the move just weren't worth it,
though. How could they possibly live in this god-forsaken country? Why, they
had driven miles and miles and hadn't even seen a tree or passed another human
being.

Mag's sister Ora and her husband, Will Stephens, had met the immigrant train at
Glen Ullin. They had even helped them load their belongings onto the wagon. But
they hadn't prepared them for the wide expanse of the rolling Dakota prairies,
unbroken by structures of any kind. As Mag looked at Ora, she was filled with
determination that if her sister could take it, so could she.

The Emigs filed their homestead claim on Sec. 6-142-87. They soon built a 10x16
wood shack to live in until the sodbusting and seeding was done. These were
trying days for both the Emigs; they had never been away from home and were
desperately homesick.

"I think our horses are smarter than we are," Mag wrote home to her mother,
"for last nite they ran away. I think they're headed for Missouri. I wish I was
running with them."

But Mag didn't run. She faced the loneliness and hardship head-on. As Ezra
walked behind his plow, with each acre of virgin soil he turned over he became
prouder and more determined to make a success of this venture.

Slowly the prairies lost the look of complete desolation and took on the warm
friendliness of a newborn pup.

When Ezra built Mag her new soddie, a large, sprawling structure with thatched
roof whose walls were less than square, they both began to suspect their
transplanted roots were beginning to take hold. Then, with the birth of their
first child in 1911, they were sure of it. Now Mag had no time for loneliness.
What with the new baby to care for, chores to be done, meals to be cooked on
her Majestic coal range, mail to be gotten (on a 23-mile trip to Nesbit and
back) and entertaining, she had a very full schedule.

New friends of many nationalities were made. Sometimes language was a bit of a
barrier, but this was soon overcome for they all had one thing in common; they
were settlers seeking a way to make a good, honest living.

If a neighbor was sick you dropped your work and went over and helped. If their
barn was destroyed you had a barn-raising. If there was a death, you comforted.
Thus life in the Aplin community, south of present-day Beulah, became one big
adventure.

In 1915 the Emigs built a new two-story frame house, and although Mag was
pleased as punch over the new home, she knew she could never forget those early
days in the soddie. There she had become a mother and she had added to her
title of wife the well-earned words helpmate and partner. All their regrets
were a thing of the past, for they knew this was where the Lord had meant them
to be. They were home!

        Around 1918, this photo shows an already-growing Beulah complete with
        board-plank sidewalks down either side of its Main Street, which was
        to be dirt for many years.

Charles B. Heinemeyer

No book can be written concerning Mercer County without mentioning Charlie. He
was an early settler living at Stanton, Expansion and Stoeltingville, later
named Ree, where he was the postmaster. with the coming of the railroad to
Beulah, Ree was abandoned as the farmers hauled their grains and livestock to
ship via rail rather than using the Missouri boats.

Mr. Heinemeyer made a tremendous contribution to our heritage. He compiled the
history of early Mercer County and dedicated it to the school children. The
material entailed much research and is accurate as well as a valuable source of
reference. It is the only record concerning early settlements, the
homesteaders, industries and Native Americans of the county prior to 1932.

When Charlie moved to Beulah he opened a feed and grain store selling a flint
corn variety developed by his uncle Edward at Stanton. He had less interest in
farming than he did in politics and economy marketing; nevertheless, he bought
a fine herd of registered Holsteins and engaged in a dairy operation one mile
east of Beulah.

He still had time to read extensively and with a flair for writing, had several
articles published in the Saturday Evening Post. He participated in debates of
a political nature concerning rural economy. He advocated the one for one
program-one bushel of wheat for one dollar.

During 58 years in the county he worked with the State Land Bank, was a state
legislator, teacher and worked with the Old Settlers Organization. He solicited
M.M. Mounts to open the coal mine.

"The Dirty Thirties" saw the demise of his dairy business. His wife, Martha,
and two sons went to New York state to finish their education and find
employment, but Charlie could not bring himself to make the move. He bought a
little land beside the Red Bridge east of Beulah and moved one of his farm
buildings to the site where he made his home and opened Beulah's first Ceramics
Shop. He was affiliated with the University of North Dakota as they
experimented with various North Dakota clays. Charlie experimented too,
preparing his own silt, molds and a firing oven in which to bake his  pottery.
Local clay fired to a rich terra cotta tone, but he liked to develop his own
colors using grasses, flowers and other items found on the prairie.

Charlie became ill in the spring and died in his own cabin June 9, 1940. His
final days were spent with peacefulness and quiet where his inquiring mind was
always searching. Thank you, Charlie B. Heinemeyer, for the legacy you have
given us.
"HISTORICAL DATA OF MERCER COUNTY NORTH DAKOTA-1882 to 1932."

Beulah boosters

"Be a booster for your home town. Boost consistently and continually. Let the
people know of the great opportunities your town has to offer and they will
'sit up and take notice.'"

"There is no town, however small, but has some advantages. No town but would be
a good location for a factory or mill of some kind. Look at the natural
advantages of your home town. Think how they could be utilized successfully.
Agitate clean streets, yards and alleys, and good roads, good public
institutions, a city park and things that make a town look like it is wide
awake."

"These are the things that make a town look good to a stranger and you can rest
assured your boosting has been effectual."

Peter Reese, editor of Beulah Independent, 1915

        equipment, as this photograph of a snowy Main Street shows.

Madison M. Mounts

Madison M. Mounts, former superintendent of the Knife River Coal Mining
Company, was an engineer by training and profession with an important
experience in connection with the railroad up until 1913. Matt, as he was known
locally, developed the coal property that he had acquired east of Beulah.

Madison's father was a colorful character of the Old West. In fact, he built
the first house in Bozeman, MT where Matt was born April 15, 1887. Matt
attended grade school there until he was 11 when his mother died. His father
sent him to Helena where he stayed at five separate places until finishing
grade school, when he moved to New York City where his married sister lived.

After completing high school he took a course in higher accounting, and was
employed for five years by the wholesale jewelry firm of Charles L. Trout and
Co.

He returned to the west in 1907 and went to work for the Cook Construction
Company of St. Paul in the accounting, engineering, and construction department
of this organization. Cook was employed in railroad building and general
construction in Montana, North Dakota and Minnesota as well as Canada. His
training as an engineer came from the severe school of actual practice;
however, he later took up a special course in mining engineering. He was with
this company from 1908 to 1914, and was given the duties of superintendent of
construction.

His last important railway work was the building of the extension to the
Northern Pacific between Stanton and Killdeer. He had charge of all the lot
sales in all the townsites along the line as representative of the Tuttle Land
Company.

Ads were placed in the Bismarck, Mandan and Stanton papers and lots in Beulah
were sold Oct. 29, 1913. This property was former railroad holdings acquired by
John C. Tweet in 1905, who sold it to Dr. Norman Vredenberg in 1911. At this
time it was plotted and named Troy. Several months later Tuttle Land Company
bought the land and the company president named it Beulah to honor his niece.

Mr. Mounts had considerable experience in mining properties in Montana and he
bought land east of Beulah from Mr. Semmler who had been mining coal with
little success. After drilling test holes it was found to have enormous coal
veins from 18 to 24 feet in thickness.

In 1917 M.M. Mounts, E.A. Hughs, L.C. Pettibone and C.B. Little organized the
Beulah Coal Mining Company and took over the Mounts properties. Matt was the
supervisor and with 25 men a shaft was dug and coal mining began.

C.B. Heinemeyer secured an option for the company for additional land in 1922.
At that time the mine was reorganized as the Knife River Coal Mining Company.
The company later opened a new mine two miles north of the tipple. The tipple
was destroyed by fire in 1925, but before the year was out a new one was
constructed of steel and cement with modern appliances to unload coal cars,
screen coal and load boxcars.

A railway was built from the tipple to the new mine, and eventually electric
underground coal loading machines were installed. The dinkey locomotive hauled
40 to 50 cars to the tipple, and this became the biggest coal mine in the
state.

In 1928 the mine was sold to the United Public Service Company in Chicago, and
a year later to Insull interests, then to the Northwestern Public Service
Company of Huron, SD, and in 1947 to Montana-Dakota Utilities Company of
Minneapolis.

Mr. Mounts was retained as manager of all these companies and he did enjoy his
work and weathered the woes of building, fires and labor problems. He realized
he was too inexperienced at the onset of this venture as the company had
control of his coal properties.

During the mid-thirties baseball players, some from the minor leagues, came to
work for Knife River. Matt was a great baseball fan, so these men were given a
job and played ball too. They were fine players and with the local talent these
famous teams were a match for any in the state. It was a good publicity stunt
for Knife River Coal and the town of Beulah. They were called the "Miners." The
school was so impressed that they soon adopted the name for their teams.

Madison Mounts was married Aug. 2, 1913, at Great Falls, MT to Ella A. Jereb,
who was born in Livingston, MT. They had three children: Edwin B. who died at
five years of age, Della M. who is married and living in Minnesota and Dalton
C. married and living in Bonita, CA.

After retirement in April 1952, they remained in Beulah for several years, and
finally moved to Bismarck and spent four years there. Their last move was to
Wadena, MN, where their daughter and grandchildren lived.

Mattison died in 1964 and Ella died in 1981.

Everything was less complicated then

"A new rhyme on the much abused Ford has been making the rounds this week. We
are publishing it for the benefit of our readers:

"There was an old man and he had a wooden leg,
He had no money and he had to beg.
He had some pins and a twelve-inch board,
And he says to himself, 'I'll build me a Ford.'
A gallon of gas and a quart of oil
A piece of wire for a coil.
Four big spools and an old milk can,
He hammered it together and the dern thing ran!"
        From the Sept. 2, 1915 edition of the Beulah Independent.
