Beulah's First burial

For years I went to the Beulah Cemetery on Memorial Day to stop and ponder at a
grave that had a small bronze plaque mounted at the foot with the following
inscription:

"Pearl Edith (Roberts) Evans, June 30, 1888, at Joy O'Neill, Nebr. Married
June 2, 1915, to Joseph C. Evans at Joy, O'Neill, Nebr. Died June 21, 1915, at
Beulah, North Dakota. The first burial in this cemetery."

It seemed so tragic that the first grave in this lonely prairie cemetery was
the final resting place for this young bride of 19 days. What happened to this
young woman, who spent her last days on earth dreaming of the future she and
her new husband would share here in Beulah? Thanks to the effort of Beulah city
auditor, Bob Wendel, the mystery has been solved.

The city decided to find the descendants of some of the early settlers of
Beulah. Thinking they would live in Beulah permanently, these people bought
large blocks of cemetery lots and buried one or two loved ones, moved away and
were never heard from again. Since cemetery lots are deeded property, the city
couldn't sell them until they were either turned back or sold back to the city.

The hunt began in June, 1987, and by March, 16, 1988, Wendel had the final
piece of correspondence in the city files. He was 100 percent successful in
contacting all of the families. This was no small task, for there were 40
blocks involved.

Many had absolutely no connections in Beulah, although the names were familiar
in Beulah's early history: Sovereign, Stuhr, Mounts, Kees, Esterly, Kenyon,
Hunter, Brown and Evans.

Wendell contacted Opal Unruh, a life-long resident of the Beulah area, to see
if she knew anything about the Evans family. She remembered they were related
in some way to a Roberts family in Bismarck. Wendel contacted Roberts Floral
Shop and hit "pay dirt." They not only knew of the Evans family, but their
family had placed the bronze plaque on Pearl's grave.

They referred him to Frank Roberts who in turn guided him to Pirrung Evans, the
son of Joseph C. Evans. Wendel contacted Pirrung and bought back the remaining
Evans lots.

I got the telephone numbers from Wendel and called Pirrung at Eureka, Ca, and
Frank Roberts at Bismarck. Between the two of them I was able to piece together
the following history.

Joseph C. was the son of early Mercer County homesteader Benjamin Franklin and
Fannie (Knapp) Evans. The Evans homestead was located between the Jim and Tom
Keogh ranches. Joseph married Pearl at Joy (the Robert's family's rural home
church) near O'Neill, Nebr. After the wedding Joseph brought his bride back to
Beulah, which was then a thriving year-old community. Whether she became ill
along the way or after she arrived here is not known, but she died of spinal
meningitis, which at the time was certain death.

        Joe Evans and his wife, Pearl, posed for a wedding photograph just a
        few weeks before her death from spinal meningitis. She was the first
        person buried in Beulah's cemetery

Pearl was the daughter of Mr. and Mrs. E.F. Roberts of O'Neill, Nebr. Her
brother, Herbert J. Roberts, was married to Joseph's sister Phrona, and this
couple were the parents of Frank Roberts. They also had a homestead south of
town.

Joseph later married Clotilde Brost of the Zap area who had a son named
Pirrung. Clotilde and Fannie, Joseph's mother, were active in the community and
were charter members of the Royal Neighbors of America, Beulah Chapter. In
1918, when Pirrung was nine months old, his mother died of the flu, taking with
her their unborn child. She was 24. This time Joseph lost not only a wife but
also a child. Clotilde was a Roman Catholic and a member of St. Joseph's
Catholic Church; therefore, she was buried in the church's cemetery.

In the 1964 Beulah history book it states that a Kathlene Evans was the first
person buried in St. Joseph's cemetery; as I and others have been able to
ascertain, that was actually Clotilde. Clotilde's father was German and her
mother, French.

Pirrung said neither could speak the other's language too well but somehow got
along fairly well and raised a large family. Pirrung was named by his
grandmother Brost, who gave him a French name that had a special meaning to
her. After his mother died, Pirrung went to live with his paternal
grandparents, Benjamin and Fannie Evans.

Losing two wives in three years was not the end of Joseph's hard luck. One day
while working in his store he heard a disturbance in the back yard (it seems
that every business place had living quarters attached and many would raise
their own chickens in the back yard). Fearing that a dog was getting into his
chicken coop again, he grabbed what he thought was a broom and was going to
chase the varmint away. In the confusion he grabbed a loaded shotgun, which
somehow went off and almost shot off his hand. It was hanging by a little skin
and flesh, so he ran to the neighboring barber shop and the barber had to cut
off the hand with his barbering shears. They applied a tourniquet and rushed
him to the nearest hospital, which more than likely was at Bismarck. It had to
have taken several hours since the main mode of travel in those days was by
horse and buggy on winding, dirt roads. There were no pain killers so it must
have been a long and agonizing experience.

        Fred Flemmer, right, served customers in a grocery/drygoods store in
        Beulah 's early days. Note the gloves and socks hanging from the
        ceiling and the canned goods on the shelves.

Joseph C. moved west in 1925. He did not marry again for many years, but when
he did, he married a wonderful woman who gave him three daughters. She was a
good stepmother to Pirrung and he loved her as if she had been his own mother.

Some additional Evans family history: Benjamin Franklin Evans and his son,
Joseph, operated a general store called, "Evans and Evans Beulah Bazaar" from
1914-1924. In a corner of the store they had an area reserved for the Beulah
Post Office. Joseph was the first postmaster of Beulah. Fannie Alice Evans was
a practical nurse and midwife and delivered many of the babies in the area
until they moved to Oregon. She had such a generous nature that she raised many
foster children who, for some reason, had no place to go. Benjamin served as
Mercer County treasurer and Herbert served as deputy treasurer. Later, when
Herbert was treasurer, Ben was deputy treasurer. Herbert was elected to serve
in the state Legislature representing Mercer and Oliver Counties. He was then
appointed to the tax commission and the family moved to Bismarck in 1925.

Benjamin and Joseph bought lot 18 on block 10 from the Tuttle Land Co. in 1913.
The building, which was built in 1914, was sold to J.E. Hoffmann in 1924.
Hoffmann opened the Star Meat Market. In 1928 William and Myrtle Dohn bought
the building and in 1932 rented it to Nick Sardotz, who had previously worked
for J.E. Hoffmann. He and his family moved to Beulah and ran the Beulah Meat
Market until the late 1930s.

In 1944 Daniel Huber purchased the building and he and his son, Leo, ran
Huber's Meat market until 1953 when they built a new building and moved. John
Kessler bought the building, tore it down, and erected a new brick building
which for many years was rented to various cafe operators. The present owner is
Ruben Sackman, of Sackman Cleaners.

The above article was taken, from the Mercer County Historical Society's
Newsletter "Bits and Pieces."

        Beulah 's Main Street looked a little different after its first theatre
        building burned down, taking with it a good portion of the business
        district.

The need for good roads and services

In the year 1923, "benedict" was a newly married man, not a way to prepare
eggs. A stock buyer was a person who bought livestock, not a representative
from the New York Stock Exchange and "crying" was something done by an
auctioneer at an auction sale, as well as mourners at a funeral.

In the year 1923, what Beulah really needed was a mill, as in flour, not a
mall, as in shopping. Local basketball teams were called "basketshooters" and
radio was considered to be the greatest indoor sport yet discovered. Two local
families had installed "radiophones" and it was predicted that they would soon
be as popular as the phonograph. Indeed, the Princess Theatre was closed during
the winter months of 1923, with Mr. Mounts, the manager, stating "Radio
concerts and basketball games seem to be the most popular form of amusement."

Although "good roads" was still the cry of the land, Beulah had made many
improvements in the decade prior to 1923. A fire which resulted in the
destruction of six businesses in 1918 prompted the formation of the Beulah
Volunteer Fire Department. The magnitude of the blaze forced local businessmen
and insurance agents to think in terms of fire protection: the businessmen were
concerned about covering their investment and the insurance agents were
concerned with the prohibitive cost of insurance with no fire protection.

A fire at the Farmers' Co-op Elevator occurred during extremely cold weather in
1923, making it impossible to use chemical engines, and a number of firemen
received badly frozen faces and ears fighting the inferno.

Beulah now had phone service within the city and a telephone directory printed
in the Independent listed 75 businesses and homes on the service. The local
telephone exchange had a local central operator who relayed calls to the
desired party and the telephone service had weekday hours of 7 a.m. - 9 p.m.
and operated on Sundays from 8 a.m. - noon and from 4 p.m. - 6 p.m.

The rural areas also had received the service in the form of a party line, a
service which included from 13-19 families on the same line. The families had
to listen carefully for their particular ring, as the numbers consisted of a
series of long and short rings. One family may have a number of one long, one
short, one long rings, and the next may have one long, two short and one long
rings, etc.

The number of families on each of the six rural party lines and the difficulty
of distinguishing between the rings made an interesting combination, and it is
easy to see how the party line "click" alerted the person using the telephone
to the fact that at least one of his neighbors was listening to his
conversation. The central operator within the city and the rural party line
were memorable features of early telephone
service in Beulah.

Even as early as 1923 there were electric washing machines and irons within the
city, greatly separating the daily labor of the city housewife from the rural
one. Knife River Coal Company was closed during the summer, since this was a
time when there was not much demand for the lignite. Knife River permitted the
Beulah Electric Company to use their generators during the summer and furnished
a current every evening until 11 p.m. On Monday and Tuesday evenings,
traditionally washing and ironing days, the current was turned on earlier for
running washing machines and electric irons.

The Garage and Light Plant was considering building a large garage to light all
the towns on the northern branch, thought to be a practical move since the
overhead cost of maintaining a separate light plant in each small town was
prohibitive.

        Left to right, Alex Weigum, a Tesky, Ed Weigum, Bill Kemer, George
        Weigum, Godfred Wagner, Cliff Foster head out for a jackrabbit hunt.

Beulah's light plant was operated by Messrs. Hughes and Deiters. The current
supplied from the large AC generators at the mine was transferred into 110
volts and the service was later extended to 24-hour service at a maximum of 16
cents per kilowatt hour.

The population of the city in the year 1923 was about 1,000 citizens, resulting
in the need for a more elaborate educational system. The first high school
classes were taught in 1919 and Beulah's first high school class graduated in
1923 with two graduating seniors, Helen Moore and Lee Perkins.

The number of students attending high school class grew each year, and in 1923,
233 pupils attended the Beulah schools; 200 in the grade school and 33 students
in high school.

        Beulah 's old grandstand sat on the old county fairgrounds, just south
        of the railroad tracks where UBC Lumber is now located. Photo was
        taken in the late 1920s or early '30s.

The rural schools were a vital part of the early educational system and the
directors and clerks and all members of the rural school districts formed what
was known as the School Officers Association. When this group met in 1923, they
set the salaries for the rural teachers at the following: inexperienced
teachers, a salary not to exceed $80 per month, and experienced teachers, a
salary not to exceed $100 per month.

G.C. Poe was Mercer County's first county agent. He attended school in Fargo
and also reviewed his knowledge at an annual conference. Poe kept busy holding
meetings to inform the local farmers about feeding livestock and diseases that
would affect production, and one such meeting was held at the Princess Theatre
in 1923. Diversified farming was beginning to be emphasized by the governor's
office and a favorite theme was, "Wheat - eat more and plant less."

The county commissioners in 1923 voted to discontinue the practice of hiring a
county agent, but A.D. Brown, the editor of the Beulah Independent, led an
outcry that gathered momentum and later resulted in the establishment of a
permanent position for a county agent.

In January of 1923, coal production at the Beulah Mine had increased to 300
tons a day and it was estimated that two new miners were being hired every
three days. Over half the coal mined in Beulah was shipped to Minnesota. The
lignite business was beginning to be promoted on an active basis and the North
Dakota Lignite Coal Operation Association sponsored meetings around the state
to promote the sale of coal. Later in the winter of 1923 production was up to
400 tons per day, and the increased activity at the mine coupled with only the
most rudimentary safety procedures led to a larger number of accidents. The
local paper carried stories of a miner who scalded his foot and leg when a
steam pipe broke and another who lost two fingers in a mining operation.

        Clowning around was a young man's pastime even then, as this group,
        which included George, Ed and Alex Weigum, goodnaturedly tries a group
        wrestle on the Beulah plains.

Later in the winter the mine workers belonging to the United Mine Workers of
America walked off their jobs at the Beulah Coal Company in a protest over job
conditions.

The strike caused a division in the ranks of the miners, who differed in their
opinions about whether or not they should return to work. Fights broke out on
Main Street and rocks were thrown through the windows of a house belonging to a
miner who had returned to work. The conflict between the labor union and the
mine company over varying job conditions is a situation that still exists in
the present day.

The development of the farming lands was increasing and in 1923, Fred Klein,
manager of the Beulah Farmers' Elevator, returned from a statewide grainbuyers'
convention in Minot and reported that the 350 delegates present felt that
Beulah was one of the largest primary grain markets in the state.

Warren Harding was president in the year 1923 and the village board of Beulah
elected Robert Heihn mayor. The Federated Women's Club was campaigning for a
constitutional amendment concerning a national marriage and divorce law.
Although the national amendment prohibiting the sale of liquor was not ratified
until 1920, the state of North Dakota approved and adopted Prohibition as early
as 1880, and in the year 1923 the editor of the Independent wrote, "20 car
loads of good booze are shipped into Canada and 20 hundred car loads of poor
booze are shipped out. It's a gay life if you don't weaken."

The religious life of community members had been enhanced greatly in the decade
before 1923 with the predominant churches in Beulah at that time being the
German Lutheran Church and the Catholic Church, both active and functioning
mainstays of society.

Fashions of the day included loosely fitting knitted frocks, ankle length
dresses with pleated skirts, flounces and tiered skirts. Hats were definitely a
part of the fashion scene for women, as well as front-fitting corsets, which
were advertised by Heihn's Store in the following manner: "The unsupported
figure all too soon evidences its neglect in sagging tissues that treacherously
add perceptible years."

There were no good roads to other towns so the Beulah business men did not have
to be concerned with losing business in that manner, but there was an abundance
of peddlers who went from door to door in the village and from farm to farm in
the rural areas, hawking wares of every sort. It was a cause for concern for
the local business people, who paid taxes to support their community and
business and resented the peddlers' infringement on their business territory.

In 1923, A.D. Brown, the editor of the Independent, wrote this sarcastic
indictment against the peddler: "The peddlers seem to appear along with the
spring crocus, selling socks so strong and durable that they could be used for
harness tugs, and clothing made from rich patterns so far ahead of the small
town it will be in style for the next ten centuries. The local business people
must be content to stand in the doorways of their shops and stare mournfully at
the sky, as they have just paid their first installment in taxes."

        Archie Erickson, the little fella, is with Hans Sevallius on the
        family's Mercer County homestead just before 1920.

The tent shows that came to town in the year 1923 featured comedians, singers
and dancers, and the local citizens enjoyed the entertainment. A popular event
hosted by the high school students was a three-act comedy play presented at the
Grange Hall and entitled, "And Home Came Ned." The Field Day and Old Settlers'
Picnic was held on the Fair Grounds and featured school children from the
county in athletic contests, musical parts, scholastic exhibits and public
speaking contests. The early settlers gave an account of what it was like
opening up a new territory and the perils they encountered.

An approximate account of the businesses operating in Beulah in the year 1923
is the following: Royal Barber Shop -- Geo. M. Slowey, I.H.C. Dealer Siebert's
Barber Shop -- Heihn's Store C.C. Smith, M.D. -- Farmer's Co-op Elevator M.P.
Moore, Draying Service -- J.P. Schwinghamer, Dentist Beulah Meat Market --
Princess Theatre Mac Martell, Construction and Masonry -- Coupland Motors Rose
Hardware and Implement -- Mrs. John Erbele-Custon Suits For Ladies
Marshall-Malaise Lumber Company -- Bacal's Store Garage and Light Plant -- City
Meat Market Cole's Garage -- Roy Robinson, Barber Samuel Frank, Lawyer -- Dr.
Geo. F. McErlain

1923 was a year when sleeping sickness claimed the lives of many citizens and
printed lists of available "coal lands" were sent to interested "eastern
parties." It was a year when the Majestic Cook Stove and Allis-Chalmers
tractors dominated the advertisements and a year when many local businesses
took eggs and cream from the farmers the same as cash. It was also the year
that the Northern Pacific Railroad planned to extend its northern branch, and
the towns of Halliday and Killdeer were quarreling over the division point
before the road was built.

The year 1923 was part of a decade in which the village of Beulah began to
progress, and even though there was still much to learn and accomplish, the
village was beginning to grow.

        Barbecues were no small affairs in Beulah's early days as this whole
        side of beef roasting over the pit shows. Site is south of the Knife
        River where Riverside Park is today. Photo taken in 1922.

Beulah's theatres--always in transition

In the present day, a movie theatre is a place where one can go and buy popcorn
and a soft drink, settle back in a comfortable chair and watch a movie. Many
modern theatres also rent movie videos at the theatre for the customer to take
home and watch on the VCR.

But in days gone by, a theatre was much more than just a place to watch a
movie. Of course, there were movies at certain times for the enjoyment of the
patrons, but theatres were used for many more purposes than just movie viewing.

They were used for public dances, school programs, operettas and a host of
other community and political events. Indeed, the theatre was the only place in
town big enough to host such functions in Beulah's early years, since the
school was still a fledgling unit and there was no city structure large enough
to hold many patrons. Thus the local theatre became the meeting place for a
wide assortment of community groups and many citizens have memories of events
that were held there.

Theatres in those days were not always called theatres--the first "opera house"
in Beulah was built by Dale Sovereign. He became interested in operating a
moving- picture machine after selling his claim in the Medicine Butte community
and moving to Idaho. After he returned to Beulah, he built The Palm Theatre
while the village was still in its infancy.

He owned and operated the theatre and moving-picture business until it burned
down in 1918. Sovereign was also the first photographer in Beulah.

The next opera house in Beulah, called the Princess Theatre, was built in 1920.
This theatre also burned in the year 1929. At the time of the fire, the theatre
was under the management of Messrs. Marshall and Malaise. The Princess Theatre
was also a dance hall and the loss of the building dealt a severe blow to the
social and community life of the town. The building was a total loss, amounting
to about $14,000, only part of which was covered by insurance.

That same year Marshall and Malaise set about constructing a new theatre in
Beulah. The opera house was built west of Renden's Cash Store and was designed
by architect Leonard of Mandan who had also designed the New Salem Auditorium,
considered to be among the finest in the state. The new building was 120 feet
long, 50 feet wide and had a ceiling that was 18 feet high. A rolling partition
divided the building in the front to separate the theatre in the front from the
dance hall in the back and the dance floor was designed to accommodate 100
couples. The front of the building was 30 feet high with two openings; the west
entrance opened into a wide foyer leading to the theatre and dance hall.

The new Beulah theatre became somewhat of a community project. Financial
commitments were secured through the sale of stock to community members with
Marshall and Malaise being the principal stockholders and the company of
stockholders was called The Beulah Amusement Company.

The very first pictures shown at the new Beulah theatre were not talking ones
since it required some time to install the necessary sound equipment, but by
October of 1929 the brickwork on the building was complete, the sound equipment
was installed and the first picture was ready for viewing. The movie was "Why
Be Good," starring Colleen Moore, and it was shown October 25-26, 1929. By
November of that year, sound pictures were available and the movie "Broadway
Babies" drew crowds of up to 700 people.

About that time there began to be some talk about constructing a pavilion in
Beulah, which was met with disdain by the editor of the Beulah Independent. It
was thought that since Beulah already had a dance hall under  construction,
another certainly was not needed and the editor doubted the motives of those
who might construct a pavilion. He wrote, "A pavilion . . . will be born in
iniquity and will meet with prompt and certain failure." Of course, the
pavilion was constructed and for many decades was also a successful social
center in Beulah.

Early in the 1930's the theatre was given a name, the Roxy Theatre, a name the
theatre held for almost 60 years. Daryl Zimmerman, who operated the Roxy
Theatre from 1956-1987, said the theatre was named after a man called Roxy who
was very successful and well known in the threatre business all across the
country. Zimmerman said many theatres in that day were named Roxy after the
same gentleman.

In 1941, Arthur Zimmerman and Ed Moe bought the Roxy Theatre from the Beulah
Amusement Company and ran it until 1956, when Arthur's son Daryl took over
ownership. He ran the theatre continuously until he sold it to Ed Carlstrom in
1987. Carlstrom remodeled the interior and converted the large theatre into
twin theatres after the fashion of the day, moved the ticket booth out of the
front lobby closer to the theatres in the rear of the building (allowing
patrons to get out of bad weather) and installed a video rental display unit in
the lobby where the ticket booth once stood. He also changed the name of the
theatre to Beulah Twin Cinema.

Like many of the buildings constructed in the early years of Beulah, the Roxy
Theatre has a colorful history. In 1943 when the country was plunged deep into
war, the theatre served the multi-purpose of hosting political and community
events. A free war picture was shown to the community, depicting a documentary
history of a decade of war that led to the attack on Pearl Harbor, and parents
were advised that it was not a picture for children.

Beulah Mayor C.E. Peterson declared Copper Scrap Week in 1943 and school
children were told, "Your Uncle Sam needs copper and needs it badly!" Children
were treated to free matinees at the Roxy for every two pounds of brass, copper
and bronze they collected. The metals were used for bombers, tanks and bullets
and Copper Scrap Week proved to be a success.

Beulah's schools were not yet large enough to host events such as Christmas
programs, so the Roxy was used for these events and Santa visited the children
and presented them with a bag of treats for their efforts. Mrs. Myrtle Sailer
of Beulah was an elementary teacher in earlier days and she remembers trooping
the lines of children from the school to the theatre to get ready for the
Christmas program. Often the teachers had to set up rows of planks for the
children and parents to sit on for the performance.

The community was very proud of its theatre and often a large portion of the
front page of the Independent was used to promote an upcoming movie such as the
new film "Random Harvest," which played in 1943. It was billed as "a picture
you will always remember," and it was promoted with front-page attention for
many weeks.

In 1933 Douglas Fairbanks and Ginger Rogers were the rage and the movies "Mr.
Robinson Crusoe" and "Professional Sweetheart" were popular with moviegoers.

Admission to the Roxy in 1934 was 10 cents for children, 25 cents for students
and 35 cents for adults. Admission prices have changed since then and so have
many other features of the Roxy Theatre, but underneath all the remodeling and
facelifting is the same building that brought civic pride to Beulah citizens
when it was built in 1929. It is the same building that housed grasshopper
relief rallies in the 1930's and war pictures in the 1940's. The building now
called the Beulah Twin Cinema is a valuable part of the history of
Beulah.

        This play bill is typical of presentations by theatres in the early
        days; this particular film has become a classic and was shown in
        Beulah's Roxy Theatre.

First funeral director found it tough going

People today take for granted that, when they pass on to their reward, the
services of a professional mortician will prepare them for that final journey
regardless of their destination.

That wasn't so in Beulah's early days (or anywhere else), when families were
accustomed to preparing their own loved ones, seeing lovingly to the details of
preparing the body and the burial clothing, building the coffin and digging the
grave, most often on a little patch of land on the farm that served for family
members and sometimes neighbors, too.

So imagine the plight of the first funeral director who came to town. He had to
keep himself fed and housed while he slowly, slowly convinced skeptical,
thrifty German-Russians that it was better to spend money to give their loved
ones a professional burial than to do it the time-honored way, regardless of
how much love and attention were lavished on the deceased.

His name was Harry Orville Chilson. He established his business in Beulah in
1926, calling it the Chilson Funeral Service. He had enrolled in the University
of Minnesota at St. Paul in 1923 to pursue a degree in embalming.

He faced a number of uncertain years as the area residents reacted predictably
to his presence and, as mentioned, didn't see the value in having a paid
non-family member prepare their loved ones for burial.

Chilson's first client was the Herman family, as he acted as funeral director
for Charlie Herman's mother when she died, and thus the door opened a little.

Chilson encountered other hardships in establishing his struggling business,
such as traveling country roads to outlying farms during blizzards to perform
his services when families would not allow their loved ones to be removed from
their homes until the day of burial. In time, however, he was able to persuade
families that his establishment in town was more convenient for his work.

        Beulah's first funeral director, H.0. Chilson, faced numerous
        difficulties in establishing his business in Beulah.

The Depression of the 1930s left many of those who desired Chilson's services
unable to pay for them. During those years Chilson accepted coal and sometimes
farm produce, and traded for services he needed to ensure that modern embalming
techniques were not denied because of financial  Difficulties.

Among the numerous interesting incidents in Chilson's career perhaps most
noteworthy is the time Chilson was involved as coroner and investigator in what
turned out to be a gruesome event.

A parsonage burned down near Krem and a body was discovered in the ruins by
then Sheriff Paschadel, State's Attorney Sperry and County Coroner Chilson.
When Chilson and Dr. Rasmusson, a Beulah physician, performed an autopsy on the
body they not only discovered that the girl who had died was pregnant, but that
she had been poisoned.

An extensive investigation followed, and when the church's minister was
confronted with the evidence he confessed to the murder as a means of hiding
his indiscretion. He was sentenced to life imprisonment at the state
penitentiary in Bismarck, and Chilson received threatening letters from the man
for exposing the crime. The incident received national press coverage, and
Mercer County officials were commended for their efforts in solving the matter.

Chilson's family took an active part in his business. His wife, Mabel, assisted
in laboratory work and funeral arrangements, and his son, Orville, obtained his
North Dakota license after graduating from the New York School of Embalming. He
and his father opened a branch mortuary in Hazen which Orville operated until
he was
inducted in the military during World War II.

Chilson's daughter, Evelyn, at 16 was granted a certificate of embalming, thus
becoming the youngest registered apprentice embalmer - and probably the first
female one - in North Dakota at the time.

After many years of service to the county as a businessman and elected
official, Chilson sold his business to Bernie Halverson in the spring of 1947,
retiring to northwestern Montana near Glacier Park. He lived there for 20 years
and died in Boulder City, NV, in November 1968.

The one-room country school

One of the most memorable experiences of growing up on a farm in years gone by
was attending a country school.

The name of one such school was Antelope Valley #14. Rural schools always had
names with a number to identify the school district, and the school's name
appeared on every report card, so by the time a student graduated from the
eighth grade or his or her country school was closed, whichever came first,
each student was likely to remember the name of the school.

There was really nothing special-looking about Antelope Valley #14. It was a
plain building, painted white after the tradition of the day, and the school
sat on a hillside just a few miles east of Beulah.

There was no bus service to a country school, and most of the students walked
the distance from their homes to school every day. For some students, this
distance was two miles, and for others it was much longer. Many a student who
attended Antelope Valley #14, after trudging through the snow and cold for
several miles, wondered if the people who built the school put it on a hilltop
just to make the last half mile the most difficult of all.

In the winter, walking to school meant bundling up so tight in coats,
snowpants, scarves, sweaters and mittens that the only possible way to walk was
in a very straight and stiff manner. Older children were always given the
responsibility of seeing that the younger ones didn't dawdle along the way, and
younger students found that their muscle power was tested as they tried to keep
up with their older brothers and sisters. By the time the schoolchildren
arrived in school, icicles hung from the fringes of their scarves, and noses
and toes were numb.

Many farms had not received rural telephone service, so a worried mother could
not call the school to see if her children had arrived. And many a student who
reached the top of the hill where the school stood was stunned by the sight of
the deserted school grounds and the realization that school had been canceled
due to bad weather and he would have to walk all the way home again, without
opportunity to warm himself before facing the miles of ice and snow.

Ah, but summer on the Dakota prairies dimmed the memories of cold winter winds
in the minds of schoolchildren, and the spring breezes tempted them to linger
on for a much longer time than a waiting mother was willing to tolerate.

When the winter snows melted, the Knife River near the school was prone to
swelling, adding an interesting variation to the trip home from school. The old
red bridge over the Knife River became the focal point of the homeward journey,
and seldom was the spring day when schoolchildren weren't hanging over the
sides of that old, rusty bridge, the older ones skipping smooth, flat rocks
over the water's surface, and the younger ones simply dropping as huge a
boulder as they could lift into the waters below. It was a time for marveling
at the forces of nature and speculating about just how much school they would
miss if the river were suddenly to flood its banks. It was a time to discover
the music of meadowlarks and the beauty of bluebells, and it was a time to
revel in the outdoors.

In the spring, the hillsides surrounding the school were covered with hardy
spring flowers called crocuses, and the number of limp, lavender bouquets that
were given to mothers can only be guessed at.

Antelope Valley #14 had no running water or indoor plumbing, so students needed
to make quick trips to the outhouse when the temperatures were freezing. They
made longer, lingering trips when the warm summer sun beckoned them to stay.

There was no hot lunch program in Antelope Valley #14. Students brought their
cold lunch from home in Karo syrup pails or lunch boxes adorned with Old
McDonald's Farm or the Dancing Ballerina. It was the custom among the
schoolchildren to trade portions of their lunches with the other students
(against their mothers' orders, of course) . A bologna sandwich was worth a
piece of chocolate cake with cooked chocolate frosting, but candy of any kind
brought a dear price, and a student with a sweet tooth was apt to go hungry the
rest of the day if he traded his lunch for the sugary confection of his dreams.

One of the delightful memories of the country school is the delicious baked
potatoes which were baked in the hot coal ashes of the stove that stood in the
center of the schoolroom. Does a potato taste different when baked in coal
ashes, or was it treasured because it was a hot addition to the otherwise cold
lunch? Did the competition of seeing who could bring the biggest potato and
secure the hottest coals add to the enjoyment? It's hard to say, but the baked
potato was the most sought-after lunch of the day for the country school
children.

There was only one teacher in Antelope Valley #14. Considering modern
educational facilities, this may seem a bit disorganized, but the students
found the challenge of listening to class lectures for older students and the
importance of helping each other do their lessons. There was a bond of
fellowship and trust that could only be discovered through learning fractions
and geography maps while seated next to a student laboring over the Dewey
Decimal System. It was commonplace to see a student browsing through an
encyclopedia when there was free time.

        The Green Vale country school south of Beulah was one where
        Marguerite Herman taught and the Herman children attended.

The month of December always meant preparing for the Christmas program, which
was one of the highlights of the year. Parents were invited to this program
(the same parents who would determine who was naughty or nice), and so everyone
was encouraged to work hard and do his very best. First came the selection of
"pieces" from the books on Christmas programs. Each child had to memorize his
piece, and a student who found the art of memorization easy to master was
rewarded with an extra long selection. Then came the practices of the program
and music selections until they were second nature to the children. The school
was readied for the program by decorating it with colored pictures of Santas
with hats made from cotton balls, and a stage curtain was created by stringing
a wire across the room. Safety pins were used to hang a white sheet from the
wire, making a curtain. When the big night came, and that curtain was drawn to
expose the waiting audience of parents and grandparents there to view the
education progress of Antelope Valley #14, stage fright took its toll,
resulting in a sudden loss of memory, or worse, doing something completely
foolish like sitting on the stick pins for the angel's costume. The
"fuzzy-wuzzy" record, that was "supposed to stay on top of the bookcase, no
matter what," had mysteriously disappeared, adding to the confusion of the
moment. But somehow, the spirit of Christmas prevailed, and students were able
to heave a long sigh when another dreaded Christmas program was over.

Everything has an ending. Eventually, Antelope Valley #14 along with most other
rural schools was closed, and rural students began attending school in town.
Soon the little schoolchildren who attended the school graduated from high
school and began to follow different paths.

Now the hilltop where Antelope Valley #14 stood is the center of a sprawling
"country" residential area, featuring several beautiful homes built just far
enough outside of Beulah to offer privacy. The meadowlarks still sing, the
crocuses still bloom and the Knife River still winds its mysterious passage
through the area. The old red bridge has been replaced with a more modern
structure that would have dismayed the schoolchildren of yesteryear, for it no
longer has the high sides from which children could hang over the water and the
new bridge took a detour that skirts around the patches of bluebells that grace
the area in the spring.

Occasionally, there may be seen an adult or two, lingering near the spot where
the schoolhouse once stood or gathering bluebells in the nearby ditches. And if
they linger longer than might be necessary, perhaps they are remembering the
many games of drop the handkerchief or pump, pump, pullaway that were played
there. Perhaps the memories of laughter around an old coal stove are too
enticing to leave just yet. Or perhaps they are wishing that someone had told
them when they were schoolchildren attending their last days in a rural school,
"Say good-bye slowly and linger long, for you shall never pass this way again."

Promote that town!

"Oh, Beulah Land, fair Beulah Land,
With future fair, with prospects grand.
Our metropolitanish town
Should yield the sceptre, wear the crown.
And in the future it should be
A home of pride for you and me.

Our Beulah Land, the land of coal
Of opulence in every knoll.
The land of cattle and of grain
Of waiting wealth and verdant plain.

Let elfs of tongue and pen be loosed
And effort turned to boost.
Let every brain, let every mind
Look to the future. Leave behind
The things of petty spats and strife
And BOOST for greater, fuller life.

Yours truly,
A. Booster"
From Feb. 1919 edition of the Beulah Independent.

The Greystone Hotel

It still presides over its corner at Central Avenue and Railroad Avenue, but
the Beulah Hotel has lost much of its aura of imposing grandeur and quiet
elegance.

Originally the Greystone Hotel, the traveling man's hotel, the three-story
edifice was built in 1929 primarily to serve the needs of travelers on the
railroad and served its function quite well.

Many area residents harbor childhood memories of its elegance and the
interesting comings and goings of its clientele over the years. Its elegance
was legendary, and it is said to have been the primary social center and the
ultimate place to eat in Mercer County for many years.

An extravagance for the northern plains, the hotel sported an exotic goldfish
pond on its south side. Not surprisingly, that only lasted about a year - until
the owners found that restocking the goldfish would be an expensive, and
annual, proposition.

The hotel held three stories of rooms, small by today's standards but more than
adequate fare for the times. In the basement was the hotel's crowning glory -
an elite restaurant that served salesmen traveling down the railroad line from
Bismarck to Killdeer and back, as well as other railroad customers. It was
complete with sophisticated menu and - wonder of wonders - sumptuous white
linen napkins and tablecloths.

During the early days when Clara Wolf ran the hotel, Tuesday nights were famed
all along the line, and salesmen made a point of being back in town for that.
No one says for sure, but the big draw for that evening is said to have been a
little poker on the sly. Whatever the case, Wolf ran a high-quality operation
there.

The hotel has passed through a number of hands, with many of them having been
forgotten.

Owned by Cecil (Jess) and Gert Smith from 1965-1974, the hotel had begun to
lose some of the gloss from its glamour and the black from its profit
statements. Rooms went for $3 a night during those years and that money also
went to pay the maid and laundry woman. Even then the minimum wage was around
$2 per hour, so it wasn't a high-profit operation.

Four rooms which had been built in the downstairs area, a little larger and
more commodious, went for $25 per month and many of the construction people who
had begun to trickle into town by the early '70s stayed there. Later on, during
the height of impact, more of the rooms were rented, though by that time they
were hopelessly old-fashioned.

Herb and Ruth Feil ran the downstairs dining establishment for seven years from
1963-1970, and an old menu is a revelation to those used to high-priced modern
meals. A 12-ounce sirloin steak went for $2.25 in those days, and a thick,
juicy porterhouse with all the trimmings for a princely $3. A hamburger for the
more frugal sold for a mere 30 cents.

No one seems to be able to recall exactly when the name change from the elegant
Greystone Hotel and Cafe to the more mundane Beulah Hotel took place, and,
though many older buildings seem to attract colorful stories and those attract
embellishment as the years pass, the hotel seems to have had a relatively
unblemished background.

        The Beulah Hotel, considerably reduced from its former days of glory
        and elegance, still presides over the corner of Central and Railroad
        Avenues.

In August, 1977, the National Register of Historic Places was petitioned to add
the Greystone to its listing, but that request was denied. Since then, some
have asked the State Historical Society to grant it protection, but that, too,
doesn't seem to be in the offing.

In 1986 it suffered the final degradation to its dignity when the latest owner,
Adam Dockter underwent foreclosure. Though the building has been for sale, to
date there have been no viable offers for it.

Some people in town would like to see the building preserved for posterity;
others would like to see it razed and a parking lot installed.

Whatever the building's ultimate fate, it's certain it will never again see its
former days of glory and elegance as the ultimate hotel on the
Bismarck-to-Killdeer run for the Burlington Northern line.

He wrestled Abe Lincoln--and won

Lorenzo D. Thompson is remembered hardly more than locally except among members
of his family, yet he carried to his grave in 1875 a distinction of which he
was modestly proud and which perhaps he alone possessed - he "licked Abe
Lincoln at 'rasslin'."

Thompson, who is buried at Oakland Cemetery northwest of Bethany, Mo., was
Harrison County's (Mo.) first representative in the state legislature. He is
only imperfectly remembered by some few of the older residents of the
community, but the record of his exploit has been carried down in his family
and also was preserved in the library of the late Henry Cadle of Bethany.

The wrestling bout between the two which established athletic fame for Thompson
and also proved the sportsmanship of the future president took place at
Beardstown, Ill., in April, 1832, during the Black Hawk War. Lincoln was 23
years old at the time and was the elected captain of a company of 67 men from
Sangamon County who were enlisted for 60-day service. Historians have said that
he regarded the day of his election to lead his company the proudest of his
life. At the time, he was out of employment.

Thompson was a private in the company of Capt. William Moore of St. Clair
County.

The two companies met at Beardstown, where they were to be mustered into
service before proceeding toward Rock River where Capt. Lincoln was destined to
meet Zachary Taylor, Jefferson Davis, William H. Harney, Albert Sydney Johnston
and others who were to become prominent figures in U.S. history.

Simultaneously, the two companies came upon a desirable camping ground at
Beardstown, and it was claimed by each one. In some manner it was suggested
that Capt. Lincoln and Capt. Moore wrestle for possession of the spot. Capt.
Moore clearly was not a match for Lincoln, and he declined the proposal,
suggesting instead that a man be named to represent each company.

To this Lincoln agreed and selected himself. Moore turned to his orderly
sergeant and brother, Jonathan Moore, and asked him to select their company's
man. Sgt. Moore, with good knowledge, chose Pvt. Thompson. Sgt. Moore agreed to
referee the match, which was to be the best two in three falls.

A coin was tossed and Thompson won the choice of "side holts," whereas Lincoln
would have favored "Indian holts." There was betting on the result, even horses
and payrolls being risked.

To Lincoln's surprise, as he was then famed as a wrestled and to the
consternation of his company, Thompson threw the future president to the
ground.

"That's only one fall, and two more are due!" shouted Lincoln's men, their
faith in their leader undiminished.

"Now, Mr. Thompson, it is your turn," said Lincoln as holds were taken again.

But once more the legs of the future president went into the air, and the men
fell in a heap.

"Dog fall!" yelled Lincoln's men. "Fair fall!" retorted the men in Moore's
company.

But Lincoln's fairness was shown. Springing to his feet before the referee
could make a ruling, he exclaimed, "Boys, this man actually threw me once
fairly, broadly so; and his second time, this very fall, he threw me fairly,
although not apparently so."

Thompson came to Harrison County soon after its organization in 1845. He was
elected to the general assembly in 1846 and again in 1848. Old records of the
county court show that he had various appointments, such as land agent for the
county, township inspector of schools, and many times as administrator of
estates. He also was a member of the first grand jury called in Harrison
County. Politically he was called an anti-Benton Democrat.

"Positive in all his convictions, he was called eccentric toward the end of his
life, but all who knew him testify that he was able, upright and a good
neighbor and citizen," says a local historical note about him.

Thompson is described as having been a powerful speaker of the rough and ready
sort, for all that his education had been limited. He is recalled as having
been exceptionally strong, as he must have been to have vanquished Lincoln.

John Linville of Bethany, whose parents' home was near Thompson's, says his
impression of Thompson is that of "a big raw-boned fellow, a lot like Abe
Lincoln.'' It seems to Linville that Thompson was quiet in demeanor. Linville
remembers that he wore a mustache and sideburns.

Mrs. Shepard of Bethany, who is a relative of Thompson, gives her impression of
him from her childhood: "He was tolerably tall, must have been six feet or
more, and was tolerably big framed. His hair was getting pretty gray at the
time I remember him. He was just common in the amount of his talking and no
more; but he was very jokeative when he was around, liking his fun. When we
were little we thought lots of Uncle Dow. We liked to have him come because he
was so jolly."

At the time of Thompson's death, a local newspaper, apparently late in learning
of the happening, was sparing in its account and missed recounting the Lincoln
story. It
merely said:

"L.D. Thompson, formerly known as Dow Thompson, died recently in Butler
township. The deceased was one of the earliest settlers in Harrison County, and
its first representative in the Missouri Legislature. His name is met with
frequently in the county court records at about the time of the first
organization of the county."

Thompson was the grandfather of Manly Thompson of Beulah.

        By the 1930s, Beulah had grown to a modest but well appointed village,
        as evidenced by this panoramic photograph. The present middle school
        stands alone and a few houses are clustered around the water tower,
        but much of what is heavily developed today lies bare.

Beulah braves depression, drought and grasshoppers

Wall Street was a long way from the Dakota prairies, but the effects of the
Depression nevertheless had stunning consequences upon the town of Beulah.
Money was scarce, grasshoppers were plentiful, and the citizens of Beulah were
strongly opposed to the state Legislature levying a tax on "their" coal, an
industry that was giving local people so much work during this depressed time.

While FDR called for his "New Deal," the Beulah businessmen were calling for a
"New Deal for Beulah," asking citizens to build their community and "Buy it in
Beulah!" "Spend your wheat dollars in Beulah!" was a favorite theme of the
business people, who sought to strengthen their "village," as it was popularly
called in the local paper.

There was talk of a dam in North Dakota, at or near Garrison. It was called the
"Big Bend" dam, alluding to its location, and it was an idea that seemed to
foster displeasure in most of the village citizens. Why anyone would want to
flood the river bottomlands was a question that was hotly debated, along with
many statistics to prove that the dam would never be strong enough to stand on
its own, without collapsing and causing calamity. Soon a regular feature
entitled "More Dam Talk" appeared in the newspaper, and numerous letters to the
editor followed, all voicing their objections to the idea.

Money may have been scarce, but imagination was not, and a favorite weekly
feature in the Beulah Independent was "Fashion News From Paris." Fashion
reviews filled the pages of the paper, noting such trends as "the new winter
designs of 1933 featuring sleeve made all or partially of fur, working to the
nth degree of novelty and chic." Hat styles from Paris were showing "a great
deal of imagination," and it was generally known that the Paris dressmakers all
agreed that the simplest costume was the smartest one. Polka dots were the
fashion rage, and handkerchiefs of fine French linen embroidered with monograms
were "vogue." During this depressed time, fashion news from Paris was like
fantasizing about a tropical island in the middle of winter. It might not
accomplish much, but it was fun while it lasted.

The Community club and Women's club were active, vital parts of the community
structure, and the Boy Scouts, Girl Scouts and the Lion's club were also
important community organizations.

        Hugh Cox, a relative of Teresa (Cox) Thompson of Beulah, in 1936
        stands beside the Charles Le Raye marker noting the campsite in 1802
        of the French-Canadian explorer. The marker, less than 75 yards north
        of the old Sheep Shed, has disappeared.

The local political scene kept things interesting. It was the custom for school
board candidates to declare their candidacy and platform in the newspaper, and
the first candidate to declare his platform stated, "My platform is nine months
of school and 100 percent efficiency." An interesting idea. With budget
problems and teacher shortages, it was logical to support a platform
encouraging a full nine months of school, but how does one measure 100 percent
efficiency? The school board election became even more intriguing when the
remaining two candidates declared their platform in the paper. They were
identical to the first, "My platform is nine months of school and 100 percent
efficiency." It seems that politics was confusing even in 1933.

        A better view of the middle school, then the only school building, the
        brick ediface left of center, along with a few businesses where
        Security State Bank and West River Telephone now are.

        A 1931 view of Main Street in Beulah, looking east. The two stacks
        from the power plant are visible at the far end of the street.

        Beulah's Main Street looking west in 1931, with a good number of
        businesses visible.

Political news from the state capital in Bismarck included this announcement:
"'Ample funds remain in the state treasury to pay all bills incurred by the
previous administration and to pay all bills that may be presented later,'
according to Governor George F. Schafer."

Another interesting note from the political scene was that the year of 1933 was
the first time steps were taken to put a wheat control plan into effect in
Mercer County.

A special statewide election resulted in the sales tax proposal being badly
defeated, as was the change in closed bank law. The sale of beer was legalized
to take effect Oct. 30. Sunday movies were defeated by a close vote.

        A 1929 photograph shows an early Beulah barbershop in action. Note the
        wall calendar from L.R. Temme insurance. Farthest back is Ruben
        Buchmann, who barbered there.

        An early photograph of the Greystone Hotel, taken from a still-dirt
        Central Avenue looking North.

        A 1931 photograph of the North Dakota Light and Power Co. plant, later
        the MDU Beulah Plant, at the east end of town.

The homemaker of 1933 baked all her own bread, rolls and pastries on a wood,
electric or coal stove. Many of the citizens of Beulah were immigrants or second
generation immigrants now called "Germans from Russia' who prepared the
traditional German "dough dishes." Thus families were prone to buying flour in
large quantities of 100 or 200 pounds, enough to last the winter. Since flour
was always in demand, the advertising for the various brands of flour was very
competitive, with each stating that its flour baked the very best bread. One
brand in particular defended its higher price by advertising that 25 pounds of
its flour actually baked more bread than 25 pounds of the competitor's flour!
One can almost imagine housewives of the day, leaning over the back fences of
Beulah and discussing which flour their family prefers.

In tough times, it is important to share fellowship. 1933 was indeed a tough
year for residents of Beulah, but there were still opportunities to find
enjoyment. Double and triple weddings were very fashionable, undoubtedly due to
the economics of the times, and coverage of such events always made front page
news in the local paper. The Old Settler's Picnic was a long-planned and
eagerly awaited event, and the September Harvest Festival was another
opportunity to meet your neighbors for a visit. Beulah was just as enthused
about its athletic teams in 1933 as in the present day, and a social event of
the season was a community night to honor the high school basketball teams and
coaches. The menu was scalloped potatoes, buttered carrots, rolls, pickles,
jelly, angel food cake and coffee, all for the price of 35 cents. Another
social activity that always attracted a great deal of attention was the old-
fashioned pie social, a chance for the young people of the community to show
someone that they were interested in them.

The local paper had a chatty, even gossipy local news column called "Local
Items," and this feature always appeared on the front page. News editors were
not in the habit of writing editorials to voice their opinion on news events,
so this column provided an opportunity to share local news bits as well as a
chance to comment on them. One can only wonder at the intrigues hinted at in
this column, with news items such as, "We noticed that several men in our
village are sporting black eyes this weekly and "John Wolf had the misfortune
of breaking his car, Sunday." It was a place to brag a little about the
accomplishments of the residents of Beulah, and the editor did just that. "The
voice of our local tenor George Easton, wafted melodiously over the air from
KGCU at Mandan last Saturday afternoon. We hope the citizens of our village
heard and enjoyed his music." The column was also used to encourage citizens to
vote and help in the upkeep of the city: "The local village election is only a
month away, so trot out your candidates!" and "City announces a local clean-up
campaign, so let's all have your ashes hauled and keep our village looking
good."' The word "chic" was used to describe everything from movies to farm
machinery, and if a sports team was described as "classy," they knew they were
on the right track.

A newsworthy event of 1933 was the gravelling of Highway 49, a job that required
10 four-horse teams. The laborers were paid 90 cents an hour. Area farmers were
also beginning to demand that Highway 49 be continued north from Beulah to
Elbowoods Bridge, stating that they needed a feeder road to Highways 25 and 49.
They were beginning to organize meetings to discuss the topic and solidify
support for the idea, and their demands were growing more insistent.

The actor Tom Keene was playing at the "new Beulah theatre" in January of 1933,
in the movie "Renegades of the West," billed as a "roaring drama of love, guns
and steaming leather." Tom and Jerry cartoons were apt to be featured with the
main movie attraction, and the movie admission prices were 10 cents for a
child, 20 cents for a student, and 35 cents for an adult.

Education was another aspect of Beulah that was regarded quite highly in 1933.
The rural schools were numerous and a column called "Rural School News"
informed the local citizens of happenings in that area. Teachers in 1933 were
paid the following salaries: $145 per month for the  superintendent, $100 per
month for the principal, $85 per month for high school teachers and $70 per
month for grade school teachers. The Beulah sports teams were called the
"Beulah Bruins."

        An early version of peer pressure, a yoke would have been a handy way
        to convince a guy to go along; but these youths were just having fun.

        Looking east from the end of Main Street in 1931, the now-middle
        school is visible to the left and the elevators to the right.

Some of the Beulah businesses that advertised their wares in
the year of 1933 were:

Jacob Bacal & Son               German State Bank
Flemmer's Store                 New Beulah Theatre
Economy Hardware                Moore Dray and Transfer Co.
Huber Brothers Store            Rose's Gamble Agency Store
Ludwig Unruh Cream Station      Moe Tailor Shop
