Three new businesses opened their doors that year. The Beulah Roller Mill, a
flour mill, began business, and hot pancakes from the first flour made at the
mill were served at a farmer's meeting. The second business was the Beulah
Bakery, located east of the Rex Hotel, and the third was a recreation parlor
advertised as "an up-to-the-minute palace of pleasure."

A plant whistle from the North Dakota Power and Light Company signalled closing
business hours at 7 p.m. daily, except Wednesday and Saturday evenings, when the
stores were open longer. When the whistle blew on Dec. 31, it signalled the end
of a year that was characterized by "relief jobs," numerous suicide obituaries,
grasshopper relief rallies and the art of "making do." Yet the citizens of
Beulah prevailed, prompting the newspaper editor A.D. Brown to write in the
last edition of 1933, "We have braved a depression, drought, grasshoppers,
storms and calamity in our nation. Let us say good-bye to the old, with a firm
belief in our town, state and nation."

It happened in 1936--

Adult education classes began in Beulah.

The village of Beulah put in alley and street crossings. The sidewalks were a
WPA project.

The fountain at the Beulah Drug became popular for its "muds" and other
delights.

Beulah Creamery

In the spring of 1933, a man from Bismarck by the name of Harry Louis purchased
a frame building from Massachali-Mallaise. In that building, he installed the
necessary machinery to operate a creamery. Louis began making butter in the
summer of that year. He named his business the Beulah Creamery. The building
was located on the lot where the Bloom'n House Flower Shop is now.

Victor Stephens, who owned and operated the Arrow Creamery in Hazen, bought the
Beulah Creamery in July 1938. The name was changed to Arrow Creameries, Hazen
and Beulah. G. Krause of Hazen was put in charge of the plant.

Soon after taking over the operations, it was decided to go into the business of
pasteurizing and buttering milk and sour cream.

In 1941, Krause left Beulah to take over the management of a creamery in Mott,
ND.

Erhardt Grosz took Krause's place. Under Grosz' management, the business grew
to a very prosperous dimension. By 1943, the creamery was shipping daily
products by rail as far west as Halliday.

In the fall of 1949, the building was badly damaged by fire. Only a few feet of
the front was saved. Immediately after the fire, all the operation was moved to
Hazen.

The cream buying was also discontinued for some time, then later the front part
of the building was patched up so that it was possible to continue buying
cream, but the other operations were left in the plant in Hazen.

In the 1960s, a new brick and tile building was erected on the same site as the
old building. There was no processing of dairy products in the new building.
All the dairy products from Hazen were distributed out of the Beulah plant.

By 1970, several cheese plants sprang up in towns around Beulah and Hazen, so
farmers found it more profitable to sell whole milk rather than separated
cream. By the fall of 1975, the Hazen plant decided to discontinue operation
due to a lack of volume.

The Beulah building was used for a gathering station for the creamery in Glen
Ullin for a short time and then vacated until sold to Darell Stephens in 1980.
Darell now leases it to Connie Gegelman, who converted it into a flower shop
known as the Bloom'n House.

A tribute to the housewife of yesteryear

Eighty-four-year-old Lydia Neuberger of Beulah just chuckles when she hears
today's housewife complain about the drudgery of household chores. She has been
married to her husband August for 62 years, and together they raised four
children and operated a farm in times where there was no electricity, indoor
plumbing or good roads to the nearest town. "To be a housewife in those days
meant a lot of hard work," Neuberger says.

        Horses were used in the early days for almost all the labor which is
        now done by machines. Farm wives had to be proficient in handling
        them, along with their other skills.

        July 4, 1938, shows evidence of a rainstorm near a Beulah farmstead
        which will no doubt muddy up things and cause a long laundry day. for
        the housewife of Yesteryear.

Although she and her husband live in town now, they still manage the family farm
eight miles south of Beulah, and Neuberger has many memories of life without
electricity.

"Most of the chores a woman had to do for her family took almost the whole day,
like washing clothes. You had to fill your kettles the night before so they
would be all ready to put on the stove in the morning. And of course, I had to
carry in all the water for the wash, but I was lucky and had a pump with a
handle to use," Neuberger recalls.

Many women of the day were not as fortunate, and had to draw their wash water
from a well and carry it into the house. "Later on, we had a windmill, and then
we hoped for a wind on wash day so we wouldn't have so much water to pump by
hand," Neuberger says.

Operating a washing machine in those days took some muscle power "I had a
washing machine with wooden slats on the sides, and it had a handle that you
had to pull back and forth to agitate the machine, and at the same time you had
to pump a pedal on the floor with your foot," Neuberger says. "I'll tell you,
it was hard on the arms, and after a while you had to stop and give them a
rest." Since each load was washed twice, that meant a lot of pushing and
pulling before a family of six had clean clothes for another week.

        The E.P. Joos farm in 1936 shows equipment that today would be
        considered antiquated and inadequate, but which was common to early
        farmers.

Neuberger says that the white clothes were always boiled on the stove to get
them extra clean before they were also washed twice. "In those days, there
weren't many colored fabrics, so there were many white things to boil hard to
get clean," she says.

What became of the wash water once the clothes were finally pronounced clean?
"Well, I had to carry it out again, the same as I carried it in," Neuberger
chuckles.

The clothes that came out of Neuberger's washing machine were much wetter than
the clothes that are spin-dried in today's machines, and they took a long time
to dry. "Of course, we always hung them outside on the lines, winter or
summer," she says, "unless you had a big basement to hang them up in. And in
those days, nobody had a big basement."

Drying clothes in the winter time meant bundling up to carry load after load of
sopping wet clothes out to the line, and pin them up in sub-zero temperatures
with freezing fingers. The clothes promptly froze, and later in the day the
housewife brought them back in the house a load at a time and hung them up to
finish drying in the house. "Sometimes they'd just be dirty again by the time
you finished dragging them through the dirty snow," she said. "It was an awful
job in the winter."

Since there were no aisles of supermarket detergents in those days, the
housewives made their own detergents and laundry soaps, using lye, lard and
cracklings, the hard, pretzel-like substance left over from the process of
rendering lard. "It was hard on the hands, but it really washed the clothes
clean," Neuberger remembers.

Monday was always wash day on the family farm, and by Monday evening, after a
day of pumping and pulling the washing machine, and carrying water in and out
and wrestling with frozen clothes, Neuberger says she always went to bed early.
"I was tired and glad to have that day over," she says.

And, if the biceps did not get enough of a workout on Monday, they got a little
more exercise on Tuesday, because that was ironing day. Wash-and-wear fabrics
and steam-dry irons had not yet come upon the scene, so the housewives had
their own methods of ironing clothes. "We called them sad irons," says
Neuberger, referring to the heavy iron wedges used to iron clothing, "and I
guess that was a good name for them, because it made a lot of housewives sad to
have to use them. You kept them hot on your cook stove, and you needed two or
three so the others could stay hot. I always baked bread on ironing day so the
stove would be good and hot for the sad irons."

Neuberger says she never found the sad irons difficult to use, but they were
heavy, and in those days, women ironed everything. "I guess that habit is hard
to break," she says, "because I still like to iron my sheets so they are nice
and crisp. and I still iron August's overalls. I just can't stand to see a man
in wrinkled overalls to this day."

And of course, the Neuberger family needed more than washed and ironed clothing;
they also needed to be fed every day, and the housewife in pre-electricity
times did not have the modern microwave ovens and convenience foods. They
prepared their family's meals from start to finish and took pride in their
baking accomplishments.

"August and I took our wheat from the farm to the flour mill in Glen Ullin and
had it milled into flour and when we got it back, they also gave us the cream
of wheat for breakfast food," Neuberger says. "The flour wasn't bleached then
the way it is now and it had a much different consistency." The flour was used
to make many types of German dishes, and to bake bread, cakes, pies and rolls.

All these culinary delights were prepared on the Majestic stove, which usually
occupied a place of importance in the home. Neuberger remembers, "Oh, the
Majestic stove was really quite the thing in those days. I can still remember
the shiny top of that stove, and it baked really good bread."

There are many things about those old days that Neuberger doesn't miss, but she
says she does miss her old Majestic stove. "There were advantages to it. It
provided heat for the farmhouse and so it was welcome in that sense, even
though you had to get up early in the morning and get it fueled up."

And the modern-day crockpots had nothing on the old Majestic stove, according to
Neuberger. "The back part of the stove served as an area where food could be
simmered all day," she says. "It was a good way to make cottage cheese, and
there just isn't a better way to make a kettle of beans to this day than by
simmering them on the back of the old cook stove all day long."

        Far in the background the tiny roof of the Sheep Shed, flooded along
        with a great deal of other space, can be seen. Photo was taken looking
        north.

The water reservoir in the cookstove also provided some added benefits by
insuring there was hot water whenever the stove was going, and also by keeping
the air in the farm home moist during the winter months.

Baking bread during the summer months was a chore, since the hot stove made the
house even more uncomfortable, but Neuberger says the housewives found a way
around that too. "Using wood or coal in the stove meant that it would heat for
a long while, so we used to use corn cobs and cowchips to run the stove when we
baked in the summer," she says. "That might be a surprise to some people, but
that's what we did. They gave a fast heat and didn't last as long."

A particular memory she has of the bread baking days is "everlasting yeast."
Like the friendship cakes and sourdough bread starters that are sometimes
passed from housewife to housewife in the present day, the yeast was passed
along and kept for the bread baking and rolls. "You always needed to have
potato water on hand to keep it going," she said. "It's kind of a shame that
more women today don't do their own bread baking any more."

In the present day, a two-day North Dakota blizzard is apt to empty many a
pantry shelf, but it was not so in Neuberger's time. "Oh, there were times when
we were snowed in for months at a time, but of course we had our supplies
ready," she says. "We had the flour that we had milled, and families always
bought 100 pounds of sugar before winter, and we had our own milk and chickens
and eggs."

        Successful jackrabbit hunters, left to right, Cliff Foster, Ed Weigum,
        Englau Eid, George Weigum.

But there was one particularly bad winter when she remembers running out of many
staples, and the family ate bread, cream and eggs until August could catch a
ride into town on a neighbor's sled to get the supplies they needed. "We used
to joke that Dad would go to town as soon as he ran out of coffee and tobacco,"
she laughed.

Blizzards also were a good time to look through the "wish book," as the
mail-order catalogs were called. "There used to be so many more of them than
there are now," she says. "The stores in town were not stocked with the things
they have now, and there weren't any roads to the stores anyway. It was really
a treat to get to Bismarck in those days."

It wasn't just the rural housewife who struggled without the aid of
electricity; the farmer had his struggles too. Without electricity, farmers did
everything by hand in their efforts to make the prairies productive.

"Why, August used to mine the coal to heat our home," Neuberger says. "There
were places then where farmers used horses to uncover the earth, and then they
would pick the coal and bring it home for the family to use. Of course, the
coal was in big chunks."

Life without electricity was a life of labor that was often backbreaking, and
the miracles electricity brought made life much easier for rural North Dakotans
like the Neubergers. "We are really dependent upon electricity now, and we
don't even realize how much we need it," Neuberger says. "I guess the good old
days were good, but I wouldn't really care to go back."

Our famous weather

Weather has always played a large part in the lives of Beulah residents. A few
looks at various weather events in Beulah through the years show, clockwise
from top left, a "typical" snowstorm on Main Street on June 6, 1942; the Knife
River overflowing its banks and flooding the bottomlands in 1939; Beulah's
south side seeing the result of more spring runoff, year unknown; Jonathan
Fischer and Herb Weil atop a sky-high snowdrift in 1949; wind damage that left
a trailer demolished and its furniture setting on the ground, in June 1980; and
hail damage to a cornfield in the late 1950s.

As with all things, those who live with extreme weather must learn to live with
it, compromise with it, and sometimes just wait it out. Beulah residents, along
with all North Dakotans, have developed a fatalistic attitude toward's nature's
vicissitudes.

        Marching down Beulah 's Main Street in the cold and snow, residents
        showed their support during the war years for the country's war
        effort. Flags waved and horns played to cheer on the boys in uniform.

The war and the weather

By the year 1943, the citizens of Beulah had learned that nothing, not even the
Depression, could change the nature of their town in quite the same way as the
war did. It affected almost every detail of their existence, from food
rationing to the kind of books they read to the clothes and fashions of the
day. There seemed to be a shortage of almost everything, and if there wasn't a
shortage of a given item, someone would soon be asking to save it for the war
effort. It was much like the Depression years in that respect, yet with one big
difference: The country was unified in its efforts and it seemed easier to save
when it might help a serviceman overseas. There was a sense of doing the right
thing, and a sense that everything would be better when the war was over.

Gone were the Paris fashion reviews in the local paper. Instead, patterns for
dresses that could be sewn at home were featured, along with rules for home
canning, and guides for buying and raising your own chicks. The emphasis was on
making things at home and not using any products that might be needed for the
war effort. Home-canned items did not have to be declared as food inventory
and no stamps were deducted for them, so it became a popular process to
preserve the foods raised in the "victory gardens," as they were called. The
government produced pamphlets available to homemakers that provided information
on gardening, hardiness zones and approximate harvest times as an encouragement
for home gardening and canning. The home-sewn clothing featured in the local
paper was made from cotton prints, in princess-style frocks and two-piece,
short-sleeved suits. Selections from the Army and Navy fashion parade became
the focal point of fashion news.

The tone of the folksy newspaper of 1933, edited by A.D. Brown, changed
dramatically by 1943, when the editor of the Beulah Independent was Harold
Dally. The country's involvement in the war effort overshadowed every detail of
the paper.

Pictures began to appear in the local newspaper, especially pictures of
servicemen stationed overseas. It was common for families to publish in the
paper letters from servicemen, providing the citizens of Beulah with some
interesting insights into the culture and ways of those who lived abroad. Story
serials were provided for the reader, offering new happenings every week, and
in keeping with war concerns, the serial in 1943 was "Bombs Burst Once," by
Granville Church. "Army Nurse Writes Home" was another weekly feature, along
with a weekly news analysis of the Allied offensive and activities of the Nazi
troops. The Washington Digest relayed war news and summaries from the nation's
capital. Even advertising was geared to the nation's war effort. The Beulah
Drug Store ran this ad throughout most of 1943: "Keep well and help win the war
with rules to keep healthy and fit."

The U.S. Treasury ads urged the public to buy War Bonds and often the ads
encouraged a patriotic attitude, such as this one from a 1943 edition of the
Beulah Independent: "A Liberty Limerick: Said an acrobat named Ali Oop, I'm
constantly telling my troop, pledge all you can raise, for War Bonds these
days, and Hitler will be in the soup!"

        Flags and slogans demonstrate support for the war effort, including
        "Produce More Food," "Win the War," and others, as residents turned
        out for parades in the snow.

Beulah had a Rationing Board Office in the Sovereign Building on Main Street,
first door west of the Flemmer Barber Shop. Ration books were necessary to make
many purchases in the local stores, and most grocery stores no longer found it
necessary to do much advertising or to list prices, since most of the process
was now regulated by the government. Foods not rationed included fresh fruits
and vegetables, homecooked soups and home-canned fruits and vegetables.

Many of the men of Beulah and the surrounding area were "in the Army now," and
such a shortage of the male population also had an effect upon the town. Since
there were not enough miners to work in the mines and bring out the coal, the
governor was issuing warnings to the residents of North Dakota about the
possibility of a long, chilly winter. "Stay clear of draft dodgers," was
another warning sent from the governor's office.

Social events were few, but one that did draw a lot of attention was the
Farmers' Union Annual Picnic held at Riverside Park. It was a big community
event, and those attending were asked to "bring your own dinner. The lucky
winner of the drawing will earn a $25 free War Bond." The Dreamland Pavilion
was still having dances every Saturday night, and the featured dance group on
New Year's Eve in 1943 was Wally Kittler and his orchestra. The Roxy Theatre
became a community center of sorts, hosting the Presidents' Birthday Ball in
February, and various political events relating to the war effort. A free war
picture was shown in 1943, with parents being advised that "this is not a
picture for children. It is a documentary history of a decade of war that led
to the attack on Pearl Harbor."

Often, items needed for the war effort were obtained through a community
promotion, such as Molly Pitcher Day, a promotion used to collect bonds and
stamps. Governor John Moses declared June as Scrap Metal Month, and the citizens
of Beulah responded accordingly.

The absence of many fathers may have had an effect upon family relationships, as
Beulah's churches banded together in 1943 to organize a fight against juvenile
delinquency. A weekly "Bible Auditorium" was held in the Zap Hotel building,
and a recurring topic was, "Is this war Armageddon?"

        A 1941 photo shows how Beulah has grown and prospered over the years,
        even through the difficult Depression years. Many more houses and
        buildings now dot the area which defines the young city.

Many Beulah residents are sure to remember 1943 for something other than the
war, for in March of that year, Beulah endured what was called the worst flood
in the history of the state. A heavy, late-winter snowfall resulted in flooding
the Knife River and Spring Creek. Many families were evacuated when the Zap
railroad bridge was torn apart by the rising water, and crews in rowboats
rescued many families. For more than a week, Beulah was cut off, without
transportation service, from the outside world. The local stores were sold out
of supplies and reported that yeast was in great demand for bread baking. For
many weeks to come, residents were cautioned against drinking well water, and
immunization clinics were set up to guard against disease from the impure water.

1943 was also the year that a freak snowstorm on June 3 left the Beulah area
covered with six inches of snow and snowdrifts four feet high. Residents
reported that flowers and tomato plants were broken from the heavy snowfall
only a short month before the Fourth of July!

Mother Nature was still not through with her souvenirs for the year of 1943. On
July 29, a severe hailstorm pelted the area, wiping out the crops of many area
farmers. Beulah residents must have wondered if the enemy they were fighting
overseas was worse than the disasters they were experiencing at home.

An interesting event of 1944 was the proclamation from the governor's office
stating that as of June 11, the legal speed limit in North Dakota was 35 miles
per hour.

Some noteworthy changes occurred in the business community. The Red and White
Store, a grocery store that had done business in Beulah for many years,
discontinued business. The manager, Mr. Charvat, sold his inventory to Mike
Held, who opened another grocery store east of the post office on Main Street.
The RCU Store then moved across the street into the former Red and White
Building.

        The Beulah Miners were a hot baseball team in 1944. Shown here are
        standing, left to right, Fred Galloway, Robert Easton, Robert Swede,
        Glenn King, Helmuth Winkler, Lee Perkins, Joe Stewart, Lester Bauer;
        Front row, Elmer Maron, Helge Carlson (high school coach), L.J
        MacMillan, Freddie Younker, Bill Wallender, Glenn Wilmes, Erhardt
        Grosz, another Wallender, and Bert Webber. Lyle Grosz was bat boy

        Beulah's power plant, a bastion of modern electrical generation and
        convenience, was a mainstay of the town during the war years as well.

        The year 1942 saw growth and development, too, as new merchants came
        to the growing town. Among them was Fred Galloway shown with his first
        Super Valu store where pickles were 29 cents for two quarts.

        Taken from the north side of town out by the county 21 bypass, which

Apparently, the German community had been invaded by some Norwegians by 1943,
as an ad from the Star Meat Market advertised lutefisk at 15 cents a pound.

When the year of 1943 drew to a close, the "village" that became a town was 29
years old. The citizens had learned some hard lessons in those 29 years:
lessons of the difficulties of the Depression years, the loneliness and
sometimes hopelessness of the war years, and the constant struggle against the
elements, which seemed determined to destroy their agricultural efforts.

But the hard lessons made them strong, and Beulah ended the year of 1943 with
the largest business sector it had ever seen and a community unified behind its
men at the front. The German-Russian heritage of many of the citizens made them
a proud, hard-working people, and they would endure.

The Joachim Memorial Home

No one has yet counted the number of lives a building may have, but Beulah's
Joachim Home is already working on its third life - and its second building.

In 1945 the original frame house, which sat on the lot occupied now by the
stately brick building, became Beulah's nursing home. The house, which had
belonged to Albert Heiser, was both the first house built in Beulah and one of
the larger ones, and it was judged by nursing home promoters Rev. August Hoeger
and Rudolph Schnaidt to be the best location available.

Hoeger began making arrangements in 1944 to purchase the home and one of the
first things decided was to name the building the Joachim Memorial Home in honor
of the late Rev. S. Joachim, a local pastor who had died that year.

Through the exemplary cooperation typical of small towns, businessmen and the
Lutheran churches in the tri-county area were able to raise the money to
purchase the house and fully equip the home. But because of wartime shortages
it was difficult to obtain the proper equipment, and the home was not opened
until March 2, 1945. The first employees of the nursing home were Rose Kiesz
and Esther Lindemann of Golden Valley.

The home opened with six patients, though that soon grew to 13, which was more
than the house could comfortably hold. The waiting list grew and the nursing
home board recognized they either had to remodel or buy a new facility.
Building was the option they chose, but they wanted the same location as it was
near churches and downtown and more convenient for the residents.

The old Hillcrest Hospital building was rented for the residents during
construction and the frame house was removed and replaced by the fireproof
brick building which stands there today.

Many hours of time were donated by Beulah residents toward completing the
building. The bricklayers donated one day's work a week to the cause, and other
residents provided free varnishing, painting, scrubbing up and other vital
work. The nursing home board struggled in cutting costs and insuring efficient
construction, and the net result of their efforts and the generosity of the
community was that the building was completed at a modest cost of $38,000.
Added to the land value, that gave Beulah a nursing home for $60,000.

        The Joachim Memorial Home, operating since 1945, provided 33-bed
        service for senior citizens in its early days.

A dedication service was held for the building on Dec. 10, 1951, and home
managers were Mr. and Mrs. Albert Link - the "Mrs." half of whom was original
worker Rose Kiesz. The 33-bed capacity nursing home served the community, with
an employed staff of six people, for many years . In 1979 a merger between
Beulah Community Nursing Home and the Joachim Home was planned, and the combined
facility would be worth $ 1.4 million, including both the Joachim Home and the
remodeled building which had been intended as a hospital but was never used for
that purpose . The merger took place on Feb. 11, 1981. BCNH planned to close
and sell the Joachim Home, though it was used until June 7, 1982, when all the
residents were moved to the BCNH complex.

Beulah was far from finished with the building, however. Its sturdy brick
structure, now overshadowed by stately, cooling trees, was vacant for a while
before ANG, administrators for the then-Great Plains Gasification Associates
project, rented the structure in August, 1982, from the nursing home to use for
their local administrative offices while the plant site administration office
was under construction.

About the same time, Beulah's Senior Citizens' Club was looking for a home for
its group, a place where the members could gather, play cards, shoot a little
pool, have their meetings and just generally have a good time together; a place
they could call their own. They had been meeting in the civic center, but that
was proving unsatisfactory.

The group began a series of visits with the Beulah City Council, seeking city
aid in helping them find and/or purchase a building for that use. Their
requests were vague at first, though, and the council repeatedly told them to
come back with a more detailed plan.

Finally they hit on the idea of purchasing the Joachim Home from the nursing
home. ANG had moved its personnel to Bismarck and the plant site in mid-1983
and the city had been leasing some office space in the Joachim building to
house city overflow from the too-small city hall. After a couple more years,
lots of negotiating and plenty of jockeying, the Senior Citizens made that
purchase, obtaining the building for $35,000, $20,000 of which came from the
city of Beulah.

        The Senior Citizens building, having gone through a brief stint as an
        administration building for the ANG gas plant personnel, is now in use
        as a senior citizens center.

The seniors had five years to pay off that $ 15,000 note, but like the thrifty
pioneer stock they came from, they set to work to get that debt out of their
way. Two years later, in February 1987, they held a mortgage-burning ceremony
to celebrate that.

Most of the money to pay it off had come from city office rental, as some city
offices were still housed in the upper level of the building. The rest came
from the seniors' much-vaunted continuous rummage sale, which occupied a
portion of the lower floor of the building.

After city hall was remodeled and the city departments moved back across the
street to their rightful home, the seniors held a remodeling project upstairs
to construct their meeting room, a new, modern kitchen facility, pool room and
restrooms, and devoted the entire lower floor to their rummage sale.

Later in 1987, they moved in.

And there they stay, until their membership grows so large they must search out
yet another building. And then, probably, another use will be found for the
Joachim Memorial Home, which no doubt will still retain plenty of life in its
old walls.

Dalton C. Mounts--son of Madison and Ella

Back from war's dark limbo of the dead and "missing" has come the
sergeant-pilot, son of Beulah parents, some day to tell a story of how he
escaped the Germans when shot down in Nazi-occupied Europe. He is Pilot Dalton
Charles Mounts, son of Mr. and Mrs. M.M. Mounts of Beulah, an airman with Royal
Canadian Air Force in England since December.

For 35 days Sgt. Pilot Mounts was missing when the aircraft to which he was
assigned failed to return to its base in England after an operational flight.
Last Sept. 18, a telegram was received by his parents announcing that Dalton
had failed to return to the base in England and must be considered "missing in
active service." Over a month later, the son himself cabled his parents that he
was safe and sound. That was on Oct. 22. A few days later official reports from
the RCAF casualties officer announced that the Beulah youth was in Gibraltar,
and then in the United Kingdom.

It is known that one member of the crew with which Sgt. Pilot Mounts flew is
now a prisoner of war in Germany. This is enough to indicate that the same fate
might have befallen the Beulah man. How he escaped from German controlled
Europe is a story yet untold here, but it can be conjectured that he stole his
way through country occupied by thousands of German soldiers to Gibraltar, then
was returned to England.

The telegrams and cable received by Sgt. Pilot Mounts parents best tell his
odyssey. The messages follow: Telegram received Sept. 18, 1942: "I am commanded
by the air council to express grave concern on learning from the casualties
officer of the Royal Canadian Air Force overseas that your son Sgt. Dalton C.
Mounts has been reported missing in active service. The Wellington aircraft of
which your son was the pilot failed to return to its base on the 16th of Sept.
1942, from an operational flight.

Cablegram received Oct. 22 (without stated place or date of origin) "Safe and
sound, Love, Dalton." Telegram received Oct. 22, 1942, dated at Ottawa, Canada:
"Pleased to inform you a report has been received from the Royal Canadian Air
Force officer overseas which states that your son, Sgt. Dalton Charles Mounts,
arrived safely at Gibraltar on Oct. 24, 1942. Letter follows. RCAF Casualties
Officer." Telegram received Oct. 26, 1942 dated Ottawa: "Pleased to inform you
a further report has been received from Royal Canadian Air Force casualties
officer overseas which states that your son, Dalton Charles Mount, arrived
safely in the United Kingdom on Oct. 24, 1942. Letter follows. RCAF casualties
officer."

Presumably the aircraft of which Sgt. Pilot Mounts was pilot was on an attack
flight over Germany of German-occupied France, Holland or Belgium when it was
brought down. It may have been shot down or forced down in territory held by
the Nazis.

        It's a finish by a length, with Phyllis Bush ahead. Bea Murray follows
        in second place at this race, held at the Beulah race tracks in the
        late 1940s.

Mounts then apparently, hid and virtually crawled across enemy territory until
he reached the haven of Gibraltar, at Europe's far southwestern tip. Someday
soon, his parents hope, he may return  home to tell in full the story of how he
escaped from the Germans in their own stronghold. It was later learned that
Dalton was shot down over Nazi occupied territory and was smuggled to Gibraltar
by the underground. He parachuted from his plane, and was hidden. Guides aided
him in his escape, dressed him in civilian clothes and instructed him to follow
someone, who was always some distance ahead of him.

He felt the closest he came to being detected was at a time that he was
entering the subway and bumped into a German soldier. Dalton said "Oh, pardon
me" in English. Fortunately they were in the midst of a noisy crowd so the
remark went unnoticed.

After his arrival in England he joined the Navy Air Force and became Lt.
Commander of a Naval Air Squadron in Barber's Point Naval Air Station in Hawaii.

        The Greystone Hotel was a place for meetings, too, and this one was
        Ladies' Night for the Lions Club in Beulah, between 1942-50.

Ballad to the Mules and Mines

Gee! Haw! The black snake
Cracked on the brown mule's hide.
The mule skinner swore as he pushed and cried,
And the mule named Jack laid down and died.
He'd had enough of the cussin' and swearin'
Be damned if he'd work
Like the men who died wearin'
The black slack dust on their longjohns and bibs,
Pulled on over bellies lean, and hard, bony ribs.
The men were glad for the light lunch carried,
The pork rinds and bread that seldom varied,
But that eased the knot of hunger that growled,
While they picked and they hammered in the coal mine's bowels.

There were men who preferred to toil up above,
Whose labor below was not one of love,
But the 30s were grim, and a man with pride
Would go down below, from welfare he'd hide.
He'd take the pennies he'd earn by the hour.
To clothe and feed family, he'd use all his power,
For though he despised the darkness and dirt,
He'd go down below, he'd keep so alert.
The life down there was dank and dreary,
And a man would come up, blackened and weary,
His pay so meager, it barely would pay
To keep wolf from his door, day after day.

There was Fred, whose family arrived too soon,
Eight kids, always hungry, and a woman who ailed,
As she struggled to feed them with a grit that prevailed
In the face of hardship, deprivation and dirt,
As her man's bones ached from backbreaking work.
Then there was Tony, coal-smudged and lank,
Who used his small pay for the cheap wine he drank,
So the men eased away from his smell, raw and rank,
And only mules put up with his cursing,
While the work that he hated caused his temper to worsen,
And he only went down to the work in those caves,
So he could buy wine for the thirst that he craved.

The men would sink down in the tunnels deep,
Their helmets with carbide the only light to keep
The blackness that threatened the walls to cave,
Though we know only one who made it his grave,
And that because of a fault in the track;
When Bill Meese hollered "HAW!" and he jumped back,
The coal car buckled; Bill leapt the wrong way,
Though his mule survived, Bill died that dark day.
Left his widow no pension, his life only worth
What it cost to bury in poverty and dearth;
One thousand dollars, is not over much,
For a widow and children to survive on as such!

Those days were hard, a man's first thought his mule,
To feed and to care for him, the very first rule.
Twenty-one long-eared friends went deep down below,
Where they spent their lives come snow after snow.
They lived in darkness, never came out at all,
Except for three months from June until fall.
When the car lifted them out to the bright light of day,
How they'd buck and cavort, like spring calves at play!
Now these mules were like people, with personalities unique,
Some were more querulous, while others were meek.
There was Big Red, there was Spider, there was faithful old Maud,
All born to the light, where they should've tilled sod.

Instead the men broke them and trained them to pull
The coal cars in darkness, several tons made them full.
Yes, that mule's normal work was a mile north and a mile west,
Then sixty feet down, where they worked without rest.
The men to furnish the powder to blow,
Company paid forty-three cents a ton; picking coal, that was low!
It's no wonder the mules knew how to strike
Long before miners had heard of the like.
In summer they'd come out and work on the land,
A farmer would turn sod, and drive them by hand.
But when 4 o'clock came, those mules would stop dead!
"Underground quittin' time is 3:30," they said.

I don't know if it was the darkness and gloom,
The sealed off tunnels, the miner's tomb,
Or was it the stubborn, cantankerous mules,
That ripened their language and gave it fuel,
But it does seem true that the mules worked best,
If the muleskinner cussed and swore before they'd rest . .

Old Bud Perkins had the choicest of words,
That the mule named Spider ever had heard;
Poor Bud caught cold, he lost his voice,
Laryngitis he had, though not by choice.
As he crouched in the dark and cracked his whip,
No words came out, someone had sealed his lip!
That mule wouldn't budge, he just leaned back,
And held those coal cars still on the track
Til Bud in anger and frustration grand,
Ran up to Spider and took a stand,
He whispered hoarse, in the brown mule's ear,
"Just wait till I get my voice back, you S.O.B., do you hear?"

The muleskinners put trust in those mules, you can bet.
Electric current ran in wires, more than shocked you could get;
But those mules knew when they should duck their heads,
Pulling coal cars and stepping with most careful tread.
Glenn Murray once made his loneliest trip,
Took Old Maud, the honest, who never would slip.

        Left, Oran Abbey, and right, George Easton, tend to some of the
        mules so vital to the early operation of the underground coal mine
        at Beulah.

The country had flooded that spring of 1938,
Left the tunnels in water, it would not abate.
Lee Perkins, the boss, asked Glenn would he go
Bring coal cars out, so the work wouldn't slow.
"Take whatever mule you choose, I'll pay double time,
Just bring those cars up, we need them out of the mine!"

Eighty cents an hour, was Glenn's highest pay,
But he needed the money so what could he say?
He chose Old Maud, so honest, so true,
If he made it at all, she'd see him through.
The darkness surrounded, the water knee-high,
If her ears touched the wires, he could say good-bye,
To life up above, and living and laughter,
Electricity ran on wires that hung down from the rafters.
His only companion was Maud in the dark,
Loneliest trip of Glenn's life was no lark.
She brought him through safely, he collected his pay
A buck sixty an hour, to risk life and limb in that way!

Danger and death threatened the men in all seasons,
They found fun where they could, if given a reason.
The tracks were bonded to keep current in check,
If this was forgotten, someone sure got heck!
For with bonding neglected, the fireworks would fly
In total darkness, the sparks would sputter up high.
Glenn was driving that Spider, it just made him wild,
Glenn's first thought his mule, a muleskinner's child.
He reached to unhook tail chain, then hollered out, "HAW!"
The mule jumped to the left, that was all that Glenn saw.
For he jumped too, the car raced on down,
Hit loading machine, flew up high and around!

The sparks were flying, the wheels whizzed and turned,
If Hell's fire is brighter, the Devil would spurn!
Its memory still lingers, death nearly sounding its knell,
But the muleskinner lived, his story to tell.
By the time human ears heard a crack in the roof,
The mules would've sensed it, and left, on the hoof!
For a mule had intuition, a sense that could tell,
And more often than not, it served the men well.
If he entered a tunnel and smelled air that was foul,
That mule backed right out, left that cave on the prowl!
Big Red was a mule that could count at least up to six;
If the men hooked one more car, he caught on to their tricks!
He wouldn't pull, he'd park there and wait,
Till that muleskinner unhooked, no matter how late!

The crack that was heard on one such grim day
Left Herb Binder no time to make get-away,
By luck he was pushed 'neath his car as he fell,
Or he surely would not be alive here to tell.
The men showed their courage, they joined in the search,
Albin Sandau was there, never left Herb in the lurch!
They carried him out, his recovery was slow,
Never more 'neath the ground to dig coal did he go.
There were others like Glenn, who came out of the light,
Found work they liked better, things turned out right.

        When Madison Mounts was mine manager, this photograph was taken;
        probably 1937-38. It shows both the mine and the KRCMC power station
        at Beulah. The tipple, behind the plant, was newly built, a fire in
        1936 having destroyed the old tipple. Other buildings visible include
        mine office, car building shop, and change house. The coal was brought
        in from the underground mine in the far background by railroad cars,
        dumped in the tipple, and the circuit began again.

Finally the mines that were dug underground
Retired to stripping, new methods were found.
The men and the mules alike were all glad
To see daylight and new life did not make them sad.
The coal mines have stories, some buried below,
The few that I've told just help us to know,
These men had courage, had strength and raw will.
We know it survives in this country still!
As the miners keep working, stripping out the black coal,
We applaud what they've been, and what will be their goal,
For the story of coal, of the miners and mules,
Is Dakota's story of her richest fuel.

        This photograph, taken before 1920, depicts a "wagon mine," a small
        operation which strip-mined coal for domestic use by farmers and
        townspeople. This one was owned by John Henderson.

The underground mine--Beulah's first "black gold"

Imagine ultimate dark, a blackness so thick and heavy you can hold it in your
hand, solid as the coal surrounding it, yet insubstantial as the air it
inhabits.

This was home to Beulah's early coal miners. This was the underground.

For as long as Beulah has existed, the area's vast lignite coal deposits were
recognized as a valuable resource. Many were the early farmers who heated their
soddies by digging an exposed seam which happened to be on their property; and,
when enough settlers had reached the area, some enterprising souls began to
mine the coal and sell it.

After the railroad was completed in 1914, it wasn't long before a couple of
mines were opened. One, operated by George Schmidt, was only a couple of blocks
north of the new depot and had a slope entry with a 13' thick vein of coal, and
it was considered notable that the coal contained no water. This made it easier
to mine and better to sell, as coal with a high water content has lower heating
power, besides being more expensive to transport.

A second mine, located on Carl Semmler's land east of town, was operated by
James Hankins, Bismarck. The entry was an 8'x10' shaft which sank 38' into the
earth. Between the two mines, 50 men were employed.

The first mine was later owned by the Beulah Coal Company, organized in 1917. It
became the area's premier underground coal mine, sinking from 20' to 170' below
the earth's surface and snaking beneath the ground in winding tunnels for
several miles.

Mining several hundred tons per day, it shipped its first coal on Nov. 2, 1917,
via a special Beulah-Mandan rail run which carried the coal to market. Beulah
was proudly called "a town with a great future."

The seam in what was called the upper level, about 33' underground, was played
out in 1919. A lower level intersected a lignite seam but it was too wet to
mine, so a new operation was started in 1922 about two miles north of the
original site, where the near-buried remains of the double opening bearing the
words, "Knife River Coal Mining Co.," the name chosen by the reorganized Beulah
Coal Co., can be seen today.

Opening that mine was hard work. Fresnos, large scoops about four feet wide
pulled by four horses and dumped by tripping a lever, were used to dig into the
side of the hill. It was not work for the weak. The first coal had to be mined
and loaded by hand, using only picks and shovels, and hauled away by horses to
the tipple, located near the original mine site by the railroad tracks (near
the old MDU power plant, which closed in 1986 and which was originally powered
by coal from that mine).

Once sufficient coal had been removed to allow men and equipment inside the
mine, things became a little easier - but not much, as equipment was
rudimentary. The mine was often supplementary income for farmers as it was only
active in winter the first few years; nobody needed heat in the summer. In that
respect Beulah's coal serves the same purpose for some farmers today, w ho hold
down energy jobs and farm in their spare time, allowing them to keep a farm
they might otherwise be forced to give up.

        Gene Crandall picked rocks off the coal belt at the Knife River Coal
        Mining Company Beulah Mine in the early years of mining. Crandall was
        uncle to Philip, Ellen and Lawrence Joos.

The mine was dug in steps and slopes to follow the coal seams. Though picks and
shovels were still used, the coal was primarily loosened by blasting. Holes
were hand-drilled, using augurs, at various points in the coal seam and black
powder charges were ignited to blast the coal loose.

The coal was loaded and hauled to the mine entrance by hand for a time, from
where it was trucked to the tipple. Soon narrow gauge tracks were built inside
the mine and to the tipple, allowing steam locomotives to haul the coal.
Inside, though, the coal trains were still loaded by hand and hauled to the
entrance by mules.

Safety equipment, minimal to non-existent, would have horrified industry experts
today. The miners had only heavy coveralls, boots - not even steel-toed - and
the easily recognized cap with a carbide light perched at the front.

By all accounts, the mine was no place for sissies. Workdays were 12-14 hours,
with little pay for the exhausting physical labor.

Sometimes the fine black coal dust was so thick that the pinpoint carbide
lights could barely penetrate it. There were no masks to protect them from the
thick, choking dust, particularly after blasting, though a ventilator shaft
with a fan helped keep the air fresh. The men's mouths and teeth became thickly
coated and their mouths became so dry from the dust that they couldn't spit.
The smell of the caustic dust permeated their clothing and hair and, when they
came up from a shift, they looked as though they'd been charred black by fires
from the very coal they'd mined.

When there was no mining activity, the deep black tunnels were eerily quiet, so
much so that a person's ears would begin to ring and he would imagine he heard
voices. But most times the shouts of the muleskinners with their blacksnake
whips, cracking hard in the acrid air, the clank and roar of the train cars
jumbling together as the mules strained toward the Surface, the steady thunder
of diesel engines and machinery pounding the coal walls all echoed and
reverberated below ground to create  a thundering cacophony.

The environment in itself wasn't uncomfortable, however; the stable underground
temperatures, though cool, didn't reflect the raging extremes of heat and cold
experienced on the surface. If a guy was working, he was comfortable; he didn't
notice the chill unless he sat down a while.

The mules were well trained and made up the train of cars for the locomotives to
transport to the tipple. Oldtime miners often chuckled that the mules could
count. Once the cars were rolling, one mule could pull nine or 10 cars; but
they "got so smart" that if one more car was added, they'd refuse to pull.

As the work became more mechanized, three mules were assigned to each loading
machine, hooking the coal cars alternately. The skinners cared for the animals
as part of their jobs, and became quite fond of the contrary critters.
Occasionally a feisty mule would take exception to some direction given by his
skinner, and woe to the slow-footed who got in the way of those quick,
steel-shod hooves. Many a man spent a few days recuperating from a hard kick
delivered by an aggravated mule. Even today, some of the old-time miners tell
stories about their favorites, still calling them by name (most of which were
quite colorful). The mine even maintained underground stables for the animals,
keeping 30 to 40 at a time.

In the 1920s underground generator rooms were built throughout the mine to
provide electricity for underground equipment, though no electric trains hauled
coal until 1935. Electric drills replaced the hand augurs used to drill and
shoot. Shooting was done by placing powder seven to eight feet back in the coal
wall and blasting in rotation, so the coal broke up in uniform lumps.

The "rips" were about 16 feet wide, leaving enough room for miners to operate
the digger, with the loader following behind. The loaders carried a swing
roughly the width of the tunnel and required care in operation.

        One side in, one side out: The entrance to the Beulah underground mine
        was in good repair and kept free of debris to ensure efficient
        operation of the equipment in and out of the mine

        KRCMC's first rescue crew, around 1943-44, Fred Younker, Otto
        Voegele, Albin Becker, Clemons Becker, Clfford Sandau, Fleator
        Monzingo (Post Falls, Idaho), Howard Mohl, Harvey Sandau, John Layton,
        Herman Bertsch.

Mention of the Joy Loader brings a chuckle to an underground miner's throat. A
wicked piece of equipment, it resembled a large, flat pan with conveyor belts
attached, and two huge, flailing mechanical arms which whipped back and forth,
knocking the coal into position on the pan. The coal was conveyed back away from
the arms and loaded, still somewhat by hand, into the train cars.

All new employees started work on the Joy, and the consensus was that it "hardly
could be called a machine." Vibration from the Joy would leave a guy with teeth
still knocking long after his shift was over. It propelled itself on
caterpillar tracks and could deliver a several-ton wallop.

Mining was sometimes interrupted because of weather, and on Feb. 23, 1923 it was
noted in the local paper that the workers "got right into the collar after the
storm" to "ship their excellent coal to keep the rest of the country warm.
Beulah never need worry about running out; we have a million tons to spare."

        No, they didn't let women mine in those days. Apparently these three
        were posing for a gag picture in front of the Beulah Mine entrance.

        "Beulah Coal" was promoted as the best in the area by KRCMC and was
        used in its Knife River Station adjacent to the tipple.

A month later, the UMWA-affiliated miners were on strike and, though there was
plenty of demand for "Beulah coal," stayed that way. A later paper recounted a
striker who had returned to work and been attacked by a fellow miner. "An
indignant citizenry won't tolerate this," it was stated. "The union has
everything to lose and nothing to gain if its members are allowed to attack
those working at the mine." There were reports of vandalism and strife between
other miners.

That year production was up, but the rudimentary safety equipment led to more
accidents. One miner scalded a foot on a broken steam pipe; another lost two
fingers. By 1927 a workforce of 200-plus men produced 230,000 tons of coal
annually.

Competition between mining crews was common, and of the "friendly rivalry" sort.
Crews would watch to see how many tons the other crews recorded in a day, and
they'd do their best to beat that. On a good day, 2,000 tons would be loaded.
The "best ever" day netted a record 2,200 tons, a paltry amount compared to
today's strip-mine production, which can put out 11,000 tons in an eight-hour
shift.

        This board held a metal tab for each worker who was on shift at the
        mine. At shift's end, if any were left on the board, someone had to go
        find the miner who had remained inside.

        Mineworkers' housing was near the power plant and was provided by the
        mining company

There was fun, too, and the miners enjoyed playing tricks. When trackmen
carried in tools and ties in working on the underground rails, sometimes men
would carry them right back out "for orneriness" when they went to lunch. Or
they'd grease the switches so when a guy reached in to throw the switch, he'd
get a messy surprise.

The main tracks in the mine were set up in a loop; one side going in carried
empty cars, the other side going out carried full loads, with diagonal
crosscuts connecting them. Each "room" being mined had looped tracks, too; as
many as 25 "rooms" were worked at once, often in different areas of the
branching mine tunnels.

The mine was modernized as new equipment came along. By the start of World War
II, there were new electric locomotives, electric loading machines and other
equipment which increased production and decreased the workforce. In spite of
the decreased need for men, during the war half the underground mines were
closed for lack of personnel and a lack of coal cars shut down larger mines,
prompting then-Gov. John Moses to say, "The outlook for winter is chilly."
Starting wages for a miner then were 71 cents an hour, though the workday was
down to eight hours.

In May, 1943, work shut down during a three-day blizzard. When the men returned
to work, they found a fire raging in the underground tunnels, most likely the
result of spontaneous combustion.

Though that generally spelled the end of an underground mine, management
determined they would try to contain it. Retired miner Clemons Becker of Beulah
worked on that project, and recalled "we put in long hours trying to get it
out. We had to leave it set about three months to get it out and we worked
double and triple shifts (in other mine areas) to keep up production while the
fire was on."

Some brand-new equipment was trapped behind the fire, but the men worked their
way through the fire area and got it out. "There were places the flames filled
the tunnels," recalled Becker. Coal and slag was red-hot beside the tracks;
miners went in with masks and could stay a very short time before the extreme
heat forced them out, "streaming sweat."

To try to stop the fire, the miners sealed off successive areas of the mine by
"bradishing." Boards and plaster were put up at intervals, sealing off the room
and depriving the fire of the oxygen it needed. Becker recalls going in with
gas masks and filling in the tunnels, then going back and filling openings,
layer after layer, away from the fire.

The attempt worked, and on Aug. 19, 1943, the Beulah Independent noted, "For the
first time in the history of North Dakota, a burning mine has been salvaged from
complete destruction."

Accidents were not common, though they were often severe when they occurred.
Safety equipment wasn't much advanced over that in the '20s. A board had been
placed outside the mine, holding pegs on which each miner placed his "check" - a
metal tag embossed with his name and number. At the end of each shift, the boss
checked the tags; if any were remaining, he had to go get the man. That offered
some security in case of accident, though the best still came from the miner's
crew.

In 1952, the last year the underground mine operated, a listing shows 23
accidents occurred, nine of them serious, including fractured pelvises, feet
and hands, and hernias. Most serious injuries occurred during cave-ins, and the
mine's only two fatalities throughout its nearly 40 years both occurred when
men were trapped and crushed by coal cars against the tunnel walls.

        Steam provided power for the equipment during those days, with this
        earthmover and the little "dinkey" engine both powered by that method.

        Today, the Knife River mine entrance wall is all that's left of the
        underground days - that, plus numerous sinkholes which dot the area
        north of Beulah. The earth behind the wall has washed out to nearly
        bury the entrances where the coal trains used to ride.

That year Knife River Coal Mining Company purchased the company which had begun
contract strip-mining two years earlier and went into the strip-mine business.
By 1953 the underground mine had been phased out.

Today the only evidence remaining of the extensive underground operation is the
numerous sink holes which pock the area north of Beulah, caused by cave-ins from
tunnels which were abandoned without being filled. The Public Service Commission
has filled some of those to prevent further subsidence, but that hasn't been
entirely successful.

The era of the underground was over. No more would the harsh cries of the
skinners echo off the rough black walls, or the coal train rumble on its
thunderous way to the tipple. But, while that colorful period had come to an
end, the influence of Beulah's vast lignite deposits on the area was just
beginning.

        Sometime before 1957, the E.A. Kees office and Huber grocery stores
        were visible as some Beulah residents rode their horses down Main
        Street for a parade.

Peace and the beginnings of prosperity

With the war years gone and the Depression years a faded, if still painful,
memory, the community of Beulah began to expand its civic involvement and
business growth. There was no longer the need for a concentrated effort to aid
the war involvement, or the sheer determination to provide food for the family
one more time. Now the citizens of Beulah found they had the time and the
inclination to concentrate on building their community base, and during this
time many new organizations and businesses began to appear on the scene. It was
a time of peace and the beginnings of something that, compared to what they had
previously endured, was prosperity.

There was beginning to be a greater emphasis on entertainment, with radio
stations such as KGCU in Mandan now offering dance music, shows such as the
Green Hornet, This Is Your FBI and Drew Pearson and the News. The rootin',
tootin' western theme had invaded the scene, and the Lone Ranger was one of the
more popular heroes of the day.

Excitement filled the air with the announcement by the Webber's Store that it
intended to install an 85-foot television tower on the north side of Beulah. It
was called "one of the first community systems in the midwest." A television
set was on display at Webber's, for all to gaze at and wonder over, and it was
promised that hook-ups would be made in Beulah as soon as work on the tower was
completed. A television channel would be on the air from Bismarck some time in
the summer of 1953 to offer programming to the Beulah area. The channel would
be known as Bismarck's channel five. Anticipating the programs they would soon
be able to see in their own homes was a time of delicious eagerness for youth
and adults alike.

The Roxy Theatre and the Dreamland Pavilion were still providing weekly
entertainment, and now the Zap Theatre was also offering dances and roller
skating. Barn dances were fashionable, and well attended by those who loved to
kick up their heels.

Even the business advertising began to reflect a more relaxed atmosphere. The
Beulah Drug Store actively promoted its fountain favorites, and many a Beulah
resident has memories of enjoying an ice cream soda, sundae, malt or "mud" at
the Beulah Drug fountain when he or she was a youth growing up in Beulah.

During the previous decades, the Beulah merchants were in the habit of using the
same business ads over and over, sometimes throughout the entire year. Now
business dealers began to use varied types of advertising to promote their
wares, and many tended to be very competitive.

Easier access to roads and automobiles led more citizens to shop away from home,
and during this time, the Bismarck and Mandan businesses began advertising in
the local paper attempting to lure local buyers to Bismarck stores such as A.W.
Lucas Company. It was the beginning of the never-ending battle to keep the
Beulah dollars in the community.

        Modern civilization comes to Beulah as, about 1950, the first
        television tower was built in town.

Automobile advertising held a prominent position in the pages of the Beulah
Independent, with competing ads from Liebelt Chevrolet and Field and Field in
Beulah and Klaudt Sales and Service in Hazen. Liebelt Chevrolet was promoting
the "new 1953 Oldsmobile, the big feature car of the year, with a rocket
engine, power brakes, power steering and Frigidaire air conditioning." It was
apparent that the advancement of the automobile would create some permanent
changes in the lifestyles of Beulah residents. By 1952, America had a million
traffic victims.

In addition to the advent of television and the increasing usage of the
automobile and the roadway systems, Beulah was also blessed during this time
with a program for a five-county phone system. Plans were in the making for a
new rural telephone company for Mercer, Oliver, Morton, Grant and Sioux
counties. The group would be known as the West River Mutual Aid Telephone
Company.

The Joachim Memorial Home was now a part of the Beulah community, and
Montana-Dakota Utilities held their grand opening at their new store on Jan.
15, both contributing greatly to the services Beulah had to offer.

In May of 1953, Harold Dally, who had published the paper since 1943, sold it to
George Cokens, who was formerly the publisher of the Burr Oak Akron in Burr Oak,
Mich. A year's subscription to the Beulah Independent was $3.

If there is anything to be learned from the study of history, it is that there
is a natural human tendency to band together in times of crisis. 1953 was no
exception. It was during this time that infantile paralysis, or polio, was
taking a toll in the lives of many children and young adults, and the Beulah
community, like so many others across the nation, responded with deeds and a
sense of commitment to fight the dreaded disease that crippled so many healthy
young limbs. "Turn on your light for one hour in Beulah tonight for the
mother's march against polio," requested a local news plea, while organizations
and individuals were participating in the program to raise money and public
awareness about the dreaded disease.

Familiar political figures of the time included Fred Flemmer, who was the mayor
of Beulah, C.A. Thelander, who served as city council president, and Usher
Burdick, who served as a North Dakota Congressman.

National politics found that a "nose count" in Congress discovered 12 of those
noses were powdered, indicating that women were beginning to become involved in
politics, and it was also at this time that Joe McCarthy was making headlines
for his enthusiastic seeking-out of "pro-Communist" activists.

News on the fashion scene of 1953 included rayon blouses, nylon hose and pure
nylon dresses, all made more enjoyable to own after the scarcity of the fabrics
during the war years. The nylon dresses, available at the Federated Store in
Beulah for $7.98, were advertised as "pure joy to own, with no ironing, quick
drying and a forever crisp quality."

The Women's Club and the Lions Club were active in community life, and
homemakers' clubs were also active in the area. Bowling had become a popular
community pastime, with bowling leagues springing up throughout the city.

Rural schools were still a part of the educational system, with most of the
students moving on to attend high school in Beulah after they graduated from
the eighth grade. In 1953, as well as in many other years, it was the custom to
include the graduation ceremonies for the rural eighth graders with the
ceremonies for the seniors graduating from high school. In 1953, 58 students
graduated from the town and rural eighth grades, and Beulah had the largest
graduating class in its history, with 33 seniors.
