        March, 1950, saw a good blizzard as a calf later decided to munch on the
        roof of the shed - something he could do easily as the drifts allowed
        him to reach the top.

The decade involving the year 1953 truly was a decade of progress for the town
of Beulah. The expansion in the business and community sectors gave a depth to
the services that the town had to offer, and the greater availability of
leisure time meant that individuals and organizations would be able to devote
themselves to upgrading the place where they chose to raise their children. It
was a time of peace, a time of growth, and a time of progress for the town that
was now 39 years old.

Seeking an airfield for the growing town

Beulah had a landing field as early as 1946, but no airport. There were,
however, two airplanes in the area, less than a mile southwest of Beulah on a
little strip of land between country road 25, the Knife River and Spring Creek.
The land was owned by John Maier, who allowed the pilots to use his hayland.

The two plane owners were Ray Retterath, manager of Farmers Union Oil Station,
who owned a 1941 65-horsepower Piper Cub in exceptionally fine condition, and
Jess Thompson, a veteran war pilot who had spent $2,000 of his combat pay on a
J-3 Piper trainer, also 65 horse, with dual controls.

Thompson's plane, with wings detached, had been shipped in a boxcar to
Williston, ND, where Thompson assembled it and then flew it home. Thompson
built a T hangar on Maier's land and flew around for fun, along with taking
other people for rides.

"Airport talk" began to be heard in Commercial Club (now Chamber of Commerce)
circles; the city fathers felt that, as other small towns had airports, Beulah,
as a forward-looking and progressive community, should consider one, too.

On the front page of the Beulah Independent on July 4, 1946, it was noted that
Jess Thompson was eminently qualified to teach beginners and would soon receive
a CAA Instructor's rating which would allow him to solo a student. Thompson was
a fighter pilot during World War II and, having a commercial license and 1,200
hours flying time (half of that in combat missions), he was considered an
expert when "talking airports" and was quoted:

        These pheasants were collected for "Pheasants for Crippled Children,"
        a benefit promoted by Beulah's airport buffs. Left is Jess Thompson, a
        long-time flight promoter in the area.

"Right now we are handicapped by not having an airport in Beulah. I way 'we'
because in the next two years there are going to be many more planes here and
many more people interested. Flying is here to stay; a considerable number of
communities even much smaller than Beulah have gone a long ways in establishing
flying schools. If we do not get an airport we will be left out of our rightful
place in the state as a live wire and growing city. Why hesitate when federal
aid is now available?"

Quite a number of Beulah people . . . have had instructions in flying
(including) Fred Galloway, Ed Vaschek, Herbert Wallender, Charles Helvik and
Dr. Lerass. Others are beginning to feel the urge to sprout wings.

Beulah, through the Commercial Club and other organizations, along with the
'village dads,' are very much interested in a new field for Beulah, along with
securing a capable instructor, such as Mr. Thompson ... the various groups have
already authorized the purchase of a nearby field on which to establish an
airport. Personally, the Beulah Independent editor feels that the city and the
organizations within it should spend many hundreds of dollars each year to
establish an airfield and flying school here.

With that seed for thought planted, then-mayor Emanuel Liebelt Sr. and city
councilman Thompson "talked airport." Talk turned to investment as they jointly
purchased land for an airport, and formed in 1947 Jess and Lie's Flying Service.

Thompson moved his T hangar to the new strip, the site of the present Beulah
airport, and Ray Retterath and Chet Haas built hangars. Liebelt left
development and operation of the business up to Thompson.

The next year saw full-scale progress with a turf runway rated "good" by the
CAA, two T hangars, the longest runway 2,300 feet and a concrete block hangar
with office space, fuel, attendant available, and aircraft and accessories for
sale. However, there were no beacon or runway lights yet, so when occasional
night landings occurred cars with headlights burning were stationed at either
end of the landing strip.

A GI flying school was in full operation with 30 students. The J-3 Piper was
used for flight training and the partnership bought a Boeing Stearman E-75, a
war-surplus biplane, in July, 1948.

The rugged Stearman saw lots of service; it was an open-cockpit craft, fun to
ride in and do loops and rolls. A fellow named Herman, dressed in a flight
suit, was seen making parachute jumps during most celebrations. Whoever
returned Herman and his chute was rewarded with a free airplane ride.

The plane had more serious business, though, as it was equipped with spray
attachments for crop spraying, which became the mainstay of the business. Fred
Galloway became Thompson's ground crew, and the low flying was rather risky when
power lines and North Dakota's winds were considered.

National Air Mail Week was held in October, 1948, and Beulah saw its first and
only air mail service. Postmaster Mary Held and her staff, the high school band
and the mayor, as well as townfolks, went to the airport to witness the event.

During 1947 and '48 the Commercial Club held a pheasant hunt on Thanksgiving
Day and 40 birds were flown to the crippled children's home by Thompson and L.
McMillan.

Beulah was landlocked in 1949 during "the winter of the big snow." Snowfall was
so heavy and frequent that travel was at a standstill, except for trains, for
nearly three months. Rural dwellers were stranded. Numerous attempts were made
to open Hwy. 49, but storm after storm filled the four-foot-plus cuts. Beulah
was dependent on the local airfield.

The J-3 was fitted with skis and Thompson took to the air, delivering mail,
dropping repairs, groceries and medicines to farmers - and cigarettes were
items high on the "needed" list. There were 57 air passenger trips in January,
88 in February, and that number dwindled to 19 in March. Dr. Vinje spent $35 on
air fare in one month - a small sum by today's standards, but then $4 a trip
was standard charge. Teachers wanted to fly out, two ambulance trips were made,
a burn victim was flown out periodically for skin grafts, an imminent mother
was taken to the hospital, a critically ill individual was rescued from a rural
church where the family was forced to seek shelter from a storm; this was the
time when Beulah became acutely aware of the importance of an airport.

In March 1951 Jess and Lie's Flying Service was dealt a woeful financial blow
and the community was without air service when 16' of heavy snow fell, crushing
three of the airport's four planes when the housing collapsed beneath the
weight. No insurance was carried, and it took about a month to restore service.

The airport saw plenty of social duty, too. Pre-Lake Sakakawea times found
people spending Sundays at the airport, enjoying coffee and cookies as they
watched or took rides, at $4 for 15 minutes - enough time to see Beulah from
the air or watch the progress at the Garrison Dam site.

A new Cessna 170 was added in 1955 and was used for ambulance service and
charter flights. Then-county agent Mac McKenzie hired the plane to take farm
pictures, Knife River Coal used the service for mapping coal lands and survey
work and Ernest Kemmet, a noted marksman, flew with Thompson over the prairies
during winter to hunt coyotes, bagging 37 in one year. The last charter trip
the Cessna flew was to take Riverdale's Cub Scouts to sightsee over their home
town. The plane was sold in 1961 to the state Game and Fish Department, and
still flew over the area.

There was plenty of work during a severe grasshopper infestation during 1956,
when aerial spraying was $1.45 an acre.

Crop spraying for Jess and Lie's ended in 1957 when the Stearman, which had
survived the '51 snowfall, was sold. More power lines in the area meant more
risk for the pilot and the plane was aging and had weathered hail and skin
repair. Others did and continue to spray off the airport, however.

In the 1960s the Knife River Squares were at the airport dancing and holding
steak fries in the hangar. The Flying Ranchers and Farmers flew in for meetings
and "fly-in" breakfasts.

Jess and Lie's Flying Service was operating an airport in the 1960s but not
giving much service. The last plane was sold to the Knife River Flying Club,
one of whose members later damaged it beyond repair. The demise of Jess and
Lie's came in 1965 when following nearly 20 years of airport work, Thompson
decided to go into a farm-ranch operation and sold his share to Liebelt.

Liebelt then gave the city a long-term lease on the land, and the Beulah Airport
Authority was formed with Thompson as chairman. Fred Galloway was on the board
and was the mainstay of the airport until 1981, when Jim Morton came to live on
the premises as base operator and manager.

Under the airport authority the municipal airport has seen some much-needed
improvements. The runways have been extended to 3,500 feet, been blacktopped,
runway lighting and a beacon have been added. Seventeen planes, as well as
helicopters, are based there.

        The mayor, the postmaster, the high school band and numerous citizens
        turned out when Beulah's air service participated in National Airmail
        Week.

Mercer County's Mother of the Year, Mrs. Friedebert Benz

Mercer County's Mother of the Year, Mrs. Friedebert Benz--or Gramma Emma, as
most townspeople call her -- had only one child of her own, but since 1961 she
and her husband Friedebert have provided a home for more than 30 foster
children. The children have stayed with the Benzes for periods ranging from a
week to four years and nine of those children came to live with them
permanently. Friedebert and Emma Benz, with assistance from daughter-in-law
Adella (Mrs. Darold) Benz, cared for the children and supervised their
activities. The farm provided work and recreation for the children.

With the exception of Betty Isaak, all of the children were from broken Indian
homes. Delano Dog Skin and his two brothers, Clement and Earl Brave Bull, came
from Cannonball on the Standing Rock Indian Reservation in January, 1970, to
stay with the Benzes. They were joined in July, 1970, by five Long Fox
children: Kelly, Kathy, Tammy, Bobbi Jo and Shawn.

Emma, who will be 73 years old in Beulah's jubilee year, and Friedebert, who
will be 77, say their happiness and health is because of their children. "If we
hadn't had those children, I think we'd be dead by now," Friedebert said. The
Benzes' one natural son, Darold, serves as Beulah's mayor.

He was married and had left home by the time the Benzes became foster parents.
Three years after his marriage, in January of 1958, Mrs. Benz began caring for
foster children. It all began in July of 1961, when Victor Bettger of Stanton,
Mercer County welfare director, drove into the Benz farmyard in an effort to
find a home for a 16-year-old boy.

"Here?" asked Mrs. Benz.

        Center back, Emma Benz, better known as "Gramma Benz, " was featured
        with some of the many foster children she and husband Friedebert had
        over the years. She was named Mercer County Mother of the Year.

"Yes," ' replied Bettger. "I've checked you out and you qualify for licensing
as foster parents."

Mrs. Benz lost track of the first boy, who came from the State Industrial
School at Mandan. Other children followed, including two boys and a girl whose
mother was attending school after losing a husband. Three boys, abandoned by
their mother, found a home with the family and a fragile six-year-old girl with
epilepsy received constant care.

After the Benzes purchased their home in town, the children returned to the farm
during the weekends and summers. The family became regular fans of high school
basketball when the boys were on the Beulah team and the children were very
active in 4-H events. "When the Mercer County Fair came around, it was just
like a nut house here," says Friedebert.

Shawn, the Benzes' youngest child, graduated from high school in 1988 and he
calls the Benzes "Mom and Dad" just like all the other children do.

The Benzes did not adopt any of the children. "They have their parents. That
was our feeling," Emma said. But even though they weren't adopted, the children
will always be a part of the Benz family. "These children are ours," Emma said.

The special qualities of the Benz family were recognized by community members in
1971, when Emma was nominated by the Beulah Jaycees for the Mother of the Year
award. According to Mrs. Richard Grosz, a member of the committee which
nominated Emma for the honor, said, "Religion has always been a part of her
life. All those who know her praise her strong Christian faith. It's not just a
ritual for Mrs. Benz, but is exemplified by her good example and her daily
efforts."

Emma Benz says, "If it weren't for God and good people, we couldn't do it," but
her only regret concerning the care she and her husband provided for children
is that "we didn't do it sooner."

How does one provide a home for more than 30 foster children?

"They have to be treated like your own," says Emma, "with self-respect and
love."

Because of the commitment of Emma and Friedebert Benz, the lives of more than 30
children have been changed. Their home provided the opportunity for love, growth
and eventually, independence. Gramma Emma and Friedebert Benz are a proud part
of the history of Beulah.

Old Tarzan--a horse with a heart

Just a run-of-the-range colt, Tarzan was foaled in the spring of 1931 with a
body of average conformity, a good leg under each corner and a head that, 22
years later, could look back over a life of loyal service that richly deserved
mention. Owned by Glen Murray, he was broke to ride as a two-year-old and from
his first day at school gave evidence of a willingness to learn, and once
taught how to do a thing properly, he didn't forget. After his first year under
leather he was perfectly safe for children and literally scores of youngsters
lifted to his back got their first thrill of riding a horse. Yet, when the
occasion demanded he could and would suddenly become vibrant with action.

His owner estimated that between the years of 1933 and 1940 he rode him in
excess of 5,000 miles to and from work while in the employment of the Knife
River Coal Mining Company, and a calculated 25,000 miles as of 1952. A glowing
tribute to his remarkable stamina that has never failed to carry him and his
rider to the end of the trail, distance or depth of snow notwithstanding. Vivid
in the minds of all residents in this territory are the floods of recent years
when the angry waters of the Knife poured over highway 49 south of Beulah for,
at times, a distance of three-quarters of a mile, closing all traffic save to
the most capable and daring. It was during those troubled times this horse
performed some extraordinary feats. School teachers employed south of the river
repeatedly sought his service and seemed to have unlimited faith in the old
mustang as he threaded his way over the treacherous grade that might or might
not be there. From first to last, he kept his batting average perfect by
depositing each precious cargo safely on the other side.

As if momentarily to bow to glamour, in 1950 he was ridden by Smiley Burnette,
popular star of screen and radio who in that year visited this area as a guest
of the annual Cowboy's Reunion Rodeo. Luckily, no locoed steer came charging
past or some of the more loosely sewn patches on Smiley's britches might have
gotten jarred loose, or what would be worse, one can easily imagine Main Street
being surfaced with little bits of Hollywood.

Obviously, it would be unfair to expect an animal of his type to be as fleet of
foot as one bred exclusively for speed. But, and this is important, by knowing
what to do and giving all he had to do it, he was used continuously from 1934
to 1948 in a relay string and track fans at those races, which brought
thousands to their feet in wild exultation, will recall Murray won far more
often than he lost.

Last time I saw this horse was in October '52 at the yards of the Beulah
Livestock Sales, where he was being unloaded from a truck that had hauled him
to the Fort Berthold reservation for the purpose of corralling a lone cow. This
salty old bovine evidently loved her range among the hills overlooking the
mighty Missouri well enough to fight for it, and up to that time had
successfully defied all efforts to dislodge her.

On that day, however, she met her match with a little left over. In pen 31 the
conqueror quietly munched hay and occasionally pushed his nose through the bars
for a friendly pat from passersby.

In pen 28 the conquered, fully equipped with the needle-sharp horns and a bad
disposition, still snorted her disgust at the humiliation of being penned by
the aging cowhorse. You just don't take a horse of questionable ability on a
mission of that kind; the margin between triumph and disaster is too narrow. As
a lover of good horses for as far back as I can remember, I fervently hope
Tarzan has, and no doubt will have, a good home till time quiets his great
heart and the saddle he carried so gallantly must be clinched on something new.

Written by E.P. Boland, Beulah, ND - 1950s

        Old Tarzan, subject of this essay by E.P. Boland, was owned by Glenn
        Murray and was legendary in his abilities and character.

The Hillcrest Hospital

From 1940-1947, the city of Beulah had a hospital call the Seventh-day Adventist
Hillcrest Hospital, later shortened to the Hillcrest Hospital. The 24-bed
facility was situated on top of the hill in the city, a site which is now
occupied by a fourplex apartment building directly north of the Judy and Murel
Spier home.

The proprietor of the hospital was Mrs. Pearl Fredrickson, a member of the
Seventh-day Adventist church in Halliday who also managed a hospital there.
She moved to Beulah in 1940 and opened the Hillcrest Hospital in a wooden,
two-story building that was previously a hotel. Several other members of the
Seventh-day Adventist church worked at the Hillcrest Hospital, but it also
employed members of other congregations as well.

Mrs. Bob Wentland of Hazen was one of the "girls" who worked at the Hillcrest
Hospital, and she has many fond memories of the facility. She says, "Oh, we were
quite close, those of us who worked there, like a family actually. Why just last
summer, I had visits from five other women who worked with me at the hospital.
It was fun to recall those days."

Mrs. Fredrickson and her sister, Mrs. Titzel, provided nurses' training for the
employees, and their standards of hospital care were high, according to
Wentland. "They had standards that we were asked to follow," she says, "and
that included the very best of patient care, and no sloppiness. Our language on
the floor was expected to be good, and cleanliness was the rule of thumb. Why,
she (Mrs. Titzel) actually used to check the tops of the doors for dust wearing
a white glove when we were finished cleaning the rooms."

The physicians who worked at the Hillcrest Hospital were the Vinje brothers, Dr.
Ralph Vinje, from 1940-1941 when he entered military service, and Dr. E.G.
(Edmond) Vinje from 1941-1945. Following his military service, Dr. Ralph Vinje
practiced in Beulah and serviced the Hillcrest Hospital from 1945-1949.

Mrs. Edmond Vinje currently resides in Hazen, and she recalls some special
memories about the hospital. "I suppose by modern standards the wooden building
would be considered a firetrap, but you know, in those days we were lucky to
have anything at all, and we felt fortunate. I remember how awkward it was to
move patients on a stretcher up the stairs."

Vinje says the hospital was a blessing to the area, as there was no other
hospital on the branch line of the Northern Pacific from Mandan to Killdeer,
for the Hazen Hospital was not yet open, and the bad roads in the winter and
spring made it difficult to transport a very ill person to the nearest hospital.

"The hospital performed surgery in cases such as an appendectomy, tonsillectomy
and hernia surgery," says Vinje, "and we never lost a major surgery."

The fondest memory that Vinje has of the Hillcrest Hospital is the birth of boy
triplets who were delivered by her husband, Dr. E.G. Vinje. The triplets are
considered to be Mercer County's only triplets. They were named Grant Edmond,
Gordon James and Gerald Keith McLaughlin, and they now live in Spokane, Wash.

"It was quite an occurrence at the hospital, and everyone was very excited,"
says Vinje. "There were no incubators in those days, so the babies were kept in
dresser drawers with a hot water bottle next to them, and they all survived
just fine."

Shortly after the birth of the triplets, the hospital received a call from the
Gerber Company, who offered to supply the family with all the products they
would need for the babies, such as diapers, formula, and baby food.

"Yes, it was an event that was most scarce," says Vinje, "yet at the time I
don't believe the newspapers did much about it." The birth of triplets is
estimated once in 7,901 births and the birth of all boy triplets is estimated
to occur once in every 20,000 births.

As the triplet boys grew up, they always remembered the doctor who brought them
into the world, and Dr. Vinje received Christmas cards from them every year for
many years.

When the Hillcrest Hospital closed in December of 1947, it was a serious blow
for the community and efforts were soon underway to reopen the institution. L.F.
Temme, a Beulah businessman, bought the old hospital building and in 1948, the
hospital was again opened under the direction of the Benedictine sisters from
Bismarck.

        Violet (Mrs. John) Neubauer delivered her bright-eyed baby Loren,
        at Beulah's Hillcrest Hospital in 1950. The nun is unidentified.

        Hillcrest Hospital was a small, unimposing building but served the
        needs of local residents for several years.

Hazen opened its new hospital in the spring of 1949, and on Sept. 1, 1949, the
Hillcrest Hospital closed its doors forever.

Mr. Temme led a commendable campaign to provide Beulah with a new hospital. He
bought all of Schmidt's Addition and had it surveyed into lots and donated the
present nursing home site to the Beulah Hospital Association. He also sold the
remaining balance and donated it to the association for cost.

But all of Temme's efforts were for naught, for the Beulah Hospital was never
to be. Even though by 1947 $50,000 was raised for the new hospital,
stockholders were in place and preliminary work had begun, the building that
was constructed to be the new Beulah Hospital eventually became the Beulah
Community Nursing Home, a facility that was also essential to the welfare of
the city.

        Manley Thompson, John Meier and Reddie Cox rode a mule-powered covered
        wagon to help celebrate Beulah's golden anniversary in 1964.

Years of growth and expansion

In the year of 1963 the citizens of Beulah were concerned with the expansion of
many of the public facilities needed to adequately provide for their growing
population and changes in lifestyles.

The years following World War II brought many changes to the field of education,
resulting in an emphasis and interest in math and science courses. More of the
rural students were attending school in Beulah and the traditional one-room
country school was very close to becoming an anachronism.

By 1963 the Beulah school had undergone several building projects to keep its
educational system from bursting at its seams, but it was evident to the school
board and administration that another project would soon have to be undertaken.

Public meetings were held by the school on the matter of selling bonds for the
construction of a new school and a remodeling project for the presently used
building, at an estimated cost of $450,000 for the entire project. The new high
school was to be located three blocks north of the present building (now the
middle school), and would be used for students in the four high school grades.
The first eight grades would use the remodeled building. School enrollment for
grades one through eight was 362, and enrollment for nine through 12 was 184, a
total enrollment of 546 students.

Full page ads appeared in the local paper asking the citizens to support the
building project, which was later approved by the voters with a 78 percent
majority. The residents of Beulah had once again shown their support for the
education of their children.

The science department at the high school was active in the presentation of
science fairs, and under the direction of science teacher Wilmer Sayler
produced several high school students who were finalists in national science
fair competitions. Harriet Tobin won first place in the state science fair and
both she and Marlyn Kruckenberg were national finalists.

President John F. Kennedy was at the country's helm in year 1963, and parents
of the schoolchildren were beginning to hear about a program called "physical
fitness for youth," a program that was introduced by President Kennedy to shape
up what he considered to be a generation of physically unfit students.

Another event of the year that undoubtedly brought joy to many Beulah sports
fans was the defeat of the Hazen Bison basketball team by the Beulah Miners,
not once or twice, but four times in regular season and tournament play. The
Miners beat the Bison twice in season play, defeated them for the championship
of the Beulah Invitational Tournament and also beat them for the district
title. It was a year that sports boosters would remember and relish for a long
while.

George Cokens was the editor of the Beulah Independent in 1963, and he was the
first news editor to begin writing an editorial giving his views and
perceptions of events happening in the Beulah area. His editorial was called
"Stickin' my neck out - by George," and he used the column to defend his
editorial and advertising policies, to comment on local organizations and
businesses and to give praise to those he felt were worthy. In 1963, the
Independent had 1,200 subscribers.

Local news items were featured in the paper in a column called "Be My Guest,"
written by L.M. Stewart, and news from the neighboring towns of Zap and Golden
Valley were also a regular feature.

The community and business community had developed to such an extent that it was
now possible to publish a paper that carried more local news than material that
was "borrowed" from the Associated Press, a feature that made the local
newspaper of 1963 unique from those that had gone before.

In the year 1963, the Independent opened a photo shop that did business on
Saturdays in the old shoe shop building next to Koppi's Jack and Jill on Main
Street.

Green stamps were given by many local businesses in that year, and the Chamber
promoted an event called "Hatchet Days" during the month of February. Lynn Aasen
served as the president of the Chamber, and the approximate Beulah businesses
were:

Beulah Gambles Store

A noteworthy happening in the business community of 1963 as the closing of the
Dreamland Pavilion, known popularly to the citizens of Beulah as "the
Sheepshed." A statement in the local paper read, "Closed due to lack of
interest in roller skating -- May 6, 1963, Quentin Bohrer manager."

        Businesses continued to grow and expand, as the Galloways moved into
        their second Super Valu store in the 1960s

That simple statement ended decades of dancing, roller skating, New Year's Eve
celebrations, wedding parties and sweet memories for most of the residents of
Beulah. It would be difficult to find a Beulah resident of 1963 whose life had
not been touched in one way or another by the memories of laughter and friends
associated with the building known as a "sheepshed."

The Beulah community seemed to be moving toward a trend of bringing well-known
entertainment into the town. In the early months of the year, a great deal of
advertising was given to the impending arrival of the All-American Indians, a
Native American basketball team that had toured nationally and would be in town
to play a team of area athletes. Another entertainment promotion was the
"world-famous Ink Spots," who provided entertainment for the city later in the
year.

        The telephone dial house was destroyed in 1967, leaving quite a mess
        to be cleaned up.

An organization that would have an influence upon the community had its
beginnings when the Bismarck Jaycees came to Beulah to organize a local chapter
among the young men of the community. Darold Benz was elected the first
president of the new chapter.

The Boy Scouts continued to be active in town, and in March of 1963, a local
troop took a 20-mile hike, leaving the city at 8:30 a.m. and returning from
their trek to Hazen at 2 p.m. The 20-mile hike was in itself quite a feat for a
boy, but it became even more so when the hike was taken in temperatures of 10
degrees and a 30-mile-per-hour wind!

1963 was also the year that other businesses decided it was time to expand. The
Sleepy Hollow Motel, first built in 1960-61, added two new sections, an office
and laundry room, and Zion Lutheran was making plans to complete its new church,
which would be located directly across from the new high school. The Bank of
Beulah bought an adjoining lot and was involved in construction plans for an
enlarging and remodeling program.

The village that was born in 1914 was now 49 years old, and like a newborn baby
that learns to crawl and walk, Beulah had learned to stand on its own. The year
1963 was part of a decade in which city businesses and organizations became
solid and progressive, with an eye to the future. The lessons they had learned
would stand them well in the next two decades, when the coal that had always
been a driving force in the everyday life of city residents would bring changes
to their town that were beyond anyone's wildest dreams.

The Beulah Drug Soda Fountain

The year is 1965. Classes have just been dismissed from the new high school and
crowds of teenagers are making their way down First Avenue, heading toward the
Beulah Drug Store. The soda fountain in the store is a popular meeting place for
teenagers after school as well as in the morning.

A young couple enters the store and strolls over to the fountain on the west
side of the store. They seat themselves on the round stools, kicking their legs
and swirling around in circles as they order one chocolate malt with two straws.

The girl is dressed in a box-pleated skirt in a houndstooth check pattern with a
matching sweater, and her hair is teased into a high bouffant in the fashion of
the day. The young man's hair is slicked into a ducktail and he wears a
short-sleeved white shirt and black slacks. Together, they enjoy the malt as
they make plans for the weekend Homecoming festivities.

Next to them, a father and a small boy survey the newest edition of baseball
cards, looking for a special Mickey Mantle card to trade, while they slurp on a
cherry Coke fresh from the fountain. The little boy spreads his cards out over
the top of the green marble surface, then runs his fingers along the
gold-colored streaks in the marble while he searches for the prized card.

The stools at the fountain fill up quickly with thirsty patrons, and the rest
of the store becomes crowded with teenagers looking at make-up, or gossiping
about the day's events at school.

Scenes like this one were common in Beulah for almost 50 years while the Beulah
Drug Store fountain was a part of the town. The fountain provided a wide
variety of beverages and ice cream treats, all at a reasonable price. There
were all flavors of Cokes, including cherry, lemon, chocolate and lime; ice
cream sodas; sundaes of all flavors; phosphates, made from syrup, soda water
and phosphoric acid which resulted in a somewhat sour but delicious
fruit-tasting beverage; and of course, the always popular "mud," for which the
Beulah soda fountain was well known. There wasn't a better place around to
enjoy a soft drink or an ice cream treat.

The fountain goes back a long way into Beulah's past, back to at least 1929.
That's when Ted Herman bought the Beulah Drug Store from Dan Hall, who later
moved to Bismarck and opened another store. The drug store was just a frame
building then, and Herman set about building a new store. He moved the Hall
building off the foundation and onto the street, doing business from it while
the present building was constructed.

Ted Herman's son Jerome, who ran the business for 22 years after his father
until he sold it to Dave Just in 1979, says he isn't sure if there was a
fountain in Hall's old building, but there was one in his father's store from
the beginning. The same fountain did not grace the Beulah Drug all those years,
but the last one had quite a history to it.

"We bought that fountain from Finney Drug," says Jerome Herman, "When they had
the back bar in their store. When we sold it in 1978, it was purchased by Pop's
Ice Cream Shop in Bismarck (located at the Gateway Mall). And when they went
out of business a few years ago it was sold to somebody from South Dakota."

Herman remembers that once when the drug inspector was making his rounds, he
remarked that the Beulah fountain was one of the few left in the state in the
late 1970's.

But the fountain seemed to be in constant need of repair. Herman says he
considered buying a new one, but when he was quoted a price of $15-20,000, he
quickly changed his mind.

The removal of the fountain in 1978 was part of a remodeling project and also a
sign of the times, for modern trends in merchandising required the space that
fountain took up, and the fountain prices did not seem to adequately pay for
its upkeep.

        The Gambles Store presented a float for Beulah's 50th anniversary
        celebration, with Herman Hauff and daughters Mary and Janice.

At one time, there were also booths in the store with the fountain, but they
had also been removed to make way for inventory.

One of the more well-known concoctions from the Beulah soda fountain was
something called a "mud." Just what was a mud?

"Well, it was a mixture of vanilla ice cream and chocolate syrup with
marshmallow cream, and lots of peanuts," said Herman. "It was served in a glass
with a long-handled spoon, and it was always mixed up to a soupy consistency."

Like the fountain from which it was served, the mud also had a history.

"When my dad graduated from NDSU in 1927," said Herman, "he worked at a soda
fountain in St. Paul that served something like our mud, and when he came back
to Beulah, he kept the concoction and served it at his fountain too."

In the early years of the fountain's existence, the muds were prepared in two
sizes, according to Herman. The small ones were 10 cents and the larger ones
were 25 cents, and they were always served within a cherry on top. In later
years, the cherry was omitted and only one size mud was prepared for a price of
50 cents

Never mind the calories, and who cares about the ingredients? The muds at the
Beulah Drug Store were well-known throughout the area, and travelers from other
states who once lived in Beulah still ask where they can find a mud when they
visit the city.

Herman says he isn't sure how the name came to be used for the ice cream
mixture, but he speculates that the combination of chocolate and ice cream
mixed together just naturally looked like the mud children use for their pies,
so the name stuck.

One can only wonder about the number of gallons of ice cream and soft drinks
consumed at the Beulah Drug fountain. One thing is for certain, the sweet
memories of the friends, fun and calories at the green marble fountain will be
a part of Beulah's history for a long, long time.

Dr. Artur Ewert--Beulah's medical institution

Go downtown for coffee one morning and ask any of the oldtimers there about
doctors.

Chances are you'll hear many, many stories about one man--Dr. Artur Ewert.
Ewert, with his unmistakable accent and way of speaking, tended the ills,
delivered the babies and cared for the injured of Beulah for two decades,
during an era when finding a rural family physician became as difficult as
striking gold.

Ewert was an immigrant to the United States, having been born Jan. 11, 1911 in a
part of Poland occupied by Russia. Most folks will recognize the proximity of
that date to the beginning of the First World War, and will have some clue as
to the kind of childhood Ewert had in Poland.

Those who have never had to flee their homes in the dead of night because an
enemy army is marching and destroying as they go cannot begin to understand the
gut-wrenching fear experienced by those whose homelands were ravaged by the war.

But Ewert knew, and he understood.

"When you are very young you don't realize how bad things really are, you just
accept them. When I became older I knew things were very bad. Life was not easy
in those days," Ewert said.

War and strife followed Ewert through much of his life. His home town, formerly
Zdunska-Wola had become Kalisz, and he was attending grade school there when
the Germans decided to make an example of the city. When they were finished,
only four houses in 10 were left standing. The young Ewert fled with his family
to Konin.

After WWI the family returned to Kalisz and Ewert finished his basic schooling
in 1930. He remembered those years in Poland as "very rough." His country was
never really at peace; turmoil always seethed just beneath the surface.

        In 1967, Beulah's swimming pool was still new Here Bruce, Randy and
        Paulette Winkler take a dip in the baby pool. In the background now
        are many more houses and to the left the Legion baseball field.

Ewert spent a year in the military and then entered the University of Poznan,
receiving his medical degree in 1937.

That event, too, was near the outbreak of a war, this time WW II, and Ewert was
working at a hospital in Lodz in 1939 when full-fledged war ripped through a
still-recovering Europe.

During the German occupation Ewert was made a prisoner of war. He was given the
choice of becoming a German citizen or going to a labor camp.

His choice led to his being drafted in 1942 into the German Army. The next few
years he spent on the infamous Eastern Front in Russia, until 1945 when he was
taken by the Russian Army and again made a prisoner of war.

No one who has been through such times likes to talk about them in detail, and
Ewert was no exception. He was married in 1941 and he and his wife, Louise,
eventually had five children. After the war he picked up his medical practice
and carried it on in Germany until 1956.

In September 1956 he arrived in Goodrich, N.D., brought to America under the
sponsorship of the town's Baptist church.

Goodrich proved not to be large enough to support a physician, so Ewert went to
Bismarck in 1957. At the time he spoke no English, though he could understand
most of what was said to him in that language. By 1959, he spoke and wrote
English and passed the required medical boards for a private practice in North
Dakota.

Ewert came to Beulah in 1960 but that didn't lead to a life of ease for him. As
the community's and rural area's physician, he had his work cut out for him,
though times were considerably easier than they had been in Europe.

Ewert is fondly remembered by many who knew him and who were his patients. He
has been described as a bit rough around the edges and lacking in an
American-style bedside manner - which is not surprising. He tended to order his
patients around and could become impatient when they didn't follow the
treatment he prescribed for them. He didn't coddle his patients and didn't
countenance chronic complainers.

Ewert was very good with older people, it's said, and was quick and accurate
with a diagnosis; if he wasn't sure about something, he would refer a patient
to a specialist without hesitation; and most times his own diagnosis was
correct.

Though he hadn't much patience with complainers, Ewert not only made house calls
but became upset if, for example, parents kept a sick child overnight rather
than calling him, even if it was three a.m.

That kind of service and dedication to his patients earned him loyalty, respect,
affection and admiration, along with the often-spoken compliment that he had "a
heart of gold." Ewert had wanted to specialize in surgery early in his career
but circumstances - including the wars that engulfed him - didn't allow him to
fulfill that dream.

On his pending retirement in 1979, Ewert commented, "I have not had much time in
my life to spend with my family. A good 10 years of it I never saw my wife. From
1942-45 I saw my wife maybe 20 days per year.

"Life was hard, but it was not all bread, we had potatoes too. Yes, those years
were hard times, but they are ancient times now. It seems like a long, bad
dream. For 10 years after the war I had many bad dreams, but that is over now.

"This country has been good to me," Ewert continued. "Beulah has been good to
me. These have been the best years of my life; I have been very happy here. It
has been wonderful not to have fear. It has been wonderful to have enough to
eat. When people here were without sugar, during the war, we were without homes.

"But now I just want to live a quiet life, do a little gardening, go fishing
and be with my family. My practice has always been first, now I want it to be
my family. They have been shortchanged," Ewert said.

His planned retirement didn't work out quite the way he expected. Ewert expected
to sell his practice to Dr. Habi Niamatali, brother to Hazen's former Dr.
Effideen Ameerally, when he came to the area under the sponsorship of Hazen
Memorial Hospital and the Beulah Chamber of Commerce. But at the last minute
Niamatali declined to buy the practice and settled elsewhere, and Ewert again
hung out his shingle.

That didn't last long, according to daughter Karen (Mrs. John Richter, Hazen),
and in December, 1979, after practicing for 19 years in Beulah, Ewert retired
for keeps.

He now lives in Lynden, Wash. and most of his traveling has involved coming
back to North Dakota to visit family. Of the five children, three still live in
the state: Karen, Heidi (Mrs. Maurice Borud), in Fargo and Angelika (Mrs.
Robert Bauste), Grand Forks. Ingrid (Mrs. Harold Carpenter) lives in Cottage
Grove, Minn.; and son Gerd, married to the former Faye Keogh of Beulah, lives
in Berkeley, Calif.

Doctors come and doctors go, and Beulah has seen its share of them since Ewert
left. But not a one will bring a twinkle to the eye and a smile to the face of
one who knew him and says, with a wide grin, "Ah, yes, Doc Ewert! He was
something!" before launching into yet another tale of the town's long-standing
physician.

        St. Benedict's Catholic Church was one of several rural churches of
        different denominations which eventually saw their congregations
        absorbed by larger churches in Beulah.

Orman's Reely Ready Lures

No one actually knows if he had an uncanny affinity for the waterborne species
or if he had a little divine help, as one Beulah Beacon editorial credited him
with.

But many Beulah residents will remember Orman's Lures and the Rev. A. O. Orman
who created, sold and regularly limited out with them.

Orman was a small man with a deeply tanned face, creases brought on by the
development of character and years in the sun searching for fish, and he peered
at the world through glasses.

Orman was a Congregational Church pastor in Beulah for a number of years, and
if a pastor can be said to have an avocation, his was fishing. By reputation he
was the best; by stringer count, that was an accurate reputation. Any spare
moments he had he spent fishing, most often at Beulah Bay which he considered a
prime spot for finny fun.

Orman had long enjoyed making his own lures, and sold his first one in 1956.

He and his wife, who was just as avid a fisherman as the reverend, hand-made
their lures, which were developed specifically to hook whopper walleyes and
pike in the chilly Lake Sakakawea waters. They opened up a business late in
1969 and several months later Orman was center stage in North Dakota Outdoors
with an article advocating his favorite pastime in his favorite spot.

Fishing in Beulah Bay, he said, was unsurpassed. In the fall of '69 he, his
wife and some friends took more than 400 walleyes, the largest topping out at
nine pounds.

Orman was scientific about his search for the whoppers. You have to have a
boat, he said, and you have to get around the fact that trolling motors can't
troll slowly enough. So you feed out line constantly and troll deeper. Fish off
rocky points, about a hundred feet from shore, he said.

Walleyes prefer live minnows over anything, he went on, and Orman preferred to
use the Pearly Flash and the Pike Special, both of which he had developed and
sold under his Orman Reely Ready Lures label.

Oh yes - and if there's a northwest wind, forget Beulah Bay. The fish go
someplace else. A south wind is okay, though.

Following his own advice, Orman's successes continued right along the top of the
line. In 1970, fishing with fellow clergyman Rev. Neubert, he hauled in a 9.5
pound walleye, this time on Orman's Beulah Spin Blitz. Later that year his wife
won a fishing derby with a 9-pound, 13-ounce walleye caught while trolling with
the Orman Pike Special, loaded with a yummy minnow.

By 1975 Orman was wanting to slow down a bit, and poor health forced him to list
Orman Reely Ready Lures for sale. By that time the lure business had grown to
such an extent that he had $18,000 worth of merchandise in his
going-out-of-business sale, served 500 dealers, employed three or four workers,
and made more than 40 types of spinners and rigs.

And he hoped to see the business go to a local buyer. Not bad for a guy who
started out with a hobby.

He had semi-retired by 1981 and moved to Hazen, and mostly fished the Garrison
Dam tailrace by then, still limiting out nearly every day.

Orman had a unique formula for catching fish, but it seemed to work for him.
Maybe fishermen today should try it as well.

"Observe other fishermen," he would smile. "Have a lot of faith - and forget
the beer!"

Pony Express Ride

In Beulah's fiftieth year, a Pony Express was run from Killdeer to Beulah and a
special anniversary stamp was used on the mail.

During Beulah's jubilee year, a similar Pony Express was planned and the special
anniversary stamp will again be used, with the year changed from 1964 to 1989.
MKM stands for Mandan-Killdeer Mountain, the original mail route through the
area.

Energy impact infuses new life

Energy impact. Those two words, and all they implied, were to change Beulah and
its people forever as energy industry development more than dominated events in
the Beulah area from the early 1970s on.

The 1960s in Beulah faded out as they did in the rest of the country, blending
imperceptibly into the 1970s. Beulah's 1969 city budget was $67,000; and its
expenditures fell $22,000 short of that. By 1982, that figure had risen to
$400,000 and by 1985 the budget was more than $1 million.

Letters printed in the newly named Beulah Beacon, which had replaced the
Independent, indicated that the greatest resource drain the community has ever
dealt with, including the impact years, was already occurring: Growing numbers
of former Beulah residents were writing their hometown paper with addresses
like Lodi and Costa Mesa, CA, Tempe, AZ, Cheyenne, WY, and other points west,
where the employment outlook was brighter (and often, so was the weather).

Beulah was warning its youth about the dangers of drugs in those days, but
police indicated there was no real drug traffic in town. That was another thing
that would change with impact, as the police chief in 1979 called Beulah "a
small town with big-city problems."

Special assessments were unpopular even in 1970, as the city council considered
a $60,000 street project several years before the massive development and
street and sewer projects necessitated by energy impact. In the early '80S,
when specials projects commonly were hundreds of thousands of dollars and the
city had taken on $2 million worth of projects, that number would have been a
relief.

All around were signs that major changes were coming. The Milton Young plant
opened at Center, utilizing experimental furnace technology and employing 260
people. Consol at Stanton was behind on reclamation, and there was a story in
the Wall Street Journal referring to the "coal rush" in the area, with
particular reference to the "ugly spoil piles" left by mining companies.

Yet Beulah was called, more than once, "a doomed town. The "Help Wanted" section
in the classified ads held one listing. Many businesses opened and closed in
the time it took to paint the signs (though a number of then-new ones still
thrive). The 1970 census showed Beulah as the county's largest town, having
gained 26 people over the decade with a population of 1,344, though the
county's population was down 9.3 percent.

The year 1971 saw a bitter fight waged over relocating the county seat to
Beulah--and lost, as Stanton rallied the votes to retain that honor. Residents
listed the biggest source of pollution as power plants and said they should be
fitted with air filters - and a few years later saw those very sources in their
backyards.

The first bubbles of energy development began to surface in 1972 as, in April,
lignite was mentioned as a solution for the energy crisis which gripped the
nation. "It is obvious domestic synthetic gas will be needed by the end of the
decade to supplement our dwindling gas reserve," stated the paper. Gas plants
and much larger-scale coal mining were proposed, and industry-environmentalist
conflicts were predicted.

Early in 1973 energy development began to awaken. A gasification plant near
Beulah was first mentioned when Michigan-Wisconsin Pipeline Co. proposed to
take water from Lake Sakakawea to supply three plants--near Beulah, Halliday
and Center - all to be in production by 1980.

That caused a wave of excitement. Talk buzzed about the 12,000 people such
development would bring to the area, and entirely new self-contained towns were
planned near the plants to accommodate them. By 1996, 36 gasification plants
were envisioned. North American Coal promised 1.5 billion tons of its coal
reserves to Michigan-Wisconsin, which residents were soon calling "Mich-Wish"
with familiar ease.

At the same time, a moratorium on strip-mining was being urged until reclamation
was proved effective, as that science was still in a very imperfect infancy.
The stage was set for conflict, and conflict came almost immediately.

Environmentalists argued that even though the plant was projected to employ
1,050 people with an annual payroll of $12 million, and a certain suture for
the bleeding away of Beulah's young people, that wasn't enough. They wanted
certainties in reclamation, guarantees about groundwater and air quality, and
assurances that agriculture would not be adversely affected--guarantees that
simply could not be given. The Sierra Club filed suit against the federal
government to halt coal development in North Dakota. It was about this time
that the word "impact" changed from a noun to a verb - a very active verb.
Mich-Wish promised continual air, water, land and noise monitoring. No one
anticipated odor monitoring, which has turned out to be the gas plant's largest
local drawback and has cost it millions in attempts to reduce the odors to an
acceptable level.

Then-mayor Wilmer Wiedrich was quoted as saying, "Our main industry is
agriculture, but all this industry coming will change our way of life." That
set the tone for the city council, and a delegation visited ABM boom towns in
the state to see how they had coped, realizing housing would be strained and it
would be difficult to maintain orderly growth.

The county became an impact laboratory as questions flew: How will industry be
taxed? How big will it be? How much gas will it produce? How many and what kinds
of problems will there be? Where will the farmers live when massive
strip-mining is on their land? Who will protect the land? How will development
affect the area lifestyle?

Schools began to worry about the number of students they could absorb as
enrollments began to grow: What would it be like with a large influx?

The burning question was: Who is going to pay?

People went to meetings, hearings and more meetings about these and other
concerns and industry representatives made promise after promise, many of which
were not kept. "I think I know how the American Indian felt when the white man
came," said one disgruntled resident.

Early in 1974 MDU planned a two-unit Coyote Station, the first to be on-line by
1981, and a mood of optimism prevailed as everyone prepared to capitalize on
coal development. Jobs for area youth were brightly envisioned, while other
small towns checked their steadily dropping blood pressure as their young
people moved away.

        An aerial photograph of Beulah in the early impact days shows a great
        deal of difference from the quiet village of 60 years ago.

Progress on the gas plant moved at a snail's pace, stumbling over public
opinion, environmentalist concerns and rampant national inflation, which hiked
construction estimates. Electrical generation was a sure bet but gasification
faced serious doubts; its biggest detriment was its connection to current
political policy - energy self-sufficiency in a time of rapidly escalating
imported oil prices. Though the federal government wanted the experimental
plant built, it wasn't overly anxious to make a long-term commitment to the
plant, and financing troubles over the next 12 years reflected that ambivalence
on the part of the then-new Department of Energy toward its illegitimate child.

The big surprise of 1974 was an agreement between Mich-Wish and Basin Electric
to build side-by-side plants at the gasification site.

Cattle prices dropped to an unbelievable low, but farmers were used to dealing
with "boom and bust" cycles in the agricultural economy and knew to diversify
and look ahead to stay financially healthy. New business came to Beulah and old
ones expanded, the county grew and the outlook, if not the present, was bright.
Plans were made to insure growth was orderly, hoping to avoid in the city a
"boom" effect and its attendant "bust."

Beulah made the New York Times for the first time, but not the last, in 1974:
"Like a toy village that has somehow been cast, upright and intact, far out
upon a rolling sea ... it seems serenely afloat on a benign biotic storm of
wheat, oats, barley ... corn, hogs and cattle."

In 1975 miniskirts were all the rage in Beulah, as they are again today, but in
place of today's "heinies" and "scalped and sculpted" hairstyles were shaggy
remnants of the '60s hippies.

Though it delayed seeking construction permits because it didn't like the tax
outlook, ANG, now directing the gasification project, filed for permits, picked
up land options and applied for a federally guaranteed loan, calling that "the
most important factor" in getting gasification off the ground. While ANG
maneuvered unsuccessfully, MDU bought land to build Coyote Station.

Alphabet soup became the byword in 1976 with the symbols, ANG, ANR, FEMA, MCLA,
ERDA, MCTF, CI0, PSA and others (which came later) peppering newspaper pages
and people's speech. The Mercer County Landowners Association was formed to
protect the rights and interests of local landowners, and immediately
circulated a petition opposing rezoning ANG's land. While "generally in favor
of development, we haven't been treated fairly and honestly," they said. A
heated meeting was held in January during which resentments were aired:
Mistreatment during land acquisition negotiations was charged, loss of the 1,500
acres of prime farmland ANG had optioned would "seriously threaten the world
food supply," water contamination, acid rain, reclamation feasibility - all
these questions were raised, with MCLA leading the way. Only two Beulah
representatives spoke in favor of development to "give area youth a secure
future."

Fallout from that hearing affected MDU as it heard opposition to the previously
inoffensive Coyote, but it went ahead with its plans.

Beulah celebrated the Bicentennial in 1976 with old-time dressing and beard
contests, the Wally Kittler band and a demolition derby. The jobless rate was
down, always a reason for celebration, and Beulah's population was about
1,600, up 300 from 1970.

        Trimming up a cow to make its best presentation is an important part
        of winning at the county fair. Beulah Beacon photo.

Additions throughout town were being rezoned to allow for development and many
residents protested: "Go somewhere else and leave us alone!" This year saw the
first in battles which intensified as impact progressed until council meetings
regularly ran into the wee hours, often attended by large groups of citizens on
opposing sides of issues, each hoping its views would prevail.

A Soviet land manager came to see North American Coal Corporation's reclamation
and was impressed. Though they were still improving, reclamation techniques had
come a long way from planting trees on spoil piles. He hoped to use some of the
techniques back home in large Soviet strip-mining operations, but remarked the
Soviet Union has "no (coal development) opposition groups as you have here."

City hall had to hire extra help in 1976 to get out the large number of water
bills, which were still done by hand. A couple of years later the city bought a
computer but its capacity still wouldn't handle the billing. It wasn't until
1987 the water billing finally went successfully on-line, having had nearly as
long a "construction period'' as the gas plant.

        Traditional activities such as square dancing were still practiced,
        with some of the newer residents becoming involved along with the
        home folks. Beulah Beacon photo.

The third annual county fair was a big success, with 10,000 attendance and
Barbara Mandrell performing to an enthusiastic audience both at the fair and on
the Roxy Theatre's stage. That audience wasn't at all surprised when Mandrell
hit the big time a few years later.

Numerous boards, task forces and committees began during early impact years,
hoping to foster cooperation among factions in the county. An editorial was
skeptical: "Basically the (Mercer County) Task Force calls for the people and
governments in the county to work together. That would be a first for the
county, which has a famous history of partisan bickering and drawing of
opposing lines. Our problem is that impact problems . . . will not honor lines
and will spill throughout the county." The various groups, for the most part,
couldn't even agree on the goals, let alone how to reach them.

The ups and downs of those who left

Dear Sir,

 We have many friends and relatives in Beulah, and I'm sure some would be
interested to know how the earthquake of Feb. 9, 1971, affected us.

 It was so fortunate for all of us in the Los Angeles area that it happened at
the early hour of 6 a.m. Our daughter, Karma was up getting ready for school
which starts at 7:30. So with the first jolt she came running into our bedroom.

 I jumped out of bed and the two of us ran though the hallway swaying side to
side, and after we turned the gas off (central floor heater) we stood in the
doorway (safest place, they claim) and swayed side to side.

 It was a strange feeling - like when you lose your equilibrium and you're sort
of dizzy. It only lasts one minute, but it seems like eternity when the ground
and floor under you are not stable and secure. Leo remained in bed!

 Our swag lamp was swinging like a pendulum; our book shelves waltzed back and
forth; the house creaked; and   only one knick-knack flew down. So we had no
damage in our home, and so we were much more fortunate than those who live at
Sylmar and the San Fernando Valley (25-30 miles north of us). Of course, Los
Angeles County extends all of this distance so other than a few miles of a
mountain pass It is a mass of buildings and homes which were damaged greatly.

 When Leo arrived at his store there was Jam, whiskey, baby food mayonnaise,
salad oil, vinegar, etc., six inches thick on the floor. The floor was stained
from grape juice, etc., and was slippery and sticky and so they couldn't open
until 11 a.m.

 They shoveled glass and debris for four hours. It is interesting now to hear
the reactions and panic of individuals, but our hearts ached for the 64
individuals who lost their lives and their families who must bear the memories
of the disaster.

 We have been out here since 1956 and this is the first one I have felt. We
have felt a couple hundred murmurs or aftershocks since that, and I think we
are more alert and aware of these smaller ones now.

 There has been an "Exodus" from California within this last month, but this is
due to the large layoffs in the aircraft industry rather than earthquake fears.

 Of course, Leo is fortunate to be in his type of business because people
always need to eat - and it is a cash business out here.

 It was quite a coincidence that when your paper was offering the opportunity
for people to send in new name suggestions, I had picked (the same name as the
contest winner).... You are doing a fine job. Keep up the good work.

With best wishes,
Leo, Joan and Karma Huber

The Mercer County Fair

What could be more representative of rural North Dakota than a county fair,
with its FFA and 4-H exhibits, sticky-faced tots wide-eyed with wonder at
carnival rides, grannies visiting and exclaiming over the winning quilts and
cool shady spots for the less adventurous?

And Beulah's offering for the Mercer County Fair held each summer is an
extraordinary example of the kind of fun expected of county fairs, involving
cooperation among community, farm and industry people throughout the county.

The fair--or a fair - was first mentioned in 1915 at a Beulah Commercial Club
meeting, which took it on as a project. A Fair Association was formed and
organized the event from 1916-22, when the reorganized Commercial Club again
took it over. A four-man fair board was elected (L.G. Rose, George Slowey, M.P.
Moore, and L.F. Temme).

The fairgrounds were located south of the railroad tracks, west of 1st Ave. W.

Farm families came to town for the whole show each fall, and one businessman
recalled a high wooden fence surrounding the grounds. Naturally, where there is
a fence, there are knotholes, and where there are knotholes, there is a
"knothole gang." So it was with the county fair.

        Standing: Donna Buchmann, Delton Herman, Ron Gunsch, Mike Connoly,
        Mike Wiedrich, Darold Benz, Ray Binder. Sitting: Amy Sorlien, Tom
        Dallman, Cliff Moine, Carrie Hafner, Leland Erickson.

        The joint Beulah and Hazen Chamber of Commerce barbecue at the Mercer
        County Fair provides plenty of food and a good time to those enjoying
        the fair's entertainment. Beulah Beacon photo.

Under county agent G.C. Poe's supervision, farm boys could take part in the Farm
Boys Encampment at the fair, allowing them to see the fair and attend lectures.
A temporary encampment of Indians from the Ft. Berthold Indian Reservation
added to the fair, as they were permitted by the Indian Agency to attend the
fairs and rodeos on condition the town would provide them with provisions.

The roots of the Cowboys' Reunion Rodeo, a long-time and recently revived
highlight of early Beulah days, were in this Mercer County Fair. The fair board
sold its property and discontinued the fair in 1925.

There was a long dry spell of almost 50 years before a new generation of fair
lovers met to organize a new county fair on Jan. 30, 1974. This fair board,
appointed by the Mercer County commissioners, consisted of Bob Albers, Hazen;
Eugene Keller, Beulah; Tom Dallman, Zap; Werner Benfit, Zap (since deceased);
Leland Erickson, Beulah; Darold Benz, Beulah; and Allen Schmidt, county agent.
Others appointed at the organizational meeting were Delton Herman of Golden
Valley and Jim Cook and Albert Kilber, both of Hazen.

        Bands are an important part of any parade, and here Beulah's high
        school band does its part to enliven the festivities. Beulah Beacon
        photo.

Benz was elected president of the Mercer County Fair Association, and all the
original members have been staunch fair supporters throughout the years.

The fair's purpose is to encourage and promote better and more intensive
farming, better bred and more profitable livestock, and advancement of all
branches of industry, as well as cultivating appreciation of fine arts and
crafts and providing good, wholesome entertainment for all ages.

Over the years a well-known entertainer has been a primary goal of the fair
board. Some who have appeared at the county fair include LeRoy Van Dyke, Tommy
Overstreet/Connie Van Dyke, Barbara Mandrell, Freddie Hart, Hank Thompson/Jana
Jae, Del Reeves, Bonnie Nelson, Connie Cato, Tommy Cash, Nat Stuckey, Whiskey
River, Ark Valley Boys and, in 1987, the Moe Bandy Show.

The fair is held the last full weekend in August and has had many activities
involving all of Mercer County. The Beulah and Hazen Chambers of Commerce
cooperate annually to provide a barbecue on the grounds. The beer garden is
manned by the various county fire departments.

The Mercer County Fair has been known for its exceptional livestock and
horticulture exhibits throughout the years, and "people activities" have
included wrestling, horseshoe tournaments, a road run, two excellent parades,
square dancing, teen dances and concerts, gospel shows, team roping, tractor
pulls, ATV races, bingo, children's activities and Beulah's own Showdeo, a
rodeo just for kids up through high school age.

Current fair board members include officers Leland Erickson, Beulah; Carrie
Hafner, Beulah; Tom Dallman, Zap; county agent Cliff Moine; and directors
Delton Herman, Mike Connolly, Darold Benz, Ray Binder, John Klein, Joe
McLaughlin, Donna Buchmann, Ron Gunsch and Mike Wiedrich. It's easy to see
there's been plenty of continuity on that board throughout the years.

Other past fair board members have been Floyd Unruh, Zap; Marvin Hafner, Beulah;
Howard Bohrer, Stanton; Harvey Wehri, Hebron; Lucille Lauf, Stanton; and Gerald
Weisenberger, Golden Valley. Benz served a five-year term as president,
followed by Klein with five years, and Erickson is currently president.

Land for the fairgrounds, adjacent to Beulah's Civic Center, was purchased from
Jim and Joan Schumaier. Much of the property in use during the fair is city
property.

The Mercer County Fair has a traditionally high attendance, with about 15,000
showing up. Many of those come all three days.

The fair involves many community people in chairing and organizing the different
events and divisions. The Beulah Chamber is a strong supporter and, without its
continued help, the fair would likely not be able to operate. Chamber members
are usually in charge of helping prepare the grounds, handling ticket sales,
parades, assisting with the barbecue, cleanup after the fair and financial help
in various areas.

When the fair began, a drive was made to collect funds from various
organizations, businesses and individuals. The original building, which today
serves as the dairy barn, was built with these donations. Today's sheep barn
was built with a $1,000 donation from Friedebert Benz, matched by the fair
board. A hog barn has been added, the 40xlOO Mac McKenzie building, the beer
garden building and a 60xlOO building used as the beef barn. The city's 60x120
public works building and 100x100 civic center are also used.

        Working against the clock, a goat-tying competitor wraps her goat's
        feet with lightning speed at the high school rodeo held in Beulah.
        Beulah Beacon photo.

The county fair is "the" event in the county during August, and most county
residents attend the fair as well as working to insure its success.

The Beulah Eagles Aerie #3728, through its gaming funds distributions, has been
a huge financial help to the fair by sponsoring much of the entertainment, and
the county commissioners have allotted part of their annual budget towards the
premiums awarded to fair exhibit winners.

Stand up and cheer

It is tradition.

"GOOD EVENING, LADIES AND GENTLEMEN . WELCOME TO THE BEULAH MINERS-HAZEN BISON
BASKETBALL GAME!" The vibrant voice of the announcer signals the beginning of
an event that is as much a part of the Beulah-Hazen area as fleischkuechle and
coal mining.

It is a time to renew once again the spirit of friendly enemies and kindle the
flames of a possible victory against the one team that each would like to
defeat more than any other it will play during the season. It is a rivalry that
has been going on for years and will continue for many more.

It is tradition.

        Time out: Lunch is a good time for a nap in the sun for many energy
        construction workers, and a hard hat makes good shade. Beulah Beacon
        photo.

There are those who say the rivalry is a negative thing, and that it is too bad
that the towns cannot get along better, since they are only 10 miles apart.
There are those who say they wish the games between the two towns were not as
intense as they are. They wonder: When did it all start?

But there are many more who understand the nature of the feelings for the
familiar rivalry that never fails to bring the tingle of excitement so
well-known to the sports fan. For both teams, it is a little like growing up
with an older brother who criticized everything you did. He had a girlfriend
before you did and a car before you were old enough, and you just lived for the
day when you'd be able to beat him at anything. To beat someone else would be
fun, too, but it just wouldn't be the same. And when all is said and done, the
bond of being brothers will still remain.

The week before this game has been a time of nervous anticipation for players
and fans alike. There have been pep rallies in both schools and the area
newspapers carried projections of the expected outcome and possible standout
athletes. The night of the game finds both sides of the spacious gymnasium
packed with fans, with Hazen green on one side and Beulah blue on the other,
facing each other across the arena like old adversaries.

The athletes are nervous, knowing that their every move will be analyzed around
the coffee tables of the local restaurants for weeks to come. A sense of
excitement is everywhere, from the musicians in the band to the small children
running in the aisles. The smell of popcorn fills the air and neighbor greets
neighbor with a spirit of friendly antagonism.

The opening buzzer jars the waiting athletes into action, and the game begins.
Every fan in the crowds has his own idea about how the games should be coached
and played and most of them are not shy with their opinions.

        Bidders at the livestock auction have to be on their toes, or they
        can get a bit of ribbing. Beulah Beacon photo.

Even during the years when neither team has been able to produce a winning
season, they have played well in this game, and it will be a close one. Tonight
they will stretch to the limits of their prowess to confront their opponent of
so many years.

As the game progresses, the tension mounts and the cheers of "M-l-N-E-R-S,
Miners, the best!" from one side are greeted with "H-A-Z-E-N, B-l-S-O-N!" from
the other.

The score is close and the cheering is frantic in the last minutes of play. The
young athlete with the ball goes inside, striving for the points that would
give his team the victory. The ball goes up, the buzzer sounds . . . and
another Beulah-Hazen game is history.

Never has the victory been sweeter, nor the defeat more stinging. There are
"high fives" on one side of the arena, and tears on the other. "Just wait 'til
next year," say the vanquished, "Just wait 'til football. We'll beat you then!"

"We're number one!" shout the victors. "We're number one!" Never mind that the
district tournament is still many weeks away and there remains a host of tough
teams to play before then.

To defeat this team means to be "number one." In the end, it is not the numbers
on the scoreboard that are the important part. It is the excitement of the play
and the nature of the enemy. It is knowing that this game is as important to
them as it is to you, and knowing that creates a bond of sorts, a bond that can
be shared with no other team.

        The sign most often seen around town during the early and middle impact
        years, "building permit" capsulizes the work of the decade. Beulah
        Beacon photo.

Many a Beulah or Hazen resident who once wore the blue or green jersey
remembers the games between the two towns with a certain nostalgia, long after
the glory days of high school athletics are gone. They will remember and they
will say, "That was the year we beat Hazen," or, "That was the year we beat
Beulah."

And, for the fans who file out of the gymnasium dejected with their loss, there
is always the realization that if big brother was too strong to defeat this
year, there is always "next year" to wait for.

It is tradition.

The last full-blooded Mandan

Mattie Grinnell was 108 years old and to the Three Tribes of Ft. Berthold she
was a treasure.

In August, 1975, when the chokecherries turned, she would have added one more
year to her life, but this was January and word was that Mattie wasn't feeling
as well as she might. The People were waiting and hoping that the last
full-blooded Mandan would see the green grass. But it wasn't to be, and Mattie
retired from conversation that evening to lie down.

That night she traveled quietly from this life and the woman who had become
living legend to The People passed into the realm of history.

Mattie was buried Jan. 9, 1975, on a barren prairie hill a few hundred yards
from the log house in which she had lived so many years on the Ft. Berthold
reservation. Services at the Twin Buttes church and cemetery were brief as the
year's first blizzard bore down on the country.

        Mattie Grinnell, the last living full-blooded Mandan Indian, clung to
        the old ways until her death at 108. Photo courtesy of Vern Erickson.

The service at Twin Buttes School was simple for a woman who had known a her
simple existence, with simple blanket-draped casket surrounded by the flags of
her country.

Mattie was known for her kindness and benevolence, fitting for a lady who always
had a hot meal or good word for a traveler or visitor. The wisdom of her years
was passed on to many, both white and Indian, who asked her advice on their
troubles.

Vern Erickson, a Bismarck artist, capsulized Mattie's essence. On assignment for
North Dakota Horizons he looked at Mattie and said, "What character. Never have
I seen such character as there is in the lines of that face."

Character. Yes. Developed and strengthened with the struggles of almost 11
decades on this earth, a period in time when her people made the greatest
transition of any people, ever. She lived it, survived it and became great by
it.

The aged Indian woman had other claims to fame. In 1971, at 104, she was granted
a Civil War widow's pension by a special Act of Congress. Three years earlier,
at 101, she had taken part in the Poor People's March on Washington.

A proud woman, whose noble visage was lined and creased with the passing of her
many years, Mattie remained physically active and mentally alert well beyond her
100th year, and those who traveled to her clay-covered log home south of Ft.
Berthold Reservation gained from her a priceless record of a way of life long
vanished from the wide Dakota plains.

Mattie was unsure of her birth date, but remembered she was born in Like-A-
Fishhook Village when the chokecherries were ripe. That village was on the
Missouri River some 20 miles south of White Earth. Her birth was later
determined, from school records, to have been in August, 1966, and the family,
she said, chose Aug. 25 as her birthday.

Her father, Bad Bull, was an Army scout, and her mother was Lead Woman. Mattie
was given the name Many Roads, she said, from the numerous buffalo trails near
her birthplace.

She attended school at Ft. Berthold four years and a teacher there named her
Mattie.

Her father died when she was 12. She recalled that the government gave them oxen
to plow their gardens.

"It was much different then, so much better," she once said. Mattie had seen the
Indian people moved from the rich Missouri River bottomlands to the hard high
country with the advent of the Garrison Dam, whose waters now cover much of the
prime reservation land along the Missouri, including whole towns, churches and
schools.

Mattie recalled making buffalo hunting trips with tribal parties to the
Badlands and the Black Hills. Feeding the hunting parties was no problem, for
there was buffalo and deer meat, corn and chokecherries and plums. The women
made corn balls for the hunters.

"We ground the corn, mixed it with berry juice and tallow and formed it into
balls. Each man took two, giving him the strength he needed for the day's
hunt," she recalled.

Mattie was the only person left in Twin Buttes who could prepare and sun-dry
beef as it was done in the "old days" and, at 102, she was still preparing corn
balls and dried beef for tribal ceremonies. As a young girl she knew all the
chiefs of the tribes and learned the religious ceremonies and dances. She
recalled Indian legends with remarkable clarity.

"I still use Indian medicine. That's why I am over 100 years old," she once
said.

When she was 18, she married a German, John Nagel, who was a Civil War veteran,
and they lived in a two-room log cabin on the reservation until he died in
1904. In 1907 she married Charles Grinnell. That marriage ended in 1935 when
she was left with four children from her first marriage and three from the
second.

In 1969 her only income was a $45 monthly Social Security payment. Friends urged
her to apply for a pension as the widow of a Civil War veteran. Because of her
second marriage, she was declared ineligible, but through the efforts of Sen.
Milton R. Young, Congress changed the law, enabling her to receive the payments.

In her later years, Mattie lived with her son, John Nagel Jr., and at her death
she was living with a daughter, Mrs. Alex Fournier, at Twin Buttes.

Mattie didn't live to see the green grass or the chokecherries turn black that
year. She died before the killing blizzard of 1975.

She died quietly, the last full-blooded Mandan Indian, her greatest honor. She
had become a legend in her own time, an irreplaceable cultural treasure that
her people will not see again.

        Despite the activity swirling around the town and the county residents
        still had plenty of time for a favorite activity - fishing Beulah
        Beacon photo.

        Talk of construction at the plants spurred construction in town to
        hold all the workers expected to move into the area. Here, Sun Valley
        Court gets its start. Beulah Beacon photo.
