        The contrast between nature and enormous power plants became a point
        of contention, both visually and environmentally during the years of
        heaviest construction. Beulah Beacon photo.

Good planning pays off for Beulah

The highlight of 1977 for most Beulah residents had nothing to do with energy,
unless it was of the "high" variety, as local beauty Kathy Powers - definitely
a high-energy girl - won the Miss North Dakota title and carried Beulah's name
proudly to the Miss America contest. Beulah, in turn, proudly boasted about
Kathy.

The energy focus shifted to Coyote as construction started on that facility. By
November the famous "bubble," a 94,000 square-foot air-supported plastic
structure under which construction could continue in adverse weather, was up
and residents were craning their necks on the way by for a look at the curious
structure. A Hazen man, Bob Burkhardsmeier, became the first Coyote fatality
when he was crushed by a bulldozer. The influx of workers led to a housing
shortage which resulted in soaring rents, only one problem a community in
transition had to deal with.

On the lighthearted side, the first and apparently only Miz Gorgeous contest
was held in 1977, with a statuesque beauty named Obscene Francene winning top
honors in the "beauty" contest. Identities are a mystery today; no one seems to
know - or would admit - who these elaborately dressed "women" were!

        Working inside an air-conditioned cab isn't like the tractors of the
        old days, but It's still hard and dusty work. Beulah Beacon photo.

A dispute between ANG and Joe and Emma Walker began over the Walkers' 24 acres,
which sat on some property ANG needed to acquire but the Walkers didn't want to
sell. It wasn't until two years later that the county commission forced a
settlement, though Basin Electric had by then picked up the option. That
incident brought negative publicity to the gasification project, as it was
charged with harassment, coercion and other unflattering tactics by some
critics. A negative image was something the project didn't need if it was to
get off the ground.

Mercer County was first called a "guinea pig," referring to it as a "rural
conservation laboratory" and it was expected to be a model for impact
mitigation elsewhere. Yet county roads were considered inadequate for impact
needs, and there was no Coal Impact Office money for funding. Where could the
county turn? No answers were forthcoming; eventually the county was advised to
use its leverage in granting permits to insure industry did what needed to be
done - before the permits were granted.

Beulah Miner fans followed their boys frenetically all the way to the 1977
state Class B tournaments, where the Miners fell to Epping 50-54, losing their
shot but coming home no less the favorite to the home-town folks. The Greystone
Hotel, long ago an elegant establishment near the railroad depot, sought but
was denied a place on the National Historic Register. A few years later it was
a dilapidated rooming house for transient construction workers; and in 1986 it
went back to the bank in foreclosure.

In spite of all the razzmatazz surrounding the energy industry, businessmen in
1978 still named agriculture as the economy's number-one underpinning; industry
came in second. Farmers simply went about the business of being the best
farmers in the world without any fanfare, as they always had; an up-and-down
farm economy certainly wasn't any harder to get along with than the
rollercoaster ANG brought to town. Farmers were long used to dealing with the
peaks and valleys of economic cycles; that resiliency no doubt was a strong
factor in Beulah's weathering those years.

Citizens expressed displeasure with county regulatory bodies that year,
particularly the county planning and zoning commission. One of its functions
was to curtail "random sprawl" but it seemed that nearly every commercial
rezoning request that crossed its table was granted, without regard to whether
in-town land for the venture was available. That took tax revenue right out of
Beulah's (and other towns') pockets, besides being unsightly, and residents
didn't like the seeming inability of the board and its boss, the county
commission, to make a decision and stick to it. Beulah was annexing land north,
south and west to make room for the construction force coming in; some 650
Coyote workers and 600 AVS workers were in town and stretch marks were
beginning to show on the burgeoning belly of the town.

Time was running out for ANG to obtain its federal loan guarantee, and in June
it sought another route to finance its syn-fuels plant, which was still a
political hot potato. At the encouragement of the DOE, a five-partner
consortium was formed to build the plant and in July GPGA was added to the
alphabet soup as Great Plains Gasification Associates came into being.

        Taking lunch hour inside a pipe is as good a way as any to get out of
        the hot, blistering sun for a little while. Beulah Beacon photo.

Mayor Wilmer Wiedrich, 22-year city veteran, stepped down and mayor Darold Benz
stepped in. Shortly he and some council members went to Wheatland, WY, which
had experienced a similar energy boom. The results, along with North Dakota
ingenuity, led in 1983 to the Department of Energy sending a team to document
the area's response to impact. DOE was so impressed with the way Beulah handled
the situation that it planned to implement similar methods in other areas.

A trend began in the Coal Impact Office in 1979 that has continued, though for
different reasons; there were so many grant requests that year only one in three
could be funded. Needs became greater over the next four years, but funding was
never sufficient for the coal severance and conversion tax-supported office.
After 1983 funds dwindled more and more; with the DOE takeover at the gas plant
the office, by then called EIO, lost its coal conversion tax revenue, and
successive Legislatures raided the office for a beleaguered general fund as the
state as a whole experienced an economic downturn. Fewer and fewer grants could
be awarded, and more and more the question at grant awards hearings became: How
is this related to energy impact? Those who couldn't demonstrate a direct,
convincing connection were increasingly refused funding.

Basin Electric decided to go ahead with AVS I whether GPGA was involved or not
as it couldn't wait any longer; GPGA was looking at a delay of another year.
Later in the year GPGA expected to start construction as soon as President
Jimmy Carter signed a bill authorizing $25 million for the politically unloved
project, but it was still almost two years before any dirt was moved.

        The recreational vehicle courts were full as transient construction
        workers set up "home" for a while, then moved on when the job was done.
        Beulah Beacon photo.

        Traditional town promotions like Crazy Days went on, with more and
        more people attending to seek out the bargains on Main Street. Beulah
        Beacon photo.

Free kraut and wieners, an annual appreciative gesture for residents sponsored
by Beulah's Chamber of Commerce (formerly the Commercial Club), was in its 20th
year and saw more and more people savor its solid German fare each year. The
first Coal Bowl, a football face-off between arch-rivals Beulah and Hazen, was
held that fall. Beulah won, 6-0, and was awarded the Coal Bowl traveling
trophy--a large chunk of Beulah lignite mounted on a walnut base.

A bad year for shoppers and a terrible year for farmers, 1980 was missed by few.
Main Street in Beulah was the focus of attention, though that, too, was energy-
related; the street suffered a four-month upheaval as it was torn up to install
a new, larger storm sewer system. All summer Beulah wondered if it would
survive the dust, the mess, the inconvenience and, in the case of businessmen,
the loss of traffic. Many people refused to be inconvenienced and took their
paychecks elsewhere, adding further to the stack of Beulah dollars drained away
by larger towns.

Farmers saw their own share of dust, mess, inconvenience and economic hardship
as a drought forced cattlemen to take their wares to the sales ring. The
growing season was dry and hot, while the harvest brought spring's wet, cool
weather; the combination resulted in a harvest only half that of the previous
year.

County schools showed deficits in their budgets even though they had new energy
facilities which should have been contributing as many tax dollars as they were
young bodies for education. But the school couldn't collect taxes until the
facility was on-line; the problem was impact didn't have the courtesy to wait
until that happened.

In a nutshell, that was the basic difficulty faced throughout the impact years:
People needed the services before the money was available to provide them. By
the time the services became available, sometimes the people were gone. It
required a delicate hand to balance the needs of temporary residents against
future burdens on permanent ones, and Beulah's leaders provided it.

Still, Beulah's taxable sales in '80 were up $7 million over the previous year,
even with Main Street construction and unemployment up as AVS construction
slowed and GPGA still waited and hoped. In July, the county's population was
9,000--higher than it had been since the 1930s, when the Depression forced the
same hemorrhage of people the pre-energy days had seen.

        In 1979 Beulah's Prairie Plaza Shopping Center went up. In its heydey,
        it held six or eight stores and offices, plus a grocery store next
        door. Now, It's owned by New Life Assembly of God and no more business
        facilities are there. Beulah Beacon photo.

GPGA finally managed to pull off a $2.02 billion federal loan guarantee in
1981, but still was seeking funding. A survey taken showed nobody cared much,
as many replied they didn't know what ANG was. The question was: Are they
apathetic about development, or saturated with blow-by-blows of the
roller-coaster ride? GPGA was called on its promises to hire locals, as
residents felt most employees were hired from out of state. When hiring was
complete in 1983, 43 percent were native North Dakotans; but GPGA quickly
explained that 70 percent of the non-technical jobs went to locals, saying
they'd had no choice but to go out of state for the highly technical personnel.
Coyote went on-line in May but almost immediately the State Health Department
was concerned about pollution, as its scrubbers were temporarily bypassed
during start-up.

With a combined construction workforce of 2,100, cries were heard as the area
hollered for "up-front money, NOW." Roads needed work, infrastructures were
insufficient, and they couldn't be improved without dollars. Many expressed the
opinion that industry wasn't picking up its fair share, that the EIO structure
didn't work, and that state government was unresponsive to Coal Country's
needs. Businesses were closing, mainly due to high interest rates and
inflation. The extra workforce bodies meant longer and longer lines on the
highways mornings and evenings, shorter and shorter tempers and attendant needs
for law enforcement. Many were the tales of people forced off the road during
the early '80s by pickups charging three abreast down the highway in a race to
get home after a day's work.

        Visiting during Oktoberfest, another time for citywide fun, is a
        favorite pastime and one enjoyed by all. Beulah Beacon photo.

Some nude sunbathers caused a ruckus in June, as the newspaper jokingly reported
they were judged "a disturbance," necessitating action by the police force, fire
department, newspaper and anyone else who thought they could half-justifiably
check it out. They turned out to be Canadians, not local girls--and anyway,
Hazen had some streakers shortly afterward. It must have been too much sun.

The post office began to split its skin like the rest of Beulah as, in early
1982, all 900-plus boxes were rented at the main office and about 150 patrons
had to rely on general delivery or share a box. A branch station was later
installed at Prairie Plaza to take care of the overflow.

After a 12-year hiatus, the Cowboys' Reunion Rodeo, formerly a big attraction in
Beulah with its reputation as a rodeo town, was reinstated, though it hasn't
regained its former attendance. One worker remarked that while the interest was
there, there wasn't enough money to keep it going; now that there was plenty of
money, people didn't seem to have the interest.

        The revival of the Cowboys' Reunion Rodeo held an irony: There was
        more money to present it now, but not as much interest as in the old
        days. Beulah Beacon photo.

Kathryn Louise Power Miss North Dakota 1977

In the year 1977, billboards in the Beulah area proudly proclaimed "Welcome to
Beulah, the home of Miss North Dakota, Kathy Power." On June 12 of that year, a
22-year-old, dark-haired singing beauty tearfully accepted the crown of Miss
Dakota on a stage in Bismarck, after also receiving the talent award with
"Adele's Audition song" from "Die Fledermaus" by J.S. Strauss.

Beulah Mayor Wilmer Wiedrich declared Friday, June 17, as Miss North Dakota Day
and the day when Kathy came home to Beulah was cause for celebration. "You're
our hometown girl," said an ad placed by the Beulah Chamber of Commerce in the
local paper. An open house reception in Kathy's honor was held on June 17 at
the civic center in Beulah and music was provided by a male quartet. It was a
time for rejoicing in the accomplishments of one of Beulah's own.

There were 12 girls involved in the Miss North Dakota Pageant and they made the
dorms at Bismarck Junior College their homes throughout the duration of the
six-day affair. "We did a lot of rehearsing," said Kathy, "and we practiced the
dancing and modeling and most of our talents."

The contestants' days were full, with rehearsals each morning and invitations to
numerous luncheons and dinners from Bismarck service organizations. Even though
they were in competition with one another and had to work hard to perfect their
performances, the contestants developed a spirit of camaraderie and a sense of
appreciation for one another's talents. "They were all special girls," said
Kathy. "They were all very talented and interested in putting on a good show.

Along with the Miss North Dakota title, Kathy received $2,500 in scholarship
monies, a diamond ring from a Bismarck jeweler and several other gifts. Her
state title meant she would be booked for appearances throughout the state at
parades, fairs and other community and state functions. "I will be traveling
all over and I hope to learn more about my state," said Kathy. The new Miss
North Dakota spent the summer with the Dr. R.D. Schoregge family in Bismarck
since she was booked for appearances throughout most of July.

One of the most exciting privileges of winning the coveted state title was the
right to represent her state at the annual Miss America pageant, always held
during Labor Day weekend in Atlantic City, NJ. It was a proud moment for her
parents, Dr. and Mrs. J.A. Power, and many other residents of Beulah.

Kathy's performance at the state pageant was not her first experience with such
functions. On Oct. 27, 1973, she was crowned Miss Mercer County in the first
Miss Mercer County pageant. She received a $250 scholarship and won the talent
division with the vocal selection "Black Swan" from the opera "The Medium" by
G.C. Menotti. Her title from the Mercer County pageant allowed her to compete
in the Miss North Dakota pageant and on June 8, 1974, she was named fourth
runner-up in the state pageant.

On Oct. 29, 1976 Kathy became the North Dakota State Potato Queen in the Park
River, ND pageant and she received a $1,200 scholarship and a $150 cash award
for winning the talent division with the aria, "So anch'io la virtu magica"
from the opera "Don Pasquale" by Donizetti. The next pageant Kathy entered was
the one at which she was crowned Miss North Dakota in 1977.

        Kathy Power waves for the camera during the Atlantic City parade for
        the Miss America pageant.

        Beulah's Miss North Dakota, Kathy Power, presents her selection for
        the Miss America talent show in Atlantic City

        Power poses in her state crown, the only Beulah girl to attain the
        honor.

Music seemed to have stamped its name on the life of this young woman at an
early age and claimed her as one of its own, for Kathy's energies and direction
seemed always to move towards music. She graduated from the University of North
Dakota in 1978 with a bachelor of music degree in vocal performance and she was
a member of the "Burning Hills Singers" in the Medora Musical in the summer of
1978.

Kathy also did graduate work in vocal performance at Moorhead State University
and at the University of Southeastern Louisiana in Lafayette, LA. Between 1979
and 1985, Kathy studied in Madrid, Spain, at the Superior School of Singing and
received the diploma of opera and concert singer.

In 1982, Kathy was married to Carlos Sampedro of La Plata, Argentina. Carlos and
Kathy have two children, Alejandro, born in 1985, and Ana Elizabeth, born in
1987. They make their home in Buenos Aires, Argentina, and they both sing with
the Colon Opera Theatre.

The young Beulah woman who was crowned Miss North Dakota in 1977 is now a wife,
mother and professional opera singer. Her musical ability and achievements are
important to the citizens of Beulah because they represent the dreams of our
youth and the belief that, every so often, dreams really do come true.

Building an underwater waterline

Anybody who's ever played in the water sprayed high in the air by a broken fire
hydrant can appreciate the amount of water carried by a city's underground water
lines, but, like everything else involved in energy development, the water
pipeline built for the Antelope Valley Station makes even that seem tiny.

The innovative $13 million water intake project was started in mid-1979 at Lake
Sakakawea, utilizing lake water for the plants' water needs. The hole for the
pipeline was dug underground by a mechanical "mole," rather than the
conventional aboveground method of digging up the ground, laying in and sealing
the pipe, and then replacing the disturbed earth. That's because the
"aboveground," in this case, was under water.

The mole operated 300 feet under water in the project, planned by ANG but
eventually finished by Basin because of the uncertainty surrounding the gas
plant construction and the fact that Basin's construction schedule wound up far
ahead of ANG's.

There were massive mechanical difficulties to overcome in building the intake,
only one of them the mole, and the weather added its woes to the pile by
breathing a cold winter wind that caused workers to complain of frozen ears.

The first step in on-shore construction was completed when a concrete caisson
was lowered to 120 feet. Workers then drilled to 313 feet, where the downward
shaft began its horizontal path to the water inlet shaft some 3,000 feet
offshore.

Beulah is used to hearing "large" when describing equipment used for mining and
power production, and the "world's largest drill bit," almost 13 feet in
diameter, used to drill the downward shaft, was no exception.

That was a reverse circulation drill. Normally a drill pushes away the material
that is in front of it, but the reverse circulation drill works like a vacuum
cleaner. It generates suction and brings material up and away from the work
site through a central stem. That was necessary, as there was no place to push
to the earth.

After the shaft was completed, the drill bit was replaced by the mole to make
the horizontal traverse. The first 150 feet of the underground tunnel were
hand-mined, and the workers erected the mole and laid 24-inch track for the
mule trains used to remove the excavated material.

        Watching over the equipment needed to build the massive underground
        pipeline needed to supply the Great Plains gasification plant and
        Basin's Antelope Valley Station. Beulah Beacon photo.

The mole bored out the length of the tunnel and, with mechanical arms, set
concrete liners in place. Moving at some seven feet an hour, it took almost
three months to complete the 3,000-foot tunnel, which terminated at the
offshore water inlet shaft.

Looking across the placid waters, nothing is visible of the intake structure.
The water inlet plug, which allows water but not fish or debris into the
pipeline, is completely submersed and rises only seven feet off the lake floor.

Water flows into the intake drain at a rate of 7,000 gallons per minute,
compared to the 250 gallons per second flowing into the Garrison Dam generating
plant.

But none of that water is returned to the lake. Originally a discharge line was
planned, but the water is recycled at the plant site through a series of
settling ponds.

When the water leaves the lake, it travels eight miles south to the plant site.
There is does its part, by no means small, in making possible the production of
energy that has for so long proved an important segment of the economy in the
Beulah area.

        Inside the plastic construction bubble over MDU's Coyote Station,
        sights took on an unearthly quality with the high-powered lights
        reflecting off the plastic. Beulah Beacon photo.

Working beneath the shimmering "bubble"

Nov. 17, 1977

Dear editor;
 I was driving back from Montana a week ago Sunday, coming north on Hwy. 49 into
Beulah, when I saw the plastic bubble had gone up over the Coyote site. The
survey crew I'm working on went inside it the next day. When I read how many
people were turned away by Bechtel (the contractor) for trying to get a better
look, I thought I'd share my experience in there.

 For those like me who've come here to work on the projects, it can get to be
routine and dull pretty quick. You folks who've lived here all your lives and
are watching so many changes coming on (could) die of curiosity for a close-up
view. And anyway, before you know it, the plastic bubble will be gone and
instead it'll be the smokestacks of Coyote I on the ridge south of Beulah.

 We are working all afternoon around the outside of the bubble, setting stakes
to mark where a construction warehouse and other outbuildings will go up. At
shift change the regular workers from Coyote emerge from the dome in a drove.
Now that they have emptied the place out, we can go inside to survey the dirt
floor to level before the first layer of concrete is poured the next morning.

 We get into our van and drive through the airlock's gaping entryway. A dark
tunnel big enough to swallow a semi-tractor whole, it gets darker as the metal
door clatters down to shut away the last afternoon light behind us. We drive
through to the opposite end, where a man in this huge space, looking small as a
fly in a web, dangles like an acrobat pulling at a chain that disappears into
the dark overhead, cranking and yanking to life the next door so we can pass
through.

 It goes up and we are suddenly washed in bright light that spills from inside.
It is dazzling. We feel like high-wire artists and daredevil stuntmen entering a
crowded circus tent, blinded by spotlights as celebrities always are. It is
huge, grand. We imagine a thundering applause, eager hoots and whistles of
welcome.

 Our eyes begin getting used to the light. Maybe on second look this isn't a
carnival tent at all, but the inside of a giant seashell with its pattern of
curving grooves arched over us, glowing a pearly opalescent white, the roar of
the ocean filling our ears.

 But no, we look again. The lights are triple-clustered thousand-watt
metal-arcs, mounted high and aimed against the ceiling of the dome, filling it.
The roar . . . is that of the diesel generators that power them. What we smell
is not the sweetness of straw and animal dung dropped in the circus promenade,
or the salty brine of the deep sea, but exhaust fumes from these chugging
engines.

Below us on the vast dirt floor, like elephants abandoned by their trainers, a
fleet of tractors and scrapers sit yellow and shiny and dead. Workers in twos
and threes, tiny in here, go about their business . . .

Johnny Lerner
Hazen

        The massive bubble looked like just that from the outside; rather like
        a blister on the gentle rolling plains which surround it. Beulah
        Beacon photo.

A look from the outside

Our journey to Beulah began in southern Colorado, where we had lived for many
years," says Lucy Doyle.

Doyle began a career outside the home after her three kids were on their own.
"In the spring of 1979 there was just myself and my husband Andy. We were
living in a home we had built in Pueblo, CO. Andy had retired from his Civil
Service job and was just getting into the field of being a self-employed
handyman," Doyle says.

"Our lives were comfortable. We enjoyed playing golf and skiing. I was involved
in my job at CF&I Steel Corp., in community activities and had recently become
involved in an amateur photography club, editing the club's newsletter.

"My first response to the phone call that came one evening asking if I would be
interested in working on a project in Beulah was to go look on the map to see
just where it was."

Several years earlier Doyle had worked for Stearns-Roger on a power plant
construction project. Stearns-Roger had a design and construction management
contract with Basin Electric Power Cooperative for the two units under way
northwest of Beulah, the Antelope Valley Station.

Having enjoyed her work with S-R and construction-related work, Doyle was
interested in the job offer, but overwhelmed with the prospect of uprooting
their lives and moving to a new community so far away.

"Andy's response to the offer surprised me. 'We don't have to live the rest of
lives here,' he said, 'and besides it might be good for us.' "

The weeks between accepting the offer and leaving Colorado in early June were
hectic. "We stored our furniture and loaded into the pickup camper just what we
thought were essentials. The house had been leased to neighbors who needed more
room for their growing family.

"We arrived during a time when many others were coming into the area because of
the construction activities. Housing was at a premium. We spent the first few
weeks here in the New Frontier Motel until we could get into one of Basin's
trailer homes," Doyle recalls. "They were putting in new units at Zap and this
was our first home in North Dakota.

        Housing going up, housing for sale was the refrain throughout the
        primary impact years. Many families who moved to town were forced to
        build, because there wasn't enough housing to suit their needs. Beulah
        Beacon photo.

"Since there were few places to rent, we began looking at houses and later that
summer bought a home.

"I settled into my job at S-R getting reacquainted with fellow employees and
meeting new ones. Andy's first job was with the real estate firm of Claire
Aune, who was putting up prefabricated houses in the area. A few months later
he became associated with Basin Electric when he contracted with them to
maintain their workforce housing units in Beulah, Hazen and Zap.

The Doyles' first impressions of the area were that the people were very nice
and most of them spoke to you on the street and in the stores. Both of us had
grown up in Bailey County, Texas, before settling in Colorado, and they found
many similarities between the two communities: both were small and located in
farming and ranching areas.

"One story told by a fellow employee was especially relished because it told us
something about the people we were living among here. One of the first  S-R
employees on a jobsite is usually the field accountant. Our first field
accountant, a young man named Bobby Baker, told about setting out to visit the
local business places in Beulah to set up charge accounts for purchasing small
tools, hardware and fuel to be used on the job. Baker had introduced himself to
one businessman as Stearns employee and said he'd like to set up a charge
account.

"After rummaging through the bottom of the cash register for several minutes,
Baker was handed a piece of paper which was covered with grime and yellow with
age. 'Just as soon as you pay this bill,' said the taciturn owner, presenting
Baker with a charge slip which was dated back some 27 years or so, to the time
when Stearns-Roger had been the prime contractor on the old MDU plant on the
east end of main Street,'' Doyle tells.

"As we explored our new surroundings, I wondered about the impact of the plant
construction on those farmers whose farms were located in the immediate
vicinity. During the first summer on the job I was to witness the reaction of
one particular farmer."

        And more, and more, until after things slowed down there were many
        abandoned foundations and empty houses where no one had bought them.
        Beulah Beacon photo.

Water for the power plant and for the future coal gasification plant was drawn
from Lake Sakakawea and delivered to the raw water reservoirs on site by an
underground pipeline. The route for this nine-mile system lay underneath
farmland that lay between the intake structure on Renner Bay and the plant.

Most of the rights of way for this pipeline had been negotiated without
incident with the exception of one segment. This farmer had posted "No
trespassing'' signs on his property and, in addition, had strung a dead skunk
up alongside the sign at the point where the first excavation was planned. He
backed up his refusal with a shotgun.

In order to maintain the construction schedule it was necessary to construct the
pipeline from either side of his place and wait for the legalities to run their
course before going onto his land. On the day the first equipment moved onto
the land, the sheriff and his deputies were on hand to ensure the peaceful
completion of the pipeline.

Doyle recalls their lives during the construction years were hectic ones. "For
recreation we played co-ed volleyball, took several ski trips with the Hazen
Ski Club to Montana and South Dakota, did some traveling in the state, watched
summer softball games and played golf on sand greens, something new to us.

"After spending four years at the jobsite, S-R transferred me to the Denver
office. Going back to the city, especially one as large as Denver, didn't suit
Andy. He had become acquainted with the community and liked living here.
Consequently, I took a job offer from a contractor and worked on the coal
gasification jobsite for several months while the subcontract work was being
completed. Since the contractor's North Dakota office was located in Mandan, we
rented our house in Beulah and spent a couple of years there before coming back
to Beulah in the summer of 1987.

Louis F. Temme, a big booster

Mention these qualities: Outspoken, staunch Republican, long-time community
servant and a phenomenal memory. If you're talking to someone who's lived in
Beulah for any length of time, those will most likely conjure up the image of
one of the city's most dedicated and controversial figures: Louis F. Temme.

        During this time Beulah saw its ambulance service become a modern,
        separate entity with its own facilities and well-trained volunteer
        personnel. Here Paul Myers takes a pulse. Beulah Beacon photo.

Temme, born Nov. 3, 1889 in Okakaville, Ill., was a pioneer businessman in
Beulah, one who didn't stop at business as his community involvement. In
addition to involvement with the German State Bank, he was school board clerk,
city treasurer and involved in numerous community organizations.

Temme came to North Dakota in the fall of 1910 when he was 20 on the
recommendation of his doctor. That physician said the cold climate would help
Temme's malaria, as it seemed to strike only in the warm, humid summer.

Temme's only prior acquaintance with North Dakota was through grade school
geography and, after two years working on the Phillip Blank farm near New Salem
as a hired hand milking cows morning and night and doing plenty of field work
with horses, he decided he preferred the geography book acquaintance.

        The old ways haven't completely died out; there are still folks who
        hitch up the horses and wagons and take a turn down the street during
        chilly weather. Beulah Beacon photo.

"I decided I didn't want any part of life in North Dakota. It might have been
good for my malaria, but it was just too cold. So when my doctor Dr. Otto Gabe
of New Salem, pronounced me free of the malaria germ, in Nov. of 1912, I went
back to Illinois."

Life in rural Illinois didn't offer too much for young Temme. He passed a civil
service test for a rural route mail carrier's job but his Republican heritage
proved a handicap. That was during the White House tenure of Woodrow Wilson, a
Democrat, and a Democrat got the carrier's job.

Temme had a chance at a job as a railway mail letter carrier, but the position
would have taken him to the big cities and he didn't want any part of that.

Somehow, when Temme looked at his options, North Dakota started to look better
and better, especially from his spot in Illinois where the cold-winter memories
could fade a bit. "I decided that North Dakota had more opportunity. So, in
1914 I headed back to New Salem and went to work again as a hired hand, this
time on the John Tellman farm north of town."

Young Temme realized that his eight years of country schooling weren't going to
provide him with enough to get ahead the way he wanted to, and he had
supplemented them with several correspondence courses in Illinois. He had read
about a new business college in Fargo, the Dakota Business College, and in the
fall of 1915 he paid the $300 tuition for a one-year business course. "That was
the best move I have ever made," said Temme. "I had a chance to learn the kind
of business I thought I wanted to get into - banking."

Positions in a bank or any other work in 1915-16 were hard to come by, and
Temme's desire to get into the banking business had to be put on the shelf.

Temme's memory was tremendous. He recalled dates, conversations, experiences
and feelings with an ease that dumfounded most, and astonished the rest.

For instance: "On Nov. 22, 1916, the Dakota Business College received a call
from Louie Oulman of Beulah. He wanted someone to set up a bookkeeping system
for a privately owned light plant. The president of Dakota Business College,
Leland L. Watkins, encouraged me to take the position. I did.

"I arrived in Beulah on Nov. 23, 1916. I came in by train at 7 p.m., maybe it
was a few minutes before seven, maybe a few minutes after, but I've always said
seven o'clock.

        As a "laboratory" for energy development, Mercer County was the
        subject of many governmentally funded studies. This one was to be a
        documentary film on how development was handled. Beulah Beacon photo.

        Main Street saw facelifts along with the new housing areas. Here,
        Fabricare Cleaners was undergoing renovation. Beulah Beacon photo.

"The Oulman Light Plant was located in an old garage building that stood where
the Roxy Theatre is now. It was a cold, gloomy place. My bookkeeping  job,
which only paid $75 a month, kept me pretty close to a big coal-fire furnace,
just to stay warm."

The turning point in Temme's long business career came on March 1, 1917. He quit
his job with the Oulman plant and went to work for Arthur Smith in a
Beulah-based real estate and insurance business. That field caught Temme's
fancy; instead of books and numbers, that business presented a new dimension to
the ambitious young man - people.

After a short training period, Temme found himself alone in the business as
Smith died shortly after that as a result of surgery. Temme was in the first
draft call for World War I, but he was allowed to stay in Beulah to clear up
Smith's estate.

Temme's military career started on March 29, 1918 and ended on March 11, 1919.
He describes his service stint as not too eventful; his business training
brought him into an Army medical headquarters office where he buried himself in
military paperwork. His Dakota Business College penmanship stood him in good
stead as he was given the job of writing military discharges, then written in
longhand. Temme got to write his own.

After that, he returned to Beulah hoping to take over the Smith real estate and
insurance business, but the asking price of $6,000 was too high. "I didn't have
that kind of money, so when P.S. Chaffee, cashier of the German State Bank of
Beulah, suggested I come to work in the bank and write insurance, I accepted."

After two years there, Temme decided to strike out on his own. "I bought my
present building site for $300 in 1921, built the office just the way you see
it, and moved in. I had various companies, but my main line was The Hartford
Company. I was going to build a new building in 1930, larger and more modern,
had the blueprints and everything, but a friend advised me to go slow. I did.
Sure, I could have built a new building, but I'm happy here, it's adequate,
it's comfortable. I have no regrets," he said in 1972.

No one keeps track of the time people spend in making a community tick. If there
was a time log, there is no doubt Temme would have contributed an average
lifetime to community service. He was school board clerk from 1919 to the early
'50s. He started the American Legion in 1919 and pumped life into it over the
years. He was city treasurer for more than 25 years. He served Zion Lutheran
Church in many capacities from 1936 on. He was active in Red Cross work,
chairman of the county rationing board and OPA during World War II, started the
volunteer fire department in 1919, and was one of the early promoters of a
transcontinental designation for Hwy. 200, serving as the North Dakota chairman
for many years.

Temme had two chances to get into his first love, the banking business; one of
them he took. The first was a chance to work for the bank at Werner, ND in
1917. Temme rode the train to Werner (now only a cemetery), looked at the
situation and came right back to Beulah. "I just couldn't see it," he said.
"Beulah just had more opportunities."

The second chance was in 1931 when he went to the German State Bank. He served
as stockholder, director and vice president of that firm until it closed on May
31, 1938.

Temme was close to the political scene. Though he was never a candidate, his
strength in the local Republican machinery was well known. In a political way
he was the father of the joint tenancy bill of North Dakota. During the 1925
legislative session, Temme did all the leg work for preparing that bill, which
was passed during that session.

Temme's childhood home was unprepossessing. His family farm was a modest 200
acres, half of that in timber. He went to a rural grade school and the Missouri
Synod parochial school for three years. "It was all German in the church
school," said Temme. "And, in a way, I suppose that the German parochial school
held me back some." He was the oldest of four, two boys and two girls.

Temme married Helga Melstad on Oct. 24, 1936 at Mountain, ND. Melstad had been
a teacher in Beulah's school. She said she recalled Temme meeting her when she
arrived in Beulah by train. "I had so many suitcases that there wasn't room for
me in the car, so he took my belongings to the rooming house--and I walked."

Temme's office belied the man's tremendous mental organization. Far from being
neat and orderly, the office was an anachronism, a skeletally functional room
that never heard the word "modernization" spoken. Around the early '60s the old
potbellied stove disappeared, and a new typewriter nested among scattered
papers on the desk in the early ' 70s. A spider web of electrical wires from an
old-fashioned ceiling cord outlet was still there in 1972.

The files were overstuffed over the years and overflowed into every nook and
cranny of the small quarters. The walls held mementos of the past--Lions Club
membership certificate, an embossed real estate license, a Crams Superior Map
of the state, photos and diplomas. Temme's calendars hung in succession from
the same hook, running backwards from 1972 to 1953.

Temme didn't always see eye to eye with everyone and, particularly in his later
years, was known for being a crusty and cantankerous character. There was never
a doubt if his opinion differed with yours; he'd tell you. "I've always
believed that if I feel I'm right, I should take a stand and stick it out until
the end. This is the way I was brought up. But when it's over, it's over and
I'd drop it and bear no grudge," he said. Temme was well known for enjoying "a
challenge" and was not likely to sidestep a confrontation.

But regardless, he was instrumental in bringing about some of the vital changes
necessary to a young and growing Beulah, changes which would stand it in good
stead as the town was flung headlong into the energy impact years of the '70s
and '80s. In a way, the town grew up along with Temme, who died Dec. 26, 1979,
at a venerable 90 years of age.

Beulah obtains a modern medical building

Beulah boasts of many things which most small towns only dream of having. It has
excellent city facilities, business community and school system; it has broad
and well-run recreation programs; it has, above all, industry which both
increases the need for and makes the other things possible.

One item, relatively new but utterly essential, is its medical arts building,
currently occupied by three doctors and a dentist. with the increased
centralization of medical care, which often requires ill or injured people to
travel distances, it's vital to have local medical facilities.

        This building was constructed as a modern medical facility containing
        office space for three physicians plus a dental suite. Originally
        Beulah Medical Arts Center, it is now known as Missouri Slope Medical
        Arts Center.

Beulah is proud to have a new, modern facility with a small emergency room,
laboratory, x-ray equipment and more, plus access to Sakakawea Medical Center in
Hazen.

The building didn't come about by accident, nor was its birth an easy one.
Early in 1979 there was a lot of talk and discussion, and many plans were made,
in trying to attract a dentist and doctor to Beulah. Many plans came up, and an
equal number fell through.

In April, the Tri-County Development Corporation went to the Beulah city
council to seek funds to build such a facility, to house doctors, dentists
and/or other professional people. The council approved MIDA bonds, which allow
financing through the city without the city incurring indebtedness, but that
effort failed as well.

By September, the Beulah Development Corporation, which had been set up by the
Tri-County Development Corporation to operate a Beulah clinic, had taken on the
project and was trying to sell $270,000 in investments to build the clinic.
Though most people agreed with the need for such a facility to attract the
necessary medical personnel, it didn't seem most were willing to invest money
in such a proposition. Their efforts to collect the money fell short by some 80
percent.

Included in the BDC group were Daryl Zimmerman, Reuben Sackman, Doug Dettmann,
Emanuel Liebelt Sr., Ernie Olhauser and Charles Thelander, among others.

The development group was not to be deterred, however, and continued to search
out sources of funding. It approached ITAT, the Inter-industry Technical
Assistance Team consisting of energy industry representatives, and asked for
financial support, explaining that other financing channels, including the MIDA
bonds, stock sales and conventional loans, had proved untenable.

About that time Mercer-Oliver Health Services stepped in. That group had been
formed about 1979, funded by the federal Health, Education and Welfare
Department (now Health and Human Services), to obtain medical facilities in the
Mercer-Oliver Counties area. While Tri-County and BDC were laying groundwork,
Mercer-Oliver had been seeking a clinic in Hazen and Center. It was suggested
the group seek funding for a Center and Beulah clinic, since Hazen was already
well supplied with medical facilities. Mercer-Oliver was eligible for federal
funding, where BDC wasn't, and that was a big plus.

In January 1980, medical clinics in Beulah and Center were financed through
Mercer-Oliver, utilizing the federal Rural Health Initiative program, and
committees were formed to begin designing clinic buildings. The facilities were
to be staffed by National Health Service doctors specializing in family
practice. NHS program doctors had part of their education paid for with federal
funds in exchange for working in rural practice for a number of years.

Beulah received $400,000 from the Farmers Home Administration, through Mercer-
Oliver Health Services, in September, 1980, to begin construction on the
building, which later became known as Beulah Medical Arts Center. Land for the
building was obtained through a grant from the city, and restrictive covenants
insure it will always be used for medical services.

The following year in August, Mercer-Oliver Health Services signed an
experimental contract with Quain & Ramstsad Clinic in Bismarck, whereby Q&R
would assign one or more of its doctors to the Beulah Clinic, which opened in
September with Dr. James Morrison as physician. A few weeks later he was
indicted for conspiracy to commit murder and extradited to New Jersey. He was
later cleared of all charges but did not return to Beulah.

Dr. Kevin Lee, DDS, came to the medical arts clinic in April, 1982, and in July
Mercer-Oliver Health Services ended the contract with Q&R, which was not working
out, and sought another doctor for the rapidly growing town.

By January of 1983, two physicians for the clinic had been sought by Beulah
Development Corporation, which was leasing the facility from Mercer-Oliver, but
had fallen through. In July, Dr. Ralph Eccles accepted a salaried position at
the clinic and became Beulah's only resident physician.

Eccles left in 1984 and was replaced by Dr. Kings Lee and, briefly, Dr. A.R.J.
Rajakumar. In 1985 Mercer-Oliver again had control of the facility and that
fall Dr. Roger Kulas, who had practiced independently in Beulah for about a
year, took over the clinic, re-naming it Missouri Slope Medical Arts Center.
Dr. Russell Emery joined him and, in 1987, Dr. Howard Eliason joined the staff
of three.

The old Red Bridge

Whizzing down the smooth paved roads which make up our vast network of modern
transportation, it's easy to forget that's a convenience that has only been
around for a very few decades.

Before that, much of westward expansion in North Dakota was dependent on the
few "roadways" there were - mostly prairie trails, two scooped indentations
weaving through the prairie grasses where many horses had pulled many wagons as
the settlers traveled west.

River crossings were another stumbling block to expansion, as bridges were few
and not always sturdy. Most often, travelers were forced to search the
riverbanks for a good spot to ford, where the water was shallow and there was a
good gravel base which would support the weight of horses and wagons.

        The old Red Bridge, southeast of Beulah over the Knife River, was
        judged an anachronism and was torn down and replaced in 1982. It was
        one of the first bridges over the Knife in the county.

Along the Knife River such a spot existed, a mile or so southeast of Beulah.
Finding it a good ford, the settlers in the area sloped and riprapped the banks
with rocks to make it better, and the Pony Express and Stevenson stage used the
ford to cross the river in making their Mandan-Killdeer Mountain run.

As the Knife River area became more settled, travel increased, cutting trail
marks in the ground which are still visible on the Beulah golf course and
marking the passing of the road from the Beulah area to Glen Ullin. But when
the mercurial Knife overflowed its banks in spring due to ice jams, when the
"June raise" occurred and when there were heavy rains, the crossing was useless
and people were stranded.

It was obvious something had to be done, and it was. The county commissioners
looked at the situation and decided to build a bridge over the Knife River at a
spot about 100 yards west of the original crossing.

This bridge, eyed with eager anticipation by the settlers whose travel still
depended on the clemency of the weather, was to become a landmark. While a
country store and post office owned by Dick Farrington were nearby it was
called Farrington Bridge. When the railroad came, the store and name were
abandoned, and the store building was moved to Beulah's Main Street where it
was still in use during the '50s as Galloway's Super Valu store.

        In spring, ice floes would break loose, float downstream and jam at
        the bridge, causing flooding in town and creaking and movement at the
        bridge site.

        Dismantling the bridge was done in summer, with modern equipment,
        where the old one was built in winter to take advantage of the hard
        water beneath. Beulah Beacon photo.

Some called it the Chaffee Bridge, commemorating an incident in which a citizen
by that name left a permanent bend in the bridge railing following a night of
revelry.

But to most, it was simply known as the old Red Bridge, a bridge full of more
mischief and good fun than Tom Sawyer and with as many tales to tell.

Land was purchased from the Farringtons and Thomas O'Neil on the north, and work
on the marvel of modern engineering began. It was a truss bridge, supported at
both ends by cement piers, with iron railings and a plank bed which rumbled and
rattled and creaked as cars passed over its surface, and iron beams and tie
rods. Painted a cheerful red, an iron plaque was welded atop its towering 16'
structure which stated it was completed in 1906, one of the earliest bridges in
Mercer County. That plaque rests in the Mercer County Historical Society
Museum, in mint condition but for a few bullet holes.

The nearest railroad was 35 miles away at Glen Ullin and bridge materials had
to be hauled by horse and wagon to the construction site. Martin O'Neil, a
homesteader and relative of the present O'Neils, spent countless days traveling
between the two communities bringing the materials to the bridge site; and in
those days, a Glen Ullin-Beulah round trip lasted two days. Construction
schedules were much more flexible, and much less predictable, than they are
today.

Methods were different, too. Rather than damming and building during summer
weather as is done today, crews took advantage of Mother Nature's quirks. Thomas
O'Neil was hired to spread manure on the riverbanks to prevent the ground at the
construction site from freezing. When the Knife River iced over that winter,
bridge construction commenced. After all, the ice made a solid bed, and a guy
knew there wouldn't be any floods during winter, so, though it was harder to
work in the cold, it was easier to drive the steel pilings into the unfrozen
ground and attach the bed to girders.

The bridge had a reputation for toughness. It was always there, faithfully,
regardless of what fickle Mother Nature could dish out. through floods and ice
jams it clung tightly to its appointed spot. Ice break-up found the Knife
swirling wildly out of its banks and both sides of the bridge were under water;
the great pressure from the upstream ice caused it to creak and groan like an
animal in pain, and sometimes give a little - sometimes as much as two feet.
But, tough as old hide, the bridge stayed put.

During these times the bridge was a favorite spot to "flood-watch," as
townspeople flocked to the Red Bridge to gauge the height of floodwaters.

One spring a massive ice jam caused some flooding on Beulah's south side, and
people became concerned as the water crept higher and higher. Dislodging large
jams with dynamite was a common practice in those days - violent, but effective.

Several Beulah citizens were trying to loosen this jam by throwing dynamite
sticks into the jam. At one point someone grabbed six sticks, tied them
together, lit the fuses and threw the whole package onto the ice. But the
dynamite didn't cooperate. it fell into the main current and drifted under the
bridge, where it exploded.

Planks flew, but the Old Red Bridge stayed put.

Over its 75-year lifespan the bridge saw washouts from severe floods, which
meant its approaches were extended and repaired; countless replacements were
made on the plank roadbed. A severe flood in 1951 called for a major overhaul .
The bridge was raised several feet and reinforced cement piers were added to
each end. New planks were placed crosswise and lengthwise, which eliminated
most of the rumble which had led some of the children to call it Thunder Bridge.

On the south side of the bridge there was a small tree-covered hideaway, a
place for picnics and parties, and it seemed someone was always hanging around
at the Red Bridge. It was a favorite fishing spot as the water was deeper there
and the bridge provided welcome shade. Children used the spot for games and as
a source for spring bluebells. People wanting to relax and get away from things
for a while would linger and watch the quiet flow of the muddy waters scribing
fluid patterns on the river's surface, or observe while a crow painstakingly
built its nest in the bridge's girders overhead.

The bridge became a favorite spot where young people would hand from the girders
for high school pictures, or jump from the wooden planks into the Knife River
during the summer. The entrances and railings were scarred and battered, mute
evidence of the many battles the bridge fought with passing cars and trucks.
This was the spot where canoes were launched to take a long, quiet trip down
the meandering Knife. This was the spot where gypsies camped. This was the spot
where, many years earlier, Charlie Heinemeyer bought a bit of land and operated
Beulah's first ceramics business.

        An early group of horsemen out for a day's ride stopped to pose by the
        Red Bridge, a favorite spot for daydreaming or picnics.

This was a spot full of life, joy and memories.

But the bridge had only a 14-foot roadbed, not only a traffic hazard for
modern-day cars and pickups but a major headache for farmers with wide
machinery to move - some of it had to be coaxed across by hand. Finally it was
determined a more modern structure was needed, and in 1982 the old Red Bridge
came down.

It was a sad day when that majestic old bridge, which had served its people so
well, lay crumpled and razed. It was dismantled and dumped  unceremoniously
into the riverbed and replaced by a functional, modern concrete structure a
short distance from the original site. That bridge, built for some $279,500, no
doubt cost many times the price of the original. It allows easier crossing and
better water flow, helping reduce flood hazards upstream at Beulah, but it has
no character.

Though some tried to have the bridge preserved on the basis of historical
value, the state museum said it was similar in structure to others in the
state. The Mercer County Historical Society could not afford to adopt and
maintain it. So down it went, yet another victim to progress.

The land on which the Old Red Bridge stood was returned to the original owners
and all vestiges of its existence, but for that plaque and the now-buried steel
skeleton covered by the swirling Knife River waters, were erased.

The youngsters and newcomers will never miss it; but many's the time an oldtimer
will saunter down to the riverbanks, to that little dell where the bluebells
grew in profusion, and reminisce about days gone by and the old Red Bridge.

        Edgar Rueb and Peg O 'Neil watch one of the last vehicles to cross the
        Red Bridge before It was dismantled and replaced. Beulah Beacon photo.

The old threshing days sometimes return

The wagons are loaded to the brim with oats bundles; the horses, eager to pull,
paw the ground raw with their hooves; men shout and laugh, women sit and watch
smilingly and children play, waiting for business to get under way.

Such is a typical scene at the occasional old-style threshing days held here
and there throughout the area. After the signal to begin, the wagons pull up to
the thresher for unloading. The tractor is started, the long heavy belt
powering the thresher begins to turn, the thresher's gears and chains creak and
groan, bundles are fed into the awaiting thresher's throat, and the grain is
separated and loaded in a pickup box as the straw and chaff are blown into an
ever-increasing pile.

Such a day is one filled with hard work, sweat, plenty of cold liquids to drink
and good food to eat, prepared and brought by all the neighbors; much
good-natured laughter and many memories for all; some for the oldsters for whom
this is the way is was in their youth; some for the youngsters who are
fascinated by what seems to them such a complicated, slow and difficult method
for performing a task done so easily today by combines.

Horses, the earliest power source, were replaced by tractors, trucks, and later
threshers gave way to combines. Conversation runs to reminiscence, ranging from
the 25-cents-an-hour salary in the old days to the friends (now departed) who
were part of the threshing crews, to activities formerly engaged in after the
harvest season, to how the land used to look - and, of course, how hard the
life actually was.

        Threshing was easier in 1956 but still was much more difficult than it
        is today

Everyone has a great time during a threshing day, pitching a few bundles or
just watching and visiting.

As a way of life, this kind of threshing was, if not easier, certainly less
complicated and it's sometimes refreshing to go back to that, experience the
simplicity, feel the aches and stiffness engendered in muscles not used to such
strenuous activity, and share the good old-fashioned fun with friends and
neighbors.

Even for a day.


        Top right: All the workers were having lunch on Theophil Ricker's farm
        in 1945 at threshing time. It was an enjoyable time for all who were
        involved.

        Center: John Scheidt stands beside a tractor during threshing days in
        1944, as in the background wheat is blown onto the pile.

        Bottom left: In 1942, Art Oberlander of Beulah was binding grain in
        preparation for threshing it out.

        Bottom right: At Dave Keller's farm in 1948, workers on Walter
        Keller's rig had just finished and were preparing to go to the next
        farm.

Bigger than big--the draglines

Draglines are as commonplace a sight in Mercer County as meadowlarks, and
there's not a blink of an eye by a county resident when driving past one of
these mammoth behemoths at work, its massive jaws wrenching huge bites from the
earth and drooling dirt as it turns.

But it wasn't always this way.

Back in 1979, the first really big - bigger than big, try enormous - dragline
was being assembled at Coteau Properties' Freedom Mine north of Beulah near the
Antelope Valley Station. The machine was far too big to be factory-built and
brought to the mine site; it had to be shipped in pieces and built on the
ground. At the same time, a similar machine was being built at Knife River Coal
Mine south of Beulah.

The maw had a capacity of 105 cubic yards. Coteau's Bucyrus Erie dragline, later
named Sakakawea, weighed 6,375 tons, including ballast; that's 12.75 million
pounds, or lots and lots of nuts and bolts. (Of that, one million pounds was
ballast.)

When completed, the dragline was more than 220 feet high, just 20 feet shorter
than North Dakota's state capitol building. It had 24 electric motors of
different sizes to juice it up for action, with one size producing 1,300
horsepower and the other 1,045 horsepower.

The Bucyrus Erie's dimensions sound staggering even now, but in 1979, when it
was being assembled, it resembled nothing so much as a prehistoric dinosaur
returned to take revenge on puny man for desecrating the remains of its
ancestors.

But, on the practical side, power plants burn more coal in a day than used to be
mined in a year, and they need a very large and steady supply of coal to insure
operation.

Putting the dragline together looked to outsiders much like playing with a
gigantic Erector set. The machine was just packages of component parts when
assembly began during the summer of '79. Some 70 men were needed to set up the
$30 million dragline, which was eventually used to remove the earth overburden
above the coal seams.

        Coteau's Freedom Mine dragline, Sakakawea, was assembled on the mine
        site because of its great size and ponderous mobility. Once a marvel,
        It's now a commonplace sight.

Work on the dragline was carried out both inside and outside; inside, workers
began on the tub, or base. The machine's feet were attached to the side while
the operating house was above. The feet and house are moveable although the
dragline actually propels itself on the tub. Ground speed is slow, at .15 miles
per hour. And it walks, it doesn't crawl, to work. Moving one across a highway
is a major chore, requiring shutdown of the road for a day or so while it plods
across.

The 80-foot diameter tub came in 25 pieces and was welded together inside a
sliding steel building, which could be taken apart and slid open on two steel
rails. Work crews began in the tub's middle, working outward. The tub's surface
was measured or surveyed to keep it level.

The house section of the dragline is proportionate to the machine, measuring 99
feet long, 80 feet wide and 111 feet high from the ground. Inside are huge
gears, some weighing as much as 22,000 pounds, and electric motors.

Attached on either side of the behemoth are operating cabs. The dragline's
operation can be controlled from either cab. Two cabs are necessary because the
operator sometime encounters blind spots and must switch from one to the other.

About half a mile of 3/4-inch cable attaches to a bucket 21 feet wide, 30 feet
long and 22 feet high, just about big enough to park a couple of cars as an
average two-car garage measures 24 feet by 24 feet. The stationary boom on the
dragline measures 335 feet, 35 feet longer than a football field.

Only three people are needed to operate the machine, despite its size. One
person sits in the cab about 20 feet above the ground, with only two pedals and
two levers controlling the monster. The pedals swing the machine while the
levers control the bucket.

The second person is an oiler, who is responsible for making sure the automatic
oilers are working and keeping the numerous gears running freely.

The third person is a gound man, who must keep tabs on the dragline's other
operations. For instance, when the dragline "walks," the ground operator must
take care the machine doesn't rest on the electrical cable which supplies its
23,000 volts, the source of the energy it needs to move.

The dragline only removes the overburden above the coal seam. Smaller loading
shovels dig the valuable black mineral and load it for transporting.

The dragline went into operation at Coteau some 18 months after construction
started. Now there are several of the lumbering giants, both at Knife River,
Coteau and at the Indianhead Mine in Zap, still ripping deep cuts of earth off
the coal seams for people to take the mineral from the ground.

Keeping the fish on ice

Every winter a familiar sight pops up, sometimes singly, sometimes in pairs,
sometimes in little clusters of fantasy villages there for a few months and
then gone again.

A stranger might do a double-take in noticing the insubstantial foundations on
which these little houses rest, as their owners obviously don't take seriously
the Biblical injunction to build your houses on rock, but to a North Dakotan
there's no mistaking them.

They're ice houses, and they're a common sight on bay and inlet waters during
the winter months.

If the lights are on, someone's home, but even if that's the case the heat
might not be on. Not all ice fishermen crave such homey comforts. Mostly the
houses just have to provide protection from the wind for fishermen and
outdoorsmen who can't wait till spring to try out their new Christmas tackle.

The houses provide the sportsmen with a welcome chance to get outdoors and get
that line in the water right now, when other sports are severely restricted if
not prohibited by the extreme cold of winter.

But ice fishing still isn't easy. First a hole must be drilled in the ice,
often three or more feet deep, and unless a power augur is available that means
lots of huffing and puffing as you press and turn a hand augur. When you're
through, you have a six-inch or so hole in the ice which reflects light oddly
down its length and gushes water as you pull the augur out. Oh - and you have
to be careful not to fall, as the gushing water makes the surrounding ice
treacherously slippery.

Then equipment has to be altered to use it through the ice. The lures and
tackle that work so well on content walleye and pike in the spring and summer
don't cut it in the cold waters of winter. The line used is much thicker and
stronger and the rods are very small. Reels are seldom used. Fish are generally
landed using just the line and maybe gaff hooks, not nets. And, of course, the
fish has to be smaller than the diameter of the hole.

Oh - don't forget longsuffering. The famous angler patience must be in good
supply regardless of the numbness of the toes.

        Ice fishing in winter brings out the tiny houses which rest on the
        ice, giving their occupants shelter from the wind and cold and a spot
        to sit to munch their lunch. Beulah Beacon photo.

Ice fishermen seem to have various concepts of the sport. For some, it's simply
a chance to be outdoors during a restrictive season. They can sometimes be
caught having skating races on the ice, particularly if there's a bit of wind
to fill their sailboats with energy. They often have their families with them,
and the little ones, when they fall down on the slippery surface, will stare
with amazement at the deep fissures in the ice and the rainbows refracted in
the air bubbles trapped beneath its surface.

Others set up their houses and spend their time going after a whopper with great
gusto and single-mindedness. It should be noted that these qualities don't
guarantee them a better catch than the first kind of ice fisherman.

Others just set up the ice house, break out the cards and the suds and act like
it was summertime, only cooler.

In earlier days maybe ice fishing was sometimes the difference between food on
the table and not, but over the years it's become one of the distinctive
recreational activities of the area. It takes a tough and determined character
to brazen it out with severe winter cold and win - much less to come home with
a tasty cold-water fish for supper.

But ah. the rewards!

A "home" away from home

The Bachelor Quarters now stand empty at the north end of Beulah, monument to
earlier days when the town was buzzing with the 500-plus workers who resided
there during peak construction days at Antelope Valley, Coyote and the ANG
gasification plant.

Some 30 employees at the BQs took care of the various operations, including
cooking and maintenance. In the fall of 1978 the quarters were open for
business, with meals being served beginning Sept. 5, though sleeping quarters
were open several days before that. At its peak, the RV pads in the complex
were full and construction workers swarmed the area, resembling nothing so much
as a community within a community--only there were no women.

The buildings, since purchased but not removed by a Minnesota businessman, were
designed and constructed to conserve energy. There were electrical hookups for
workers to plug in vehicles.

There were solar-heated shower facilities in the complex for those using the RV
pads, and total occupancy was 408 with 105 RV pads. Each room, for one
individual, contained a bed, dresser, bathroom and shower and a closet. Each
day the rooms were cleaned, bedsheets changed and beds made. All laundry was
washed and dried at the BQs. Each billet, containing 24 rooms, had its own mud
room.

It had all the comforts of home - almost.

RV patrons paid $12 a week to stay there; that included water, electricity and
sewer; meals were extra.

For others, the cost of staying in one of the furnished rooms varied, depending
on who employed them. AVS workers were charged a percentage of the per diem rate
they were paid by Basin. Coyote worker paid a flat $10 per day. Both received
room and board for those fees; and as housing, feeding and cleaning cost $38
per day, they got quite a bargain.

        Eating was cafeteria-style at the Bachelor Quarters dining hall in the
        man camp north of town. It suited the appetites of the workers who
        built the power plants in the area. Beulah Beacon photo.

There were also special laundry quarters, two television rooms and a game room
for playing cards, pool or foosball.

It wasn't heaven, but it was home--sort of--for a little while.

Since the Department of Energy fell heir to the BQs there has been a lot of
rolling around trying to figure out what to do with them. The man who purchased
the modular billets had until June, 1988 to remove them, and that deadline had
been extended before. The DOE had given the mess hall, the largest of the
buildings, to the city of Beulah, which is trying to attract some small
industry to the area to utilize the building and get it back on the tax rolls.
The city had formerly promoted the site when federal Job Corps people were
looking to build a Job Corps training center, but that didn't come through.

It may never see much activity again, and certainly not the kind it saw during
the impact years, but the quarters and the streets surrounding them stand as
mute testimony to the workers who came, built and left again, leaving a small
ghost town in their wake.

The Ballad to the Swede and the Beaver

It was late in March
When the Swede started out,
He took nothin' with him
But a little bit of stout;
As he strolled on the banks
Of that muddy old river,
His heart was heavy
And the cool air made him shiver.
He watched for the beaver
As he lounged upon a log,
He was all alone,
Never even took his dog
Oh, say oh, say
What's that I see?
A brown beaver's head
Is a-peekin' up at me?
And the muddy waters roll right on,
And the muddy waters roll right on,
That old beaver's gone, he's gone.

The Swede looked around.
His gun was 'cross his knee.
Who'd a-thought he couldn't trust
That old two-forty-three?
But he needed some snoose,
So he reached to have a chew,
And the blast that filled the air
Could be heard, but he never knew,
For he lay there on the sod,
A hole shot through his chest,
Come right out above his heart,
His head was pointin' west.
Oh, say oh, say
What's that I see?
A brown beaver's lookin';
Is he laughin' at me?
And the muddy waters roll right on . . .
And the muddy waters roll right on . . .
The Swede's life soon might be gone . . .

What does a man think?
What does a man say?
When he looks up at the sky
At the slowly closing day
And he knows there's a door
He might soon step through
The minutes now are passing,
He might have just a few.
He never was a quitter,
Oh, yes, the Swede fought for his life,
As he tried to lift his graying head
He thought of kids and wife.
Oh, say oh, say
What's that I see?
A brown beaver lookin';
He's a-pokin' fun at me!
And the muddy water rolls along,
The muddy old Knife rolls on,
Soon, so soon, the Swede will be gone . . .

But he struggled as he lay there.
He tried to clear his head,
He knew he had three more shells,
"I'll pull the trigger," 's what he said,
The roar it made did echo
Through the dim, dark trees,
Made him tremble as he lay there
And he whispered, "Lord, now please,
Just let somebody hear me,
As I fire these last two shots.
My blood is draining in the dirt,
And a hero, I am not!"
Oh, say, oh, say
What's that I see?
A dirty beaver grinning
And a wavin' at me?
And the muddy waters roll right on,
And the muddy waters roll right on . . .
The Swede may soon be gone . . .

As he lay in the cold
On the wet, hard earth,
The Swede took his measure,
What his life was really worth,
And he knew he would live,
He would hunt again,
He would get the beaver's pelt,
If he only knew just when,
For his heart was slowing
And his thoughts drifted too,
As he waited for his woman
Or a friend to help him through.
Oh, say, oh, say,
What's that I see?
That ain't no beaver,
It's St. Peter greetin' me!
And the muddy waters roll right on,
Will the Swede pass over and be gone?
Will he greet his maker and be gone?
And the muddy waters rolled right on . . .

Fran Erickson

        Inside the Great Plains Gasification Associates gasifier building,
        looking at the ash locks. The building is several stories high, and
        the huge pipes and other equipment dwarf the people who operate the
        plant.

Pulling together for the future

The Year of the Great Ice Storm, 1983 saw "the most devastating damage in
county history" when, in March, Mother Nature draped everything in sight with
her beautiful but deadly frozen crystalline sculptures. Electricity was out for
96 hours, much of the state was declared a disaster area and life came to a
slippery halt as nature again declared her supremacy over man.

A pneumonia epidemic filled the Hazen Memorial Hospital wards to overflowing,
with people coughing in corridors and reports of having to share vapor tents;
many were sent to Bismarck but there, too, hospitals were full.

The Great Plains partners first threatened to abandon the project in 1983 as
they sought to apply some political pressure of their own; they asked the
Synthetic Fuels Corporation, which held the purse strings on federal synfuels
support, for $2 billion in price support subsidies, an amount in line with what
other synfuels projects in the nation had received. When the SFC wouldn't talk,
they threatened.

        The city's new water treatment plant resulted from impact.

        The civic center, originally the Tri-County Neighborhood Facility was
        built in the early impact years.

        After the ruckus died down, city hall was given a renovation and
        facelift, too.

It worked the first time; the SFC came to the negotiating table. Two years
later, after using the same tactic a couple more times, the SFC tired of
listening to GPGA cry, "Wolf!" and called the consortium's bluff. It turned out
not to be one.

Trouble loomed on the horizon already in 1983 but no one paid much attention, as
AVS II construction schedules were slowed because generating needs were down.
That was the beginning of a trend toward needing less electrical generating
capacity, which was to affect the industry more and more in years to come. In
June, AVS I went on-line.

GPGA's start-up in mid-'83 produced noises (which were expected) and foul odors
(which were not). They became worse and caused more troubles for the plant in
terms of public relations than any other single factor. In July the first
commercial gas hit the pipeline, but a metering station in the southwest part
of the county blew up, killing one and injuring five.

Water was rationed the summer of 1983, with Beulah homeowners watering their
lawns every other day; the Beulah water plant was operating 24 hours and
couldn't keep up with the demand. The city stepped up its efforts to get
another treatment plant, which started up in 1985. With 5,600 people now in
town, according to a special census, a water plant built years earlier couldn't
handle the load.

Beulah saw its greatest congestion from energy impact in that year. Parking
downtown was at a premium, with long-time residents complaining about the
traffic and newcomers, many of whom had come from major metropolitan areas,
wondering, "What traffic problem?"

People saw more and more unfamiliar faces as they walked Beulah's streets, as
fewer of the town's citizens had lived here all their lives. Newcomers, who had
been told of small-town hospitality, were sometimes puzzled that it didn't seem
to be as obvious as they had thought it would, while natives didn't quite know
how to respond to the here-today-gone-tomorrow residents typical of
construction and start-up.

Recreational facilities and programs were stretched to the bursting point, and
new parks and playing fields were built to accommodate the load. Houses were
going up at a record rate, and many families who came to town found they had no
choice but to custom-build, as too few houses were available to satisfy many of
their needs.

The Bachelor Quarters were closed in 1984 and the construction force was down to
a comparatively skeletal 900, giving the town space to heave a brief sigh of
relief. The area began to feel the force of what came to be called "negative
impact," those things which occur when people leave the area quickly, as
opposed to the "positive impact" of influx with its associated money and jobs.
It was to get much worse very shortly.

Still asserting that farmers were number one, local businessmen instituted Ag
Appreciation Days. The Beulah Miners basketball team made it to the state Class
B finals again, but lost in opening round action to the Hillsboro Burros.
Summer saw Jacques Cousteau's crew in the county as his scuba divers explored
the Missouri River system for an upcoming film but, though there was interest
on the part of local residents, Beulah had become too used to being in the
public eye to do more than blink a couple of times. In the same area, the county
planning and zoning commission was being asked to rezone some lakeshore land so
lakeside development could be started.

The following year was the pivot point by which all the impact years, before and
after, are measured: In 1985 came Black Tuesday, Aug. 1, when the five-partner
consortium that owned Great Plains followed through on its third threat to
abandon the project when it could neither begin repayment on its $2.1 billion
federally guaranteed loan nor maneuver any longer for breathing room.

Threats to close the plant were heard, and panic perched on the shoulders of
county residents, business and workers. There was much behind-the-scenes
activity in trying to keep the plant open; a pep rally was held in Beulah which
attracted nearly every dignitary in the state and some from Washington, D.C.;
the General Accounting Office, the federal budget arm, predicted more than $242
million in losses to local, state and federal governments if the Great Plains
plant shut down.

It was rally time. Even those who had voiced strident opposition to the plant
in early years softened their tone and spoke of support; whether because public
relations had improved or some of their relations now worked at the plant, no
one knows.

Along with the energy blight came a grasshopper plague. Area farmers and
ranchers fought this one just as quietly as they had always gone about their
work, and more successfully than those who fought the gas plant battles. Some
good news came even in a difficult year in the form of a 5 percent tax
reduction for residents, to bring Beulah more in line with what the rest of the
county paid.

New questions arose, echoing a harsh counterpoint to those raised in the early
