impact years: What will happen? Will we have a job tomorrow? How will we pay for
all these improvements? Where will we go? What can we offer our young people?

        The dunking machine has been a popular item in such celebrations as
        Crazy Days for a number of years - how else to get even without
        getting in trouble? Beulah Beacon photo.

As it was the first time, the burning question was: Who is going to pay?

A great deal of money had been invested in building to meet impact needs. Much
of that debt still remained to be paid. People began to leave the area,
"getting out before the ship sank." The bottom dropped out of the housing
market, with homes built during peak impact years losing 30 percent or more of
their value within a few months.

Schools saw panic times, and midnight budget sessions for all political
subdivisions were the rule for a while. Beulah was faced with more hard facts:
The DOE did not have to, and had no intention of, paying any property taxes or
special assessments despite the fact that the plant on which it had foreclosed
owed a great many of them. Conversion tax money was also lost to the schools,
the county and the cities, making quite a dent in their budgets. With plant
abandonment came a flurry of new requests for the EIO, and it had fewer and
fewer dollars to hand out.

Things began to settle out somewhat in 1986, with the plant foreclosure sale
taking place where more commonplace ones did, on the courthouse steps in
Stanton, with the DOE the only bidder.

A great deal of ingenuity, persistence and nose-to-the-grindstone hard work on
the part of officials that year led to relative stability, though the
population was decreasing and business had dropped off proportionately. Beulah
was looking at numerous financial problems, including a narrowed tax base from
which to pay for improvements which, to some extent, were no longer needed.

But, thanks to a traditionally conservative approach to things fiscal by
Beulah's city council and forward-looking policies when impact began, Beulah
was in relatively good financial shape, especially when compared to surrounding
communities which had depended more on promises for tomorrow than on realities
of today.

        Door prizes were drawn at the Oktoberfest in 1985, with Curtis Schulz
        doing the honors while Al Schock holds the box. Looking on are Verna
        Almen and Erma Voegele, with Nancy Northrup in the background. Beulah
        Beacon photo.

        After the snow and wind stopped, digging out began from drifts that
        were more than kid-high. Beulah Beacon photo.

When local leaders went to the Legislature in 1987 to plead their case, they
had to slap at hands that were still reaching for their pockets. Too many
stories had been heard about Mercer County's "streets of gold" for legislators
to take seriously their requests for funding to mitigate impact.

"But impact is over," they were told repeatedly. "You don't have a large influx
of people any more. They're all leaving." It seemed futile to try to convince
them that a large egress of people created an even larger financial burden on
the people who remained, as there were no governmental provisions anywhere for
such a change and there were fewer people were left to pay taxes that paid for
the improvements designed to meet impact.

        The April, 1984, blizzard which brought the town to a standstill was
        fought all the way, as this resident attempts to pull out his pickup
        and keep going Beulah Beacon photo.

Special assessments that were outstanding on properties owned now by the DOE
became a point of contention. The DOE saw them as taxes and refused to pay them.
On top of the property and conversion taxes it was already not paying, the loss
of specials was a serious blow. But again, dogged persistence paid off, as the
DOE began making "community impact assistance" payments to the schools and
eventually came to a settlement with the city about its specials.

During 1987 the DOE was also developing an elaborate marketing strategy to sell
the plant to a private owner, getting it off the DOE 's unwilling hands and
back onto county tax rolls . Hiring the investment bankers Shearson-Lehman
Brothers to market the plant, the DOE's criteria for sale included strength for
the purchasing company and a long-term commitment to run the plant, to keep its
900 people employed and Beulah's economy on an even keel. That was enough to
give Beulah a sigh of relief, as a people used to dealing with uncertainty saw
that as a kind of stability.

Early in 1988 the DOE announced it would shortly begin negotiating with some of
the companies which had submitted firm bids on the facility, which Shearson-
Lehman's marketing analysis showed has enormous potential for by-products
expansion.

        Main Street still saw changes. The old, original cash store with the
        tall front was torn down and made into a drive-through for Fabricare
        Cleaners.

        Present city councilmen: Herb Dittus, Robert Schutt, Fred Galloway,
        Jim Schaefer, Norris Abrahamson, Milton Flemmer; seated, mayor Donald
        Benz, Darrell Bjerke.

        Many hands made light work as the senior citizens of Beulah banded
        together to fix up the old Joachim Home into a home for their club. A
        second remodeling has now been completed. Beulah Beacon photo.

Though a possible purchaser might be expected to raise anxieties and more
questions, like layoffs, reorganizations, salary and benefit cuts, Beulah's
reaction was: "Fine, get it over with, and let's get on with our lives."

What will happen in succeeding years in this long, drawn-out saga remains to be
seen. Beulah's Ag economy, though not yet healthy, has shown signs of recovery,
and it must be remembered that these farmers have descended from the pioneers
who had the courage and dogged persistence to settle a harsh and inhospitable
wilderness.

Other area industry is stable, and there are creative and continuing efforts
being made to attract employers to the area, to fill in the gaps in the
economy, to turn the town's debits into assets. The hard work and sacrifices
over the years have provided Beulah's young people with the choice to make
their homes near home. The town isn't about to give that up.

It will work. It may take time, but it will work.

What has been seen is that Beulah and its people have met the test. Over the 75
years since Beulah was born, when faced with challenge, its people have risen to
meet it. When adversity struck, they have taken it in stride. When belts had to
be tightened, they pulled in a notch farther than necessary. And through it all
they stuck together; working, playing, marrying, burying, sharing their lives.

Though living in a modern world with microwave ovens, television, and
innumerable other conveniences their forebears would never have been able to
dream of, Beulah's people have proved to be of the same hardy stock as their
forebears. They will turn adversity to advantage and come out on top, as they
have for the last 75 years.

        And down went another phase of Beulah history as the coal storage from
        the MDU Beulah Plant at the east end of Main Street was torn down in
        October 1986. Beulah Beacon photo.

        Following the Beulah Plant's shutdown, the now-useless cooling towers
        were burned and the fire department used them for practice in July
        1986. Beulah Beacon photo.

Beulah's public library has spacious new home

Those who think a day isn't complete without a good read have had plenty of time
now to celebrate the Beulah Public Library's newest home, in the remodeled and
spacious accommodations it now has in city hall. It moved into its latest home
in June 1987.

Quiet and well appointed, these quarters are a bit of heaven for some of the
dedicated members of the Beulah Women's Club, which organized the original
library and has seen it through all its growing pains over the years, and still
views it as an important club project.

For several months in 1987, the library spent its time hibernating in boxes
while construction was going on. It was a great relief - and a great deal of
work - to get all the books out, cleaned up and on the shelves, ready for
patrons.

But the library is an old hand at moving, having had five homes and seven moves
since its birth in 1931. And it's grown a lot, as well, having gone from its
original 373 donated books to having accession numbers in the 9,000s now. That
doesn't mean there are 9,000-plus books on the shelves; it means there have
been that many recorded over the years. It isn't certain how many books there
are.

        Beulah's public library has spacious new quarters in city hall.

The original library, called the Marion Moore Memorial Library, was housed in
the east foyer of the Roxy Theatre. It issued 30 books its first day and saw 51
paid memberships, a practice which was discontinued in 1941 when the library
made its first move to city hall.

Mrs. I.J. Niedermeyer wanted to start a library some six years before the
project became reality, and enlisted the help of Mrs. L.G. Rose. together the
two convinced the newly federated Beulah Women's Club in 1930 to sponsor a
library project and served as the original library committee.

Then-president Mrs. F.P. Rasmusson and a Mrs. Marshall also joined the
committee, and when club members sharing library duty on a rotating basis proved
unsatisfactory, Mrs. Marshall became the first librarian.

This was two years after the library was born and it had already outgrown its
shelves, so its first move and remodeling were undertaken. The move wasn't far,
though, going from the Roxy's foyer to the balcony, and new double book stacks
were built.

Beulah proved appreciative of its library and by 1935 yet more space was needed.
The possibility of building a log cabin-style library as a WPA project was
aired in 1935, and the Women's Club began to raise money in earnest for such an
eventuality.

With a target of $300 for the building, the members threw themselves into the
project, but the money was placed in a library building fund when the project
was tabled.

Raising money for the library was especially difficult during the Depression
years, but the Women's Club served dinners, catered, held home-town plays and
did anything else it could to raise funds. Though it was hard during those
years, the members had a lot of fun; and expectations during an economic
downturn weren't quite what they are during a prosperous cycle.

One funding standby was the club's annual rummage sale, which it still holds.

In 1936 the library built a new nest once again, this time being housed in the
school building, where it remained until its first move to city hall.

Until this time, library patronship had been by paid membership; when the
facility was moved to city hall, this was abolished and it became a free
lending library. Another first simultaneously was the first non-Women's
Club-member circulation librarian, Gertrude Younker.

Always the public servant, the Beulah Independent featured the changes to the
library's situation on its front page.

Shortly after, the library was moved to the old American Legion Hall because the
World War II Rationing Board needed city hall for its functions. The following
year it returned to city hall.

By 1957 the library had outgrown its surroundings again and the Women's Club
went on record favoring a new city hall with a library room. Shortly after
Beulah's residents voted in a new city hall meeting those specifications, and
in early 1959 the new library room was ready, with much the same anticipation
this new one has received.

At the same time, the library began receiving city funds and no longer had to
depend solely on donations and Women's Club fundraising projects to support it.
The money previously placed in a library fund intended for a building went to
fixtures and other things needed to furnish the city hall library room.

Until then, the library moved around because it had no permanent home. Someone
always offered it a place to stay and when it became inconvenient or too small,
its supporters packed it up and moved it someplace else.

The library has always seen a lot of use, with people's interests as diverse as
the selection of books available to the library.

One thing the library makes a point of keeping up to date is its section on
North Dakota history books and regional authors, maintaining a special section
for them.

The State Library has been instrumental in the Beulah facility's success, and
currently the library has an interlibrary loan agreement with both the state
and regional library, Mercer-McLean Regional Library, allowing it to borrow any
book its patrons request providing the other library has it. Also inextricably
linked with the library and its growth and expansion was Rags Thelander,
long-time librarian and library champion, who died early in 1988.

Currently the library receives a one-mill levy from the city to support it,
some $3,000 a year, in addition to personnel funding from the regional library
which pays for the salaries of the librarians.

The Women's Club maintains its library committee, still dedicated to keeping the
library strong and growing, but the governing body is now the city library
board. Funding comes from the city and is vouchered through the library board.

The Dreamland Pavilion

It took a one-man city crew only 15 minutes to knock down the old Dreamland
Pavilion building in May of 1985. The next day a match was lit and the rest was
history.

But what a history it was . . .

If the walls of the building commonly known to city residents as the "Sheep
Shed" could talk, there would be quite a story to tell, for its history spans
six decades of dancing, roller skating, boxing and wrestling matches and
political gatherings through years of Prohibition, Depression, war and city
expansion. The townsite that became a village and then a town changed greatly
throughout those years and so did the residents, but the popularity of social
activities at the Dreamland survived. For many decades, it was the social
center of Beulah.

The building that was razed by the city's front-end loader in 1985 didn't look
like much anymore. After being closed in May, 1963, the building had been
vacant for some years and then was re-opened as an auto body shop. The once
beautiful hardwood dance floor had been scratched and mauled beyond
recognition, the walls and roof were deteriorated and collapsing and there was
little to suggest its years of former glory.

        The famous Sheep Shed, dilapidated and disused, just a bit before its
        destruction.

        Following its razing, the former Dreamland Pavilion was torched and
        burned to the ground.

        Before the decision was made to destroy the building, it was
        temporarily used for a body shop. It bears little resemblance to the
        dance hall of earlier days. Beulah Beacon photo.

Before the building was demolished, officials from the Mercer County Historical
Society toured the site, hoping to secure enough pieces of the hardwood floor
to use in making keychains as mementos for the next all-school reunion, but the
floor was no longer usable.

The building had become an eyesore along Highway 49, next to the Knife River and
close to the entrance to the Riverside Park. For those who had not grown up in
Beulah, the demolition of the Dreamland Pavilion meant very little, for many
others it was the end of an era.

When the building was first constructed in 1929, it was not a pavilion at all,
but a bowery. Built by a chiropractor named Dr. Meiers, it was just a platform
to dance on, with no walls or roof. Of course, North Dakota weather soon proved
that a bowery was not very practical, and the good doctor soon ran out of money
and sold the bowery to Ben Kittler and his sons Walter and Herb, who operated
the business for the next 20 years.

Wally Kittler and his wife now reside in Mandan, and Kittler has many fond
reminiscences about the Dreamland. He says that after his family purchased the
building, one of the first efforts was the addition of walls and a tar papered
roof. "We had to make sure that we could have a longer dance season," said
Kittler, "and some of the best crowds we had was when it rained and the farmers
had time to come in, so we just did the remodeling piecemeal, until we were
done."

Wally Kittler had a musical group consisting of from five to nine musicians,
and the Wally Kittler Band was a popular feature at the Dreamland for many
years. "We played there every Saturday night for 15 years," said Kittler, "and
gosh, we had some big crowds too. It got so we would average 500 people at our
dances, and one Fourth of July we sold over 1,000 tickets."

Kittler recalls the dances drawing people from the entire area, including
Hazen, Zap, Killdeer, Glen Ullin, Hebron and Golden Valley, and the ferryboats
brought more merrymakers from across the river in Underwood and Washburn.

Kittler says his band played "old time" music, and they had a good reputation
at other dance halls, too. As a matter of fact, that's where he found the name
for the bowery that was turned into a pavilion, which is defined as a light
structured place of entertainment.

"Once, the band played in Fairview, Montana, at a place called the Dreamland
Pavilion. I thought it was a great name, so I brought it home for ours. So I
guess I was the guy who named the pavilion," said Kittler.

How did a dance hall with a romantic name like the Dreamland Pavilion come to be
nicknamed the Sheep Shed?

"Well, it happened when we were putting tarpaper on the roof," said Kittler.
"One of our ticket takers looked up at the roof and said, 'This place looks
more like a sheep shed than a pavilion.' And don't you know, that name stuck."

Whether the place had a name that was fancy or plain, its reputation was good
enough to draw bands from as far away as Nebraska. Kittler said the out-of-town
bands always played on Wednesday nights.

"Many people considered the Dreamland to be the best dance hall in the state,"
said Kittler, "and the bands that were on the road going to Fargo or Minnesota,
or traveling to Montana always wanted to play here. We were located in a
convenient spot for them to stop, and our middle of the week booking gave them
a chance for travel time. So many of them didn't care if they made much, just
enough to cover their travel expenses."

Another business technique that Kittler used to promote the Dreamland was the
scheduling and promotion of dances on a regular basis. "There were other dances
in the area," said Kittler, "but when we had posters printed that said we would
have dances every Saturday night, that was good for business, because then
people never had to wonder if there was a dance or not."

The inside of the building featured a large dance floor and a big pillar in the
center. There were rows of chairs around the inside of the pavilion, and a beer
parlor was added after the repeal of Prohibition. "At first, the beer parlor
was on the south side of the building," said Kittler, "and then it was moved to
the northwest corner." 4 by 4's were used on the ceiling to create the look of
a wagon wheel and Kittler made an agreement with "the Chesterfield man" to use
their advertising on the stage if he in turn would show him some ways to
decorate the pavilion with crepe paper. "We had the Chesterfield posters on our
stage for a good many years," said Kittler, "and of course after that, the
pavilion was always decorated well."

Kittler says he consulted with some color psychology people and determined that
the colors they would use to decorate the pavilion would be orange and blue.
"The orange was to make them happy, and the blue was to keep them cool," he
says.

When the Kittlers ran the pavilion, a 12-ounce beer cost five cents and a
hamburger was 15 cents. Kittler says the orchestrations, or arrangements of
music for his band, cost 50 cents in those days, and he now works with some
young musicians who can't believe the price stamped on his old music. "Today
that same music will cost from $25 to $50, and it's the very same thing," says
Kittler.

A St. Patrick's Day blizzard in 1943 was a memorable one for Kittler and many
others who attended the dance at the pavilion that evening. "The blizzard
lasted two or three days, and people were stranded everywhere trying to get
home from the dance," says Kittler. "When all that snow melted, we had three
feet of water in the pavilion." The Kittlers' three-room house was built close
to the pavilion and also received a foot of water.

        Inside the Dreamland Pavilion in earlier years - this photo in  January
        1955 - the Knife River Squares started their square dance group in 1954.

About 1950, the Kittlers sold the pavilion to Ted Rodgers, and there were other
managers throughout its history. The last owner of the Dreamland Pavilion was
Adam Keller, who sold it to the Beulah Park Board.

Yet Wally Kittler, who is now 79, was one of the major forces in the popularity
of the site. Kittler is still very active and interested in music. He has
taught music at the State Penitentiary for the past 20 years, is associated
with Ace Booking Company, serves as secretary for the local musicians union and
is involved with the Jazz Jamboree every year.

Lest it be thought that the pavilion was noted only for its dances, it should
be noted that roller skating was an event that was also widely enjoyed and many
a Beulah resident received his first black-and-blue knees and elbows while
learning to roller skate at the pavilion.

The large column in the center of the room gave beginners a place to break
their fall a bit, and the "piped-in" music that was a part of the pavilion's
later years made it possible to vary and perfect many styles of skating. It was
a great place for families and youth to meet and have fun.

In its early years the pavilion also hosted many political gatherings, since it
was the only place in town big enough to do so. When baseball was king in
Beulah, it was the custom to hold wrestling and boxing matches in conjunction
with the baseball tournaments, and many of those events were also held at the
pavilion. Free wedding dances were commonplace and many special promotions
were held, such as the Thanksgiving Eve Dance of 1947, during which five live
turkeys were given away as door prizes. The only catch was that the winners had
to catch the turkeys first, after they were released inside the hall!

When events at the pavilion were in progress, there were those who thought that
the fun to be had inside the building was nothing compared to the fun that
could be had outside--in the parking lot.

"Oh sure, there was a lot going on outside too," says Adam Keller, longtime
resident of Beulah and the last owner of the pavilion. " Cars filled up the
parking lot and were often lined up along the highway. The parking lot used to
be much bigger, but when the new bridge was built in the 60's the highway was
raised about five feet and that made the parking lot smaller."

Keller says there were plenty of fist fights and car races in the parking lot
and along the highway next to it, while the more sedate patrons found it a
comfortable place to visit with their friends during the cool summer evenings.

During the early years of the pavilion, Wally Kittler remembers that the
parking lot was the place where a bottle of home brew could be bought from a
bootlegger and many a merrymaker kept a bottle stashed under his coat.

The pavilion had its own power plant, since in those days the electric companies
refused to go outside city limits, where the pavilion was located. This
provided yet another opportunity for merrymakers to have some fun, and Kittler
remembers that the lights were often dimmed by practical jokers tampering with
the power source and boiler.

Some Beulah residents have memories of the pavilion that are more special than
others. Fred and Betty Hausauer of Zap have been married for 29 years, and the
first time they met was at a New Year's Eve Dance at the pavilion when Betty
was 15 years old. They were later married and had their wedding reception at the
Dreamland.

Betty Hausauer remembers that social events were handled quite differently in
those days. "When we were kids we went to dances with older brothers and
sisters, so we learned how to dance and socialize when the adults were present
too," she says. "The Dreamland was a good place to go. Because of the shape,
you could dance around in a circle, and I remember how well it was decorated."

Yes, if walls could talk, the old Dreamland Pavilion could have told quite a
story. It would be a story of first loves, wedding dances, roller skating
memories, wrestling matches, practical jokers, bootleggers, fistfights, car
races and some fancy dancers. It would be a story of a people that grew up
along with their town and spent their playful moments at a place called the
Dreamland Pavilion.

Rags Thelander--Beulah's Renaissance woman

When Clare Boothe Luce died in 1987, Time magazine called her "the preeminent
Renaissance woman of the Century." And so it seems, if the timbre of a life is
measured by honors and glory. At 34 she had understudied Mary Pickford; been a
suffragette flying gliders; and the cheeky managing editor of Vanity Fair.

Luce's detractors believed she got everything she wanted. It was only at the
end of her life, when she was alone in her apartment, that some friends began
to wonder if, for all her ambition and power, it might have occurred to Clare
that she had got things slightly wrong.

There are people who, with much less noise, get it right. One of those was
Beulah's Rags Thelander.

If there was a Renaissance woman in Beulah's cultural life, it was Thelander.
"More a liker than a disliker, better at putting things together than taking
things apart, a very positive lady in love with life" are some descriptions of
her. She knew where she was going and exactly how to get there, and along the
way she collected, besides an array of accomplishments, a considerable number
of friends.

        Die Deutsche Stammhalter Chapter of the Germans from Russia Heritage
        Society is a very active heritage preservation group in Beulah.

        Though the underground mines are long gone, remnants surface
        occasionally as in these sinkholes the Public Service Commission
        reclaims. Beulah Beacon photo.

Ragnhild (pronounced "Runghild," roll the R if you like" Jelstrup was born Feb.
20, 1906 at Greenbush, MN to Dr. Marcus Frederick Christian Bang Jelstrup and
Andrea Haabjorn. Jelstrup was a physician/pharmacist and moved the family
frequently following his profession, and Thelander graduated in 1924 from
Petersburg High. She attended the University of North Dakota, where she was
elected to Phi Beta Kappa, member of Alpha Pi International Fraternity. In
1928, Thelander graduated with a degree in home economics and German.

After graduation, she taught in New Salem until the UND dean of languages asked
her to teach German at Grand Forks High School. She did, but not for long. She
had met Carlyle Thelander in New Salem and on July 27, 1933, they were married.

According to son Charles, Thelander was a "white-gloves" lady before she met
Carl. A ride in a sleigh with her father to visit patients was all the
"outdoors" she had done. She had been taught "there was a right and there was a
wrong," cultivated to be a "proper thank-you-very-much" sort.

Yet she could be surprisingly flexible; her honeymoon was spent in a canoe in
northern Minnesota. Through Carl, she developed a deep, abiding love of the
outdoors, became an avid hunter and camper. Her favorite spot, besides her
garden, was the family place at Lake Sakakawea, where the family still holds
Rags annual New Year's picnic.

Friend JeAnne Selby's first camping experience was with Thelander. "She had this
large Ford station wagon, which we slept in. And in the morning she got up too
early to talk about, marched down to the river and filled a huge enamel
coffeepot full of river water. I thought, 'Oh, no! Surely we aren't going to
drink that!' We were, and we did. She made coffee out of it, and it was the
best I ever tasted," Selby recalled.

Charles recalls Thelander's last boat ride on the lake in 1987 with amusement
and amazement. "We were 20 miles out on the water when the boat broke down. We
got it running but so slowly it took us five hours to get to Red Butte Bay,
where friends came to the rescue.

"For a while things were looking fairly serious and other passengers began to
demonstrate their lack of water-worthiness. In the middle of all this is a very
'not-to-be-concerned' 81-year-old lady calmly enjoying herself," Charles
recalled.

Even Thelander's favorite poem, "To A Waterfowl," by William Cullen Bryant,
rests heavily on a symbolic nature. According to Thelander's friend Merilynn
Liebelt, this poem might have been the metaphor for her life.

        Rags Thelander, a prominent figure in Beulah's history is best known
        as champion and stalwart supporter for the city's library first as a
        Women's Club project and then as a public library. Beulah Beacon photo.

Charles says Thelander was as heavily involved in bringing up their two
children as she was in community affairs, yet she never allowed a conflict of
interest. When her children reached school age, she resigned from the school
board.

Obviously there were high standards. "Oh, gosh, did she have high standards,"
laughed Charles. "Of course, I was the delinquent, so maybe I am not the one to
ask." His eyes twinkle and one is reminded of all the Tom Sawyers there ever
were. "High standards and dinner at a regular hour always. She was an excellent
cook and my buddies loved to come."

Honesty and education were her two prime motivators, mixed in with industry. "I
recall this especially when she took over the family business. There was a very
by-the-rules, regular, proper, thank-you-very-much way to run a business. If
she had been at the helm of our country's treasury, there'd be no deficit," he
said.

"She felt education was the absolute beginning of everything - not a how-to for
acquiring money, but a way of life."

After he married Rags, Carl became a partner in the RCU Store in Beulah, a
general mercantile.

When Carl died in 1965, Rags added running the store to her busy agenda. "She
didn't know how to run a business," explains Charles, "but what was that to
her?" She did what the Ben Franklin people said and ran the store alone until
Charles finished college in 1972, when they became a successful management team.

Her accomplishments, while she raised a family and worked full time, read like
several Who's Who resumes. She was a member of the Congregational Church, where
she taught Sunday school and was active in Ladies Aid. She was past matron of
the Order of Eastern Star, past member of the Chamber of Commerce and Country
Club, and member of the Woman's Club, serving as a local, district and state
officer. She served on the Small Business Administration board as a local
advisor, was active in the county historical society and the county fair arts
division. She was one of the people most responsible for the growth of the
Woman's Club Library, now the public library, serving on the board and as
librarian for many years. She was a long-time member of the Mothers Club, and,
along with Agnes Herman, was a tireless worker in preparing Beulah's hospital
building for an occupancy it never saw. She took great pleasure in welcoming
new people to town and making them feel at home. She read voraciously and loved
poetry; was active in the Woman's Club annual poetry contest. In the early
'40s, Thelander served on the school board. She was active in Beulah Boosters
and the golf club.

By contrast, Thelander never drove a car. Charles' eyes twinkle. "I can remember
driving the car with her as passenger and she began back-seat driving," Charles
recalled. "I asked her if she knew how to drive. She said no. And that was,
forever, the end of it. She could somehow discern what was worth the effort of
controlling and what was not."

Thelander made time for people, with a talent for intergenerational friendships.
Liebelt, more than 20 years younger, holds many warm memories.  "We had many
common interests and our age difference really was never an issue," smiled
Liebelt. "When Rags first came here, the area was composed of nearly all
German-Russians. There was this intense ethnic thing and you were not accepted
if you weren't the right nationality. I thought I'd have to learn German--this,
in America! - and we were two rebels attracted to one another."

Thelander was 100 percent Scandinavian, Liebelt half, both were UND graduates,
teachers and avid readers. "Getting new books for the library was an adventure."

Liebelt's daughter also connected with Thelander. "When Rags was dying, my
daughter called to find out how she was. She said she felt Rags had been an
example to all of us; full of enthusiasm, never complaining about her own
situation, simply aggravated that she couldn't walk right, that her body was in
the way. She was less fearful of her own impending death than she was
interested in others and their efforts to grow," said Liebelt.

Selby was 40 years Thelander's junior when they met, renting a room from her for
four years. "I would introduce her as my landlady and it wasn't long before she
made it clear that was not acceptable. So I called her my second mom. And
that's what she became," Selby said.

        Michael Schmidt enjoys the free kraut and wieners, a feed put on
        annually by the Beulah Chamber which has been on-going for more than
        20 years. Beulah Beacon photo.

"She was such a multifaceted person, with incredible energy and understandings,"
continued Selby. ''She was a fantastic conversationalist. She could talk to
absolutely anybody, discuss any topic. I remember her at the library - she
loved to give the first-graders their first library cards, just to see their
reactions and talk with them."

Among the things the two had in common were home ec degrees. Selby was
fascinated with Thelander's homemaking skills, including the way she set a
table.

"She had three sets of dishes," said Selby, "and she used all three. Most
people with multiple sets only use one, but not Rags. She used them all, even
for just her family and friends - of course, family and friends were high on
her list."

Selby was often incredulous at Thelander's accomplishments. "I know how she did
it," laughed Selby. "She never slept! She stayed up until 1 a.m., that's how
she got all her stuff done. Then I'll bet she read in bed another hour--she was
a voracious reader--before she went to sleep. And she was up at 6 a.m."

Charles recalls her "night owl" tendencies, too. "She really was enchanted by
what was going on in the world around her. Let's say I come home at 1 a.m., and
seeing the Northern Lights, decide to wake her up. She would be delighted," he
said.

"I absolutely adored the lady, yet we had our differences," Selby continues.
"She would give you the space to disagree. Maybe this is why she had friends of
such varying ages. That's not ordinary. She connected with everyone, regardless
of years."

Daughter-in-law Angie Thelander adds, "Heritage meant so much to her that she
traveled to Norway to her ancestral home of Trondheim three different times. She
kept up close contact with her various relatives, so close in fact that one
year a family of Norwegian relations came to spend Christmas with us."

Instead of seeing an American Christmas, "you name the Norwegian custom, we had
it. Rags was a stickler for tradition and had never celebrated Christmas
American-style," Angie said.

Thelander was a woman of definite ideas, sometimes even imperious, but still
open to the beautiful in the universe, willing to share it, able to convey it.
She wrapped herself in a rich web of connections and left a fabric of
impressions in the hearts of those she loved.

Thelander died Jan. 2, 1988. "You may not believe this, but I think my mother
willed herself to live until after the holiday season," said Charles quietly.
"I think she wanted us all to remember Christmas joyfully, not as the time when
Grandmother died."

When Clare Boothe Luce was dying from a brain tumor, as did Thelander, she was
alone, without loved ones to buoy her spirit. She had become an angry, bitter
woman. "You know, I have had a terrible life," she finally said. "I married two
men I really didn't like. My only daughter was killed in a car accident. My
brother committed suicide. Has my life been a life for anyone to envy?"

Thelander never made national news, never waltzed with Buckminster Fuller. Her
funeral was no celebrity event at St. Patrick's Cathedral. She only lived a
life as rich as Norwegian dessert and was mourned by those who loved her. Hers
was a life, not to envy, but to emulate.

And items too numerous to mention

It's one p.m. on a hot, cloudless, perfect North Dakota summer day. You can't
hear the soft whisper of grain nodding in the breeze, or the occasional low of
cattle, or even the distant buzz of farm machinery cultivating the fields; what
you hear is humming, punctuated by a sharp burst of laughter or a quick chuckle.

You fan yourself with the big sheet of paper you brought with you, which boldly
proclaims, "AND ITEMS TOO NUMEROUS TO MENTION," as you stroll around the
farmyard looking in the various boxes, bags and bins of items of all sizes,
shapes, descriptions, uses and stages of disrepair.

You stop by a concession booth and buy a pop to quench the thirst that suddenly
clutches your dry throat, and grin at the sticky-faced kids who are trying to
finish their ice cream before it melts off the stick.

Then, suddenly, everyone around you falls silent and begins to drift
purposefully toward a man climbing up in the back of the truck, trailing a
microphone.

This is what you're here for; the show is about to begin, and the name of the
show is AUCTION.

Auctions have long played a big part in the lives of people in North Dakota.
They're both a bane and a blessing; often, with a farm auction, it's a way to
raise as much money as possible off the place before moving to another area to
start fresh (often California or Arizona) . When an auction is used that way,
it robs North Dakota of its strongest and best asset--its people.

But for those who come to auctions - and there are great numbers of them who go
regularly, whether they buy or not, just because they like to look at the many
different kinds of merchandise, or they're looking for a particular item, or
they like the visiting with friends and neighbors and other auction-goers, or
the ubiquitous "items too numerous to mention" - they are a great blessing.

        Look at the merchandise, decide on your price limit, and put in your
        bid at any auction in the area. Beulah Beacon photo.

Need a part for that '47 washer? Maybe there's one at the auction. Looking for
a good wrench but at a good price? Try the auction. Need some furniture but
don't want to lay out a lot of bucks because the kids will be rough on it? No
doubt, you need an auction. Just want to visit a bit and while away a beautiful
afternoon in the sun? That's right, the auction's your best bet.

Each auction has its own character, its own flavor, its own atmosphere; as a
"selling off" of the effects of the family involved, each reflects the
character of that family.

Auctions hold the same standard items repeatedly - tools, tires, old electrical
gadgets, pictures, knicknacks and mismatched spoons.

But there's also the unique involved in each one; the antique tractor that
Grandpa never took out of the barn; the never-opened carton of French porcelain
service for 12; the highly polished and age-mellowed sturdy oaken table;
jewelry to outfit a queen, some real and some not so real; a cedar chest that
guards secrets of the hopes and dreams of some long-dead girl growing up on the
prairie; an old and well preserved Victrola.

You name it. Chances are, if it's not in this auction, it was in last week's,
or it'll be in next week's.

Many people use auctions as a source to fill out collections that are their
hobbies. Depression glass used to be plentiful at auction sales, but isn't
quite so available any more; miniature scale farm equipment is a big item. Now
and then a shoe last, dainty in a size 4, pops up. Collectors are often the
people who follow the auction circuit, looking for vintage pieces of almost
anything to add to their stores.

        Does this get auctioned off, too? There's no way to tell if you don't
        ask and no one's shy when looking for a bargain. Beulah Beacon photo.

There are different types of auctions and all are self explanatory: Household
auctions, farm auctions, ranch auctions, estate auctions, antique auctions and
on and on. Depending on the type, out-of-state folks often attend, particularly
antique dealers and those who seek antique farm equipment.

The auctioneer is more than a seller standing above the crowd crying his tune;
he has an interaction with his audience, with his bidders, that sometimes
reflects long acquaintanceship, sometimes a friendly antagonism as he tries to
squeeze out the most he can for any given item. In all cases, he's fun to watch
as he leads the audience through their paces.

Didn't find what you wanted this time, or maybe somebody out-bid you7 Come back
to the next one; there's always another one, and they all have "items too
numerous to mention."

Partners in progress

What were the changes Beulah saw during the impact construction years? What
sacrifices had to be made, and what advantages were gained? How did the city
cope with such rapid change, and what problems did it run into?

Each person who lived through those years has a different story to tell, but
from a city standpoint, probably no one is closer to the broad perspective
involved in telling the energy impact story than Beulah's mayor, Darold Benz.

Benz was elected mayor about the time the first shovelful of earth was turned
for the first of two units at Basin Electric's Antelope valley Station, which
was to be constructed side-by-side with the then-hypothetical gasification
plant. He guided Beulah through the construction years and, when Black Tuesday
saw the construction consortium abandon the gas plant project in 1985,
continued to guide Beulah through what has since been dubbed "negative impact."

Benz points out that Beulah didn't wait for energy impact to look to future
needs; before impact, in 1972, the Jaycees proposed building a civic center.
The progressive townspeople were in favor of the idea and the building became
reality a few years later. In addition, mill levy increases to support
education have been passed over the years, and Beulah's current school
facilities were built with little Energy Impact Office assistance.

That progressive attitude carried over into general support for coal development
when it came. The ease with which industry moved into the area probably sprang
partly from familiarity with and dependence on the coal industry, as the town
had lived with the Knife River Coal Mining Company's underground mine for some
four decades and many local residents had worked there.

Born and raised in Beulah, Benz recalls that the MDU power plant, fueled by
KRCMC's coal, was a central figure in the community. Softball players would go
by the Beulah plant to shower before heading home from a game, and in those days
Beulah's water quality was a far cry from the sparkling clean liquid of today.
When community members held a gathering, coffee was not made from city water;
it was brewed using a couple cups of coffee grounds tied in a cloth and placed
in a cream can full of water condensed from the power plant's steam - clear,
sweet, pure and, some still say, the best coffee there ever was.

Though KRCMC operated a strip mine outside of Beulah, the community had been
through a decade of stagnation when a 1971 study showed the possibility of
converting coal to energy on a large scale. Beulah had barely maintained its
population of 1,200, and surrounding towns were declining.

At some of the first meetings called to discuss coal development, Benz met Art
Seder, who was to become a key figure in Beulah's coal gasification plant,
following it from inception to reality. At the time Seder was employed by
Michigan-Wisconsin Pipeline Co., a firm interested in coal conversion.

        Arthur Seder, Jr., a staunch supporter and tireless mover for the
        gasification plant now located at Beulah, played a prominent part in
        the energy drama during most of the impact years.

Seder envisioned developing the technology to produce synthetic fuels from
lignite, thus giving the United States an alternative to dependence on Middle
Eastern oil, which was suddenly and painfully in very short, very expensive
supply during those years.

"It was an idea of Art Seder's and his original intent was that this
gasification plant would become a showplace. He wanted to show what can be done
with coal gasification, that it could be done, and it could be done in a small
town without corrupting the community and without bankrupting them financially.

"We all worked together. The goal was that we wanted a project everyone would
talk about for a long time, to look back on years later and say, 'It's been
good.' Throughout the years we've stood shoulder to shoulder with the industry
in the development of the resources here. We often used the term 'partners in
progress,' " said Benz.

Primary opposition to coal development came from landowners in the Dickinson and
Mott areas, those who, for the most part, owned the surface but not the rights
to the coal beneath the soil, Benz explained. He speculated that perhaps
because they didn't stand to gain from developing mineral resources, they
joined with environmentalists and others who opposed constructing large-scale
industrial plants in the western part of the state.

One group, which dominated the earlier meetings, was called the United
Plainsmen, Benz recalled. They adopted a scoop shovel as an emblem and showed
up at public meetings bearing on their shoulders the symbol of their
opposition. The Mercer County Landowners Association, later organized to
provide a forum for those disagreeing with resource development and presenting
concerns about the possible adverse environmental effects of large plants,
carried the opposition standard locally.

"We were all aware that this project would displace some farmers in the area.
And some were good, strong families that had been born and raised on those
farms, perhaps even homesteaded by their grandfathers. Financially it wasn't
such a bad deal for them to sell their land, but emotionally it was tough to
leave their farms. Some pulled up stakes and left the area entirely," Benz said.

One family displaced by energy development was that of Eugene Keller, who had a
farm near the plant site. Keller was one of those opposed to the proposed
construction of a gasification plant, and waged a two-year battle before
eventually selling the land and moving to Huff, south of Mandan. Floyd Weigum
was another; that family relocated to New Rockford. Both men had children who
were friends with Benz's children.

"It got a little tight once in a while," said Benz, "when you knew you were
going to be promoting an industry that would eventually displace families. But
to be realistic you had to look at the several hundred jobs you would be
creating for others in the area."

        Beulah mayor Darold Benz was convinced that good planning was the
        key to managing impact.

Relations between neighbors and friends with differing points of view sometimes
got touchy. Benz recalls running into a neighbor, who was negotiating about his
land with energy companies, one day and commenting about his new pickup. "Yes,
I guess you think it came from the coal  company," was the defensive reply.

Benz recalls with satisfaction the foresight of the city planning commission in
planning for orderly growth during construction, with its heavy influx of
workers; 2,000-plus at one point. Early on city officials visited boom sites
Langdon, ND (site of an anti-ballistic missile installation), and Wheatland, WY
(where a power plant was built), so they could learn first-hand from other
officials, fire chiefs and law enforcement officers what could be expected in a
"boom." Those trips brought forth recommendations for Beulah to handle its own
energy boom.

Based on its new knowledge, the city refused to commit funds to pay for
improvements made by housing developers. It was common for a developer to offer
to "do the city a favor" and construct needed housing if the city would
underwrite the cost of improvements. Because policies were in place when that
happened and the city fathers "hung tough," requiring developers to pay up
front, Beulah does not now have large areas of unoccupied developed lots for
which taxpayers must pay improvement costs.

The city implemented policy regarding real property valuations which, while not
popular, proved beneficial. "There were many objections to the assessment of
lots for mobile homes at $120 a lot, and some of our own people howled about
the value when compared to neighboring towns. But we determined that the amount
was necessary to prevent a financial burden and were able to maintain, and in
the last two years even to lower, the valuations here," said Benz.

Benz recalled skirmishes over coal industry taxation. Along with then-state
senator Bob Stroup and House majority leader Earl Strinden, local
representatives created a coal severance and conversion tax package that was
acceptable to both industry and to coal country communities.

"We did continue with a planning commission and as a city council we have
evaluated over the years what we needed to do in our growth, how and where to
develop a residential and business areas. So we've had orderly growth
throughout this whole time," said Benz.

The city fathers have used impact funds through grants which have helped pay for
such city improvements as better water and sewer treatment (no more coffee from
condensate, though some would say that's a pity), better police and
fire-fighting facilities and equipment and more and larger snow removal
equipment, among others.

"Our immediate challenge for the next few years is to continue our efforts to
develop the by-products from the plant," Benz said. "Of course, first to ensure
a stable ownership for the plant," which was supposed to have been sold by
September, 1988.

Forming an "energy park" for the area adjacent the AVS plant brought interest
from High Country Rose, which proposed to build a greenhouse and heat it with
waste heat from AVS. Funds were allocated to promote further development, and
officials took other steps to attract employers to the area.

The focus may have had to shift a little, but it's no less sharp: Nothing but
progress and improvement will satisfy the wishes of Beulah's people or its city
fathers.

        A typical classroom from Beulah's early years.

Education was and is - important

The education of their children was of great importance to the German-Russian
immigrants who settled in the Beulah area. In the early days of Beulah there
were many rural school districts that brought education to the children of
those who tilled the prairies, and these country schools were usually one-room
buildings with a cloakroom, sometimes a small library and always an outhouse.

The teacher who taught at any country school had many other duties in addition
to the education of the students; she also was the janitor, health nurse,
school counselor and sometimes referee among students who sometimes were much
larger and stronger than she was.

In 1923, inexperienced rural teachers were paid $80 per month, while those with
experience were paid $100 per month. These salaries were set by the School
Officers' Association, which was composed of all the directors and clerks of
the rural school districts.

Rural school terms were not always nine months long, as they are now. The terms
were often shortened so that the children, especially the older boys, could
help their families with the planting and harvesting seasons.

One of the more difficult problems faced by the early rural school districts
was the German-English language barrier. There are many local residents who
recall attending their first day of school when they could speak only German
and their rural teacher could speak only English! With time, the passing of
generations and the determination of many German mothers, the students learned
to speak the English language and it began to be accepted in every aspect of
the society they lived in.

Eighth-grade examinations and graduation were an established part of the rural
school process, since the eighth grade was the finishing point for a student's
education. It wasn't until 1923 that Beulah graduated its first students from
high school. Thus, it became a difficult task to study for the exams, and
students often had to walk long distances to another school district to combine
with other students to take the exams, which were administered by a
representative of the County Superintendent of Schools.

Even after the advent of the high school educational system within Beulah, the
rural schools remained in force for many more decades. It became the custom to
hold the graduation ceremonies for the rural and city eighth graders in
conjunction with the graduation exercise for the high school seniors. In the
1960's, the rural school districts began to diminish in size and soon they
became almost obsolete.

        Beulah 's second school house, now called the old Legion Hall, was
        completed in 1918.

Beulah's pride and joy - its first school

In 1915, Beulah built its first schoolhouse, a little frame building that was
the pride and joy of the community. An entire day was set aside for the
dedication of the new structure, and dignitaries from around the state were
present to offer their congratulations to the citizens. The construction of the
school as a symbolic achievement for the town; it represented a yearning for
education and the beginnings of progress.

The school was built according to the latest state requirements and was
considered to be a very modern structure. At the time it was built it was part
of Spring Creek school district. On July 14, 1917, Beulah School District #27
was organized and the new district received this building as its share of the
Spring Creek school district property. The original school building was used by
the local school district until 1930.

The expansion of the Northern Pacific Railroad and the lure of western lands and
coal beds caused steady growth in Beulah, and by 1918 the Beulah school district
was again in need of additional classroom space. This prompted the construction
of the building now known as the Legion Hall, which is across the street from
the Beulah middle school. This school building was intended to be used as a
temporary structure until a more permanent building could be constructed. In
1918, the Legion Hall was built for $1,695. The principal was Katherine Barlow.
A year later Lawrence Williams became principal. Abbie Tyrell started teaching
primary grades in the above school house and continued to teach in the Beulah
school system for 22 years.

The officials of the school district wisely recognized they would need more
room for future expansion and they purchased the entire block #16 for their new
brick school house and started building in 1919. The first brick building in
Beulah was the building now called the Beulah middle school, which was finished
in 1920. It was considered quite an elaborate school for its day, for it had
four classrooms, a small library and an assembly room that could be partitioned
into two large classrooms. With the completion of this school, Beulah could
offer a four-year high school curriculum, and in 1923 the school graduated its
first high school class; Helen Moore and Lee Perkins. By 1925, this building
was also overflowing with students and the school district had to use the old
frame buildings once again.

The first addition to the brick school was completed at a cost of $38,000 in
1930. Leonhard was the architect and J.C. Beattie was the contractor. This new
addition added seven new classrooms, a large assembly room and a large gym
which for many years was considered to be the finest in the area. This new
addition allowed the school district to go on without building for about 19
years.

Following World War II, the field of education saw many changes in teaching
methods and curriculum. Students were taking a greater interest in science and
math courses, more of the rural youngsters were going to high school and the
Beulah school kept pace with the trends. In 1949 the second addition was added
to the brick building. This addition housed the home economics, vocational
agriculture, and the science department. This addition was built by Chase
Construction at a cost of $45,809.

In 1953 a new gymnasium was added with a seating capacity of 1,200. The gym also
serves as an auditorium with the stage located on the south end. New locker
rooms and dressing rooms were built in this part of the building. Half the old
gym was converted into a music and band room and the other half into a
hot-lunch facility.

The third floor on the west wing and the gym were built at a cost to the
taxpayers of $166,287. This addition also provided four additional classrooms
for junior and senior high use.

Ten years went by. The school district was not under any indebtedness and the
building was bursting at its seams, so in 1963 the school district asked the
voters to approve another building project.

        Beulah High School.

The present Beulah High School

The present high school is located three blocks north of the middle school and
has been in use since the fall of 1964. Arlo C. Beattie, the son of the
contractor who built the first addition, was the architect and Lunn
Construction was the contractor. The estimated cost of the new school was
$420,000 and there was also a $30,000 remodeling project on the building now
called the middle school.

When the new high school opened, the Beulah school system was operated on the
8-4 program: the first eight grades were in the middle school and the four high
school grades were in the high school building. There were an additional three
teachers hired to bring the faculty to 24 instructors. The 1964 school budget
was $212,000.

In 1976 a junior high wing was added to the west side of the high school and a
new lunchroom and vocational agriculture department was added to the east side.
The new vo-ag department became more diversified and offered courses in
carpentry, mechanics and the traditional shop courses.

Continued expansion-- the elementary school

In 1978 the city of Beulah as well as the school system was feeling the
pressures of energy impact, and the school district found it necessary to build
a new elementary building just north of the present high school. Grades one
through three were housed in this facility. To expand the sports program, a new
gymnasium was added and annexed to the high school. The multi-purpose gym
provides areas for physical education classes, wrestling, weight training and
concerts as well as basketball. The seating capacity in the gym is between
2,000 and 2,400 people. The cost of the gym and elementary building was
$2,925,000.

In 1982 a wing was added to the west side of the elementary building, which
provided additional space for kindergarten students. Music room and additional
classrooms were also part of the expansion project. The multi-purpose room was
remodeled in the high school to provide a band and choir room, which resulted in
more practice room for individual students.

Presently, the new elementary building houses grades K through four. The old
elementary building, now called the middle school, handles grades five through
seven, while the junior high and high school contain grades eight through
twelve. Each building has areas of physical education, music and a hot-lunch
room. Each school is provided with special-needs personnel such as speech
therapists, learning disabilities instructors and a basic skills teacher.

The 1987-88 school budget was $3,023,320 and the projected income was
$3,232,000. The Beulah school district is planning to construct a greenhouse and
commons area and a studio for interactive television along with renovating the
middle school kitchen.

        Beulah Elementary School.

The National Merit Scholarship Program

Students in their junior year of high school know the importance of the National
Merit Scholarship Program. In 1987, 1.2 million of the nation's high school
juniors participated in the testing. The competition is tough and only the
academically excellent survive.

The first step of the national competition is the Preliminary Scholastic
Aptitude Test/National Merit Scholarship Qualifying Test (PSAT/NMSQT). This
exam measures reasoning ability. Students are presented with verbal and
mathematical information and asked to reason with it. Students with a
designated score on this test earn the title of "Commended Student." Once
commended students are honored, advanced selection procedures begin.

The second elimination round reduces the ranks considerably and a group of
qualifying students then advance to the status of semifinalist. The final steps
which, when completed with a high qualifying score, will earn the distinction
of being named a National Merit Scholar, include: completion of the Scholastic
Aptitude Test, a test which confirms their academic performance; an academic
record of consistent high performance in grades nine through twelve;
recommendation by a school official; submission of a Merit Scholarship
application form.

The National Merit Scholarship program began in 1956, and since then more than
100,000 students have met the rigorous standards applied in the merit
scholarship selection process and have won scholarship awards worth
approximately $310 million. Throughout the years Beulah High School has been
honored with some 10 students who have been recognized as a Commended Student
or a National Merit Scholar. The latest was Chris Hoper as a National Merit
Scholar and Jon Kulas as a Commended Student in 1988.

The number of Beulah students who have achieved distinction in the Merit
Scholarship program indicates the high academic achievement that is
characteristic of Beulah High School.

        Beulah school superintendent Dale Gilje.

The strengths of the Beulah school system

I would have to say that the most obvious strength of the Beulah school is the
constant support of the community, said superintendent Dale Gilje. "The people
of Beulah are committed to a good education for their children and you just
can't improve on a strength like that."

The support of the community is shown in many ways, says Gilje. "The amount of
scholarship monies from the community and organizations shows how they feel
about their school, and the manner in which the school functions are attended
and supported by the parents is also an indication," he says. Gilje says that
even before he became Beulah's superintendent in 1974, he recognized the
commitment to education that was evident in the community.

"In this community there is a history of a demand for a strong academic
background that is recognized throughout the area," he says.

Gilje says the residents have been flexible throughout the impact years, which
gave the Beulah school district many challenges, and he feels the community
deserves to be commended for how well they provided the needed facilities and
services for the additional students who arrived during impact. "We had good
planning in those times because the community assisted us in making decisions
to meet our demands," he says. The support of the community plus a dedicated
teaching staff make a combination that is the cornerstone of the Beulah school
system.

Evidence of long-term support is shown by the fact that a building bond issue
has never been defeated by the Beulah voters. The residents have always
recognized and supported the need for continued expansion to meet the growing
needs of the community.

A commitment to academic excellence has resulted in the Beulah school system
holding the highest accreditation rating in the area, according to Gilje. "We
are presently at a Level II accreditation, and we are the only one in the
area," he says. "We are also the only North Central (Association of Colleges
and Schools) accredited school in the area."

How has the focus of education changed since Beulah's golden anniversary in
1964? "I believe that the focus of education has changed greatly in the last 20
years," says Gilje. "The nature of education used to be specialization, and the
schools attempted to instruct students in specific subject areas like math and
science, for example. Now the focus is coming around to an emphasis on the
basics of education and the belief that it is a more traditional structured
setting that will result in the best academic education for the student. You
could call it going back to the three R's."

Gilje says that schools can no longer teach just facts and expect to produce
students who can cope with the present world. "Students today need a wide
variety of information and abilities, not just in the academic sense, but also
in their abilities to interact with one another and their abilities to cope
with conflicts. They need to understand different cultures and to accept the
global realities of the world," he says.

French Club (Le Cercle Francais)

The French Club was organized in 1984 by high school French instructor Peg
Miller. The most outstanding achievement of the group has been a summer
excursion to Paris, France in 1985. In addition to Miller, her son, Erik, and
traveling companion Merilynn Liebelt, the following BHS students enjoyed the
memory that would last a lifetime: Mark Cazalas, Donna Crain, Denise Darby and
Julie Sparks. The Beulah students traveled with a group of students from Hazen.

While in France, the group found the sight of Paris at night to be breathtaking
and the immensity of the palace and grounds of Versailles were impressive. A
concept of history that could never be learned from a book and an understanding
of the culture and language of the French people were obtained when the
students were immersed into the French-speaking world.

The club also visited the French Language Village in Bemidji, MN in 1987 and
plans another trip to Paris and London in July of 1989.

The Future Farmers of America have been very active in Beulah High School. They
have received numerous awards including a superior chapter rating every year
since 1984.

They have also received a 100 percent plus Chapter since 1984.

Leann Erickson and Aneica Hafner have both received special honors in this club.
Leann was the state secretary and Aneica was state sweetheart.

the fair have been top mechanics in the state (1987); top mechanics exhibiting

place (1981).

Some other awards include numerous gold placing and district winners, various
state farmer degree winners, and top chapter at McLean and Mercer County fairs,
1984-88.

Beulah Adult Education Program

The Adult Education Program has been in place for the past 13 years. Diane
Wallender was the coordinator for 10 years, followed by Karen Brook. The Beulah
program is a satellite of the Dickinson School District and is promoted by the
Beulah School District as a method for area residents to complete a high school
degree, brush up on basic skills or become a part of the literacy program.

Students wishing to complete a high school degree must study and prepare in five
areas: math, science, social studies, reading and writing skills. They are
tested on each area and must obtain a designated score to obtain their degree.

The basic skills program is a convenience for those wishing to review an area to
enhance a job skill, study for citizenship or study English as a second language.

The literacy program is an attempt to help anyone who wants to learn to read.
Tutors are selected and the learning process is completed within the program.

The Beulah Community Education Program

Community Education is a program for the education and enrichment of the entire
community and an attempt is made to offer a balance in the classes offered. The
instructors are chosen on the basis of their education and experience and their
ability to conduct a meaningful classroom experience.

The community education program has a grassroots beginning which evolved from
several classes that were being taught to community members using the Beulah
school as a meeting facility. The Beulah school district soon recognized the
need for a more complete program, and the present class structure began in 1983
with Beverly Johnson as its first coordinator.

The community education program offers a series of classes twice a year, in the
fall and early winter. Classes are open to Beulah residents as well as those
from the surrounding area interested in education or enrichment. The program
makes an attempt to offer classes that represent several broad topics of
learning and enrichment, such as business skills, cooking classes, craft
classes, safety/health, parenting, money management and hobbies and skills.
Each session offers from 15-30 classes of varying topics and the registrations
from the classes are used to pay the instructors' fees.

The current coordinator for the community education program is Jo Ann Miller.
She has a degree in secondary education and her responsibilities with the
program include locating instructors, arranging publicity and facilities at the
school for the classes, supervising registration and class fees, paying
instructors and notifying students of class changes and cancellations.

The Alpha Enrichment Program

The Alpha Enrichment Program began in 1984 and focuses on students who could
use an extra challenge or enrichment they normally would not receive in the
regular classroom experience. Students are recommended by their teachers and
administrators and must have good academic standing.

Colleen Compton, who coordinates this program, became interested in an
enrichment program after seeing methods and results of a summer school program
for talented students at Minot State College Lab School. While Compton observed
the classes and saw the program's effectiveness, she decided to work toward a
similar program for Beulah students. In December of 1984 she was hired by the
Beulah school board to coordinate such a program for Beulah students.

The Alpha Enrichment Program is a mentor-assisted program that allows anyone in
the community with a skill, talent or knowledge to share it with a group of
students who have a similar interest. The classes meet after school or in early
evening.

The program was first introduced to the fifth through seventh graders. Classes
offered at the middle school level include creative writing, art, puppetry,
math games and brain teasers, computers, drawing, painting, beginning chess,
CPR, geology, conversational Spanish, and others.

During the fall of 1987 classes were also offered to the third and fourth
grades, including beginning Spanish, Scienceworks, drawing, creative writing
and Junior Great Books.

As coordinator, Compton locates mentors, arranges the facilities for the
classes and notifies parents and students of class listings. Compton has an
elementary teaching degree and can often be found teaching one of the classes
offered in the program.

Drama Club

Drama club consists of 30-50 members per year. This group is responsible for
presenting a fall and spring drama production.

During the last few years such productions as "Oklahoma," "The Sound of Music,"
"Heaven Can Wait," and "Gramercy Ghost" have been done.

The renovation of the old stage in the middle school gym was a great improvement
made in 1984-85.

The club is advised by Sherry Houdek.

Senior High Acalympics

The Acalympic academic interschool competition was started by the principals of
the I-94 Conference high schools in 1985. It has been held in Center High
School each year in the month of November.

Each high school brings a team of five students in grades 10-12, who work
together to answer questions in the areas of math, science, social studies,
language arts, current events and various electives.

The top three teams advance to a lightning round to answer more questions and to
determine who receives the first-, second- and third-place trophies.

The Beulah team placed fourth in 1985, second in 1986, and second in 1987.

Music Boosters

The Music Boosters of the Beulah public schools became a formal organization on
Oct. 28, 1986. The purpose of the group is to arouse and maintain interest in
music, to lend all possible support, both moral and financial, to the music
programs of the schools, and to cooperate with those in charge of the music
departments and the administration to help make the music departments at all
three schools the best they can be.

The original officers were co-presidents, Janice and Terry Towers; vice
president, Susan Legg; secretary, Colleen Compton; and treasurer Joan Schauer.
These officers and the three music teachers meet regularly to plan activities
and offer assistance.

It is impossible to state the size of this organization because all parents of
music students are considered boosters along with teachers and others in the
community who show interest and are great supporters. Volunteers are recruited
for specific projects.

        Kayla Duerr participates in a hula hoop contest during the 50's-60's
        concert sponsored by the Music Boosters.

The first year activities included serving lunch and providing dessert to
students attending the choral clinic, playing one game of bingo at boys'
basketball games as a fundraiser, collecting donations at music concerts,
conducting a raffle and helping with candy sales. Four scholarships for half
tuition to International Music Camp at the Peace Garden were given to two
students at the high school and two at the middle school for the summer of 1987.

The school year of '87-88 saw many fund-raising activities in preparation for
the high school choir trip to Colorado Springs in June of '88. The club sold
Miner pins and sweatshirts, raffle tickets, held a rummage sale, worked at
concession stands for the choral clinic and PT0 Carnival, conducted bingo games
at basketball half-times, collected donations at concerts, helped with candy
sales, had a booth at the spring craft fair and staged a 50's-60's dinner in
conjunction with the spring concert. The club hoped to give the four
scholarships to music camp again in 1988, aid the choir financially on its
trip, provide partial payment for a new mallet instrument for the elementary
school and to give some financial assistance to the state centennial band
student.
