        The 1987-88 Beulah High School choir and director, Kathy Enervold.

The Beulah School Choirs

The Beulah school has an eighth grade choir, honor choir, senior high concert
choir and swing choir. In recent years, the size and appearance of the school
choirs have been greatly enhanced, largely due to the efforts of director Kathy
Enervold. The choirs have grown in number and the high school choir members now
wear tuxedos and long gowns for their performances, which contributes to the
dynamics of the performance.

The middle school honor choir includes honor students who must maintain their
grade average to sing with the group. They have performed at many community
functions and have been a welcome addition as an after-dinner musical group
numerous times. The eighth grade choir is a large and enthusiastic group which
promises to provide many senior high choir members in upcoming years. The senior
high concert choir and the swing choir have consistently received a star rating
at regional musical festivals for many years. The concert choir also received
the Outstanding Choir Award at regional competition in 1986 and also in 1988.
Several choir members have received individual honors, such as being named to
the UND Honor Choir and the North Dakota All-state Choir.

In June of 1988, the high school choir attended a national musical festival,
"Music Maestro, Please," in Colorado Springs, CO. The choir received a superior
rating for its performance, something only seven percent of schools receive
nationally. The festival included four days of competition, clinics, rehearsal
time and some sightseeing events, including Pike's Peak. It is the goal of the
school choirs to attend such a national festival every four years.

        Janell Reich, participant in North Dakota Centennial Band.

Beulah High School Band

Beulah High School's concert band has received a #1 rating in three of the past
six years. It also was selected as outstanding brass group in the 1986 district
contest. The band has marched in the Fall Festival parade for the past five
years and has made several tours to area schools in the past six years.

The stage band has been honored by receiving a #1 rating for the past six
years. Both of these groups are presently conducted by Tom Mandigo.

Janell Reich, a Beulah High School junior, was selected to play in the North
Dakota Centennial Band which will perform for the state's celebration in 1989.
Reich was one of 200 North Dakota students selected to be a part of the elite
group which will comprise the band. A seven-year student of the alto saxophone,
Reich was selected through taped auditions by adjudicators who evaluated all
the tapes submitted on each instrument. Reich played part of a sonatina and a
solo, "Passe Pied," by Claude Debussy.

The Centennial Band, organized by the high school band directors in the state,
performed throughout North Dakota during the state's centennial year in 1989.
The Rose Bowl Parade in Pasadena, CA, was one of the highlights of the
performances and culminated a national tour planned for Dec. 25-Jan. 4, 1989.
Other performances for the Centennial Band included an appearance at the
official opening ceremony of the North Dakota Centennial on November 2 and in
the State House on the first day of the 1989 Centennial Legislature.

Janell is the daughter of Ted and Norma Reich, Beulah.

High school sports

There is perhaps no other area within the school that is more enthusiastically
supported than that of high school sports. Within the community of Beulah,
there is a great deal of pride in the accomplishments of our athletes. Over the
years our community has gained a reputation for consistently producing teams
and individuals who take pride in their ability to be able to compete
athletically.

High school sports

1988 was a banner year for high school athletics as far as the Miners were
concerned. The Miners were considered to be a favorite as the Class B all
sports-champion by Steve Thomas of the Bismarck Tribune sports staff,
indicating that Beulah High School had a successful all-around sports season.

        Action from this Beulah-Hazen basketball game found the usual
        high-spirited competition that always exists between the two rivals.
        Left to right are Kelly Heier, David Lausen, Michael Heihn and Todd
        Wagner.

Tom Petrik's cross country teams started out Beulah's year in good fashion,
finishing fifth in the boys meet and sixth in the girls. Doug Olson's football
team advanced to the first round of the 11-man playoffs before losing 45-28 to
eventual state runner-up Kenmare and finishing 6-3.

Joe Bren took the Miner girls basketball team to the regional finals before a
54-42 loss to Watford City left them with a 19-4 record.

Coach Dave Stuart's wrestlers finished eighth in the state and Olson's boys
basketball squad went 18-6, bouncing back from a 77-62 semifinal loss to Crosby
Divide County to take third in the Region 7 tournament.

Connie Schmidt's girls volleyball team finished second to Park River in the
all-state invitational, giving Beulah points in seven of a possible nine
sports. The two sports in which Beulah did not place were nine-man football and
gymnastics, neither sport is offered at the school.

After a 98th place finish among the state's Class B schools in 1981-82, the
Miners advanced to 77th in 1982-83, leaped all the way to 12th in 1983-84,
improved to fifth in 1984-85 and were third the next two years after that. The
athletics and coaches of Beulah High School, according to a May 1 article in
the Bismarck Tribune, are "sitting on top of the Class B Athletic world"

State athletic titles

Six basketball teams from Beulah have competed in the state basketball
tournament, a record to be proud of. The 1938, 1949, 1951, 1970 and 1984 teams
participated in the prestigious state tournament.

The 1938 state tournament found two former state champions in the field as eight
teams gathered in Minot for the sixth annual State Class B Basketball
Tournament: Fairmont, the 1933 winner and the 1936 champion, Lakota, were
joined by Bismarck St. Mary's, Minot St. Leo's, Stanley, Beulah, Enderlin and
Bowman.

Undefeated Lakota, with 26 straight victories, and St. Leo's were the
pre-tournament favorites. The Beulah team was coached by R.J. Stegmeier. St.
Mary's and Fairmont opened the first round at 3:00 in the afternoon and the
Saints prevailed 39-32. In the afternoon's second game, Stanley built up a 18-7
half-time advantage over Beulah and went on to a 31-18 victory. The scoring
leader for Beulah was Harold Bates with 7.

In the evening round of the 1938 tourney, St. Leo's defeated Beulah with a
score of 46-18. Consolation play on Friday saw the Miners defeat Fairmont by a
score of 15-14. Joe Muhlhauser led Beulah with six points. In the final round
of consolation play, Fairmont prevailed over Bowman and in the battle for fifth
place, Enderlin stopped Beulah 38-36 in overtime. Wayne Murray pumped in 24
points for Beulah and was named on the second all-tournament team. St. Leo's
captured the state title with a 32-27 victory over Stanley.

        The 1986 Beulah Miners state track champions.

The 1949 team that participated in the state tournament at Minot placed fourth.
Jerome Helvik was named to the All State Team. In 1952, the Beulah basketball
team that went to state defeated Lisbon in the first round of play with a score
of 49-38, lost to Bottineau 54-52 and then defeated Beach 48-40, to place third
in the state.

In 1956, the Miners' baseball team earned another coveted state title.

The 1984 Beulah basketball team entered the state tournament with an undefeated
record after beating Crosby-Divide County 57-49 in the finals of the Region 7
basketball tournament in Williston. Their 23-0 record fell in first-round
action when they were defeated by the Hillsboro Burros 64-45. In the first of
two consolation rounds, Beulah lost to Towner 63-60. In the last consolation
round, Beulah defeated the Kindred Vikings 93-70 to earn seventh place in the
state tourney. Beulah guard Mark Aanderud was named to the All-Tournament Team.

The first ever state boys' track title was won by the Miners in 1986. The
girls' team finished third at the state meet. Both teams were coached by Tom
Petrik. The boys' team had a fourth place finish in the 1600 meter run, a third
in the 800 and fourths in the 400 and 1600. The teams were made up of Jeff
Rhodes, Mike Aanderud, Mark Lausen, Tom Dallman and Matt Kivisto. Greg Kuch won
four second places, in the 100, 200,400 and 800 meter runs. Tom Petrik received
the Coach of the Year award.

In 1987, both the boys' and girls' track teams won the state championships
aided by student athletes, the performance of Greg Kuch and Chris Hoper.

        The 1987 girls state track champions.

Beulah's boys ran away with the title, running up 85 points to second place New
Town's 49. The girls had a long lead as well, with 50 team points to Center's
second place finish of 38. In addition, Greg Kuch captured the boys' Class B
Athlete of the Year award and Beulah track coach Tom Petrik received his second
Coach of the Year honors. Kuch led the way with three first place finishes.
Mark Lausen and Lawrence Anderson collected 18 points in the discus and Jason
Pulver brought home a third in the long jump. The Beulah relay team of Kent
Jaeger, Kip Jaeger, Chuck Nicoli, and Matt Kivisto set a new record in the 3200
meter relay with a time of 8:10.56. Chris Shereck brought home a second place
for the girls in the discus and shot put, with 128'1" and 38'2". Chris Hoper
placed fourth in the 300 hurdles. Hoper also placed first in the 100-yard dash,
400 yard-dash and was part of the winning 1,600 relay team: Kristi Knodel,
Neelam Trividi, Ranae Schiltz. 1988 was the third consecutive year the Beulah
Miner boys brought home a state track title by running up a decisive 74 team
points. Two new meet records were set, in the discus and 1600 meter relay. With
a new record of 3:26.78, the relay team was Jeff Rhodes, Kent Jaeger, Randy
Helm and Matt Kivisto. Lawrence Anderson set a new record in discus with a
distance of 168'11".

The Beulah girls track team also brought home a second consecutive state title
in 1988. Chris Hoper, named the most valuable girl athlete at the close of the
meet, scored 40 of the total 54 points earned by her team in defending their
state crown. Hoper took first in the 300 yard hurdles, and the 100, 200 and 400
meter runs. She set a new meet record in the 300 hurdles and a new Class B and
overall record of 25.65 in the 200 meter dash. The girls relay team of Kristi
Knodel, Stacy Schnaidt, Krista Dallman and Jus Hoper placed second.

Coach Tom Petrik was again honored with Coach of the Year award.

A salute to the Beulah school athlete

As the high school expanded, the need of varying types of athletic activities
became more evident, and additional sports competitions were added to the
curriculum. Wrestling was first introduced in Beulah in the year 1960, and at
the present time, the program reaches down into the elementary grades, and has
produced many high school state qualifiers. A track program for girls was
introduced in 1966 and the fruits of that labor became evident in later years.

The state distinctions earned by the athletes of Beulah are indeed noteworthy,
and there have been numerous other titles, awards and honors earned by a
multitude of athletes from the community over the span of 75 years. However, in
its finest form, high school athletics is not intended to be merely a vehicle
to obtain a laurel or ensure the victory, but rather a means of using physical
activity to improve the student's ability to increase his or her
self-confidence, endurance and team cooperation.

A salute to the Beulah school athlete means to salute to a young, man or woman
who participated in basketball, track, golf, volleyball, football, wrestling,
cheerleading or drill team, whether in 1914 or 1989. It is a salute that is
equal in meaning to a state qualifier or a second grader struggling to learn
the basics of wrestling. The athletes of the Beulah School have consistently
brought honors to our town and their day-to-day efforts are characteristic of
the people who will one day be the leaders of our community.

        Tom Petrik, state track coach of the year, 1987 and 1988.

Beulah Alliance Church

At the peak of the Great Plains project, Dan and Rachel Kramer were appointed by
the Rocky Mountain District of the Christian and Missionary Alliance to begin a
new Alliance church through a bi-vocational church-planting ministry.

The first church service began in November of 1983 with three people. By July
1984, 17 people met in the pastor's home. With such a congregation the church
was moved to the New Frontier Inn conference room. An additional room was
rented for a children's church ministry. Soon another room was needed. Only a
few months later the congregation was again moved, this time to a building on
the corner of Highway 49 and Seventh Street. Forty-five people attended the
first anniversary celebration of the newest church in Beulah.

Like other congregations the Alliance Church lost many people as people lost
jobs. In July of 1986 only a handful of people were left. God blessed as new
families began attending. Once again, the Alliance Church has about 25 people
who call her their church. Estimates of the size of the church, if people had
not moved, are about 70 in attendance, and that in only four years.

Some of the people who have faithfully attended the church are: Bonnie Thompson,
Betty Herbst, Lance and Kim Sabot, Bruce and Judy Schael, Lars Painter, Kelly
Doll, Val and Sonja Lundin, Marc Thompson, Anita Evermann-Gibbs, Mike and Peg
Miller, Toni Hoff, Marie Armbrust, Ted and Melinda Chick, Ron and Sue Kuhn,
Jeff and Carolee Halvorson, Pat and Anna Marie Baughn, Linda Aguilar, Robb
Roberson, Randy and Elaine Morris, Chris Paulson and their families.

The Beulah Alliance church has faithfully ministered God's Word through
community Bible studies, newspaper, radio, children's ministries, youth
ministries and church functions. Truly, Beulah is better with this addition.
And the Beulah Alliance Church will continue to seek to do God's will to
benefit a fine city.

Most recently the congregation has moved to the Seventh-day Adventist Church
facilities. Pastor Kramer also was ordained on Sept. 23, 1987 and left in early
1988 to fulfill a long-term goal of being a missionary to China.

        Beulah Baptist Church

Beulah Baptist Church

Pastor John Miller of Baptist Temple Church in Mandan led the people of his
church to begin a mission in the Beulah area. It started as a Bible study in
the basement of a home in Beulah in the summer of 1978. Ron Moore was called as
pastor from Texas.

Land was purchased at the corner of Ninth Street and Highway 49 and the present
church facility was built debt-free in 1979 by the generous donations of
Southern Baptists from Texas, Kentucky and other states. Donations were
received from local persons also. Countless hours of volunteer labor built the
building.

When the church began in 1978 it was known as "The Coal Field Mission." From
1979-1982 it was called "The Beulah Baptist Chapel." On May 15, 1982, the
status of the mission was upgraded to a church. Since then it has been known as
Beulah Baptist Church. Jim Eller was called as pastor in August of 1980.

Peak membership during "the boom" of 1983-1984 was approximately 100 members.
Present membership is about 50. We have served people from as far as Washburn
to the east, Golden Valley to the west and approximately 15-20 miles to the
north and south.

We are proud to be a part of this community and look forward to God's blessings
as we go forward into the future.

        Church of God - Robert L. Burget, pastor.

The Church of God

The Church of God, Beulah, ND, had its beginning in Golden Valley, N.D., in the
Elmer Walker home, in 1919, with 53 members. It was organized by the Rev. G.T.
Stargel and Rev. William Hance. Rev. Stargel pastored the church for quite some
time, after which Rev. Charles Cook became the pastor.

In 1925 the work began to progress and grow, so that this membership was moved
to a country church, north of Beulah, known as the Ree Church of God. In 1930 a
branch church was organized in Beulah, a building was moved in and remodeled on
the east end of Main Street. It was during this time that Rev. Paul H. Walker
became the first pastor in this church and later organized the church. The Rev.
Charles Bowen was the pastor placed there later. The clerk at that time was
Court Foster.

In 1952 the desires grew for a new modern brick church, plans were made,
resulting in the erection of the present church, now located on Third Street,
Beulah. The Rev. Milton Sandberg served the church while the basement was
built, and it was during the time that Rev. E.E. Coleman was pastor that the
church was completed. The board of directors at that time was: the clerk,
Reinhold Reich; trustees, Emanual Becker, Reinhold Reich, Albert Pfenning.

The pastors who served the Church of God were: Paul H. Walker (first pastor and
organizer), Charles Bowen, Eugene Inches, Ralph Brostrom, James Reesor, Oscar
Beckman, E.E. Colman, M.L. Lowe, Anton Meyers, Milton Sandberg, N.B. Wills,
Bernard Knispel, Arnold Erikson, M.D. Haar, C.W. Batson, Dennis Batt, James T.
Pender, Robert James and present pastor Robert L. Burget. The board of
directors at this time is: clerk, Albert Pfenning; trustees, Leo Sayler, Otto
Pfenning, and Art Boeckel.

The Ladies Willing Workers Band was organized on Sept. 27, 1953, during the
pastorate of the Rev. N.B. Wills.

The purpose of this organization is to assist and aid in the development and
maintenance of the church, and to create interest and good will in every
possible way for the general welfare of the congregation. Their activities have
consisted of donations to the church funds; serving meals for special
occasions, such as weddings, funerals, etc.; donations given both to home and
foreign missions; and visitations made to the sick and shut-in.

They meet in the church once a month. Devotional periods are observed, business
is transacted, and the remainder of the time is taken up discussing of new
projects.

The church and pastor's council are: Ted Reich, Art Boeckel, Larry Pfenning, Don
Boeckel and Clarence Sayler. The church clerk is Ken Peterson.

The Christian Education Board is: Calvin Buechler, Gaylen Boeckel, Larry
Pfenning, Ken Peterson, Carol K. Boeckel, and Caroline Buechler.

The Ladies Willing Workers Band has become Ladies Ministries with the following
officers: Polly Pender, president; Shirley Schlafman, vice president; Norma
Reich, secretary-treasurer; and Hazel Burget, adviser.

The congregation built a new parsonage to the north of the church in 1966. They
completed a major remodeling in the downstairs area this year.

        Concordia Lutheran Church - Robert Pfau, pastor.

Concordia Lutheran Church

In the 1890s, Mercer County, south of the Missouri River, was still typical
Wild West. The German settlers in this county were accustomed to a more
comfortable village life in Russia, where many of them had grown up. After
their arrival here, they found many hardships. Markets were 50-60 miles away
and poverty and want made the first years in the new home unforgettably bitter.

Among the first settlers of this large region were a number of Lutherans who
settled in and near Kronthal. Besides their lack of the material things, their
greatest regret was that they sat upon the wide prairie without spiritual care.

Their heavenly Father did not forget them, however, and their joy was great when
soon after settling in this county, a Lutheran missionary visited them to
preach the truth of salvation to them as well as administer the sacraments.
Some of the first missionaries who made long journeys to serve this vast
territory were Revs. H. Arndt, J. Duerr, F. Mathias, Wm. Schmook, P. Siegel and
E. Bliss.

The Lutheran congregation at Kronthal was organized in 1898 with the guidance of
P.L. Wohlfeil, who served at the Lutheran congregation at Hannover. Shortly
after, Rev. Wohlfeil helped with the new congregation, which became Trinity.
The Rev. H. Arndt, who served Hazen and Baldwin until 1901, assisted the
congregation.

The names of the men who, as far as could be ascertained, were active in
founding Trinity Lutheran congregation are Bernhard Galster, Joseph Boeshans,
Fredrich Wiedenmeyer, Peter Wiedrich, George Miller, Andreas Muller, Martin
Zeiszler, John Kochler and Peter Stern. Several others were living in the area
and joined the congregation shortly there after but were not present for
organization. Trinity's congregation dissolved in 1963.

While it is necessary to consider Trinity (rural Beulah) in the roots of Beulah
Concordia, the focus of attention is now upon the "church in town." While
dreams of such a congregation were being shared in 1942, it wasn't until the
end of World War II that three pastors were able to carry their dreams into
reality. The Rev. Wm. J. Israel of Trinity Lutheran Church of Kronthal, the
Rev. Fred Riedel of St. Paul Lutheran Church of Otter Creek and the Rev. G.H.
Fiechtner of St. Matthew Lutheran Church in Hazen were able to gain support for
their dreams in 1946.

During the summer of 1946 six men started a new ministry in Beulah: Sam Miller
Jr., Albin Becker, George Perman, John Reinhardt, John Maier and Franz Kasper.
On July 17, 1946, the history of the new congregation was started. Five days
later, on July 22, 1946, Emanuel Lutheran Church of the Synod of Missouri, Ohio
and other states and the church of the Lutheran House adopted its constitution
written in the German language. The name was changed to Concordia Lutheran
Church in January of 1948.

In August of the first year, the congregation purchased the Emanuel Lutheran
Church building of Bremen, N.E. of New Salem, ND. This church was dedicated
March, 9, 1947. With this big step out of the way, the congregation readied
itself for its full-time minister by buying a parsonage in 1947. The Rev. G.H.
Fiechtner served the congregation in the early going and assisted the first
council in issuing a call for a shepherd. In June of 1947, the Rev. Fred Riedel
accepted the call to serve the congregation.

By 1950 the congregation had outgrown its building and purchased the Peace
Lutheran Church building of Hazen. This building was moved in 1951 to newly
acquired property in the north part of the city of Beulah, and was dedicated on
March 9, 1952.

Through the years, Concordia was served by the Revs. Samuel Meske, Edwin Rossow,
Hans O. Carlson, Melvin Meyer, Jerry Markel, Sam Christensen, and presently, Rob
Pfau. Vacancies were served by neighboring pastors Revs. G.H. Fiechtner, H.
Burgdorf, Vernon Mickow, Ron Erber and Curtis Olimb.

On July 30, 1947, the Ladies Aid Society of Concordia Lutheran Church became
affiliated with the International Lutheran Women's Missionary League of the
Evangelical Lutheran Synod of Missouri, Ohio and other states (later changed to
The Lutheran Church Missouri Synod). This auxiliary of the Lutheran Church
Missouri Synod serves to support missions in our country and throughout the
world. Currently some 50 women from Concordia are actively involved with this
group in three different guilds.

On Nov. 15, 1976, Concordia Lutheran Laymen's League was established. This
auxiliary was to carry on the important mission work over and above what The
Lutheran Church Missouri Synod was doing. Two programs which are best known as
being supported by the Lutheran Laymen's League are "This Is The Life," a
half-hour television program, and "The Lutheran Hour," a half-hour radio
broadcast. Currently some 20 men and women from Concordia are actively involved
with this group.

While active youth work was common at Concordia through such groups as the
Walther League and Active Christian Teens, it was on Nov. 16, 1979, that the
youth of Concordia joined Lutheran Youth Fellowship of The Lutheran Church
Missouri Synod. While this is not an actual auxiliary of the synod, many
congregations have youth groups who belong. Currently Concordia as about 30
youth involved with this fellowship.

In July, 1978, a vote was taken to build a new structure. Groundbreaking
ceremonies were held on Oct. 15, 1978. A farewell service to the old church,
cornerstone laying at the new church and entrance into the new church were held
on April 27, 1980.

In October of 1986 the congregation voted to add the current education facility
to the existing church building. Work began almost immediately and the building
was ready for occupancy by May 10, 1987. A dedication service was held June 14,
1987, with the Rev. Jerry Markel serving as guest preacher.

It has been over 40 years that Concordia Lutheran Church (LCMS) has been in
existence. During that time this congregation has been blessed immensely. At the
present time, by the grace of God, there are some 475 baptized souls with about
95 in Sunday school.

Because it is God's will that Christ's disciples preach the Gospel to the whole
world, and in order that Christ's mission for His church might be carried out
according to His will, He has commanded that Christians unite in worship,
practice fellowship with one another, witness to all men, help each other grow
in the Word, serve the needs of all people in Christian love, administer the
office of the keys as His Church and maintain decency and order in the church.
Therefore, we at Concordia ask that God might enable us and empower us to
continue to carry on these important functions in our midst and throughout our
community in the years to come.

        Congregational Church - Edward Horst, pastor.

Congregational Church

The Congregational Church of Beulah had a forerunner in the Brush Creek
Congregational church, organized in the country south of present Beulah in 1906.
This congregation first met in the Hollister home. Later when a school house was
built services were held in it. The early ministers came from Glen Ullin to
preach to this rural group. Later regular pastors were called. One--the Rev.
Gray - drove from Richardton to serve both Brush Creek and a church near Fort
Clark.

When in 1914 a need was felt by some of the people in the new town for an
English-speaking church, a meeting was called and the Rev. Rood from the
Congregational State Office was asked to come to help organize the
Congregational Church of Beulah. At this meeting, held in the Johnson Hall, in
March of 1914, it was voted to list the members of the Brush Creek Congregation
as charter members of the Beulah church. There were 47 members.

The records show people of many denominations affiliating with this church in
the early years. Services were held in Johnson Hall until February 1918 when
the services were held in the white school house on the hill north of the
Legion hall. Then in 1920 the church was built on its present site. Except for
one hired carpenter the labor was all donated by members and other interested
people. The first services were held in the church on Dec. 5, 1920. The need
for securing a bell to sound the call to worship presented a problem which the
women solved. They made little aprons with big pockets and sent them "back
east" to relatives and friends with the request for pennies to "ring the bell."
These contributions plus a generous anonymous donation by a Beulah businessman
made the purchase of the bell possible in time for the New Year's service. The
Ladies Aid was organized in 1917 with 23 members.

The young people organized as a Christian Endeavor group in 1922. This active
group was the predecessor of the present Pilgrim Fellowship.

The present Congregational Church is located at 112 3rd Ave. NW, which was
formerly the Zion Lutheran Church. The Parsonage and church were purchased in
1967.

Cornerstone Baptist Church

The Cornerstone Baptist Church began in 1979 through the efforts of seven
families meeting in a home south of Beulah, under the leadership of Pastor
Keith Gamble from the Baptist Church of Manning, N.D. The main purpose of the
church is to spread the gospel and reach people who do not have a church home
or do not attend church.

The church became organized in the fall of 1980 Pastor Jonnie Eastwood was
called to be their first pastor.

Cornerstone Baptist Church was the name chosen, taken from the Bible in
Ephesians 2:20: "Jesus Christ himself being the chief cornerstone.

In December of 1980, they located a place to rent in Beulah. For the next five
years the church met in the Seventh-day Adventist Church.

        Immanuel Baptist Church - Gordon Voegele, pastor.

        Cornerstone Baptist Church - Keith Gamble, pastor.

On Oct. 3, 1982, Keith Gamble became the pastor. There were 13 charter members.
In 1984, the church bought property in the Country Club Estates. In June of 1985
ground was broken and the church building was started. In March, 1986, they had
their first service in the new building. Fifty-seven people were in attendance.
In June, 1987, the church had a special  dedication service as the church was
complete and also debt-free. They have had a high of 100 in attendance.

Immanuel Baptist Church

The Immanuel Baptist Church of Beulah was organized in 1910 when 24 people in
the Beulah area felt the need for Christian fellowship. They invited delegates
from Hebron, Washburn and New Leipzig to meet with them and to seek their
advice. After much consideration an agreement was reached and the German
Baptist Church was organized, known as the Immanuel Church at Evans, N.D.

These people were strong in the faith. Before the church was organized, they
built the first building which was dedicated the day after the organization
meeting. The building cost $1,204.45, of which $935.68 was paid, leaving a debt
of $268.77. In 1913 the Women's Missionary Society was organized with eight
charter members.

The early years were filled with hardship for these pioneers. The following
story relates one incident. When Rev. Blumhagen accepted the call in 1913, he
moved his family to a mud and stone homesteader's cabin north of Beulah,
located on the land where the GPGA plant now stands. On Sunday, March 15, 1914,
Rev. and Mrs. Blumhagen went to the Gottlieb Klaudt home to hold services,
leaving their children at home. In the fall of 1913 a farmer north of Golden
Valley burned a straw pile which, unknown to him, smoldered all winter. This
particular day in March was especially windy and stormy. The dormant fire was
fanned into flame and burned several farms before descending into Antelope
Valley where the Blumhagen home was. Homesteaders' children were taught to
remain in the house when there were storms but the Blumhagen children were new
to this land and thought they could outrun the fire. One boy ran south and made
it, but the two other children ran east trying to reach another farm. However,
the fire overtook them and the little girl was killed. The boy was seriously
burned and needed medical help in Bismarck. The only means of travel was by
horse and wagon so after several horse changes they reached Bismarck the
following day. The boy lived only another two days.

It was decided to move the church building to Beulah in 1914 and to build a
parsonage. During the later 1920s when Rev. Trautner was pastor a mission church
was begun in Zap. The pastor from Beulah served the Zap church for many years.

The second church building was erected in 1930 and the parsonage was enlarged.
In the late 1960s a new parsonage was erected next to the church and a building
fund was established for construction of a new church building.

In the late 1970s there was a need for a new church building and a
ground-breaking ceremony was held in October, 1978, with construction following
at 432 Sunny Drive. Much of the labor was done by the church people, and the
sanctuary was completed in August, 1980. The old church and parsonage were sold
shortly thereafter. The debt on the new building was paid off and a
mortgage-burning ceremony was held on Aug. 7, 1983. There was still a need for
classrooms and a fellowship hall so again the people took a step of faith and
construction of the educational unit was begun on May 10, 1984, with completion
on Dec. 19, 1984. Dedication was held in February 1985.

An AWANA program was begun in January 1985 with large numbers of boys and girls
in attendance.

The following pastors have served the church through the years: Rev. Frederick
Pahlke, 1910-1912; Rev. Samuel Blumhagen, 1913-1925; Rev. Fred Trautner,
1925-1928 and 1947-1952; Rev. Daniel Kline, 1930-1935; Rev. Arthur Fischer,
1935-1937; Rev. Peter Schilling, 1938-1944; Rev. William Jaster, 1945-1947; Rev.
Ernest Lautt, 1952-1957; Rev. John Wood, 1957-1962; Rev. Edwin Voight,
1962-1965; Rev. George Neubert, 1965-1976; Rev. Herman Kesterke, 1977-1979; and
Rev. Gordon Voegele, 1979 to the present.

New Life Assembly of God

        New Life Assembly of God - Lloyd Hohn, pastor

New Life Assembly of God fellowship began with four families meeting together
for Bible study. During this time, a pastor interested in pastoring a new home
missions work contacted the North Dakota Assemblies of God. Through God's
leading and through these four families, the North Dakota District Assemblies
of God, along with Pastor David Davidson, his wife Pauline, and their three
children were all brought together. Their first Sunday service was in June,
1983, at which time they became a home missions fellowship of the North Dakota
District of the Assemblies of God. The second Sunday, a foreign missions
speaker shared in the service and support was pledged toward a missionary going
to Belize, Central America. This was a beginning to missions support which
extends to 11 foreign missionaries today.

The New Life Fellowship had new visitors every week and outgrew its original
meeting spaces with an attendance of more than 30 when it moved into a large
space in the Clarence Jaeger Building at 12th Street North and Highway 49.
Through the following years, the fellowship saw more than 500 people come and
go during the construction of the coal gasification plant. The regular
attenders, consisting of area residents and permanent people, continued to grow
in number also.

Pastor Davidson left in July 1986 to pastor a home missions church in
Frankfurt, IL. Pastor Lloyd Hohn, his wife Mary, and their six children came to
Beulah from Neillsville, Wi. in November 1986. New Life continued to grow and
the North Dakota District of the Assemblies of God and New Life Assembly of God
purchased the former Prairie Plaza complex in July 1987, moving into the unused
spaces in August of that year while remodeling the west wing of the complex
into a sanctuary, Sunday school rooms, offices, and fellowship hall. They
formally moved into the finished sanctuary in November 1987.

The fellowship enjoys praising and worshipping the Lord and music. The
attendance average during Sunday worship services is more than 90, with Sunday
school classes for all ages, an active youth group, weekly home Bible studies,
and exciting fellowship as added ministry.

The main focus of the church is ministry to the Lord, ministry to each other,
and ministry to the non-Christian in the community.

Peace United Methodist Church

The Peace United Methodist Church had a forerunner in the Evangelical United
Brethren Church. It was organized in March 1921 with services held in the John
Unruh home and later in the school.

Oct. 7, 1923, dedication services were held in the newly erected church in the
300 block of west Main Street.

In 1946 the church became the Friedens United Brethren Church and in 1968 it
became the Friedens United Methodist Church.

        Peace United Methodist - Linda Harris, pastor

In February 1969 the church was destroyed by fire. After the fire the membership
transferred to Salem United Methodist Church in Hazen.

On May 5, 1978, an organizational meeting was held at the Beulah City Hall for
all parties interested in starting a church again in Beulah. After several
meetings and picnics in the park and with much help from the Western District
Superintendent, Cameron Johnson, Rev. Peter Aakerman of the Hazen Methodist
Church, Naomi Unruh, a member of the church and the conference, the
congregation was able to get another church started in Beulah.

The former Concordia Lutheran Church, which was shared with them while their
new church was being built, was purchased.

The first service was held Sunday, Sept. 10, 1978. On Sunday, Oct. 1, the church
was recognized and became a parish with a special service led by the district
superintendent.

The first pastor was Marc Nagel, a Bismarck native, who at the time was a
seminary student at Andover Newton Theological School in Boston, Mass.

From October of 1978 we were yoked with the Congregational church in Zap, with
the Peace pastor serving both churches. In the fall of 1982 Zap was dropped and
Peace was then yoked with the Methodist church in Riverdale. In the summer of
1983 that yoke was dropped and Peace became a station church.

Charter members at the time the church was organized were Charles, Carol,
Carolyn and Carla Desper, Phil and Deborah Eastgate, Naomi Unruh, Walter and
Jeannette Zeiszler, Randal and Barbara Salzer, Kenneth and Betty Parent, Jody
and Rodger Young, LeRoy and Sandi Peterson, Lorraine Radtke, and Rosena and
Katie Huber.

In June of 1979 Brian Harmon, a Fargo native, became the pastor and served for
three years.

The Peace congregation shared the church with the Concordia Lutherans until
Sunday, May 4, 1980, when the first service was held in the church that they
could finally call their own.

In June of 1982 another pastor, Mark Brickzin, a native of Wahpeton, N.D., came
to Peace. He was here one year. June of 1983 brought another pastor, Walter
Elmer, who was a native of Hebron, N.D. He was here until June 1987 when he
retired.

After Rev. Elmer came Linda Harris, a native of Fargo. After serving five years
with the Church World Service in ministry-related programs in such countries as
Malaysia, the Philippines and the United States. she entered the seminary and
graduated from St. Paul School of Theology in Kansas City, Mo., just before
coming to Beulah.

In June of 1987 Peace was again yoked with another church, the Methodist church
in Center.

A parsonage was obtained in the summer of 1982 when the church purchased a home
from the Gordon Eiders.

The United Methodist Women of the Church were organized in September of 1980.
They have been very active, having bazaars, rummage and bake sales with most
proceeds going to missionary projects, which are their main objective. There is
also a yearly mother-daughter banquet which is attended by all in the community
and the UMW sponsors the local Daisy Scout troop that has met weekly in the
church since 1985.

Since the beginning, Peace has had a very active Sunday school program for all
ages, from preschool through adult classes. Through the years, it has had a
youth group which has been involved in many projects such as car washes, bake
sales and chili suppers to raise money to go to camp and state youth
conventions. In the fall of 1983 two of the youth went with the North Dakota
delegation on a trip to the United Nations in New York and to Washington, D.C.

In September 1981 a free baby sitting service was started called Parents' Time
Out. It was started with grant money from the National United Methodist to aid
in the energy impact area for one year.

The St. Anne Altar Society

The St. Anne Altar Society is affiliated with St. Joseph's Catholic Church and
offers open membership to any lady of the parish. It was organized prior to the
construction of the first church and could easily be considered the oldest
continuous organization in Beulah. During early times the ladies met in each
others' homes.

The purpose of the society is to bring faith, fulfillment and acts of charity
to its members and perpetual care for the needs of the altar.

The meetings consist of prayer and enrichment lessons. The society has held
retreats at the home, church and also at the Abbey at Richardton. A special
mass is offered each month as well as a mass for a deceased member.

The group has been so committed to the needs of St. Joseph that it is
impossible to mention the many fund-raising activities. In addition to an
annual church dinner and bazaar, the society has made numerous personal
donations, maintained a cleaning program and purchased many pieces of
equipment, including a piano. Some of the very special donations have been the
tabernacle, veils and the papal and U.S. flags, which were purchased in 1951
and are still in use. A financial commitment has also been made towards a bell
tower.

The Catholic Daughters were sponsored by this group and aid was given in the
establishment of a library. A pamphlet rack and other reading material has been
made available to the congregation. The society trains the altar boys, teaching
them the responses in Latin when such masses were celebrated. They have
organized and taught the religious and confirmation classes and trained those
making their First Holy Communion.

St. Anne's has sponsored a Welcome Wagon at various times to visit new members
and the sick or elderly. For charity activities they send shoes, clothing and
blankets to foreign and domestic missions. They furnished a room at the
hospital and maintained flower beds at the cemetery. They have maintained a
food pantry for the needy and distribute food baskets.

Social functions of the church have been under their jurisdiction. In addition
to dinners, picnics, parties and receptions for the priests or bishop,
enjoyable times have been arranged for the children of the parish and even a
few dances in the old church hall. The first Sunday of each month has been
reserved as a time for coffee, rolls and friendship.

Other than religious needs, the society's main commitment is to the needs of the
altar. It supplies candles, linens, altar breads, vigil lights and vestments.
There have been hand-made vestments and surplices for the altar boys and
priest. The ladies of the early days purchased yardage and altar linens were
hand-sewn and embroidered.

The St. Anne Altar society will assist those of every faith.

        Shrine erected at the site of St. Benedict's.

Saint Benedict Catholic Church

In 1904, the first priest, Fr. Alois Strigl, came to the Saint Benedict
Community to offer mass and organize a Catholic parish. During 1904, mass was
offered at the Martin Schutt farm home. In 1906, mass was offered at the
Wendlin Zahn home, by Fr. Benedict Peter.

Construction of Saint Benedict Church began in 1906 and was completed in 1907 at
a cost of $2,000. The labor was donated by the parish members. A six-acre tract
of land was donated for the church site, about 13 miles south and two miles
east of Beulah.

Saint Benedict was consecrated by Bishop Werhle of the Bismarck Diocese. The
first baptism in the new church was Joseph Deibert, administered by Fr. Peter
on June 15, 1908. The first holy communion class was received in 1910 and the
first confirmation class in 1917. Priests from the Assumption Abbey in
Richardton, ND served the parish.

In 1925, an addition was built to the church for $1,800. It was enlarged again
in 1926, at another $1,200. In 1930, a parish house was constructed for $7,000.
All of these building projects were accomplished without any expenditures for
labor, as it was an donated.

After the completion of the parish house in 1930, Fr. Nickolois Fox became the
first resident pastor of Saint Benedict parish. Helen (Lynch) Skalsky was the
first housekeeper. She was also organist for 30 years.

Fr. Fox was replaced by Fr. Joseph Meiser who served until his death. Fr.
Bernhard Eichner was the last resident priest. Two priests are buried in the
Saint Benedict cemetery; Fr. Joseph Meiser and Fr. Bernhard Eichner.

Saint Benedict parish has an inspiring record of religious vocations: one
brother, Martin Heier; seven nuns, Magdeline Heier (Sr. Sylvia), Bardella
Weiand (Sister Coletta), Claudia Weiand (Sister Virginia), Ann Deibert (Sr.
Mary Margaret), Delores Skalsky (Sr. Lambert), Margaret Eberle (Sr. Martha) and
Alice Weiand (Sr. Sylveria).

The maximum number of Saint Benedict families numbered about 45. They sponsored
various activities, such as bazaars and dinners in the 1920s, 30s and 40s to
help finance the needs of the parish. With the church receiving the constant
attention of the parishioners it was maintained in a becoming manner until it
closed in 1968. All but three members joined Saint Joseph Catholic Church in
Beulah.

Several years later the church was dismantled and the lumber sold. The parish
house was sold and moved.

The statue of Saint Benedict was enshrined at the cemetery. A fence was built
around the shrine and the cemetery. It is viewed as a gem of the one-time
western prairie where Almighty God lent a helping hand to those who needed Him.

        St. Joseph Catholic Church (the new church).

St. Joseph's Catholic Church

Faith was one of the Beulah area settlers' most important characteristics, as
that was often what enabled them to get through the harsh winters, insect and
dust plagues, prairie fires, small graves mounded near their homes, and the
other hardships they faced every day.

Many German-Russians brought with them their Lutheran faith, and as they
predominated in the area that became the largest denomination.

It was by no means the oldest.

St. Joseph's Catholic Church had fledgling roots in this area before Lewis and
Clark voyaged up the Missouri River, long before the advent of the Germans from
Russia, when French fur traders and trappers, traditionally Catholic, brought
the faith to their Indian families. They hunted on the prairies and trapped
along the waterways near Beulah.

Dreams of profit were not the only motives of the French ministry; the
conversion of natives was also desired. Missionaries began to arrive and one of
the earliest was the beloved western padre, Father Jean DeSmett. Historians
have documented DeSmett's baptisms and other sacraments performed at Ft.
Berthold north of Beulah.

At this time St. Joseph's belonged to the archdiocese of Rouen. By 1879 the
church became the vicarate of Dakota. Catholic immigrants, mostly Irish and
Germans from Russia, began to arrive but brought no priests.

It would be many years before Beulah would enjoy its own church building.
Traveling Benedictine fathers served the area, with records maintained at the
Halliday mission.

The railroad brought priests to Beulah. Fr. Bonaventure Goebel was one of the
first, coming in 1914 with the railroad and living in Bismarck. Mass was seldom
celebrated more than monthly in the upstairs room of Joos Hardware (now Coast
to Coast). All the early priests came from Richardton Abbey.

The May, 1916 Beulah Independent said Fr. E. Bubic came each third Sunday,
holding mass and conferring other sacraments. Mary Eva, daughter of John and
Margaret (Geisinger) Usselman, was the first child baptized June 1, 1916. The
first marriage was Frederick Allmendinger and Katherine Bosch, Jan. 12, 1919.
The first burial was Kathlene Evans, 24, June, 1918.

A building committee was formed consisting of James and Thomas Keogh, J.H. Kuhl,
Max Martell and A. Landarf. They, along with Tom Farrington, were later named
first trustees.

Pearl S. Chaffee, credited as Beulah's staunchest promoter, donated $500 and
some land to open the way for a church. The small prairie church later became a
landmark on top of the hill overlooking Beulah. Donations of $100 each came
from Thomas O'Neil, James and Thomas Keogh, and Mr. Evans, listed as St.
Joseph's founders.

Fifth-generation descendants of two founding fathers have maintained
Catholicism: Mathew, Thomas and Lucas O'Neil; and Kyle and Michael, children of
Laura and Delry Schwalbe, trace to James Keogh.

Encouraged by so much interest, the bishop approved a church on July  18, 1916.
Additional money came from private donations and a grant from the Catholic
Extension Society in St. Paul. The church was dedicated Oct. 15, 1916 and St.
Joseph was chosen as patron saint.

After a successful dedication, the bishop wrote a letter to the Independent
commending the kind businessmen of Beulah for their acceptance and splendid
cooperation towards this new church, thanking Mr. Sovereign of the Palm Theatre
opera house and Mr. Joos and the band for their assistance.

Following WWI Bishop Wehrle asked the Precious Blood Community of Ohio,
dedicated to serving needy areas, to staff the Mandan-Killdeer rail route with
priests so the German-speaking people wouldn't lose touch with the church.
Precious Blood priests serving Beulah included Rev. Evaristus J. Olberding,
1921-27; Rev. Charles A. Bauer, 1927-37; Rev. F. Herman Schwitzer, 1937-41;
Rev. Harry Wibbles, 1941-48. Until then, St. Joseph's was still missionary in
character as the priests lived in Hazen. There is little information on the
early priests, except for Bauer. He was a popular church and community figure.
Tales of his friendliness and participation in sports are still told.

        St. Joseph Catholic Church (the old church).

The congregation increased beyond capacity early in the '30s. Times were tough,
but the Altar Society held women of unending ambition. They held many
fundraisers until finally, with another Extension Society grant and a loan from
the bishop's aid fund, there was enough money to begin a new structure.

The old church was dismantled and mass was held in the school while the basement
was completed. Many hours of donated labor led to a new St. Joseph's Church in
1938. It took years to pay off the loan; the parish was so poor that the old
pews were used in half the church. Between 1915-1940 such progress was
remarkable, considering these were years of great depression on the frontier.
It is a convincing demonstration of the people's spirit of faith and sacrifice.

        Rev. R. Guillozet, first resident priest.

In 1948 Beulah's Catholic population warranted a resident priest and Fr. Raymond
Guillozet served from then until 1955. Along with pastoral duties and tempering
the financial woes of the parish, Guillozet built a rectory. His artistry in
wood showed up everywhere in the church. The holy water font and carved
candlesticks are still in use. He also found time to supervise and do some
carpentry on the Beulah Country Club clubhouse and fashioned white crosses for
unmarked graves.

Guillozet returns periodically to visit and substitute; he celebrated his 50th
anniversary in the priesthood at St. Joseph's in 1986. He said, "Since I am
over 80 I have curtailed my activities considerably; however, I still play golf
and Believe it or not, I had a drive of over 300 yards!" This devout, gentle
priest is remembered tenderly.

Fr. Rupert Landoll, 1955-63, worked on educational facilities and his
professionally trained sister formed a high school choir of surprising talent.
He advocated coal and gas development and spent time and travel in that cause.

Fr. R. Alphonse Jungwirth, 1963-68, was an intellectual, inspiring and
no-nonsense priest. He was demanding of his altar boys, the catechism classes
and the whole parish. His tenure was a time of intense learning.

Fr. Louis Telegdy, 1968-70, held the youth's interest by being involved in all
aspects of their lives, from spirituality to sports, even converting the
parking lot into a ball diamond.

Several priests served the parish for a short time, including Fr. Schroeder, who
arranged social activities and introduced a monthly post-mass fellowship.

The building years for St. Joseph's were not at an end, as a third church was
to be built on Chaffee's land given more than 60 years earlier. People from the
disbanded St. Benedict parish south of Beulah joined St. Joseph's.

A building fund had been growing for years and a new church was discussed
frequently early in the 1970s. A 1975 parish vote unanimously approved a
$650,000 church, hall and rectory complex. With donations, pledges and a loan,
the building fund goal was reached.

Fr. Harold Roth, 1970-84, secured a plan and an energetic building committee
went to work. 1977 saw the completion of a brick-front building with a seating
capacity of 500. It was just in time, as it was completed during the rapid
energy impact growth.

The first mass in this building was celebrated April 16, 1978, and the Solemn
Dedication was held June 4. Bishop Hilary B. Hacker of Bismarck, Roth and area
priests took part in the inspiring ceremony.

During the construction period in this area a tremendous fluctuation in
membership was experienced as the workforce changed constantly. When St.
Joseph's moved from the old church, 167 families were registered. By 1979 there
were 232, and between 1980-84 there were more than 370 families. 1986-87 saw a
noticeable decline as people left this area.

Roth saw the most challenges. He was an excellent counselor and instructor and
very knowledgeable, with a go-get-em attitude that made St. Joseph's very
active spiritually and materially. The church made great strides in all areas,
from maintenance to ministerial assistance. During this time mass changed from
Latin to English and Vatican II permitted laypeople to assist with ministry.
Roth implemented many changes with little stress to the people, along with
handling the frustration of a growing and changing congregation.

Roth had made Beulah home after a military career and worked on his hobbies,
gardening, hunting and fishing. St. Joseph's people were his family. Though he
cried with the church when farewells came, he still returns to hunt and assumes
pastoral duties while here.

Fr. Joseph Hajduch, 1981-84, was harnessed with Roth, and the two had a good
working relationship as well as friendship. Fr. Joe's infectious sense of humor
brought a light spirit to the solemn religion; he was beloved by the children
and the nursing home residents.

        Fr. Edwin Volk, resident priest.

The Precious Blood priests were withdrawn in 1984 after 63 years of service. St.
Joseph's was reassigned to the Bismarck diocese, which sent Rev. Edwin Volk to
the parish in 1984. The church was in need of renovation because of
construction errors, and Volk jumped right in to correct them and direct a
major landscaping project. This congenial priest installed the Renew Program,
an extension of Faith and Prayer, in conjunction with the Marion year.

The congregation has always asked that God choose St. Joseph's men and women to
the religious life. Ima Hamilton, daughter of Ida Helvik, became a Benedictine
nun, serving as nurse and teacher. Gary Schneider, son of Clarence and Leona,
became a Paulist priest involved with U.S. missions, and was ordained May 13,
1976. St. Joseph's was proud to have Fr. Gary celebrate his first mass in
Beulah and held a reception in his honor.

The music department has grown and changed. In 1916 Mrs. Marshall was the first
organist, directing a choir of high school girls. Alice Abbey, a widow with nine
children, organized a choir which sang the difficult Latin mass. Now there are
adult and youth choirs and five organists, plus guitarists.

Throughout the years, stretching back before the days of settlement, the
Catholic church has cradled its people, as St. Joseph's continues to do today.

Zion Lutheran Church

As Lutheran people settled in the Beulah area, Rev. A. Schult from Stanton
occasionally came to serve the small group of Lutherans that had settled here.
Later on, Rev. John Mau served as pastor. The first official service was held
in a school house two miles north of Beulah where the congregation was
organized. This was on Jan. 10, 1914. A parsonage and a church were built that
same year in the village of Beulah. Rev. John Mau served the congregation in
1914-1915. From 1916-1918 Rev. Al Lieberodt was the pastor. Rev. M. Baudler
served the congregation from 1919-1923. During his time the parsonage was
enlarged and a garage was built. From 1923-1926 Rev. W. J. Siefkes was the
pastor.

Rev. S. Joachim became the pastor, Oct. 1, 1926. During his time the
congregation grew. It was a time that was hard for the congregation. It was a
time of drought, depression, language questions and building. Yet the
congregation grew. It was due to his wise leadership that the congregation was
able to overcome many obstacles. The parish which he served was divided,
enabling him to give his attention to the Zion church. The parsonage was
modernized. The biggest achievement was the building of the church which was
dedicated in November 1940. Rev. Joachim continued to serve the congregation
until his death, Jan. 1, 1944.

        Zion Lutheran Church - Pastors C. Hoper and Schuessler

Rev. Henry Dirks served the congregation from October 1943 to April 1949. It was
during his ministry that language questions of the congregation were solved.
Double services were started and the language became a side issue. During the
vacancy, from April 1949-Nov. 1, 1949, the congregation installed a new heating
system in the church. It was decided to build a new parsonage.

Pastor John Kammerer arrived in Beulah on Nov. 1, 1949, and served the
congregation faithfully until August of 1961 when he accepted a call to Ashley,
N.D.

In 1956 a building fund was started and the congregation made plans to build a
new church.

In 1962 plans were proposed to the congregation and soon adopted to build a new
church and education unit on new property. Shortly after, the congregation
purchased the land north of the Beulah Community Nursing Home.

Pastor M.J. Schumacher arrived in January of 1962 and was installed as pastor on
January 7. During his ministry the new church was begun in September of 1963.
Pastor Schumacher writes, "There were many, many hours of labor given by people
throughout that time. The work consisted of hauling brick, rocks, lumber, sand
and gravel, building and assembling, painting and cleaning. The list could go
on and on. The tasks were varied and the willing people many. People made the
lights in the sanctuary, the brass work on the communion rail, the altar cross
and candelabra. They scrubbed floors, laid tile, assembled pews, sanded and
waxed ceilings. There simply wasn't much they didn't do.

At first there were not so many each day, but as the time for dedication
approached one could sense a feeling of unity and urgency. The place during the
last few weeks was alive with people. They built part of themselves into that
building and while they were building a house with hands, God was building His
temple, not made with hands, His church, the people of God.

On Nov. 1, 1964, the new church at a cost of $172,000 was dedicated with about
1,000 people in attendance at the worship services. With the new church built
the congregation directed its attention to build a new parsonage. By 1968 the
new parsonage was completed. From then on the most urgent concern of the
congregation was to pay off its debt. Rapid progress was being made in paying
off the indebtedness and by the time that Rev. Marvin Schumacher accepted a
call to Zion Lutheran Church of Ashley, N.D., in December of 1973, the
congregational indebtedness had been reduced from $86,000 to $22,500. On Nov.
28, 1976, the debt was retired with a note-burning service.

A few years after the new church was completed the membership was increased by
Lutherans who came from churches which closed their doors. On Jan. 1, 1967,
Peace Lutheran Church, south of Beulah, officially merged with Zion and most of
its members came over to Zion. One year later, March, 1968, Peace Lutheran,
north of Beulah, ceased to hold services and a good many of these members
joined at Zion.

Some interesting changes helped the mission of Zion. In January 1968, monthly
communion was introduced. In March, 1971, an arrangement was established with
Emmanuel Lutheran Church of Zap to share its pastor with Zion 25 percent of the
time. Up to this time, Zion, even though it had grown in membership, still had
no church secretary. The first secretary, Jan Schulz, was hired in February,
1972.

In January, 1974, Pastor R. Markwart began his ministry at Zion. The first
significant change was a reorganization of the church council which came
through a revised church constitution. A few years later it was found necessary
to establish church council guidelines which simplified the operation of the
church.

With the increase in the population of Beulah other changes soon were made. In
November, 1974, two worship services were introduced. This was followed up in
September of 1983 with a weekday school which was intended to relieve the
pressure on the Sunday school and two Christmas programs the Sunday before
Christmas. A bus ministry for the older members was established in 1977 to help
them get to church.

The work for one pastor was mounting with the size of the congregation and its
many programs. In September, 1977, Alan Schwochou, an intern from Trinity
Seminary, arrived to share in the work of the congregation.

After his departure it was decided to call a second pastor instead of another
intern. The first associate pastor, Ronald Bolinger, arrived in May, 1979. He
contributed much to the music program, youth and visitation ministry. In
August, 1983, he accepted a call to Red Wing, Minn.

In February, 1984, Rev. Clifford Hoper arrived with his family. Pastor Hoper
contributed to the development of the church's organizational structure,
broadened the youth program, other than church school, to include the children
down to the fifth grade.

The arrival of the associate pastors created a need for a second parsonage. In
1980 the second parsonage was built for $80,310. When Pastor Hoper arrived in
1984 the basement was completed at a cost of $12,000. The indebtedness for both
of these projects ended August, 1986, and June 1986, respectively.

In May 1987 Pastor Markwart submitted his resignation, having accepted a call to
Gloria Dei Lutheran Church, Williston, N.D. Immediately the church entered into
a process of evaluation to determine its staff needs.

Following the evaluation, the study and call committee presented to the
congregation on Oct. 11, 1987, a call to Pastor Hoper as senior pastor. The
voters overwhelmingly approved the committee's recommendation. Pastor Hoper
accepted the call at the same meeting.

There is much more which could be included in such a brief history of the
congregation. Zion's baptized membership is 1,480 persons. What will be obvious
to any careful reader of this history is that God has blessed Zion with capable
leaders over the years, who were not afraid to work and were open to His
guidance. May God continue to bestow His grace on the members of Zion and use
them in His ministry in the Beulah area.

Business community

Aarthun-Goetz Funeral Home

The Aarthun-Goetz Funeral Home opened in Beulah on April 23, 1988 under manager
Jay Seibel. The owner is Glenn Goetz of Washburn and Terry Sayler is the
manager of the chapel at Hazen.

Jay R. Seibel was born Nov. 3, 1961 at Thief River Falls, MN to Mr. and Mrs. Ben
Seibel, Jr. He moved along with his family to Harvey, ND, at the age of three.
He attended school and graduated from Harvey High School in 1980. He attended
Jamestown College from 1980-1984. He married Karen Grad on June 5, 1982 at
Selz, ND. He attended Central State University of Oklahoma 1985-86. He graduated
from CSU with a bachelor of science degree in mortuary science in 1986. He
worked for Baggerley Funeral Home of Edmond, OK from 1985-1986. They then moved
to Minot where Jay was with the Thomas Funeral Home from Sept. 1986 to April
1987 when they moved to Beulah.

Karen G. Grad was born Sept. 3, 1963 at Rugby, ND to Mr. and Mrs. Emmanuel
Grad. She attended school and graduated from Harvey High School in 1981. She
attended Jamestown College from 1981-1985 when she received her bachelor of arts
degree in nursing. While they lived in Oklahoma, she worked at Presbyterian
Hospital in Oklahoma City and at Edmond Memorial Hospital in Edmond, OK. While
in Minot, she worked at St. Joseph's Hospital. She is presently working as a
registered nurse at Beulah Community Nursing Home.

Jay and Karen purchased a home at 743 3rd St. NW, Beulah in Oct. 1987.

        American Family Insurance - Gary Miller, agent.

American Family Insurance

In June of 1977, Gary Miller became the insurance agent for American Family
Insurance in Beulah. Adam Keller of Beulah had previously been the company
agent. Gary is a native of Golden Valley and graduated from high school in
Beulah. After teaching and coaching for several years in North Dakota schools,
he decided to make a career change to the insurance business.

Gary's first office was located in the Professional Building on Main Street.
Since the agency was small, it took many years of hard work before the phones
began to ring steadily and in the first few years of business, Gary's
secretarial help was part-time only.

In 1981, Phyllis Baskerville was hired as a full-time secretary; she has been
with the agency as a valued employee ever since. It is not uncommon to find
Phyllis at the office in the early morning hours or on a weekend, trying to
finish her insurance paperwork.

In 1983, the agency moved to an office in the Prairie Plaza Shopping Center and
stayed at this location for three years. During this time, the multi-line agency
continued to increase in size and the phones became busier.

In 1985, the agency expanded its office facilities by building an office
structure with two other partners. This building, located along Highway 49, is
called the Hillside Office Complex and also houses the Mercer County Women's
Action and Resource Center, the ASCS office, Mercer County Extension Office,
Interstate Engineering, and Kootsikas Law Office. In 1986, the agency added
another part-time secretary, Lucy Emter, and opened an extension office in
Hazen, managed by Mary Adler.

The agency has grown considerably in size throughout the years. In 1977 the
agency started with 300 policies and has now grown to over 3,600 policies and
is the third largest American Family agency in the state.

The Bank of Beulah

As related in the 1964 jubilee history book, the Bank of Beulah is actually the
third bank to open its doors in Beulah. The First State Bank operated from
1913-1924, the German State Bank from 1915-1938, and the present bank actually
received its charter as the First State Bank of Zap in 1915. The members of the
initial board of directors were: John Young, P.S. Chaffee, and R.M. Stroup.

When the German State Bank failed in 1938, the First State Bank of Zap moved
down to Beulah and became known as the Bank of Beulah. The board of directors
were: T.F. Zimmerman, A.T. Zimmerman and Ludwig Fuchs. In 1955 the Bank of
Beulah was sold to F.K. Flemmer, D.H. Dettmann and Robert Keogh, Sr.

At that time the capital stock was $50,000. Surplus and undivided profits were
$102,497.55. Total deposits were $1,709,977.43 and loans were $148,404.88.

In 1956 the old, wooden two-story structure was torn down and a new 25-foot by
100-foot brick building was constructed on the site. During construction, bank
business was carried on as usual in the old Marshall-Malaise Hardware Building
which was the only building in town with a walled-in vault. In 1963 the bank
bought the adjacent Main Bar Building and in 1964 a 25 foot by 100 foot
addition was built. By 1978 the growing need for modernization led to the
construction of a 30-foot by 50-foot addition with a drive-up window and room
for an in-house computer system and employee lounge with full basement for
storage.

In 1966 Gertrude Buscher joined our ranks when she purchased Bob Keogh's bank
stock and became active in the general operation of the bank, serving as vice
president, office manager and member of the board of directors. F.K. Flemmer
remained on the board until he retired in 1986. In 1983 Kenneth Hintz, who had
worked for the First Bank System for 16 years, was hired as vice president. As
of December 1987 the bank officers are:

  Doug Dettmann--President
  Gert Buscher--Executive Vice President & Cashier
  Kenneth Hintz--Vice President
