During the last 25 years we've seen many changes and the biggest influence in
these changes was the building of the ANG plant. During "Impact" we would have
a line two to three blocks long at the drive-up window and on Friday nights the
bank lobby would be wall-to-wall people waiting to cash their pay checks.
During this time our help "hung in there," never losing their cool under some
very stressful conditions. This change has also brought us some good
experiences. We have had customers from all over the world and have made some
very good business relationships.

Basin Electric Power Cooperative

The partnership between Mercer County and Basin Electric goes back to 1961 when
the cooperative was formed.

Basin Electric Power Cooperative was founded as the supplemental power supplier
for rural electrics in the region because hydroelectric power from Missouri
River dams could not meet the region's ever-increasing demand.

Because Mercer County had abundant supplies of lignite coal and water and was
strategically located close to federal transmission lines, Basin Electric's
first plant was built near Stanton. When the Leland Olds Station became
operational in 1966, it was the largest lignite-fired electric generating plant
in the western hemisphere.

Since then Basin Electric has added a second unit to Leland Olds Station in
1975 and construction began on the first of two units of the Antelope Valley
Station north of Beulah in 1975.

        Basin Electric Power Cooperative - Antelope Valley Station.

Besides these generating plants, Basin Electric has a partnership with the ANG
coal gasification plant, sharing the railroad facility, water intake structure,
water treatment facilities and mining operations at the Coteau Freedom Mine. In
addition, Basin Electric's subsidiary, Basin Cooperative Services, owns and
operates the Glenharold Mine near the Leland Olds Station.

Basin Electric today has 118 member systems serving more than 1 million people
in North Dakota, South Dakota, Montana, Minnesota, Wyoming, Iowa, Nebraska and
Colorado, the largest geographic base of any other non-government utility in the
nation, covering 400,000 square miles.

One of Basin Electric's member systems is Oliver-Mercer Electric Cooperative,
headquartered in Hazen, which serves rural electric consumers in Mercer County.

Basin Electric's number-one mission is to provide a reliable power supply for
its members at the lowest possible cost consistent with sound business
practices. The more than 400 employees living in Mercer County and employed at
the Leland Olds Station, Antelope Valley Station and Glenharold Mine are
helping carry out this mission.

Basin Electric salutes the fine people of Mercer County and the contributions
they have made toward providing a reliable power supply to Basin Electric's
member systems.

Basin Electric congratulates the city of Beulah on its 75th jubilee and looks
forward to many more years of association with it.

Beulah Ben Franklin

Beulah's Ben Franklin Store, a variety store offering merchandise ranging from
crafts and fabrics to clothing to household goods to pets, had its roots in the
RCU Store which was opened in 1932.

Under the ownership of Carl Thelander, Albert Wolf and Charlie Wiegman, the
original store was a combination Federated Store and grocery establishment. The
RCU Store followed that.

In 1954 Thelander and Wolf switched to a Ben Franklin franchise and converted
the store, which became a full-line variety store.

On Nov. 26, 1955, Wolf died, and his wife, Elsie, assumed the partnership. The
store was run in this way until 1965, when Carl passed away.

At that time, Mrs. Rags Thelander, Carl's widow, became the sole proprietor of
the store and set about learning to run it - and very successfully.

        Ben Franklin Store (old building).

        Ben Franklin Store (new building).

        Ben Franklin Store (new building) - Charles Thelander, owner.

She ran the store alone until 1972 when son Charles graduated from college and
returned to Beulah, and the two formed a very successful family management team.
At that time they built the facility which serves as the main part of today's
Ben Franklin Store, on the corner of Main St. and Central Ave. in Beulah.

The business began to feel the same growing pains as all other Main Street
businesses during the energy impact years. People moved to Beulah and required
more and a larger variety of items to serve their needs, and Ben Franklin
responded in 1982 by adding the adjacent building (formerly Modern Barber and
Beauty Shop) and increasing its floor space and merchandise.

Rags and Charles ran the store together until Rags passed away on Jan. 2, 1988.
Charles continues the family operation.

The store continues as a full-line variety and department store with emphasis on
fabrics, crafts, stationery, ready-to-wear clothing, toys, toiletries and
housewares.

        Ben's Muffler Shop--Ben Muhlhauser, owner.

Ben's Muffler Service

Ben's Muffler Service, 221 West Main, was built in 1941 by Ben Muhlhauser, Sr.,
a Blue Grass, ND native, as a gasoline station and automotive repair shop in
1941. He utilized his railroad section-boss experience from Zap and Montana and
back to Beulah, plus the apprenticeship skills he learned from John Field. The
store grew after 1946 with the addition of a Kaiser Fraiser dealership, a 1950
Ferguson tractor dealer-ship and an Allis Chalmers dealership in 1958.

Ben Muhlhauser, Jr., the current owner, took over in 1958 and returned the
company to a gas station and automotive repair shop. In 1977, he began accepting
service and muffler repair work only. Today he specializes in muffler repair.
He has customers in the Beulah/Hazen area, as well as Killdeer, Pick City,
Bismarck and the coal mines.

Ben is a member of the Beulah Eagles Club and the Beulah Chamber of Commerce.
He enjoys riding his motorcycle with other members of the Exit 22 Retreads Club.

Benz Insurance Agency

The Benz Insurance Agency was formed in 1961 with Darold and Adella Benz as the
sole owners and operators. The Benz Insurance Agency has been a general
insurance agency with numerous companies, including such national companies as
Allstate and Allied. Darold has primarily handled the casualty business,
including auto, farm, homeowners, business, etc., while Della has worked in the
personal medical, nursing home and Medicare supplement type of insurance.

While being active in the insurance business on a local level, Darold has also
been president and chairman of the board of the North Dakota Professional
Insurance Agents. In his year as president the organization moved its office
from Fargo to Bismarck and went from a part-time staff to two full-time people
and nearly doubled its membership.

During the first years of business the Benz Insurance Agency had part-time help
usually recruited from the Beulah High School sophomore class, but when Diana
(Heier) Schulz was hired in 1969 as a sophomore, she worked part-time and today
is still with the agency.

In addition to spending many years building an insurance agency, Darold and
Della have both been very active in the community. Della is involved in the
Women's Club, church women, Mercer County Fair, Mrs. Jaycees and Church
Council. Darold has been president of the Mercer County Fair, Zion Lutheran
Church Council, Beulah and North Dakota Jaycees, North Dakota Association of
Fairs, Professional Insurance Agency of North Dakota and is president of the
North Dakota League of Cities for the year 1988. Darold is also in his third
term as mayor of Beulah.

        The new Beulah Beacon building was constructed in 1983 and houses
        modern facilities.

Beulah Beacon

If any single business pulses in rhythm with its community, it's the community
newspaper. Dependent on advertising revenue for its existence, it is fat in
flush times, lean when the going gets rough. Dependent on community support, it
is sometimes brashly controversial, but more often gently chiding when it sees
something that needs changing.

The Beulah Beacon, Beulah's community newspaper and official county newspaper
since 1978, is no exception.

The Beacon has a long and colorful history, like most small-town newspapers.
Often in the early days a town would exist for several years before some
enterprising young printer's devil would exchange his soul for ownership of a
press and some paper and become the town's conscience.

With Peter Reese, an outspoken fellow who nagged his readers incessantly about
community improvements, as its first editor under owner A.D. Brown, the first
Beulah Independent was printed in 1914, the same year Beulah was incorporated,
in conjunction with the coming of the railroad. Reese was a forward-looking man
who badgered his readers about good roads and was certain that Beulah's future
depended on and was assured by its vast lignite deposits and the attendant coal
industry.

Two years later, Brown took on the dual shackle of publisher and editor, moving
to Beulah after Reese left.

The Independent was, like most rural papers, printed with less than
state-of-the-art equipment, though they did keep up with technology. Type was
hand-set in the early days and the paper was printed on a George Washington
hand press. That was replaced in the late 1920s by a power-driven press.

In 1935 the George Washington was put on display in the University of North
Dakota museum, billed as the last hand press in North Dakota. A used Linotype
machine was bought, meaning type could be set by machine rather than by the
laborious hand method.

Brown died in 1938, but his wife, no doubt having inhaled enough printer's ink
to affect her own bloodstream over the years, continued to run the paper until
she sold it in 1943 to Harold Dally.

Things sailed along pretty steady over the years with Beulah, small but stable,
being reflected in its newspaper of the same vein.

Along with skyrocketing inflation and bad economic times in the late 1960s, the
Independent saw some rough times, too. It was bought by Glenn Elliot, who
couldn't make a go of it. After a one-year hiatus in 1967-68 during which time
the town was without official news, the Independent was purchased by Lyle Suhr
and Richard Berg, with Elliot writing an open letter to the town hoping they'd
learned their lesson and would support the paper. At the time Suhr and Berg
bought it, subscriptions were $4 a year for a four-page paper.

Those two printed their first edition on Oct. 2, 1969 and, though they and their
wives struggled and sweated over the Independent, their last edition came off
the press on Jan. 21, 1970. It was only two pages and was published only to
keep their second-class mailing permit current.

Early in May, the paper was purchased by Don Gackle, who owned the McLean
County Independent, and became part of the BHG Inc. newspaper chain of three.
Ken Beauchamp, who had been production manager for Gackle's third paper The
Hazen Star, moved to the tiny apartment above the colorful but cramped
Independent offices in Beulah, which were behind the Bank of Beulah, and, on
May 7, put out the first issue containing his first editorial column ever.

That first issue also marked some major changes in community news coverage.
Where formerly front-page news had included few photos and lots of engagement
announcements, now it carried pictures and a "hard news" story about a spill of
crude oil into the Knife River upstream from Beulah. That philosophy - acting
as watchdog and community informant as well as the social register - has been
adhered to and has won the Beacon much respect over the years.

Rather than keeping the "Independent" name, in which Gackle felt people no
longer had confidence, a contest was held for a few weeks during which people
could submit their ideas for a name for the baby newspaper.

During that time it was published as The Beulah Newspaper. Not original, but
functional until the winner was chosen.

That proved to be Mrs. Ralph Johnson, Zap, whose "Beulah Beacon" was chosen from
among 68 entries. She was awarded a $50 prize. Later in 1970, one of the
Beacon's longest-term employees began her long-standing column, "Have You
Heard?" Then, she was Carol Flemmer; now Carol Buchmann, and she still writes
the column.

The Beacon's first subscription rate was $4.50 annually with servicemen (this
was during the Vietnam era) getting a break at $3 per year. The paper started
at six pages with a circulation of less than 400 and by September that year
published its first county-wide edition, going to an communities in the county,
with 14 pages of local news.

Shortly after came energy impact, and the Beacon grew flush along with other
businesses in the community. By mid-1975 community interest brought about the
development of a sports page and volume dictated hiring a sportswriter.
Beauchamp chose Bob Link, then a high-school sophomore, who served as the
Beacon sports editor for 10 years, endearing himself to his readers as
SportLink.

By 1976 impact was in full swing and the Beacon had doubled in size, running
several energy impact-related stories each week regarding construction, permits,
pollution and public hearings, as well as weather reports from Washington,
D.C., as the winds that blew there reached all the way to the Dakota prairies.

Circulation was up to more than 2,000 with a weekly page count of 16-18, not
counting Info which was soon to become The Common, a section devoted primarily
to agriculture-related news, which is shared with sister paper The Hazen Star.
The increase in business demanded Beauchamp spend more time on management,
overseeing both the Beacon and Star, so Mark Miller was hired as news editor
for the Beacon and Beauchamp became general manager.

A milestone and a celebration came in the 1978 election year as the Beacon was
chosen by county voters as its official county newspaper, ousting the Star from
that long-held place of honor. That designation meant that, with publication of
county government legals, the Beacon could offer a larger page count each week
and thus more "news hole" with which to inform and entertain its readership.

Link took a hiatus with the National Guard and, when he came back in 1979, times
were more than flush. The Beacon carried 20-plus pages each week and had on
staff an editor and two writer/photographers. A year later writer Tim Kjos was
made news editor, a position he held for seven years. When Info became The
Common in early 1981, the paper's circulation was 5,200. By mid-'81, it
carried 38 pages, along with an editorial commending its advertisers for their
loyalty and support.

Optimism ran high over the next few years, as the power and gasification plants
were completed and went on-line. The Beacon built new offices on the bypass at
the east end of town and the old Independent office became a parking lot. Then,
in August 1985 on Black Tuesday, the bottom dropped out: The five-partner
consortium that had constructed the gas plant abandoned the project, leaving it
in the hands of the Department of Energy.

The repercussions were instant and harsh, felt all over the county. The Beacon
underwent a major change at the same time, as Kjos and Link both left and
current editor Nancy Northrup went on-line the same week the plant threatened
to close.

Businesses closed, advertising dropped for the Beacon, optimism crashed,
uncertainty, doubt and worry reigned among the community. A downward spiral
continued for quite a time until things began to level off.

There they have stayed. The community and the newspaper have become more
stable, though all are still troubled by gusts of uncertain political breezes.
The Beacon dropped from that high 38 to an average of 20 pages, still better
than its earlier years when the community was almost completely
agriculture-dependent, but not able to provide the same coverage with a third
the staff and half the page count as in earlier years.

Nevertheless, its search for excellence continued. Kjos had won top honors for
the Beacon in 1984 in the state newspaper association competition, and Northrup
followed suit in 1986, both having the honor of dusting a traveling trophy which
rested in the office during each of those years.

Though forced to squeeze by inflation and economic downturns, having reduced
page size and increased all rates (a subscription was now $16), the Beacon was
still performing its original function: Informing, entertaining, lauding and
chiding its readers.

And so it continues to do.

        Shirley Muhlhauser in R.C.U. Store.

        Beulah Cash Store has had a long, colorful history.

Beulah Cash Store

The Beulah Cash Store was started by H.Z. Rosen in approximately 1945. At this
time the store was located in the old pool hall (the Schilling building) on
Main Street. This building is no longer standing. In its location is the
present Fabricare Cleaners.

Joseph Muhlhauser began working for Rosen in 1947 and bought the business with
Shirley (Herman) Muhlhauser as a partner in 1951. They bought the George Kuch
building on Main Street. The Coast to Coast addition is presently located where
the Kuch building had been. This store prospered by selling dry goods, shoes
and boots and men's and women's clothing. It was truly a family business, as
both Joe and Shirley and their three daughters, Jay, Jill and Tara, could often
be found working behind that big wooden counter measuring fabric or operating
the old cash register.

In 1973, the business moved directly across the street to occupy a larger and
newer building which was formerly occupied by Galloway's Super Valu. Shirley
Muhlhauser remained an active business partner until 1977, and Joseph
Muhlhauser operated the store until his death in March of 1988.

        Beulah Clinic.

Beulah Community Nursing Home

The Beulah Community Nursing Home, which in 1987 celebrated its 25th
anniversary, was incorporated on March 1, 1960, as a North Dakota non-profit
corporation.

The building in which the home is located was originally built in 1952 to be
used as a hospital, but it was never used for that purpose.

The Rev. Joachim Memorial Home board of directors started the Beulah Community
Nursing Home as a community-owned home in response to an increasing need for
care for the area's elderly residents.

An earnest-money contract was presented to the directors for a proposal to
purchase the hospital building in April, 1961. With a 3 Percent loan from the
Bank of North Dakota, the work began.

        Beulah Community Nursing Home.

In 1962 service to Beulah as a 24-bed nursing home began. Because of the
original intent of the building, rooms in the original quarters are less than
uniform, and that difference is noticeable today. The current board of
directors is considering remodeling the area to improve its usefulness and
efficiency.

Six residents were admitted the first day the home was open. When the original
home was first opened there was quite a scramble to insure there was enough
furniture for the residents. Mattresses and other furniture were donated by
people throughout the area, and some had been stored in barns and other
unlikely places.

As a result, much of the cleanup the first few weeks consisted of making sure
all the oats and other surprises were out, and employees who have worked for
BCNH since those early days still recall with a laugh how they opened those up
and the oats fell out.

Two years later 18 more beds were added, allowing the home to provide skilled
care to 42 residents. During this time the home continued to develop a
reputation for quality care and services. From the early 1960s the demand for
nursing care and services for the aged increased rapidly, as did governmental
rules and regulations, which still are the biggest obstacles the nursing home
staff must fight to give quality care at an affordable cost.

In an effort to better serve the area elderly and to expand the services of the
home, a merger between the Beulah Community Nursing Home and the Joachim
Memorial Home of Beulah was brought about on Feb. 11, 1981. This merger phased
out the basic care Joachim Home, which then was used by ANG coal gasification
administrative personnel and later was sold to the Beulah Senior Citizens, and
allowed the Beulah Community Nursing Home to construct an additional 50 beds
and offer basic intermediate and skilled nursing care to area residents.

With the additional services and living space at the community nursing home
comes a continued commitment to providing personal care to the individual needs
of each resident. Concern and professional services have been and continue to
be the trademark of the Beulah Community Nursing Home.

The home's first board of directors was Sam Miller, Ed Schulz, Herb Engbrecht,
Fred Flemmer (who now lives in the home) and Fred Galloway. The home has seen
three administrators and four nursing directors since its inception: The Rev.
John Schmeier in 1962, Herb Feil in 1966 and Dave Almen in 1980; nursing
directors have been Ira Wing, 1962, Marge O'Neil, 1962, Julie Knodel, 1975 and
currently Loretta Greni, who started in 1982.

The first addition to the home was financed with a 6 percent loan from Gate
City and in July 1965 it opened, at a total cost for construction and
furnishings of $175,000. By contrast, the second addition, opened in 1982, was
financed by $2.16 million in MIDA bonds.

The nursing home is regulated by the North Dakota State Health Department and
has 88 residents today, compared to the six it began with, and has a capacity
of 90. Current medical director is Dr. Harjeet Singh, following the term of Dr.
Ewert, who retired in Dec. 1979.

The home's first volunteer workers were the Gray Ladies, which included about
100 volunteers. That group disbanded in 1981 to be replaced as a formal
volunteer group by the Beulah Community Nursing Home Auxiliary.

Religious services are provided to the home by the Mercer County Ministerial
Associates. Two services are provided for residents each week, with the
ministers rotating these duties.

Unusual among nursing homes, BCNH is owned by county residents. Anyone over 21
and a resident of Mercer County is legally part owner of the home and is
qualified - and encouraged--to take an active part in working with the home.

That makes for a number of advantages for the home's residents. They can vote
for members of the board of directors, on building projects, major changes in
service or any other major decision involving the home, giving them an active
voice in how the home serves them.

Though that means BCNH doesn't have to answer to any corporate office as do
homes owned by chains, giving total local control, it also means the home
doesn't have access to some of the experience and advice large corporations do.
Certain medical and geriatric specialists are not available to the home because
there is no large corporation to retain their services. And since the home is
not church-affiliated, no single church group is obligated to support the home
on a continuing basis.

Of course, that also gives the home the freedom to work with all the area
churches, and the local control and direction more than makes up for the
minuses.

The nursing home has seen and is still struggling with its share of problems,
notable cutbacks in financing on the state and federal level coupled with
increasing state and federal regulations with which the home must comply. When
the original home opened in 1962, rates charged residents were $80 per month.
Today, that figure is $60 per day. In addition, staff has increased from 67 to
107.

Beulah Dairy Queen

The Beulah Dairy Queen is known as the "treat capital of the world" and it is a
special treat as well as a surprise to have such as enterprise in Beulah. The
Dairy Queen advertising is a familiar symbol nation-wide, attracting people of
all ages. The present business is fairly new and is one of the three top
ranking Dairy Queens in the state of North Dakota in size, seating capacity and
modernization. It is situated on Highway No. 49 - another good reason for its
popularity, as it is just a hop off highway 200 and easily accessible to those
traveling that route.

The business was opened in 1983 and featured landscaping with sizable trees, a
drive-in service window, ample parking, an indoor area that seats 68 and a
comfortable outdoor picnic spot.

The number of daily customers attests to the fact that the quality of food and
service is special.

Phillip Eastgate, operations manager since it opened, is a familiar person in
the community, as he has been here since 1975. He was formerly employed by the
Beulah school system as teacher, coach and principal. Phil, his wife Debbie and
daughter Ashley live in Beulah.

Phil states that the Dairy Queen is proud to have the distinction of being the
largest employer of high school students in Beulah. The employment is somewhat
seasonal ranging from 20-30 during the summer months and about 75 percent of
these are high school students. They are well trained under the guidance of Mr.
Eastgate and are courteous, pleasant ambassadors of the Dairy Queen.

Originally the enterprise was owned by Gary Allard and Robert Alexander Inc. as
C. & D. Properties. Alexander is now the sole owner after he purchased the
property from his partner in the spring of 1984.

Although Dairy Queens are considered fast food establishments, complete food
preparation is done at the store. All the specialty items and treats are also
made there with a full line of preparation equipment. Beulah's Dairy Queen is
somewhat unique as it has one food specialty that customers probably won't find
in any other fleischkuechle.

        Beulah Drug - Dave Just, owner.

Beulah Drug Store

The present business was purchased by Ted Herman in December 1928, from the
George Thamert estate. The present building was erected in 1930. Pharmacists
preceding Mr. Thamert in Beulah were a Mr. Kuhl, L.G. Stutsman and Dean Hall.

Ted Herman graduated from NDSU school of pharmacy in 1926 and, after purchasing
Beulah Drug in 1928, operated the store alone until 1957 when his son, Jerome,
joined him in the business after graduating from NDSU school of pharmacy. Ted
passed away in January 1977 after which time Jerome operated the drug store
until its sale to Dave Just on Nov. 1, 1979.

When Just bought Beulah Drug, there were three part-time employees. In October
1987, there were 11 full-time and two part-time employees. Clarence Schnieder
had been with Beulah Drug for 35 years, starting Feb. 1, 1946, until Jan. 31,
1981. He now works in a semi-retired position.

The store had been recarpeted and the interior remodeled right before Just
purchased the store. Since Just has had the store, he has rearranged
merchandise, bought new fixtures, tried different card companies, run sales and
expanded the gift line.

The Justs have expanded their family from one son to one son and four daughters
since coming to Beulah.

        Beulah Lumber Company - Les Heringer, owner.

Beulah Lumber Company

Les Heringer was the last of three brothers to establish his own lumberyard,
following in the footsteps of his father and grandfather. That first lumberyard
was established 45 years ago in Anamoose, ND, and growing up with the business
allowed Les to become well-versed in the selling of lumber.

Preparing a feasibility study on beginning a new business was a class project
for Heringer in college, but he took it more seriously than most. Upon
graduation from UND in 1978, Beulah Lumber was opened for business. Land was
purchased at the intersection of Highways 49 and 200 from local farmer Carl
Schnaidt. First constructed was a pole building and, for a time, Les' desk was
a unit of plywood. Soon the office was built, followed later by a second pole
building, to allow for more inside lumber storage.

Employees have numbered from three to 11. Currently, Beulah Lumber employs six
full-time people and two part-time, including Les' wife, Barb. She often brings
their two children with her, right in step with the Heringer family tradition.
Current employees include Milda Frei, Gary Wallner, Stan Rambough, Dave Gramm
and Wanda Etzel.

At one time, most of Beulah Lumber's business was done in units at a time, but
that has slowed with the changing economy in Coal Country. Heringer has always
backed his product with "service after the sale" and also promises that "you'll
remember quality long after price is forgotten." Other services include free
estimates, delivery, drafting and glass repair. Beulah Lumber has also been a
part of introducing innovative building techniques to the area, such as earth
homes and double-wall energy-efficient homes.

As Beulah celebrates its Jubilee, Beulah Lumber will begin its second decade.
We are proud to be a part of this thriving community!

        Ed Carlstrom, owner of Beulah Twin Cinema, provides up-to-the-minute
        releases for Beulah movie-goers.

Beulah Twin Cinema

Giving new life to an old building, Beulah Twin Cinema is in the building
formerly operated as the Roxy Theatre and, before that, the Princess Theatre.

Owner Ed Carlstorm, who purchased the building from Daryl Zimmerman, remodeled
the spacious theater into two theatres after the current fashion. The smaller
has a seating capacity of 163 and the larger will seat 215. The larger theatre
contains the original stage and curtain used in the Roxy.

Carlstrom rents videotapes as well, with a stock of 1,500 which continues to
increase. The video rental side of the business actually came first, as it was
opened in October, 1987, followed in November by the movie theatres.

The vintage 1929 building was vacant for about three years, two and a half of
which Carlstrom spent searching out funding for the theatre venture. $40,000 of
that went into the remodeling project.

In addition to the theatres and video rentals, Beulah Twin Cinema rents
videocassette recorders (VCRs) and will soon rent video cameras. Carlstrom also
offers a video transfer service, by which patrons may have 8mm movies
transferred to videotape for more convenient viewing.

Video equipment is also sold, including VCRs, videocameras, televisions,
videotapes, and related supplies.

Beulah Vision Center

Dr. James A. Power, since his arrival in Mercer County in Aug. 1953, has
provided the area with consistent, high quality vision care. He opened his
office in a recently completed building on Main Street in Beulah. The structure
was built by Ted Herman, former owner and operator of Beulah Drug. The building
was shared with Dr. Robert Peterson and later with Dr. Leo Misslin; both were
dentists.

In 1975 Dr. Power constructed an office building on the site of the E.A. Kees
building. Increased space had become a necessity with the gradual addition of
new diagnostic instruments, the expansion of a frame inventory that has grown
from the initial 50 frames to the present 1000, and the addition of contact
lens fitting to the practice.

        Beulah Vision Center - Dr. James A. Power and Dr. Michael J.
        Hammerschmidt, optometrists.

        LaVon Kirchmeier, Lois Scherer, Saly Battest - employees at Beulah
        Vision Clinic.

LaVon (Mrs. Dennis) Kirchmeier joined the practice in 1964 as receptionist.
Since that time her position had developed into optometric assistant, frame
specialist and office manager. She is assisted in the office by Sally Battest
and Lois (Mrs. Brian) Scherer.

Between 1964 and 1978 Dr. Power maintained an office in Glen Ullin, practicing
there one day each week. When the press of activity in the Beulah practice
forced him to close that office he was recognized by the Glen Ullin community
for his service there.

Dr. Michael Hammerschmidt, a Richardton native, went into partnership with Dr.
Power in Aug. 1983. Dr. Hammerschmidt, a 1976 graduate of the University of
North Dakota and 1981 graduate of Illinois College of Optometry, had practiced
in Dickinson previous to his arrival in Mercer County. Mrs. Hammerschmidt is the
former Nancy Nelson of Dickinson. She is employed as an account clerk at MDU's
Coyote Station.

Dr. Power is a 1950 graduate of UND and a 1953 graduate of Southern College of
Optometry. Born in Minot, his home was Crosby, ND. Early schooling was received
in Crosby schools and, following high school graduation, he served in the U.S.
Navy. He is married to the former Phyllis Kjerstad of Grand Forks. Dr. Kjerstad
was a former president of Dickinson State College.

Mrs. Power is also a graduate of UND. She has been an active participant in
local, area, and state church and community and musical activities. Dr. Power
has served as president of the North Dakota Optometric Association and the
Board of Examiners in Optometry. He was appointed and served as a member of the
ND Health Council, elected to the Beulah school board and has been active in
area fraternal and community activities.

The Powers are the parents of four daughters; the first born in Memphis, Tenn.,
and the others in the Hazen Memorial Hospital now Sakakawea Medical Center. They
are: Paula (Mrs. Thomas Berg) of Rapid City, SD, Kathryn (Mrs. Carlos Sampedro)
of Buenos Aires, Argentina, Elizabeth (Mrs. Bruce Hawkinson) of St. Peter, Mn.
and Holly (Mrs. Scott Bommersbach) of Rosseau-Greenbush, Mn. There are five
grandchildren.

        Bloom'n House--Connie Gegelman, owner.

Bloom'n House

Business is blooming at the Bloom'n House, Inc.! Connie Gegelman purchased the
florist shop, which was begun by Karl Menge, from Gaylen Sailer and opened
Bloom'n House, Inc. at 113 Central Avenue in March of 1979.

Gegelman feels the business has grown stronger every year thanks to local
support and the able help of "bookkeeper" husband, Jeff (who helps in his spare
time from their kennel business), "delivery" sons, Shawn and Shad, and
part-time staff Darcy Thompson, Nancy Mathern, and Esther Bauer.

The Bloom'n House specializes in fresh flowers and plants for weddings,
funerals, parties, and seasonal and special occasions. Gegelman has also added
gift items.

        Connie Gegelman and Stella Stern of the Bloom'n House.

One of the most memorable orders Gegelman has prepared was the 500 carnation
corsages for GPGA/ANG women staff, wives and dates for their Christmas party in
1984.

For the past nine years Gegelman has prepared 200 carnation corsages for the
ladies of Knife River Coal Company for the annual company Christmas dinner.

Bloom'n House staff prepares funeral floral arrangements for the communities of
Beulah, Hebron, and Glen Ullin.

Gegelman's favorite part of the job includes the lovely spring flower bouquets.
The very best part of the business is seeing the delighted smiles of joy on the
faces of her customers when she makes her daily deliveries.

Coast to Coast

The Coast to Coast Hardware store is owned by Al and Suzan Schock and is located
at 116 West Main Street. The business was purchased from Helmuth and Helen Hilz
on Oct. 1, 1978.

The Schocks are natives of Turtle Lake, ND. Prior to purchasing the Coast to
Coast store Al was employed in a similar retailing hardware and lumber
business. Suzan has a degree in nursing and was employed at the Turtle Lake
Hospital.

During the past 10 years the store has grown from a staff of four to its
present staff of nine with additional part-time help added during special
seasons. With a third of a million dollar inventory, the store offers the
shopper a complete line of hardware, housewares and related items from its 10
major departments.

        Coast to Coast Store - Al and Suzan Schock, owners.

Much local history is associated with lots 13 and 14, on which the Coast to
Coast store is located. These lots were the site of the first building built in
Beulah; in fact, it was built by Dr. Norman E. Vredenburg of Hebron in 1911. He
also built a large house about a block away, which later became known as the
Joachim Memorial Home. Vredenburg named his town Troy, but he never lived in
the house nor occupied the two-story building. Many people thought he had
speculated about the railroad coming through this area and was going to be
ready for the boom. But he jumped the gun three years too early and finally
sold the building to the Tuttle Land Company. So the town of Troy died before
it had a chance to live.

        Employees of Coast to Coast. Back row - Left to right: Al and Sue
        Schock, owners; Kely Rudolph, Helmuth Hilz, Wilma Hausauer. Front row:
        Sharon Frank, Esther Fleisher, Melita Scherer.

In the early years of Beulah, this building's second story was used in many
different ways. In the beginning, it was living quarters, then meeting rooms, a
dance hall, church and revival meeting rooms, and then in later years it was
used for storage.

Eventually the Tuttle Land Company sold the building to Lorenz Joos, who opened
the first hardware store in Beulah. He opened the Lorenz Joos Hardware Store in
1914. Joos sold the store to L.G. Rose, who operated the L.G. Rose Hardware and
Implement in 1929 and into the late '30s. W.H. Esterly bought the building and
rented it to many different tenants, including Church's Gambles Store, Jose's
Gambles Store and then in 1942 a young man from Rolla came to town and rented
it for his new grocery store, Galloway's IGA, which later became known as
Galloway's Super Valu. After Fred and Lillian Galloway moved their business
across the street to what is today the Beulah Cash Store, the building was torn
down and for a number of years the two vacant lots were used for a downtown
ice-skating rink.

In 1916, Fred and Emma Tesky constructed a building on this site and used it as
a confectionery store and pool hall. They sold the building to Ted Muhlhauser,
who sold it to Dr. Oliginey. It is not known whether the doctor ever used the
building, but records at city hall show that he died on July 6, 1931.

Rudolph Stuhr Sr. bought the building and opened a cafe. Rudolph worked in the
grain elevator. The Stuhrs were homesteaders who lived south of town and
operated a small mine on their land. When their oldest son, David, was killed
in the mine the family moved to town. When Rudolph Sr. died, his widow Carrie
rented the building and living quarters to Albert Sailer and his family, who
also operated a cafe and pool hall.

According to the abstracts, Hadley Graves bought the building in 1934 for
$1,000. He sold it to Tillie Flemmer who, with her sister, Helen, operated a
beauty shop and lived in the quarters in the back of the building. In those
days when a woman got a permanent it would take so long that many times she was
served lunch so she wouldn't get too hungry.

When they moved to California they rented the shop to Elite Beauty Shop, to Ida
Zeller and Tina Krieger. They operated the business until after World War II
when Jack and Evelyn Chilson bought the building and for many years operated
Jack's Barber Shop. When Jack and Evelyn moved to Libby, MT, they sold the
building to George and Helen Kuch. George used it as a barber shop for a few
years and then he and Helen moved their variety store into the building. It was
later purchased by Shirley and Joe Muhlhauser, who operated the Beulah Cash
Store, a clothing and dry goods store.

In 1955, Helmuth and Helen Hilz decided to go into the hardware business and
purchased the Corner Hardware store from Fred Flemmer and D.H. Dettmann. In
1961, the Hilzes joined the Coast to Coast family and soon found the need to
expand their building. In 1963, they bought lots 13 and 14 of block 10 and
built a 50' x 85' building. In 1968, they again felt the need to build so they
bought the Beulah Cash Store from Joe and Shirley Muhlhauser and expanded into
what is now the Coast to Coast store.

The Coteau Freedom Mine

The Coteau Properties Company, a wholly-owned subsidiary of The North American
Coal Corporation, operates a 9.9 million ton-per-year surface lignite mine
located 10 miles northwest of Beulah, ND.

The Freedom Mine supplies 5.2 million tons of lignite annually to Basin
Electric's Antelope Valley Station and 4.7 million tons annually to the ANG
coal gasification plant.

        Coteau Freedom Mine.

Coal deliveries to the Antelope Valley Station began in August, 1983, and to the
gasification plant in March, 1984, with delivery contracts for a period of 35
and 25 years, respectively.

Surface mining is achieved by utilizing large mining equipment, including
105-cubic-yard draglines, 20-cubic-yard capacity shovels, and 170-ton capacity
coal haulers.

As of November, 1986, 240 North Dakotans were employed at the mine site, with
the majority of these employees residing in Hazen and Beulah.

Since it first opened, the mine has been in full compliance with both state and
federal reclamation regulations, which require that the land be restored to its
original productivity.

        MDU's Coyote Station.

Coyote Station, Unit No. 1 Montana-Dakota Utilities Company

During the early 1970s, five electric utility companies found their customers'
needs for energy increasing rapidly. To satisfy this need, a consortium was
formed to construct one large 410-megawatt electric generating station to serve
all five utilities. This generating station is Coyote Station, Unit No. 1.

Construction began on Oct. 10, 1977, on a low hill southwest of Beulah. Four
years were necessary to construct and start up Coyote Station. On May 1, 1981,
Coyote was declared commercial, ending its construction period and beginning
its service life.

Coyote Station supplies power through the Mid-Continent Area Power Pool (MAPP)
to the customers of its owners: Minnesota Power, Montana-Dakota Utilities
Company, Northern Municipal Power Agency, Northwestern Public Service Company,
and Otter Tail Power Company. Montana-Dakota Utilities Company also acts as
Coyote's operating agent.

Coyote directly employs approximately 100 full-time people. All full-time
employees live in Beulah, Hazen, Zap, or the surrounding area.

Coyote also contributes to the local economy through fuel contracts with its
fuel supplier, Knife River Coal Mining Company's south Beulah Mine.

The challenges that Coyote now faces, providing cost-effective energy and
simultaneously meeting environmental obligations, will not diminish. These
concerns will surely intensify in the future.

Coyote's dedicated and capable employees will be a valuable asset in meeting
these obligations.

        Dakota Helicopter Service. Helicopter with microfoil boom and
        hypodermic spray nozzles.

Dakota Helicopter Service

Few local people are aware of the extensive, modern helicopter services
operated at the Beulah Municipal Airport by Jim Morton, who came here in 1981
as airport manager.

Dakota Helicopter Air Service was located at the Beulah airport through the
encouragement of Fred Galloway, giving Beulah "bragging rights" to a federally
approved base operator specializing in helicopters. The service is the only such
facility in the state and enjoys an excellent reputation for efficiency and
professionalism. It sports four Bell 70 helicopters on the field, valued at
about $70,000 each, mounted with an $18,000 boom which will cover a 30- to
40-foot swath while spraying, with no chemical drift.

Special spray nozzles, some 56 mounted on a microfoil spray boom with hypodermic
needles, enable Morton to crop spray in most conditions for weed and pest
control.

        Dakota Helicopter Service - Jim and Shawn Morton, inside hangar.

Much of Morton's and son Shawn's work is contracted for the government or power
companies, doing mapping, survey or patrol work. They work rough terrain for
weed control and wildlife surveys, and charting and patrol work for the State
Game and Fish Department. They also check power lines.

Interestingly, the Mortons take their landing pad with them when they head out
for a job - it's mounted atop a large truck which goes with them, along with a
camper where they live until the job is done.

Morton has flown since 1960 when he farmed and worked with a regular spray plane
at Larimore, ND. The farm was sold that year and he began giving helicopter
lessons to family. Feeling a move would be beneficial, he eventually moved his
operation to Beulah, partly because of the odds of securing work with oil or
seismographic companies.

Morton lives on the Beulah airport premises and he and Shawn helped build the
spacious hangar which houses spray and dispersal equipment (which is
manufactured there also), an office area, waiting and rest rooms, a telephone
and records and computer space, in addition to a comfortable three-bedroom loft
apartment. Jim built this and it is available for pilots when necessary.

Beulah is an excellent location for the Mortons' work, because it is centrally
located as they cover the state from border to border --even venturing into
Minnesota where Jim once flew for some film work on "Wild Kingdom."

Beulah's airport is mainly a helicopter service, and the Mortons are annually
inspected by the federal government. Flight instruction licenses are renewed
every two years and mechanic inspection occurs annually. Jim and Shawn are both
licensed by the federal government, the Environmental Protection Agency, state
aeronautics board and the county. Jim is also a certified airplane and
helicopter instructor.

Jim operates a flying school and, during energy construction days, had more
than 25 students, most of whom were construction workers. During those days,
there were 30 and sometimes 40 planes on the field at once; too many, said the
Mortons. Now, traffic is mostly pleasure planes, running to 10 or 12 a week.

The largest plane trying the field, against Jim's advice, was a Convar 440, a
30-Passenger airplane, which was considered much too large for the Beulah
facility. It proved much too heavy, and broke through the seal just before
lift-off.

Nowadays, practicing to handle heavy loads in the 800-horse Sikorsky results in
some strange sights--large hay bales become airborne and seem to float through
the sky.

A certified helicopter pilot's license requires 150 hours of flying time, at
from $160 to $500 per hour. It takes a rich man to get a rating, and experience
to land a job in the oil fields; 500 practice hours are need before a pilot can
even apply for an oil-related job.

Jim and his wife, Audrey, have twin girls who attend Beulah High School and
their daughter, Lisa, works at Cenex. The other half of the partnership, Shawn,
and his wife, Dawn, and their two children live in Beulah. A familiar, almost
family, figure is Rocky, the Malamute who came to live with them when the
hangar was built in '81.

Elite Hair Stylists

In 1954, Frieda Wiedrich located her Elite Hair Stylists in the building next
to Ben Franklin, which is now incorporated into the Ben Franklin Store. At that
time she was in business with her husband, the late Wilmer Wiedrich, a barber.
Wilmer was mayor of Beulah for eight years and served on the city council for
16 years. In November, 1979, Wiedrich moved to her current location in Prairie
Plaza Shopping Center.

During the energy boom, five people worked in the shop. Now three do. Since
1981, Ava Ost has worked at Elite. Leta Tupa and Paula DeHaven also work there.
They attend seminars in Bismarck, offered by supply houses, and go to the State
Hair Dressers Convention. Frieda writes "Beauty Tips," an advertising column in
the Beulah Beacon. She has been doing this on a weekly basis for a year
and-a-half. She has also taught beauty tips in high school classes.

The Elite Hair Stylists salon is a full-service salon offering men's cuts and
perms, perms, cuts, color, bleaches, frost, manicures and eyebrow waxing.

Twyla (Frieda's daughter) and Steve Larson opened Elite Body Fitness on July
20, 1987. The shop features exercise machines, toning and firming. Two hours on
the exercise machines are said to produce the equivalent value of 14 hours of
aerobic exercise.

Els Sanitation Service

Els Sanitation Service was established by Ray Mohl as a supplement to his
water-well drilling operation. It provided both a much-needed service and a
supplemental income during the slack periods in his well drilling business.

In 1903, the business was sold to Fred Ost, who operated the business under the
name of Ost Septic Tank Service. In 1972, Fred Ost sold the business to his
son, Wally.

Wally operated under the same name until 1978, when he expanded the business to
include chemical toilet rental and services. At that time, Wally changed the
name to Ost Sanitation Service. In 1979, Wally purchased a high-pressure sewer
jet to provide sewer line cleaning to cities, farmers and power companies. He
also built a new shop in partnership with his cousin, Gilbert Ost. In the new
shop, they installed a front-end alignment machine and started doing minor
automotive repairs and tune-ups. The name was once again changed (to Ost
Services, Inc.) until the business was sold to Industrial Contractors, Inc., in
1982.

On April 1, 1983, the business was sold to Lyle D. (Del) Els. The business
continues to operate under the name of Els Sanitation Service. The business
continues to serve farmers, ranchers, municipalities, power companies, and the
general public when the services are required. Chemical toilet services are
still provided to anyone who needs them for various activities, including
family reunions, wedding dances, barn dances, rodeos, auction sales,
construction sites, etc.

        Fabricare Cleaners.

Fabricare Cleaners

The business located at 116 Main in Beulah, Fabricare Cleaners, was begun in
1984 by owner Eileen V. Vowell. When the building was purchased from Herman and
Vivian Hauff it was known as Knife River Woodworks, a custom woodworking shop
owned and operated by Steve and Don Pollock. It had previously been a Gambles
Store, a carpet store, bowling alley and pool hall. Major interior changes
including insulation, wiring, sheetrock and flooring were added. The exterior
was remodeled by adding new windows and a glass door. The false front building
to the east, Beulah's first Cash Store, was demolished to provide space for a
covered canopy drive-through to protect customers from the weather.

Services provided at Fabricare Cleaners include tailoring, alterations, drapery
pleating, down coat and comforter cleaning and rehabilitation and covering
pillows with ticking.

Formal wear rentals include a full line of tuxedos, bridesmaids and prom
dresses. Special storage boxes for wedding dresses and special occasion clothes
(christenings, proms, graduation, and the like) are also available.

A machine called a "mileage booster" has been installed to collect cleaning
chemical fumes from the atmosphere and clothes. It allows recycling of a
portion of the chemicals, reducing costs and providing a more pleasant working
environment and finished product.

Staff members working with owner Eileen Vowell include full-time presser
Lorraine Sarge and two alterations experts, Donetta Kunkel and Lori Steffen.

        Aerial view of Beulah with Farmers Union Elevator, a landmark.

Beulah Farmers Union Elevator Company

The Beulah Farmers Union Elevator Company was organized in 1917. The articles of
incorporation were filed on June 29, 1917, and the first board of directors
consisted of Peter Boeckel, Joseph Zeigler, Carl Stephens, David Keller, and
Jacob Hafner.

The elevator opened for business in the fall of 1917, enabling it to purchase
grain and provide service for area farmers. Business was brisk in the first
years of operation, but the Depression and drought years of the 1930s were hard
on the elevator. By the end of the 1930s, the business was in the red and
seemed to be heading for bankruptcy.

Being in financial difficulty, on Aug. 5, 1939, the board of directors decided
to lease the elevator to the Farmers Union Grain Terminal Association of St.
Paul, MN. At a special stockholders meeting held on Sept. 16, 1939, the
stockholders voted to reorganize a new elevator company. On Jan. 23, 1940, the
deal was completed. One hundred four farmers bought stock at $100 per share to
pay off the old company. The first annual stockholders meeting of the new
company was held on May 18, 1940. Elected officers at this meeting were Henry
Conrath, president; Joe Zeigler, vice president; Ernest Hafner, secretary;
Victor Strom and Gus Buchfink, directors.

The warehouse capacity in 1939 was 35,000 bushels. In 1941, a wooden annex was
added and the capacity increased to 70,000 bushels. Due to increased business,
additional space was required and, in 1951, four concrete tanks were
constructed. In 1958, more concrete tanks were built with the remodeling of the
office area, bringing the storage capacity in 1961 to 312,000 bushels. The
volume of grain and increased numbers of patrons required more expansion. In
1978, the Peavey Elevator was purchased. Remodeling of this plant started in
1980. Also in 1980, a grain dryer was added to the plant. In 1983, two
40,000-bushel steel tanks were added to further provide needed storage. The
total capacity of the elevator has grown to 585,000 bushels.

More than a million bushels of grain are handled by the Beulah Farmers Union
Elevator Company each year. The elevator provides full service for the
customers: selling feed, seed, chemicals, grain drying, cleaning grain, and
purchasing all varieties of grain.

The present board of directors includes Marvin Hafner, president; Duane Walz,
vice president; Darell Herman, secretary; Maynard Blohm and Joe Keller,
directors.

Edward Wasichek was the first manager when the elevator was reorganized in 1939
and remained until 1947. Following that time, John Reinhardt managed the
elevator until 1968 when Paul Ross became the manager and remained the manager
for 10 years.

Steve Garrison is the present manager and accepted that position in 1978. Steve
and his staff (Roger Krueger, Casey Voigt, and Donalda Whitecalfe) provide the
services needed by over 1600 patrons.

It is the teamwork between patrons, directors, and management that makes the
Beulah Farmers Union Elevator an outstanding cooperative. It is this
cooperation that insures its continued success.

        Farmers Union Insurance--Gary Murray

Farmers Union Insurance

Farmers Union Insurance has been on the move both economically and physically
since Gary Murray came back to Beulah and opened his business July 1, 1966. Gary
began selling his insurance and moved his office three times in the space of
nine years. His very first office was in the basement of the old post office
building and from there he moved to the present Ziman's Jewelry Store. From
that site his office was moved to the old Beulah Farmers Union Oil Company
building where Bronson's Super Valu Store is now located. Just north across the
street was the Field building, at that time called Farmers Union Hardware and
Appliance Store. Gary secured office space there and operated from that
location for five years.

When Gary moved back to Beulah the population was about 1300 people and it was
easy to walk up the street and recognize everyone. Now with some 4500 people,
you still greet them, but there are many who are unfamiliar.

The quality of life has always been good, but now it is even better. More people
mean more business. This factor led to Gary's next, and perhaps final move. Gary
purchased his own building on July 1, 1982--just 16 years after returning to
his home town. His present address is 112 West Main Street and from this modern
office he offers a full line of insurance which he says is the best.

Gary's wife Marjorie worked as secretary in the office for 12 years. Three
years ago in 1985, she quit the insurance business and went to work at the
Missouri Slope Medical Arts Clinic. Debora Creel has been the full-time
secretary since that time.

Gary and Marjorie closed the office on many occasions to support the boys as
they were either playing basketball, football or track. This started in 1970
when the oldest son, Mike, was a freshman and lasted until the youngest son,
Glenn, graduated in 1981. Michael, Wade, Steve, Dan and Glenn were all very
active in sports. Many days the Murrays had three different games to watch as
the boys were on three different teams. These were very enjoyable years
watching the boys participate and improve in their sport. Gary and Marge still
follow the high school teams, but it is not quite the same as when the boys
were playing.

Farmers Union Oil Company

In order to obtain a dependable supply of products at a fair price, a group of
local farmers decided to start a cooperative corporation. The Beulah Farmers
Union Oil Company received its charter on May 12, 1930. The main purpose of the
company is to obtain petroleum products and farm supplies on a cooperative
basis, returning all of the net savings to the members.

The original incorporators were C.B. Heinemeyer, F.B. Conrath, Peter Boeckel,
Ernest R. Hafner, H. H. Hauser, Jacob Fuhrman, John Weiss, Glen Voeltz, Henry
Conrath, John Eisenbeis, Theo. Hafner, John L. Schmid, William Weiss, John
Polriesz, and Ira Miller. A board of directors was appointed until a regular
board was elected. The first manager hired by this board was Ira Miller.

The first service station facilities were located on the Northern Pacific
Railroad right-of-way. Until Farmers Union Central Exchange, presently Cenex,
was organized, gas was purchased from Standard Oil Company on a contract basis.

In 1931, the service station on the Northern Pacific right-of-way burned,
destroying most of the merchandise and the company records. The company rebuilt
at this same location.

From 1931-1947, the company operated substations at Golden Valley, Hazen,
Stanton, Center, and Zap. In 1947, the substations at Hazen and Stanton merged
and separated from the parent company. It now operates as Hazen Farmers Union
Oil Company. All the other substations have since closed.

        Farmers Union Oil--Ron Mongeon, manager.

During 1939, a new building was constructed on Main Street and the business was
moved there. In order to meet the demands of the patrons for more products and
services, this building was remodeled and enlarged in 1958. A fertilizer plant
was built on the original Northern Pacific right-of-way site and later was
enlarged to meet the growing demand by the patrons for fertilizer products.

Additional property and a building were purchased across the street from the
main business in 1970. After extensive remodeling, a new hardware and appliance
store was opened in this building. In 1977, the company added an anhydrous
plant in order to meet the increased demand by area farmers.

In 1983, all the property on Main Street was sold and a new modern building was
constructed at 1300 Highway 49 North, which is the present location of the
company. Included in this building are an auto service and repair center, a
hardware store, offices, and a warehouse. A large pump island and a convenience
store were added at the same location. Through the years, many new products and
services have been added for the convenience of the patrons of this company.

The following is a list of farmers who have served on the board of directors of
this company: Rudolph Miller, Oscar Erickson, Ernest R. Hafner, Albert Binder,
Fred J. Miller, C.B. Heinemeyer, Peter Boeckel, Felix Conrath, John E. Weiss,
Ernest Bohrer, Jacob Mohl, Gust Buchfink, August Anderson, Ernest Herman,
William Binder, John Lindemann, John Kusler, Wilford Herman, George P. Cline,
August Miller, Christ Bieber, Emmanuel Stuhlmiller, Myron Hafner, Fred
Boeshans, Jake Lindemann, William Heth, John Zau, Norman Sailer, Wilbert
Flemmer, Francis Pulver, Jerome Skalsky.

Presently serving as directors are: Ted Reich, Jerome Boeshans, Kenneth Richau,
Tom Frank, Roger Buechler.

Ron Mongeon has managed the company since 1985.

The company's success can be attributed to the courage and foresight of the
original incorporators; the dedicated boards of directors, employees, and
managers; and the loyal support of the patrons of the company.

        Gamble Store--Herman and Jerry Hauff.

The Gambles Store and Hardware Hank

The Gambles Store at 116 East Main was purchased by Herman and Vivian Hauff
from John Brazzell in November, 1950.

In the early years, most farmers and ranchers made only one trip to town a week.
The busy day was Saturday and Saturday night. The stores had no closing time;
rather, the old rule of thumb that "when everyone went home, the business doors
closed." Many a Saturday night included open store hours until midnight.

1954 was the year for electrical excitement . . . TELEVISION CAME TO BEULAH!
Gambles began selling television sets. Reception in the Beulah valley was nil
to poor. Herman took a set to John Scheidt's farm south of Beulah to give the
farm neighbors their first look at this electrical wizard. Reception there was
better than in Beulah.

The Hauffs changed the store from Gambles to Hardware Hank in 1976. They sold
the merchandise in November 1979 and closed the store.

Donald and Eileen Vowell purchased the building in 1984 for a dry-cleaning
establishment.

        ANG coal gasfication plant.

Great Plains Coal Gasification Plant Project History

A large-scale coal gasification project was initially conceived in the late
1960s, when planners from American Natural Gas Company, now American Natural
Resources Company (ANR), identified coal gasification as a promising supplement
to traditional gas supplies. An evaluation of available coal supplies in 1970
led to the selection of North Dakota lignite as a suitable feedstock for the
development of a gasification plant.

In the early 1970s, Michigan Wisconsin Pipeline Company (at that time, a
subsidiary of American Natural Gas Company), the predecessor of ANR, took
several steps that were essential to project development. Among other things,
Michigan Wisconsin acquired rights to lignite, water and the plant site and
initiated preliminary engineering, testing, and environmental work.

In March, 1975, ANG and Michigan Wisconsin filed applications with the
predecessor of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), requesting
regulatory authorizations necessary to proceed with the construction and
operation of a coal gasification plant capable of producing 250 million cubic
feet of SNG per day. A year later, however, in recognition of potential
financing and socioeconomic impact problems associated with a project of that
magnitude, the applications were amended to propose the plant to be built in
two phases, each designed to produce an average daily volume of 125 million
cubic feet of SNG.

To reduce the financial burden on ANR and to obtain the support of the
Department of Energy in the ongoing regulatory proceedings before the FERC, the
participation of additional gas systems in the project was sought in 1977 and
1978. In 1977, Peoples Energy Corporation (the predecessor of MidCon) agreed to
co-sponsor the project. A partnership was formed between Peoples Energy and
American Natural Properties (ANP), a wholly-owned subsidiary of ANR. The
agreement provided for equal ownership and receipt of SNG. The following year,
when three additional companies agreed to sponsor the project, the Great Plains
partnership was formed. The original Great Plains partners (ANP, PGC Coal
Gasification Company (now MCN), Tenneco SNG, Transco Coal, and Columbia Coal
Gasification Corporation) agreed that each company was to own 20 percent of the
project and that each company's pipeline affiliate was to receive 20 percent of
the SNG.

In 1979 and 1980, the FERC issued decisions that provided the regulatory
authorization necessary for Great Plains to proceed with project development.
Accordingly, detailed engineering design work, procurement, and initial site
work was commenced in the summer of 1980, with the assistance of funds provided
by DOE under a cooperative agreement. In addition, Great Plains sought loan
guarantee assistance from DOE under the Federal Nonnuclear Research and
Development Act and President Jimmy Carter signed a conditional letter of
commitment for a $250 million loan guarantee on July 18, 1980.

However, the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit
subsequently set aside the FERC's opinions on jurisdictional grounds and
remanded the case to the FERC for further proceedings. Columbia thereafter
withdrew from the Great Plains partnership. The remaining partners agreed that
their respective interests in the partnership would be 32.5 percent, 5 percent,
15 percent, 30 percent, and 22.5 percent and further agreed that the pipeline
affiliates' respective shares of the SNG produced would be 25 percent, 20
percent, 30 percent and 25 percent, as now provided for in the Gas Purchase
Agreements.

        Aerial view of Great Plains plant site--1984.

Following negotiations in early 1981 with the other parties to the FERC
proceedings, Great Plains and the pipeline affiliates filed an offer of
settlement with the FERC which requested authorizations for the pipeline
affiliates to recover the payment to be made to Great Plains under the Gas
Purchase Agreements through the purchase gas cost adjustment provisions of the
pipeline affiliates' respective tariffs. The commission subsequently issued an
order which approved the offer of settlement. During the same period, Great
Plains sought increased loan guarantees from DOE and President Ronald Reagan
ultimately approved the issuance of a conditional $2.02 billion loan guarantee
on Aug. 5, 1981. Meanwhile, construction work on the project began in earnest
and engineering design, procurement, and site work continued.

The loan guarantee assistance required for project development was ultimately
obtained on Jan. 29, 1982, when Great Plains and DOE executed the loan guarantee
agreement and related agreements. Construction work accelerated in 1982 and was
43 percent complete by the end of the year. Detailed engineering work was 95
percent complete by year-end. Pacific acquired a 10 percent interest in the
project from ANP and Transco Coal during 1982.

Further progress in construction activities was achieved in 1983. Procurement
was more than 99 percent complete by the middle of the year and construction
was more than 90 percent complete by the end of the year. Moreover, operator
training was conducted, start-up activities on the first train began, and the
SNG pipeline was completed.

Early in 1983, it became apparent that substantial declines in projected energy
prices since 1980 would require Great Plains to obtain additional financial
assistance to complete and operate the project. Since it appeared that such
assistance might not be available, later that year Great Plains notified DOE
that it was seriously considering abandonment of the project.

Great Plains submitted an unsolicited application for price guarantee
assistance to the U.S. Synthetic Fuels Corporation (SFC) in September, 1983. In
January, 1984, the SFC issued a solicitation for coal or lignite gasification
projects and Great Plains promptly filed a responsive proposal. Following a
series of negotiations, a Letter of Intent to provide a price guarantee
commitment of up to $790 million to Great Plains was executed on April 26,
1984. Subsequent negotiations resulted in an agreement by SFC to provide a
price guarantee commitment of up to $820 million, which included additional
equity obligations of the partners.

Meanwhile, construction, plant operations, start-up, and testing continued.
Initial deliveries of SNG commenced from the first of two trains on July 28,
1984. From that date on, SNG production increased at rates far beyond anyone's
expectations. The original goals for production were to achieve 70 percent of
design in 1985 and increase that by 7 percent per year, reaching 91 percent in
1988. The plant actually received 79.6 percent in 1985 so a new goal of 91
percent in 1986 and beyond was set for the plant. For the first three months of
1986, the plant achieved 99.1 percent, 99.6 percent and 104.9 percent,
respectively.

On May 21, 1985, the Secretary of Energy voiced objections to the April 26 price
guarantee commitment on the ground that it did not ensure long-term
participation by the partners in operation of the facility. The SFC board of
directors, later that same day, failed to act on final approval of the April 26
commitment. On July 18, 1985, the SFC board of directors presented a new price
guarantee package; this new package was in negotiation among the DOE, SFC, and
the partners when, on July 30, 1985, the Secretary of Energy communicated to
the SFC chairman that there was no support on the part of the administration
for the July 18, 1985, price guarantee package. On Aug. 1, 1985, the Great
Plains Gasification Associate partners announced their withdrawal from the
project, thereby defaulting on the $1.54 billion DOE-guaranteed construction
loan.

On Aug. 15, 1985, the Secretary of Energy agreed to keep the Great Plains plant
operating for several weeks while state officials discussed ways to meet
certain DOE conditions for continued plant operation until the spring of 1986
in order to give DOE time to determine the future of the plant. The DOE
indicated that it was considering several options for disposition of the
facility, i.e., to continue to operate the plant, sell it or lease it to a
corporation, shut down the plant until a buyer or lessor is found, mothball it,
or scrap it. To obtain title and increase its options, DOE filed action to
foreclose on the property on Aug. 29, 1985, in federal district court in North
Dakota. In the meantime, the DOE negotiated an interim agreement with ANG to
operate the project until DOE decides on its future.

The DOE has stated its objective is to see the plant operate over the long term
at no further expense to taxpayers.

In February, 1986, the DOE asked for statements of interest from companies
interested in purchasing or participating in the financial operations of the
plant. Nine companies filed statements by the April 4 deadline.

U.S. District Court in North Dakota ordered a public courthouse sale of the
plant to facilitate foreclosure and transfer title to the DOE. That sale took
place on June 30, 1986, at the Mercer County courthouse in Stanton, at which
time the DOE bid $1 billion for the Great Plains Coal Gasification Project and
acquired title to the assets.

On Nov. 21, 1986, the DOE extended the deadline to December 1 to investment
banking firms to submit proposals for assisting the agency in the divesting of
the Great Plains Coal Gasification Plant.

ANG Coal Gasification Company signed a project administration agreement with the

A milestone for the project was reached on Jan. 18, 1987--Great Plains

Knife River Coal Mining Company

Knife River Coal Mining Company, one of the largest lignite producers in North
Dakota, began operation as the Beulah Coal Company in 1917. In that year the
company sank an underground shaft located northwest of the Beulah power plant
within the city of Beulah.

From 1917-1919 most of the mining was done on what was called the upper level.
This vein was located about 33 feet underground and averaged approximately 11
feet in thickness. Two years later plans were formulated to start an entirely
new operation to be located approximately two miles north of the main line of
the Northern Pacific railway. This was due to the inability to continue
underground mining operations in the original location.

The company reorganized in 1922 under the name of Knife River Coal Mining
Company and opened the new underground properties. A narrow-gauge railroad was
constructed from the Beulah power plant site to the new operation and coal was
transported by steam locomotives.

Lignite was loaded entirely by hand and all the underground hauling was done by
mules in the working area and four-ton, direct-current, trolley-type
locomotives in the main areas. By 1927 the mine was producing approximately
230,000 tons per year.

Knife River was acquired by Montana-Dakota Utilities Co. in 1945. Additional
loading machines and haulage locomotives were installed and by 1950 the mine was
producing 418,000 tons with a work force of 125 men.

In 1952 Knife River purchased a large electric walking dragline along with
additional equipment to work a new surface mining area east of the underground
property. The underground operation was subsequently discontinued and by early
1953 all lignite was produced from the new operation, known as the North Beulah
Mine.

Along with the North Beulah Mine purchase in 1952, Knife River bought a small
coal mine near Gascoyne, ND. Over a period of years, this mine supplied coal to
the Montana-Dakota Utilities Co.'s plant at Mobridge, SD and the Otter Tail
Power Company plant at Ortonville, MN. This mine, in addition to lignite,
produces a slack lignite which is not a very satisfactory fuel but is used as
an ingredient for thinning mud in drilling oil wells. It is also used as an
ingredient in certain water softeners for industrial use.

In 1958 the company began operation of a small mine near Savage, MT. The mine
produces approximately 250,000 tons per year, which is used by Montana-Dakota
Utilities Co.'s plant at Sidney, MT and a nearby sugar refining operation.

Knife River opened another mine in 1963 approximately three miles south of
Beulah. In September 1973, the North Beulah Mine was closed down as all
recoverable commercial coal had been removed. During 1974-1975 the company
expanded its Gascoyne Mine operation to fulfill a contract with Otter Tail
Power Company to supply lignite for a new power plant at Big Stone City, SD. The
plant started operation in January 1975 as was on firm operation by May of that
year. This plant, at full operation, consumes an average of 2.5 million tons of
lignite each year and in peak years may consume almost 3 million tons.

In the fall of 1979 expansion of the South Beulah Mine, now called the Beulah
Mine, was under way. The expansion of the mine was required to meet the fuel
requirements of the new Coyote I power plant, which was being built
approximately one quarter-mile west of the Beulah Mine facility area. The
Coyote plant went into commercial operation in May 1981. It is estimated to
have a net production of 410 megawatts and burns 2.3 million tons of lignite
each year.

Lignite produced at Knife River's mine sites is shipped to various utilities
and/or industrial users within the states of North Dakota, South Dakota,
Montana and Minnesota.

Today Knife River is a major operating subsidiary of MDU Resources Group, Inc.
The coal company has, for the past two decades, sold primarily to the
industrial section, such as electric utility generating plants and sugar
refining operations. Recently, however, because the rapid price escalation of
alternative heating fuels, an old coal market, once nearly extinct, has
reopened. Knife River has constructed and is operating two stoker coal tipples
for sales to homes, small businesses, schools, hospitals, nursing homes, and
light industry. With other energy costs substantially higher than lignite,
Knife River is optimistic about the expanding markets for stoker coal.

Knife River Coal Mining Company is proud to be part of the Old West heritage.
For the past several years the coal operation has produced and sold more than
5.5 million tons of lignite annually. Along with the production of lignite
coal, the company is firmly committed to reclamation of mined lands. Knife
River has pledged its expertise and resources to return all mined land to a
productive state and today the record clearly indicates this goal is being
accomplished.

Early on the emphasis was on land rehabilitation for both domestic livestock and
wildlife use. During the past decade the emphasis has been on returning mined
lands to an equivalent or better use generally for agriculture crop production.
Current activities are directed not only toward agriculture but also such
reclaimed land use as wildlife management and industrial uses. During the past
several years, a variety of crops has been produced on reclaimed lands at the
Beulah and Gascoyne mines.

Today all mined land is restored to a gently rolling topography seen in western
North Dakota and eastern Montana. Crop production on reclaimed lands has been
gratifying. On any given day at Knife River's mines deer may be seen grazing,
partridge and pheasant feeding, ducklings maturing, a farmer planting wheat and
another baling hay or harvesting barley. The company displays proof at its mines
every day that reclamation works. Productivity levels for alfalfa, tame hay and
cereal crops have been similar to surrounding unmined farmlands and equivalent
to production averages published for the counties in which the mines are
located. Reclamation of mined lands at Knife River is a reality accomplished
through commitment.

Knife River Veterinary Clinic

Beulah is fortunate among small towns to have a veterinary clinic; many rural
residents must drive long distances to professionals who can care for their
animals. In the case of farmers, this is particularly important as some of
their income often depends on the health and well being of their animals.

The Knife River Veterinary Clinic, which serves all the Mercer County and part
of Oliver County areas, was started in the summer of 1968 by Dr. James Olson,
from Iowa, and Dr. Harold Balas, from Minnesota. The original clinic set just
where it does today: along highway 49 on Beulah's south side.

Dr. Wayne Boland joined the clinic in 1985 and Dr. Roberta Amsden has also
worked at the clinic.

The clinic specializes in "companion pet" care. The veterinarians expanded their
small-animal facility to provide for the increase in business experienced
during the energy boom.

The largest percentage of the clinic's time, however, is spent with the farm,
ranch and dairy cattle herds which predominate in the area. They provide
pregnancy exams, bull evaluations, vaccinations and surgical techniques to
their rural customers.

Support staff members provide many services appreciated by their customers.
Ralph Murray, Connie Beckler and Kathy Best, veterinary technologist, serve in
this capacity.

Dr. Balas graduated from the University of Minnesota in June, 1957, and two
weeks later opened a practice in Hazen. In August of that year he married JoAnn
Hlavinka, who was from Lark, ND. The family now has three children, Tom, Mike
and Beth. Dr. and Mrs. Balas live in Hazen.

Dr. Olson graduated from Iowa State University in 1958 and married Connie
Hainly, from Mitchell, SD, two years later, in 1960. Dr. Olson practiced
veterinary medicine in Harvey, ND, until 1966 when he joined the Army
Veterinary Corps. In 1968 he returned to North Dakota and became a partner in
the Knife River Veterinary Clinic. The Olsons have one daughter, Julie, and
they live in Hazen.

Dr. E. Wayne Boland graduated from the Oklahoma State University School of
Veterinary Medicine in 1968. He practiced in Billings, Mont., until 1983, when
he moved to Beulah, where his family still owned a ranch, and he became a
partner in the clinic in 1984. Dr. Boland has one son, Lynn, living in
Tallahassee, Fla. Dr. Boland lives on the family ranch eight miles southeast of
Beulah.
