Metropolitan Federal

Today, with more than $2 billion in assets and more than 60 years of service to
the Heartland, Metropolitan Financial Corporation, through its subsidiary
Metropolitan Federal Bank, fsb, has established a tradition of providing
quality financial products and services to its customers.

Beginning in September 1926 as Metropolitan Building and Loan with assets of
$25,000, the organization's ongoing story was one of growth and success.

Its early history was, for the most part, quiet and uneventful, characterized
by a commitment to customer service and an upstanding reputation for safety and
security. The years between 1953, when the 27-year-old company changed its name
for the first time, and 1973, when Metropolitan became a federally chartered
institution, were years marked by substantial growth throughout the state of
North Dakota.

That growth was intensified in the early 1980's when Metropolitan Federal merged
with three other North Dakota savings and loan associations and emerged as the
state's largest financial institution.

The next step in Metropolitan Federal's growth was the conversion from a mutual
savings and loan association to a publicly held company. In March, 1983,
Metropolitan Federal completed its initial public offering of 2.1 million
shares of common stock and raised more than $20 million of capital to help fund
its continued expansion.

In January 1984, the Midwest Federal office in Beulah became Metropolitan
Federal and continues to serve the financial needs of the Beulah community with
friendly and knowledgeable personnel and a variety of financial products.

Metropolitan Financial Corporation has other subsidiaries engaged in mortgage
banking, real estate development and sales, travel and insurance. The bank's
savings accounts are insured by the Federal Savings and Loan Insurance
Corporation, an agency of the U.S. government, up to $100,000.

The Metropolitan story is one we are very proud of. And we're proud of our
commitment to friendly, caring service. At Metropolitan, we're dedicated to
being the financial institution that puts your concerns first and provides you
with the utmost in full-service investment opportunities.

Current employees are: Kay Ramsbacher, office sales manager; Debbie Morast,
clerk/teller II; Sylvia Zeiszler, clerk/teller I; Shirley Boyce, clerk/teller I
part time and Colleen Wiest, clerk/teller I part time.

In mid-1984, Metropolitan Federal changed its charter from a federal stock
savings and loan association to a federal stock savings bank. That change
allowed Metropolitan Federal to add the descriptive noun "bank" to the
company's title, a word which more aptly described the products and services
offered by Metropolitan Federal. Later that same year, the bank acquired its
first South Dakota office through the acquisition of Mitchell Home Savings in
Mitchell.

The South Dakota market was expanded in February 1985 when Metropolitan Federal
acquired the Sioux Falls-based Dakota Savings and Loan Association. At the same
time Metropolitan Federal underwent a corporation reorganization, the result of
which was Metropolitan Financial Corporation, a thrift holding company.

Montana-Dakota Utilities Co.

On March 14, 1924, Montana-Dakota Utilities Co. was incorporated under the name
of Minnesota Northern Power Co. It began operating as an electric company in the
Glendive, Mt. area with its general office located in Minneapolis, MN.

In 1925 MDU expanded its eastern Montana properties and became a pioneer of
cross-country transmission lines and central power stations.

Most of the smaller communities such as Beulah owned their own generating
stations, which were quite costly to operate and would only provide electricity
for a few hours a day. The cost of electricity these plants produced was
between 16 cents and 25 cents per kilowatt-hour.

As MDU expanded its electric operation, it purchased many of the city-owned
power generators. Many of the early systems had to be converted from direct
current to alternating current and were connected to central transmission
systems. Many of the local power plants could be shut down because of this. As
towns were connected to the central transmission lines, MDU adopted uniform
rates which were consistent with the size of the community. Incentive rates for
cooking, refrigeration, and water heating were also established. These rates
were generally considerably lower than when electricity had been produced by
the city-owned plants.

MDU entered the natural gas business in 1926 when it constructed an eight-inch
pipe-line from the gas field north of Baker, MT., to Glendive to furnish fuel
for generating electricity at the power plant and for local distribution in
Glendive.

The company continued to expand its gas and electric operations over the next
few years, and by 1929 had acquired gas properties in North Dakota and South
Dakota, including Bismarck, Mandan, Valley City and Rapid City. In the early
'30s, depression and drought set in and no further major expansion was
undertaken.

In 1935 federal legislation was adopted directed at the elements of holding
companies. It was decided to merge several companies holding ownership of whole
electric and gas systems into a single operation. Through the 1936 mergers of
Montana-Dakota Power Company, Montana Cities Gas Company and Montana-Dakota
Utilities Co., MDU became a single operating company.

The most significant impact on our electric business came in 1945 when a
transmission line from Glendive to Baker was completed, which joined our
isolated systems in eastern Montana and western North Dakota. The company also
entered into a contract with the Bureau of Reclamation to purchase hydro power
generated at Fort Peck for delivery to the Glendive system. One of the
provisions of this contract required that the company "wheel" government power
over its lines to the bureau's preference customers, including irrigation
projects and rural electrification cooperatives. This "wheeling" agreement was
the first of its kind in the United States.

In October, 1945, after extended negotiations, MDU purchased the Dakota Public
Service Properties, which included power plants, transmission lines and
distribution systems in 91 towns in North Dakota and South Dakota. It was
through this transaction that MDU began serving Beulah. Included in this
purchase was the stock of Knife River Coal Mining Co., which was operating an
underground lignite coal mine north of Beulah.

When MDU purchased the Dakota Public Service Properties, the city of Beulah was
receiving its electricity from a plant located in Beulah. The original power
plant was constructed in 1925 at which time it had a rated capacity of 400 KW.
In 1927 the reciprocating engines were replaced with a new steam turbine,
bringing rated capacity to 2,500 KW. In 1928 the plant increased its capacity
to 3,500 KW and in 1937 to 6,000 KW. This was considered a large
lignite-burning power plant at that time.

In 1949 MDU constructed the Dakota Station Addition onto the Beulah plant. This
7,500 KW addition was built under an agreement between Montana-Dakota Utilities
Co. and the Dakota Electric Cooperative, Inc. which was a generating and
transmission organization made up of 14 REA cooperatives located in North and
South Dakota. The plant provided electricity for the cooperatives as well as
for MDU. After many years of providing reliable service, the plant was closed
on May 1, 1986, and was scheduled to be demolished in 1988 - 1989.

When MDU acquired the Knife River Coal Mining Co. stock, they were operating an
underground lignite coal mine near Beulah. In 1950 Knife River Coal entered a
new era by converting some of its Beulah lignite mine operations to open strip
work. This conversion resulted in the closure of its underground mine, complete
with mules, in 1953.

Today Knife River Coal Mining Co. continues to operate as a wholly-owned
subsidiary of MDU Resources Group, Inc. and has coal reserves of more than 500
million tons of low-sulfur lignite. Knife River Coal has strip-mining
operations in Savage, Mt., and near Gascoyne and Beulah in ND. Knife River Coal
Co. employs 244 full-time people, many who live in and around the Beulah area.
In 1986 coal sales for Knife River Coal Co. were 4.7 million tons.

Since 1945 Montana-Dakota Utilities Co. has continued to grow and expand its
electric and gas operations. In Sept. 1968, MDU moved its general office from
Minneapolis to Bismarck. Also moving were approximately 100 of their 135
employees.

Growth in MDU's service area was creating a demand on electric generating
facilities. In the early 1970's we became a partner along with two other
electric utility companies in constructing a 415-megawatt electric generating
station. The power plant, which is located in Northeastern South Dakota, is
called Big Stone. Knife River Coal Company provides the 10,000 tons of coal
required daily to operate this plant from their Gascoyne mine.

Before the completion of Big Stone, another electric generating station was
being planned. This facility, very similar to the Big Stone plant, would be a
joint venture between five utility companies; Otter Tail Power Company, Fergus
Falls, Mn.; Minnkota Power Cooperative, Inc., Grand Forks; Montana-Dakota
Utilities Co., Bismarck; Northwest Public Service Company, Huron, SD; and
Minnesota Power and Light Co., Duluth, Mn. Three were also owners of the Big
Stone plant.

Because of proximity to both coal and wate4 Beulah was selected as the site of
the 410-megawatt electric generating station, named Coyote. Bechtel Power
Corporation of San Francisco, Ca., was chosen as consulting engineer and
general contractor for the plant. Otter Tail Power Company served as
construction agent and when completed, Montana-Dakota Utilities Co. became the
operating agent.

Construction of Coyote Station began Oct. 10, 1977. To enable workers to remain
on schedule, a 360 x 250 foot air-supported structure was placed over the power
block area. This vinyl-coated nylon bubble, which rose 60 feet above the
prairie, was heated in winter, allowing foundation and concrete work to
continue.

Building the plant called for 2.2 million feet or over 400 miles of electrical
conductor. In excess of 64,000 cubic yards of concrete was utilized in the
structure. Siding used to cover the plant totaled over 1.3 million square feet
- enough to cover more than 22 football fields. The 498-foot stack is the
tallest structure at Coyote and marks the plant's location from a great
distance.

Water used for producing steam and for cooling the plant is provided from the
Missouri River through a 36-inch pipeline which begins at the intake structure
located south of Stanton, some 26 miles away. Return water back to the river is
provided through a 12-inch pipeline.

Knife River Coal Mining Company provides the two million tons of coal required
annually from a nearby mine to operate the plant. After nearly four years of
construction, Coyote began commercial generation in May, 1981.

Coyote Power Plant plays an important role in providing power for Mid-continent
Area Power Pool (MAPP), which was formed by 35 power suppliers in the eight
upper-Midwest states in 1972.

By utilizing combined facilities of the federal government, public power
districts, rural electric cooperatives, investor-owned electric utilities and
municipal electric utilities, MAPP members produce and distribute an adequate,
reliable and economical supply of electric power. The complex system of the
MAPP network allows members to buy power when needed or sell when they have
excess. This benefits both producers and customers by providing a constant
source during peak demand or during shutdown of facilities by an individual
member.

Since the completion of the Coyote Station in 1981, MDU has purchased additional
megawatt interest in both Coyote and the Big Stone plant. MDU also had a
contracted agreement with Basin Electric to purchase 41 megawatts of capacity
from Antelope Valley Station II located near Beulah.

Through long-range planning, Montana-Dakota Utilities Co. will continue to meet
the needs of its customers and continue to provide reliable electric service.

Montana-Dakota Utilities Co. operates as a division of MDU Resources Group, Inc.
which is a multiple dimension resource corporation with businesses operating in
Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota and Wyoming.

Other enterprises operating under the MDU Resources Group are Williston Basin
Interstate Pipeline Co., a natural gas acquisition, storage, transportation and
marketing firm; Knife River Coal Co., a coal extraction, handling and marketing
organization; and Fidelity Oil Co., an oil investment and development company.

Montana-Dakota Utilities Co. today serves 111,373 electric customers and 176,116
gas customers in 247 communities in the four-state area.

At the time of this writing, MDU employs five people in the Beulah district
office. They are Janice Sigman, Alvina Hagler, Raymond Voegele, Gary Younker
and district supervisor, Don Wetzel. MDU is proud of its long tradition of
providing an adequate and reliable supply of electric energy at the lowest cost
possible in our service area. Our employees have been and still are loyal and
dedicated servants to our customers, both large and small. Our employees are
typically active citizens contributing their time and talents to local
community affairs.

MDU is proud to be a part of the Beulah history, and to have served the
community most of the last 75 years as its supplier of electricity. We join the
many well-wishers in congratulating all present and former Beulah residents on
their Diamond Jubilee.

Moos Construction

Moos Construction, owned and operated by Elmer Moos, has been in business in
Beulah since 1963 when they started building houses in the Beulah area and
employed 11 people. Elmer also built cabinets and his wife, Hildagard, did all
the finish work, varnishing and painting.

Over the years as more contractors came into town, Moos Construction stopped
building houses and did strictly concrete work and eventually started doing
excavating, sewer and water lines and hauling dirt and scoria along with the
concrete.

Curtis, Elmer's youngest son, is now operating the business after his dad
suffered from illness. Curtis has had 12 years experience working with Moos
Construction which has been servicing Beulah and the surrounding communities
for 24 years and hopes to continue in the future.

Neuberger Oil Company

Neuberger Oil Company was started on May 10, 1948, by Reinhold Neuberger. The
business started out with one Studebaker truck with an 800-gallon tank.
Deliveries were first made to various farm accounts and three service stations.
When a delivery was made, five-gallon cans were used to measure the products
since there were no pumps or meters at the time.

It wasn't until 1954 and three trucks later that a 1,000-gallon tank truck was
purchased. This was also the first truck to have a pump and meter. Presently,
the business operates with two trucks, one with a 2,000-gallon tank and one
with a 1,500-gallon tank.

In the beginning of the company, the products were shipped via railroad cars,
but then transport trucks took over and, to the present, semi-trailer trucks
bring the product from the terminals.

When Reinhold started the business, he worked as a commissioned agent for Oval
E. Carter, Enco and Exxon. These were all the same company, but the name kept
changing. In 1972, he changed the business to a family-operated small business
by buying out the franchise.

In 1975, his son, Doug, purchased the business. With Exxon leaving the state on
North Dakota in June 1986, the product now comes from Conoco, Amoco and
Sinclair.

Oliver-Mercer Electric Cooperative

The Oliver-Mercer Electric Cooperative was organized on Feb. 23, 1945, by
farmers living in Oliver and Mercer Counties.

At the first organizational meeting, R.J. Sailer, acting chairman, and Charles
H. Carl, REA field representative, explained what REA is for and how REA co-ops
are organized and function.

The aim was then, and still is, to provide dependable central-station
electrical service to an farmers living in the area.

Members of the first board of directors were H.H. Henke, Wm. R. Van Oosting,
Philip Maier, Nels Porsborg, E.A. Bohrer, Rudolf Miller, Wm. Raab, Albert
Hoffman and Adolf Raeszler. These men were charged with organizing and getting
electric service under way to their neighbors. They served long hours without
pay.

The steps in organizing the Oliver-Mercer Electric Cooperative were these:
First, a sign-up of an prospective members was made to determine if there were
enough to make electrical service feasible. Then, when feasibility seemed to be
likely, an engineering firm was hired to plan the system.

The engineering firm drew up plans which were submitted to the REA in
Washington, D.C., where a further study again proved feasibility. A loan was
granted to the Oliver-Mercer Electric Cooperative to start building lines.

Contracts were then let by the board of directors for 100 miles of line in the
first approved area. This system of building lines area by area was adopted to
speed service and to simplify handling the huge building task. The first lines
of the Oliver-Mercer Electric Cooperative were built in the Center area in
Section A. In all there were five sections built.

The first Oliver-Mercer substation to go into service was just west of Center
in 1948. The following was taken from the March, 1948 issue of Lite Rays, the
monthly newsletter sent to an members at the time. It was topped by a full-page
banner proclaiming "Electricity is Coming--Electricity for Everyone." The
newsletter explained how Oliver-Mercer obtained and distributed its power at
that time. The Center substation was connected to the 44,000 volt line owned by
Montana-Dakota Utilities Co., and through the substation the electricity was
transformed from 44,000 volts to 7200 volts, the voltage that would pass
through the lines.

At each farm was placed a small transformer that would transform the voltage
from 7200 volts to 120/240 volts, the voltage the farmer would use. The power
originally came from the Fort Peck Hydro Dam and arrived in this area by a line
owned by the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation.

The first consumer on Oliver-Mercer Electric Cooperative lines was Sigrud
Lovold of Center. He was first connected to the co-op's lines on March 2, 1948.

During the first few months the average usage was only about 76 kilowatt hours
per month. This contrasts with the average of 1,400 kilowatt hours used every
month now by Oliver-Mercer Electric Cooperative's consumers.

Forty years ago and the first years that followed were exciting in rural
electrification. The electricity was a luxury that now practically everyone
could afford. In those early years, everyone wanted to know who was buying what
kinds of electrical appliances and Lite Rays published a list of its members'
purchases, such as electric stoves, refrigerators and maybe even a newfangled
milking machine.

The minimum monthly bill was figured on 40 KWHs per month and any member using
more than 200 KWHS per month was included in the Kilowatt Club in the next
month's Lite Rays.

A few years later, farmers were well aware of the fact that electrical power was
capable of doing much more around the farm and home than just lighting the house
or barn or operating a refrigerator or iron.

In the 1960's, electric home heating was being mentioned. There were many
skeptics who were sure it wouldn't work. It would be too expensive or the
outages would prevent electric heating from being practical, they said. Over
the years, electric heating has proven to be a very safe, clean, dependable and
stabilizing load.

In the decade of the '70s, electrical usage continued to climb until the energy
crisis occurred. That period of time changed the whole energy situation in the
United States and had a very detrimental effect on electrical usage. For the
first time in their history, electrical consumers were instructed to conserve
on electrical consumption. Although the energy crisis was short-lived, the
attitude toward energy efficiency and conservation is still affecting the
electrical industry.

The area served by Oliver-Mercer Electric has been fortunate to have had several
major construction projects, including the power plants and the gasification
plant. Because of these projects and the major loads created by those and water
pumping plants and coal operations, the amount of KWHs sold has grown by leaps
and bounds. There were 9.5 million KWHs sold in 1964, compared to 148.5 million
KWHs in 1984.

With these loads, Oliver-Mercer has been fortunate to have one of the lowest
rural electric rates in the state. However, as we complete the '80s, new
challenges face the rural electric cooperative. Load management systems are
being installed to reduce peak usage and make more efficient use of the
existing power plants, dual-fuel operations are being promoted so surplus power
can be utilized, and the current federal administration has not been supportive
of the REA funding programs.

It has been exciting to look back and see what has happened to make this area a
better place to live because of the development of rural electrification. Yet
we must realize this is history and we must plan for tomorrow, for that is the
most important time.

The managers who have served the co-op are: Frank J. Belinskey, 1945-1952;
Richard B. Gabe, 1952-1954; Miles Handy, 1954-1962; Kenneth Ervin, 1962-1978;
Garland L. Sagen, 1978-1986; Clayton O. Hoffman, 1986-present.

Many dedicated directors have served Oliver-Mercer Electric Cooperative over the
years. Their names and the years they served are: Nels Porsborg, Judson,
1945-1950; Ernest A. Bohrer, Hazen, 1945-1948; Herman H. Henke, Hannover,
1945-1969; Philip Maier, Blue Grass, 1945-1947; Wm. R. VanOosting, Hensler,
1945-1961; Albert Hoffman, Zap, 1945-1946; Wm. Raab, Golden Valley, 1945-1960;
Adolf Raeszler, Beulah, 1945-1949; Rudolf Miller, Hazen, 1945-1950; Albert
Bauman, Golden Valley, 1946-1976; Herbert Becker, New Salem, 1947-1956 and
1964-1975; David Isaak, Hazen, 1949-1952; John Kusler, Beulah, 1949-1963; Oscar
Letzring, New Salem, 1950-1954; Fred J. Miller, Hazen, 1950-1963.

Herbert Schlender, Hazen, 1952-1953; Herbert Hafner, Beulah, 1953-1969; Fred W.
Kuch, Center, 1954-1970; Ernest Becker, New Salem, 1956-1957; Raymond
Retterath, Stanton, 1957-1960; Dale Ford, Hazen, 1960-1964; Ernest Isaak, Dodge,
1960-1982; Ed Orgaard, Center, 1961-1971; Bill C. Heth, Beulah, 1963-1986;
Eldor Rasch, Hazen, 1963-1982; Ed Unruh, Zap, 1969-present; Harold Schulte,

Performing Arts School of Dance

Performing Arts School of Dance opened in Beulah in January, 1982. Initially
classes were held at the Beulah civic center. After two more changes in
location, Performing Arts School of Dance now resides in Room 217 in the Beulah
middle school.

Classes are held three days a week and draw students from Halliday, Stanton,
Riverdale and Glen Ullin as well as Beulah and Hazen.

Three kinds of dance are taught: ballet, tap and jazz. Students range in age
from four years through adult.

The school year traditionally ends with a public performance in the spring. In
May of 1987 Performing Arts School of Dance produced and directed a benefit
performance for the Arnold Knodel Memorial Scholarship Fund entitled
"Memories." This event raised more than $1,000 to help send local teens to the
North Dakota Teen Institute on Substance Abuse camp that summer.

The dancing school has provided entertainment for a number of community events:
the Good Sam Convention, the Hazen Holiday Fair, and the Beulah Lioness Club, to
name a few.

The school is directed by Eva Marie Schaffer, who moved to Beulah in the fall of
1981 with her husband, Bob, and their two children, Camille and Andrew. She
received her early dance training in Michigan where she became a soloist with
the Flint Civic Ballet, dancing leading roles in the Nutcracker, Coppelia and
Swan Lake. She continued her studies in New York City at Ballet Russe, American
Ballet Theatre and the Robert Joffrey School of Ballet. She performed in a
number of musicals on Broadway, at Lincoln Center and on tour throughout the
United States.

        Jim Robideau Photography:

Jim Robideau Photography

Jim Robideau Photography, established in North Dakota, more specifically,
Beulah, in 1983.

Robideau, a native of Moorhead, MN, spent his early years in the Fargo-Moorhead
area, graduating from Moorhead High School and working in Fargo until his
entrance into the armed services in 1967. After his discharge he secured a
position with International Harvester Company in Minneapolis.

Jim discovered an interest in photography when, in an effort to utilize some GI
benefits, he enrolled in night school. The first course covered black and white
processing and printing. The second, more comprehensive, addressed many more
aspects of the trade. In 1976 he received his certificate in the fundamentals of
professional photography from the Elkins Institute and over the years has
studied under Monte Zucker, Charles E. Lewis and the late Bill Stockwell.

While in Minnesota Jim belonged to the Minnesota Professional Photographers
Association and to the Professional Photographers of America.

Jim continued working at International Harvester Company and spent weekends
photographing weddings and creating portraits until 1982, when the company sold
the branch office and left 40 men without employment. At the time, more than
90,000 people were seeking work in the Twin Cities.

After actively looking for a job for six months, they decided to seek their
livelihood elsewhere. Connie's sister and family, who lived in Bismarck,
mentioned the growth at Mercer County and, after much deliberation, the family
made the decision to relocate. In August of 1983, Jim and Connie and sons,
Charles and Michael, arrived in Beulah and opened a studio there.

Jim was accepted into the Professional Photographers of North Dakota in the
spring of 1984, and remains a member of the Professional Photographers of
America, as well as Wedding Photographers International.

Since his acceptance into the organizations, Jim has won several awards in print
competition on the state, regional, and national levels. His "Nite Cap" is a
still life which was accepted into the National Loan Collection and is
permanently retained at headquarters for the Professional Photographers of
America.

In 1988, "Serenity," a wedding candid print entered into competition at the
Upper Midwest Convention, received the North Dakota Candid Award as well as the
Gallery Award, a crystal trylon, suitably inscribed and made for Kodak by
Tiffany & Co. Both awards are presented for prints that, in the eyes of the
judges, are technically and visually superior and outscored others in the same
category.

A photographer constantly strives for improvement in his work and Jim is no
exception. As his partner, Connie is most proud of how far he's come in the
short while he has been a full-time photographer. Under less than ideal
conditions he is producing portraits and wedding prints that consistently
please his customers.

"We are proud to be a part of this fine community and look forward to years of
continued growth and prosperity," Connie writes.

Roughrider Mobile Homes, Inc.

In January 1977 brothers Willie and David Schaper purchased the existing
business known as Suburban Mobile Homes in Dickinson, ND and renamed it
Roughrider Mobile Homes. After a few months they took on a third partner, a
nephew, Arvid Mittelsteadt. In 1979 they expanded by purchasing Suburban's
Beulah branch just east of highway junction 49 and 200.

Willie and Della Schaper began managing the Beulah office in January of 1979,
commuting from their farm north of Halliday until they moved to Beulah in the
fall of 1979. Willie's brother Marvin transferred from the Dickinson office to
head up the service department. And so the business got off the ground.

In 1988 the Schapers celebrated their 10th anniversary. Son Rob joined the
Beulah branch in 1982. The Schapers have seen and felt the many effects of
Beulah's growth. Product demand has changed from 14-foot-wide single mobile
homes for the transient customers in the early impact days to more permanent
housing for today's customers. There is a growing trend toward mobile-home
living in the rural and farm area. Willie and Rob are very optimistic about
their future here in Beulah and invite you to stop in and visit with them.

        Spier Sales and Service.

Spier Sales and Service, Inc.

Back in the '40s it went from buggy and horse to tractors. After the war you
could sell equipment faster than you could get it in stock, but it did not last
long. In the '30s if you got a 20-bushel crop it was considered a bumper crop,"
writes Spier's Sales and Service owner Henry Spier.

"My father and mother came from Romania. They first settled in Tripp, SD in
1898. In 1901 they came to Mercer County and homesteaded south of Zap up to
their retirement in the '60s. There were seven children in the Henry Spier Sr.
family, five boys and two girls. My brother, Daniel, was a missionary in New
Guinea."

Spier Sales and Service.

The Spiers are members of Zion Lutheran Church in Beulah. Henry Spier Jr., was
born and raised in Mercer County, five miles south of Zap. From 1936 to 1948, he
farmed on the homestead. In 1948 an auction sale was held on all the farm
equipment, cattle, horses, etc. The farm was leased to brother Fred. In March of
1949, Spier purchased a half interest in Field International Harvester Company.
The agreement was half share and after one year he could purchase the other
half. After the good sales on farm equipment, cars and trucks, the Fields
refused to sell the other half as originally agreed. Therefore, Spier sold back
his half share in 1951.

On March 16, 1952, Spier purchased the Ford and Moline agency from Fred
Flemmer. In 1959, he built the first self-setting pin bowling alley in the
area. This was operated for 14 years by the family, but was sold when the two
businesses became too much for them to care for.

In 1980, the coal gasification plant was being built. The main street of Beulah
became too congested for parking equipment, and the building was too small for
the large combines and tractors. It meant expanding to the new area or getting
out of the business. In 1981, a new building was constructed north of town. And
now, with the city expansion, Spier's is back in town.

Presently Ford, Mercury, Lincoln farm equipment and short lines are sold. "With
prices on equipment going up every year and the economy the way it looks
nowadays, you sometimes wonder if it's worth all the grief you have to go
through in business," writes Henry.

Murel Spier, son, is part owner in the business. Murel and his wife, Judy, have
two children, Travis and Valerie. Mr. and Mrs. Henry Spier also have two
daughters, Dell and Diana, who both live in Bismarck.

Classic Club Convention held in Springfield, MO.

Thomas has restored a 1951 Hudson originally owned by John Unruh when he was

include a 1926 Model T, a 1946 Chevy pickup, a 1959 Cadillac and a 1963 Chevy
convertible. Thomas is a member of the Beulah Chamber of Commerce.

Mercer County Women's Action and Resource Center

The Mercer County women's Action and Resource Center was established in 1979
with a grant from the Law Enforcement Assistance Administration. At that time,
North Dakota was recognizing and identifying domestic violence as a problem
within the state and six domestic violence projects were implemented. The center
was one of the original projects set up as an effort to meet the needs of women
involved in abusive relationships by assisting with safe shelter, protection
orders, referrals to counseling or whatever else might be indicated in order to
them to improve their situation if possible.

Mercer County was targeted as a site for a number of reasons, including the high
incidence of alcoholism, child abuse/neglect and suicide statistics. Many of
these problems are often inter-related. Limited services were offered at that
time because of limited funding.

In 1979 the center was basically operated out of a private home with a 24-hour
crisis line. A need to expand services became apparent after only a short
period of time, and when gaming became legal, additional sources of funding
became available.

Also, the definition of domestic violence began to change. Traditionally it is
defined as physical abuse such as pushing, shoving, hitting, slapping, biting
and beating. Other aspects began to emerge as abusive and perhaps more
devastating to self esteem, including sexual abuse, economic abuse, emotional
abuse and psychological abuse. Therefore, services were expanded to include
crisis intervention for sexual assault, rape crisis advocacy, a suicide
network, food pantry, short-term counseling, referral, library service and
education in the areas of parenting, child abuse/neglect prevention and sexual
assault prevention, which can all be considered part of domestic violence
prevention.

Prevention education and helping the child victims of domestic violence is
society's best bet for changing the incidence of abuse in the home.

The county's population base was stable until the coal gasification plant
impact when it grew rapidly in 1982-83. This impact, in addition to stress
caused by a quickly changing environment, brought to the surface long existing
and newly developed violent incidents within homes. When the population boom
receded, many families experienced months of unemployment and hard times. With
the farm economy likewise suffering setbacks, violence often became the outlet
for pent-up stress. No single population base or type of family is responsible
for the statistics. Domestic violence crosses all racial, ethnic and economic
boundaries.

The Women's Action and Resource Center is affiliated with the North Dakota
Council on Abused Women's Services (CAWS), and meets the requirements set forth
by the North Dakota State Department of Health. Sixteen domestic violence
projects are in existence across the state. The center is dedicated to
providing crisis intervention and help for those who have the least amount of
power in our culture. WARC has expanded this role to include prevention
education of abusive situations and other related factors.

Wilfred's Texaco, Exxon, and Conoco

In October 1964, Wilfred Schumacher started a service station with Texaco on
east Main Street in Beulah. He rented the Texaco station from Mrs. Rose Gleich.
After renting for five years, the lot where the station was located was sold.

Since Wilfred had to move, he decided to make a loan and, in 1969, built a new
station near Highway 49 in west Beulah. He bought one-and-one-half lots from
Bill Unruh in an area known as the Unruh Addition on June 30, 1978. The prime
contractor for the new building was Keller Construction Company, Bismarck (Ralph
Keller, owner). Concrete work was performed by Tri-County Corporation (Clarence
Jaeger, owner). Electrical work was performed by Hazen Electric (Richard Roshau,
owner). Plumbing work was performed by Unruh Plumbing (William Unruh, owner).

Texaco Inc. canceled its contract in North Dakota and some other states. So, in
July 1978, Wilfred signed an agreement with Newberger's Exxon. Neuberger's
Exxon has been in Beulah for many years distributing Exxon products. Wilfred
became an Exxon dealer until June 1986 when Exxon Company USA canceled its
contract in North Dakota.

Wilfred's Conoco has employed one to four people, depending on demand. Wilfred
Schumacher has owned a station at the same location on Highway 49 for about 25
years, servicing the Beulah area and beyond.

Yamaha Farm

Don Boeckel purchased his first motorcycle in the fall of 1965. Whatever repair
work needed to be done, he began to learn on his own. After some time,
neighbors began to bring their bikes to Boeckel to work on, as did other people
that he rode with. The repair work business spread by word of mouth and
eventually it was called Don's Cycle Repair.

Sometime in the late 1960s or early 1970s, Liebelt's, a local Chevrolet dealer,
purchased the Bridgestone motorcycle franchise. When Boeckel heard about it, he
talked to Mr. Liebelt about the possibility of working for him as a mechanic.
After working on Bridgestones for approximately one year, Boeckel recommended
to Mr. Liebelt that he purchase the Yamaha franchise, which he did. Boeckel
continued repairing motorcycles for Liebelt's Inc. from 1971 to 1981. He would
pickup the bikes at Liebelt's shop, take them out to his farm, do the necessary
work, and then return the repaired bikes to Liebelt's.

In July 1981, Boeckel heard Mr. Liebelt was dropping the franchise. He had
become acquainted with the Yamaha representative over the years and the
representative called him about the possibility of setting up a Yamaha
franchise. Upon the purchase of the Yamaha franchise from Liebelt's Inc., it
became know as the Yamaha Farm.

The Yamaha Farm has always been a family business. During the construction boom
years, son Dean also worked in the shop. The shop's best method of advertising
is still by word of mouth.

Ziman's Jewelry

Ken Ziman, a Dodge, ND native, studied watch making and repair at St. Paul
Vocational School in 1971. He worked for two years in Albert Lea, MN at Stadheim
Jewelers. Reuben Sackman, Beulah, was instrumental in encouraging Ken to locate
a business in Beulah.

In March 1977, Ken opened Ziman's Jewelry on Main Street next door to his
present location. His original inventory has expanded over the years to include
special occasion jewels for baptism, graduation, christenings and wedding gifts,
trophies, necklaces, watches, clocks and rings.

        Ziman's Jewelry-Janet Morast and Ken Ziman.

Black Hills gold is the shop's most popular item. Ten to 15 years ago white
gold was the customers' favorite. In 1977, gold sold for $150 per ounce. It has
now risen to a 1988 price of $442 per ounce.

Ken's wife, Cindy, is the company bookkeeper. Janet Morast has been with Ziman's
since 1986 as sales clerk.

The American Legion Argonne 85

The American Legion in Beulah was organized by Louis F. Temme by petition on
Oct. 8, 1919, with 10 World War I veterans signing. They were L.F. Temme, P.T.
Janski, H.W. Benson, C.L. Foster, Fred Tesky, Edward Adolf, O.I. Chadwick, John

Theo. J. Hafner, August Keller, and Dan Huber also joined the organization.

They agreed that the post should adopt the name "Argonne" in memory of their
comrades-in-arms who made the supreme sacrifice at the Battle of the Argonne
Forest in France.

A temporary charter was issued to the Legion-the Argonne Post 85 on Nov. 5,
1919. The permanent charter was issued Aug. 20, 1920. There were 52 names
listed on the permanent charter.

Beulah Airport Authority

The Beulah Airport Authority was established in 1965 due to then-mayor Lynn
Aasen's concern about the future of the city's airport and air service, as Jess
and Lie's Flying Service had been discontinued. Landowner Emanuel Liebelt
agreed to grant the city a longterm lease for a municipal airport on the
property.

The airport authority is under the auspices of Beulah city government and is
responsible for supervising airport maintenance and management, applying for and
distributing grant funds available to the airport through various agencies,
acting as a grievance board if problems come up and observing state and federal
flight regulations.

Aasen and the other first board members, Jess Thompson, Fred Helm, Wilhelm
Keller, and Mr. Schock and Mr. Aanderud, met May 14, 1965 and elected officers.
It was decided later that the city auditor should act as treasurer for the new
authority, and the group was granted a four-mill levy to fund its activities.

In 1966 the airport lease was signed with Liebelt, an engineering consultant was
hired, applications were made for available funds and a contract was let to
surface the turf runways.

Dedication for the spruced-up airport was held Sept. 18, 1966, with State
Aeronautics Commissioner Harold Varva attending, along with the Flying Ranchers
and Farmers. All were treated to a breakfast and lunch and toured the newly
improved airport.

        The first airport hangar.

Five private planes were then based at the airport, and by 1967 there were four
hangars. A surplus truck from Ellsworth Air Base in Rapid City, SD was granted
to the airfield and in 1970 a grant for $1,750 was secured. That allowed for
more work on the runway, taxiway, lighting and installation of a beacon. Other
improvements over the years included removing the office space in the old
hangar, installing a telephone booth, lighting the windsock, seal-coating the
surfaces, burying power lines and extending the runway 500 feet.

The airport saw a lot of heavy use in 1976, prompting the airport authority to
call a meeting with members of the Federal Aviation Administration to discuss
proposed plans for a county, area or joint airport. Several sites were
presented in an attempt to build an airport centrally located for industry and
cities and funds were appropriated to study the sites. A field was not found
which both Beulah and Hazen could agree on as compatible, and Beulah obtained
funds and an overlay on the parking area. A taxiway helped ease the problem
caused by the increased traffic.

        Fred Galloway Ralph Murray Walter Hafner.

In 1981 a fixed base operator was obtained when Jim Morton began to serve as
airport manager. He built a spacious hangar and has his own business, Dakota
Helicopters, which flies from the airport.

The airport authority has seen little change in membership, except when board
members have moved away. Only two chairmen have served: Thompson from 1965-70
and 1977-79, and Fred Galloway from 1970-77 and 1980-present. Other members
have been Aasen, Helm, Jim Kantack, Harold Herseth, Bill Sayler, Roger Smith,
Herb Scherbinske and Kevin Lee. City planner John Rogers was secretary-
treasurer for the authority until 1986, when he moved, and Robin Dettmann
volunteered to take over for him.

The airport authority plans to reseal and extend the long runway in the latest
of its continuing efforts to provide for Beulah and the surrounding area a
modern, well appointed, convenient airport for its use.

        1985 Alumni Association picnic.

Beulah Alumni Association

When the golden anniversary of the city of Beulah was held in 1964, the idea
took shape to hold a special reunion for all former Beulah students and
teachers. Ray Binder was elected president, secretary-treasurer was Teresa
Thompson and vice president was Selma Koppi. The project took a lot of effort
obtaining addresses of teachers and students with emphasis on the graduating
classes. The reunion was such a hit, with the more than 500 returning teachers
and students, that the organization was urged to continue the event at five-
year intervals. The Beulah Alumni Association was born.

Since that first reunion in 1964 there was one held in 1969, 1975, 1980, 1985
and the upcoming 1989. Hereafter reunions will be held in years ending in zero
and five.

The first graduating class to receive high school diplomas from Beulah school
was in 1923, with two graduating seniors. Since that first small beginning
there has been a graduation each year at Beulah high school, with classes
continually increasing in size. People now travel from nearly every state in
the U.S. and some foreign countries to attend the alumni reunion.

In the past the Alumni Association has sponsored varied activities: barbecues
at the park with as many as 900 people attending, banquets with 600 in
attendance, hospitality places around the city, dances at the gym and the
Eagles Club with the building overflowing with laughing people, tours of plants
and schools, breakfasts and programs. For the programs there have been choirs
organized from past school members, recognition of students who graduated 25
and 50 years ago and renewing acquaintances of former administration and
teachers.

The Alumni Association strives to host an event that has something for everyone
for a very small fee. The association has been assisted in the past by many
other city organizations, the many local alumni, as well as the alumni that are
no longer living in this area.

Perhaps one of the most popular events at each reunion is the hospitality and
registration room where everyone can mingle, share a cup of coffee and a hug,
leave messages for others and look at an the pictures of the schools and
students from the past.

Each former student is a member of the Alumni Association and every effort is
made to contact each of them before a reunion. A file system is established,
and an attempt is made to keep addresses current as well as information of
interest concerning the former students, teachers and graduates.

The Alumni Association is a rather loosely organized group with Gert Buscher,
Selma Koppi, Joan Schumaier and Ed Kittler overseeing the organization.

        Aaron Moos, 14 years old, son of Lona and Bob Moos. Eagle Scout, March
        20, 1988.

Beulah Boy Scouts

The Boy Scout program in Beulah was first organized in April 1929. Those
helping to organize the program were L.G. Rose, A.D. Brown and Rev. S. Joachim.
Rev. C.G. Eslinger was the Scoutmaster and Johnnie Lofthouse the assistant.

In 1933 the Beulah Lions Club became the sponsor and continues to sponsor the
Boy Scouts today. The troop is a member of the Roughrider District, which is a
part of the Northern Lights Council.

Beulah's first Scouts were Harley Kees, Ivan Iverson, Harry Lautermilch, Orville
Chilson, Clair Kearns, Lyle Wagonveldt, Bertram Heinemeyer, James Moore, Herbert
Kettler, Lonnie Tysver, Irvin Bates, Lester Segman, Elmer Bates, Walter Teske,
Ralph Sigman, Lester Roessle, Monroe Crystsal, Osborne Herman and Wm. Keller.

In 1933 Bert Webber was Scoutmaster. In 1938 B. Aanderud took over and then
Nels Husom. In 1947 Rev. Tyler Kriedeman and then in 1954 Edgar Goodman was
Scoutmaster. In 1960 Darold Benz took over for the next few years. Following
Benz, Don Kuch served for approximately 11 years. Then following was Darrel
Bjerke and then Gil Hanson.

The troop had had some years of inactivity but was again revived in 1987 by a
group of interested adults. Through the reorganization, Bob DeMaria emerged as
the present Scoutmaster with Larry Reinhardt serving as associate.

Through the years the troop has seen many boys come and go. A lot of the
activities have remained the same.

Camping is the big activity for the boys. They go camping in the area and also
go to Heart Butte a lot. They have gone skiing at Lake Metigoshe and some of
the boys at one time traveled to Philmont in New Mexico. The last two years the
boys have traveled to Camp Wilderness in Minnesota for a week-long camp earning
merit badges while at camp.

The boys are also involved in the community doing service work. They've been
involved in city cleanups, collecting books, eyeglasses (as part of Aaron Moos'
Eagle project) and tree planting (as part of Scott Schutt's project--he is
currently working on Eagle Scout status).

Since Beulah's Golden Anniversary in 1964, Eagle Scouts coming from Troop 19
were Donald Wolf, Larry Thompson, David Willis and Aaron Moos.

There are approximately 24 boys in the troop at the present time. Serving on the
Scout committee at this time are Darrel Bjerke, Bob DeMaria, Larry Reinhardt,
Lisa Reinhardt, Jennie Niska, Dave and Roxanne Salisbury, Bob and Jean Schutt,
Lona Moos and Aloha Simenson.

Beulah Chamber of Commerce

The Beulah Commercial Club was formed in 1914 with C.B. Heinemeyer elected the
first president. The Commercial Club was a busy organization and played a very
important role in the success of Beulah's business community.

The club had many projects over the years, ranging from constructing a new
bridge over the Knife River in 1914 to plank street crossings and a community
band in 1916. In the 1930s financial assistance was generated to send John
Moses to Washington, D.C., to promote water conservation and in the same year
the club also founded a local development corporation to build a movie theatre.

During the next 20 years the club struggled with projects and promotions. Many
committees were formed and the efforts of the members were spread very thin.

In 1954, the Commercial Club and its many smaller committees decided to
consolidate and form the Beulah Chamber of Commerce. On Dec. 21, 1954, the
Beulah Chamber of Commerce was incorporated as a nonprofit organization and was
registered with the secretary of state.

Over the next 30 years the Chamber started new projects and promotions. Some of
these have continued through the years. The annual Sauerkraut and Wiener meal,
recently expanded into the Oktoberfest, was begun in 1959. The meal started out
slowly but in 1963 it took off. The Chamber was ready for approximately 1,200
people, but when it came time for the meal it wasn't nearly enough. The day was
set in history and became part of Beulah's traditions.

        Beulah 's Chamber of Commerce has come a long way from the days when it
        was a small group, then called the Commercial Club.

In the late 1950s many ideas were pursued and some materialized. In those days
TV reception was poor, so they pursued a T.T. booster. Today the chamber still
funds the tower's insurance and assists with maintenance and power.

Also in the late 1950s a swimming pool to cool a person off on the hot summer
days was one of the chamber's number-one goals. Shortly after, the chamber and
other groups made the pool a dream come true.

In 1961 a terrific wind storm destroyed the rodeo grandstand. Many felt there
would never be another rodeo in Beulah. However, Lynn Aasen, Chamber president
that year, pushed for the reconstruction of the rodeo grandstand. By rodeo time
in 1962 a new earth-rolled amphitheater was in place. The Chamber was proud of
another job well done. In the years since 1962, the Chamber has assisted the
Rodeo Association in any way it could, from taking tickets and parking cars to
paying for the power at the rodeo grounds crow's nest.

After the construction of the Garrison Dam in 1953, the Chamber had various
committees working on the recreational aspects of the lake. In early years the
Chamber centered its efforts on cabin sites, waterside parks, boat ramps,
picnic areas and roads. In 1962 it sponsored what it hoped would be an annual
event at Hafner Bay (now Beulah Bay). The water carnival showed signs of being
one of the Chamber's better promotions. Unfortunately, due to varying weather
conditions and the distance from town, interest in the promotion faded away.

In 1986, the idea was tried again. Attendance and enthusiasm was good, but again
Mother Nature didn't cooperate. The committee, wet and tired, lost interest
just as the committee 24 years before had.

Over the years committees have worked on recruiting new business. In 1981, the
Chamber decided to open its own business. It contacted the motor vehicle
registrar and negotiated a contract to open a motor vehicle branch office. Off
and on since 1958 the Chamber had used the city hall as headquarters. So, when
it needed a home for the new public service business, it went to the city
council for permission to open the office in the city hall. Permission was
granted and the Chamber was moving again.

In January 1982, the business was ready to open. They hired their first-ever
full-time employee. The Chamber had dreams that this person would not only run
the Motor Vehicle Branch office but would also serve as public relations
person. During these past years the office has grown to serve as the hub of the
Chamber, the newly formed Convention and Visitors Bureau and the Booster
Committee.

Another project undertaken by the Chamber in 1981 was the erection of "Welcome
to Beulah" billboards. One was erected at each entrance into town. However, soon
this project became too costly for the Chamber to handle alone so other
community organizations and the city were contacted to contribute. To date we
still have billboards welcoming people to our fine city.

The Chamber has grown over the years to a current membership of more than 200.
It continues to do the projects that were started many years ago. Some of the
traditional projects that are still handled by the Chamber include cleaning the
entrances into town every spring, helping ready the swimming pool for the busy
summer season and financial support of various school activities, both
recreational and educational. The Chamber also handles many of the functions at
the county fair, including the construction of the booths in the exhibit area,
ticket-taking at the gates, a Saturday afternoon barbecue and coordinating the
county parade.

During these past 75 years, the Commercial Club/Chamber has continued to show
what faith and hard work can accomplish. The members are proud of their
community and they plan to make the next 75 years as productive as the first. As
always, the quality of life in Beulah is the number-one concern.

Beulah Christian Women's Club

The Beulah Christian Women's Club was started by a small handful of women in
1978 who met weekly for prayer and planning. By midsummer of that year a
representative from Stonecroft Ministries, Trudy Gilbert, arrived to select the
first slate of officers and plan the first luncheon which was held Aug. 7, 1978
at the Sleepy Hollow Inn.

Christian Women's Club is an associated ministry of Stonecroft Ministries, a
nondenominational, non-profit, Christ-centered organization. The objective of
every phase of the Stonecroft Ministries is to present the Biblical message of
salvation through our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. The Beulah Christian
Women's Club provides a unique avenue through which Christian women may present
the claims of Christ to their friends.

The unusual and stimulating program, designed to be presented in secular
surroundings, has an appeal which draws many to Jesus Christ. There is no
membership or dues. The format of each luncheon consists of a delicious noon
luncheon, a special feature which creates a party-like atmosphere (fashion
shows, antiques, photography, crafts, modes of cooking, sewing, etc.), special
music, and a speaker.

Other features include the sale of Christian books and publications, unique
decorations coordinating each month's theme, Friendship Coffee Bible studies
which are held in several homes throughout the surrounding communities, and
prayer coffees held at least once a month in individual homes on a one-time
basis.

The Beulah Christian Women's Club grew rapidly the first three months,
necessitating a move to larger facilities at the Beulah Civic Center, where the
monthly luncheons were catered by the Beulah Jayceettes for six years. In
November of 1984 the club moved to the Beulah Eagles Club and continues there
today.

Past chairwomen have been Sharon Lentz, Carole Dallman, Kathryn Helm and Debbie
Suelzle. The 1988 officers are as follows:

Eldora Sailer; book chairwoman, Margaret Oler; assistant book chairwoman, Irene
Rohde; decorations chairwoman, Claudia Kruckenberg; assistant decorations
chairwoman, Pat Grossman; hostess chairwoman, Audrey Morton; assistant hostess
chairwoman, Darlene Bauman; life publications chairwoman, Nikki Fagan; name tag
chairwoman, Florence Winkler; assistant name tag chairwoman, Audrey Sailer;

chairwoman, Bernice Scheid; ticket chairwoman, Helen Maxson; assistant ticket
chairwoman, Hertha Borth; treasure4 Debbie Suelzle; and assistant treasurer,
Genevieve Kamoni.

Numerous other ladies serve in various capacities to make this club as
successful as it is; such as table hostesses, telephone callers, study guides
and hostesses.

Beulah Fire Department

Beulah started out with two fire departments - one city and one rural, both
volunteer--but in August, 1961, they were consolidated. There is no date for
formation of the rural group. The most likely reason for the formation of the
original group can be found in a Sept. 13, 1918, newspaper clipping which
details the loss of six businesses on Beulah's Main Street early that morning,
netting a $17,500 loss for those six businesses. In 1918, that was no small
amount.

After that, businessmen and fire insurance salesmen alike began considering fire
protection for the young town of Beulah. The businessmen wanted to prevent or
reduce loss, while the insurance men wanted to lower rates to make their service
affordable.

To solve this, the first Beulah Volunteer Fire Department was organized Aug. 13,
1920. Fritz Schnitker served as first chief, with E.F. Munro assistant and L.F.
Temme, instrumental in the group's formation, as secretary-treasurer.

Those courageous firemen fought with the most primitive of equipment; two hand-
drawn two-wheel chemical carts.

The first fire for which the men were called out was at the Princess Theatre in
February, 1921. Though the damage was small, it pointed out the importance of
such an organization. Those members who had responded to the fire call were
paid $1; those who had not were fined the same amount. That method of assuring
the firemen came when needed continued until 1923.

The department held its annual fire inspection during fire prevention week each
fall. Some of the early inspection reports mention prairie chimneys, exposed
haystacks, kerosene stoves and coal sheds. Those serve as a reminder of the
department's longevity.

The first motorized equipment was a 1929 Ford truck, which served until 1940
when a new Ford unit complete with all the latest equipment was purchased. The
first electric siren was installed in 1933. The year 1952 saw the acquisition
of grappling equipment to aid in lake rescue work. In 1953 a Pnealator
breathing device was purchased and in 1960 Scott Air Pack mask and rescue
equipment was purchased. A civil defense-approved siren was acquired in 1963.

Some of the more spectacular fires the department has fought over the years
include the Johnson home, Coupland Garage, two Knife River Coal Mining Company
tipple fires, Shilling Pool Hall, John Frisco home, Buschbaker Blacksmith Shop,
the Princess Theatre film-room fire, Arrow Creamery and Klaudt Garage at Hazen.

The Fire Hall.

Serving as chiefs over the years have been Fritz Schnitker, Ted Muhlhauser, A.D.
Brown, Irv Niedermeyer, John Smith, C.L. Foster, Jim Stoppler, Fred Galloway,
Erhardt Grosz, Leonard Pulver and Lester Schlitz (1975-present).

When the departments were combined in 1961, combined equipment included a 1951
Ford, a 1962 Dodge, a 1964 van and a 1975 Chevrolet pickup. The reorganized
group was called the Beulah Rural Fire Protection District and became a
tax-supported entity.

Beulah began to expand about a decade after the departments consolidated, and
the fire department followed suit. A new 60 x80' fire hall was built at Central
and 7th St. in Oct., 1976. The department purchased turn-out gear for 30
members (at $325 a set), a 1979 Chevrolet 2-1/2 ton fire truck, an 1981 GMC
2-1/2 ton fire truck, and a 1983 GMC minitruck, all set up with the most modern
equipment available. They also have volume, high pressure and foam pumping
ability.

In 1985 a 1982 Chevrolet Suburban 4x4 was purchased for the fire chief's car,
and in 1986 a 1977 Freightline tractor was purchased and a pump and
3,800-gallon tank was installed. Also a 40'x50' extension was added to the fire
hall.

In 1987 land was purchased in Beulah's Industrial Park and a three-story 16'x16'
training tower was built, to give fire fighters experience in dealing with
doors, stairs, windows and obstacles in difficult conditions.

Much of the equipment purchased over the last decade or so has been with the
assistance of the Energy Development Impact Office, which often furnished
matching grant funds for the equipment the department needed to adequately
protect its grown town and rural areas.

Hanks, A. Emter, M. Spier, C. Galloway, F. Wright, D. Knudson, P. O'Neill, M.

Tesky, G. Sailer, D. Herman, M. Weidrich, and S. Garrison.

Beulah Municipal Golf Club

The Beulah Municipal Golf Club had its beginnings back in the early 1920s. Some
of the local people who had played an occasional round of golf decided Beulah
should have its own course. The search was on to find the appropriate place.

A parcel of land south of Beulah, school land owned by the state, was selected
as the prime spot. The land was leased by Johnnie Maier. Johnnie and the golf
course worked out what they thought to be the perfect arrangement. In the
summer the land would be Beulah Country Club and during the winter Johnnie
would use the land for his cattle to graze.

During the summer of 1926, 15 men constructed five holes. The sand greens were
constructed by digging a circular hole 10 inches deep and 40 feet in diameter.
The hole was then filled with six inches of clay and four inches of sand. A
high grade of used oil was sprayed on the sand and mixed thoroughly. In 1944
four new holes were added, expanding to a nine-hole course. This was also the
first year of the Beulah Invitational Tournament.

In 1954 a building was purchased from Knife River Coal Mining Company and moved
to the course to serve as the club house. This building, with numerous
modifications, remains an active part of the course today.

Beulah Country Club continued as a sand green golf course sponsoring numerous
annual tournaments, several high school regional tournaments and the State High
School Sand Greens Tourney in 1970.

In the spring of 1984 the Beulah Golf Course made a decision to change and
upgrade the facility to a grass green course. The dream of all the Beulah
golfers began to take shape and finally in June 1985, play on the grass green
course began. The transformation required tremendous work and support on behalf
of many individuals, local businesses and the city of Beulah.

A few of those people instrumental in the development were: Ray Hagen, Rich
Bronson, Al Power, Gerry Burling, Ken Ziman, Charlie Thelander, Don Bradley, Ben
Lenzen, Bob Jesswein, George Koppi and Fred Menge. The initial cost of over
$200,000 was a major investment and countless hours of donated labor required a
genuine team effort of which Beulah can be proud.

Today that commitment, cooperation and hard work is evident as the Beulah
Municipal Golf Club continues to grow and improve. The club has grown to include
over 200 full-time memberships and a total of over 10,000 people playing rounds
of golf in 1987.

A ladies' group, organized in 1955 to assist the men in the upkeep and
furnishing of the clubhouse, is still active today. Their total membership
today is 30 strong. The ladies meet on Tuesdays for golf and lunch and are
responsible for planning many of the mixed tournaments, socials and other
important course projects.

Officers and directors for the 1988 season are as follows: president, Brent
Sullivan; vice president, Art Schilke; treasurer, Phil Eastgate; secretary,
Larry Duppong. Directors: Dennis Voegele, John Dschaak, Bob Grant, Ethie
Pierce, Stan Piasecki, Rick Ziegler and Kevin Flaagen.

Beulah Girl Scouts

Girl Scouting in Beulah was reorganized because of the request of little Dawn
Marie Goetz. While passing a Girl Scout display at the Mercer County Fair, she
told her grandmother, Alma Kasper, she thought "we should have Girl Scouting in
Beulah."

In the fall of 1974 a Neighborhood Association was formed, consisting of one
Brownie troop and one Junior troop. Mariann Sayler agreed to serve as the first
Neighborhood chairwoman.

Kasper persuaded the Beulah Veterans of Foreign Wars and the V.F.W. Auxiliary to
sponsor Girl Scouting that fall. During the next 14 years, they purchased troop
flags for all registered troops, provided numerous camperships, full leaders'
dues, leaders' resource books, local cookie incentives for the Girl Scouts, and
partially funded Wider Opportunities or trips for older girls and adults.

Sayler served as Neighborhood chairman from 1974-1977. She was followed by
Lindarae Eisenbeis, who served the Neighborhood Association for one year. She
was succeeded by JeAnne Selby in the fall of 1978. She remained at the helm for
nine years, expanding the adult volunteers into a Neighborhood service team as
the girls' membership increased. Pat Mohl assumed chairmanship of the local
association in fall, 1987.

One of the first three Daisy Troops piloted in Sakakawea Girl Scout Council was
started by the Beulah Neighborhood in January 1985. Daisy Troop No. 4191 was
composed of 11 kindergarten-aged girls. Mohl was instrumental in securing the
pilot program for the Beulah Neighborhood and served as the first troop leader,
assisted by Lynn Mohl. She subsequently provided council-wide training for new
Daisy leaders. This troop has been sponsored since its inception by the United
Methodist Church Women.

The Beulah Girl Scout Association has been very active locally, in Hidatsa
District and in Sakakawea Council. Several older Girl Scouts and adult
volunteers have attended Wider Opportunities in other councils as well.

The Neighborhood has generally hosted an Investiture Ceremony each fall to
welcome new Girl Scouts. Brownies have delighted in helping welcome many new
Brownies with these words from the familiar Brownie story: "Twist me, turn me,
show me the elf. I looked in the water and saw--myself!"

Troops take turns making tray favors for the patients at our local nursing home
for various holidays throughout the year. Troops enjoy caroling each year
during the holidays also.

One of the more unusual local troop activities was a Brownie troop picnic in
1981. Brownie Troop No. 4102 honored their fathers with the picnic and outdoor
games and prizes.

Local Junior and Cadette troops have taken sight-seeing trips a number of
summers to the Badlands and Medora.

Local Girl Scouts have earned money for troop activities and camping through the
annual Girl Scout Cookie campaign. February, 1988, was the first time Brownies
in Sakakawea Council were allowed to sell cookies. Other council-approved troop
fund-raising activities include magazine subscription sales and the sale of
Girl Scout calendars.

The local Neighborhood has celebrated National Girl Scout Week each March with
various special troop activities, church bulletin inserts and Girl Scout
participation in worship services. In 1978 the Neighborhood started sponsoring
International Friendship Day (or Thinking Day) programs on or near Feb. 22,
which is designated as Girl Scout Thinking Day. The program and ceremonies
reflect the thoughts of Girl Scouts and Girl Guides around the world. Special
guests each year have been people who are from other countries or who have
lived or traveled in foreign countries.

Window displays representing activities, projects and badge-work selected from
the world of the arts have been placed in Sveum's Department Store to celebrate
National Girl Scout Week annually since March 1981.

        Daisy Scouts. Seated: Nicole DeMaria, Sarita Harris, LaRae Busch. Back
        row: Leader Sandy Keys, Tanya Boeckel, Katie Larson, Elizabeth Keys,
        Laura Jo Petrik, Leader Linda Harris.

In 1986, because of a shortage of printed church bulletin inserts, Neighborhood
chairwoman JeAnne Selby designed a localized insert using local troop pictures.

Each May the V.F.W. and Auxiliary host the annual Girl Scout family potluck and
bridging ceremony, sometimes called "fly-up," which is graduation from one troop
level to another. Also that evening, individual membership pins, badges and
patches are presented in a Court of Awards.

The Beulah Girl Scouts participated in the 1987 Mercer County Fair parade.

The Beulah Girl Scout Association has hosted the Hidatsa District Brownie Fun
Day three years. They hosted the 1976 District Girl Scout Camp for Girl Scouts
of all ages at the Riverside Park. Local troops have participated in District
Brownie and Junior Fun Days as well as camps at Camp Sakakawea and Heart Butte.

Troops have either sponsored booths or participated in the little theater
productions at the annual Girl Scout Expo in Bismarck each spring. In 1986 the
council began awarding only a first, second and third place ribbon in each
troop level. That year the combined Junior Troop No. 4112 and No. 4113 received
the second place award out of a field of about 60 to 70 Junior troops. In
February 1988 the same group of girls, now registered as Cadette Troop No.
4121, again received second place among the council's 20 or more Cadette troops.

In 1978 Holly Power and Miriam Sayler were selected to attend Cadettes on
Horseback at National Center West, Ten Sleep, Wyo. They attended two sessions of
the two-week Wider Opportunity.

Rhonda Mosbrucker, Power and Ann Scheidt attended Senior Sports Spectacular at
Billings, Mont., in 1979, chaperoned by troop leader Stephany Schneider.They
participated in karate, silk screening, synchronized swimming, mime, stage
make-up, powder-puff mechanics, photography, disco and racquetball.

Power and Sayler were among the 15 ninth-grade Cadette and Senior Scouts who
attended Sakakawea Girl Scout Council's first Career Probe '80, receiving
on-the-job experience in observing the duties, qualifications and job
opportunities at St. Alexius Medical Center in Bismarck.

Senior Scout Ann Scheidt was one of 200 Scouts and Guides who attended a Wider
Opportunity at New Haven, Conn., in 1980, which included a sight-seeing trip to
New York City, an overnight hike in the Appalachian Mountains and 11 days of
camping and "home hospitality" in two Connecticut homes.

In April 1985 Daisy leader Mohl and Neighborhood chairwoman Selby participated
in four-day national workshops for adult volunteers in New York City.

In 1987 Daisy co-leaders Paula Goldman and Ann Kok attended the Workshop for
Leaders of Daisy and Brownie Girl Scouts, also in New York.

JeAnne Selby served on the board of directors for Sakakawea Girl Scout Council
from 1973-79, also serving one term as first vice-president of the board and
chairman of the council membership operating unit.

Sandra Rudolph, a former local Brownie leader, was elected secretary of the
Sakakawea Girl Scout Council board of directors in April, 1987. Prior to that,
she served in the position of Brownie program coordinator for the council
program unit.

The only original member of the finance committee is Diane Mutzenburger, who has
served since 1978. This committe fulfills the Neighborhood's local, district and
council financial obligations.

The Beulah Girls Scout Association has become a vital part of Sakakawea Council
during the past 14 years. It quickly grew from two troops and 30 girls in 1974
to four troops and 55 girls in 1979, eight troops with 80 girls in 1984.
Currently, the Beulah Neighborhood has seven troops with 61 registered Girl
Scouts and 17 adults.

Mercer County Historical Society

On May 31, 1977, 11 people met for the purpose of officially organizing the
Beulah Historical Society. They were Daryl Zimmerman, Julius Orth, Martha Heihn,
Catherine Scherbinske, Althea Seifert, Selma Koppi, Rags Thelander, Teresa
Thompson, Gertie Buscher, Millie McKenzie and Kathryn Helm. First officers were
president Daryl Zimmerman, vice president Kathryn Helm, secretary Millie
McKenzie and treasurer Gertie Buscher. Gertie Buscher was instructed to check
further into the possibility of being designated as the Mercer County
Historical Society. There were 100 charter members and 11 life-time charter
members.

It was at the June 21, 1977, meeting that the first plans for a building of
their own were discussed. Zimmerman agreed to contact the city about some land
near the civic center. Tillie Dettmann, George Benz and Zimmerman were
appointed to serve on the building committee.

On Dec. 20, 1977, they officially became the Mercer County Historical Society.

Ground breaking was Aug. 31, 1978. Officials from the North Dakota State
Historical Society were in attendance.

The building was erected in October, 1978. It was completely finished and open
to the public by the spring of 1980. The total cost of the building was
$42,109.28. On April 21, 1981, on behalf of the society, Millie McKenzie and
Zimmerman signed a mortgage with the Bank of Beulah in the amount of $30,000.
Officially the loan was paid up in April of 1986.

Being debt-free was a good feeling, but it wasn't for long.

In August of 1987 the group gave Western Steel a down payment for a steel
building 60' x 100'. The building was started in October and will be used for
cold storage for the present time. The cost up to the present time is $45,794.
As soon as our debt is retired, the group hopes to pour a concrete floor in
order to expand the present display area. It now has a $32,000 mortgage with
the Bank of Beulah.

Officers as of January, 1988, were president Leland Erickson, secretary Millie
McKenzie, treasurer Gertie Buscher; board of directors at present time are
Teresa Thompson, Martha Heihn, Tillie Dettmann, Peggy Wolff, Esther Scheidt,
Herb Feil, Chip Unruh, Milton Flemmer, Fred Menge, Erik Holland, Millie
McKenzie and Althea Seifert.

Membership fees for the historical society are: Individual $5, business
membership $25, lifetime membership $100.

At present time there are 41 lifetime members and seven deceased.

The society has an ongoing memorial fund and the money is used for equipment and
artifacts.

Beulah Homemakers Club

The Beulah Homemakers Club was organized in the early 1920s by Mercer County's
first agriculture agent, Grover Poe. Mrs. Poe was the club's first president.
In 1935 the club was reorganized by county agent, O.K. Cline. The club
membership was 26. Mrs. C.B. Heinemeyer was the president and three club
members, Mrs. I. Vincent, Mrs. C.B. Heinemeyer and Mrs. A. Gilchrist, were
appointed by the Mercer County Council to draft a constitution for the county
Homemakers Clubs.

Many women of varied interests have joined the Beulah Homemakers Club over the
years. Since 1971, the club has had 38 different members. During Beulah's
construction boom of the late 70's, the club enjoyed the participation of many
new members from diverse backgrounds and locations.

Club meetings are held on the third Thursday of each month in members' homes.
Club dues have changed from five cents per month to $1.00 a year in 1965 to
$5.00 a year in 1988.

The Mercer County Extension Service offers a selection of interesting lessons.
In 1935 members were advised to listen to the radio for topics pertaining to
homemaking. In 1988 many of the lessons are presented via video. Some members
use their own talents to teach hands-on craft projects. Now, as then, the club
meetings consist of a lesson and social time. Yearly activities include a
dining out, Christmas party, picnic, pot luck dinner and the Mercer County
Homemakers event.

Current progressive officers are: president, Margie Lee; vice president, Mildred
McKenzie; and secretary-treasurer, Marcie Burling.

Beulah Lions Club

The Beulah Lions Club was originally organized under the auspices of the
Bismarck Lions Club. On May 12, 1930, the Beulah Lions Club received its
charter from the International Association of Lions Clubs.

The International Association of Lions Clubs is the largest civic organization
in the world. The motto of every Lion is simply, "We Serve," and the slogan of
Lionism is "Liberty, Intelligence and Our Nation's Safety."

During the 1930's and 1940's the Beulah Lions Club was a weekly luncheon club
which met on Mondays at noon.

A major contribution to the community has been its long sponsorship of the Boy
Scouts. Previously they sent Beulah boys to Boy's State. The Lions Club was also
active in developing better roads for Beulah.

The Beulah Lions continued actively in the community until February of 1971,
when the club was dissolved.

Fortunately in 1975 some men of Beulah still retained the strong feelings of
Lionism and initiated action to reorganize the Beulah Lions Club. On January
31, 1976, the Beulah Lions Club received its charter from the International
Association of Lions Clubs. The Elgin Lions Club was the sponsor for the Beulah
Lions Club. One hundred thirty-three people enjoyed charter night. Charter
night was held at the Beulah Civic Center.

Cities represented were: Elgin, Carson, Beulah, Bismarck, Glen Ullin, New Salem,
Minot, Hazen, Stanton, Dickinson and Hazelton. The 22 charter members of Jan.
31, 1976 were: Ken Beauchamp, Darold Benz, Virgil Biloff, Douglas Dettmann, Lyle
(Del) Els, Roger Endreson, Tim Ernst, Fred Galloway, Dale Gilje, Ron Gunsch,
Herman Hildebrand, Helmuth Pfenning, Helmuth Hilz, Wilhelm Keller, Gary Miller,
Ernest Ohlhauser, Mark Sayler, Wilmer Sayler, Clyde Schulz, Curtis Schulz, Al
Splichal and Charles Thelander.

Many Beulah men have provided leadership to the Beulah Lions Club by holding a
variety of offices. All positions are important to the club. Presidents since
the 1976 Charter are as follows: Wilhem Keller -- 1975-76 and 1976-77, Clyde
Schulz -- 1977- 78, Charles Thelander -- 1978-79, Dean Moos -- 1979-80, Al
Schock -- 1980-81, Mark Sayler -- 1981-82, Jim Selby -- 1982-83, Al Splichal --
1983-84, Norris Abrahamson -- 1984-85, Richard Bronson -- 1985-86, Marvin Aberle
-- 1986-87, Mark Wagner -- 1987-88.

The Beulah Lions Club plans and conducts a variety of community and humanitarian
projects. Some of them are: July 4th Demolition Derby, Lions Auction, sale of
mints, contract flag service, sponsoring of Boy Scouts, awarding scholarships,
sponsoring Blue and Gold Boy Scouts Banquet, sponsoring the High School Honors
Banquet, maintenance of the Lions Park and collection of used eye glasses (2700
pairs collected in two years).

Donating money, labor, and materials to other organizations involved with
seeing eye dogs, helping the blind, assisting diabetes programs and Quest
programs associated with educating youth to the dangers of drugs and alcohol
are other Lions projects.

The above mentioned projects require that the Beulah Lions Club members be
involved in a variety of fund raisers so that donations can be made to worthy
causes, which parallels Lionism.

Some of the other activities that Lions members have participated in are as
follows: paper drives, breakfasts and brunches, horse shoe tournaments,
sponsored beard contest and issued shaving permits, provided picnic tables for
the Girl Scout Camp, house numbering project, contributed toward July 4th
fireworks display, sponsored Christmas Socials, sponsored bus trips to
historical sites for senior citizens, acquired glasses for individuals that
could not afford them and held raffles to earn money and held hard water golf
tournaments at Renner Bay.

The Beulah Lions Club has also made donations to the Lions hearing guide dog
project, Mercer County parade fund, drug awareness program, West River
Transportation Service, Mercer County Ambulance Service, Beulah Chamber of
Commerce, drug abuse work shops, the School for the Blind, Brian Gamble electric
wheel chair fund, Beulah Civic Center, the Beulah Municipal Golf Club, Beulah
Gymnastics Club and possibly the most important of all, The Lions Clubs
International Foundation, which responds to international disasters.

The Beulah Lions Club is active and busy in 1988 working towards the completion
of several community and club projects. With the interest of the members and
enthusiastic leadership, the Beulah Lions will continue to be the dynamic club
it has been in the past.
