Beulah Mothers Club

The Beulah Mothers Club was organized in September, 1935 at the W. Esterly home.
Twelve young mothers formed a social and child study group which has met
continuously since then on the third Thursday each month. The original
membership was changed from 12 to 13.

Mrs. Esterly was the first president. The charter members were Mrs. Halbeisen,
Mrs. E. Shirley, Mrs. P. Keogh, Mrs. W. Esterly, Mrs. Bert Webber, Mrs. T.
Carrigan, Mrs. A. Lang, Mrs. S. Frank, Mrs. T. Herman, Mrs. A. Roedel, Mrs. O.
Swanson and Mrs. S. Bacal. They affiliated with the Homemakers Program in 1948.

The program was originally a study of child behavior based on Parents' Magazine.
They were the sole sponsor of the summer kindergarten. The first kindergarten
was started in 1939 with Abbie Tyrrell as the first teacher. Another big
accomplishment was sponsoring Miss Marta Kassik, a displaced person, as a
full-time piano, voice, and organ teacher for Beulah and the surrounding
communities.

The club's aims have remained the same with the exception of sponsoring a
kindergarten, which is now provided by the Beulah public school system. Members
still try to have one foods lesson a year, usually something of an ethnic
nature as members are from various ethnic backgrounds and often rely on their
own resources.

The club tries to have one or two crafts a year, sometimes bringing in guest
speakers or demonstrators, and tries to keep membership at 13 to best
accommodate living room space.

Present membership of 12 consists of Helen Morman, a member since 1938; Gertie
Buscher, 1946 to 1952, 1966; Selma Koppi, 1951; Phyllis Power, 1953; Tillie
Dettmann, 1955; Althea Seifert, 1961; Teresa Thompson, 1961; Carole Bjerke,
1965; Angie Thelander, 1972; Karen Bronson, 1982; and Cheryl Younker, 1983.
These members represent 315 years of membership.

Note: Rags Thelander, a member of 47 years, passed away on Jan. 2, 1988. She
gave some of the club's most interesting and memorable lessons and is sadly
missed by the entire club.

History of the Beulah Police Department

The first available history of the Beulah Police Department is back in the
1930's, when Ed Carmichael was Beulah's policeman.

In the 1940's the following served as Beulah's policemen, or marshalls as they
were called in those days: Manley Thompson, Fred Schutz, and Mike Weiand.

On April 1, 1941, Manley Thompson was called upon to arrest Fred Sinerius at his
son's farm just west of Beulah. Sinerius had gunned down V.P. Wolf, 29, field
man for the Bank of North Dakota, and Joseph Runion, 47, a Mercer County
deputy. The two men had gone out to Sinerius's son's home to try to recover
some storm windows, storm doors and lumber, which the elder Sinerius had
removed from his former farm after being evicted. Sinerius surrendered to
Marshall Thompson without resistance.

Fred Hanck served as Beulah's policeman from 1948 until the mid 60s. He
performed other duties as well, such as operating the Austin Weston grader and
reading water meters. He was succeeded by Rudy Kovak, Jake Weisinberger, Ervin
Tischer and Harold Kiesz.

Harold Kiesz was Beulah's policeman in 1969 when the city was invaded on a
Saturday morning by approximately 3,000 students from various colleges in the
United States, who had been run out of Zap by the National Guard that Friday
evening when things got out of hand at the now infamous "ZIP TO ZAP." Many
Beulah citizens were deputized that morning to assist officer Keisz in
protecting downtown businesses from vandalism, and in evicting the rowdy
students. This was accomplished with the assistance of the National Guard, when
the students offered only token resistance.

One incident of note occurred when a student from Minnesota became belligerent
and refused to move, and got prodded in the backside by the bayonet of a
National Guardsman. The student had to be taken to the Beulah Clinic where he
was sutured by Dr. Ewert, and then left town with a mark of distinction which
he will carry with him all of his life.

The 1970's, the early impact years, saw quite a turnover of officers. Jerry
Beeman, William Taplen, Windy Rose, Mark Sayler, Al Rebhahn (part-time), Joe
Foley, Harry Johnson, David Paetz, and Gordon Leingang.

The city of Beulah had only one full-time policeman with the assistance of a
part-time officer and one police car until the mid-1970's, when the city was
impacted by construction workers from the Coyote and Basin power plants,
Antelope Valley Station, and then the ANG coal gasification plant.

The city then had to increase its police force to meet the impact. The following
individuals served as policemen during that era: Mark Gilbertson, Mark Erhardt,
Tim Ernst, David Paetz, Kevin Swalley, Patrick Testa, John Willoughby, Greg
Stone, Donald Tittle, Rodney Sagen, Michael Lynk, Gilmore Hanson, Gary
Thompson, and John Rendell. With the complete turn of events and increased
crime rate, whereby stabbings, rapes, burglaries, drug traffic and increased
vehicle traffic had to be coped with, the city was required to acquire more
sophisticated equipment and trained officers.

In the later months of 1983-1984, the construction phase of the coal
gasification plant was winding down, and they were pushing for plant start-up.
The police department at that time consisted of Chief Mark Gilbertson, Sergeant
David Paetz, patrolmen Rod Sagen, Michael Lynk, Gilmore Hanson, Gary Thompson,
and John Rendell.

In January of 1984, Gilbertson resigned and took a position with the ND State
Training and Statistics Division. David Paetz became chief, and John Rendell
became sergeant. Later that year Gary Thompson left the department and moved to
Minnesota. That left the police department as it is today, Chief David Paetz,
Sergeant John Rendell, and patrolmen Rod Sagen, Michael Lynk, and Gilmore
Hanson.

The police department is located in the City Hall building on Central Ave N. In
1985 the police department purchased a computer system for record keeping, and
is rated fifth in the state for city police departments with such systems. In
1986 city hall was renovated, which gave the department much needed room. Also
in 1986, the department hired Lisa Eissinger as secretary dispatcher. 1987
found the department with a new radio system for the city and police
department, and a new four-wheel drive vehicle to go along with the two police
cars.

Beulah Quarterback Club

The Beulah Quarterback Club was organized in September of 1975 by a group of
Beulah citizens interested in promoting sports within the community. The
organization quickly grew and found many areas within the school and community
in which they could lend their financial and manpower support.

Promoting youth involvement in athletic competition has always been one of the
goals of the club and it has served the community well in many areas. The club
has contributed totally or partially to a wide variety of events and equipment
throughout its years of existence, totaling over $50,000 in financial
assistance to the youth of the community.

An annual event sponsored by the Quarterback Club is the pancake and sausage
breakfast held in conjunction with the district tournaments. The proceeds from
this project are donated to the Beulah park board, which uses the funds to
sponsor the summer recreation program for the youth of the city. The summer rec
program includes t-ball and baseball for boys, the American Legion team and
girls' softball.

The club donated the championship banner in the high school gymnasium and the
upcoming events sign on the outside of the gym. A free-weights set was donated
to the high school weight room and $800 was given to the Beulah Gymnastics Club
to assist in the purchase of operating equipment.

In addition to the many avenues of financial support, the club provides
manpower in the form of ushers, ticket takers, etc. for both the boys' and
girls' district basketball tournaments which were held in Beulah in 1987-88.
Manpower was provided for the multiple dual wrestling meet held in Beulah and
the club provides oranges for both the Beulah team and the visitors at every
high school athletic event.

Another annual event sponsored by the club is the Beulah Quarterback Club
Invitational Track Meet.

Current officers are: Bill Misslin, president; Sally Kivisto, secretary;
Loretta Greni, treasurer; and board of director members Jim Aanderud, Rex
Wenko, Edgar Rueb, Lawrence Anderson, Elroy Herman and Mike Hammerschmidt.

There are currently 90 families and 21 single memberships in the Beulah
Quarterback Club.

        Beulah Senior Citizens Center

Beulah Senior Citizens' Club

A group of 25-30 Beulah citizens organized the Senior Citizens' Club in 1968.
The newly organized club held meetings once a month at the city hall and civic
center until the club bought the former Joachim Memorial Home from the Beulah
nursing home in November of 1984. The total purchase price was $35,000.

The city of Beulah gave $20,000 towards the purchase price, leaving the balance
of $15,000 to be paid by the club. The club rented out four rooms of the
building and the garage for $400 per month and in this manner raised most of
the funds necessary to pay off the mortgage by November of 1986.

Through the proceeds of the on-going rummage sale held in the basement of the
center, the club has been able to remodel the center and convert the pool room
into a larger area which is still used for pool. A large kitchen and 48'x 50'
dining hall were added to the top floor and the kitchen that was formerly
downstairs is now a small unit used only by workers.

The entire downstairs, except for one room that is used for quilting, is now
used for the on-going rummage sale, a concept that was begun in 1984 when Ted
and Martha Heihn lent their idea to the center. Community members donate
clothing and other items to the center which then sells them at a rummage sale
which is open in the center basement Wednesday, Thursday and Friday. The
average monthly income from the rummage sale is estimated to be $600 per month,
which helps keep the club financially secure.

The Senior Citizens' Center provides a place where Beulah's seniors can meet and
play pool, whist or pinochle, quilt, donate time to the rummage sale or just
visit with neighbors. The center also is available for rent for occasions such
as family reunions, anniversaries, etc.

        Beulah's Senlor Citizens Club has many many members both women . . .

        . . . and men, who keep the club, its building and its projects
        going.

The establishment of the center and the fact that it was paid for so quickly
are both tributes to the enthusiasm and determination of Beulah's senior
citizens and a reminder that age has little to do with the ability to
accomplish a task.

Beulah Soccer League

Soccer has become very popular in the U.S., particularly as a game for young
children. The reason for this is that it has a high energy level and as a
result, satisfies their natural enthusiasm and exuberance. Furthermore, the
degree of participation by all players is high, which is appreciated by the
children. No special equipment is necessary to play and, within any particular
age group, the size of the child is not important as the rules discourage
intentional physical contact.

The Beulah Soccer League, established in 1983, completed its very successful
sixth season in 1988. A total of 210 players ranging from five to 14 years
competed in four age groups and were assigned to 14 teams. In 1987 there were
approximately 25 percent more players than in 1986. The league is coed and
girls were on each team. In addition to Beulah, players were drawn from Hazen,
Golden Valley, Pick City, Stanton and Zap.

The primary objective of the league is to make soccer an enjoyable experience
for each player. While all the players and their teams try their utmost to win
the games, no record is kept of their performance, and no champion teams in the
various age groups are declared.

        The soccer team getting advice from Coach Mark Goldman.

Each team is carefully selected to achieve a balance of age and experience. The
result is that the teams are well matched and no team succeeds in winning all
of its games. League rules ensure that each player plays at least half of each
game, and this allows everyone to develop his or her self-esteem and feel a
valued member of the team. The registration fee per child is very affordable
($8.50 in 1987) and for this the child is given a team shirt with an individual
number.

The 1987 season started with the Beulah school year and lasted for about six
weeks. During this period at least six games were played against other Beulah
teams. Weekly activities were intense, with typically two practices and one
game taking place. Games were played either on Saturday morning or during the
week.

Each game consists of four 12-minute quarters with substitutions of players
allowed at any time. In addition to this local competition each player in two
higher age groups was offered an opportunity to broaden his or her experience
by playing home and away games against Bismarck and Minot.

The league is run at the local level, with vital parental support. Parents
coach and referee.

All soccer activities take place on the softball fields. The soccer league
received a $500 contribution from the Eagles, and of this amount $400 was
donated to the softball league in appreciation for allowing use of the softball
fields for soccer.

Beulah Women's Club History

The G.F.W.C. Beulah Women's Club was organized in 1930 with the following
charter members: Mrs. C. Ellinger, Mrs. A. Gilchrist, Mrs. H.J. Halbeisen, Mrs.
H. Harold, Mrs. M. Held, Mrs. W. Lane, Mrs. A. Lang, Mrs. C. Malaise, Mrs. F.P.
Marshall, Mrs. M.P. Moore, Mrs. I.J. Neidermeyer, Mrs. F.P. Rasmusson, Mrs. L.G.
Rose, Mrs. T. Scholz, and Mrs. I. Vincent.

The Beulah Women's Club, an affiliate of the General Federation of Women's
Clubs, is a study club whose major project throughout its existence has been
the growth and improvement of the local library.

        Beulah Women's Club. Standing: JeAnne Selby, Myrtle Sailer, Inez
        Sommer, Helen Maxson, Carole Bjerke, Deanna Knudson, Helen Morman.
        Sitting: Merilynn Liebelt, Karina Singer, Suzan Schock, Mariann
        Sayler, Angie Thelander, Della Benz.

The library was opened on Feb. 1, 1931, in the east foyer of the Roxy Theater.
Throughout the past 57 years, it has been six homes and eight moves. Its most
recent move was in May of 1987 from one area of city hall to another larger one
resulting from extensive remodeling. The library was closed from Jan. of 1987
until its open house, held in conjunction with the open house held for city
hall on Sunday, June 14, 1987.

The library opened with 51 paid memberships, a practice which was discontinued
in 1941.

During the years 1956-57, the Beulah Women's Club went on record as favoring a
new city hall with a library room and offered to campaign for this civic
project. As a result of these efforts, the library moved into a new room at
city hall. Also, about this time, the library began receiving funding from the
city, alleviating the financial obligations of the Women's Club somewhat.

In the fall of 1958, the library linked up with the McLean-Mercer Regional
Library in Riverdale. This liaison has provided local patrons with additional
books, bookmobile services and local librarians' salaries.

A municipal library board was established on Feb. 6, 1985, with original board
members Herb Dittus, Carol Schwartz, JeAnne Selby, Rags Thelander and Judy Welk.
Through the cooperative efforts of this board and the library committee of the
Beulah Women's Club, the library opened in its newest quarters in city hall
last June.

The Women's Club has maintained an active library committee through the years.
The specific duties have varied, but were always directed toward the promotion
of the library. The club has been in charge of the annual library teas the past
25 years, which the club has hosted during National Library Week each April.
Programs have varied, but have generally included art displays and/or
demonstrations featuring the talents of local artists and craftsmen as well as
high school art students and the musical talents of the Grannies and the
Mammas, an all-female group which originated from a common interest in music
among women's club members.

The club has had numerous fund-raising projects on behalf of the library,
including spring rummage sales, lunches at rodeos, dinners, benefit card
parties and home talent plays. They also collected coins using a sheet from
spectators at basketball games. In the mid 1940s club members took turns
writing local news items for the newspaper, then the Beulah Independent. The
club was paid by the printed inch for their efforts and these proceeds went
into the library fund as well.

In 1964 and 1965 club members took turns hosting a children's story hour every
other week for pre-school children. A weekly story hour was again provided to
children during the summer of 1986.

In its early years, the Beulah Women's Club helped with local health clinics,
funded a nurse's scholarship during World War II, conducted a war bond drive,
helped with the first local March of Dimes and promoted "get-out-the vote" '
campaigns (especially for local improvement projects).

In 1950 the Women's Club distributed 15,000 trees donated by Zap Collieries for
the beautification of the area.

The club cooperated with other local organizations to buy a sterilizer for the
proposed Beulah Hospital. They later raised money to furnish a room in the
hospital also.

The Beulah Women's Club has promoted academics and liberal arts throughout its
58-year history. The promotion of creative writing among members years ago has
given way to the promotion of poetry and art contests for local high school
students. The talents of many local high school students have been recognized
in both areas at the state G.F.W.C. level.

In 1975 the Beulah Women's Club was one of ten clubs from G.F.W.C. District VII
which donated $1000 for a plaque at E'lan Gallery in Bismarck.

The club has provided partial scholarships for local high school students
attending the International Peace Gardens Music Camp for over 25 years.

Each spring the club sponsors an annual music program, featuring the music of
the Grannies and the Mammas as well as high school and community musical
talents. The programs have featured various kinds of music through the years.
The general pubic is also invited to attend this annual program and reception.

Two years ago the Women's Club also began partially sponsoring a local high
school student to the Hugh O'Brian Youth Foundation Leadership Seminar held each
summer.

The Beulah Women's Club sponsored the Junior-Senior School Spring formal annual
from 1948 to 1958. The formal, similar to today's junior-senior prom and
banquet, did not have the blessings of local school officials at the time and
was not held at the school, as is today's custom. Women's Club members also
prepared the banquet meal.

Another club tradition begun in the 1940s is the annual senior girls tea held
each May, honoring the girls in each graduating class.

Club members share many cherished memories of years of annual Christmas socials,
which always include husbands. One meeting each spring is the annual "night
out." That 'meeting' is solely entertainment - at a play, concert or dinner
theater. Members have particularly enjoyed the years when dinner theaters have
come to Beulah.

The program committees have attempted to coordinate some of the monthly
programs with state and national celebrations. Programs celebrated our nation's
Bicentennial in 1976, the history and restoration of the Statue of Liberty in
1986 (including a donation to the restoration fund) and the Bicentennial of the
U.S. Constitution and its founding fathers.

The Beulah Women's Club participated in the G.F.W.CX. Bicentennial Plate project
during the years 1973 to 1976. The series of four luncheon-size collectors
plates, selling at $10 each, celebrated the 200th birthday of the United States.

Club members now have the third of a series of four G.F.W.C. eight-inch
Centennial figurines depicting classic women's costumes from each
quarter-century of G.F.W.C. existence. The figurines, averaging about $28 each,
represent the 1940-1964 fashion era. Members received their first figurines in
1983, ordering one every two years thereafter. The fourth and final one will be
available in 1989.

The club has volunteered many hours to many community projects, the most
important of which is the library. There have been a few other projects which
have also given members satisfaction, joy and pride.

During the 1930s the club sponsored a two-day hobby show, which drew exhibitors
from all over Mercer County as well as some from Morton County.

The Beulah Women's Club was thrilled to be able to sponsor a "welcome home"
celebration for Miss North Dakota 1977, Kathryn Power, on June 17, 1977. She is
the daughter of clubwoman Phyllis and Dr. Al Power.

The club marked its 50th anniversary with a dinner and program at the New
Frontier Inn the evening of September 11, 1980. The brief program included
music by the Grannies and the Mammas along with the history of the club. The
fifteen active members were pleased to share the gala evening with ten former
members who were able to return.

The Beulah Women's Club participated in the G.FW.C./Prudential Walking Challenge
from November 1984 through March 1985. The walking project, chaired by Jeanne
Selby, received first place in North Dakota competition and third place in
national competition. The national recognition in June 1985 was accompanied by
a $500 check to the club.

The club was pleased to make arrangements for a concert presented by Kathryn
Power and her husband Carlos Sampedro on Sept. 12, 1985, at Zion Lutheran
Church. They were accompanied by Merilynn Liebelt at the piano. The concert and
reception were jointly co-sponsored by the G.P.G.A. Women and the Beulah
Women's Club.

Though the primary focus of the club has been of a local nature, the club has
also played an active role in the district and state organization. The Beulah
Women's Club has hosted numerous District VII annual fall conventions,
including the district's golden jubilee the fall of 1958. With reorganization
of district boundaries, the local club is now part of District VI. Members most
recently hosted the annual fall meeting in September 1987, providing tours of
the Great Plains visitor's center. Local club members made God's eyes as favors
for one of the banquets at the 1982 International G.F.W.C. Convention held in
Bismarck that June. Most of the members were able to attend the state night
banquet and program.

Several district and state officers have come from the Beulah Women's Club. R.J.
Thelander and Helen Morman have served as district presidents, Agnes Herman
served as district secretary, and Marion Moore and Bernice Dally served as
district historians. Rags Thelander and Mary Held served as state directors.
Ruth Solberg was installed as state president in May 1974.

Current club members include Della Benz, Carole Bjerke, Deanna Knudson,
Merilynn Liebelt, Helen Maxson, Helen Morman, Phyllis Power, Myrtle Sailer,
Marianne Sayler, Suzan Schock, Althea Siefert, JeAnne Selby, Inez Sommer and
Angie Thelander. Karina Jenssen Singer is an associate member.

History of Beulah Women of Today

The Beulah Women of Today organization is a community group that emphasizes
community involvement, training in leadership and civic consciousness and an
interest and participation in the state and national organizations.

The organization was first chartered in 1966 and the name of the chapter was the
Mrs. Jaycees. At that time, the organization was affiliated with the Beulah
Jaycees, and the state and national organizations were also affiliated with
their Jaycee counterparts. An age limit of 18-36 years applied to both the
Jaycee and Mrs. Jaycee organizations. In 1977, the name of the state and local
organization was changed to Jayceettes, and this name was used until 1983, when
the North Dakota Jayceettes voted to change the name of their organization to
the North Dakota Jaycee Women, a change they hoped would project a professional
image and also reflect their Jaycee auxiliary status.

Then, in 1985, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that women could join the previously
all-male Jaycees, a decision that was going to change forever the nature of both
organizations.

Some women did join the Jaycees, and some Jaycee Women chapters in North Dakota
and other states chose to merge with the Jaycee organizations in their
communities. But the majority of the women wanted their own organization,
without the auxiliary status. It followed naturally that, in May of 1985, the
Jaycee Women organization in North Dakota voted to disaffiliate completely with
the Jaycees and form a new organization, called the North Dakota Women of Today.

Even though all of these name changes have occasionally made it difficult for
the group to be recognized, the basic thrust of the community organization has
remained the same since its original charter in 1966. Community projects such
as blood drives, well-child clinic, businessmen's appreciation day, Mercer
County fair kiddie parade and fair meal, faculty welcome, Halloween carnival,
Christmas angel tree, and style show are among the many service projects
completed by the chapter each year. Many of the community projects are
completed on an annual basis and have become anticipated by community members.

The leadership training emphasized by the organization takes its emphasis from
courses available to its members, such as leadership training, communications,
finances, personal enrichment, stress, women's issues, and spiritual enrichment,
which provide opportunities for members to grow personally as they serve their
community.

Throughout the years, the organization now known as the Beulah Women of Today
has had a distinguished history. The group has been fortunate to have several
local presidents who have been recognized as outstanding local presidents by
the North Dakota state organization, and the chapter has won numerous awards
for projects in the community service and individual development areas. The
Beulah organization has also had several local members who have been elected to
the position of president of the North Dakota organization. Carrie Hafner
served as president of the Mrs. Jaycees in 1973-74, and Doreen Schilke served
as president of the North Dakota Women of Today in 1986-87. Diana Grosz was
appointed to the position of national coordinator of Jaycee Auxiliaries in
1972-73, a position which was considered to be the equivalent of the first
national president of the women's organization. In addition, many of the local
members have served the North Dakota organization in the state officer capacity.

One of the changes brought about throughout the years was the elimination of the
18-36 years as an age requirement for members, thus allowing the group more
flexibility in obtaining interested members. Because of the interest and
dedication of the chapter members and officers, and the support of the Beulah
business community, the organization continues to be an active and productive
part of the city of Beulah.

        gavel from 1987 President Joe Friedlander.

The Mercer County Extension Service

The mission of the NDSU Extension Service in Mercer County is to be a part of a
nationwide university-based educational resource dedicated to improving people's
lives. The Extension Service has had a big impact on the area by bringing new
ideas and methods to homes and communities. It offers new challenges and it can
easily be said that much of the progress made in agriculture within Mercer
County was motivated by the county agent and his associates.

Grover C. Poe was the first agricultural agent in this county and his office
was located in Beulah. His services were secured through the efforts of the
Beulah Commercial Club after they sponsored petitions to secure the services of
an agent.

Poe's program emphasized diversified farming and his motto, "Hogs and Hominy,
Cows and Clover," was a well-known theme in the area at the time. He was county
extension agent from June 1920 - December 1924, and from February 1924 -
September 1926.

The Federal Farms Programs started in 1933 and during that year Omar K. Cline
was appointed the agent. His job consisted of organizing and administering the
federal farm programs from his office in Stanton. He served from 1933-1935.

When Cline resigned, Robert J. Montgomery was appointed to work in the office
and he did a large amount of work in organizing the 4-H clubs and homemakers
clubs that remain an active part of community structure. Montgomery served the
county from October 1935 - August 1937.

When Montgomery resigned his position, Donald R. Groom was appointed county
agent, until 1940, when Melvin J. Berdahl became the agricultural agent.

Berdahl was very active with 4-H clubs and homemakers clubs and he was also
charged with the responsibility of many of the War Emergency committees. When
Berdahl, a reserve officer, was ordered to active duty, he was replaced by
Harold C. Schultz. During Berdahl's tenure the Mercer County office was moved
from Stanton to Beulah. Schultz also entered the service and was replaced by
Lawrence Restemeyer, who was the agent from 1942-1944.

The Extension office was without an agent until December 1946, when Wayne W.
Owens assumed the position. His work with the office centered around
reorganizing the 4-H and homemakers clubs and he was also responsible for the
initial work of Soil Conservation Districts and rural electrification.

Thomas Martindale took over the position in 1949 and stayed until 1954; he was
the first agent who stayed long enough to become acquainted with the county and
its needs. He completed the post-war adjustment work, dealing with REA and soil
conservation districts and did much educational work for the rural telephone
service. Martindale was also responsible for completing much of the initial
work in the establishment of the Fort Clark Irrigation District.

H.R. "Mac" McKenzie was appointed agent in 1954 and served until his death. Mac
was a strong advocate of diversified agriculture and he continually encouraged
livestock programs, especially livestock feeding. Under Mac's direction, many
livestock quality programs such as the Dairy Herd Improvement Association,
artificial insemination, beef performance testing and calfhood vaccination
programs were evident and flourishing.

The next county agent was Allen J. Schmidt, who served until 1982. He built a
strong 4-H Junior Leaders' Program with a special emphasis on the abandoned
vehicle project. Private applicator pesticide certification, landscaping and
livestock performance testing were also promoted by this agent. Schmidt also
promoted AGNET, the agricultural computer network designed to assist a wide
variety of users in three general areas of applications: problem solving,
information sharing and communication.

David Ramsey was employed as county agent from November 1982 - August 1987.
During this time the extension office was moved from the basement of the Bank of
Beulah to the Spier Building next to the Post office in 1984. During the fall
of 1986, the office moved to its current home in the Hillside office Complex
along Highway 49.

Amy Sorlein was employed as county home economist July 1, 1984. Her position is
split between Mercer and Oliver counties and her work brings expertise in
consumer skills, family strengths, financial education, nutrition, diet and
health and leadership in educational programs, 4-H and homemaker projects.

Clifford N. Moine was employed as county agent Jan. 1, 1988 and serves now.

Each Extension office has been equipped with a computer, video recorder and
television in keeping with the electronic age. Many of the club programs and
study topics have been transferred to videotape, allowing more accessibility to
the services of the Mercer County Extension office.

        3rd Annual Dakota Classics Show and Shine at Beulah, 1986.

Dakota Classics

Dakota Classics was formed in 1983 as the first classic car chapter in North
Dakota. The club is 100 percent affiliated with the International Classic
Chevrolet Club. This Mercer County-based group allows only 1955-56-57 Chevrolet
owners as members. Members come from a radius of 150 miles. Until 1986 it was
the only club of its kind in the state. Keeping the classic cars, music, dress
and the fun of the 50s alive is its purpose.

The group meets monthly. Three or four times a year members drive their cars
through the state's smaller towns in parade fashion to let others relive the
times and reminisce about the classic cars. The Bismarck Rocking 50's Cafe has
been one such destination. The poker run is another favorite outing. Each
driver draws a card at each of five stops. At the end of the drive, the best
poker hand wins the pot.

Dakota Classics sponsors an annual Show and Shine event in Beulah. It is
usually held in conjunction with the Mercer County Fair. The Chevrolets have
become a favorite feature of the fair parade as well.

officers are: Don Retterath, president; Deen Brecht, vice president; Darwin
Roeser, secretary and Darlene Brecht, treasurer.

4-H Clubs

4-H provides learning experiences that enable youth, with the assistance of
their parents, interested adults and other 4-H members, to grow personally as
they develop skills for living and for responsible citizenship. Membership is
open to all youth from ages 8-19.

The "learning by doing" philosophy of 4-H emphasizes the importance of involving
members in the learning process. What people hear, they may doubt; what people
see, they may possibly doubt, but what people do, they cannot doubt.

The mission of 4-H is to assist youth in acquiring knowledge, developing life
skills and forming attitudes that will help them to become self-directing,
productive and contributing members of society.

There are currently 10 4-H clubs in Mercer County with three in the Beulah area;
Knife River 4-H, club leaders Leland Erickson, Jan Gunsch and Lou Ella Smith;
Riverside 4-H, club leaders Mark Hafner, Virginia Hafner and Wayne Boeshans; and
Galloping Ghosts, club leaders Berna Ost and Joyce Gazur.

With over 1,500 projects to choose from, youth can learn about rocketry or
forestry, nutrition or clothing, pets or livestock, safety or photography.

Die Deutsche Stammhalter Chapter of the Germans from Russia Heritage Society

Beulah has held a Germans from Russia music day since in the 1960s. It started
from a love for German music and a start in preserving our heritage.

The time was right as, on Jan. 9, 1971, an organization was formed in Bismarck
for just that purpose. It was called North Dakota Heritage Society of Germans
from Russia. On June 20, 1975, 17 people met at Beulah city hall to become a
chapter of that organization. A five-member board of directors was elected with
Curtis Schulz as president, Albert Hoffman as vice president, and Gert Buscher
as secretary. Serving as directors were Sam Miller and Ed Kittler. Kathy Helm
was appointed treasurer. All were from Beulah.

The name the group became known by was the Beulah Chapter, In 1979, NDHSGR
underwent a name change to Germans from Russia Heritage Society as they became
an international organization with chapters in Canada, Montana, North Dakota and
South Dakota. On March 18, 1984, the Beulah Chapter adopted the name, "Die
Deutsche Stammhalter," which means, "the German family keeper." The chapter
colors are black and white.

        Germans from Russia.

On June 4, 1988, Die Deutsche Stammhalter Chapter hosted its 18th Annual
Musikfest, which has been held the first Saturday in June at the old middle
school for years. Record attendance was more than 800 people in 1986 for the
afternoon and evening programs. Oct. 12, 1984, the group began hosting a dinner
called a "Deutsche Schmeckfest," featuring only food of our German-Russian
ancestry, in conjunction with the Beulah businesses' Oktoberfest. In 1984 we
served about 350 people and in 1987 we served about 200 people. In December
1985 we started a German Advent Church Service which was held in the Immanuel
Baptist Church, in 1986 in United Methodist Church and in 1987 in the Zion
Lutheran Church. These church services have been non-denominational and have
been well attended.

The local chapter has been well represented on the international GRHS board of
directors with Herb Messmer, Curtis Schulz and Vi Schielke, all of Beulah,
currently serving on the board. Curtis Schulz has just finished serving three
years as GRHS president. Currently we have about 50 members from all over
Mercer County and members in Dunn and Oliver counties. Our board of directors
locally as of July 1, 1988, are president Willie Adolf, Beulah; vice president
Walter Morast, Zap; secretary Carole Kessler, Stanton; treasurer Mel Miller,
Golden Valley. Directors are Edna Galster, Hazen; Elmer Weisz, Dodge; and Leo
Wiedrich, Zap.

Grannies and the Mammas

This odd title was assigned by one of the original members of this group of
"singing ladies." Merilynn Liebelt and Phyllis Power, both music majors at the
University of North Dakota, decided in 1963 to start a quartet, with Phyllis as
first soprano, Merilynn as second soprano, Linda Barta as first alto and Gladys
Misslin as second alto.

The debut for this group was Beulah's Golden Jubilee program, and they've sung
at various gatherings including talent shows since then.

In time the number of singers grew to nine, then settled to six, which still
include Merilynn and Phyllis, Susan Schock, Jill Galloway, Jan Schulz and
Deanna Knudson. Each year the group plans a public music program under the
auspices of the Beulah Woman's Club, with such widely varying themes as opera,
folk music, or patriotic music.

The Northern Star Homemakers Club

The Northern Star Homemakers Club was organized in May of 1952 north of Beulah.
Tom Martindale, County Extension Agent, assisted in organizing the club.

The club meets the first Monday of each month. Social activities include an
annual family picnic and a Christmas banquet with exchange of gifts.

The present members are: Viola Boeckel, president; Rachel Mosbrucker, vice-
president; Erma Voegele, secretary; Eleanor Beckel treasurer; Irene Rhode and
Norma Sailer, program chairman. Selma Ost and Linda Voegele are the greetings
senders.

The charter members are Erma Voegele and Norma Sailer.

The Pan Handlers Club

The Pan Handlers Homemakers Club was organized Feb. 3, 1966, with membership
set at 13.

The first officers elected were Mrs. Duane (LaVaun) Johnson*, president; Mrs.
Jack (Donna) Thielman*, vice president; Mrs. James (Joan) Schumaier*,
secretary; and Mrs. Ernest (Marlys) Mosbrucker*, treasurer.

Other members were Mrs. James (Leeta) Aanderud; Mrs. Ray (Sandi) Binder; Mrs.
Duane (Donna) Hartwig*, Mrs. Helmuth (Helen) Hilz*, Mrs. Norman (Kathy) Kessler;
Mrs. Donald (Margaret) Kuch*, Mrs. Robert (Rosemary) Renke; Mrs. Gordon (JoAnn)
Schmidt and Mrs. Albert (Adeilne) Aanderud*.

Other members throughout the club's history were Mrs. Ruben (Eunice) Sackman,
Mrs. Roy (Loretta) Neuberger, Mrs. Delmar (Audrey) Erickson, Mrs. Bernard
(Eileen) Keller and Barbara Kato. Present members are Mrs. Gary (Marge) Murray,
Mrs. Jerome (Dee) Koppi, Mrs. Glen (Marlene) Sasse and Mrs. Marvin (Sally)
Stiefel.

We have secret sisters with whom we exchange birthday, anniversary and Christmas
gifts. At our annual Christmas party our husbands are also included in the gift
exchange.

At each meeting we have a door prize. Members who have had a 25th wedding
anniversary are presented with a gift from the group.

Some of the club's projects have been adopting a foster child from Formosa,
fleischkuechle sales, bake sales, quilt raffle, and selling helium balloons at
the County Fair.

Donations were made to All Faiths Chapel in Grafton, School for the Deaf,
swimming pool, county servicemen in Viet Nam, school speaker system, civic
center, high school band uniforms, Mercer County ambulance fund, Beulah
Community Nursing Home, and Toys for Tots and Food for Families.

From February, 1970, to September, 1981, we had a traveling gypsy basket. At
each meeting a name was drawn and that person brought a basket filled with baked
goodies to the next meeting.

Since April, 1980, the group has not been affiliated with the Mercer County
Homemakers Council. Now each hostess plans a lesson or project for the meeting.

Since January, 1985, each member has paid $1 for roll call at each meeting. At
the end of the year we donate this money to a charity.

When a member has a wedding or anniversary in the immediate family, we help
each other by baking bars and preparing and  serving lunch.

Beulah Parks and Recreation Department

The Beulah Parks and Recreation Department is involved with a number of
activities for both young and old. For the youngsters, the activities range
from the baseball programs, which include Pee Wee, Midget and Babe Ruth teams,
to tennis and golf lessons. There is also a girls' softball program. These
teams play intra-city teams and also have a schedule of games with surrounding
towns. For the older youth there is an American Legion team. There is also a
gymnastics club in Beulah for interested youngsters, and it expects to field a
team for competition soon.

        The Beulah Park Board, L-R, parks and recreation director Randy Pachl,
        park board secretary Bev Sullivan, Gary Younker, Kelly Heihn, Ken
        Ziman, Bill Keller, Bill Misslin.

Beulah also has a soccer league, a parent-run organization which teaches the
sport of soccer, which is somewhat new to this area. Again the kids are
involved with intramural play with some of the older kids playing teams from
outside the area.

On the adult side of recreation, there is also a variety of programs. There are
both men's and women's softball leagues. These programs are very popular and
well supported in Beulah. The city of Beulah is also well represented by the
teams through their tournament accomplishments.

Other programs offered during the summer are horseshoe leagues, scuba diving
classes and aerobics classes.

In the winter there are adult co-ed volleyball and men's basketball leagues.
Both are very popular activities. The men's basketball league also has
participants in the state amateur tournament.

The Royal Neighbors of America

The Royal Neighbors of America, a fraternal life insurance society, is the
oldest organization in Beulah.

Beulah West Camp #8324 was issued a charter June 22, 1917, and numbered 24
charter members. In the formative years, monthly meetings were held at the Palm
Theatre, Grange Hall, and the Legion hall. Along with the family protection,
pioneer members considered "lodges" a social outlet, and were the major
proponents for promoting community activities.

Seven decades later, Beulah West Camp retains its charter, with 90 adult and
juvenile members, plus 79 paid-up members. A small group of active members,
singly and in groups, continue the principles of fraternalism, locally and
nationally, as exemplified by the doctrines of the National Society.

Locally, the society annually donates to charitable causes. A relief committee
remembers the sick and bereaved, and visits shut-ins. Each year on Memorial Day,
flags are placed on graves of deceased RNA members. Camp activities are stages
to promote interest and local involvement.

Support of several national services includes the RNA Fraternal scholarship
program, the Royal Neighbor National Home for the Aged, and Help to Hear and
Dogs for the Deaf programs.

        Royal Neighbors of America officers. Back row: Catherine Scherbinske,
        Ruth Johnson, Marguerite Herman. Front row: Mildred McKenzie, Lois
        Stewart, Emma Easton. Not pictured: Lena Heihn.

Throughout its history, Beulah West Camp has achieved a distinctive record of
service. Current officers are Catherine Scherbinske who has served as recorder
since 1952, Lois Stewart who has served as treasurer since 1957; Marguerite
Herman who has served as oracle and vice oracle many years; Emma Easton and
Lena Heihn who have held various offices; and Mildred McKenzie, who has held
office as well as being a district deputy since 1974.

Beulah West Camp is a member of Logan District 8 in North Dakota and
representatives attend annual district meetings and the quadrennial state
meetings.

Sakakawea Art Association

The history of Sakakawea Art Association goes back to the late 1960s when a
group of people, interested in learning to paint, got together and asked Bob
Watts, an artist from Dickinson, to come to Beulah and teach an oil painting
class. Many men and women in Beulah became interested in painting through these
workshops. Some of the students continued to take art classes from many other
art teachers. These were the people who started the Sakakawea Art Association.

The art association reorganized in 1982. They met at the Beulah Public Library.
There were about a dozen people present at the meeting which Mrs. C.A. (Rags)
Thelander chaired. Three members of the Hazen Art Association attended.
Discussion was held regarding combining the two clubs. The Hazen delegates
decided not to merge with the Beulah group.

Sakakawea Art Association was chosen as the name for the club. Gert Smith was
elected president, Carol Tomroy, vice president, and Rags Thelander secretary-
treasurer. Dues were set at $5 per year, and the year ran from April 1-March 31.
New members joined in 1982 and 1983. The members voted to have an annual
outdoor art and craft festival at the Riverside Park in Beulah, co-sponsored by
the Beulah Park Board.

One of the art association projects was to sponsor the art exhibit at the
county fair. Mrs. Thelander chaired this committee until 1987. In 1987 Mrs.
Kenneth (Elaine) Reich chaired the committee. Interested art members had
sponsored this exhibit since the Mercer County Fair began having an art
exhibit. At one time the art association tried to find a trailer suitable to
house the art exhibit.

The members gave up the idea due to the lack of funds. The art exhibit at the
fair has been held in various buildings on the fair grounds as well as in the
Mercer County Historical Building.

In 1983 Leonard Thomas was elected president of the association and Carol Tomroy
was re-elected vice president and Rags Thelander continued as
secretary-treasurer.

The group also held its first art and craft festival in 1983. It contacted
people from the surrounding area who were interested in displaying and selling
their arts and crafts and charged a $5 registration fee for the use of a table.

Berna Ost, an artist from Almont, ND, demonstrated oil painting throughout the
day. The Barber Shop Quartet entertained with song, and Eva Marie Schaffer's
ballet students delighted the audience with their dancing. The chuck wagon from
the Kozy Korner Kafe furnished refreshments. The public enjoyed the festival
and encouraged the club to continue it as a yearly event.

In 1984 Glenda Newton was elected president, Elaine Reich, vice president, and
Rags Thelander was again elected secretary-treasurer.

The second outdoor art and craft festival was held on June 23, 1984, and in 1985
due to rain the festival was held in the Beulah grade school. The attendance in
1985 was very poor so the club voted to discontinue it.

Throughout the art association's existence, the art members have continued to
take workshops and lessons from art teachers. Many of their pictures and
photographs have won ribbons at art shows and county fairs, and have been
chosen for display at business places in Bismarck, Mandan and surrounding
towns. Most of the artists paint for their own enjoyment, and being able to
sell their paintings and photographs gives them encouragement to continue their
hobby.

In 1987 the Sakakawea Art Association decided to put out a Beulah Centennial
Calendar. This calendar consisted of paintings and photographs of old buildings
and events of the past.

        Trophy Takers Salmon Club - Joan Chadborn.

Trophy Takers Salmon Club

The Trophy Takers Salmon Club began as a group of six in October, 1984.
Currently the group has more than 80 members. Since inception, the club has
strived to increase the knowledge of salmon fishing in North Dakota, improve
facilities on Lake Sakakawea and contribute to the expansion of the trout and
salmon fishery on the Missouri River system.

Three successful Black Jaw Salmon Derbies in 1985, 1986 and 1987 have provided
funding for marina lighting and ramp improvements at Lake Sakakawea State Park
and completely financed the feeding of 436,000 salmon smolts to be planted over
a two-year period in the lake. In addition, monies generated by the club have
been used to improve the facilities at Hazen Bay, Beulah Bay and Beaver Bay.

The salmon are raised directly in Lake Sakakawea in a cage system. In 1986,
116,000 salmon were raised to smolt size, and in 1987, with the help of the
Trophy Takers, the operation tripled to 320,000 fish. The Trophy Takers
supplied $1,500 for high-quality food pellets to feed the fish.

The Trophy Takers derbies are so successful they result in more than 100 percent
participant payback, produced a registered catch of more than 2,000 salmon, and
provide excellent low-cost entertainment for nearly 2,500 fishermen from 14
states. Proceeds from additional annual derbies will be allocated to other
worthy projects.

The current officers are: Mike Peterson, president; Tony Johnson, vice
president; Bob Stark, treasurer; Bill Roach, secretary and Ron Crowley,
membership.

The Trophy Takers Salmon Club is a non-profit organization of amateur fishermen
whose purpose is to promote salmon fishing on Lake Sakakawea and to exchange
information about fishing patterns and techniques. The club meets monthly and
new members and visitors are always welcome.

VFW Post 7759 and Auxiliary

The Herman Schmidt Post #7759 was organized by Otto Kasper, Gottlieb Wiedrich
and Delmar Grishkowsky and officially chartered May 27, 1946, with 51 charter
members. It was named in memory of Herman Schmidt who was killed in action in
the Philippine Islands on Dec. 20, 1941.

Of the current membership of 187, the following are charter members: Roger
Endreson, ElRoy Herman, Walter Johnson, Otto Kasper, Edwin Krieger, Leonard
Krausz, Albert Pischel, Andrew Sailer, Henry Schmidt, Albert Wallender, Henry
Winkler and Gottleib Wiedrich. Included in the membership are 50 lifetime
members.

During the early years the meetings were held at various places in Beulah. In
1972, a dream came true and the new club house was constructed on land
purchased from the county. The building committee was Ray Galster, chairman;
Allen Simenson; Emil Frank; Joe Muhlhauser; Leonard Krausz and Ervin Eisenbeis
of the Post and Thelma Hyttinen, Helen Ondrasek and Naomi Unruh of the
Auxiliary and non-members. After many months of hard work and cooperation by
both men and women, our club house was ready for our first meeting March 6,
1973, under the leadership of Allen Simenson, commander, and Freda Kriege
Auxiliary president. Open house was held May 20, 1973.

For the next few years, much voluntary work by active members and non-members
made it possible for this veterans organization to hold a mortgage-burning
ceremony in May, 1979.

The Auxiliary to the Veterans of Foreign Wars, Post #7759 was officially
chartered June 13, 1950, with 27 charter members. Of the current 167
membership, the following are charter members: Evelyn Eisenbeis, Minnie
Endreson, Thelma Hyttinen, Alma Kasper, Freda Krieger, Esther Wallender, Olga
Weiss, Agnes Wiedrich, and Frieda Wiedrich.

        VFW Auxiliary Standing: Amanda Bauer, Marian Brecht, Helen Ondrasek,
        Janet Morast. Seated: Helen Renner, Irene Loeffelbein, Evelyn
        Eisenbeis.

During the history of both the Post and Auxiliary, several members held local,
district, state and national offices. Those holding district #1 commander
positions are Otto Kasper, Emil Frank, Allen Simenson, Ray Galster and Lynn
Amsden. Amsden also served as state commander 1967-68.

Auxiliary member Thelma Hyttinen was North Dakota State Auxiliary president in
1975-76 and national councilwoman in 1982-83.

Otto Kasper is currently Mercer County Service officer, a post he has held for
nine years.

The VFW Auxiliary has two members who are Gold Star Mothers, having lost sons in
active duty: Rose Wolf, whose son, Mike Wolf, Jr., was killed in the Vietnam
War on Sept. 10, 1967, and Rose Welk.

Most activities are held jointly with Post and Auxiliary, such as the Christmas
Cheer baskets which are filled with fruit and distributed for Christmas to the
lonely and shut-ins in Golden Valley, Zap and Beulah by our own Santas and
helpers.

The Auxiliary members make homemade cookies and candies and mail to all service
men and women from Mercer County who are stationed overseas and cannot be home
with their families at Christmas time.

Our Post and Auxiliary hold the annual Memorial Day Services at the Beulah
cemetery and have a potluck dinner following the services at the club house,
which is open to the public.

Post members hold military funeral services when requested by a veteran's
family.

An annual pancake and sausage supper is held at the club house every Veterans
Day in November. It is open to the public.

Bingo was started in 1974 and is held Thursday evenings with gambling proceeds
donated to community activities in Mercer County, including local schools,
senior citizens, parks, nursing home, ambulance, Boy Scouts and Girl Scouts.

The VFW sponsors Girl Scouts Voice of Democracy in schools as well as furnishing
many American flags in the community. American flags and North Dakota state
flags have been furnished for the schools in Golden Valley, Zap and all three
schools in Beulah. Flag etiquette books and flag demonstrations have been given
to the schools upon request. The flags and holders displayed at the Beulah
cemetery on patriotic days were donated by the VFW Post to the Lions Club.
Small American flags are placed on veterans' graves each year on Memorial Day.

The Post and Auxiliary have received many awards from the North Dakota State
Department for membership and projects, including the annual special fund
raising project for Cancer Aid and Research.

The 1988-89 officers from Post #7759 are: Ed Siegel, commander; Greg Foss,
senior vice commander; John Mohl, Jr., vice commander; and Gus Morlock,
quartermaster.

The 1988-89 Auxiliary officers are: Helen Ondrasek, president; Evelyn Eisenbeis,
senior vice president; Irene Loeffelbein, junior vice president; Janet Morast,
secretary; and Ellen Renner, treasurer.

Monthly meetings are held the first Tuesday for Post and Auxiliary members at
the club house.

This history is dedicated in memory to all our departed comrades and sisters of
VFW Post #7759 and Auxiliary.

                And the people . . .

Beltram and Halda Aandelud

Beltram married Halda Mindt on May 1, 1932, at Beulah. They lived in Beulah
until 1944 when they moved to the strip mine camp. In 1950 they moved back to
Beulah where they lived until their deaths.

They were active members of Zion Lutheran Church. They had six children:
Richard, Albert, Mrs. Donald (Margaret) Kuch, Jim, Mrs. Orville (Janet) Miller
and Mrs. Bill (Glenda) Misslin, deceased.

Beltram was born on March 11, 1907, at Hamberg, ND to August and Barbara
Aanderud. He had five brothers and three sisters. Beltram graduated from Maddock
High School and attended business college in Fargo. He moved to Zap in 1930
where he was employed at a bank and later employed at a bank in Beulah. When
the bank closed in 1938 Beltram or "Andy," as he was known, began working for
Dakota Collieries between Zap and Beulah as the office manager. When the mine
was sold to North American Coal, Andy continued working until his retirement
(due to ill health) in 1963.

The family lived at the strip mine camp until 1950 when Ralph Richardson decided
to close down the camp and the Aanderud family moved to Beulah.

Beltram "Andy" was city treasurer for many years and also served as treasurer
for the Beulah School District. He also served as scout leader, taught Sunday
school and sang in the church choir. He was a member of the Zion Lutheran
Church, church council, Lutheran Brotherhood, and Lions Club.

A victim of MS for 16 years, he died at Hazen Memorial Hospital on March 8,
1967.

Halda was born on May 16, 1910, at Bluegrass, ND to Jacob and Margaret Schwagler
Mindt. She attended the Beulah School and was a lifelong member of Zion Lutheran
Church. She had three sisters and two brothers: Mrs. Ralph (Arletta) Berkley,
Eva Harper Duppong, deceased, Mrs. Julius (Alma) Bitterman, deceased, Edmond
"Sonny" and William "Babe," both deceased.

Halda belonged to various homemakers clubs and was a charter member of the
Mission Circle at Zion. She died at home on Oct. 19, 1983. She was a diabetic
for many years but never lost her faith.

Alan and Janice Abbey

Alan L. Abbey, son of Oran and Alice (Herman) Abbey, was born Sept. 25, 1941.

Oran Abbey was killed in 1943 in an automobile accident, widowing Alice with
nine children, of whom Alan was the youngest.

The family remained on the farm three miles south of Beulah until 1947, at which
time they moved into Beulah.

Alan went through school in Beulah, worked locally, and traveled with
construction until he was employed with Knife River Coal Mining Co. in 1963.

On April 25, 1964, he married Janice Welk at St. Joseph's Catholic Church in
Beulah. Jan is the daughter of the late David Welk and Pearl (Bowers) Welk.

Mrs. Welk resides in Mandan, which is where they made their home in 1964 when
Dave retired from the U.S. Army and started working for the state purchasing
department in Bismarck.

Even though Dave was an Army career man, the family, including one son, Jerry,
spent a lot of time in North Dakota. David was twice stationed at Fort Lincoln
near Bismarck. They also lived at Battle Creek, Mich. Jan graduated from high
school in Highland Park, Ill., while David was stationed there at Fort Sheridan.

While Dave was in Korea, and again when he was in Germany, Pearl and the
children resided in Beulah.

Jan was employed at the Hazen Memorial Hospital soon after her graduation and
was working at the MDU office in Beulah when she and Alan married.

Jan's brother, Jerry, was killed in an automobile accident in October, 1982.
His two sons, Jason and Jamie, live with their mother in Glendive, Mont.

David passed away in June, 1985.

Alan remained with Knife River Coal Mining Company at Beulah until 1974, at
which time he was transferred to their Gascoyne Mine near Scranton, N.D. In
1980 he returned to Beulah where he is now mine superintendent for Knife River
Coal.

Alan's mother, Alice, passed away in the spring of 1982.

Alan and Jan were blessed with three children: Alana Marie, who is attending
Moorhead State University; Gregory Oran, serving with the United States Army,
2nd Infantry Division, Camp Essayons, Hijongbu, Korea; and Alicia Pearl, at
home.

Marvin and Debra Aberle

Marvin B. Aberle, an auto mechanic, was born on Sept. 23, 1955, to Joseph and
Rose Aberle in Linton, N.D. Joseph and Rose still live in Linton.

Debra (Debbie) E. Schlosser, housewife, homemaker, and babysitter, was born on
March 19, 1957, to Joseph and Neldamae Schlosser in Jamestown. Joseph and
Neldamae presently reside in Edgeley, N.D.

Marvin and Debra have four children: Tonya Jean, born July 27, 1977, in Oakes,
N.D.; Blaise Joseph, born Nov. 17, 1978, in Hazen; Aaron Lee, born Dec. 9, 1980,
in Hazen; and Amanda Dawn, born June 28, 1982, in Hazen.

"Marvin was transferred to the Farmer's Union Oil Company as foreman," writes
Debra, "where he wanted to advance further, so he went into his own business.
When he had the opportunity to sell out, he did so, and is now self-employed at
Mann's Automotive.

"Before moving to Beulah, we moved around a lot. We started in North Carolina,
where Debra was in the Marine Corps. We then moved to Oakes, N.D., where Marvin
worked for a farmer. Then it was on to Edgeley, N.D., where Marvin worked for
the Farmer's Union Oil. Finally, we came to Beulah.

"We first came to Beulah during the height of the energy boom. When we moved
into the Dana Trailer Court, in March 1987, we were the first trailer on the
upper level. By August, the whole court was filled. We thought, 'Boy, Beulah is
really going now! "

" We noticed right away the effect the boom was having on the older people, the
ones who had lived their lives here and for whom all the changes were making
life foreign and uncomfortable. There were so many strangers here, people who
only came for the jobs and were not interested in investing themselves in the
community. Once it had been a place where everybody knew everybody. Because of
all the strangers, I seemed to be aware of a lot of 'German talk' whispered
under the breath, a way to stay private in all this explosion of people.

"Now that's not so frequent any more since the lifestyle here has gone back to a
steadier pace.

"We have become involved in a number of community activities. Marvin is a member
of the Beulah Lions Club and is a past president. He was involved in soccer as a
coach and is now the financial secretary in the Knights of Columbus.

"Debra is a member and president of the Beulah Lioness Club. She is also
president of Merry Mrs. Homemakers, is involved in Soccer Club, and is a den
leader for the Cub Scouts."

        Joel and Kathy Allen. L to R: Dusty, Kathy, Joel, Ben.

Joel and Kathy Allen

Where is Beulah, North Dakota? That was my first question to husband Joel when
he was being transferred there.

I wasn't sure what I had gotten myself into that June day in 1975. We arrived in
Beulah with most of our worldly possessions and one dog in the back of a 1972
Ford pick-up.

Being my first time away from home and entering this German-flavored community,
I figured I'd better put aside my Irish heritage. Joel, on the other hand,
being of German descent, fit right in, although to this day he still goes to
wieners and sauerkraut day alone. There is a limit as to what I will try.

We settled ourselves in. We joined a bowling league and met some new faces.

On Jan. 18, 1976, our first little bundle of joy was born. We named him Dustin
Joel. Dusty, as we so fondly call him, is presently a sixth grader at the
Beulah Middle School. He enjoys soccer and football. His favorite pastime is
drawing.

On April 20, 1978, shortly after a flood in Beulah, our second little bundle of
joy arrived. Benjamin Joseph, affectionately referred to as Ben, enjoys all
sports and loves to be outside working and playing. He is presently a fourth
grader at the Beulah Elementary School. He enjoys collecting toy guns.

Joel has worked for Knife River Coal Mining Company for 13 years here in Beulah
and six months in Savage, Mont. He is presently the supervisor in charge of
pumps and blasting. For the previous six years his responsibility had been the
draglines.

Joel George Allen, named for his two grandfathers, is a home-grown North Dakota
boy. Born in Williston on Jan. 11, 1947, to Harvey and Louella (Hickel) Allen,
he is the oldest of eight children. He was raised on a farm 13 miles south of
Ray, N.D. He went to a one-room country school until the end of the eighth
grade. He then attended and graduated from Ray High School in 1965.

Joel is a 1969 graduate of Minot State University, with a double major in
physical education and mathematics. He taught school for two and a half years
in Savage and Baker, Mont. He farmed for a while and also worked on a
construction crew.

Joel married Kathleen Marie (Reed) on Aug. 31, 1974, at St. Michael's Catholic
Church in Savage, Mont. Our wedding was the first one held in that little
mission church in 40 years.

Joel now enjoys bowling, fishing and spending time with his kids. He is a
member of the St. Joseph Catholic Church, where he serves as a lector. He also
belongs to the Knights of Columbus and is a member of the Beulah Eagles Club.

I was born in Seattle, Wash., on June 10, 1957, to Joseph and Diane (White)
Reed. I am the fourth child in a litter of six. We moved a lot while I was
growing up. We lived in Lakeview, Ore., Frazee, Minn., Bellevue, Wash., and
Savage, Mont. I attended my last two years of high school in Savage, where I
graduated in 1975 in a class of 16.

When we moved to Beulah almost 13 years ago, I never dreamed the wheatfields
north of town would be covered with houses. Joel and I have seen a lot of
changes in Beulah in the few short years we have lived here.

I also never dreamed I would ever get so involved in a community. I enjoy
bowling in two different leagues, one of which I am the president. I am a
member of the Chamber of Commerce and a member of the Mercer County ambulance
squad. In 1982, I started my own cleaning business, Splash and Mop Kleaners,
and have had a contract with Knife River Coal Mining Company since I began. I
am also spearheading the project of getting this 75th anniversary book
together. So if you are reading this, all the others that worked on the jubilee
book and I must have been successful.

        Mr. and Mrs. Reinhold Allmendinger and family

Reinhold and Marthela Allmendinger

Reinhold and Marthela (Bopple) were both born in Odessa, Russia. They were
married in 1906 and came to the United States in 1907. Their first home was in
Tripp, S.D. In August, 1907, they moved to Golden Valley. They later moved to a
farm south of Dodge. They had six children: Ida, Emma, Edward, William, Otto,
and Irene.

Reinhold and Marthela moved to Bismarck in 1944. She worked at MedCenter One
and Reinhold worked at the Nelson trading post until his death in June 1959.
Marthela spent her last years at the Baptist Home until her death in 1979.

Ida Allmendinger married Ed Wolf. They also had six children: Clarance, Elmer,
Ralph, and Harold (all of Dodge); Norma, who married Leslie Voltz of Dodge; and
Allen, Scotts Bluff, Neb. Ed passed away in 1946 and Ida passed away in 1984.

Emma Allmendinger married Ted Kust. They moved to Chaffee, N.D., with their two
children, Deloris and Clarance. Deloris, who married Bob Obliniss, resides in
Seal Beach, Calif. Clarance married Rose Lintz and resides in Bismarck. Ted
passed away in April 1976.

Edward Allmendinger married Lorine Raub of Golden Valley and they have two
children, Larry and Billy. Larry is married and resides in Las Vegas. Billy,
also married, resides in Topeka, Kan.

William Allmendinger married Viola Pitts. They had six children: Gladys,
Eunice, Guy, Lee Ray, James and Dean. Gladys married Elmer Isaak and resides in
Richardton. Eunice married Norman Sebastian and resides in Hebron. Viola passed

Henry John and Blanche Baker

In 1865, the Civil War ended and President Abraham Lincoln was assassinated. In
that same year, three brothers sailed to America from Sommerset-Shire, England.
They settled in Michigan. These three brothers were William, George and Henry
Baker. George was 13 years old. Henry moved to Canada. Later, William and
George moved to North Dakota.

George Baker was born in 1852 and died Feb. 13, 1935. In 1884 he married Mary
Elizabeth Giles, who was born at Houghton, Mich., in 1862. She died June 29,
1933. They lived in Moorhead, Minn., for five years. To this marriage were born
two sons, William Claud Baker (born March 31, 1885 and died Jan. 13, 1939) and
Henry John Baker (born March 10, 1894 and died April 5, 1963).

Henry John Baker was born in Grass Lake in Pierce County. He attended grade
school there and the seventh and eighth grade in Cando. He attended the
Presbyterian Church in Wolford and attended some grades in Wolford School. In
1911, Henry entered Aaker's Business College in Fargo, where he attended two
years. In 1914 he entered Valparaiso University in Valparaiso, Ind., for one
year of additional business administration. In 1916 he entered barber college
and received his diploma for barbering from the Twin Cities Barber College in
Minneapolis, Minn., in the spring of 1917.

Baker entered the military service of the First World War in September of 1917
in Des Moines, Iowa. He was with the 338th Field Artillery there and in the
335th in Camp Pike, Ark. He was honorably discharged with a "valvular heart
disease" as a result of the flu, in April of 1918. He was unconscious for three
days with the epidemic.

Baker then barbered for three years in Sykeston, Carrington and Underwood.

In 1921 he married Myrtle Blanche Beck in Minneapolis, Minn. Miss Beck was a
school teacher in the Rugby area and they had corresponded during the war.

Myrtle Blanche Beck was born in Zenobia (now Albany) in Clinton County,
Kentucky, on Jan. 15, 1892. Her paternal grandparents were Ben Beck (born Nov.
12, 1818 and died in 1899) and his wife, Rachael (Ballow) Beck (born in 1822,
died in 1877).

Myrtle's maternal grandparents were Ben Young (no information on his birth or
death) and his wife, Tabitha Radford who died in 1868. Myrtle's parents were
Gilbert B. Beck (born Oct. 10, 1854 and died Jan. 15, 1938) and his wife, Sarah
Victoria (Young) Beck (born Sept. 16, 1866 and died Nov. 12, 1912). Myrtle was
one of eight children. Her brothers and sisters were Helen, Flossie, Ben,
Lowell, Eva, Elbert and Lewis Orbin. Of these, Eva lives in Lewisville, Ind.,
and Lewis Orbin lives in Albany, Ky.

The Beck family attended the Methodist Church in Albany. Myrtle attended grade
school at York's Chapel, Ky. She entered Berea College at the age of 15 and
attended there until she was 18.

In 1912, nine girls from Berea answered a plea from North Dakota for the need of
teachers there. They arrived by train at Dickinson. There Myrtle taught school
south of town. The following summer, she attended Valley City Normal School and
in 1913 she taught in Litchville. In Valley City, she did office work in a
dental office in 1914. One summer she worked as a cashier in a cafe in Fargo.
Another term she spent at Ellendale Normal. She taught in the Leonard School in
Eddy County. She was a personal companion and secretary for Mrs. Wm. (Bill)
Lemke when her husband was a lawyer in Fargo. He later became a senator for
North Dakota. In 1919, she taught school at Hamar for one term. Then that
summer she attended Mayville Normal School (and not one penny of support from
home! That took stamina and perseverance!).

In 1920, she taught school north of Rugby at Hurricane Lake in Pierce County,
where she met Henry John Baker. Actually, they had met years before and
corresponded during World War I. They were married in Minneapolis, Minn., in
1921.

They moved to Fingal in Barnes County, where Baker barbered in his own business
for 10 years. In Fingal, three children were born to the Bakers--Burrel Arnold
(born April 29, 1922 and is still living), Joan (born Jan. 16, 1929 and is
still living), and Lloyd Kenneth (born May 26, 1930 and died July 10, 1987 at
age 57).

In 1931, the Bakers moved to Beulah, where Henry barbered. Remember seven
barbers at 25 cents a haircut - and the barber chair in the Baker living room?
He also did common labor, bookkeeping and payroll work for WPA, clerked on the
Ration Board, did harvesting, etc., until he left Beulah in November 1942. It
was wartime and Seattle, Wash., had advertised they needed workers in the
defense plants, so Baker hitchhiked to Seattle. His intentions were to move the
family to Washington once he was established, but instead they chose to remain
in Beulah. Instead of wartime work, Henry got a job with Albers Mining Co. on
Nov. 11, 1942; and he worked for them until he retired in 1959, a total of 17
years.

Due to poor health, Myrtle Baker was confined to N.D. State Hospital in June
1948. Due to her incurable condition, they were divorced Nov. 14, 1949. Seeking
new happiness, Baker married Anna (Cote) Jacobson on June 30, 1950, in Seattle.
In 1968, the first Mrs. Baker, Myrtle, was transferred to Prairie View Nursing
Home in Underwood, where she resided until her death on June 30, 1985, at age
93. She had not returned to her home in Kentucky for 73 years. Anna Baker still
resides in Seattle, and she was 90 years old in 1987.

Henry Baker lived in North Dakota for 48 years and in Seattle for 21 years. He
died of a heart attack in Seattle on April 5, 1963, at age 69.

At the time of her death, Myrtle had six grandchildren. Burrel had two sons,
Joan had two daughters, and Lloyd had two daughters. Myrtle also had three
great-grandchildren and 15 nieces and nephews.

Burrel presently lives in Sun City, Calif., with his wife Ruth (Reynolds)
Baker. Joan married Leo R. Huber and they live in Salt Lake City, Utah. Lloyd's
wife, the former Alice Rueb, lives in Costa Mesa, Calif.

Henry Baker is buried in the Garden of Devotions, Washington Memorial Park,
Seattle, Wash. Myrtle Baker is buried in the Beulah Cemetery. Their son, Lloyd
Baker, is buried in Harbor Lawn Memorial Park in Costa Mesa, Calif.

"The kind of ancestors we have had is not as important as the kind of
descendants our ancestors have." (Anonymous)

In Memory of John Bauer

"When I grew up my father owned and operated an underground coal mine," says
Ella Bauer Madche, daughter of John Bauer. "Some of the things I remember best
are how well we could keep apples and potatoes in it. Pumpkins and carrots kept
well and oranges and grapefruits. My dad used to buy a truckload of apples,
oranges and grapefruit around Thanksgiving and keep them in the mine and sell
them to his coal customers.

"He'd make 50 cents on every box. We had apples and oranges in our lunch box for
school from Thanksgiving on through spring. We could always count on apple and
pumpkin pie for Thanksgiving.

"When my dad first started in the mining business he got $1.50 for a ton of
coal, or when people said they couldn't pay, he let them charge, and some he
even let have the coal for nothing. A lot of the ones that charged never paid,
either. My mother used to ask him what he'd get for the coal he gave away, but
he said they didn't have anything he needed and he couldn't just let them
freeze. Times were hard on everyone.

"We had an old horse named Nance that he used to pull the coal cars out of the
mine. The cars went down into the mine on their own if you gave them a little
shove up to where the tracks branched off into other rooms. That's where we
kept Nance. They pushed the cars up to there by hand.

"We used to walk into the mine in the dark and she never hurt us if we bumped
into her. One day my sister came back to the house and told my mother, 'Mama,
vich vas Nance hate gesact hot?' Translation, 'Mom, do you know what Nance said
today7'

"Mom said, 'Nie, vas had sie gesat?' or 'No, what did she say?' and my sister
said, 'Pfblt.' (The sound horses make blowing through their lips.)

"By the way, the lights that they used in the mine were called carbide lights.
They burned something that looked like rock salt and was called carbide. My dad
used to get a charge out of telling people it burned if you put it in your hand
and spit in it, which it did; it got hot.

"But people thought he meant they would see a flame. He pulled this trick on one
man and he called my dad a 'Dunear veater.'"

Darold and Adella Benz
