University, and Laura is also a Bismarck State College graduate. At the present
time, Matthew and his wife Amy (Tokach) have two children, Justin and
Cassandra, and Matthew is employed at the Great Plains coal gasification plant.
His wife Amy is a teacher in the Beulah school system. Laura and her daughter
Amber live in Beulah where Laura works at the Dakota Farms Restaurant, and
Marsha is in Denver, Colo., managing Braun's Department Store.

Mathias Benz and his wife Christina came to America from Krem, South Russia, in
1893. They were accompanied by their sons Jacob and his wife Rosina, Mathias,
Phillip and John. They traveled to Freeman, S.D., by covered wagon, arriving in
October. In December of that year Jacob Benz Jr. was born.

Mathias and Christina started north in their covered wagon with their
children, two horses, a cow and some chickens. They arrived at Cannonball,
N.D., but had to hold up at that point for three days as one of the horses had
a colt and it was necessary to wait until it was strong enough to follow.

They arrived in the Beulah area and built their home, a sod house, and planted
potatoes on what is now the Helmuth Pfenning farm Sec. 23, 146.88. One of the
horses ran away to the east and of course, Benz pursued it. When he finally
found his horse, it was about 10 miles away. While searching for his horse, he
noted that there were more people residing in that area, so he returned home,
dug out his potato seed and moved his family east to what was soon known as
Expansion. Here four more children were born, Kathrina, Freda, Paulina and
Minnie.

On Dec. 26, 1907, son Mathias was married to Rosina Morast. They had 10
children, Herbert, Friedebert, Henry, Erhard, Julius, Lydia, Rose, Martha,
Pauline and Lea.

Friedebert Benz and Emma Zeller were married in 1934 and made their home at
Kronthal. Friedebert was born May 5, 1911, about 14 miles north of Hazen. His
father Mathias died Oct. 3, 1955, and his mother Rosina (Morast) passed away
Dec. 15, 1978. Emma was born Nov. 10, 1915, to Frederick and Kathrina
(Wiedrich). Frederick passed away Jan. 2, 1973, and Kathrina passed away Sept.
28, 1981.

Friedebert and Emma had one child, Darold. There have been seven generations of
Benzes in Mercer County and the Beulah area.

Friedebert has been (and still is) the Republican Precinct Committeeman for
some 30 years. They have also been foster parents for over 26 years, and the
last 17 years have been parents to eight Native Americans from two families,
three boys from one family and five from another.

The Sheep Shed and the Legion Hall were great for dances years ago. Back in the
'30s on the Fourth of July, it rained so hard they couldn't get home because of
a bridge that had washed out. After working hard all week farmers went to town
on Saturday night for groceries, and the stores stayed open until midnight or
maybe until there were no more people in town.

Friedebert and Emma have seen lots of changes in Beulah through the years and
like it much better now with all the nice streets. stores. churches and schools.

        The David Betz family

David and Martha Betz

David Betz was the son of Jacob and Katherin Pfaff. He was born in 1872 at
Watertown, NY. His father immigrated to the United States from Darmstadt,
Germany to avoid military conscription only to be inducted into the Union Army
during the American Civil War in 1862. David's parents were married in 1860. In
1883 most of the family moved to Scotland, SD, while the oldest children stayed
in New York.

        The David Betz family

David met and married Martha Karlin in 1901. They had 10 children: Henry,
Benjamin, Helen (Mrs. Gottlieb Mindt), Bertha (Mrs. Otto Reich), Elsie (Mrs.
Emil Reich), Ida, Edna (Gramm, Erickson), Martha (Mrs. James Thomson), Emma
(Mrs. Christ Bentz), and Laura.

The Betz and Karlin families moved to the Beulah area together in 1902. The
Karlin family homesteaded on the south side of the Knife River and the Betz
family homesteaded directly to the north across the river. While the railroad
was under construction, Martha supplied the crews with vegetables and baked
goods.

As the Betz family grew, they decided to move to a larger place near Otter
Creek, southeast of Beulah, in 1912. They raised some good wheat and flax crops
on the bottomlands. A schoolhouse was built a quarter mile away so the children
did not have far to walk.

In 1925 the family moved to the Walter Stephens place where they built a house.
That fall David entered the tuberculosis sanitorium at San Haven. He died three
years later. A daughter, Laura, age four, died of an accidental gunshot wound
in late 1927. A son, Henry, died of illness at age 26 in 1928.

Martha continued to raise her family by selling farm produce. Her son, Ben,
helped out by working at the mine and putting in the crop. Martha moved her
family to Beulah in 1933.

During the 30s Martha worked for the WPA, sewing and cooking for the school
lunch program. Her daughter Ida remained living with her until Martha's death
in 1961 at age 79.

        Michelle, Mary Kay and Barry Bjorklund.

Mary Kay Bjorklund

Mary Kay Bjorkland was born in Bismarck, ND on Oct. 29, 1944 to D.H. "Bud" and
Gertrude Flemmer Buscher. She lived with her parents in Beulah until 1952 when

Ervin and Bertha Boeckel

I, Ervin Boeckel, was born north of Beulah on March 21, 1920, to Ludwig Boeckel
and Dorthea Morast Boeckel. I grew up on the family farm north of Beulah, the
land that now belongs to ANG.

In my lifetime so many firsts have happened. My father bought his first tractor,
threshing machine and truck in 1928. Plowing was done with tractor and horses.
Seeding and harvesting was all done with horses. Six horses were used to pull a
two-bottom plow and four horses were used to pull the seed drill. Harrowing
was also required. Hay was cut with a four-foot mower pulled by two horses. It
was also raked and hauled home again with a team of horses and a wagon. Feeding
livestock in the winter was also done with horses, with wagons or sled. Milking
was done by hand and cranking the cream separator was also a hard chore that
had to be done twice each day, morning and evening, hot or cold. We went to
school with the horse and buggy or sled, depending on the weather.

        Bertha and Ervin Boeckel.

In 1938, my father bought a U Moline tractor and that was a big help. We then
used the tractor for seeding and plowing.

My wife Bertha (Flemmer) and I were married on June 27, 1941. Her parents were
John W. Flemmer and Rosina (Voegele) Flemmer. We lived with my parents until
fall when we fixed up a quarter of land that we got from them. In October 1941,
my parents quit farming and had an auction sale, and moved to town. So back to
farming with horses for me. In June 1942, I bought my first tractor, a W4
International with a three-bottom plow and packer drill for which I paid $1100.
I paid $100 down and $500 per year after that. I had to sell a horse for the
down payment. On June 12, 1942 our son Dale was born. The bill for the hospital
and doctor care was $35. I sheared sheep for my brother Albert to earn the
money to pay this bill. I was paid 10 cents per head of sheep.

In the spring of 1943, we moved west of Beulah. While there our daughter Donna
Mae was born, on Nov. 24, 1943. The hospital cost was much more then, but I
don't recall the amount.

In January 1944, we moved north of Beulah where our son Dale and wife Claudette
now live. Everything was done by hard work. The coal for heat was dug, hauled
home, unloaded by hand and then carried into the house by buckets. Water was
also carried into the house by buckets - no running water unless you ran to get
it! Ashes and used water were carried outside again with buckets. Milk was
carried into the house in the winter to separate with buckets, and after it was
separated, out again with buckets. Plus, there were dozens of other chores that
required using buckets.

On Dec. 1, 1946, we lost our home to fire and that was a real hardship. It was
so very cold. We moved an old house on the place and many a morning snow was on
the bed. When there was a wind we had no heavy clothes to wear. But the Lord
comforted us and we did manage because people were so kind and good to us. In
1962 we started raising Charolais cattle and continued to raise them until we
quit the cattle business in 1975.

On Aug. 27, 1963, a tornado struck our farm, doing severe damage to the
buildings and injuring my wife and me. We were both in the hospital. I did get
out for the funeral of my mother, but had to go back to the hospital again
after the funeral for some time.

In 1966, we moved 11 1/2 miles south of Hazen where our daughter Donna and her
husband Gary Soland now live. In 1967, we bought our first four-wheel drive
tractor, which was surely a big help.

REC electricity, super airplanes, TV, satellites, computers, men in space and a
decent telephone all are now a common thing, but have been a first in my
lifetime. We moved to the city of Hazen on Oct. 1, 1974, where we now live, but
still farm. We attend church at Beulah, the Church of God, and have both been
active in different departments. My wife's hobby is making quilts and it seems
there is always someone in need of one. I like to go snowmobiling if it is not
too cold.

We were blessed with two children. Dale Ervin Boeckel married Claudette Schulz,
daughter of William and Lenora Schulz. They have one son, Darnell, who is in his
second year of college at Wahpeton, ND. Dale farms and Claudette works for a
local law firm. They also own the Hitching Post Western Shop in Beulah. Our
daughter, Donna Mae, married Gary Soland, son of Lawrence and Agnes Soland from
Bottineau, ND. Donna Mae went to beauty school and worked several years as a
beautician. They live south of Hazen and farm some and Gary works at Indian Head
Mine at Zap.

They have three sons: Wade is now working in Florida; Darin is in the U.S. Army
and is married to Robin Goodjohn and they have one son, Bryant; Jamie is an
eighth grader at the Hazen school.

Our children, grandchildren, and now the great-grandchild are all such a
blessing to us. Our favorite Bible verse is John 3:16.

Otto Boeckel

My name is Otto Peter Boeckel, born to Johannas and Caroline Boeckel on Jan.
22, 1903, on a farm eight miles north of Beulah. My mother died in April 1906
when she fell from a spring seat on her wagon after she fell asleep, and the
front wheel ran over a rock. She had helped my dad haul wheat in two wagons to
Glen Ullin and was returning home, following my dad. He picked up her limp body
and brought it home.

I had one brother and four sisters. In 1907 my dad married Mrs. Hartwig who had
four children. There were two children born to that marriage. My dad Passed away
Aug. 10, 1910. That fall my stepmother had an auction sale, selling all
livestock and machinery. After the sale our family was split up because my
stepmother remarried.

I was taken in by Mr. and Mrs. George Slowey who were close neighbors and were
good friends of my dad. In 1911 a Baptist minister, Reuben Blumhagen, moved onto
my dad's homestead with five children. In March 1912, a raging prairie fire
swept through, burning all the buildings on my dad's farm, also two of the
Blumhagen children, who were alone while Mr. and Mrs. Blumhagen were gone
preaching on a Sunday. They then moved to the Beulah area, where he was the
first Baptist minister.

I enjoyed living with Sloweys on the farm. We moved into Zap, house and all, in
the spring of 1913. Slowey built a pool hall and his business was good. In 1916
he started the International Harvester business, which he sold J.B. Field in
1918. He then moved to Beulah in 1919 and started the International Harvester
business, in which I had a part.

In 1920 Dad Sturr, who ran the grain elevator, started a coal mine two and a
half miles south of Beulah with his two sons, David and Rudy. They had a
steam-powered tipple which operated satisfactorily for several months. But one
morning the boiler blew up, killing David and breaking his son Eddie's leg.
Everything burned down, leaving the coal in the mine on fire. The State Bureau
of Mines sent a railroad car of equipment to fight the fire in the mine which
was under the supervision of Jess Crowe, who was appointed by the state. I was
one of the many volunteers who fought the fire with gas masks and other
equipment. It was no use, I worked a couple of days but we could not put it
out. But sometime later, Ed Carmichael opened it up and made a go of it.

I worked with Slowey in the implement business. On Nov. 8, 1926 I married Helen
Rousseau, step-daughter of Mike Haider who had a butcher shop in Beulah. Helen
and I had three children: Yvonne (died at eight months), Ramona and Otto, Jr.,
all brought into the world by that wonderful Doctor Rasmusson, his equally
wonderful wife assisting. We had another son, George, born in 1941 in Kellogg,
Idaho, the only one born in a hospital.

(Otto died in 1983 in Portland, Ore. and Helen died Aug. 17, 1987 at Gladstone,
Ore.)

Michael and Susan Boland

As with most of our pioneers, it was the desire to become landowners rather than
tenants that brought the Michael H. Bolands to settle in this area.

Born near Toronto, Ontario in 1937, Michael Boland moved, with his parents, to
Mower County, MN, in 1848. He married Susan Crowe, a native of Maryland, at
Johnstown, Iowa on Aug. 5, 1876. To this union were born 11 children: Mary,
Nellie, John, Tom, Susan, Ray, Elizabeth, Kate, Ed, Maude and Mildred.

The family resided in southeastern Minnesota until November, 1902, when they
boarded immigrant cars and set out for their newly acquired homestead on the
Dakota prairies.

The first winter was spent on a farm south of Glen Ullin and the following
April they moved to their homestead on S18-T143-R87 in Oliver County. Michael,
with a son and two daughters, John, Mary, and Nellie, each proved up on a
quarter-section. Shacks were built on their respective quarters near the center
of the section so they would be settled together.

They had brought very little with them; however, they did have four horses,
three cows, two wagons, a breaking plow, a harrow and a meager supply of
household goods.

Breaking 10 acres of ground and seeding flax composed the first spring's
farming. With succeeding years the farming became more diversified and a band
of brood mares was built up to supplement the family income.

Water was a definite problem. Springs were non-existent and numerous wells were
dug, but to no avail. All the water used for household purposes and for the
livestock was hauled five miles daily.

The family lived mostly on homegrown foods, buying very little except staples
such as flour and sugar. Very little clothing was store-bought - most of it was
made by Mary, a seamstress by profession. What trading there was, was done in
Glen Ullin. They would go down one day, stay overnight and return the next day.
As can be readily imagined, this trip was not a frequent undertaking.

Of the boys, Ed was the rancher while John and Ray were the farmers. It was John
who bought the first tractor shipped into Beulah. It was an iron-wheeled
International.

Tom was the hunter and trapper. To stimulate the sport of hunting he imported
the first pheasants to this area. These he acquired from the State Game and Fish
Department.

Michael lived to the age of 91 years, dying on Oct. 16, 1928. His wife Susan
died April 6, 1935.

Of the 11 Boland children, one survives, Mrs. Maude Carmichal of Billings, MT.

Ruben and Emma Buchmann

What makes a guy come home after 50-plus years away?

For Ruben Buchmann, it was partly a desire to be near the old family homestead
which he still owns, but which he was tired of trekking back yearly to check on.

Buchmann was born with the new century some 25 miles south of what would become
Beulah. His family, with many others, lost the original place in 1923 but
Ruben, determined to keep his roots, saved until he could buy it back.

"It was my mother's place, where we were raised," he explained.

Ruben recalls Beulah's birth pangs. "In 1912 they'd just come into town with the
railroad," he says. "I was just a little fella, 12 years old."

Winters were tougher then, he recalls, with a couple of feet of snow on the
level. Though most people had cars, they were useless in winter and horses and
bobsleds were the rule. Many people used that method to get to church and smoky
kerosene lanterns hanging from the ceiling provided flickering illumination for
such entertainment and gatherings as Christmas programs.

If a person got sick, a bobsled was necessary to reach the doctor; but then
doctors still made house calls. Some folks had party lines and could call.

And some had ingenious ways to hook on to the party line. "Sometimes they would
connect the phone line from the house to the fences, and it would go half a
mile this way and half a mile that way," Buchmann gestured expressively. "It
wasn't real good, but it worked."

Entertainment for the Buchmanns was music. Guitars, fiddles, accordions and
"mouth organs" provided background for singing and dancing; all the family was
musical, Ruben recalls.

Ruben married Emma Gramm on Jan. 16, 1927. The couple has two children, Jim, a
musician for Walt Disney World in Florida, and Cleo (Buchmann) Herndon,
Gladstone, Ore. There are two grandchildren and three great-grandchildren.

After his marriage, Ruben started working as a barber. He opened his barbershop
in Beulah in 1928, with three barbers including himself. Men's and women's
haircuts were 50 cents, shampoos were 50 cents and a shave, 25 cents. Face
massages were $1, Ruben recalls, but men never took advantage of that service.

He operated the shop for 11 years, next to the old Roxy Theatre in what is now
the basement of Sears Catalog Store. Each year Ruben held a three-day special
when he gave children entering school a free haircut, knowing not many had the
35 cents required.

Emma worked hard those years, raising the children and helping at the shop. She
kept the tools and clothes clean; clothes were hung out wet and "freeze-dried,"
then brought inside to thaw and dry again. At least, she recalls, the sunlight
removed stains.

Main Street looked different then, with only 18-20 businesses including his own.
Ruben recalls during the Depression men who needed haircuts would gather coal
from the railroad tracks and trade that for Ruben's skills.

In September, 1936, he sold the business to Pius Hoffart, then moved with Emma
and the kids to Ft. Peck, Mont., a boom town where they stayed four years before
moving to Oregon City, Ore., where they spent the next 50 years.

Ruben's goal, repurchasing the family farm, was realized in 1944, 21 years
after it was lost and eight years after he'd left Beulah, when he finally was
able to save enough. He and Emma returned annually for 42 years to check on it
and take care of the land.

Finally the trip became too hard and they decided to move back home for keeps.
"Now we can go out to the farm every week if we want to." Ruben smiles.

Gertrude and D.H. "Bud" Buscher

DuWayne Homer Buscher, better known as Bud, was born Jan. 13, 1921 in
Breckinridge, Minn., to Benjamin and Mary Hubard Buscher. The Buschers moved to
Beulah in 1937. Bud served in the CC program for two years, stationed near
Watford City at the northern entrance of the Theodore Roosevelt National Park.
After returning to Beulah he attended Beulah High School and graduated in 1941.
After graduation, Bud went to work for the Knife River Coal Mining Company.

Gertrude was born Dec. 20, 1922 on a farm in rural Beulah to Fred K. and
Katherina (Voegele) Flemmer. Gertie attended school in Beulah and graduated
from Beulah High School in 1941. She attended Concordia College and then on
Aug. 23, 1942, she and Bud were married at Zion Lutheran Church in Beulah.

Bud was employed by Flemmer Sales & Service Ford Garage, and then in 1943 he
and Gertie managed the local Gambles store.

In April of 1943 Bud enlisted in the Merchant Marines and was sent to Sheepshead
Bay, N.Y. Gertie followed him in June. While Bud was stationed in New York,
Gertie worked for the United States government in the Lend/Lease to Russia
Program.

When Bud was sent overseas in the summer of 1944 Gertie returned to Beulah and
went to work at the Comer Hardware, which was a combination of the former
Economy Hardware and Gamble Stores.

On Oct. 29, 1944 their first daughter, Mary Katherine, was born in the Bismarck
Hospital. Gertie and Mary Kay lived with her parents, the F.K. Flemmers. Gertie
continued to work at the Corner Hardware until Bud came home after the war in
1945. He worked at the Ford Garage with Flemmer Sales and Service until April of
1952 when the garage was sold.

On May 19, 1950, their second daughter, Lindarae, was born at the Bismarck
Hospital. During their years in Beulah, the Buschers were members of Zion
Lutheran Church. Gertie taught Sunday school, Bible school and was very active
in the WMF. Bud served on the church board for several years. He belonged to
the Beulah Fire Department, Beulah Athletic Club, Commercial Club. Gertie was
also a member of the Beulah Mothers' Club.

After the sale of Flemmer's Sales and Service and after 10 years of living in
Beulah, they moved to Thermopolis, Wyo., where they bought the Rainbow Motel.
They were very active in church and community affairs. Bud served as mayor of
Thermopolis, president of the Wyoming Motor Court Association and was also on
the National Motel Association board of directors.

Due to Bud's severe heart attack in 1958, they were forced to sell the motel.
They bought it on Tuesday, July 8, 1952 and sold it on Tuesday, July 8, 1958.
The Buschers moved to Billings, and it was here, while Bud was on a plane en
route to Billings from Jackson, Wyo., he succumbed to his last heart attack on
Feb. 5, 1959.

Gertie and the two girls moved to Bismarck where Gertie attended Bismarck Junior
College and later opened a ceramic and hobby shop. Mary Kay graduated from
Bismarck High School and married Steven E. Bjorklund.

In 1966 Gertie purchased Bob Keogh's shares in the Bank of Beulah. On July 1,
1966 she started at the Bank of Beulah. In August of 1966 she and Lindarae
moved to Beulah. Lindarae completed her junior and senior years at Beulah High
School and graduated in 1968.

Gertie has belonged to the Beulah Chamber of Commerce and Beulah Boosters,
Beulah Quarterback Club and was a charter member of the Beulah Eagles Auxiliary,
Beulah Mothers' Club, Beulah Country Club and a charter lifetime member of the
Mercer County Historical Society on which she has served as treasurer since the
society started in 1977.

She was a charter member of the North Dakota Historical Society and Germans from
Russia and has served on the alumni reunion committee since 1970. Gertie has
been a member of Zion Lutheran Church and in the past served as a council
member for six years. At the present time she is a member of the North Dakota
Bankers Association, Executive Council and was a member of the National Bank
Women's Association.

Lorence and Shirley Christmann

Lorence Christmann was born Dec. 24, 1941, near Beulah to Alfred and Martha
(Hintz) Christmann. He was raised and attended school north of Beulah where he
worked on the family farm and grew to manhood.

Lorence married Shirley Krausz on Oct. 5, 1963. Shirley was born Oct. 9, 1944,
in Beulah to Leonard and Hilda (Winkler) Krausz. She attended Beulah schools and
graduated from Beulah high school. She also attended Dickinson State College for
one year before her marriage.

This couple lived in Beulah for eight years, where Lorence worked for Farmers
Union Oil Company and the Beulah Livestock Sales. Shirley worked at the Beulah
Community Nursing Home. In 1971, they moved out onto the family farm north of
Beulah where they were engaged in farming and ranching. In 1980, they were
employed at the Antelope Valley Station by Industrial Contractors Inc.

They both loved to hunt and fish and were enjoyable company to have around and
were well known for their generosity and were always willing to lend a friend or
neighbor a helping hand.

Lorence and Shirley died in a tragic accident on Nov. 2, 1981 at the
intersection of Highway 1806 and County Highway 27 north of Hazen when they
were sideswiped. True to their benevolent nature, they were returning home
after giving a stalled motorist a lift to Pick City.

        Mr. and Mrs. Lorence Christmann.

They were members of Beulah Congregational Church.

Mary L. Cox

Mary L. Cox grew up and attended school in Beulah. Molly taught several schools
in the area including the Spring Creek School for 13 years. Her teaching career
continued in the Beulah public school system for 25 years. Molly retired from
her fourth grade classroom in 1978 and continued her involvement with education
through substitute teaching until 1983.

During the early years of her career, Molly attended summer sessions at
Dickinson State Teachers College where she received her B.S. degree in
elementary education. She was a lifetime member of St. Joseph Church.
Fraternally she was affiliated with Royal Neighbors of America and the Eagles
Auxiliary. Professional activities included membership in local, state and
national education associations.

Molly made her home with her sister, Catherine Scherbinske and family until her
death in 1983.

Molly will be remembered as a person dedicated to her family and friends. Her
students will remember Miss Cox as a caring, fair teacher who took a personal
interest in each of them.

        Heather, Debora and Dave Creel.

David and Debora Creel

Debora Creel was born in Dickinson, ND on April 30, 1956 to Harry and Mildred
Hanks. She lived in Werner with her parents, three sisters and one brother
until the family moved to Beulah in June, 1964. She attended grade school and
high school in Beulah where she participated in choir and track.

David Creel was born in Newcastle, WY on Nov. 29, 1955 to Joseph and Georgene
Creel. David lived in Dickinson with his mother and one sister until August,
1969 when his mother married Ken Schulz and they moved to Zap. He attended high
school in Zap and was active in basketball and participated in class plays.

Debora and David were married on Dec. 31, 1973 in Beulah. They made their first
home in Reeder, ND where Dave worked at the Reeder Grain Elevator. They had an
opportunity for Dave to get some training in appliance repair so in June, 1974
they moved to Glasgow, MT and Dave went to school. After Dave finished school
they moved to Dickinson, Zap, and finally made their home in Beulah. Dave went
to work for Peavey Lumber in October, 1975. They had lived in apartments until
May, 1976 and they wanted their own home and bought a mobile home. Dave worked
for Peavey until May, 1978 and then he went to work for Knife River Coal where
he operates different machinery.

Debora was not idle as she did babysitting for several years. She decided it
was time for a change and went to work part-time for Sveum's Department Store
for one year and cleaned the Beulah Civic Center for several years. In the fall
of 1978 they decided to sell their mobile home and build a house, now living at
612 Cypress Drive in the Gateway Addition. They kept busy that fall doing
painting, varnishing, and staining the interior of the house. They did most of
the landscaping the next spring but have added shrubs and trees a little at a
time.

In February, 1982 Debora went to work full-time at Peavey Lumber, now United
Building Center. She worked at United Building Center until July, 1985 when
there was going to be a reduction in personnel, and she started working for
Farmers Union Insurance at the end of July. The secretarial work and insurance
work being different than she had ever done was a real change, but it didn't
take long and she decided she enjoyed her new occupation.

Heather, the couple's daughter, was born in Hettinger, ND on May 2, 1974. She
attends the Beulah school and is active in band. She enjoys listening to music
and reading. She has a poodle named Pepi that the family enjoys playing with.
Heather enjoys taking friends to the lake for swimming and boating. She enjoys
riding the tube pulled behind the boat.

David has been active in several organizations including the fire department,
softball where he coached and played, and bowling. Dave enjoys going to the
lake and fishing. As a family they spend most of their weekends at the lake
camping, boating, and fishing. Debora enjoys going for long walks, bowling, and
just visiting with friends, but by herself she enjoys various crafts including
cross-stitch.

        Douglas and Tillie Dettmann.

Douglas and Tillie Dettmann

Little did Doug know that he made a permanent move when he signed the contract
to be Beulah's Veteran's Ag Teacher in September of 1948. After living in
Beulah for 40 years he's convinced he made the right decision at that time.

Doug, son of Hugo and Agnes (Ims) Dettmann, graduated from Judson High School
in 1937, attended and graduated from N.D.S.S. in 1939 with a degree in commerce.
He graduated from N.D.A.C. in 1948 with a degree in animal husbandry. While at
N.D.A.C. he was a member of the Alpha Gamma Rho Fraternity and the Alpha Zeta
Honor Society. His two degrees proved to be very compatible when he became
associated with the Bank of Beulah.

Doug was drafted into the U.S. Army in July, 1942, serving 40 months, 33 of
which were spent in the European Theatre. He was honorably discharged on
November, 1945, and then went to the N.D.A.C. (N.D.S.U.) on the G.I. Bill.

Since coming to Beulah he has belonged to the Beulah Lions, Cowboys Reunion,
Beulah Livestock Association, Beulah Development Corp. and Zion Lutheran Church
Council. He is presently a member of the Beulah Chamber of Commerce, charter
member of the Beulah Eagles, Mercer County Historical Society, Beulah VFW,
Beulah American Legion, N.D.S.U. Alumni Association and the Beulah Country
Club.

Doug has always been interested in anything pertaining to agriculture. He
served on Mac McKenzie's first committee to start the West River Judging
Contest and has worked on it ever since, missing only two contests. His love of
horses got him involved with the State 4-H Horse Camp at Washburn and he
remembers how he and Mac had to cross the Missouri by boat in order to work
with the construction crew. He worked with the local VFW when they sponsored
the first High School Rodeo in the State of ND. He was presented the N.D.S.U.
Alumni Agriculturist Award in 1979.

Tillie (Flemmer) Dettmann has been a life-long resident of Beulah. She was born
on July 22, 1926, in the small family apartment behind their grocery store. The
Flemmer Grocery was located where the present U.S. Post Office was built. She
graduated from Beulah High School in 1943, attended Concordia College in
Moorhead, Interstate College, Fargo, and the University of Montana at Missoula.

She taught school at Elgin High School from 1948-1950 and at Hazen 1950-1951. In
those days teachers were not paid extra for extra-curricular activities and
Tillie remembers being very busy being advisor to the pep club, school paper,
school annual, Jr. Class play and prom. She also taught a baton twirling class
of 50 students and taught ballroom dancing at the high school dances, all for
$1755.00 a year. When she taught the sixth grade in Hazen she had 39 students
in her room.

Tillie has been a past member of the Beulah Women's Club, charter member of the
ND Germans From Russia Historical Society, and served on the first state board
of directors of this organization.

She is presently a charter lifetime member of the Mercer County Historical
Society, serving on its board of directors. She has been a member of Beulah
Mother's Club since 1955, the Beulah Alumni Association, chairman of the 1964
Jubilee History Book, and Sunday School teacher in both the English and German
Sunday Schools of Zion Lutheran Church. Her present project is chairman of
Zion's 75th Anniversary Book.

Doug and Tillie Dettman were married April 8, 1951, at Zion Lutheran Church,
with Pastor J. Kammerer officiating. They had two children; Michael Douglas,
born March 11, 1953; and Kathleen Ann, born July 22, 1955.

        Kathleen Dettmann.

Kathleen Ann Dettmann

Kathleen Ann Dettmann graduated from Beulah High School in 1973 as a National
Merit Scholar and graduated summa cum laude from Concordia College with a
double major in English and history-political science. She also graduated from
Lutheran Northwestern Seminary in St. Paul with a master's degree in divinity.
She did her internship at Colfax, WI.

Kathleen was ordained at Zion Lutheran Church in November of 1982 and served at
the Butte-Balfour Parish. In 1985 she entered law school and expects to get her
law degree in May of 1988.

Kathleen was a Legislature intern for the North Dakota Legislature 1987 session,
working in the insurance department. She has been selected to serve as a law
clerk to Judge H. Meschke of the North Dakota Supreme Court from Aug. 1, 1988 -
Aug. 1, 1989. She plans to move to Bismarck in July of 1988.

While attending law school she continued to preach at various churches in the
Grand Forks area whenever a parish was in the need of a supply pastor. She
hopes to continue doing this after graduation.

        Agnes Easton family - L to R: Andy, David, Graeme, George. Seated, L
        to R: Agnes, Alex, Bob, Wilson and John.

        Jim Easton

Agnes and John Easton

Agnes (Wilson) Easton was born in 1871 near Glasgow, Scotland. She married John
Easton, a coal miner in Lanackshire County, Scotland. The Eastons were a very
musical family. In fact, Agnes and John met each other in a Presbyterian choir.
They were later married in that same church.

They were parents of 10 children when John Easton came to America to work in the
coal mines in Indiana, where he died in 1918 of the flu. He was born in 1865.

Agnes Easton came to America in 1916 with her sons to her brother, David
Wilson, at Wilton, N.D., where her sons found employment in the coal mines
there. In 1923 some of the Easton sons found employment in the Beulah coal
mines so that within a few years the whole family lived at Beulah.

Agnes Easton spoke with a very Scottish brogue. Many times someone had to
interpret to the store clerk for her as in Beulah much German was spoken and no
one was familiar with the Scottish accent.

After the family arrived in Beulah they were active in the Congregational
Church and choir. A quartet consisting of sons Alex, George, David, Robert and
Graeme often sang quartet music. David and Graeme also played piano for church
services. George was also active in church music and band. George directed a
Beulah band as well as choir music at St. Joseph Catholic Church. A dance band
made up of Alex, George, David, Robert and Graeme often played in this area.

Wilson Easton finished his education in the Beulah school system. Robert Easton
also played baseball with the Beulah Miners during the '30S and the early '40S
when the Beulah Miners were a well-known baseball team.

The Easton family was saddened when Alex lost his life in a gold mining
accident in Lead, S.D. in 1930. He had been married to Gladys Jensen, a
fourth-grade teacher at the Beulah school.

John Jr., James and Andrew lived in Beulah for a short time. James worked in
Colorado mines and Andrew found employment in Chicago, as did James and Wilson,
where they later married and died. John, Jr. came to America after his mother.
He was married and his wife could not adjust to a new country, so they returned
to Scotland a short time later. They had a son, John.

In later years only Robert, David, Graeme and George lived here. They married
and were employed by Knife River Coal Mining Company. All had families that are
now living elsewhere. Agnes, Alex, George, David, Robert and Graeme are all
interred in Beulah Cemetery.

The Easton children: Mary was born in 1889 and died in 1891 in Scotland at 18
months.

John, Jr. was born in 1893 in Scotland and died there in 1964.

James was born in 1894 in Scotland and died in 1968 in Chicago, Ill.

Andrew was born in 1896 in Scotland and died in 1983 or 1984 in Chicago, Ill.

Alexander was born Sept. 29, 1898 in Scotland and died July 10, 1930, at Lead.
S.D. He was married to a schoolteacher, Gladys Jensen. They had no children.

George was born Oct. 17, 1900, in Scotland and died Dec. 29, 1977, at Coeur
d'Alene, Idaho. He was married to Josephine Morgan who was a schoolteacher. They
had three children, George, Alex and Mary.

David was born Oct. 5, 1903, in Scotland and died May 1, 1974, at Beulah. He
married a schoolteacher, Emma Spitzer, and they had four children: David,
Donald, Marilynn and Richard.

Robert was born Oct. 5, 1903, in Scotland and died June 9, 1982, at Bismarck. He
married a schoolteacher, AnnaBelle Iverson. They had no children.

Graeme was born March 21, 1905, in Scotland and died April 21, 1976, at Beulah.
He married Esther Grannis. They had one son, Delvin.

Wilson was born in 1908 or 1909 in Scotland and died in 1985 at Chicago, Ill.

David and Emma Easton

David Easton was born to John and Agnes (Wilson) Easton in a mining town near
Glasgow, Scotland, on Oct. 5, 1903. Agnes Easton and eight sons came to Wilton,
N.D. in October, 1916. Their father, John Easton, came to Indiana before the
rest of the family came in 1916. He found employment in the coal mines in that
state. He died shortly before his family came to North Dakota, where he was to
join them. David Easton came to Beulah in 1925 to work in mines. He worked for
local mining companies until he retired in 1968. The last 10 years he operated
a mine for Knife River Coal Mining Co. at Savage, Mont. That mine supplied coal
for Lewis and Clark Station, built and operated by Montana Dakota Utilities Co.
at Sidney, Mont.

        Donald, Marilynn, Richard and David, Jr., Easton.

        David and Emma Easton

David married Emma Spitzer at Bismarck on June 29, 1926. She was born July 22,
1904, on her parents' homestead near Wilton. Her parents were Ludwig and Rosina
(Brenneise) Spitzer. She attended rural schools there until finishing elementary
grades. She graduated from Bismarck High School and taught in rural schools
before her marriage. She also taught rural schools in Mercer and Oliver
counties and in Richland County in Montana in later years. They were parents of
four children, all married and living in other areas. David died May 1, 1974,
and rests in the Beulah Cemetery. Emma is still living alone in her home in
Beulah.

David Easton, Jr. married Elsie Dee Kaufman in Tacoma, Wash. They have two
daughters and one son. All are living in the Seattle area.

Donald Easton married Evelyn Hedges at Antelope, Mont. They have two daughters.
One daughter and her parents live in Billings, Mont. The younger daughter lives
in California.

Marilynn married Paul Swanson, a former Beulah school teacher. They live in
Bismarck. They have three sons, one in Bismarck, one in Chicago, and one in
Lincoln, Neb. with his wife and family.

Richard Easton married Judith Rice. They have three daughters. All are living
near Amherst, N.H.

The Easton families were interested in music and took part in band, orchestras
or church music. All are happy to see how much their home town has improved
since their early years here.

Erwin R. and Evelyn Eisenbeis

Erwin R. Eisenbeis was born July 1, 1921, in Ree, N.D., and has been a farmer
all his life. His father John passed away May 1963, and his mother Lena (Ries)
passed away in August of 1969. Erwin married Evelyn (Morast). She was born
north of Zap on Sept. 17, 1923. Her father Carl passed away Sept. 9, 1984, and
her mother Ida (Mittelsteadt) resides in the Beulah Community Nursing Home.

Their children are as follows: Betty Loud (Gadberry), born Feb. 3, 1945, in
Beulah; Carol (Weigum), born Dec. 7, 1947, in Richardton; Myron, born Nov. 2,
1950, in Hazen; Mary Ann (Brunmeier), born Nov. 10, 1955, in Hazen; Julie Ann
(Madche), born Aug. 23, 1957, in Hazen; Erwin Wayne, born Jan. 1, 1964 in
Hazen; and 10 grandchildren, seven boys and three girls.

Erwin and Evelyn are active members of Concordia Lutheran Church in Beulah and
also VFW members of Post 7759.

Erwin and Evelyn (Morast) were married in Wittenberg Church north of Zap, April
9, 1944. They moved to the Jake Eisenbeis farm for one year. Erwin was in the
service during World War II and served in the U.S. Infantry in the Pacific
Theatre with the 63rd Artillery Battalion stationed at Kurma, Japan. After he
came home in 1947, he took over farming where he had left off in 1945 and still
farms.

Growing up in the Beulah area was different years ago. For one thing there was
no television. People had lots of fun riding horses and sled riding down the
hills in the winter. Cocoa was never as good as when you came in from the cold.

Shopping in town was fun. First you dropped off the cream at the creamery and
then went shopping and visiting with the other people because you knew
everyone. Erwin started fishing with the children as soon as they could hold a
fishing pole and they still all go fishing today and the grandchildren go also.

John and Mary Ellen England

John England and his Mary Ellen Gibson came from Borndard, Mo. John was born
March 8, 1862, and his wife, Mary Gibson, was born in Sept. 18, 1860. They were
married on Aug. 18, 1884, when John was 22. They lived for a time in Missouri.
To this family were born eight children, all deceased. One daughter, Mary, was
married to a farmer of Beulah, Bill Kosbab, but they later separated and she
later married a farmer down in the Oakes area. When she died she was 92. Her
sister Viola married a man from Bismarck. They lived there for many years until
they moved to California. When Aunt Vi passed away she was 92 and would have
been 93 in a few months.

On May 30, 1904, Mary England passed away. She is buried at Belgrade, Neb. Two
years after her death in 1906, John moved his family to North Dakota. They
settled on a farm south of the present Beulah in 1907.

It was the following spring that John England planted his crop on his new farm.
He planted flax. The crop was fairly good. He had to haul his flax far to
market.

        John W. England.

        Mary Ellen (Gibson) England.

John Anderson raised a large potato crop and supplied the NP railroad
construction with potatoes. In the fall of 1914 John England, who was then
employed by the NPRR Co. in Killdeer, was hired to haul the potato crop to the
consumer after it reached Killdeer.

In 1915, Grandpa England was taken ill. He was hospitalized at Brainerd, Minn.,
then the nearest railroad hospital. There he passed away on July 20, 1915. One
of his favorite hobbies was playing the fiddle, which he did very well.

In 1918 or 1919 his daughter Hulda Jean married Edwin P. Joos.

Edwin P. Joos was living on the farm owned by his parents. When times were
tough, he often helped out ice-cutting in the winter, mined coal and at one
time worked as an oiler at what is now the North American Coal Mine--also known
as the Indianhead Mine. Many times he helped in the local garages, as he was
very good at fixing things. Several times he had to help the county sheriff.
Suppose one could say he was a jack of all trades. When need be he could whip
up a batch of bread, or set a good table.

Edwin P. Joos and Hulda Jean England Joos had three children: Philip P., Ellen
G. (known as LuEllen when she was in school), and Lawrence J.

        Earl Erdman

Earl Erdman

Emil Earl Erdman, Jr. was born Sept. 18, 1951, in Hazen to Emil Erdman Sr. and
Hulda (Pfenning) Erdman. He grew up on the family farm east of Golden Valley.

His grandfather, John Erdman, had homesteaded the land one mile east of Golden
Valley and his father took over the family farm. His brother, Jim, still
operates the family farm.

Erdman was raised and attended school in Golden Valley, graduating from Golden
Valley High School in 1969. Erdman attended Minot State College for three years,
from 1969-72, and then joined the Navy, serving from January, 1974, to June,
1976.

In 1977 he graduated from Mt. Hood College at Portland, OR, and received his
North Dakota funeral director and embalmer's license on July 1, 1978.

Erdman started work for Bernie Aarthun the same day and later bought the
business from the Aarthun heirs on Jan. 1, 1980.

He still operates the business under the name Erdman Funeral Home.

Erdman has two children: Shawn, born Jan. 11, 1973, in Denver, CO, and Shane,
born Aug. 31, 1975 in Great Lakes, IL, near Chicago. Erdman's father passed away
Feb. 28, 1983 and his mother lives in Golden Valley.

Erdman is active in the Elks, Lions and Beulah Chamber of Commerce as well as
sponsoring an annual Toys for Tots-Food for Families benefit at Christmas time.

        Archie and Emma Erickson

        Delmar, DoLores, Emma and Archie Erickson

Archie and Emma Erickson

Archie Erickson was born in Cambridge, Minn., on May 27, 1904. He was eight
years old when his parents, Harvey and Christene (Pederson) Erickson, moved to
North Dakota and homesteaded 10 miles south of Beulah. The elder Ericksons had
been born in Sweden and emigrated to Minnesota.

As a young boy Archie worked out most of his single life. When the Beulah Mine
was started he worked there for a while, hauling coal with the wagon and lead
team to the Beulah tipple. He helped grading the road to the mine to lay the
track.

He also worked for Ed Carmichael hauling coal to town with the team, delivering
coal to residences. When Highway 49 was built he was on the finishing group,
using the Fresno and driving four mules.

Archie married Emma Fischer in 1933, the daughter of Henry and Elizabeth (Weil)
Fischer, Emma was born June 5, 1909.

The couple lived in a tent for a couple of weeks, until Ben Ivarie moved out of
the sod house and the Ericksons could move in. They lived there from spring to
fall. During the summer Archie got cottonwood from the Missouri River, cutting
trees to build a shack on the place where they now live. That was also in 1933.

"In beet time, 1934, after the little crop we had was harvested," Emma recalls,
"Archie, Floyd Erickson, Victor Strom and George Cline went to Montana to work
in the beet field to earn some money. They came home with $50, which had to
stretch over the winter."

Also on July 27, 1934, daughter Do'Lores was born to the Ericksons. Archie
walked a mile every morning to work for Robert Johnson for a dollar a day,
helping out in Robby's crop. Then he'd walk home to put in his own crop after
he was done.

The drought was very bad that year. The Ericksons' shack wasn't finished on the
inside, so Emma papered it with newspapers to keep the sand from blowing in.

On June 18, 1943, son Delmar was born. Times got better and in 1946 the
Ericksons began to build around the shack and finished it in 1947, complete
with a bathroom, running water and a coal furnace, for which they were very
grateful.

Emma taught Sunday school for many years and is a 23-year member of the Aplin
Homemakers. She has belonged for many years to the Friendly Circle of the
Congregational Church.

        Before moving to Beulah, the Harvey Erickson family lived in Minnesota.
        Harvey, Christine, Cora, Clifford, Archie, Myrtle, Floyd, and Grandma
        Erickson.

Harvey and Christina Erickson

The Harvey Erickson family came from Minnesota and homesteaded eight miles
south of Beulah in 1909. Harvey was married to Christina Peterson Strom. They
had seven children, Cora, Clifford, Archie, Floyd, Myrtle, Beatrice and
Lawrence, who died at age two.

Christina passed away on March 3, 1914. Later Harvey married Margaret Voltz.
They had one son, Harold, whereabouts are unknown.

Harvey farmed until he was about 85 and then moved to Beulah. He passed away
Oct. 3, 1967 at the age of 93.

Archie and Floyd still farm south of Beulah and Bea lives one mile east of
Beulah. The rest of the children have passed away.

Arthur Erickson and Anna Sevallius Erickson also homesteaded 10 miles southwest
of Beulah in 1909. They had eight children, Gladys, Francis, Esther, Bernice,
Roger, Lloyd, Edward and Marion. Esther, Bernice, Roger and Edward have passed
away.

William and Betty Fetch

William (Bill) Fetch was born Aug. 15, 1914, in Beulah. His father Mike passed
away July 21, 1969, and his mother Katherine (Heier) passed away April 30, 1963.

Barbara (Betty) Jacob was born Oct. 13, 1914, in Napoleon. Her father Valentine
passed away April 14, 1956, and her mother Veronica (Haegele) passed away Oct.
24, 1967.

Bill and Betty are both retired from farming and now reside in Beulah.

Their children are as follows: Wilfred, born Feb. 9, 1942; Cary (Fetch)
Unterseher, born Dec. 12, 1945; and Angeline (Fetch) Braun, born Feb. 23, 1947;
all born in Beulah.

The Fetches are members of the Eagles Club, senior citizens group and the St.
Joseph's Catholic Church.

Bill has lived in the area all his life and grew up in the Blue Grass area
until he married in 1938. He then moved to a farm eight miles south of Beulah
in 1945. From 1938 to 1945, after he married Barbara Jacob, they farmed in
Oliver County on rented land until he purchased his farm south of Beulah in
1945.

His parents Mike and Katie came over from Russia and Germany as children and
lived around the Beulah area most of their lives. Bill grew up with the horse
and buggy trend and then came the automobile. Beulah grew right along with Bill
and changed as he did. First it was wooden sidewalks and dirt roads, and now
there are cement sidewalks and paved roads. The coal mines helped the town grow
and then came along the power plants.

William and Barbara had three children who also grew up around Beulah. They
attended country school and high school in Beulah. They are all moved now. Bill
and Barbara retired from the farm in 1976 and built a new home in Beulah.

Abraham and Maria Fischer

Abraham Fischer, a lifelong farmer, was born in Bessarabia, Russia, on Dec. 20,
1876, to John Fischer, Jr. (d. Sept. 25, 1919) and Rosina (Hoersch) Fischer (d.
Dec. 28, 1913). His parents came to America the year before he did, in 1898.
He, being 21, was forced to stay behind and serve one year in the Russian Army
before joining his parents and brothers and sisters.

Abraham hired out as a farm laborer near Parkston (also called Scotland), S.D.,
where he met his wife, Maria (b. July 2, 1882, Parkston), daughter of August
Mattheis, Jr. (d. Nov. 23, 1939) and Maria Baier Mattheis (d. 1889) . They were
married on March 24, 1907.

Abraham and Maria homesteaded three miles east of Zap, where they farmed for 20
years. "There was nothing in the early years," says Emma, now 76, the fourth
child of Abraham and Maria.

"My father got a quarter of land because of the Homestead Act. But his parents
had come to Zap the year before and that helped," continues Emma, describing
the act of making a life from nothing as a standard achievement, which, then,
it was.

"Somehow, Father got together a team of horses," she says, unsure of whether he
borrowed them, bought them, or shared them, "and later a cow. A friend gave
them, as my mother always called them, a 'cluck with some chicks.' "

Emma recalls that her childhood home was built of stone and sod. There were, at
first, two rooms and a shingled roof. Later, two more rooms were built on for
what would become a four-room house for eight people. This was home from
1907-1927. This was where all the Fischer children came into the world. Abraham
and Maria were blessed with eight children, but William (d. 1909) and Magdelina
(d. 1910) died in infancy. The remaining children were Theodore (b. 1908, Zap),
Emma Rosina (b. 1911, Zap), Rudolph August (b. 1913, Zap), Robert (b. 1916,
Zap), Amelia Regina (b. 1917, Zap) and Paulina Rebecca (b. 1919, Zap).

Emma remembers the sleeping arrangements - three to a bed, boys on one side and
girls on the other. The parents had their own room.

Abraham would talk about life in Russia, Emma says, "but we children wouldn't
listen, and so I don't remember enough. I do remember that, when we were eating
and didn't like the food, he would tell us if we were in Russia we would be
licking our plates for the hunger. People there, he would tell us, weren't able
to raise what they needed." The Fischer family raised all the vegetables they
needed for the winter for the family of eight, each summer. Things were not
that rich in Mother Russia.

Abraham was proud that he became a citizen of the United States and said many
times how this was something he had to do. It was important to him, a
validation for everything that was so difficult.

In the summertime, the children would play baseball; in the winter there was
school and chores. Emma recalls washing clothes, hanging them out to "freeze
dry" and then bringing them in to "house dry."

Christmas celebrations were spare. They didn't celebrate by gift-giving unless
it was much-needed clothing. Usually, they baked a lot, shared nuts, candy and
some fruit. Fruit, so scarce in this part of the country at that time, was the
most special gift of all.

In 19Z7, the Fischers moved three and a half miles west of Beulah. Emma married
in 1937, at 26, and moved to Beulah.

In 1938, the life work of Abraham Fischer succumbed, as did that of thousands of
other small farmers, to the Great Depression and the desolation of the Dust Bowl
years. "There were no crops in those times," says Emma. So, Abraham had a farm
auction and sold 31 years of work for just enough money to buy a house in
Beulah. "The only thing electric in the house was the lights,"' says Emma,
"until a wringer washing machine was added."

By placing a lien on the house and hiring himself out as a farm laborer once
again, Abraham, now 63, and Maria made a go of it on $11 a month. And so it was
for him until he died on Jan. 1, 1953. Maria lived until she was 94, passing
away on Oct. 11, 1976.

Of the Fischer children, Theodore married Clara Ehli. Their children were Joan,
Mavis, Larry, Betty, Shirley, Ralph, Doris, Curtis and Jerome. Emma married Emil
Heihn. Their son is Gerald (Sam) Heihn. Rudolph married Emma Soeman. Their son
is Duane Fischer. Robert married June Whiting. Their children are Sharon Johnson
and Audrey Ostrowski. Amelia married Thor Ulvestad. Their son is Steven
Ulvestad. Pauline married Charles Byrnes. Their children are Charles, Jr. and
Mary Kay.

It was a hard living for Abraham and Maria Fischer, who were perhaps among the
truest children of their times. "They had nothing special," says their fourth
child in a quiet voice. Nothing special, if one does not count great courage
and the ability to raise children who keep in close touch no matter the
distance --the youngest sister calls and writes from, as she calls it,
"Longlegs, New York," a brother and sister from Seattle, another brother from
Olympia, Wash. "Only my oldest brother (d. 1985) and I stayed to live out our
lives in North Dakota," states Emma.

        Barry Fischer family: Billy, Kim, Barry, Becky

Barry and Kim Fischer

Barry Ray Fischer was born Sept. 18, 1955, at Hazen to Ray L. and Irene
(Boeckel) Fischer.

Kim (Zachary) Fischer was born April 18, 1959, to Verlin and Sharon (De Grace)
Zachary at Tokyo, Japan.

The Fischers have two children: Becky Kim, born Nov. 29, 1980, at Bismarck and
Billy Ray, born Sept. 29, 1982, at Fort Worth, Texas.

Kim first came to North Dakota in 1972. She moved here from the Chicago area
when her family came to this area with the construction of Stanton's power
plant.

She has lived in many different states around the country and she thinks North
Dakota has a lot of advantages for people. She points out, "You have to look at
the positive to overcome many of the disadvantages." Kim still finds it
difficult to adjust to the wind and long cold winters but she says, "I think
the honesty of the people and the strong family ties are great aspects of this
area."

Barry is a rancher and Kim is a member of the All Thumbs Homemakers.

They are members of the Cornerstone Baptist Church in Beulah.

        David Fischer family

David and Mathilda Fischer

David, son of Christian and Christina (Kirshman) was born on Oct. 31, 1894, in
Nebraska. He was the eighth child of 11 born to this family.

Mrs. Fischer, Mathilda E. Kroh, was born in December 1893 at Bluegrass, ND, to
Lewis and Elizabeth Moos Kroh. She grew to womanhood in that community and was

his family and came to Bluegrass to go to confirmation school where they met.

After their marriage they farmed at Otter Creek (near Center). Mathilda
delivered mail here with horse and buggy. Here three children were also born.
They were Ruth, Reuben, and Edna (Mrs. Virgil Biloff). Next they moved to a
farm south of Zap. Here two more children were born, Ray and Eileen (Mrs. Frank
Morely). Ruth died here at this farm at the age of 12. This farm is now the
Bernhardt Flemmer farm.

Then in 1942 they moved to another farm south of Beulah. Here they farmed until
they retired and moved to Beulah in 1950. Mathilda died at the age of 63 in
1957. David then married Eva Voegele in May 1958. On May 24, 1969 David died in
a Bismarck hospital.

There are 12 grandchildren and as of this date 34 great-grandchildren, and four
great-great-grandchildren.

Reuben A. and Alma Fischer

Reuben married Alma Ballensky, who was born Nov. 2, 1927. Both her parents are
deceased; Wilhelm, Dec. 13, 1980 and Dorothy (Allmer), Feb. 17, 1965.

Clarence and Mavis Flemmer

Clarence Flemmer, a lifelong farmer, was born to Christ and Mary (Vietz)
Flemmer in Glen Ullin, N.D., on Aug. 3, 1927. His parents still reside in Glen
Ullin. Clarence's wife, the former Mavis Elaine Loewen, was born to Leonard and
Fran (nee Albers) Loewen on Nov. 8, 1937. Her parents are still living in
Hazen, N.D. Mavis has been a housewife and mother all her married life.

Together, Clarence and Mavis have had six children. Debbie, born Sept. 16, 1956;
Darcy, born June 6, 1958; Wyatt, born Feb. 27, 1960; Vicki, born March 6, 1966;
and Amy, born May 25, 1973, were all born in Hazen. Jennifer, the second-to-last
child, born Sept. 9, 1970, has the distinction of being the only Flemmer not
born in Hazen. She was born in Mandan.

Writes Mavis, "Our family formerly lived five miles north of Hazen on the
Leonard Loewen farm until 1970. Then we moved to Hazen. We lived there until
1975 when we bought the Ervin Mohl farm two and a half miles west of Beulah.

"Not having grown up in Beulah but in neighboring towns as small children, we
didn't know Beulah as it used to be. But, from 1950, when we first visited, we
found it to be a uniquely warm and friendly town. Our children adapted
especially well to Beulah. Of course, the friendly home-town attitude has
changed some with the growth in size Beulah has experienced since the building
of the plants."

Fond memories include, of course, Sunday nights at the old Roxy Theater. For a
teenager at that time (the '40s and '50s), the Roxy really was "the only show
in town. There just wasn't all that much else to do. Sunday nights were the
best. "Everybody who could afford it came, kids from Hazen and Zap. Then, there
were our youthful memories of the famous Cowboy Reunion, a two-day occurrence
around Labor Day, which still happens annually. It's always been a family
affair where cowboys compete in rodeo events and kids come to be greatly
impressed. As children, of course, we were definitely impressed. Then you grow
up and things don't excite you so much. But actually, all that's really
changed, besides the kids who grew up, is the location. The Cowboy Reunion used
to be in the park at the football field and now it has moved to the rodeo
grounds on the hill."

Then, there is the memory of Saturday nights in Beulah when everyone would come
uptown to shop and visit. Clarence shares vivid images of this. "There was a
whole different emphasis then, before Garrison Dam (1957). Beulah then on a
Saturday night was like the Fourth of July--busy. Just busy. The stores were
open until nine and 10 o'clock, people really working long hours. There was
reason to, of course, because nobody was always going up to the Lake
(Sakakawea) all the time and traveling out-of-town to shop."

He also remembers being 14 years old, sitting at the breakfast table with his
family, and hearing the news of the Japanese bombing of Pearl Harbor come over
the radio. "Course, I was just young and dumb enough not to be able to put it
all together at that moment. Mostly I just couldn't believe it. But the message
got through on Dec. 8, the day after. That's when the rationing began. That was
believable. And so were the thousands of our boys returning home without arms
and legs. I learned the meaning of the word 'appreciation' in more ways than
one," Clarence recalls.

"I was just a good ol' country boy," he continues. "I used to trap and hunt out
on the prairie back in 1941. I remember sitting on a hill at night, maybe
around Christmas, looking around me and seeing three churches and half a dozen
schoolhouses in a country mile, all lit up. That didn't happen often, except
when something special was going on. Then there were no radios--much--and no
TVs. The once- or twice-a-year special Christmas program or pie social was a
very big deal. That's when the buildings would be lit up, everyone (except
possibly the dying) came, watched the program, loved it, ate the food, and
played games until midnight. We really looked forward to this sort of event.
With those churches lit up like that, they were like a giant magnet. The closer
you got, the more you wanted to get in and be a part of the light."

Clarence feels sorry now for some of the changes that have occurred since those
times. "Things are way different," he says. "But, then, the perspective isn't
finished yet."

        Fred Flemmer

Fred K. Flemmer

When Fred Flemmer retired in 1985, it marked the end of sixty-two years of
being in business in Beulah.

The Flemmers began their business career when they opened a cream station on
Dec. 4, 1923. They had previously started a dray business but the truck burned
before they had a chance to get started.

This was the first of many business ventures. From 1925-1934 they operated a
grocery store in conjunction with the cream station. They sold Wear-U-Well
Shoes, Crosley Radios, clothing, had a hide and fur buying business, bought a
service station and bulk dealership in 1932, a cream trucking line from Grassy
Butte to Mandan on the old MKM Trail, started selling Ford cars in 1933 and
built their first garage building in 1935.

They had to put their garage and gas business on hold during WW II as gas and
tires were rationed, new cars were pulled off the market and there just wasn't
enough business. Fred kept on buying scrap iron and decided to buy Edwin Jose's
Gamble Store. Later he bought Irv Niedermeyers Economy Hardware and combined
the two which became known as The Corner Hardware which was sold to Helen and
Helmuth Hilz in 1955.

After the war, in 1947, they built a new Ford Garage, for Flemmer Sales and
Service which was sold to Henry Spier in 1952. Spier still owns it and the site
is now occupied by Pizza Galore, Magic Touch and Coal Country.

In 1955 the F.K. Flemmers, D.H. Dettmanns and Bob Keogh bought the Bank of
Beulah. Other than buying and feeding cattle this was his last business venture.

From 1969-1986 Fred lived alone in his house that he built on the old Bacal
place. Since he was always an independent person he did his own cooking and
cleaning and had a big garden out at the lake. It was a hard decision for him
to give up his home and move into the Beulah Community Nursing Home, of which
he had been a member of the organizing board.

He is the first to voice his thankfulness that there is a place to take care of
people like him who no longer can live alone.

He loves to go down to the Bank of Beulah lobby and visit with his former
customers, many of whom are the fifth generation to do business with him.

At 89 he still takes an active interest in what goes on in Beulah's business
community. He is a charter member of the Beulah Eagles and looks forward to the
times when he can go up to the club-house for an evening out with the family.

Fred has always been proud of the fact that America has been very good to this
German from Russia immigrant boy with a sixty day formal education, who became
an independent businessman, mayor of Beulah and president of a bank.

This is one of the reasons he feels so strongly about his obligation to vote
and has never missed a chance to exercise that privilege. Even as a resident of
the Nursing Home, he makes sure that someone gets him to the polls bright and
early. He has always been an avid "electioneerer" for something he believes in.

His service station and garage were always a "hot-bed" of politicking. During
the thirties when Bill Langer was in his heyday, he made a special trip to see
Fred at the gas-station to discuss their differences of opinion. Needless to
say Fred didn't change Bill Langer's views and Bill Langer didn't change Fred's.

Fred was in business in Beulah longer than any other individual.

He has seen many changes on Main Street, from a muddy country road, to graveled
highway to pavement and finally paving throughout the town. When he started in
business there were no houses beyond 2nd Street North. There were cement
sidewalks only in front of the business places in downtown Beulah and the rest
were wooden which had a tendency to move whenever there was a flood.

During the early 30's there were eight grocery stores and competition was very
keen. All the stores had to diversify in order to survive; Franks, Pitzers,
R.C.U. and Bacals all had a complete line of general Merchandise; Hubers and
Sardotz's had a fresh meat market and produce, home-made sausage, sovereigns
had confections and ice cream and they also were a member of a grocery chain,
the I.G.A. Stores.

There were more that 40 businesses in 1933. One of the messes he remembers is
when water and sewer came to Beulah in 1929. It was an especially wet year and
Main Street was one big mud hole. Many was the time when someone had imbibed a
little too much at one of the local "watering holes" and would try to cross the
street and would end up sliding into one of the open tranches, or end up
joining other merry makers in a mud fight--similar to modern day mud-wrestling.

Beulah has always had a reputation of having a lot of fun-loving practical
jokers and in those days one of the favorite jokes occurred if one
over-indulged at night. He might find himself the next morning, nicely "laid
out" in a casket in the local funeral parlor, holding a lily.

During the "dirty thirties" there were many times when farmers had absolutely no
cash and couldn't pay their spring gas bill and would pay their bill with
cattle and that was how Fred got into the cattle business.

Katharina Flemmer

Katharina Flemmer was born Aug. 18, 1902, in Gluckstal, South Russia, to Michael
and Fredericka Goetz Voegele. She immigrated to Mercer County in 1905. She
married Frederick Flemmer on Dec. 4, 1921. She and her husband moved to Beulah
in 1923 where they owned and operated a grocery store and cream station until
1934 when they sold out to Bill Froehlich. They owned many businesses in their
lifetime: A Ford agency and garage, a gas service and bulk station, a hardware
store, and finally were part owners of the Bank of Beulah.

Katharina was an excellent seamstress and could design and sew any kind of dress
without a "bought" pattern. All she needed was a picture or sketch and an old
newspaper, which she used to cut out her pattern. She was always blessed with a
green thumb. Her yards were always a showplace of flowers of every kind and
color. In later years she became an avid fisherman and spent many an hour on
the banks of Lake Sakakawea.

Katharina has two daughters, Gertie Buscher and Tillie Dettmann; four
grandchildren and eight great-grandchildren.

Since 1979 Katharina has lived in the Beulah Community Nursing Home, the Pioneer
Home at Hazen, and at present time she is a resident at Marion Manor, Glen
Ullin.

Ludwig and Bernice Flemmer

Ludwig Flemmer was born south of Beulah on Feb. 22, 1917, to Jacob W. and
Christiana (Voegele) Flemmer. Louie, as his friends call him, grew up in the
Beulah-Zap area, attended schools here, and then in April of 1942 enlisted in
the United States Army. He served three and one-half years in the Army, of
which one year and nine months were spent overseas with duty in France, England
and Germany. He took part in the D-Day operations at Normandy, France. He
received the Purple Heart. In November 1945, he was discharged.

        Louie Flemmer family

They moved to Beulah in 1950, at which time Louie worked at the Grishkowsky Coal
Mine and then did mechanic work at a garage. In April of 1956, he started work
for Mercer County, operating the maintainer, a job at which he is still
employed.

Louie and Bernice have two children, Carol, who was born in February 1947, and

        Elizabeth and Emil Frank

Emil and Elizabeth Frank

Emil Frank was born in Dodge, March 4, 1921. His father, Phillip, passed away
April 28, 1948, and his mother, Ottilie (Weidner), passed away June 6, 1936.
His wife Elizabeth (Keller) was also born in Dodge, April 8, 1924. Her mother,
Anna (Lange) passed away June 28, 1965, and her father Wilhelm passed away Jan.
7, 1950.

Emil and Elizabeth have five children: Clyde Malcolm, born Feb. 10, 1946, in
Bismarck; Thomas Gene, born July 1, 1947, in Bismarck; Robert Phillip, born
Jan. 6, 1953, in Hazen; Walter Emil, born Feb. 1, 1959, in Hazen; and Dwight
James, born April 14, 1961, in Hazen. All children attended school in Beulah.

The Franks live on a farm 14 miles south and three and a half miles west of
Beulah. They are retired but still live on the farm. Emil grew up on a farm
north of Dodge. He was 14 when his mother died, and he worked with the family
in the beet fields at Sidney, Mont., during the Depression to help make ends
meet. When Emil was old enough, he joined the Civilian Conservation Corps. He
was at Sidney, Mont., for six months and at Watford City and Medora for one
year. One of the CCC projects he helped with was to restore the Marquis De
Mores Chateau.

After coming home from the CCCs, Emil engaged in farming and trucking on a small
scale in the Dodge area. After losing the family farm, Emil's father rented a
farm south of Beulah from the Fuchs Brothers. There the family started over
again in 1942. Emil remained in the Dodge area two more years farming and
trucking before joining the family south of Beulah and continuing with trucking.

On June 2, 1944 Emil and Elizabeth were married. Due to the uncertain date of
Army induction, they stayed with Emil's father and Emil continued trucking. Emil
served in World War II from Jan. 18, 1945, to Nov. 13, 1946, serving nine months
and 10 days in the United States, one year and 17 days in the Philippine
Islands and with the occupation force in Japan after the atomic bomb was
dropped. He was a sergeant when discharged.

They then moved to Beulah where Emil worked at Fields Implement from November
1946 to November 1948 as a parts man and salesman.

Emil's father died in the spring of 1948. In November 1948 they moved to the
present farm where Emil's father farmed until he died. They also rented from the
Fuchs Brothers until 1964 when they were able to buy the farm. The family was
busy remodeling buildings, putting up fences, etc., when the heavy rains came
and flooded the farm. They had to redo all the buildings with the help of many
good friends and neighbors. This happened in June 1966, two years after the
property was purchased. There was a loss of personal property, cars and
livestock. They made their home in a nearby church that was vacant for several
months.

Emil worked for the Agriculture Stabilization and Conservation Service (ASCS) in
Beulah. He also served on the ASCS county committee and was district chairman,
member of Concordia Lutheran Church as an elder, treasurer of rural Peace
Lutheran Church (now closed and moved), member of VFW Post Beulah and post
commander for three years and district commander for two years, and a school
bus driver for the Beulah school district for six years.

Since retiring from farming, Emil likes to help with farming when needed. He
likes to putter, fix things and play cards.

Elizabeth grew up on a farm east of Dodge and graduated from Dodge High School
in 1942. She taught country school with a second grade elementary certificate
for two years in the Dodge area and three years south of Zap. She worked at the
State Hail Insurance Department in Bismarck after Emil left for the Army. She
was a member of Concordia Lutheran Church and the Lutheran Women's Missionary
League. She held the offices of president, secretary and mission service for
Naomi Guild, unit LWML president, taught Sunday school and vacation Bible
school; member of Medicine Butte Homemakers Club, held office of president,
secretary and treasurer; county Homemakers Council president, member of VFW
auxiliary; held office of secretary and was community service reporter.

Clyde and Eunice Frank live in Dickinson. Clyde graduated from Beulah High
School, National College of Business, Rapid City, S.D. and Dickinson State
College. He is a Vietnam veteran and is now employed as office manager for
Fischer Sand and Gravel in Dickinson.

Eunice (Gegelman) Frank graduated from high school at Alexander, N.D., and
Dickinson State College. She is now teaching second grade at Jefferson
Elementary in Dickinson. They have two sons, Scott and Tyler.

Thomas and Sharon live on a farm south of Beulah. Thomas graduated from Beulah
High School and Dickinson State College. After teaching in Killdeer for five
years, he started farming.

Sharon (Breen) Frank graduated from Beulah High School. She worked for Montana
Dakota Utilities in Bismarck, as an Avon saleslady in Killdeer and now works at
the Coast to Coast store in Beulah. They have three daughters: Daron Reinhardt,
Cheri and Amy.

Robert and Marlene live in Washburn. Robert was born at Hazen and graduated
from Beulah High School. He served one term in the Air Force and was stationed
in Greece. Robert is an instrument technician for United Power at Coal Creek,
Underwood.

Marlene (Stevens) Frank was born in Great Falls, Mont., and graduated from
Dawson County High School in Glendive, Mont. They have three sons: Christopher
(born in Greece), Eric and Aaron.

Walter and Leslie live in Beulah. Walter graduated from Beulah High School. He

Dwight lives south of Beulah. He was born at Hazen and attended Beulah High

        Andrew Froescher family: Myra, Andrew, Hildegard, Ramona and Lou Alice

Andrew and Hildegard Froescher

Andrew Froescher was born on June 13, 1907, at Halliday to Barbara (Sailer) and
Christian Froescher. His parents immigrated to Mannhaven, N.D., from Krem, South
Russia, and homesteaded north of Halliday. He attended grade school in Halliday
and moved to Beulah in 1927 to begin work in the Beulah coal mine.

Hildegard (Sandau) Froescher was born in Otter Creek, N.D., on June 15, 1909, to
Jacob and Magdelana (Hein) Sandau. Her parents immigrated to Otter Creek from
South Russia via Kansas City, Kansas, and Menno, S.D. The Jacob Sandau family
homesteaded at Otter Creek and later moved to Beulah, where they farmed.
Hildegard attended grade school in Beulah in the old "Scout" hall which was
located just east of the present Middle School.

Andrew and Hildegard were married in Beulah on Jan. 22, 1928, and became the
parents of a son, who died in infancy, and three daughters.

Andrew worked in the Beulah mine until 1948, when he and Hildegard took over
management of the Joachim Memorial Home for several years. he then was employed
by the Hanewald-Benz store until his retirement. He was a member of the Zion
Lutheran Church, Zion Lutheran Brotherhood and the Senior Citizen's
Organization.

Hildegard, as a housewife, baked pies and rolls for the Huber Store snack bar
for several years. She also found much enjoyment in caring for the Wilmer
Wiedrichs' children, Timothy and Twyla, and the Larry Quasts' children, Tiffany
and Phillip, after her own children were grown. She was a member of the Royal
Neighbors of America Organization and served as their recorder for eight years.
She was a member of the Zion Lutheran Church, Zion Lutheran Church Women and
the Beulah Senior Citizens Organization.

Their daughters, Lou Alice, Ramona and Myra, all attended and graduated from
Beulah High School.

Lou Alice married Herb Messmer in 1948 and they lived in Grand Forks for 32
years before returning to Beulah in 1982. Herb attended and graduated from the
University of North Dakota and served as general manager of the Northern
Equipment Supply Corp. of Grand Forks for 30 years. Lou worked at the Payroll-
Personnel office of the University of North Dakota as retirement clerk for 15
years.

They have two sons, Marc and Kevin, and a daughter, Karen. Upon returning to
Beulah, Herb took a position as buyer expeditor with the newly created synthetic
fuels company, ANG Coal Gasification Company. Lou Alice was employed in
December 1982 by the West River Telephone Co. at their Hazen office in their
accounting department.

Ramona graduated from Beulah High School in 1950. During her senior year and the
year following graduation she was employed as office secretary for Mercer County
Agent Thomas Martindale. Ramona married Ralph Johnson in 1951 and they lived on
the Albert Johnson farm southwest of Zap where Ralph was engaged in farming-
ranching along with his father, and his brother, Art Johnson.

In the fall of 1952, Ralph and Ramona moved to a farm (the former Halpern family
farm) along the Knife River southwest of Zap, where they presently live and
continue with their farm-ranch operation. For several years Ramona was the
"South Zap News" correspondent for the Beulah Independent and also the Beulah
Beacon. They have two sons, Russell and Paul, and a daughter, Randie.

Myra married Wilmer Weltz of Zap, and they lived in Riverdale, Minot, Grand
Forks and Blytheville, Ark., while Wilmer served as a civilian employee of the
U.S. Air Force. Wilmer passed away in 1981 and Myra continues to live in
Blytheville, Ark. where she is employed at the Chickasauba Hospital. They have
four daughters, Deborah, Vicki, Joleen and Diana.

In June 1978, Andrew and Hildegard celebrated their golden wedding anniversary.
Hildegard passed away in September, 1982. Andrew married in December 1984 to
Otillia Springer in Salem, Ore. They continued to live there until his death in
January 1986. Andrew and Hildegard are buried in the Beulah Cemetery.

an opening for high school principal for which I was hired." The following year
he was hired as superintendent of schools. "The support and dedication of the
staff, students and school board has made our stay rewarding," states Dale.

When asked what special memories or impressions they would have of Beulah in the
early years, Dale states, "Hectic would be the word I would use to describe the
Beulah area when we first moved here. We were involved in many meetings, studies
and reports on energy development. Presently things are operating smoothly
because of the timely planning and commitment of the community."
