Ellen G. Joos

Ellen, known as LuEllen to her early schoolmates, was born and raised on her
grandparent's farm just west of Beulah. Her parents were Edwin and Hulda Jean
England Joos.

Ellen attended the Beulah schools. Her early years were of helping her dad run
the family farm. It was a job that she loved as a young child and still does.

When World War II began in 1941, she soon followed her older brother Philip into
service, joining the WACs. Her first choice was the WAF, but due to a mix-up she
became a member of the WACs. She spent three years in that branch of the Army.
She was stationed in Texas and then in Georgia. During her service time, she
became an expert in many of the Army's weapons and she worked quite a bit with
cars and trucks. While stationed in Georgia, she earned her wings as a glider
worker, using her jeep and equipment in many of the army's exercises during the
use of gliders. The first few times, she said she nearly lost her meals.

When she returned home after the service, she returned to help her dad with the
farming. Not long afterwards, in the fall of 1947, she began working as a
postal clerk in Beulah. This job was to be a long one, as she had in
twenty-some years when she retired. She loved the postal work as her hours were
such that she could still help on the farm. When she started at the post
office, Mary Held was the postmaster. Ellen had many of the very early hours,
as at that time the mail was brought in by train, called the "galloping goose,"
which was the forerunner of the trains we have today. She had to be at the post
office around 5:30 or 6 in the morning as the train came from Killdeer at that
time, and it returned to Killdeer in the evening about 5. The mail then was
hauled from the depot by truck to the post office. This included everything,
baby chickens, freight, all sorts of parcels, packages and bags and bags of
mail. During the spring and summer it wasn't too bad, but come the holidays
during winter, the hours were long and hard.

Regardless of when the mail arrived in the evening, it still had to be put out
and this included all the junk mail. She also had to clean the sidewalk of snow
and take care of the old furnace that at times refused to cooperate in giving
out heat. Besides filling the hopper with coal, she also had to carry out the
ashes and clean the basement. Taking care of the furnace was a seven-day-a-week
job in the winter. But despite all this, Ellen says that working in the post
office was a very rewarding job. She had wonderful co-workers, like Jess and
Teresa Thompson, Albert Wallender, Clyde Stickney, who was a rural mail
carrier, and R. Schnaidt, another mail carrier. Another employee at the time was
Christ Iverson, another mail carrier.

She enjoyed meeting the public. Besides the above-mentioned postal employees
there were others whom Ellen enjoyed working with, if only briefly.

Shortly after her retirement from the post office, she began working as night
watchman at the Knife River Coal Mining Company, a job that lasted until she
retired from there. Again, she found working at something different to be
rewarding.

She still runs the family farm, enjoys fishing, and sometimes a small vacation
trip. When time permits, she says, she wants to take up golfing and bowling
again, even on a part-time basis.

She wishes the very best for the town of Beulah on its 75th birthday.

        Philip, Ellen, Lawrence Joos

Lawrence "Larry" Joos

Larry, the son of Edwin and Hulda Jean England Joos, was born and raised on the
family farm. It was said by the mid-wife who was present when he was born, that
his arrival was badly timed, as she had had a Fourth of July date with a
rancher near Beulah. So it would seem, as he always says, that his badly-timed
arrival was the start, and he still messes up the lives of others. Sometimes
good, and maybe, just maybe, not so good, it all depends on who's telling it.

Larry attended the Beulah school system and shortly after World War II broke
out, he entered the Army, following his brother and sister. He spent three
years in the service, part of which was in Italy.

When he was discharged, Larry decided to finish his schooling so in 1947 he
returned to school and at the same time he began working at the Roxy Theatre. In
1950 he graduated and from 1950 until May of 1952, he helped out on the farm and
did house painting. He still worked at the theatre at night.

In May 1952, he began working for Montana Dakota Utilities Co. at the old Beulah
Power Plant as company clerk under Lester H. Bowers, who was at that time the
chief engineer. He also worked part-time at the Jack and Jill store owned by
Mike Held. He also began working at the post office as submail carrier and
janitor. In September, 1963, he resigned his job at the theatre, a job he held
for 16 years, and worked under Mr. Ed Moe and Mr. Art Zimmerman.

When the job of mail carrier began to extend into more time than he could
muster, he resigned.

During the years he worked at the power plant, he wore out four plant chiefs.
When Lester Bowers retired after 40-some years, Edward S. Morman became the
plant chief and then later, Elroy C. Herman and lastly, Richard Dube, who later
moved to Mandan at the closing of the plant. What does Larry say about the 30
some years working at the plant.

"I think I really enjoyed all those years, because I got to meet many different
people, those that I worked with and the outside people I came in contact with
each and every day. I saw many improvements during those years, went through
one strike, had several electrical fires and in the spring, the floods. When I
began working in 1952, I became assistant to Mr. Bowers in taking care of the
weather station that was at the plant. Later I was appointed to take over the
job, which I still do from my home. I think over the 30- some odd years, I
worked with nearly a thousand different people. I was there when Eddy Morman
retired, Jack Fiergola, L.G. Murray, Herb Wolf and Paul Brenner. There were
many more. I think I felt the sadness for the employees who lost a loved one
and rejoiced when they were happy. I knew the families and became close to many
of them over the years."

During the 1960s Larry began a hobby which he hopes will begin to pay off some
day. He began writing. He has had three books published and is at present
working on a fourth.

He has a number of articles published in several nation-wide magazines, won an
honorable mention in the company magazine. In those few years, he has lectured
in several schools. It's his enjoyment of mystery writing that keeps him
plugging away at the typewriter.

He still lives on the family farm, helping out when needed.

Lorenz and Lucy Joos

Lois (Boutch) Joos) family came to the United States in 1855 and landed at
Quebec, Canada and then traveled to Wisconsin. Of the earlier Boutch's family
that were born in Poppelau, Germany, only three of the 10 children of Casper
and Hedwig Boutch lived: Lorenz, Albert and Sebastian.

Lorenz Boutch married Anna Skroch (1827-1896). They too had about 10 children,
some of whom were born in Germany. Lorenz Boutch was educated in Germany and
became a graduated blacksmith. He had two brothers, Albert, who became a
mechanic and a miller, and Sebastian, who graduated in woodwork.

When Lorenz married Anna they soon left Germany and boarded a ship in Holland.
It took them three months to cross the ocean because of unfavorable weather.
They were short on food and water and the grain used for food was buggy. They
settled in New Lisbon, Wis., for a few years. The two brothers also settled in
Wisconsin at a town called Independence, which was located along the
Trempealeau River in Trempealeau County.

        Lucy Boutch Joos

Here Albert made a mill pond for his mill, Sebastian made implements, wagons,
etc., and Lorenz made the iron parts for the mill and machinery. They also
farmed their own farms. A granddaughter of Lorenz visited the mill in 1925. It
was still operated by water power and making No. 1 refined flour. This
granddaughter again visited the mill and it was still in business in 1940,
making feed for livestock.

Lucy Boutch Joos was one of Lorenz's daughters, and she was born in Fountain
City, Wis.

In 1879 Lorenz Boutch moved his family to Jamestown, N.D. He took up a
homestead in what is now Ashland Township in Stutsman County.

When Lucy Boutch grew to womanhood, she married Lorenz Joos, son of Martin
Joos. Lorenz Joos' ancestry has been traced back to Vassar, Switzerland, to the
year 1630. The original ancestral home of the Joos family is still in the
family, and still pretty much the same after an these years, though some of the
history has been lost.

Lorenz Joos also settled in Fountain City, Wis. There is no record just when
Lucy Boutch and Lorenz Joos were married. They did have three children: baby
Louis died at birth, Philip E. was killed in World War I and Edwin, father of
Philip P. Ellen G. and Lawrence J., all still living. Edwin died in 1962 after
a lengthy illness. He is buried in Jamestown.

A church was built in 1887 in Fried, N.D. Lucy Boutch Joos' father was the
custodian of the church. It was called Sacred Heart Church of Fried. The first
mass was held on May 3, 1887. The church celebrated its 100th anniversary on
June 14, 1987.

        Philip, Lorenz, Lucy Joos

Lorenz and Lucy Joos lived in Fried for a time and then moved to Jamestown where
they operated a County "Poor Farm.' Later they moved west to the coast and then
returned to North Dakota after a few months. After a short time they moved to
Beulah in the early 1900s and moved to a farm west of the town. Lorenz operated
the farm with his sons until World War I began and his son Philip was called
into service. He was killed in France just before the war was over. Edwin Joos
worked the farm during this time. During the early years of Beulah, Grandfather
Lorenz also operated a hardware store, where the Coast to Coast now stands. The
upstairs of the store was often used for church services and other meetings.
Shortly before he died he sold the store and business to L.G. Rose, who
operated it for many years. Some of the supplies Grandfather Lorenz sold
included cream separators, farm equipment and windmills, some of which are
still in the country along with water pumps.

Lorenz Joos died in 1931. Grandmother Lucy still farmed with the help of her son
Edwin and grandchildren. She raised a big garden, raised chickens and milked
cows, from which she made butter to sell and cottage cheese. She raised her
grandchildren. She knew many of the old-time healing cures and used them often
on her family. She passed away in 1941, just before the start of World War II.

It was her wish not to live through another war, especially since her
grandchildren were getting to that age. She died about six months after her
brother, Richard D. Boutch of Jamestown, and a few weeks after her sister, Anna
Boutch DeMers of Oregon.

Lorenz and Lucy Joos' son Edwin soon met and married Hulda Jean England in 1918
or 1919.

        Katherine and John George Karlin

Johann Georg and Katherine Karlin

Johann Georg Karlin was born in 1859 in Friedenstahl, Preussen. His family came
to America and settled in Nebraska. From there they moved to Tripp, SD, where he
married Katherine Heihn.

The children of this marriage were Martha (Mrs. David Betz), Ida (Mrs. Jack
Arlt), George, Rudolph, Jacob, and Emil, all born in South Dakota.

In 1896 they moved to Decatur, TX, where they purchased land from a land dealer
who, unknown to them, was unscrupulous and did not legally own the land. They
lived in Decatur long enough to plant and harvest a cotton crop. While on this
farm, one child, Katie, was born and died. The family was ordered off the land
at gunpoint by the legal owner.

From Texas they moved to Scotland, SD, where Mathilda (Mrs. John Sagmiller) was
born.

In 1901 Johann and his son-in-law, David Betz, came to North Dakota to file
homestead claims near the Knife River southeast of Beulah.

They returned to South Dakota and began moving the family to North Dakota in
September 1902. They arrived in North Dakota in November with three covered
wagons and a herd of cattle and horses. Martha Betz (with a two-month-old child,
Henry) and her sister Ida drove one wagon while Johann, Rudolph, George, Jacob
and David Betz drove the other two wagons, cattle and horses. On the journey
they encountered a prairie fire that stretched for miles. They ran the herds
and the wagons through the fire line. Ida, who was on foot, wrapped her head in
her shawl and ran through it also.

The family forded the Missouri at Bismarck. The wagons were ferried across, but
the livestock had to be forced to swim across and several cows and calves
drowned.

The Karlin-Betz family arrived so late in the year that there was no time to
build shelters. They spent the winter with Carl Heihn Sr. (Mrs. Karlin's
father) and Jacob Isaac. The next spring they moved to their homesteads four
miles southeast of Beulah and built sod houses.

One of the Karlin sons, Jacob, ran a livery stable in Beulah for several years
beginning in 1913.

        Lydia and Emil Karlin

As of this writing the only living member of the Johann Karlin family is Emil,
age 94, living in Missoula, MT. Emil is a World War I veteran. During World War
II he worked at an airplane repair plant in Utah where he mended airplane
fuselages damaged by bullets.

Otto and Alma Kasper

Otto Kasper was born March 24, 1917, in Beulah. His father Franz passed away

Edward A. and Mollie Kees

Edwin Andrew Kees of Minneapolis went to Expansion, N.D. in 1911, where he
joined his brother Walter Charles Kees in operating The Security State Bank. He
married Mollie Peterson of Montevideo, Minn., in 1915. They lived in Expansion
for several years and had sons Harvey Mathias in 1916 and Lowell Edwin in 1917.

After World War I, the bank was moved to Krem and eventually closed when the
early towns of Krem and Expansion found it too difficult to compete with the
thriving new railroad cities, such as Beulah and Hazen. The family continued
with operating The First State Bank of Beulah during the 1920s, with Walter
Charles Kees eventually continuing banking at Ollie, Mont., and The Bank of
America in California. Edwin Andrew Kees remained with the Beulah bank until it
was forced to close by a "run on the bank" in the mid-1920s.

Thereafter, the family ran the Milligan Hotel (Rooms: $1 per night) on Main
Street in Beulah for several years, and Edwin Andrew Kees conducted a real
estate, insurance and investment business until his retirement in 1959. He also
served several terms as Beulah village clerk and as justice of the peace. He
moved to Saint Paul, Minn., for retirement and died in 1967 at almost 90 years.
His wife Mollie also died in St. Paul, in 1966, at 92.

The sons Harvey Mathias and Lowell Edwin withstood all 12 grades of the Beulah
public schools, and both graduated from the University of North Dakota in the
late 1930s. Harvey became a radio engineer, serving at Harvard University Radio
Research Laboratory during World War II and in other research and development
activities thereafter, Lowell became an accountant, served with the U.S. Army
in the Pacific Theater during World War II and retired from the Minnesota
Highway Department as auditor.

Harvey M. Kees now lives at Route 2, Poseyville, IN 47633, phone 812-874-2873;
Lowell E. Kees, 11077 West Forest Home Avenue, Apt. N106-36, Hales Corners, WI
53130, phone 414-425-1857.

        Joe Keller, and his invention - fence post remover.

Joe and Elaine Keller

Joe Keller, son of Mike and Mary (Goldade) Keller, was born on Feb. 4, 1934, in
western Oliver County. There were nine children in the family: seven boys,
Sylvester, victor, Ralph, Joe, Pius, Wilhelm and Francis; the two sisters were
Barbara and Loretta. Elaine, daughter of Joe and Frances (Weiand) Schumacher,
was also born in western Oliver County on March 7, 1940.

Joe and Elaine were married Aug. 26, 1957, at St. Benedict's Catholic Church
south of Beulah. Joe continued to farm with his father until they purchased the
family farm in 1962.

Their two children are Julian, born Feb. 16, 1958, and Melissa, born Oct. 13,
1972. Julian married Shelly Boschee from Glen Ullin on June 11, 1982, at St.
Joseph's Catholic Church in Beulah. They have one daughter, Angela Rose, born
July 1, 1986. Julian is service manager for Bergstedt Implement, Hazen. He also
plays drums with the band Midnight Ride.

Melissa is a freshman at Beulah High School. She was a cheerleader for girls'
basketball and participates in the choir. In track her events are sprints, 100-
and 200-meter run plus the 400-meter relay.

Joe has had many interests in addition to farming. He studied music at an early
age. From age 16 he played guitar for countless wedding dances, public dances,
at bars and nightclubs and for barn dances around the country. Joe served on
the Burt school board and the St. Benedict church board. He has served on the
Beulah Farmers Union Elevator Board for 25 years.

Joe has loved hunting and fishing all his life. Since there was no fishing
available nearby, he decided to build a dam large enough to stock with fish. In
1964 the Keller Dam was constructed. It was stocked with large-mouth bass and
bluegills in 1965. It has provided good fishing for countless fishermen. In
addition, the State Game and Fish Department uses stock from the dam to supply
other lakes around the state every five years.

In 1982 Joe and Elaine took an interest in state politics. The District 33
Democratic Non-Partisan League endorsed Joe for the North Dakota House of
Representatives. He was elected to represent Oliver and Mercer Counties. During
the 1983 session he served on the house agriculture and judicial committees. In
1984 he was re-elected for a second House term. Joe won the Senate seat from
District 33 in 1986. That session he was on the labor committee. Interim
assignments included the house judicial process committee dealing with marital
properties and uniform laws plus the senate job development committee.

The Kellers recently formed a family operation, Keller Enterprises. officers
are Joe Keller, chairman; Elaine Keller, secretary; and Julian Keller,
treasurer. Their main product is the newly patented Keller Post Puller. The
invention has been exhibited at the Jamestown Inventors' Congress and at the
Capitol during North Dakota Inventor and Entrepreneur Week. The puller has been
featured in local and state newspapers. Articles have appeared in Dakota
Farmer, North Dakota REC/RTC and Farm Industry News.

        Susan Keller

Susan Keller

Susan, a resident of the Beulah Community Nursing Home, says she is as happy
there as she would be anywhere. "What more could I want?" was her cheerful
response. Her friends claim she has used hundreds of miles of yarn as she
crochets everything from afghans to doll clothes for charitable purposes and
for those who love her. Her hands are always busy, and that is the story of her
life, "busy."

Susan's parents, the Jake Hipfners, homesteaded some 14 miles north of Beulah at
the turn of the century. There she was born the fourth of 12 children, eight
girls and four boys.

When asked what Beulah was like way back then she said, "I really wouldn't know.
We were a big family and when we did leave home it was with a horse and buggy.
Our outings were to church, many miles away as we went to St. Benedict's Church
which is about 15 miles south of Beulah. We crossed the river at the low places.

"I made my first communion and was confirmed there. My sister and I stayed with
friends of my parents and took our religious instructions. We knew some of these
families well as they were friends of my parents before they came to America. We
attended a country school near us, but I finally had to quit as mother needed
help at home," she says.

When Susan was 18 she married Joseph Goldade. The families were friends and it
was not uncommon for parents to plan the wedding for their children. Susan said
she really didn't mind as she didn't really know any other young men. Susan and
Joseph bought a farm of their very own south of Beulah from Carmichael, the
veterinarian. There were times that crops were poor and there went the cream
money.

Money was scarce, but they managed to buy two more quarters of land and replaced
the small two-room house with a four-bedroom home which had a furnace. Susan
and Joseph had 10 children: Florence, Steve, Pauline, Ida, Clementine, Jake,
Marian, Helen, Anne and Marlene--all born at home, except Marlene when Susan
said, "I'm having this one in the hospital."

Farm life was not easy in those days. This little lady had to be tough as just
doing the laundry was a chore. The water was carried from the well, heated on a
coal stove, used for washing and carried out again. The dryer was the outdoor
clothesline.

Susan advanced from a washboard to a hand-powered washer, then the luxury of a
washer with a gas motor which she bought with her "turkey money." There was no
refrigeration, butchering was done twice a year, and the meat was canned or
salt-packed. A used Singer sewing machine which cost $5 saw many useful years
as she sewed most of the clothes for her family.

Although milking, gardening, canning, stacking hay, shocking grain, raising
poultry and caring for the family seemed like a 24-hour job, Susan found time
to enjoy friends with her children and Joseph as they entertained or visited at
other homes. Usually someone played the accordion at these parties. St.
Benedict's annual carnival was another festive event for the family.

This home had room for one more and Joseph's mother, now in poor health, came to
live with them for six years. She spent 10 months as a bed patient and died at
the age of 95. Naturally she was in need of much care and attention. "I don't
know how I did it, but I had to. The children spent many hours playing outside
so as not to disturb Grandma.

"I thank the Good Lord that my children were healthy and had good marriages,"
said Susan.

Farming came to an end for the Goldades as they moved to town and bought a
house in Beulah. Joe, a World War I veteran, began to have health problems and
died in 1955.

It was Susan's nature to be ever busy and she found a way. There were no school
buses at that time and rural high school students stayed in town during the
week. She provided room and board for so many that she found it hard to keep
track. It was like cooking for a threshing crew every day as those boys had a
hearty appetite.

Soon she began caring for children. How fortunate the home was that had Mrs.
Goldade. She was a dear mother and friend. The delightful German dishes,
especially fleischkuechle, kuchen and pfeffernusse pleased everyone.

After being alone for about 10 years Susan married her long-time friend, Mike
Keller. Russell just said, "How come he is so lucky to get her?" He was lucky.

It was a happy marriage and their companionship and sharing many hobbies lasted
15 years. Mike became ill with terminal cancer and she gave him constant and
efficient care. Following Mike's death things were not the same, as she
developed some health problems and was lonely. She and her daughters decided
that she should move to the nursing home where more care was available, as well
as friends and companions.

June 1987 marked Susan's 85th birthday, and her children honored her with an
all-day celebration. Besides many friends and relatives, brother Joe and
sister Theresa were there, too.

Susan, an ever faithful Catholic, feels the Good Lord watches over her and
helps time pass pleasantly, and God's will has made her life what it is.

        Walter and Katie Keller

Walter and Katherina Keller

Walter Keller was born Feb. 27, 1906 to Gottlieb and Emma (Fischer) Keller on
the family homestead, where he grew to manhood attending the Keller School and
later farming with his father. As a young lad on the farm he did a lot of
rabbit and coyote hunting. He reloaded his own shells. The days on the farm
were not all this carefree, for his father was a hard worker and expected the
same from his son. As a young man he started helping and later operated a
threshing rig. Walter did this for 30 consecutive years, including the year
that his leg was in a cast.

On Dec. 2, 1928, he married Katherina Becker on the family homestead north of
Beulah. The Rev. S. Joachim officiated. Katherina was born March 12, 1908, to
Henry and Elizabeth (Voegele) Becker. As a young girl she attended the nearby
Klundt School. Katie's mother died when she was only eight years old. Her father
later married Karolina Voegele who died when Katie was 15 years old and she
assumed the responsibility of managing the Becker home with the help of her
brothers and sister, Ann. This she did until she married.

Walter Keller's family lived on the Gottlieb Keller home place. They did not
live with the senior Kellers though, for they each had their own home. Walter
farmed with his father until 1948 when his father retired and Walter took over
the management and operation of the farm. They raised grain crops and Hereford
cattle. Walter's pride and joy was his farm workshop where he spent the winter
months repairing his own and the neighbor's machinery, cars, trucks, tractors
or whatever was in need of repair.

Walter served 26 years on the school board. His family were members of Zion
Lutheran Church at Beulah. The Kellers had four children: Ivan, living on the
family farm; Violet (Mrs. Marvin Schnaidt); Judy (Mrs. Wilbur Elder); and
Larry, all living at Beulah. There are eight grandchildren and nine
great-grandchildren. Katie passed away Oct. 31, 1975, and Walter passed away
Aug. 26, 1977.

Kessler family history

In the early 1890s, Lorenz and Rosina (Geist) Kessler and their daughter, Lydia,
emigrated from Gluckstal, Odessa, Russia to America and settled 18 miles south
of Eureka, SD. This is where their two sons, John and Herman were born. In 1899
they moved to Mercer County to an area six miles north of present-day Beulah,
which was open for homesteading. They built a three room sod house and broke
sod for farming. Since Beulah was not yet established, their address was Krem,
ND, where they also did their trading. They prospered on their homestead until
Lorenz died of an injury.

Lorenz Kessler was born Jan. 14, 1862 and died Nov. 16, 1918. Rosina Kessler was
born May 25, 1863 and died April 17, 1930. Both rest at Zion Lutheran Cemetery
at Beulah. They were parents of three children: Lydia (Mrs. Gottleib Teske),
John and Herman. Herman remained on his parents' homestead until about 1935
when he moved into Zap. Later Herman moved to Spokane, WA, where his wife,
Lydia Hagel died in 1975 and Herman in 1984.

John Kessler was born July 5, 1894, at Eureka, SD, to Lorenz and Rosina (Geist)
Kessler. He was married on July 9, 1916, to Lydia Beck. Lydia was born near
Odessa, Russia on June 20, 1896, to John and Matilda (Ott) Beck. John farmed an
adjacent farm to his parent's homestead where Bertha and Elizabeth were born.
In 1921, they sold the farm and moved to Beulah where Emma was born. Later the
family moved to the strip mine at Zap and in 1928, they bought the Bower farm
three and one-half miles west of Beulah. They farmed there until 1941 when they
moved to the Nefstad place. After retiring from farming they moved into Beulah.

They were parents of three daughters and five granddaughters. Bertha was born
July 20, 1917, and married Julius Orth in 1941. She lives at Beulah. Elizabeth
was born Nov. 15, 1918, and married Ace Kusler in December 1941. Ace passed
away in 1982. She makes her home in Beulah. Emma was born Oct. 14, 1925 and
married Frances Fitzgerald. They live in Bismarck and have five daughters;
Joan, Cinthia, Debra and the twins, Fay and Faith.

John Kessler died Sept. 14, 1974, and Lydia Kessler died on July 26, 1954.

Otto and Phyllis Kessler

Otto Kessler was born on March 24, 1912 to George and Karolina Kessler. He was
born on the family farm north of Beulah and was the youngest of eight children:
George Jr. (deceased), Mrs. Fred (Christine) Saeman, Rosa (died at the age of
10), Jake (deceased), Christ and Fred (both residing in Beulah), Mrs. Pius
(Lydia) Usselman of Hazen and Otto of Beulah.

Otto's father passed away in 1945 of a heart attack at the age of 78. His mother
passed away in 1952 at the age of 83.

Otto was educated at a country school two miles north of Beulah. In 1935, he
married Phyllis Hipfner. They made their home on a farm four miles northeast of
Beulah. They spent their working years farming. They were blessed with two
children, Norman and Ardella. Ardella was born in 1938 and Norman in 1940. They
were raised and educated in Beulah and later graduated from Beulah high school.

As a young boy, Otto recalls the many times they rode to the Knife River on
horseback to go fishing and swimming. Later on, he enjoyed going to baseball
games and dancing at the Sheep Shed.

Times were tough for many. Otto tells how they brought eggs and cream to town to
sell. In return, they bought their groceries which would last for one week. One
3-gallon can of cream brought them $1.50. Otto can't recall what the eggs sold
for, but it was very little as everybody sold eggs at that time.

The mining operations were very different in those days. Everything was
underground. The horses had to be backed into the pit to load the coal and
sometimes that was a very lengthy ordeal as horses, like people, like to know
where they are going.

In 1957, Otto and Phyllis gained a son-in-law when their daughter, Ardella,
married Jerome Miller, son of the Otto Millers of Hazen. Jerome and Ardella
have two adopted daughters, Ruby and Amy, and one grandson, Joshua. All are
living on the family farm north of Hazen where they farm and raise cattle.

In 1963, a daughter-in-law was gained when Norman married Kathy Albers, daughter
of Emil Albers of Hazen. Norman and Kathy have six children, Charles, Melissa,
Tom, Lori, Karen and Mary. They have one grandson, Braden. Norman and Kathy
reside in Fessenden where Norman manages the ASCS office.

In 1970, Otto and Phyllis sold their farm and moved into Beulah. Phyllis passed
away in October of 1981 after a two-year battle with cancer.

In October of 1983, Otto married Alice Running of Hazen who had been widowed
since 1980. Her husband was the late Oliver Running. Former residents of
Columbus, ND, they moved to Hazen in 1967 when Oliver was transferred
to Glenharold Mine, Stanton.

Alice has a family of seven children: Mrs. Mertie (Roberta) Stompro, Randy
Running, and Mrs. Greg (Beth) Loken, all of Watford City; Mrs. Vern (Vicki)
Oakum of West Virginia; Mrs. Jim (Beryl) Dschaak of Roundup, MT; Mrs. Myron
(Denice) Mutzenberger and Mrs. Bill (Tami) Thomas, both of Hazen. Alice has 10
grandchildren and five step-grandchildren.

Otto and Alice made their home in Hazen until 1986, when they moved to Beulah
and rented an apartment. In 1987, they bought the former Fred Renner house. They
are very happy and lead very busy lives. They are active members of Zion
Lutheran Church in Beulah. They enjoy dancing and playing cards and fishing.
They are active members of the Beulah Eagles and Auxiliary and Golden Eagles
and they are members of the Beulah Senior Citizens.

Edwin and Jeannette Kittler

Edwin Kittler was born May 5, 1948, at Hazen to John G. and Edna (Brunmeier)
Kittler. "Ed" has always lived in Beulah and is now an accountant at Basin
Electric. On Sept. 6, 1975, he married Jeannette Raszler. Jeannette was born
Jan. 23, 1952, at Hazen to Otto and Agnes (Schopp) Raszler. Jeannette grew up
southeast of Beulah on her parents' farm. She remained in Bismarck after her
graduation from Bismarck Junior College until her marriage. She now is employed
by the Bank of Beulah. They are parents of one daughter, Kimberly Jeanne, born
Oct. 23, 1984. They are members of Zion Lutheran Church where Ed has served for
19 years on the church finance committee. Both are members of Beulah's chapter
of Germans from Russia. Ed is a member of the Beulah Eagles Club, and Jeannette
is on the Beulah Girl Scout finance committee.

        Edwin, Kimberly and Jeannette Kittler

Ed writes, "I have many fond memories of growing up in Beulah. I remember the
quiet Sundays and observed holidays where you had a quieter and closer
fellowship and companionship with your family and friends. I remember when all
the stores were open for business on Saturday nights. It seemed like everyone
shopped that night. How about the Beulah Drug soda fountain? My, how tasty the
muds, sodas, etc., were! I remember the old Sheep Shed. I remember the German
language being spoken a lot by everyone and of course German church services. I
remember the old Main Street and how it has improved in appearance and number
of businesses. I remember us being a small town which has now grown with more
businesses and more residents. This tells us that Beulah is a wonderful city
with wonderful people working together.

        Edna and John Kittler

John G. and Edna Kittler

John G. Kittler was born May 10, 1920, at Golden Valley to John and Magdalena
(Meissel) Kittler. His parents were born in Alt Arzis, Bessarabia, Russia, and
came to Mercer County to homestead in 1904. His father died July 1, 1962, and
his mother June 9, 1939. John G. Kittler married Edna Brunmeier on Feb. 23,
1947, in Hazen. Edna was born June 25, 1919, at Krem to Christ and Lydia
(Schimke) Brunmeier. Her father was born in Lincoln, Neb. and died Nov. 26,
1972. Her mother was born at Krem and died July 8, 1979.

John and Edna Kittler lived in Golden Valley prior to moving to Beulah in 1948.
John worked in the underground coal mine in Beulah until the day it shut down.
He retired with Burlington Northern Railroad and is presently working part time
for the city of Beulah. They are members of Zion Lutheran Church. They are
parents of two sons: Edwin, born May 5, 1948, at Hazen, married Jeannette
Raszler of Hazen. They have one daughter, Kimberly. Wilmer was born May 9,
1953, at Hazen and married Diane Scherr of Modesto, Calif. They have one son,
Lucas.

Scott and Julie Knodel

Scott Knodel, the son of Ted and Clara Knodel, grew up on his parents' farm in
Bowden, N.D. He graduated from Bowden High School in 1966 and went on to
graduate from Moler Barber College in Fargo in 1967 and barbered in Bowden,
Sykeston, Garrison and Pettibone while helping out on the family farm. He
served in the U.S. Army as a Spec. 4 from August 1970 until February 1972 and
was stationed at Anchorage, Alaska.

After completing his tour of duty he returned to the family farm and worked in
the fertilizer department of GTA in Fessenden until moving to Beulah in
December 1973 to work in the fertilizer department of Farmers Union Oil
Company. He also worked for Mann's Automotive from 1977-78 when he was employed
by Knife River Coal Mining Company as the storekeeper/warehouse manager at the
Beulah mine.

He is involved in athletics through refereeing girls' volleyball and basketball
and coaching community soccer. He is a member of the parish council and choir
at St. Joseph's Catholic Church.

Julie, the daughter of Clifford and Blanche Cossettte, grew up in Fargo, N.D.
and graduated from Shanley High School in 1969. She received her associate
degree in nursing from NDSU in 1971 and began work as a registered nurse at St.
John's Hospital in Fargo and Bethany Homes until moving to Beulah in 1975.
Scott and Julie were married in June 1975. Julie was employed as director of
nursing at the Beulah Community Nursing Home from June 1975 until January 1984.
She then worked as a part-time staff nurse until October 1985 when she started
working for Home Care Services as branch supervisor for Mercer County.

Julie is a member of the Sunflower Homemakers, Beulah Women's Aglow, a member
of the advisory board for Home Health Care at St. Alexius Medical Center, and
has served on the parish council of St. Joseph's Catholic Church.

Scott and Julie have three children: Janine and Jared, twins, born April 25,
1976. Both attend the Beulah middle school and are in the sixth grade. Jared
has been involved in city soccer and baseball teams since age five. Janine has
been involved with the Performing Arts School of Dance and taken piano lessons
for four years. Jacob was born June 17, 1987.

Edward E. and Brenda Kraft

Edward E. Kraft was born in Mobridge, SD on May 12, 1953 to Casper and Catherine
Kraft. He grew up in the Mobridge area and married Brenda Newman, also of
Mobridge, and daughter of Ole and Donna Newman.

Ed worked for the Montana Dakota Utilities Company of Mobridge until the plant
closed. He and Brenda then went into business for themselves for two
and-one-half years until Ed decided he preferred power plant work. An opening
at the old MDU plant in Beulah brought the Krafts to this area, which they now
very happily call home.

Ed is very involved in softball, basketball, tennis and is a cable TV watcher.
Brenda is a piano teacher and full-time mother of four children: Heather Dawn,
born in 1975 in Mobridge; Kevin Edward, born in 1977 in Mobridge; Hayley Marie,
born in 1982 in Hazen; and Todd James, born in 1986 in Bismarck.

The family has grown very fond of the Beulah area and has special memoires here
since two of the children were born here. The most precious times they have had
have been in raising the children, and with Brenda teaching piano lessons, the
opportunity to stay home and be a full-time mom has been greatly enriched.

        Leonard Krausz family. Back row: Dianne, Judy, Shirley, Donna. Seated:
        Yvonne, Leonard, Hilda, Richard.

John and Katharina Krausz

John Krausz was born in Alt Fridenstahl, South Russia on Oct. 16, 1893, to John
and Susan (nee Moser) Krausz. He had a brother Richard, born in 1895, and a
sister Eimlie, born in 1897. John's father passed away in 1897 when John was
only four years of age. His mother later married Jacob Schlecht who was a
widower with six children.

At the age of 16, John along with his step sister Elizabeth, who later became
Mrs. Fred Rueb (nicknamed Luisa), decided to go to America. So on May 8, 1910,
they bid their parents and family good-bye and set out for the strange new land.

They were to find out later that on that very same night baby sister Barbara
came into this world. John arrived in Hebron on June 22, 1910, and went to live
with a farmer southwest of Zap, named Pete Neumiller. Since John was too young
to take up homesteading, he worked at various jobs around and in the Mercer
County area working for such people as: Emil Klundt, J. Schlichenmeyer, August
Ziemann, Karl Heihn and Jake Heihn's Livery Stable. He then began operating his
own farm and was married to Katharina Rueb.

        Krausz family: Leonard, Oscar, Emilie, Erma. Seated: John and
        Katherina Krausz.

Katharina Rueb was born in Hoffnungsthal, South Russia, on June 10, 1895, to
Fredrick and Charlotta (nee Schopp) Rueb. In 1905 Katharina came to the United
States with her parents and arrived on Nov. 20, 1905. They lived in Velva until
August of 1906 when they moved to Mercer County and took up a homestead just
east of the area which later became known as Beulah.

John and Katharina were married on Dec. 1, 1974, at the Zion Lutheran Church of
Beulah by Pastor J. Mau and were the first couple to be married in the new
wooden church. They farmed north of Beulah for 11 years on land which they
rented from Christ Frist. Then they moved to a farm east of Beulah which they
purchased from George Karlin in October of 1924.

In January, 1950, they retired from active farming and moved into the town of
Beulah where they resided at 104 4th Ave. NW. John Krausz served on the town
board for years. John and Katharina celebrated their Golden Wedding Anniversary
in 1964 the same year that the city of Beulah celebrated its golden jubilee.
They were married 66 years when John passed away on July 26, 1981. Katharina
lived alone until April, 1983, when she moved to the Beulah Community Nursing
Home where she lived until Jan. 1, 1985 when she passed away.

John and Katharina were members of the Beulah Congregational Church.

Leonard and Hilda Krausz

Leonard R. Krausz was born Sept. 17, 1919, north of Beulah to John and Katherina
(Rueb) Krausz. The first four years of his childhood were spent on the Christ
First farm located northeast of Beulah. Later his parents moved onto the George
Karlin farmstead east of Beulah. In October, 1924 John and Katherina bought
their homestead. Here Leonard attended rural school and grew into his manhood.
In November, 1942, he enlisted in the U.S. Army.

He married Hilda Winkler on Aug. 30, 1943, at Marysville, CA, where he was
stationed.

Hilda Winkler was born Jan. 12, 1924, south of Beulah to Albert Sr. and Eva
(Nies) Winkler. She was raised and attended rural school south of Beulah.

Leonard and Hilda lived in Brownwood, TX, until Leonard went overseas. Then
Hilda came home and stayed with her parents. When Leonard returned to the United
States on July 23, 1945, Hilda went to stay with her husband at Camp Boye, CA
until his discharge on Nov. 1, 1945.

In Feb. 1946 Leonard and Hilda returned to Beulah, where they spent the rest of
the winter with Leonard's parents. In the spring of that year they established
their own farmstead where Leonard resides and farms today.

Leonard and Hilda were blessed with six children: Shirley, born Oct. 9, 1944,
graduated from Beulah High School and attended one year of college at Dickinson
State College. She married Lorence Christmann on Oct. 5, 1963. They had no
children and died together in a tragic traffic accident on Nov. 2, 1981.

Richard, born July 29, 1946, attended rural school and graduated from the eighth
grade. He worked for local farmers in the area and held odd jobs until he left
Beulah in 1975. He presently resides in Utah with his wife Margie.

Dianne, born Aug. 1, 1948, graduated from Beulah High School and married Donald
R. Tesky on June 9, 1967. They have four children; Leonard, Bradley, Lorie and
Becky. The Tesky residence is located in the Beulah area just east of the city
limits.

Judy, born Nov. 19, 1949, graduated from Beulah High School, Josef's School of
Hair Design and passed her state board test in the fall of 1968. She married
Brian Langmaack on June 6, 1969 and they presently reside with their two sons,
Kelly and Corey, in Ontario, CA.

Donna, born Oct. 17, 1951, graduated from Beulah High School and Josefs' School
of Hair Design and passed her state board test in the fall of 1972. She married
Douglas E. Lindquist Sept. 24, 1977 and she is employed at the Beulah Community
Nursing Home in Beulah and resides in Hazen with her husband and two children,
John and Kathrina.

Yvonne, born Jan. 4, 1957, attended Beulah Schools until 1974, then she
completed her high school education by night school and graduated in 1979.
Yvonne married David Entzel July 17, 1976. David is presently employed at North
American Coal and they reside in Beulah with their two children, Melissa and
Scott.

Leonard and Hilda were members of the Beulah Congregational Church. Leonard is a
VFW lifetime member of Herman Schmidt Post 7759 and Hilda was a member of the
VFW Auxiliary.

Hilda passed away on Dec. 26, 1984. Leonard resides on the farmstead where he is
still engaged in farming and occupies himself in the winter time by hauling coal
locally.

Edwin Robert and Freda Krieger

"Eddie" Krieger was born on Oct. 26, 1915, in rural Stanton to Fred and Matilda
(Lauf) Krieger. The elder Kriegers lived in Hazen, Zap, and, lastly, Beulah.
Fred passed away in April of 1966, Matilda in November of 1978.

Freda is the daughter of George and Christina (Flemmer) Unruh, born Nov. 28,

her father, October, 1979. The elder Flemmers were formerly residents of Zap.

Eddie lived in rural Stanton, moving to Hazen as a young child, then to Zap. He

duty including Alaska, Texas, Hawaii and 15 months overseas. He returned to
Beulah, where he presently resides with Freda. Eddie and Freda have two

Eddie has been a tavern owner in Beulah for 29 years, first owning the Mirror

spent 10 years as a Tupperware dealer.

Freda writes, "We are members of Zion Lutheran Church, charter members of
Eagles, VFW and the Women's Auxiliary, the Elks in Dickinson, and the American
Legion. We have, for 40-some years, been members of the Beulah Country Club.

"For our children, Beulah was a great place, a good school system, a clean and
safe city."

        Kruckenbergs: Michael, Claudia, Dwight, Curtis Kruckenberg

George A. and Martha Kuch

George A. Kuch was born Jan. 23, 1906, at Hannover to Karl M. and Pauline
(Schulz) Kuch. His father died Aug. 7, 1960, and his mother died March 21,
1971. They later lived at Hazen. George Kuch was married at Hazen on Jan. 27,
1929, to Martha Rose Nei. Martha was born Sept. 17, 1905, at Mannhaven to
Ludwig "Louie" and Lydia (Huber) Nei. Her father was born Sept. 10, 1876, and
died April 23, 1954. Her mother was born July 12, 1886, at Menno, S.D., and
died Aug. 24, 1957. After their marriage George and Martha Nei moved to Zap
where George had a barber shop and Martha gave piano lessons. While in Zap all
three of their children were born.

In 1945 they moved to Beulah and purchased a barber shop. The living quarters
behind their shop was their home, which was located where Coast to Coast Store
is today. Around 1948 they bought the Variety Store on the corner (where
Sveum's is located today) and shortly after they moved the Variety Store in the
building where George had barbered. The Variety Store was sold to Mr. Art
Tabert in 1952 or 1953. George was a member of the Lions Club and a deacon at
Zion Lutheran Church. Martha was organist at Zion Lutheran Church and pianist
for the Ladies Aid and many town functions. Martha died of cancer on April 22,
1954, a day before her father died, and is buried at Zion Lutheran Cemetery at
Beulah.

George married Helen (Faut) Kramer in 1955 and they moved to Mott, where he

        John Kusler family Jim, Johnell, John, Alma, Milda, Jerry

John and Alma Kusler

John and Alma Kusler both grew up in the Beulah area. John was born Oct. 17,
1908 to Emanuel and Louisa (Schrink) Kusler. Alma Buechler was born May 31,
1910 in Canada to Christ and Helen Buechler. The Kuslers lived in Beulah; the
Buechlers in Zap. They were married Nov. 5, 1933, in a double wedding with
Alma's sister, Kay, marrying John's brother, Paul. Alma and John began their
life together moving to a farm south of Beulah, where they still have a home
today and which is now farmed by John and his son, Jim.

Alma and John's life together was affected almost immediately by the drought and
Depression. In 1934 John went to work for six years in the underground coal
mines while Alma managed the farm.

Both John and Alma have been extensively involved in community service and
activity during their lives. John was involved in the organization of the
Farmers Union Education Association, serving as chairman of the county
committee for a number of years. He also held the office of chairman of the
local school board for 10 years and was a director of the Aplin telephone
company for some years. In the late '40s John became involved in the
reorganization of the Beulah Farmers Elevator into the Farmers Union
Elevator, which he then served as chairman of the board for over 20 years. His
service as chairman of the board of the Farmers Union Oil Company of Beulah
also extended over 20 years.

During these years Alma became involved in the work of the Farmers Union
Association, the local 4-H program and was a charter member of the Aplin
Homemakers Club. She has been a member of the Aplin club for over 40 years,
serving that group in all its offices including president. She has also been a
member of the Beulah Congregational Church Ladies Aid association for 40 years
and is a founding member of the Beulah Community Nursing Home Auxiliary.

In the 1950s another major responsibility arose through John's work with the
organization of the Oliver-Mercer Electric Cooperative where involvement in the
negotiations for the construction of the Basin Electric generating plant took
him into Washington, D.C. regularly for a number of years. John served as
chairman of the board at Oliver-Mercer for 12 years until the mid-1960s.

It was also during the 1950s that John was elected to the state senate. He
served his first term at the state Capitol in 1951, continuing through 1959, an
exciting decade in North Dakota when the oil industry first came into the
state. John's work in Bismarck meant that Alma became a farm widow a second
time. Alma also became the chief chauffeur for the many community activities of
their four children, including 4-H, Farmers Union, FHA, FFA, music lessons,
drama, speech, choir, band, sports and church group organizations.

A new phase of life began in 1965 when they built a home in Beulah, though they
continued to operate the farm. John's community service after their move into
town included chairing the Beulah Community Nursing Home Board during a period
in which the nursing home was merged with the Beulah retirement home. Alma began
work for the Beulah Community Nursing Home in 1965 and was later promoted to
dietary supervisor, a position from which she retired in 1986.

Members of John and Alma's family include Jerry, Milda, Jim and Johnell. Jerry,
born Aug. 7, 1934, is living in Bismarck, married to Loretta Reiger, and is the
production director for Colonial Life Insurance for North Dakota and Minnesota.
Their three children are Becky, David and Shad.

Milda, born May 25, 1940, is living in St. Paul, Minn., married to Edwin
Fogelman, and is a professor of politics and media at Augsburg College in
Minneapolis. Their children are Scott and Simon.

Jim, born Dec. 10, 1947, completed a master's degree from the American Graduate
School of International Management in Arizona, is living on the home farm in
Oliver County, served on the staff of Gov. Art Link for several years and was
the state senator for the legislative district including Beulah, the same
district his father John represented in earlier years.

Johnell, born June 16, 1951, is living in Minneapolis, Minn. and is working as
the accounting manager for Tennant Company, an international manufacturing
firm, after obtaining her master's degree from the American Graduate School of
International Management in Arizona. She is also completing her certified
public accountancy degree.

        Emanuel and Anne Maye Liebelt

Emanuel and Anne Liebelt

Emanuel Liebelt was born July 10, 1902 near Rhein, Oliver County, N.D. His
parents, Joseph and Louisa Liebelt, homesteaded in the late 1890s and built a
sod house at the site. Portions of the home are still visible.

The family moved to Colorado for two years but soon returned by covered wagon,
returning eventually to the original homestead. They gradually acquired more
land and farmed in the area until 1919.

Emanuel worked nights when he attended business college in Bismarck. He became
manager of the bank in Coleharbor, N.D. which led him to a job in the Bank of
North Dakota. During a change in bank administrations, the selling field began
to look more promising, so the Fuller Brush Company gained a new salesman.
Emanuel worked his way up to assistant branch manager at Fergus Falls, Minn.

In 1924, Emanuel and Anne Maye VanVleet were married. She was born in
Galesville, Wis. to Edwin and Corabelle (Abbott) VanVleet on May 20, 1905,
moving with her family to Driscoll, N.D. soon after. She graduated from
Bismarck High School and worked in the North Dakota hail insurance department
and the Bank of North Dakota.

Emanuel eventually moved to Hazen and began selling Chevrolets for Tokeim
Chevrolet. He became general manager of a Chevrolet organization in New Salem
and then owner of his own automobile agency in Glen Ullin. Thirteen years after
opening in Glen Ullin his agency burned to the ground with nary a bit of
insurance and he decided to move to Beulah. In 1941 he bought Service Chevrolet
and in 1948 began construction of Liebelt Chevrolet at 208 E. Main. Emanuel
received his 50-year gold plaque form General Motors in 1980 in honor of his 50
years as an active Chevrolet dealer. He retired in 1983 when the business was
sold to Rick Wolf.

For more than 45 years the Liebelts were involved in business and civic
organizations. Anne Maye was head of such varied organizations as Royal
Neighbors of America, the American Legion Auxiliary, Beulah Homemakers Club,
Congregational Ladies Aid and Sunday school. Emanuel served for many years on
the Chevrolet Motor Division Dealership Planning Committee. He helped to
organize the Commercial Club into the Chamber of Commerce and served as
president of the organization for three years. During this time he was part of a
movement to have Beulah's status changed from village to city government, and
for one and a half terms served as mayor of Beulah. For 22 years he was a
charter member of the Beulah Tri-County Development corporation and is a life
member of the Elks. With Jess Thompson he owned a flying service and developed
the first Beulah airport facilities. He has been awarded several patents from
the U.S. Patent Office and received much publicity from his development of the
anti-rapist glove with articles appearing in newspapers from coast to coast. In
the 1950s he and Emanuel Jr. owned Liebelt & Sons, a steel structure firm.

The family's three sons, Emanuel Jr., Beuhl and Jonathan, all received their
diplomas from Beulah High School.

Emanuel Jr. and Merilynn Liebelt

The oldest of three sons born to Emanuel and Anna Maye Liebelt was Emanuel Jr.
He attended grade school and two years of high school in Glen Ullin. When his
father opened an automobile agency in Beulah in 1941, Emanuel Jr. came along as
a bookkeeper and graduated as valedictorian from Beulah High School in 1942.

He enlisted in the U.S. Navy in the fall, serving in the Pacific theatre of war
as a Lieutenant JG until 1946. Then he enrolled at the University of North
Dakota, graduating in 1950 with a bachelor of science degree.

        Emanuel, Jr., Merilynn, Lon and Lori Liebelt

After his marriage to Merilynn Taintor at Grand Forks in 1952 he was active in
sales and construction of Stran Steel buildings in a seven-county area.

The family, which now included a son, Marlon, and a daughter, Lori, moved to
California in 1957, where "Lee" was employed as purchasing agent in guidance and
flight control for Lockheed, Missiles and Space Division. They returned to
Beulah in 1963, where he managed Liebelt Inc. until his death.

He was a member of the Beulah Congregational Church, Masonic Order, Shrine,
Lions, Beulah Chamber of Commerce, Beulah Boosters and a charter member of the
Beulah Eagles Club. He actively worked with Housing and Urban Development in
Mercer County.

Merilynn Liebelt, also a UND graduate, taught in Bend, OR, for two years, then
in schools in the Beulah area after her marriage. She is active in the Beulah
Woman's Club, Beulah Homemakers, Knife River Chorale and various church groups.
She plays the organ for church services, including weddings, and piano for
various school and community activities.

Dr. Marlon Liebelt, a graduate of Beulah High School and Northern College of
Chiropractic, is currently working in the Chicago area. Lori Liebelt, also a
graduate of Beulah High School, with a bachelor of music degree from the San
Francisco Conservatory of Music, is studying music and German in Cologne and
Munich, Germany, where she lives with her husband, Jorg Weinbrenner.

Douglas and Donna Lindquist

Donna Mae Krausz was born on Oct. 17, 1951, in rural Beulah to Leonard R. and
Hilda (Winkler) Krausz. The elder Krauszs still reside there.

Donna grew up knowing farm life well and attended a country school. It was up
at 5 a.m. to milk 18 cows by hand, separate the milk, clean the separator and
feed all the animals. Then there was breakfast and a one and a half mile walk
to the little schoolhouse on the hill. Donna brought bag lunches, consisting of
jelly-bread sandwiches and sausages. When she was in the fifth grade, the
school finally closed, and she continued her education in Beulah.

Until that time, it was classic "country'' all the way, with a classroom well
lit by huge paned windows, wainscoting, chair railings, hardwood floors and a
wood stove. Water was hauled in by cream can, frozen or not, and poured (or
chipped) into a big glass water jug. On storm days, school closed at 1 p.m.

Donna recalls that the yearly Christmas program was looked forward to by
children and adults alike. Wire was strung from wall to wall, sheets were hung
from them to create a stage, and decorated cardboard was used to recreate the
manger scene. Attendance was not required; everyone came regardless for the
light, the togetherness, and of course, the gift-giving. It was different then.
Donna's wondrous gift consisted of nuts, candy, and best of all, a fresh
orange. "If you got apples or oranges, it was a thing to get excited about,"
said Donna.

"You always wore pants and boys' shoes," continues Donna. "You hardly ever wore
a dress, and didn't know what to do with yourself if you did." Girls worked and
played hard and dresses were limiting. She remembers, "I loved jumping in,
around, under, anything, on snowbanks. They were big, wonderful, and all over
the place. Once I thought I could tackle this snowbank, so I gave it my best -
and my left overshoe. It came off my foot when I pulled myself out. I had to go
back into the school, in front of everybody, get the shovel, and dig it out. I
was very red-faced."

Yet it is clear that whenever the light is right, the children (now long grown)
of Edwin Raszler, Andy Sailer, Eugene Sasse, Herb Reub, and Pat O'Neill still
come out for a game of baseball on the playground of Donna's mind, their shouts
ringing on into the twilight of every pale spring evening. "I loved it," says
Donna with a big smile in her voice.

At the bottom of a draw near her childhood home, there existed a U-shaped creek
formation, left by meandering water. "We called it The Lake because water always
collected there - we must not have seen many lakes--and by the Lake grew a large
tree. This was the tree where they had hung cattle and horse thieves in the old
days," Donna recollects. "Everytime we'd hay I'd see that tree and think about
its history."

"Then there was the time I went picking chokecherries with my sister, Shirley
(now deceased). We were near a washout," Donna says, "a sort of hole in the
side of a hill, with water in the bottom. And I had to go to the bathroom. My
sister said, "Here, I'll hold you over (the edge of the washout" ." You guessed
it. She dropped me. On purpose."

In the 1960s, when Donna became a teenager, the perspective changed. Getting to
go to town, to the Roxy Theatre, on a Saturday night was very exciting. Main
Street, Beulah, was on that evening a celebration, with everyone coming into
town to do their shopping and visiting. She recalls Hildebrand's Barber Shop,
stripped pole and all, with men stacked up like a log jam, waiting for a
haircut. On Saturday night, his shop closed at 10 p.m.

Summer brought the circus and the Cowboy Reunion, complete with clowns and
Brahma bulls. The VFW Auxiliary 7759 would sell lunch.

Donna can dearly recall the Otter Creek flood, which occurred during that
decade. "It rained for three days,'" says Donna. "South Beulah had the most
water. The back roads to Beulah were all under water Whole fields became lakes.
Bridges went out and you could see bodies of cattle and pieces of furniture
floating by. Josie (Mrs. Link) Reinhiller had to carry her girls out in her
arms to escape a big wall of water."

After she graduated from high school, Donna went to Joseph's School of Hair
Design and became a beautician in 1972. On Sept. 24, 1977, she married Douglas
E. Lindquist (b. April 4, 1940) from Wilmer, Minn., and is presently a nurse's
aide at the Beulah Community Nursing Home. Douglas and Donna make their home in
Hazen and have two children, John (b. July 25, 1978) and Katherina (b. Aug. 14,
1981). A son, Mark, died in infancy in 1990.

George Loning

George Loning was born in 1867, in Beschotenweg, Germany. In 1893, he came to
the United States with his mother Ann Kadus and his half-brother Lewie Kadus.
They first lived in Iowa, then Litchville, N.D., before settling in Rhine in
1903.

In 1913 he married Maggie Cornelius, who was born in Emden, Germany, in 1885.
Their son Anton was born in 1915 and lived in Beulah most of his adult life.
Maggie died of cancer in 1927 after doctoring in Bismarck and Minneapolis.

In 1928 George married Klasena (Clara) Cornelius Kadus, who was born in 1899, in
Emden, Germany. She was the widow of his brother Lewie and a sister to Maggie.

The couple had an instant family with his own son Anton, now 14, and her
children: Ann 10, Fred, 8, and Pearl, 5. Geraldine had died as a baby in 1926.
The couple had three more of their own children: Margaret in 1929, Louie in
1932 and Henrietta in 1935.

In 1945 the family moved to Beulah. The following year George died at Hillcrest
Hospital in Beulah. In 1950 Klasena married William Rettke, who died in 1959.
Klasena is now a resident of the nursing home in Beulah.

The children are-Anton, 1915-1977, married Rose Unruh Teske; Ann, 1918-1983,
married Edward Bumann; Fred, 1920, married Dorothey Vreeland and later Addie;
Pearl, 1923, married Carl Opp and later Pete Lane; Geraldine died as an infant
in 1926; Margaret, 1929, married John Kottre and later Paul Rettke; Louie, 1932,
married Marion Ashly Simms and later June Watts; and Henrietta, 1935, married
Bennie Guenthner. She graduated from Beulah High School in 1952.

Kirk and Linda Maize

Linda and Kirk Maize are well known in the Beulah area for their interest in
and work with the American quarterhorse.

Kirk and Linda moved to Beulah in 1975. Kirk ran his own machine shop from 1975-
78. In 1978 he began his present job as a machinist for Basin Electric
Cooperative.

Linda taught school in Golden Valley for three years, coming to the Beulah
school system in 1978, where she still teaches elementary school.

"Since we have been in Beulah we have been involved in a variety of
organizations, but our main interest is raising quarterhorses," writes Linda.
"We own a select brood mares whose colts have gone on to win shows ranging from
the Quarterhorse Congress in Columbus, Ohio, the largest quarterhorse show in
the world, to the San Antonio Stock Show in San Antonio, Texas.

In addition to those, their quality animals have won numerous state fairs,
circuit championships and have placed at the AQHA World Show in Oklahoma City.
The two belong to the American Quarterhorse Association and the North Dakota
Quarterhorse Association.

Because of their hobby and their love for quarterhorses, the Maizes enjoy
country living and the small-town atmosphere which enables them to pursue both
their careers and their interest in raising good-quality animals.

"We enjoy the small-town atmosphere in Beulah. It's nice to be in a small town
where everyone knows everyone else and everyone works together," Linda
continues. "The people have been very friendly."

Along with other families who moved to Beulah just before or during the energy
impact years, the Maizes have seen many changes occur in the time they've lived
in Beulah. "We both work in new facilities which didn't exist when we moved
here. New people brought a variety of new ideas to the area. There have been
improvements in the town's appearance and an increase in the variety of
recreational programs offered," Linda tallies.

"We're looking forward to seeing the changes the future brings to our town."

Rudolf and Lydia Mattheis

The parents of Rudolf and Lydia Mattheis came to the United States from South
Russia. Rudolf was born May 14, 1904, to Emanuel Sr. and Christine Miller
Mattheis.

Emanuel Mattheis, Sr. was born Oct. 14, 1867, at Brienne, Bessarabia, South
Russia. Christine was born Nov. 25, 1867. They were married Dec. 2, 1890.

For 12 years thereafter he followed the profession of carpenter and tradesman
in the home village. In 1902 they emigrated to America, settling on a homestead
five miles northeast of Beulah, where they resided until 1929 when they retired
and moved to Beulah.

Christine died July 26, 1933. Emanuel died March 28, 1935. They had been blessed
with 11 children. There were four children living at the time of his death:
Emil, Emanuel Jr., Rudolf and Bertha Sabrowske.

        Mattheis family Back row: Emil, Emanuel, Anna, Rudolf, Bertha, Mr. and
        Mrs. Emanuel Mattheis.

Emanuel Sr. was a charter member of Zion Lutheran Church and its carpenter.
Rudolf and Lydia were lifetime members of Zion Lutheran Church and their son
Raymond and his family have always been members there.

Lydia was born Oct. 8, 1908, to Fred and Margaret Zuern Wiedrich. She came from
a family of five girls and four boys.

Rudolf and Lydia were married March 30, 1930. They lived on the family farm
homesteaded by his parents. They sold the farm to John Zuern in 1951 and
purchased the Konrad Wiedrich farm 15 miles northeast of Beulah. Their lifetime
together in Mercer County was short. Lydia died March 15, 1953, at the age of 44
and Rudolf died March 9, 1957, at the age of 52.

Rudolf and Lydia had three children: Elaine, Raymond and Betty. Elaine is
married to Benjamin Scheid. They are grain and livestock farmers south of Hazen.

Bennie is a licensed cattle buyer and they operate the Scheid hog buying at New
Salem. They also own Scheid Trucking. They have four children: Richard, married
to Wanda Hildebrand, has one son and they live south of Hazen.

Ricky, who lives north of Hazen, is married to Zola Morast and has two
daughters.

Linda is married to Mark Klein and they live in Hazen. They have one son and one
daughter. Mary Lou is married to Bret Losey and has one son. They are living in
Chugiah, AK, where Bret is with the National Guard.

Raymond is married to Leona Voegele and they live on the family farm and are
livestock and grain farmers. They have three sons: Carey, Dwight and Eric of
Hazen.

Betty is married to Herbert Hintz and they are cattle and grain farmers and
live south of Hazen. They have three sons: Steven is married to Stacy Meidinger
and they live at Mesa, AZ; Kevin lives at Hazen and Kelly lives in Gillette WY.

        McKenzies: Mary Jo, Mac, Milly Vickie, Scott

Mac and Milly McKenzie

The Mac McKenzies moved to Beulah on June 1, 1954. Mac and Milly were born in
Grand Forks County, North Dakota, where Mac graduated from Logan Center High
School and Milly from Northwood. He went on to attend the Agricultural College
at Fargo. Soon after his 18th birthday he received a call from Uncle Sam and
spent the next two years in the Army, serving as a litter bearer in the Medical
Corps. He was awarded the Bronze Star for meritorious service in combat in the
Po Valley in Italy.

Following military service he returned to school at the agricultural college in
Fargo. Mac and Mildred Grina were married at Northwood, N.D. They lived in
Fargo one year while Mac completed his college education. Following graduation,
they moved to Mayville, N.D., where Mac was the veteran's agricultural
instructor until moving to Beulah where he was employed by the North Dakota
Extension Service as the Mercer County Extension Agent until the time of his
death in July, 1973.

During his time at Beulah he was actively promoting 4-H Clubs, Homemakers Clubs,
and earned many state awards in livestock judging and other phases of 4-H work.
He was also active in civic and church groups such as the Beulah Chamber of
Commerce, the VFW serving as post commander and district commander and serving
as president and secretary of Concordia Lutheran Church.

During his spare time he enjoyed square dancing and calling. He and Milly
traveled North Dakota, Montana, South Dakota and a couple of Canadian provinces
pursuing this hobby.

Mac and Milly had three children. Vickie is married to Rod Helm, and they live
at Park Rapids, Minn., with their three children: Sarah, Luke and Rachel.

Mary Jo is married to Kent Larson, and they live in Beulah with their two
daughters, Anne and Kathryn.

Scott lives at Fort Benton, Mont., with his wife Patti Wallender, and three
children Peter, Angela and Samuel.

After Mac's death Milly continued to live in Beulah. She was employed as the
executive secretary of the Mercer County Selective Service Board for several
years. More recently, she worked for the Knife River Coal Mining Company and
also as an insurance representative for the Royal Neighbors of America
Insurance Society. She is a member of the Beulah Homemakers Club, the VFW
Auxiliary, the Sons of Norway Lodge and Concordia Lutheran Church.

Beulah is a warm and friendly community and a wonderful place to raise a family.
Milly will be looking forward to renewing acquaintances with friends returning
for the Diamond Jubilee celebration in 1989.

        Carl and Ida Menge

Carl and Ida Menge

Carl "Charlie" Menge was born on May 29, 1908, in Boradena, Bessarabia, South
Russia, to Johan (d. 1961) and Elizabeth Seigloch Menge (d. 1973). He came to
America with his parents in May 1910, where his father had found work at the
Hebron Brick Yard in Hebron, N.D.

Carl writes, "In 1911, Dad homesteaded a farm five miles north of Hebron and, in
1918, bought a farm 12 miles north of Hazen. I received my education in the
rural school there.

"From 1933 to 1934, I joined the Soil Conservation Corps and was stationed in
various places. After that, I went to my parents' farm."

In 1936, Carl married Ida Katherine Mindt in Beulah. She is the daughter of
Gottleib (d. 1956) and Katherine Buchmann Mindt (d. 1960), born July 11, 1916,
in Blue Grass, N.D. At the time of their marriage, Carl was employed at the
Knife River Coal Company.

"In 1949, we built a greenhouse and florist shop in Beulah and operated it for
23 years, until 1973. I also that year retired from the coal mine, where I was
employed for 36 years," he writes.

Carl and Ida had two sons. Eldon Carl was born April 13, 1937, and died May 1,
1937. Delvin Carol was born Aug. 3, 1940. He graduated from Beulah High School
in 1958. In July that year, Delvin enlisted in the U.S. Navy until 1961 and
after his discharge, he entered the University of North Dakota, graduating on
June 6, 1965.

On June 12, 1965, Delvin married Georgia Lon Stephenson from Valley City, N.D.
After their marriage, they moved to Tulsa, Okla., where Delvin entered the
school of law at the University of Tulsa. He graduated in 1969 and was employed
by Marathon Oil Company.

Delvin and Georgia have two children. They live in Houston, Texas, where
Marathon Oil Company has its main office.

The Menges are members of the Zion Lutheran Church where Carl served for a
number of years as an officer. He has been a member of the Beulah Chamber of
Commerce and has served on the city board.

Writes Carl, "Ida and I always loved Beulah and enjoyed living here. We always
thought it was a great little city. And I intend to spend the rest of my
retirement here."

Fred and Hella Menge

John and Elizabeth Menge immigrated to the United States in 1910 and
homesteaded near Hebron. Fred Menge, born Jan. 9, 1918, was one of 16 children
born to John and Elizabeth. The family later moved to a farm north of Hazen.
Fred's father died March 18, 1961, and his mother died June 26, 1973.

Fred served in the Army during World War II with the 29th Infantry Division. He
was wounded while serving in France on Aug. 12, 1944. He received the Purple
Heart and two battle stars.

Fred retired from Knife River Coal Mining Company after 33 years of employment
with the company. He is an avid golfer and has many trophies to attest to that.
During his retirement years he is able to spend a lot of time on the golf
course, not only playing the game but helping out doing volunteer work where
needed.

He is on the board of directors of the Mercer County Historical Society, is a
member of the Beulah Eagles, the V.F.W., the American Legion, Disabled American
Veterans and Zion Lutheran Church and has held various offices in each
organization.

Hella Voegele, born July 25, 1925, is the daughter of Christ Voegele and Eva T.
Fischer. The Voegele family came to the United States from Southern Russia in
1905 and homesteaded south of Beulah. Her father died Jan. 9, 1973. Her mother,
Eva Fischer, resides at the Sunset Manor in Glen Ullin.

Hella is employed as a cook at Beulah High School. She is a member of the Eagles
Auxiliary, Beulah Nursing Home Auxiliary and ALCW of Zion Lutheran Church.

Fred and Hella have three children: Alice Fredericka was born Feb. 17, 1950 at
Hazen, graduated from Beulah High School and the University of North Dakota. She
is employed as a social worker in Minneapolis.

Jerome Fredrich was born Nov. 9, 1951, at Hazen, attended school in Beulah and
graduated from Beulah High School. He is a graduate of Moorhead State College
and is employed by Basin Electric in Bismarck as an electrical and designing
engineer. His wife, Beth Stroup is the head coordinator at Heartview Foundation
in Mandan.

Jodi Allen, born Aug. 12, 1968, graduated from Beulah High School and is
presently attending Concordia College in Moorhead, MN, majoring in accounting
and business and hospital administration.

Albert and Louisa Miller

About 1908, Michael Miller immigrated to America from Krem, Russia, and settled
in the area northeast of Halliday. His first wife, Mary (Frosch) Miller, died
in Russia. Michael and Mary had four sons: George, Christ, Albert, born in
1898, and Gothart, born in 1900.

All four sons were born in Russia and immigrated to the United States with their
father. George Miller married Lidya Mittlesteadt, Christ Miller married Rosa
Glass, Albert married Louisa Faser and Gothart married Helen Weidenmeyer.

Following the death of his first wife in Russia, Michael Miller married
Kristene Kempf in America, and they had six children: Emma, Elizabeth, Fred,
Bob, Ida and Freda. Michael Miller died about 1916.

Throughout their married years, Albert and Louisa (Faser) Miller lived on a
farm near Twin Buttes and also farmed nine miles north of Golden Valley. They
bought the Valley Bar in Golden Valley in the 1950s and sold it in 1952 and
moved back to the farm near Golden Valley.

Albert and Louisa had eight children: Edwin, Norman, Lorraine, Vera, Mardella,
Gladys, Dale and Gerald (Gary).

Albert Miller died December 3, 1960, and Louisa Miller died March 23, 1959.

August and Tillie Miller

August (Augie) Miller was born to George and Dorothy (Kasper) Miller on July 23,
1905. His father passed away in March 1931 and his mother in September 1938.
Augie's occupations have included being a farmer, school bus driver, and county
assessor.

Tillie was born to Jacob and Katherina (Fisher) Weil on Aug. 12, 1905, at Java,
S.D. Tillie's father passed away in December, 1951 and her mother in September,
1969. Tillie's occupations have included being a housewife and nursing home
craft coordinator.

Augie and Tillie were reared in Mercer County. Augie was born in the farmhouse
north of Beulah that was also his residence until 1959. Tillie was two years
old when her family homesteaded south of Zap.

August Miller's avid love of baseball made him known to many Mercer County
citizens. His playing began as a young man in Krem, N.D. He then played with the
K&E Team, Hazen, Pick City and Beulah. He also enjoyed bowling and later was a
frequent spectator at the high school basketball games. His love for play was
synonymous with his love for young people. He had many mementos given to him
that indicated the young people that made up his bus route enjoyed his humor, his
encouragement and his good, firm discipline.

While farming, Augie did a lot of custom work. His favorite was the threshing
rig he supervised for many years. When combining became prevalent, he spent
many hours swathing grain and hay. While his girls were in school, he served
the Woodrow School District #31 as a school board member. After Augie lived in
Beulah, he sometimes served as town marshal for events that brought crowds to
the community. One such event was the "Zip to Zap" youth confab.

Tillie's earliest recollection of family living centered around a grandparent's
farm and then the activities of her church. Then, like her husband, there were
many chores and hard work that occupied most of their growing-up years. Tillie
was often the hired girl in neighborhood homes when there were additions in
those families and when the threshing season demanded another cook and helper.
This was the experience she had when she married August on Nov. 29, 1929, at
the Emmaus Congregational Church. They then lived on the Miller farm north of
Beulah until September, 1959, when they moved into Beulah. Besides being a
housewife, Tillie was a Gray Lady volunteer, a member of the Congregational
Church, and worked in the nursing home for two years. No matter what she had to
do with these occupations, Tillie always had time to crochet, give perms to her
friends, do some quilting and gardening.

Augie and Tillie didn't grow up within the boundaries of Beulah. Tillie,
however, remembers a walk she and the other students of her school took from
their school building to Beulah so that they could see the first train which
came to the area. They both remember the progress made as the town of Beulah
developed, added businesses, built new churches, and then added hard-surfaced
roads with curbs and gutter.

The Fourth of July celebration of 1938 stands out in their memories too. After
a day of visiting and revelry, the rain came. The rain brought a flash flood to
the community. For many residents, along with Augie and Tillie, this meant that
they either spent the night in a car or in a home along the main roads north of
town.

Augie and Tillie have four children: Cleo, married to Fred Kulish, was born
Oct. 5, 1929; Florence, married to Robert Kostelnak, was born Nov. 8, 1930;
Mardell, married to Carlos Tatum, was born Dec. 5, 1934; and Janet, married to
James Tysver, was born Aug. 20, 1942.

Cleo began her teaching career in Mercer County. She now lives in Dickinson
where she's still teaching. She had two children: Marlowe of Moorhead, Minn.,
and Carma of Sao Paulo, Brazil.

Florence also taught school in Dunn, Billings, and McKenzie Counties. She and
her husband presently operate the Knife River Trading Post at Manning. They
have two daughters: Zola of Great Falls, Mont., and Renae of rural Killdeer.

Mardell lives in Abilene, Texas. She taught in North Dakota and Montana for six
years before she joined the Civil Service. She has a son, Marty, who is with
the U.S. Navy in Rhode Island, and a daughter, Carla, who lives in Abilene.

Janet is presently residing in Artesia, N.M. Janet and her husband have moved
extensively within the oil-producing states because Jim was in seismographic
work. They are the parents of Jackie, Joel, and Jay.

        David Miller family: Cindy, David, Aaron, Brent and Barbara
