Gary and JoAnn Miller

Gerald (Gary) Miller was born Jan. 30, 1948, at the Hillcrest Hospital in
Beulah. He attended rural Golden Valley schools; Beaver Creek school grades
one-four, and grade six; grade five in Beulah; grades seven-ten he attended
school in Golden Valley. Gary attended Beulah High School during his junior and
senior years and graduated in 1965. He attended Dickinson State College for two
years and Mayville State College for two years, graduating in 1969 with a
bachelor of science degree in social studies and physical education.

He married Jo Ann Raszler on June 7, 1968. Jo Ann is the daughter of Edwin
Raszler and Frances (Kuk) Raszler. Jo Ann was born Nov. 19, 1947, at the
Hillcrest Hospital in Beulah. She attended rural schools and Beulah High
School, graduated in 1965 and also attended the University of North Dakota. She
graduated from Mary College in 1973.

Gary's first teaching job was in Alexander, N.D. during the years of 1969-1971
where he taught social studies and was head football and assistant basketball
coach.

From 1971-1975, Gary taught social studies at Flasher, where he was also head
track coach, and assistant football and basketball coach. While they lived in
Flasher, Jo Ann drove to Mary College every day for two years and graduated in
1973 with a bachelor of arts degree in English and French. Jo Ann taught high
school English for two years in Flasher, and also supervised the Pep Club, the
paper staff and the Drama Club.

Their daughter Camella was born Feb. 16, 1974, at the Bismarck Hospital. She was
about one year old when the family moved to Tuttle, where Gary and Jo Ann taught
social studies and English. Gary was head cross country, basketball and track
coach, and Jo Ann supervised the paper staff, the Drama Club and also was the
high school librarian.

        Gary Miller family: Camella, Gary, JoAnn and Michael

In 1977, they moved back to Beulah when Gary accepted a position with American
Family Insurance. Jo Ann substituted in the Beulah school system and also taught
English from 1978-79.

On Oct. 4, 1979, their son, Michael Gerald, was born at the Bismarck Hospital.
Since that time Jo Ann has done free lance writing at home, works as the center
page editor for Oliver-Mercer Electric in Hazen and coordinates the Beulah
Community Education Program.

Jo Ann was very active in the Jayceette and Jaycee Women organizations, and
served the local chapter in several offices and the state organization as
programming vice president and personal growth program manager. She is also a
member of the Crafty Corner Homemaker's Club, is secretary of Zion Lutheran's
church council and teaches weekday school at Zion. Jo Ann is a member of
Beulah's 1989 jubilee committee and is the co-editor of Beulah's jubilee
history book.

Gary was also active in the Beulah Jaycees and served as chapter president and
other offices. He is also a member of the Beulah Chamber, the Lions Club and
the Eagles. Gary serves on the Zion Lutheran church council as a member of the
stewardship and finance committee and also on the Parent Advisory Committee for
the Beulah Elementary School.

Growing up in Beulah has many special memories. Jo Ann says, "I remember roller
skating at the old Sheep Shed on Saturday night when I was a kid and thinking
it was great fun. The high school dances in Zap are also a special memory
because it was a place where you could always meet some friends. Having a 'mud'
at the Beulah Drug Store fountain was a special treat, along with the cherry
and lime cokes. I remember Mr. Sayler's tough science classes at Beulah High
School, and how there were only two girls from my graduating class who took the
science and math courses. Needless to say, we got a lot of attention! It was a
strange feeling for me to find myself teaching in the same halls where I once
was a high school senior at Beulah. There are many wonderful people who live in
our town and it is a great place to raise children."

        Sam and Rufina Miller

Sam and Rufina Miller

Sam Miller, born Oct. 27, 1908, came to Mercer County with his parents, Samuel
Miller, Sr., who died Sept. 3, 1964 and Maria (Boeckel) Miller, who died Aug. 8,
1917. The Millers arrived in America in May 1910 from Crimea, South Russia, to
homestead north of Golden Valley.

Sam grew up and received his education in this area. After he finished his
school, he worked part time on the farm and in the winter months, he worked for
different coal mines. In 1932, he started working with his father in his
blacksmith shop at Zap where he was taught the blacksmith trade.

Rufina was born Aug. 21, 1910, and was raised seven miles north of Zap, where
she received her education and grew up. Rufina moved to Zap in 1929 with her
parents, Adam Herrmann, who died April 17, 1954, and Christina Walz Herrmann,
who died Oct. 14, 1938.

On Oct. 21, 1933, Sam was united in marriage to Rufina. After living in Zap for
five years, Sam decided to go into business for himself, so the Millers moved
to Beulah in March 1939 where Sam started his own shop, which he operated until
1975 when he retired. Sam and Rufina had three sons: Myron, born April 2, 1936,
David, born Sept. 20, 1946 and Charles, born July 21, 1949.

Myron, who now resides at Madison, IN, is married to Carol Hafner, daughter of
the late Leo and Katie Hafner. Myron is an anesthetist at King's Daughter
Hospital in Madison, IN. Myron and Carol have three children. Kimberly, married
to Dr. David Wilson, is employed as a physical therapist at an Indianapolis
hospital; Karla, a registered nurse is also employed in Indianapolis; and Marc,
who is a freshman in the School of Pharmacy in Indianapolis.

David, who resides in Beulah, married Barbara Younker, daughter of Esther
Reinschmidt and the late Gust Younker. They have three children: Cindy, a
freshman at Moorhead State College; Brent, a sophomore at Beulah High School
and Aaron, a seventh grader at the Beulah school. David is employed at North
American Coal.

Charles, who resides at Fargo, married Joan Weil, daughter of Herb and Leona
Weil of Beulah. They have three children: Tasha, Michele and Karena. Charles is
employed by LaVelle Lumber in Fargo.

Sam was active and served on the city council for eight years and was a member
of the Chamber of Commerce, director for Joachim Memorial Home and Beulah
Community Nursing Home and an honorary member of Beulah Volunteer Fire
Department. Sam and Rufina took an active part at Condordia Lutheran Church,
where they were charter members. Rufina is also active in the Lutheran Women's
Missionary League. Sam Miller passed away April 22, 1987.

        Walter and Hertha Mittlesteadt

Walter and Hertha Mittlesteadt

When Walter and Hertha Mittlesteadt were married in 1938, there was no
electricity, running water or any other modern conveniences on their farm. They
lived in a stone/mud house the first 10 years of their marriage. All the
farming was done with horses.

Walter, son of Fred and Julia Mittlesteadt, was born Nov. 25, 1915, on a farm
five miles north of Zap. Hertha, daughter of John and Christina (Tesky) Pischel
was born Sept. 24, 1915, north of Beulah. They were married Nov. 6, 1938, at
Zion Lutheran Church at Beulah in a double wedding ceremony with Walter's
brother, Adolph, and Hertha's sister, Alvina.

        Walter and Hertha, Adolph and Alvina Mittlesteadt

They started farming in 1940 on a farm seven miles northeast of Zap, using
horses. Walter purchased his first tractor, a Minneapolis-Moline, in 1942. In
1949, they built a new house on their farm. Electricity (REA) came in 1951.
They continued to grain farm, had range cattle and also a dairy operation until
1975 when they moved to Beulah. Their only son, Clyde, who was born April 20,
1940, took over the farming operation. Walter continued to make daily treks to
the farm to help with the farm work. Hertha is an avid gardener and starts her
own plants inside early in the winter and is one of the first people in town to
plant her garden in the spring of the year and has fresh vegetables early in the
summer.

They are members of Concordia Lutheran Church and the Senior Citizens' Club in
Beulah.

Clyde married Cheryl Mohl and they have four children: Brent Lee, born Sept. 30,
1977; Crystal Ann, born Dec. 22, 1980; Tiffany Rae, born Aug. 4, 1985 and Cody
Ryan, born Sept. 14, 1987.

They are members of St. Lukes Lutheran Church in Zap and their children attend
Zap public school.

Myron and Cindy Mitzel

Myron Mitzel was born on March 21, 1958, to Frank M. and LaVern Mitzel in Cando,
ND. Frank and LaVern Mitzel currently live in York, ND.

Myron married Cynthia Kay Keller on June 16, 1979. Cindy was born May 11, 1958,
to Clarence and Gloria Keller, in Devils Lake. Cindy's parents live in Lansford.

Myron and Cindy lived in Devils Lake until moving to Beulah in May of 1980. A
job at the Indian Head Mine in Zap brought them to Beulah. Myron transferred
from Indian Head to Coteau in 1985, where he is currently employed as production
supervisor.

Myron and Cindy have two children: Chandra Kay was born March 3, 1982, in Minot
and Jaden John was born Jan. 20, 1986, in Beulah.

Betty Mohl

Betty L. (Miller) Mohl was born on a family farm 14 miles north of Hazen on
Sept. 24, 1929, the daughter of Albert Miller and Emma (Weigum) Miller. There
were three children in this family: Norma (Mrs. Reuben Richter) of Fargo, Betty
L. Mohl of Beulah, and Helen (Mrs. Helmuth Hilz) of Beulah.

        Betty Mohl

Betty's father, Albert, was born March 20, 1895, on the family farm and died
Oct. 11, 1981. Mother Emma was born Feb. 5, 1900, on her family farm north of
Hazen.

Betty attended school at Krem District 4, school number three, where she
received her eighth grade education. She was baptized and confirmed at St.
Peter's Congregation, a family church, about one and a half miles from her
childhood home.

Her childhood home was the source of many memories--she loved the country, the
family farm, the baseball games, the surrounding hills where such interesting
items as Indian hammers might be found on a lazy autumn afternoon.

Since those days, Betty has gone on toward the achievement of a number of
goals. In May 1986, she received her high school diploma as well as a
certificate in human relations from Century High in Bismarck. She has also gone
on from artifact hunting to searching for history of another sort--genealogy.
She has made up books of the family records of Jacob (Kuoch) Kuch, Peter Mohl,
Anton Mohl, Alex Mohl, and Christian Buchfink. Some of these histories go back
to 1639. Betty writes, "It was so interesting to get all these records and
share all the blessings, joys, and sorrows of family members."

The same year she "graduated from high school," she also organized a Miller
family reunion which has been held every two years in Hazen or Dryden, Wash.

And in July 1986 she organized another reunion, celebrating the 100th
anniversary of her great-great-grandfather's arrival in America. This was held
in Hazen.

Betty, prior to her marriage to Raymond Mohl, was employed at the Hanewald and
Weigum Store, a grocery and clothing shop where Betty's aunt, Helen Weigum, was
owner with Mr. William C. Hanewald of Hazen.

On Sept. 30, 1951, Betty and Raymond were married at Peace Lutheran Church of
Hazen. Raymond was born Aug. 9, 1922, the son of Alex Mohl and Eliza Buchfink.

Betty is the mother of two children, Pamela, born in 1952, and John, born in
1955. Pamela is married to Dale Kinslow of Fargo, and they have three children,
Shannon, Nellie, and Bridget. John is married to Carmen Kruckenburg and resides
in Beulah with his three children, Jason, Amber, and Caty. Betty enjoys her
children and grandchildren and hopes they will continue the history she has
started.

Betty was employed at the Beulah nursing home for eight years as an activity
director. She spent much time with the elderly people listening to all the
blessings and hardships they had known in life and felt this was a great way to
share and care for people.

"All in all, it was a very rewarding job,"' says Betty. Later on she worked for
the Beulah Cash Store.

Betty is a member of Zion Lutheran Church, ALCW, Church Women Society,
Christian Women, Eagles, and senior citizens. Betty and Ray were divorced in
February 1983.

"I have lived in Beulah since 1954 and this is where my children went to grade
and high school. I continue to make my home in Beulah and enjoy my family and
my life here," Betty says.

        John Mohl family: Amber, John, Carmen, Caty and Jason

John and Carmen Mohl

John Raymond Mohl, son of Betty L. (Miller) Mohl and Raymond Mohl, was born
June 22, 1955 at Bismarck Hospital. John attended Beulah public and high school
at Beulah and one year of college at Minot College. John has one sister,
Pamella (Mrs. Dale Kinslow) of Fargo.

Her mother, Janis, daughter of Emil and Olga Sailer, moved back to Beulah with

To be close to her family and also Orley's family (Hattie and Louie

Carmen then attended Beulah public school and high school, graduating in 1976.

John and Carmen make their home in Beulah. Carmen went with John when he did
out-of-state testing till the family expanded and son Jason John was born on

Beulah and hope that they can continue to make their home in Beulah.

        Philip and Emma Morast

Philip and Emma Morast

Philip Morast was born in 1898 to John and Elizabeth Morast in the Hazen area.
Emma Morast was born in Russia in 1899 and came to the United States with her
parents Christ and Christina Scheid when she was three. The family came to New
Salem on the train and were met by friends.

When Philip and Emma were growing up there were small communities close by, but
they had to go by oxen to get feed and groceries from New Salem. There were nine
children in Philip's family, three girls and six boys.

They farmed using oxen and mined their own coal and hauled it home with
horsedrawn wagons. They also gathered cow chips for their fire in cooking.

Philip and Emma were married in 1919 and moved to land he bought 15 miles
northwest of Hazen. They built a small house and a barn. The barn was struck by
lightning and burned to the ground three years later. They had to start all
over again since they lost a lot of things in the fire.

They farmed with horses until in the late 30's when Philip bought a tractor.
They milked cows, raised hogs, ducks, turkeys and chickens. The cows were
milked by hand.

When the children went to high school they had to board in town as there were no
school buses running then.

They had six children: Ida (Giesinger) born in 1920; Ray Morast, born in 1921;
Erna (Galster), born in 1923; Hulda (Isaak), born in 1927; Lorena (Olson), born
in 1931 and Agnes (Luft), born in 1939. All the children were born in Hazen.

Philip and Emma moved to Hazen in 1951 but kept on farming. Philip worked in the
Farmer Elevator in Hazen a few years as well as selling insurance. He served on
the A.S.C. office, school board, a church officer, Democratic committee, and
was a Farmers Union County board member.

Philip retired in 1962. Philip and Emma celebrated their 60th wedding
anniversary in 1979.

Emma died in 1983. Philip lives in the Hazen Pioneer Home now and is a member
of the St. Matthew's Lutheran Church of Hazen.

B. Harvey and Edith Moxley

B. Harvey Moxley was born July 17, 1865, to Joseph and Rhoda (Cummins) Moxley
at Sarnie, Ontario, Canada.

Edith Clarice (Vrooman) Moxley was born July 10, 1876, to John and Eliza
(Thomas) Vrooman at Windsor, Ontario, Canada.

B. Harvey Moxley was a farmer, carpenter, butcher and elevator operator.

B. Harvey and Edith had six children: Blanche was born Feb. 2, 1900, in
Michigan; Murray was born Oct. 19, 1901, in Michigan; Leonard was born Aug. 12,
1904, in Hesper, ND; Clarence was born Dec. 16, 1906, in Maddock, ND; Hazel was
born Jan. 29, 1910, in Mercer County and Leone was born Feb. 15, 1910, in
Mercer County.

Harvey was sworn in as a deputy sheriff at Ree, ND to maintain order at the
dances he sponsored weekly in that community. People came as far away as Beulah
and Hazen to attend the dances. He also had a butcher shop in that community in
1923.

The Moxleys were one of the few English-speaking families to settle permanently
in the Missouri River bottoms north of Beulah. Harvey had operated a butcher
shop and elevator in the Maddock/Hesper area prior to coming to Mercer County
in 1909 to file on a homestead immediately east of the reservation boundary on
the Missouri River bottoms. This land is now flooded by the Garrison Dam.
Harvey kept a journal of the spring breakup on the Missouri River which was
later published in the Beulah paper. His sons operated a sawmill at the
farmstead for many years.

Harvey owned one of the nine original Dakota cars which were licensed in North
Dakota. He purchased it new for $675 (including magneto) in 1910. His 16 hp,
two-cylinder car was later destroyed in a shop fire in Beulah where he had
taken it for repairs.

Dancing was a favorite activity of the family. When a visiting aunt from Detroit
chided Harvey for letting the girls go to so many dances, he asked how many was
too many. She replied, "Four dances in eight days is too many!"

The boys worked in the mine at Beulah while Hazel and Leone attended school for
several years. Fishing was another favorite family activity.

Hazel once caught a 34-pound sturgeon. Leone ran the mile home to ask Harvey to
bring a truck to get their big fish, but he wouldn't believe her "fish story!"
Leone's future husband used the fish as an excuse to get acquainted when he
called the first time. Harvey moved the farmhouse into Beulah after the
"taking" for the dam and lived there many years.

Murray C. and Hazel Moxley

Murray C. Moxley was born Oct. 19, 1901, to B. Harvey and Edith (Vrooman) Moxley
in Michigan.

Hazel (Houghtaling) Moxley was born March 24, 1910, to George and Eda J. (Couch)
Houghtaling in McLean County.

Murray and Hazel had two children. Murray C. Moxley Jr., was born May 7, 1933.
L. Joyce Moxley Gustafson was born Feb. 28, 1935. Both of their children were
born in Hazen.

Murray and Hazel were married during the Depression. They filed on a homestead
north of Beulah on the Missouri River bottoms and built a log cabin to live in.
They took a horseback pack trip up the Missouri River on their honeymoon and
earned over $25 in magpie bounty when they returned. Murray farmed with his
father, worked a sawmill with his brother and operated several country stores
in the area before moving to Beulah in 1945. Hazel taught in rural schools in
the area for many years.

Growing up in Beulah meant knowing everyone and trusting everyone. It was a town
that had a lot of pride in its school and its athletic programs. It was also a
town that cared about its children and a place to laugh, learn and grow.

Swimming in the Knife River in the summer with the big kids watching over the
younger ones, slumber parties that ended up with early morning breakfast at the
Beulah park, dances at the old Sheep Shed where whole families would go together
(but not necessarily leave together), the Cowboys' Reunion when we would have
beds all over the floors to accommodate all our guests from out of town, are all
memories of growing up in Beulah. Now old faces are no longer with us, buildings
have been refurbished and given new fronts, and the city limits have moved out
into old fields. The town has grown and changed and will never be the same.
Maybe that's good, but it's kinda sad too.

Joseph and Shirley Muhlhauser

On May 18, 1920, Joseph Jacob Muhlhauser was born in Beulah. His parents were
Ted and Ottillia Muhlhauser. He grew up in Beulah, attended both grade and high
school, and graduated in 1938. He served in the military from Nov. 1942-Nov.
1945, and attained the rank of tech. sergeant.

After the service, Joe returned to Beulah and worked in the RCU store for Carl
Thelander for two years. He also worked for H.Z. Rosen until 1951 when he
purchased the Beulah Cash Store from Rosen. He and his wife, Shirley, owned and
operated the Beulah Cash Store from 1951 until his death in March, 1988.

Joe was a city building inspector for Beulah for 10 years and served on the
Beulah school board for seven years. He was a lifetime member of the Beulah VFW
and a lifetime member of the North Dakota Firemen's Association. He was also a
member of Zion Lutheran church and served on the church council as treasurer
and as a deacon.

        Joe and Shirley Mulhauser

Shirley Catherine (Herman) Muhlhauser was born in Golden Valley on Nov. 11,
1921. Her parents were Emanuel C. and Emelia Herman. She grew up in Beulah and
attended grade and high school in the area.

Upon graduation from Beulah high school in 1940, she embarked on a trip to
Minneapolis with Mary (Molly) Cox to find work as a nanny. Shirley and Mary
spent several years in Minneapolis employed as nannies. She came back to Beulah
to work for the Thelander family in the RCU store. On Aug. 14, 1943, she
married Joseph Muhlhauser in Sacramento, CA.

Joe and Shirley lived in California and Texas while Joe was serving in the
Army. After his tour of duty, they returned to their home town of Beulah. She
worked together with her husband as a business partner until she became ill in
1977.

Shirley was well known in the area and across the state for her abilities as a
seamstress and a quilter. She won many awards for her quilts and her quilts have
been displayed in local museums. She was a member of Zion Lutheran Church and
was a founding member of the O.W.L.S. She died in December of 1982.

This marriage was blessed with three daughters: Jay (Muhlhauser) Brennan, who
lives in West Haven, CN; Jill (Muhlhauser) Galloway, of Beulah, and Tara Lee
Muhlhauser of Bismarck. Joe and Shirley also had five grandchildren of which
they were very proud: Joel, Joshua and Matthew Galloway; and Katie and Molly
Brennan.

Gary and Marjorie Murray

Gary Murray was born Sept. 14, 1935, at Bismarck, to Glenn and Beatrice Murray.

        Left to right: Dan, Steve, Wade, Glenn, Mike Murray

        Gary and Marge Murray

Gary and Margie have been members of the Beulah Quarterback Club for 11 years.
Gary has been a Beulah chamber member for 21 years and served for two years on
the Beulah School Board. He is also a charter member of the Beulah Eagles Club.
Margie is also active at Zion Lutheran Church and is presently serving as
treasurer.

Gary writes, "When I was a kid, Saturday night was the 'big night' in Beulah.
Everybody came to town! Stores stayed open late. The kids ran up and down the
streets playing with other farm kids. In my high school days, the drug store
was the big hang-out during noon hour and after school. The fountain was very
popular for cokes and the famous 'mud.' On Saturday night we all went to Zap to
the dance. Sunday night was spent at the Roxy Theatre in Beulah. Beulah had
good basketball teams when I was growing up and that tradition has continued. I
don't miss the old muddy Main Street we used to have!"

        Glenn and Bea Murray

        Glenn Murray family: Peggy, Gary, Phyllis, Bea and Glenn

Glenn and Beatrice Murray

Glenn Murray, a retired farmer, was born Sept. 22, 1908, to Charles and Anne
Murray of Beulah. His mother passed away in 1959 and his father in 1971. Glenn
has lived in Mercer County all of his life. His father, Charles Murray, was a

His wife, Bea, was born Sept. 5, 1910, to Harvey and Christine Erickson. Bea's

Glenn and Bea say that surviving the "Dirty Thirties" was an achievement. In
the early years when they were kids, they only came to town three or four times

Glenn is a member of the Beulah Chamber of Commerce and the Beulah Rodeo

the "relay race" that was held during the Beulah Cowboys Reunion Rodeo.

Ralph and Ella Murray

Ralph F. Murray was born Oct. 3, 1911, in Beulah. His father Samuel passed away
March 27, 1957, and his mother, Myrtle Elwilda (Wyatt), passed away Aug. 20,
1951. Ralph married Ella Voegele who was born April 6, 1923, in Beulah. Her
father John passed away March 9, 1958, and her mother, Christina (Stauss),
passed away Sept. 9, 1940. Patience Marie was born Nov. 28, 1960, in Zap. She
graduated from Beulah High School and the University of North Dakota. Patience
was married Aug. 7, 1981, to Calvin C. Sayler. They have a son, Joshua, and a
daughter, Elizabeth, and live in St. Louis, Mo.

Ralph was arena director for the Cowboys' Reunion Rodeo from 1939-1954, 4-H
leader for 10 years, charter member and director of the Beulah Chamber of
Commerce and the Mercer County Farm Bureau, a member of the North Dakota
Stockmen's Association for 43 years and served on the church board.

Ralph's parents came to North Dakota in 1905 from Missouri and took up residence
three miles south of Beulah where he was born and grew up. Ella's father was
born in South Russia, came to this country at the age of 20 and took up a
homestead 15 miles south of Beulah. Her mother was born in South Dakota and
moved to Blue Grass, N.D., where she grew up. Ella was born on the family farm
and has lived in the area all her life.

From 1936 until the spring of 1942, Ralph worked as a mule-skinner for the Knife
River Coal Mining Co. Wages back then were 64 cents an hour, working 10 hours or
more per day. Three mule-skinners would haul about 200 cars of coal per day,
each car hauling about three tons. When Ralph quit working as a mule-skinner,
he was making 67 cents an hour. In 1948 he bought the Tom Keogh ranch south of
Zap.

Ralph and Ella were married Dec. 17, 1957, and became parents of a
daughter, Patience, in 1960. In 1971 they sold the ranch to Don and Kay Voigt,
moved to Beulah and built a home where they still reside. Ralph worked for the
Knife River Veterinary Clinic until 1985 when he retired. Both are members of
the Beulah Congregational Church and enjoy high school sports, rodeos and
traveling.

LindaKay M. Naas

LindaKay M. Naas was born in Sharon, N.D., on July 18, 1943, the daughter of
Lester K. and Harriet (Ronningen) Naas. Originally, Harriet and Lester were
from Kloten, N.D., but now they reside in Devils Lake, N.D., and Weslaco, Texas.

LindaKay has lived in a number of North Dakota communities before moving to
Beulah. Kloten was home, Fargo was where she attended North Dakota State
University, in Hazen she was a vocational home economist and, in Bismarck she
was staff assistant for the State Board of Higher Education. She was a
vocational home economist in both Mandaree and Stanton, N.D., before she became
a senior standards analyst for Great Plains Gasification Associates at Beulah.

Of her move from Stanton to Beulah, she recalls, "The morning after an October
ice storm, my car slid into the ditch twice - the second time on Buffalo Hill
with 17 other vehicles. Suddenly commuting to GPGA lost its charm. I decided to
move from Stanton before the snow fell. Since it was the height of Great Plains
Gasification Project construction/start-up activity, few places were available.
However, two days later, I was settled in Sun Valley."

Ms. Naas is heavily involved in a number of community and state organizations,
among them the Sons of Norway--Sverdrup 107, Democratic Non-Partisan League
District 33, Beulah Chamber of Commerce, American Association of University
Women, Business Forms Management Association, Association for Business
Communication, American Society of Professional Women, Knife River Indian
Villages Advocates, Theodore Roosevelt Nature and History Association,
Bismarck-Mandan Genealogical Society, and Phi Upsilon Omicron, as well as Coal
Country Toastmasters.

August A. and Lydia Neuberger

August (Gus) A. Neuberger was born Nov. 20, 1903, on a farm close to Mannhaven,
N.D. Gus has been a farmer all of his life and is presently serving on the
equalization board here in Beulah. August's father, John, died Nov. 5, 1934, at
home, and his mother, Rosalin, died Sept. 7, 1966, in the nursing home. August
married Lydia (Boepple) and she was born Sept. 30, 1903, in Tripp, S.D. Lydia
(Shortie) worked as a school teacher for four years and is presently a
housewife. Her father and mother are both with the Lord. George Boepple passed
away July 15, 1953, while in a nursing home in Minot. Katherine (Goetz) passed
away May 14, 1943, after a stroke.

Gordon was born Aug. 10, 1927, on a farm eight miles from Mannhaven. Elmer was
born Oct. 20, 1928, also close to Mannhaven. Elaine was born Sept. 25, 1933, on
the farm five miles south of Beulah. Elaine took sick in 1983 with a brain
tumor and passed away on New Year's Eve. She lived on a farm in Minnesota about
40 miles out of St. Paul. Lucille was born May 19, 1941, in Beulah.

The Neubergers lived on a farm close to Mannhaven and in the spring of 1929
moved to the Christman farm close to the reservation. Then in the spring of 1933
they moved south on the Shattuck farm for a while and then over to the Vincent
farm; in two years they moved to the Stuts farm south of Beulah.

During this time things were rough on the farmers, no rain and lots of dust
storms. Things were so bad they had to cut thistles to feed the cattle. Then
the government came in and shot the cattle in the barn. They were paid $10 a
head.

The Neubergers have seen many changes in Beulah and also in the county. Many
farmers had to move when the Garrison Dam project was started years ago. In 1942
they purchased land in Oliver County that was Sagmiller and Gressle land.
Farming was good there, good crops and lots of hay back then. When Elmer and
Rita married, August and Lydia moved into town. The first year Lucille and
Elaine went to Bismarck schools after they moved there over the winter and came
home in the spring.

Reinhold and Selma Neuberger

Reinhold (Reinie) Neuberger was born and raised in Mannhaven, N .D., the son of
John and Rosina (Sayler) Neuberger. His birthday was June 22, 1910, and he lived
there until 1944. His father, John, died on Nov. 8, 1934, and his mother
followed on Sept. 12, 1966.

Selma was born in Krem, N.D., to Karl and Fredericka (Link) Rathjen on March 26,

After their marriage in 1944, Reinhold and Selma lived in Zap until 1952, when
they moved to Beulah. Reinhold made his living as a dealer of gas and oil.

Selma writes, "When we first came to Beulah all of the streets were dirt and
the town was small and everyone knew each other. Many changes have taken place
over the years. Who would have thought we would, having never moved, now live
next to a busy highway7 It is still amazing to us, how this dusty little town
grew up around us. The hill next to us used to be a favorite source of
wintertime entertainment - sledding. Now there are houses all over it.

"We hold many fond memories of the way Beulah used to be and of the way it is
now, with so much growth since the opening of the power plants and ANG."

The Neubergers have two children: Carol Jean Schiermeister, born May 13, 1945,
in Bismarck, and Douglas Richard, born Feb. 14. 1957, also in Bismarck.

Richard and Nancy Northrup

Between them, Richard and Nancy Northrup have lived at the four extremes of the
United States--both coasts and the Canadian and Mexican borders.

Perhaps typical of many "impact people," who moved to Beulah because of energy
development, the places where they were born, went to school and grew up had
several different names.

Richard was born Aug. 16, 1947 in Syracuse, N.Y., the only son of Richard and
Catherine (Nocera) Northrup. His parents were later divorced and he spent his
first 11 years in New York with his father, then moved to Albuquerque, N.M.,
where his mother lived, attending seminary for a time and finishing high school
in Sante Fe.

Following high school he enlisted in the Navy and saw much of the world from
underwater for the next four years, as he was on a nuclear submarine.

Meanwhile, Nancy had been born Nov. 5, 1952 in Stillwater, Okla. to B.E. and
Emma C. (Hulse) Lawson. Wanderlust was strong in that side of the family, as
both parents had been born in Missouri - and before she was six Nancy had lived
in at least as many houses.

        The Richard Northrup family left to right: Ricky, Richard, Nancy,
        Ryan and Christopher Northrup.

Her parents both taught (her father high school math, her mother home
economics)and the first house she remembers was a "teacherage," a small house
owned by a school district for a faculty member to live in. Another, much more
fun, was a farm with a big haystack she wasn't supposed to jump in (but did).

At seven, her parents made the move to a speck in the desert called Carrizozo,
N.M., where she grew up. Spanish came naturally--and of necessity, as Anglos
were a minority in town - though a love of hot chili, as made by the abuelitas,
had to be painfully acquired. As was sunburn. A lot of sunburn.

Nancy graduated as valedictorian in 1970, when Richard was just getting out of
the Navy. They both enrolled in New Mexico State University in Las Cruces,
Nancy on an academic scholarship and Rich on the GI Bill. They met through a
friend who insisted she was going to marry Rich, but Nancy had other plans.

So did Richard. He told her point-blank she, at 18, was too young for him, a
ripe old 23.

They were married a year and a half later on July 8, 1972. Both graduated with
honors, rather amazingly considering the amount of time they spent playing in
the muddy, swirling waters of the Rio Grande, racing motorcycles and riding in
the desert, and moved to Riverside, Calif., in 1974 when Richard was employed
as a supervisor with Kaiser Steel Corp. in Fontana, Calif.

Riverside was a beautiful city with palm trees and sunshine galore;
unfortunately it also had people galore and the Northrups didn't like crowds.
Nancy worked with several advertising agencies and public relations firms in
the area and did a stint as assistant advertising manager for a large regional
grocery chain.

In 1978 they moved to Fontana, partly because Rich was tired of driving 40
minutes one way to work and partly to buy property with some land (two and a
half acres is a "ranchette" there). Richard got busy planting gardens and trees
and, by the time they left in 1983, there were oranges, grapefruits, lemons,
peaches, avocados, pears, plums, walnuts and almonds, an apple or two, apricots
and more to prove how much earth he'd dug. (They were also just ready to bear
their first real crop when the Northrups moved to Beulah.) There were grapes,
strawberries and a very large garden, and Nancy made an art of finding reasons
why she shouldn't pull weeds.

On Feb. 2, 1979, the couple's first son, Richard J. IV, was born on a 75-degree
day and immediately developed heat rash. Nancy stayed home to do what mothers
are supposed to do with babies and the family continued the kitchen remodeling
project they'd begun when they moved to Fontana. Ricky knew all about plaster
dust, nails, spackle, plumbing and electricals first-hand - before he was two.

Bursts of creative carpentry coincided with babies, and after a bath remodeling
project Ryan was born on March 14, 1981. A big, strapping 11-pound boy, the
nurses all asked why a three-month-old was in the newborn nursery. Nancy just
sighed.

The garden grew and so did the boys, and the family's two Irish wolfhound
puppies outstripped them all. Rumors began that Kaiser Steel was going to close
down, but no one much believed it. In the melee, another son was on the way
(along with a two-story house addition Rich built) and shortly before his birth
Kaiser did indeed shut down.

Not long after Christopher's birth on Jan. 28, 1983, and the remarkable ease
with which he was integrated into the family, Richard was hired on the Great
Plains Gasification Associates project and the family moved to Beulah.

It was crowded at first, with five bodies in 750 square feet, and limited
available housing dictated building a home. Everyone breathed easier when that
was finished and they could move in.

The whole family immediately took to the area. It was clean and spacious and
uncluttered - and best of all, uncrowded. The lake rapidly became a favorite
spot, and both parents were delighted they could let the kids play outside
without paranoia.

That fall Nancy hired on as proofreader-copy editor for BHG, Inc., catching
typos for the Beulah Beacon and Hazen Star, while Rich soaked up the complicated
technology necessary to starting up the sophisticated gas plant. The boys
continued to do what little boys do best, unknowingly providing Mom with
unending material for a column she soon began writing for the Beacon.

The first winter was a shocker for Nancy. Rich had been through Connecticut
winters in the Navy and had some idea what to expect, but driving home from
work in -50 degree weather on Christmas Eve 1983 Nancy discovered ANYTHING will
freeze if it's cold enough - hoods, batteries, doors, windows, hands, gas
lines, garage doors and tears.

Rich chuckled and the boys squealed in delight, having discovered with Mom that
cars do fun things on the ice, but she survived and learned.

Rich has switched areas in the plant several times, racking up a good overall
knowledge of much of the technology. Nancy was moved to editor of the Beacon in
1985, the same year Ricky started first grade. In 1989 youngest Christopher
started first grade, putting all three boys in the Beulah grade school.

Rich and Nancy belong to the Beulah Chamber of Commerce. They did a stint as co-
presidents of the Parent-Teacher Organization and Rich has been on the swimming
pool board for four years. He has been instrumental in renovating and updating
the 20-year-old structure. In addition to chasing news, Nancy was co-editor of
this history book project.

        Art Oberlander family Back row: Diane, Don, Kathleen, Glenn and Fred.
        Front row: Una, Art, Vera and Nancy

Arthur and Vera Oberlander

Arthur Oberlander retired after 43 years of farming. He was born Nov. 30, 1915,
south of Halliday in Dunn County. His parents were Fred and Eva (Zuern)
Oberlander. He married Vera Herrmann, daughter of Theodore and Hilda (Reiner)
Herrmann, who was born Oct. 11, 1920 at Zap.

Art and Vera farmed 10 miles north of Beulah of Art's father's farm where they
raised their eight children: Diane, Kathleen, Fredrich, Glenn, Una, Neal, Nancy
and Don. Art purchased the farm in 1940. This farm was homesteaded by Art's
grandmother, Eva Zuern, who had come from Russia in the 1800's. Art's father
had homesteaded eight miles south of Halliday but they moved to Grandmother
Zuern's farm when Art was five.

Art served on the Center school board for nine years and on the election board
for six years. Art and Vera are members of Concordia Lutheran Church and the
Senior Citizens Club in Beulah.

Arts writes, "Farming has changed a lot. It used to be all hard work, digging
rocks by hand. All farm work was done with horses. There was no electricity.
Today farmers use all hydraulic machinery and there isn't as much physical
work. Without electricity, we had to pump water by hand, and baths were taken
in the washtub.

Art lived north of Beulah before the Garrison Dam was built. It took a lot of
timberland away which was used for firewood. Coal was stripped using horses
during the summertime to have enough coal for winter use.

Glenn and Colleen Oberlander

Glenn, son of Arthur and Vera Oberlander, was born at Hazen on June 23, 1953. He
grew up on his parents' farm north of Beulah. He attended rural schools and
graduated from Beulah High School. He entered the Army in June, 1973, and served
in the 4th Infantry Division until June, 1976. Glenn is presently employed by
MDU Coyote Station.

Colleen was born April 21, 1962, at Benson, Minn. She is the daughter of Floyd
and Hazel Guyott. She graduated from Benson High School and attended St. Mary
College in Minneapolis, receiving an associate degree in special education.
Colleen operates a day care center in Beulah.

Glenn and Colleen's children are Christina, born April 6, 1984; Victoria, born
Aug. 5, 1985; and Jonathan, born March 31, 1987.

Jacob Orth

Jacob Orth was born at Artas, SD, on Sept. 19, 1885. He came to Mercer County
as a grown man to take up a homestead and put up a few buildings. He then went
back home to get married on Aug. 25, 1907 to Susana Barreth.

Susana was born Aug. 4, 1887, at Menno, SD. Her parents later moved to Zeeland,
ND. After their marriage they came back by train to Glen Ullin and brought with
them furniture, machinery, wagon buggy, also five horses, one cow, one heifer,
two pigs and a few chickens.

They had two daughters and seven sons with four of the sons passing away at a
young age. Robert Orth married Mary Tabbeth and lived at Glendive, MT. He is
deceased. Rueben Orth married Cecelia Thomas and lives at Fargo. Julius Orth,
now deceased, married Bertha Kessler, and they lived at Beulah. Eva Orth
married Tex Bronson and lives at Kellogg, ID. Ella Orth married John Burkhardt
and lives at West Fargo. Jacob Orth passed away Nov. 18, 1938 and Susana Orth
on May 23, 1972. Both rest at the Beulah City Cemetery.

Julius Orth was born May 26, 1915, on his parents' homestead south of Beulah
where he received his eighth grade education. On Oct. 18, 1941, he married
Bertha Kessler. Bertha was born July 20, 1917 at Beulah to John and Lydia
(Beck) Kessler. They farmed south of Beulah until 1971 when they moved into
Beulah. Julius was active in the community and served 30 years on the Farmers
Union elevator board and was secretary about 20 years. He also was instrumental
in completing the Mercer County Historical Society building and served on that
board. He was chairman of Knife River Farmers Union and helped start the rural
fire department and was secretary of that for a number of years. Julius was very
enthusiastic about restoring cars and tractors. He belonged to two car clubs
that he helped start and won many trophies in that field. At the time of his
death on July 30, 1985, he was president of the Beulah Senior Citizens.

Bertha still makes her home at Beulah where she keeps busy with crafts, reading
and gardening. At the present time is serving on the Beulah Senior Citizens
board and is a member of the Congregational Church at Beulah.

Fred and Selma Ost

Frederick "Fred" Ost was born north of Beulah on April 3, 1907, to Johann and
Fredericka (Boeshans) Ost. He married Selma Ida Mohl on Sept. 11, 1923, at

Gilbert and Violet Ost

Gilbert Ost was born Sept. 8, 1930 at Beulah to Christian and Bertha (Wiedrich)
Ost. His father died in 1964 and his mother in 1965. Gilbert married Violet
Lorenz. Violet was born Feb. 1, 1932 at Watauga, S.D. to John and Margaret
(Bitterman) Lorenz. Her parents moved to Zap. Her father died in 1943 and her
mother in 1953.

They are parents of four children, all born in Hazen.

Vicky Violet, born Jan. 21, 1950, married Jimo Menge. They have three children;
Jak is 16 years old, Tara is 14 and Jason is 12. They live in Fountain, Colo.
Jimo is plant foreman at an electric plant and Vicky is a nurse, employed at
the hospital in Colorado Springs.

Cary Lee, born Jan. 16, 1954, married Ava Rebhahn. They have two sons, Casey, 6,
and Cody, 1 1/2 . They live north of Beulah on the home place. Cory is an

at Elite Beauty Shop.

Joette Fay, born April 9, 1955, married Terrance Maericke. They have two

attending Mary College and Joette is a secretary for Hobb Industries.

Linda Carol, born Dec. 21, 1957, married Perry Wolf. They have two daughters,
Jessica, 7, and Angilee, 5. They live on a farm north of Zap. Perry is a miner
at Knife River Coal Mine and also raises cattle. Linda is account
representative for Production Credit Association in Beulah.

The Osts have been members of Immanuel Baptist Church for 33 years. Gilbert has
served as church deacon for over 30 years, Sunday school teacher over 25 years
and a church moderator for about 15 years. He has also been a Gideon about 15
years, served as chairman of the board of the Beulah Community Nursing Home
for two years, served as the first vice president of the Mercer County
Landowners Association and past president of the local chapter of Germans from
Russia, Die Deutsche Stammhalter.

Violet belongs to the Happy Hour Bowling League, is a member of Die Deutsche
Stammhalter Chapter, member of Women's Missionary Society, taught Sunday school
for over 25 years and belongs to the Gideon Auxiliary serving as president.

Gilbert writes of his special memories, "I was born and raised in Antelope
Valley. I got married and raised my children there. It was home to us until
1979 when we moved into Beulah. I'm still actively engaged in farming my land
there. When I stop to think what that valley was like then and what it is
today, a giant industrial complex, I can scarcely comprehend it. Gone are many
of the farms, fields, and meadows that we roamed as children and worked as
adults. Gone is a way of life we thought would go on indefinitely. Gone are
many of the friends and neighbors that were so much a part of our lives.

"When I stop to think what Beulah was like when I was a child, I would see it
from the back seat of my dad's Model A Ford as they came to town once a week to
sell their produce and buy their supplies, and what it is today. It's just mind
boggling! The streets were dirt, or mud if it rained. On Saturday night, at
midnight, the street lights were turned off. The small frame buildings on Main
Street. The very small cream station where you sold cream at the front door and
skunks, hides and scrap iron at the back door.

"The school was huge (without the gym on the east side) and scary. The stock
yard was in the middle of town, south of the tracks, next to Chaffee Road.
Which brings to mind shipping time in the fall of the year when the neighbors
up the valley from us would turn his cattle to be sold, out on the road. As
they passed the second farm more cattle were added, same at the third farm and
so on until cattle from six or seven farms were collected into one herd.

"This herd was then brought by saddle horses to town, usually on Friday. On
Saturday morning the cattle were loaded into cattle cars. The train came down
the line from Killdeer, picking up cattle cars in every town, building a
livestock train, which then headed for St. Paul, Minn. All this and more
changed!

"Whether change is good or not could be and has been debated long and hard but
one thing we know, it will always be with us. God grant us the ability to
change with it!"

Ost Family History

The Ost family history can be traced back to Poland to Heinrich Ost, born in
1811 in Wilhelmsdorf, Ostrow, Poland, and his wife, Anna Marie Schmidt, born in
1808 in Ostrdingen, Poland.

When they settled in Klostitz, Bessarabia, Russia, is unknown, but Klostitz was
founded in 1815 and the Osts' first child was born there in 1831. They were
married in 1830 and had at least 10 children, including Christian, all born in
Klostitz.

Christian, born March 3, 1840, married on June 23, 1860 at Klostitz, Bessarabia
to Karolina Wolt. Karolina was born June 24, 1840, at Klostitz to Andreas and
Margaretha (Krownwolt) Wolt.

Christian and Karolina were parents of at least eight children: Gottfried, Mrs.
Konstantine (Fredricka) Stohler, Mrs. Adam (Katherina) Baisch, Johann, Mrs.
Jacob (Louisa) Dschaak, Mrs. Peter (Barbara) Dschaak, Friedrich and Mrs. Jacob
Christman.

On Oct. 6, 1900, Christian and Karolina Ost, with their youngest daughter,
Anna, age 16, arrived at New York from Hamburg, Germany, on the ship, Patricia.
They traveled to North Dakota by train, coming to Krem, where their daughter
Katherina and her husband Adam Baisch had settled. He opened a shoe and harness
shop at Krem which he operated the rest of his life.

Christian Ost died Aug. 20, 1921, at Krem. His wife, Karolina (Wolt) Ost, died
June 20, 1911. Their children all came to America, settling in Mercer County
except Mrs. Konstantine (Fredericka) Stohler, who settled in Dunn County, and
Friedrich Ost, born 1878, who was serving in the Russian Army and lost his life
in 1904 before he could join his family in North Dakota. Friedrich was married
to Natalie (of Russian descent) and had several sons when the others left for
America in 1900.

Johann Ost was born Nov. 9, 1869 at Klostitz and was married there to Fredericka
Boeshans on Feb. 20, 1894. Fredericka was born April 25, 1874 at Klostitz to
Wendelin and Katherina (Hirt) Boeshans. In 1902 they left Eupatoria, Crimea, for
America on the ship Armenia. Their departure was Nov. 4, 1902, from Halifax to
New York. Their children listed on the passenger list were Christian, 6,
Katharina, 3, Emelie, 2, and Jacob, 2 months. From New York to New Salem, N.D.,
they traveled by train, then from New Salem to Krem to his parents, the
Christian Osts. The Johann Ost family settled north of Beulah where they raised
their family. Johann Ost died March 25, 1936, his wife Fredericka (Boeshans)
Ost died Sept. 11, 1933. Both are buried at Peace Lutheran Church Cemetery
northwest of Beulah.

Their children are Christian, born March 18, 1896, at Klostitz, married on Nov.
21, 1920, to Emma Kruckenberg. He died on Dec. 12, 1972, at White Fish, Mont.

Katharina, born in 1899 at Klostitz, died as an infant.

Emilia, born March 24, 1900, at Klostitz, married Christian Jose on March 23,
1923, lived at Wing and Beulah, remarried Jacob Buchmann on July 27, 1966, died
July 10, 1980, buried at Beulah Cemetery.

Jacob, born in 1902 at Klostitz, died as an infant.

Robert, born Oct. 9, 1903, at Beulah, married Oct. 10, 1924, to Alvina Herman,
lived in Beulah; Fairview, Mont.; Havre, Mont., and Livingston, Mont.; died
Sept. 9, 1975;

Gottfried, born Dec. 21, 1905, at Beulah, married Bertha Wolf on Nov. 2, 1932,
died April 1, 1955. His widow Bertha still makes her home in Beulah.

Frederich, born April 3, 1907, at Beulah, married Selma Mohl on Sept. 11, 1932.
He farmed and lived at Beulah all his life, he died Sept. 20, 1984. Selma
resides at Beulah.

Martha, born Dec. 4, 1912, at Beulah, married Feb. 29, 1932, to Carl Jose. They
live in Bismarck.

Nathalia, born April 28, 1914, at Beulah, married Jacob Pfenning on Jan. 22,
1935. They live at Mandan.

Sharold and Caroline Oster

Caroline Fern Heihn was born March 1, 1939, at the Bismarck Hospital. She is the
daughter of Theodore (Ted) and Martha (Pfenning) Heihn, of Beulah.

Caroline attended and graduated from Beulah High School in 1957. She was very
active in band, choir, FHA, editor of the school "Dial," Drama Club, speech,
Science Club, and soloist for various competitions. She graduated from the
Milwaukee School of Nursing in 1960, and worked toward her degree at the
University of Minnesota from 1960-1962.

On Dec. 27, 1962, Caroline married Sharold Edwin Oster, son of Edwin and Freida
(Mattheis) Oster at the Zion Lutheran Church in Beulah, with Pastor Marvin
Schumacher officiating. They moved to Fargo, where Sharold attended North Dakota
State University. Caroline was a registered nurse at St. Lukes Hospital in
Fargo.

In 1963, they returned to Hazen, where Caroline worked at the Hazen Memorial
Hospital for over 10 years. She worked several years as a surgical nurse. She
was an active member of the Peace Lutheran Church in Hazen, the American
Lutheran Church Women (ALCW), Community Choir, soloist at various wedding and
activities and was very active in the local community affairs. Caroline died of
cancer on March 17, 1975 at the age of 36.

        Albert Pischel family Left to right: Anna, Pauline, Gerald, Albert,
        Marva, Judy, Alice

Albert and Pauline Pischel

Albert Pischel was born July 10, 1925, five miles north of Beulah to John and
Christine (Teske) Pischel, one of their 11 children. He was drafted into the
U.S. Army on June 28, 1944, and on Christmas Day, 1944, left for the war
theatre in the South Pacific.

Albert is a 100 percent disabled veteran of World War II and was honored with a
Purple Heart. He was wounded in Okinawa on April 30, 1945. He doesn't remember
how long it was before someone found him, but when he came to he was in one of
the tents which served as field hospitals during that war.

And, he was in a cast from his toes to his neck. Amazingly, the doctor who
looked after him in the field hospital was Dr. Ralph Vinje, who was a Beulah
doctor before the war. Albert remained in the field hospital until he was
strong enough to be flown to another hospital at Pearl Harbor, where he spent
three weeks and received his Purple Heart. From there he was flown to Ft.
Lewis, Wash., where he stayed until he was able to come home.

After spending some six months in the hospital he was discharged Oct. 18, 1945,
and returned home to farm.

Albert married Pauline Goldade on Feb. 18, 1946, at Hazen. Pauline was born Dec.
29, 1925, south of Beulah in Oliver County to Joseph and Susan (Hoepfner)
Goldade. She came from a family of 10 children.

After their marriage they moved to a farm northwest of Beulah, the Reinhold
Renke farm, where they lived from 1946 until the fall of 1949 when they moved
to his father's farm. They still live there but had to give up farming in 1970
due to Albert's health.

They have five children: Anna, born July 29, 1948 at Beulah and married to Donny
Miller and later Fred Buechler; Marva, born May 22, 1950, at Hazen, married to
Duane Keller; Judy, born June 25, 1953, at Bismarck, was married to David
Keller; Alice, born July, 1958, at Hazen, married to Tim Bosch; and Gerald,
born Jan. 29, 1960, at Hazen, married to Carol Sobeski.

They also have 10 grandchildren and two step-grandchildren.

Jacob and Rosina (Heine) Raszler

There are many stories to be told of the early German-Russian settlers who
homesteaded in the Beulah area. Rosina (Heine) Raszler is only one of the many
Germans who settled here and made a life for herself, yet her history is unique
because she brought her four sons to America alone as the head of her family and
homesteaded an area close to Otter Creek. Because of the determination of their
mother, the sons grew to manhood on the prairies of North Dakota, instead of on
Russian soil.

        Adolph and Emella Raszler with one of their 20 grandchildren

        Adolph and Emella Raszler on their golden anniversary

Rosina was born in 1865. She was the daughter of Christoph Heine and Elenora
(Kunz) Heine, who were Germans living in Bessarabia, South Russia. She married
Jacob Raszler and they had four sons; Gottfreid, Adolph, John and David, all
born in Russia. Rosina's husband, Jacob, died while serving as a soldier in the
Russian Army. The Germans who served in the Russian Army were not treated well
and it is thought that Jacob died from a ruptured bladder at the approximate
age of 45.

Meanwhile, living conditions in Russia had become almost unbearable for Germans,
who were forced from their land and holdings and deprived of their religious
beliefs. Germans by the thousands were immigrating to America for the promise
of free land and free speech and religion. Rosina's brother Gottfried and his
wife and family immigrated to Krem, ND, in 1894.

Should she keep her family in Russia where she knew what the perils would be, or
should she take them to America, a land of which she knew virtually nothing? It
must have been a difficult decision for a mother to make without the help of
her husband. Would she be strong enough to face the hardships of a new land?

One can only guess at the thoughts that went through her mind, but in 1905, she
made her decision. She would go to America.

The voyage across the ocean must have been a difficult one for a mother alone
with four children. Even though there wasn't much food for the voyage, many
people were seasick, so the food seemed to last. Rosina's son, Adolph, was 12
when the ocean journey was made.

After her arrival in America, Rosina spent some time with her brother and then
"hired out" for some years to raise enough money to file her homestead papers
and buy the necessary supplies to begin her farmstead. Rosina's homestead
papers were filed in 1916, but it is not known how long she lived on the land
before she actually made the filing.

Rosina never re-married, but continued to raise her sons and farm the homestead
she had been freely given in the land called America. Thus she lived for about
14-20 years, until her death in 1930. She is buried in a graveyard one mile
north of Hazen. Her character was typical of the many Germans from Russia who
settled in the Beulah area: she was strong, determined, and had the ability to
endure the hardships that life gave her.

Adolph Raszler, Rosina's son, was 26 when he bought his farmland from Adolph
Goetz on Dec. 4, 1919. When he was 27 he married Emelia Wiedenmeyer, who was
born Sept. 7, 1898, in South Dakota to Fredrich and Chrestena (Horn)
Wiedenmeyer. She moved along with her family as a small child to Kronthal, ND,
where she attended schools. The family moved from South Dakota to North Dakota
in a covered wagon and it is remembered that Adolph said the Wiedenmeyers would
have gone all the way to Canada if the Missouri River hadn't stopped them!

Adolph and Emelia were married on Feb. 17, 1920, at Kronthal. After their
marriage, they farmed on Adolph's land southeast of Beulah, where they were
blessed with a family of nine sons and one daughter. Their children are: Edwin,
born Dec. 14, 1920; Arnold, born Jan. 25, 1923; Oswald, born Dec. 30, 1924;
Herbert, born April 26, 1926 (he died from whopping cough two months later);
Otto, born June 24, 1927; Raymond, born Jan. 10, 1930 (he was killed in a
car/train accident with his wife, Esther on May 25, 1980); Edgar born April 25,
1931; Walter born Sept. 29, 1933; Albert, born Jan. 22, 1939 and died Feb. 10,
1957; and Eileen, born Nov. 1, 1941.

Raising a large family and farming in times when there was no electricity or
modern conveniences was a 24-hour-a-day job for both Adolph and Emilia. Of
course, one can well imagine that a family of so many boys could always find
some mischief to get into, and the boys who are now grown men with children and
grandchildren of their own, sometimes reminisce about sliding down haystacks,
walking across the top of the old Red Bridge on the Knife River or reading
storybooks in their hideaway in the old granery.

Adolph's grandchildren remember him for bouncing them on this knee while he sang
a favorite German tune to them, or entertaining them with his false teeth or his
favorite "I stole your nose, trick, in which he used his thumb stuck between two
fingers to trick small grandchildren.

The family farm home may not have been a large one by today's standards, but it
housed the family and provided shelter for all the children very adequately.
Emelia cooked many of the German dishes that are still popular in the area, and
she enjoyed gardening and raising flowers. Her grandchildren remember the
irises that grew around the farm home.

The family was not without its hardships, and particularly difficult times for
the family were the deaths of their son Herbert, two months old, and Albert,
who died from a gun accident in 1957. He was 18 when he died. Another terrible
tragedy struck in 1980 when Raymond and his wife Esther were killed in a
car/train accident.

"Butchering days" were always a time when the family would gather together and
spend several days butchering beef and pork, making homemade sausage and
enjoying the freshly cooked beef liver. Strange that so few enjoy it in the
present day and it was considered a delicacy then. The grandchildren were
always intrigued by the sausage stuffer and the "casings" that were used to
hold the delicious sausage.

One of the first pieces of furniture bought by Adolph and Emelia was a rocking
chair - purchased with one of their first wheat crops. Their oldest son, Edwin,
can remember many of the children being rocked by their mother in the old
rocking chair which is still in the family.

After Albert's death in 1957, Adolph and Emelia moved to a home in Beulah.
Living in town was a different experience for them after farming for so many
years, but they seemed to adjust. Adolph could be seen walking down the hill to
get the mail almost every day when the weather and his health permitted, and
Emelia became involved in quilting for the mission circle at Zion Lutheran
Church. Adolph and Emelia Raszler were married for 58 years.

The farmstead where Adolph and Emelia lived and raised their family is now
abandoned. The wind that still turns the farm windmill whistles through the
failing walls of the home that once held the activity of a large, busy family.

Only a few miles away, across the prairie hills is the huge Coyote Station. Its
sight would have amazed Adolph and Emelia. The presence of the huge
technological structure across the hills from the Raszler farmstead and only a
few miles from Rosina Raszler's homestead is a true testimony to the striking
changes that occur within two generations.

Adolph Raszler died March 11, 1978. Emelia was a resident of the Beulah Nursing
Home from 1975 until her death on Easter Sunday, April 3, 1988. Adolph was a
faithful visitor at his wife's room at the nursing home every day as long as
his health permitted. Their children remember them singing German hymns when
they still lived on the farm, and their enjoyment in the hymns brings comfort
to those who mourn the loss of Adolph and Emelia Raszler.

Thus the Raszler family has grown, from Jacob Raszler, who died on Russian soil
and Rosina Raszler and her four sons, who immigrated to a strange land in 1905,
to a family of hundreds of members in 1989, who all bear the legacy of the
pioneer woman named Rosina Raszler.

        Otto and Bertha Reich

Otto and Bertha Reich

Otto Reich was born Feb. 10, 1901 in Russia to August and Wilhelmina Reich. He
came to America with his parents while still a baby. For a short time they
lived in Kulm, ND and then Krem, ND. Later his dad homesteaded nine miles south
of Hazen. Otto grew up there and went to Red Butte School. He married Bertha
Betz on July 3, 1928 and they lived on the farm near Red Butte for 27 years.

Bertha (Betz) Reich was born on May 11, 1908 to Mr. and Mrs. David Betz on her
parents' homestead four miles east of Beulah near the Knife River. Their first
house was a sod house. Later they bought a farm two miles southeast and built a
house there. Bertha went to school a short distance north of their home. Her
mother always had a big garden. All the girls had to hoe the weeds. They also
had to pick potato bugs and put them into a bucket of kerosene. How they hated
those bugs!

After her marriage, Bertha and her husband lived near Red Butte. She was
assistant leader for the girls in the Red Butte 4-H Club. She also was the
clerk for the Red Butte School District. The school burned down on Jan. 5,
1952. There was so much snow that winter, the fire truck was unable to get
through. After the school burned down, the local election had to be held in the
entry of the Reich home.

In 1955 they bought a ranch from Fred Flemmer, located six miles south of Zap
along the Knife River. In 1965 they sold the ranch to their sons Delvin and
Kenneth, and moved to Beulah. Otto passed away on July 18, 1973.

They have four children: Raymond (born 1929) was married on Sept. 16, 1957 to
Norene Buchanan in Seattle, WA. They have two boys, Kenneth and David. Raymond
lives in Stanwood, WA, and has been employed at Boeing since 1955.

Delvin (born 1932) was married on Nov. 18, 1967 to Joyce Boland. They have three
children, Jack, Stephanie, and Joseph. In 1961 Delvin was named North Dakota
all-around champion cowboy. He received three saddles and several buckles. He
now lives south of Zap. Joyce passed away on Jan. 20, 1984.

Kenneth (born 1936) was married to Elaine Becher on Nov. 5, 1971. They live
south of Zap on their ranch. For the past 25 years, he has been a brand
inspector for the Beulah sales ring.

Carol (born 1943) was married in 1975. She has one son, Daniel, and they live in
Beulah.

        Bill Rettke

William "Bill" and Johanna Rettke

Wilhelm Johannes Herman Rettke was born in 1878 in Pomerania, Germany to Herman
and Johanna (Potratz) Rettke. In 1882 the family came to the U.S. and settled
in Kossouth County, Iowa. They later moved to Niagara, ND. In 1901, he married
Elizabeth Behm at Niagara. The same year they moved to Wenatchee, WA. In 1902,
Elizabeth died during the birth of their son Herman. Bill carried the surviving
infant back to Niagara in a basket.

In 1905, he took a homestead 10 miles southwest of Beulah. Here he married
Johanna Potratz, the widow of Rev. G.F. Potratz who was a pioneer missionary for
the Lutheran Church, Missouri Synod in North Dakota. Bill and his wife had three
children, Paul, Otto and Ernest. The Potratz children were Agnes, Erna, Werner
(Dick), Gerhard (Gay) and Gunther (Guy). Another son was missing in action in
World War II, and another drowned on the farm.

Johanna died the day before Christmas Eve in 1945. In 1950, Bill married Lasena
"Clara" Loning. They lived on the farm until 1955 when they moved into Beulah.
He died in November 1959. Clara lives at the Beulah Community Nursing Home.

Bill served two terms in the North Dakota Legislature in the early '40s and was
involved with the Non-partisan League.

Frederick Jr. and Elizabeth Reub

Frederick Reub Jr. was born in Alt Hofnungstahl, South Russia. He was the
oldest of the Reub children. He received his education in the schools in
Russia. He was a young man of 20 when his parents decided to emigrate to
America.

In 1906 Fred filed claim on 160 acres east of Beulah. He broke the land with a
walking plow and a team of horses.

In 1911 he married Elizabeth Schlect. She had come over from Russia with her
step-brother John Krauz, in 1910.

Fred and Lisa were married on Oct. 1, 1911, by Rev. Schult, a Lutheran pastor.
There was no organized Lutheran congregation, so they were married in a nearby
school.

The couple lived on Fred Junior's homestead until 1939. All of the children
were born here and grew to adulthood on this farm.

When they needed steel for the East Bridge (near Beulah) Fred Junior was one of
the men who went by wagon to New Salem to haul the steel. So that the long trip
over wasn't made with an empty wagon, he'd haul over a load of wheat. Fred also
dug many wells in and around Beulah. Many of these are still in existence today.

In 1939 the Reubs moved into town, although Fred continued to farm with the help
of his sons until 1952. He sold 240 acres to Knife River Coal Co., gave Herbert
the home place and Jake received another quarter. Jake lives on the Frederick
Sr. and Charlotta Reub farm.

The Reubs were charter members of Zion Lutheran Church, of which they remained
members.

Even after retiring Fred remained active and liked to putter. Every house he
lived in he would improve and remodel. The last house the Reubs moved in and
remodeled was Grandma Reub's.

Fred suffered a stroke from which he never fully recovered. After a long
illness Fred passed away April 14, 1961. Lisa passed away on April 23, 1965.

The Reub children are Clara, Mrs. Bill Werner of Mandan; Jake of Beulah
(married to Pauline Heihn); Herb of Beulah (married to Ida Weil); Erna, Mrs.
Howard Johnson of Underwood; Elsie, Mrs. Gordon Goetz of Sundance, Wyo. There
are sixteen grandchildren and 17 great-grandchildren.
