        Theo Ricker family: Ellie, Esther, Hanna and Walter. Seated: Frieda
        and Theo.

Theophil and Frieda Ricker Theophil Ricker was born on Aug. 27, 1903 in
Neubajaut, Crimea, Russia, to Thomas and Christine (Boeshans) Ricker. Theo's
great-grandfather, Georg David Ricker, immigrated from Rohrbronn, Germany, to
this southern part of Russia by the Black Sea in 1840 to establish a weaving
mill.

Shortly after Russia entered World War I in 1914, Theo's father was shipped to
Kologriv, Russia (400 miles northeast of Moscow), for internment along with
other Germans living in Russia who had retained their German citizenship. In
the spring of 1915, Theo, his mother, two sisters, and three brothers traveled
by train to Kologriv to join Thomas after Thomas had sent secret code messages
embedded in his letters to his family.

While the family was under constant surveillance in Kologriv, they were free to
come and go through this lumber industry town from 9 a.m. - 9 p.m. They were
unable to get a job and had to live on what money they had. Luckily, Thomas had
been a wealthy farmer and so the family survived quite well and helped friends
who had little money.

Theo and his family, along with other Germans in Kologriv, were placed on ships
and traveled down the swollen river to Moscow in May of 1918. They traveled for
six weeks by rail to Petersburg, Russia, to the Weichsel River by Poland, and
finally to Stuttgart, Germany. Their freedom had been negotiated by the Swedish
Red Cross after the Bolshevik Revolution in the fall of 1917.

Theo's uncle Joseph Boeshans signed for Theo, age 19, to immigrate to the U.S.
in July 1923. Theo worked on Joseph's farm north of Beulah for 200 days to pay
for the $200 trip across the ocean.

While working on a farm north of Golden Valley, he met his future wife, Frieda
Henke. Frieda, born on July 14, 1910, north of Golden Valley to Ferdinand and
Caroline (Klaus) Henke, had six sisters and eight brothers and lived on a farm.
Her father and mother were both born in Russia, married in Russia, moved to
Hebron on April 10, 1899, and then moved to Golden Valley.

Theo and Frieda married on Oct. 3, 1929. They then rented farm land and bought
what they needed to begin their life together. Frieda remembers that $100 was
allotted for household goods and so she bought a bedroom suite with dresser,
vanity, and nightstand for $24, six chairs for $2 each, a butcher knife for 47
cents, a cast iron frying pan, and a nice new wood stove. She was given an old
table and cupboard which her grandfather had made.

Their three daughters, Esther, Ella, and Hanna, and one son, Walter, were born
during the Great Depression. This was a difficult time for them as they had to
pay rent for the farm land and support their family. A bushel of wheat brought
only 24 cents, a big cow $25, pigs 25 cents a pound, cream 17 cents a pound,
and eggs eight cents a dozen. But while they weren't rich, they weren't hungry
either. They raised everything they needed and bought only sugar and flour.
Despite this hardship, they still sent money to Theo's parents still living in
Germany.

After renting for 12 years, they purchased a half section of farm land 16 miles
north of Beulah in 1941 from the Bank of North Dakota for approximately $2,000.
They moved from the farm to Bismarck in 1961, to Beulah in 1966, where they
retired, and to Golden Valley in 1980.

Theo died on May 6, 1982, after a long struggle with heart problems and fluid
in his lungs. Frieda, at age 77, still lives in Golden Valley. Esther is
married to Ray Eisenbeis and lives in Beulah, Hanna is married to Harold Link
and lives north of Golden Valley, Ella is married to Steve Dassinger and lives
in Glendive, MT, and Walter is married to Lois Zepik and lives in Hamilton, MT.

        The Robideau family: Charles, Jim, Connie, Michael

James and Connie Robideau

James Neil Robideau, son of Wayne and June Robideau, was born and raised in
Moorhead, MN. Connie Nadine Halvorson, daughter of Alvin and Alpha Halvorson,
was born in Rugby, ND, spent her early years on a farm near Maddock and later
moved to Devils Lake. Jim and Connie were introduced by mutual friends in June
1970.

On Sept. 11, 1971, they were married at St. Olaf Lutheran Church, Devils Lake.
Since his discharge from the Army, Jim had been employed as a parts man at
International Harvester's Motor Truck Branch at St. Paul. A move to Fargo would
not have been practical so they settled in Fridley, a northern suburb of
Minneapolis. Connie, while settling in, soon discovered many ways to get to and
from places without the use of freeways.

Early in 1972 Connie accepted employment at Medtronic, Inc., a worldwide
manufacturer of cardiac pacemakers and related medical appliances. Late in 1972
they purchased a home in Columbia Heights, south of Fridley but north of
Minneapolis. This was home until their move to Beulah.

Charles Christopher was born Feb. 25, 1975, at Golden Valley Health Center. He
attended kindergarten through second grade at Valley View Elementary School in
Columbia Heights. Charles has actively participated in baseball, soccer,
football, basketball, Cub Scouts, band, honor choir and various other
activities.

Connie continued to work at Medtronic until Michael Warren was born on Nov. 6,
1978, also at Golden Valley Health Center. Michael was the youngest of many
children on their block in Minneapolis and Connie recalls a day when he and
another little boy wandered blocks away from home, during peak rush-hour
traffic, across several busy streets before they finally found them. He was
only three years old.

Michael attended Little People Preschool shortly after the Robideaus' arrival in
Beulah. He is active in Cub Scouts, baseball and soccer and has already picked
out the Avias he wants when it's time to play basketball.

Before Michael's arrival, Jim spent a considerable amount of time attending
night school, learning the basics of black and white photography, processing
and printing, composition, color processing and printing and lighting. He soon
discovered he had far more interest in photography than he had given himself
credit for.

After school, he was pleased to capture many a couple's wedding day on film,
learning more each time. He continued to work at International Harvester days
and do photography part-time weekends until, in 1982, after 15 years with the
company, he, along with 40 other veterans, lost his job following a sale within
the company. This sale took place at a time when more than 90,000 people were
searching for work in the Twin Cities alone.

After canvassing the job market for better than six months, to no avail, the
family decided it was time to search elsewhere for a livelihood.

Connie's sister Faye and husband Larry Rolfson live in Bismarck. They had told
Connie and Jim a little about the energy development in the Beulah/Hazen area
so in March, just in time for the great ice storm of 1983, Jim drove to Mercer
County to have a look around and visit with some of the natives. He was excited
about the response; many were interested in having a photographer in the area.

During the Easter holiday the Robideaus traveled to Bismarck to visit the
Rolfsons as well as drive to Beulah to look for housing. They had decided to
make a move.

On a cloudy day, over damp terrain, Jim introduced Connie to Beulah, the spoil
banks and nearby power plants. Oh! Woe to he who thinks North Dakota is flat!

They spoke to available realtors, most specifically Gary Allard of West River
Realty, who was also a native of Devils Lake. Gary took them around in a 4x4,
in borrowed boots that were too clad with mud to bother to clean, in order to
look at some homes they were in the process of building - for someone else. At
this time there wasn't an apartment or mobile home to rent or buy and anything
large enough for a family of four was already spoken for, so if they wanted to
relocate it was necessary to build. They chose a lot based on blueprints Gary
had his office and by looking north of 12th Street at corner markers - there
were no streets north of 12th at that time.

They returned to Minneapolis to prepare for the move to Beulah. Summer went
quickly as anticipation grew. Their home of 12 years sold, they packed and said
goodbyes and departed.

The Robideaus arrived in Beulah a couple days before the Mercer County Fair. Jim
had secured a booth in which to display his photographs; however, their
intention was to continue the photography part-time, much as they had in
Minneapolis. This was not to be. Numerous attempts to seek local employment
proved fruitless so when asked about occupation, both would respond with
"photographer . . . " and that is what he is.

Connie enjoys working at the Beulah Beacon. It's been a wonderful way to become
acquainted with names and faces. In addition to the time she spends at the
Beacon, she assists with the photography in the evenings and weekends as the
need arises. Connie has been active as a Cub Scout committee member is on the
church council and is forever attempting to fulfill her role as wife and
mother. In her spare time, of which there is precious little, she enjoys
various craft projects.

Being part of a smaller community makes for essential involvement in church,
community, school, clubs and organizations. The Robideaus have found that,
regardless of how busy they are, it's still more rewarding being on the inside
looking out than on the outside looking in.

"We are grateful for the opportunity to share our lives in some small way with
the rest of the residents of Beulah and look forward to growth and continued
prosperity. . .we can't afford to relocate again," laughs Connie.

        The Rueb family: Herb, Ida, Marlin, James, Karen, Sharon

Herbert and Ida Rueb

Herbert Rueb's father, Fredrick, was born in Hofungstahl, South Russia. When he
was 20 years old his parents decided to immigrate to America. In 1911 Fredrick
married Elizabeth Schlecht, who came to America in 1910 with her stepfather,
John Krausz. Elizabeth and Fredrick farmed east of Beulah and on April 9, 1918,
Herbert was born. The family continued to farm until 1939 when they moved into
town.

On Oct. 13, 1940, Herb married Ida Weil, whose parents, Jacob and Katherine
(Fischer) Weil, also immigrated to the United States with their parents from
Russia in the early 1900s. Ida's parents homesteaded near Java, SD before
coming to Mercer County in 1908 to homestead eight miles southwest of Beulah.
On June 15, 1917, Ida was born.

After Herb and Ida were married they lived on the Fred Rueb home place until the
land was sold to Knife River Coal Mining Company in 1952. Since there was not
enough land left to farm, Herb worked for Reine Grishkowsky in the mine south of
Beulah and also started his own trucking business, which he continues to operate
today. In 1959, the Ruebs moved into Beulah and continue to marvel at how the
town has grown and changed since the energy boom began. Herb hauled coal from
the North American Indianhead Mine at Zap to the eastern states for testing as
part of the pre-work-up for ANG.

In their teen years, they fondly remember Saturday nights in the summertime in
Beulah. Benches lined both sides of Main Street where people sat and visited
during the evening until the stores closed at midnight. The youth attended
movies at the Roxy Theatre, mainly westerns and comical attractions.

Herb and Ida have four children. The oldest, Marlin, was born in August 1941, and
married Ruth Mehling on Feb. 9, 1963. They live south of Beulah and have three
children: Brenda Lee, born in 1963; Todd Emil, born in 1966; and Audry Jo, born
in 1974.

James Herb was born in October 1942, and married Linda Schaper on June 11,
1966. They now manage the Super 8 Motel in Beulah and also have three children:
James Allen, born in 1966; Rhonda Lynn, born in 1969; and Robert Alan, born in
1972.

Herb and Ida's third child, Karen Katheryn, was born in February 1944 and
married Gerald Knoell on Oct. 5, 1962. They live west of Hazen and have three
children: Brent Edward, born in 1964; Kristie Kay, born in 1966; and Kinberly
Kaye, born in August of 1971.

Herb and Ida's fourth child is Sharon Elizabeth, born in March of 1945. Sharon
married Robert Tesky on May 29, 1966 and they now live in Mandan and have two
children; Patricia Lynn, born in December 1968; and Ronny Ray, born in January
1973.

The Herb Rueb family attends and belongs to Zion Lutheran Church, carrying on
the tradition of the Rueb family.

Ruben E. and Eunice Sackman

Terry Dawn Cornelius was born at Turtle Lake on June 1, 1946. She lives at

The twins, Karen Ray and Sharon Kay, were born on April 22, 1947, also at Turtle

        Christ and Norma Sailer

Christian and Norma Sailer

Christian Sailer was born on Oct. 17, 1917, on a farm north of Beulah. His
parents were Karl and Christina (Erdman) Sailer. Christ worked at various
places and farmed with his parents until his marriage to Norma Reiner on Nov.
25, 1945, when his parents retired and moved into Beulah. His dad, Karl, passed
away Oct. 3, 1946, and his mother followed on Oct. 12, 1974.

Norma Reiner was born June 11, 1926, to Theophil and Elizabeth (Herrmann) Reiner
north of Zap where she lived until her marriage to Christ. Her dad passed away
Nov. 20, 1971, and her mother still resides in Zap in the Mercer County Housing
Unit.

After their marriage, Christ and Norma continued to farm on Christ's father's
place until 1957 when they bought the land from his mother. They farmed until
1975, when because of poor health, Christ had to retire, sell the cattle and
rent the land. They continued to live on the farm until Sept. 22, 1986, when
they bought a house and moved to Beulah. Up to that day, Christ had lived more
than half a century on the same farm: 69 years.

Christian and Norma were blessed with three children. Rodney married Linda
(Thomas) on March 6, 1971, and they and their two daughters, Nicole and Jodi,
live in West Fargo. Dean married Edna (Heiszler) on Feb. 1, 1975, and they live
with their daughter, Christina, in Missoula, Mont. Pamela married Wes Wenger on
Aug. 29, 1981, and lives in Bismarck with their daughter, Lindsay.

The Sailers are members of Concordia Lutheran Church. Christ is an active member
of the Beulah Volunteer Fire Department. Norma is a charter member of the
Northern Star Homemakers Club.

Emil J. and Olga Sailer

Emil Sailer farmed the home place, the John Sailer farm, where he was born and
raised until he retired in 1970. He was born on Jan. 1, 1912, at the farm home
located about five miles northeast of Beulah, to John and Magdalena (Kunz)
Sailer.

On Oct. 3, 1937, he married Olga Koehler at Zion Lutheran Church at Beulah. Olga
is a Golden Valley native, born May 31, 1920, the daughter of John and Franszi
Weidrick Koehler.

During their early days of farming, the Sailers' weekly trip into town for
necessities was considered by them to be a "Saturday evening outing." After
Saturday evening chores were finished, they brought their eggs and cream to
town and did their weekly shopping. Olga used the egg money to purchase
groceries. During the summer, the cream check likely bought repairs; during the
winter it bought clothing and large quantities of staples to stock Olga's
sheves against adverse weather.

Emil and Olga have two children, nine grandchildren and six great-grandchildren.

Janice, now married to Lawrence Taylor and living at Beulah, was born on April
23, 1939, at a maternity home (a private home operated by a widow) in Hazen.
Janice, a homemaker, and her husband have seven children. Carmen, 29, is
married to John Mohl. They live in Beulah and are the parents of two daughters
and a son. Darcy Kruckenberg, 25, lives in Tempe, Ariz. Paula, 24, is married
to Gordon Guthmiller. They have one son and live in Beulah. Joan, 22, lives at
Grand Forks with her husband and two daughters. Douglas, 19, serves with the
U.S. Air Force in Japan. Holly Taylor, 13 and Crystal Taylor, 10, are both at
home.

The Sailers' son, Duane, was born at Bismarck Hospital on April 25, 1943. He is
married to the former Mary Barby of Bismarck. They and their two children,
Paul, 17, and Letty, 10, live in Bismarck. Duane works at the Amoco refinery at
Mandan.

Emil and Olga Sailer were charter members of Zion Lutheran Church. Emil has
served as church deacon and was active on the finance committee at the church.
Olga belonged to a church circle, an Extension Homemakers Club and worked as a
volunteer for the Red Cross.

        The George Sailer family Front row: Frieda, Bertha, George, Regina,
        Gertrude, Andrew. Back row: Emma, Lillian, Hildebert, Gotthold, Hugo

George and Regina Sailer

George Sailer was born April 23, 1880, at Neusatz, Crimea, Russia, to Andreas
and Dorothea (Stiefel) Sailer. In 1905 in the Crimea, he married Regina DeWald,
who was born in 1883 at Zurichtal, Crimea, Russia, to Henrich and Dorothea
(Rapp) DeWald. They decided to come to America as some of George's family had
come to the United States as early as 1883 when his half-brothers, Jacob and
Adam, and half-sister, Susana (Mrs. Carl Semmler) homesteaded in the Krem
area. The Semmlers had the hotel and Adam Sailer a retail store there. They
were farmers, businessmen and politicians. Carl Semmler was instrumental in the
early settlement of Mercer County.

In 1911 George and Regina left the Crimea with their three sons: Hugo, age 6,
Gotthold, age 4, and Hildebert, age 2. They immigrated to Calgary, Alberta,
Canada, traveling by train from Halifax, Nova Scotia, Canada to Calgary. George
attended night school while in Calgary and became a Canadian citizen. During
these years in Calgary two more children were born: Lillian in 1912 and Emma in
1914. In 1916 they immigrated to the United States to the Krem area. They
rented a farm from Fred Bohrer and later purchased the Werner farm. During this
period three more children were born: Frieda in 1916, Bertha in 1919 and
Gertrude in 1921. They now had children born in three countries. Because of
water shortage they sold this farm and purchased the Freer farm south of Hazen.
The children attended the Red Butte Consolidated School. In 1928 there were 96
students in attendance. Jack and Irene Riedel and Chester and Adelbert Peterson
were the teachers in 1928-1936.

Because of a serious hip injury George sustained in an auto accident in 1935 and
because of the Depression, they were forced to leave the farm. They moved into
Beulah in 1936. The move made it possible for Gertrude and Andrew to graduate
from the Beulah High School. George passed away in 1964 and Regina in 1967. Both
are interred at Zion Lutheran Cemetery at Beulah.

        The Gothold Sailer family: Jeannette, Gotthold, Mike, Alvina, Donna,
        Donald, Rosalie

Gotthold and Alvina Sailer

Gotthold Sailer was born Aug. 22, 1908, at Crimea, South Russia to George and
Regina (DeWald) Sailer. In 1911 Gott immigrated with his parents to Canada. They
landed in Halfax, Nova Scotia, then went by train to Calgary, Alberta, Canada.
He remembers the many (30) days on the ship, a freighter. In 1916 the Sailers
came to the U.S. by train, settling by Krem in Mercer County.

He attended rural school there and also in Stanton. In 1929 he began work at the
tipple of Knife River Coal Co. On July 17, 1932, he married Alvina Sailer.
Alvina was born Dec. 4, 1910, on a farm near Beulah to Andreas and Lydia
(Pischel) Sailer. Her parents later moved to Circle, MT. Her father died in
1944 and her mother in 1970. Both Gotthold and Alvina came from a family of
nine children each. His father died April 7, 1964 and his mother on March 21.
1967.

In 1943, they purchased the Jake Bacol Store in Beulah. It later became the Red
Owl Store. Gott also did custom combining. In 1968 they had Beulah's first
laundromat, selling it to Barney Baszler in 1976 when they retired. In 1978
they sold their home in Beulah and purchased the Erdman house in Golden Valley,
ND. Gott and Alvina completely remodeled and restored the house. With Gott's
excellent carpentry and Alvina's artistic touch they did a beautiful job. They
still reside there. They are members of Zion Lutheran Church in Beulah.

They were the parents of six children: Donald married Darlene Miller and lived
in Tennessee and Vancouver, WA. Donna married Robert Hartwig and lives in Golden
Valley, ND; Rosalie married Milton Unruh and lives at Palm Desert, CA; Jeannette
married Jim Bently and lives in Escondido, CA; William "Mike" married Deniece
Koehler and lives at Cando, ND; Allen died in infancy.

        The Ludwig Sailer family Front row: Loren, Ames, Deborah. Back row:
        Louis, Myrtle, Gretchen, Glenn

Ludwig Sailer family

In the book The Origin of North Dakota Place Names the following appears: "Troy
was located on the present site of Beulah, ND. Dr. Norman E. Vredenburg of
Hebron, had the land platted in 1911. He named it Troy. He built a home and a
large store, but leased them both to Carl Hanke, who put in a stock of hardware.
Before the close of the year the doctor sold his holdings to the Tuttle Land
Co. who later replatted the site and called it Beulah."

According to this the Sailer family is virtually native to the Beulah area.
Ludwig Sailer, born in 1883 in Johannestal, South Russia, came to America in
1902. He spent six weeks in South Dakota before moving to Mercer County. His
wife, Salome Erdmann, born in 1891 in the province of Bessarabia, South Russia,
arrived in Mercer County in 1907. She was married to Ludwig Sailer on Jan. 1,
1911. They homesteaded two quarters of land just north of the present Highway
200, about three miles from Beulah, and lived there until 1932. Knife River Coal
Company bought that land and the Sailer family moved to the farm west of Beulah.

The couple has 10 children. They were Otto (married Delores Weigum); Selma, who
died in infancy; Ludwig M. "Louie" (married Myrtle Melby); Hertha, (Mrs.
William H. Wahler); Adolf (married Esther Singer); Jacob (married Lilly
Schock); Lorraine (Mrs. Raymond Mohl); Arvada (Mrs. Clayton Schramm); Reuben;
and Florence (Mrs. Virgil Sailer). The men in the family are deceased except
Jacob who lives in Beulah. The other family members listed presently live in
the Bismarck-Mandan area.

Ludwig Mathias Sailer, the son of Ludwig Sailer and Salome (Erdmann) Sailer, was
born Feb. 11, 1913, at Troy, the forerunner of Beulah. The only time in his
life he lived away from Mercer County was in the 1930's when he worked briefly
loading and hauling sugar beets in the Sidney, MT area, and when he served in
the Civilian Conservation Corps in Utah and Arizona. When he came home he
bought an old truck with his savings and began hauling coal for Beulah
customers while living and working with his parents on the Sailer farm about
one and one-half miles west of Beulah.

This farm was purchased in 1932 and has an interesting history. A ranch just
south of town on the Knife River (owned by "Four Paw" and Tom Farrington) was
sold to Gideon Henderson in 1890. John Henderson came to Mercer County in 1896
and filed on the homestead which is the present L.M. Sailer farm. Mrs. Manley
Thompson (Belle Henderson), now deceased, was a daughter of this pioneer
family. In visits to the farm she recounted cutting hay on the meadow which is
now Beulah. They sold the farm in 1917.

On Oct. 22, 1944, at Glendive, MT, Louie married Myrtle Melby, who had been
born in Manfred, Wells County, ND, on March 14, 1914, to Martin K. and Alma
(Haugen) Melby. She and Louie met when she came to Beulah in 1939 to teach.
Their first residence was on the Clyde Stickney farm, part of which is now the
Lorraine's Addition to Beulah. In 1945 they purchased the Alec Sasse farm about
four miles southwest of Zap and lived there six years, selling that farm to the
Gideon Scheurer family who still resides there. In 1951 they purchased the Karl
K. Sailer farm located 14 miles south of Zap. In 1957, when Fred and Elsie
Entze bought that farm, they moved to their present location.

Five children were born to the couple: Glenn Martin, May 15, 1944, married to
Marie Evelyn Truax from Crosby. Their first child, Ross Evan, died shortly
after birth; Denise Ann, married to Gregory J. Lauinger on March 29, 1987,
lives in Mandan; Leah Joanne is a sophomore in Rapid City, SD Central High
School, where her parents moved in 1987. Glenn works at McKie Ford Body Shop.
He is a graduate of Beulah High School and Wahpeton State School of Science.

Gretchen Mary, born Sept. 4, 1948, graduated from Beulah High School and married
Burt Mason, Bemidji, MN. Both of them graduated from NDSU in Fargo. Burt served
in the U.S. Air Force and they were stationed at air bases in Arizona,
California, Grand Forks, ND, and at Ellsworth in Rapid City, where the couple
now resides. Their three sons are Christopher Burt, a senior at Central High
School; Eric Paul, a freshman; and Jeffrey Ryan, in grade three.

Deborah Deane was born March 7, 1950, and graduated from Beulah High School and
from Dickinson State College with a BS degree in secondary education. She
attended summer school after her marriage to Timothy D. Huber and also completed
the elementary education degree. She taught in Golden Valley and then joined
the faculty at the Beulah school, where she is now employed. The family lives
in Hazen with their two children, Bryan Timothy, age 8, and Rebecca Ann, age 5.

Loren Michael was born Feb. 18, 1952, and graduated from Beulah High School and
attended Dickinson State College, the University of North Dakota, and NDSU in
Fargo where he graduated with a BS degree in education. After teaching in the
Hendrum-Perley School in Minnesota, he returned to NDSU where he was employed
by the university while attending classes pursuant to a master of education
degree in guidance-counseling which he completed in 1986. He is employed in the
Lambert, MT, public school system.

Ames Ludwig, born Aug. 11, 1953, graduated from Beulah High School and Wahpeton
State School of Science. He worked as parts man in garages in Forsyth, MT,
Wahpeton and Bismarck in North Dakota, and is now employed at Coal Creek
Generating Station, Underwood, ND. He married Marilyn Axtman from Williston,
ND. She also graduated from Wahpeton State School of Science and works as a
dental hygienist at Dental Associates in Mandan. They are parents of two sons,
Ryan Michael, age two, and Cory Daniel, born Jan. 25, 1988.

Louie died June 18, 1968, in Bismarck Hospital. The family remained on the farm,
rented for several years to the oldest son, Glenn, and now leased out. Myrtle
taught in Manfred, ND; Jurdsfield, ND; Jerome, Idaho; Plentywood, MT; Zap, ND;
and in Beulah, where she taught 19 years. She retired from teaching in 1981
with 35 years in the profession.

Family memories of Beulah are many. While the children were in Beulah schools
they participated in many activities - all of them were in 4-H Clubs; Glenn,
Loren, and Ames in FFA and Gretchen in FHA; Gretchen, Deborah, and Loren in
music-vocal groups, small and large, in church choir at Zion Lutheran, and in
band. Loren was a member of the North Dakota All-State Band and Chorus in 1969
and 1970. Deborah attended State Music Camp some summers and at Dickinson State
College played in the Symphonic Wind Ensemble, traveling on concert tours with
them.

On the farm they learned to be responsible for the many farm chores, but there
was time for fun, too. Mother was not always happy with their swimming in
Spring Creek, and with all the vehicles on wheels--from bicycles to Doodle-Bugs
(motor scooters) to motorcycles, and finally to cars so they could drag Main
once in a while. There were always horses to ride, too, and activities
connected with Beulah's rodeos.

Saturday night was "town" night. Stores were open late. Sometimes we sat in
cars or on benches at the stores while we visited with our neighbors. We did a
lot more visiting at the homes of relatives and friends those years. Winter
evenings were spent playing checkers and card games and listening to the
crackly battery-operated radios. There were no telephones on the farms we lived
on for the first 15 years or so, and, worse yet, no electricity.

We enjoyed family picnics at the parks--no Lake Sakakawea with its water sports.
Fishing was generally good. There was very little eating out, and no fast-food
places or car hops until Mr. and Mrs. Herb Flowers opened the first drive-in
that I can remember in Beulah.

My memories of teaching in Beulah from 1939-1942 include the shared experiences
of my friends and co-workers, Blanche M. Knutson and Lucille Hoeft (Mrs. Ewald
Jungnitsch) . We were in charge of the annual school Christmas programs held at
the Roxy Theater and always performed for a packed house. Scheduling practices
there was nearly impossible. The building was large and probably difficult to
heat. We (the three of us) had to carry in wooden cases of full beer bottles on
which to arrange planks for seating the school children.

The junior high chorus sang from the balcony, a long ways from the piano. It was
difficult to hear the pitch and Lucille thought they sang off-key. I can't
remember about that. Other than those programs, the only functions I remember
at the Roxy were the annual President's Birthday Balls. In 1939-1940 there were
13 the following years.

Because there were few single teachers we were often invited to the homes of our
patrons for meals, as well as to Ladies Aid, club meetings, etc. We really
appreciated not having to have our meal tickets punched at the Greystone Hotel
and Cafe. Each slight (like $2.50 per month) raise in our salaries was
accompanied by a hike in meal ticket prices.

Some of our Sunday afternoon recreation wouldn't be tolerated today - riding
down Main Street on toboggans being pulled behind cars, or driving down the
hill east of the school in Shorty's Model A. When he hit the brakes we made
several circles on the ice at the bottom of the hill. Dances and roller-skating
at the Dreamland Pavilion, popularly known as the Sheep Shed, were well
attended. Wally Kittler is still playing the "Muskrat Ramble," but not in
Beulah.

One summer (1942) I stayed in Beulah to direct summer band and to teach
individual lessons. Saturday night band concerts were played in the  bandstand
just north of the depot. One high school student who played the drums liked his
Saturday evening free, and I had to go to his home and beg him to play in the
concerts. What would a band be without a drummer! Later the bandstand was moved
to what is now the playground just north of the telephone building. It was a
dandy place to sit and watch the children at play.

Living and teaching in Beulah was far from dull, especially when I think of
having from 40 to 50 second-graders in one small classroom my first three years
here. Now I really enjoy meeting those first second-graders, and seeing their
successes as adults. Then, too, I taught many of their children in junior-high
English classes the last 16 years I taught in Beulah.

The memories would fill more than one book. I have never regretted living in
this community - it's just a great place to call home.

Herb and Audrey Sasse

Audrey May (Wolf) Sasse (Feb. 28, 1937) is the daughter of Herb and Lydia Wolf.

Wilmer R. and Mariann Sayler The Saylers moved to Beulah in 1956, when Bill was
employed by the Beulah school system as high school science teacher. He had
taught four years previously at Gardner, N.D. and two years at Lodge Grass,
Mont.

Bill, the son of Albert E. and Elizabeth R. Sayler, was born in McLean County,
N.D. He received his grade school education there, and graduated from Underwood
High School. He attended Jamestown College, graduating with a bachelor of
science degree and has done graduate work at UND and NDSU.

He was on active duty with the Navy, serving from September, 1943, through May,
1946, and also served in the Naval Reserve and the Army National Guard for 20
years. Bill served two terms on the Beulah school board in the '70s, served on
the board of trustees at Beulah Congregational Church, is a past master of
Meridian Masonic Lodge 116 at Hazen and is a past secretary of the Beulah Lions
Club.

Mariann, daughter of Nelson and Edith King, was born and raised at Jamestown.
She graduated from Jamestown High School and attended UND at Grand Forks.
Mariann is a member of the Beulah Women's Club, the Congregational Ladies Aid
and past member of Beulah Mothers Homemakers Club. She is presently employed by
Century 21 in real estate sales.

Willie and Della Schaper

Willie and Della Schaper were no strangers to Beulah, having grown up on
neighboring farms north of Halliday just 28 miles west of Beulah.

Willie is the ninth of 13 children born to Henry and Katherina Schaper (both
deceased). Della is the oldest of six children born to Adolph and Esther Kisse.

Willie's first time away from home came in 1953 with a two-year tour of duty in
Uncle Sam's Army. Upon his discharge in March, 1955, Willie rejoined his family
with the farming operation and played his accordion and sang in the Schaper
family band.

Della graduated from Halliday High School in 1954 and attended Dickinson State
College. She taught rural schools in the Dunn Center and Halliday area.

Della and Willie were married July 29, 1956. They moved to Fargo in January 1957
where Willie attended Mohler Barber College. Later they lived in Killdeer and
New Rockford, where he served his apprenticeship.

Upon moving to Killdeer, Willie and Della bought their first mobile home, 8'
wide by 28' long, including the hitch. When they moved to New Rockford Willie
pulled it with their '54 Ford car.

In 1961, a change of career came for Willie, from barber to butcher. Willie
purchased and operated the locker plant at Halliday, selling it a year later to
go back to farming, his first love. The farm income was supplemented with
part-time barbershops in Dunn Center, Dodge and Golden Valley, along with
running the movie theatre in Halliday.

Mobile homes had gotten longer and wider since their first one, but moving a
mobile home couldn't be much different from moving haystacks, so Willie bought
a mobile home toter and ventured into the mobile home transporting and repair
service.

In 1977 he, along with two partners, purchased the existing Roughrider Mobile
Home dealership in Dickinson, followed by the 1979 purchase of the Beulah
branch, which led to Willie and Della moving to Beulah along with sons Steve
and Rod. Another son, Robert, then in college, has since joined the company.

Robert, his wife Sheri, and twin sons Dane and Ryan live in Beulah. Willie and
Della also have a daughter, Brenda, who lives in Watford City with her husband,
John Fulwider, and their sons David and Bryan.

Reuben and Berniece Scheid

Reuben Carl Scheid was born Sept. 6, 1934 north of Hazen to Arthur Fredrich and
Hilda Eva (Link) Scheid. His parents had 10 children: Reuben of Beulah, Elmer
and Leo of Terry, Mont., Delores Bauer and Alvin of Hazen, Mrs. Lloyd (Viola)
Keidel of Mandan, Mrs. Aaron (Bernice) Beick at Spokane, Wash., a baby died as
an infant, Irene who died as a teenager and Clemet died in 1982. The Scheid
sodhouse is still standing on their farm located 15 miles northwest of Beulah.
In 1967 they moved into Hazen. Arthur Scheid died Sept. 4, 1971. In December,
1981, Hilda moved into the Joachim Home in Beulah and in March, 1985, she
entered the Beulah Community Nursing Home. She died Aug. 21, 1986.

        Berniece and Reuben Scheid

Reuben Scheid was married to Berniece Martha (Boeckel) Winkler on June 17, 1977.
Berniece was born March 5, 1939, north of Beulah to Albert and Bertha
(Oberlander) Boeckel. Reuben is a truck driver for Mercer County and does some
farming. They also clean the PCA office once a week. Berniece collects bells,
likes crafts including quilting and crocheting. They like to go camping when
they can. Berniece belongs to Christian Women's Club and her highlight of the
month is their monthly luncheon. She held various officer positions with
Christian Women's Club. Berniece is a member of the Congregational Church and
Reuben belongs to St. Matthew's Lutheran Church at Hazen. They live in Beulah
and enjoy living here.

Berniece writes of some of her memories growing up in Beulah, "I remember the
old creamery which Ludwig Unruh ran or owned. I used to watch him test the
cream and he would give me treats such as bubble gum, etc. Friendly man! We
used to get 25 cents when we got to town, then we would buy candy to last the
week. Sugar Daddy or Black Cow caramel suckers were our favorite because they
lasted longer, so it took longer to eat them. We usually bought them at the RCU
Store or the drugstore."

She misses the soda fountain there and the good muds they used to make. She also
remembers the Legion Hall had church conventions and weddings where she had so
much fun.

        Arthur and Anne Erickson

Gladys M. Scheidt

Gladys M. (Erickson) Scheidt is my oldest living grandparent. She was born
Sept. 5, 1906 and now lives in Beulah. John Scheidt (her husband) and Gladys
raised five children who were all born on the farm south of Beulah. They are:
Herbert Scheidt of Beulah, Mrs. Herman (Vivian) Hauff of Beulah, Mrs. George
(Willa Jean) Weaver of Wheatland, WY, Mrs. Chris (Carol) Kaelberer of New
Salem, who is my mother, and Mrs. Raymond (Darlene) Schuh of Bismarck. Gladys
also has 21 grandchildren.

Grandma's mother's parents were Anna (Strom) and Carl Sevallius. Carl was born
in Sweden around Orso in the year 1848. Anna Strom was born in Orso, Sweden,
Jan. 2, 1860. They were married in October of 1885 in Sweden and migrated to the
United States as a young couple. They settled around the Red River Valley in
Minnesota, later moving to Starchfield, MN. They lived there until coming to
North Dakota in Oliver County, 10 1/2 miles southeast of Beulah, and took up
homestead in 1907.

        A.W. Erickson family Back row: Gladys, Esther, Marion, Lloyd, Edward.
        Front row: Arthur, Roger, Berniece, Anna

Sevallius was an iron ore miner deep underground in Sweden, MN. They did mixed
farming and lived in a sod shack. Anna died Aug. 13, 1925 on her son's homestead
south of Beulah. Carl died Dec. 2, 1930 in Wisconsin at his son's home while
visiting there. They had six children: Hans, born in Sweden in 1880, and died
Aug. 21, year unknown.

Anna (Mrs. Arthur W. Erickson), who is my great-grandmother's mother, was born
in Sweden, Feb. 11, 1886. She died Nov. 24, 1957. Emil was born Feb. 2, 1889 and
died in February 1920. Mrs. John Stephens was born April 26, 1891 and died Dec.
26, 1970. Arvid was born March 19, 1896 and died May, 1977. The last child was
Clara (Mrs. Milo Stephens) who was born in 1900 and died on Feb. 8, 1924. These
people all lived in the Beulah area.

Gladys had many pleasant memories of her grandparents, Carl and Anna. During the
summer at harvest time, when they were shocking grain, Carl was no good with
driving horses but his sons were grown so they did the farming in North Dakota.
Anna milked the cows and made butter to sell. She also made cheese. She spun
yarn from the few sheep they had and knitted the kids' mittens and long
stockings. Anna also had rug looms that she would weave on, besides the house
work that she did. She smoked a corncob pipe because she had gotten the habit
while a young girl in Sweden.

Grandma's father's parents were Greta and John Erickson. Greta's maiden name is
unknown. Greta was born in Kallmar, Orso, Sweden in 1842. She immigrated to the
United States in Minnesota in 1863. John was born in 1848. John and Greta were
married in Chicago, IL on Feb. 5, 1864. They then took homestead at Grandy, MN
in Isanti County.

They raised six children and the youngest was Arthur William, who was grandma's
father. John farmed potatoes and cleaned the land of wood and brush. Greta
loomed and made clothes for people. Grandma never knew John, but she had
memories of Greta. Greta homesteaded in North Dakota three miles west of
grandma's parents home in Mercer County. She lived in a sod shack and was a
midwife. She was called around in Minnesota and North Dakota.

My grandmother's parents were Arthur William Erickson who was born March 1,
1882, in Isanti County, MN and died March 31, 1957 in Beulah, and Anna
(Sevallius) Erickson who was born in Sweden on Feb. 11, 1886 and died Nov. 24,
1957. They were married on March 18, 1905. They had eight children: Gladys
Margaret (Grandma), born Sept. 5, 1906, Frances Luella, April 9, 1909, Roger
Alfred, Aug. 20, 1911 - March 26, 1972, Lloyd Morris, March 25, 1914, Edward
Theodore, July 18, 1916 - May 25, 1947, Marion May, May 5, 1919, Elizabeth
Esther, Nov. 19, 1924 - July 7, 1982, and Bernice, Oct. 11, 1928 - July 26,
1952.

Grandma came to North Dakota in 1910 in Mercer County 10 1/2 miles southwest of
Beulah with her parents when she was four years old. They homesteaded on one
quarter of land from Isanti County, MN where Grandma was born. When they got to
Mercer, she and her parents lived in a sod shack before they built a two-room
wooden house. One of the rooms was used for the kitchen and living room and the
other room was a bedroom. It was heated by a coal heater and they used a coal
range for cooking. They never had indoor plumbing and they didn't get
electricity until 1950. Grandma used kerosene lamps for light. They also had a
cellar under the floor with a trap door where they kept their perishables.

In the winter, they harvested ice and stored it in a dugout with straw. About
1925, they had a wooden ice box, but before that the food was cooled in cold
water or hung by a rope in a shallow well. They had their own well and they
used a pail to pull the water out. Later they got a pump. They saved rainwater
and melted snow in winter for washing clothes on a board in a tub. They also
made their own soap.

Grandma was the oldest in the family and had to do whatever she was able to do.
She plowed when she was eight years old. She also mowed hay, shocked grain,
picked rocks, milked, fed calves and cared for the chickens. She also had to
watch for prairie fires. If there was a prairie fire Grandma was told to go out
on the fire break. That was a strip that her father had plowed around the home
to keep fires from burning the buildings. Her mother planted potatoes on the
fire break.

Grandma's mother did all the cooking but the kids always had to help. They never
had store-bought groceries, except for flour, sugar, coffee, salt and matches.
They washed wheat and soaked it. They cooked it all day and it was used for
cereal or it was cooled and sliced to fry as a main dish. When the neighbors
had wheat to sell, several farmers would get together and travel to Glen Ullin
by sled or wagon and stay there overnight. The men got whatever was needed and
the grocery store would always give them about two pounds of free candy (the
hard kind like a Christmas mix we get now). Grandma would get a piece every now
and then. They had to make it last as long as possible. Grandma's mother and
grandmother sewed coats and pieced quilts. They got a lot of hand-me-downs from
relatives in Minnesota. Grandma's father usually fixed all the shoes.

They kept in touch with relatives by writing letters. Grandma got her mail from
a post office in Oliver County about four miles east of where they lived. Later
mail was hauled from New Salem and Glen Ullin until the railroad came to
Beulah. There was a post office east of where Beulah is, called Farrington,
where they had to go and get their mail. Shortly thereafter the mail on rural
routes came; also mail was at Aplin, in Oliver County.

Grandma remembers a very special pet that she had. It was a collie dog and the
dog would go everywhere that Grandma went. He would even pick out the milk cow
and take her home. Grandma also remembers a pony that she had. The pony took
them to school by sled when there was snow on the ground.

Grandma always had something to do. She washed the dishes, swept the house,
studied and sometimes she popped corn. Grandma also helped with the garden.
They grew all kinds of vegetables, but they didn't have any fruit trees.
Grandma said that there wasn't much canning done when she was a child, except
for store bought pears and prunes. Grandma's family raised hogs for meat and
chickens for meat and eggs. They had a cow and they sold cream. Pork was
butchered in the cold season and cured in salt brine in a barrel. In the spring
it was smoked for summer use. On the farm, they grew corn, wheat, oats and
barley.

Saturday meant baking, cleaning house, washing hair and taking a bath. Sunday
was a day of rest and when Grandma was a teenager they had Sunday school at the
schoolhouse. The whole family went to church with the horse and buggy.

As a child, Grandma was taught not to go barefoot out in the field and to wear
long, woolen stockings in the winter to keep warm. Grandma remembers one bad
blizzard when Hazel Minor froze to death near Center, ND. She said it was
terrible.

For recreation, Grandma went visiting or else they had company on Sundays. In
the summer, they went on the prairie and picked wild flowers. They also picked
juneberries, chokecherries and wild plums.

In the winter, Grandma enjoyed sled riding and reading books. Grandma didn't
have any hobbies, but when she was in grades 6-8, the teacher organized a boys'
and girls' club. They learned how to can and then they demonstrated canning at
the county fair in Beulah. They had a pie social and program at school and they
bought library books with the money from the sale of the pies.

Grandma went to school in Ash District #1 in Mercer County, a one-room
schoolhouse heated by a big coal stove. The stove was filled in the evening and
by morning it was very cold. When Grandma was small her father took her to
school with the sled pulled by horses. She was bundled up with straw and sat in
the wagon box. As Grandma got older she could drive a single pony and finally
she had to walk about 1 1/2 miles. Sometimes her lunch froze on the way to
school. The school had grades from primary to eighth. Grandma only got an eighth
grade diploma.

John Scheidt, the man grandma would marry, lived with his family a mile from
Grandma's. John's parents were Conrad Scheidt, born Nov. 14, 1854 and died Nov.
26, 1928, and Maria (Schroeder) Scheidt who was born Oct. 24, 1860 and died May
25, 1944. They came to the United States from Kettwig, Germany in 1887 and lived
in Scotland, SD. In 1907, they came to North Dakota and took homestead 10 miles
southwest of Beulah.

Grandma was married to John Scheidt on Jan. 11, 1927 at the court house in
Stanton, ND. They did not go on a honeymoon. Grandma and grandpa's first home
was 15 miles south of Beulah. They rented a house made of mud and stone. They
lived there for two years and in March, 1928, they bought a quarter of land nine
miles south of Beulah. They raised cattle and chickens and farmed grains. John
died Jan. 16, 1965 and Grandma had an auction sale and moved to town.

Grandma feels electricity has been the greatest invention since she was a
child. She has a lot of concern for her family, keeps busy, and has a lot of
patience. Grandma is worried about the possibility of war and what the
devastating effects could be. She also has much concern over the rising prices.
Grandma has led a very enjoyable life and hopes it continues in the same way.

Kyle Kirchmeier

Herb and Catherine Scherbinske

Herb Scherbinske and Catherine Cox were married Sept. 7, 1946. Catherine was
born and reared in Beulah. She taught rural schools in the area and during the
World War II years she was a welder in the Kaiser Company ship yards in
Portland OR.

Catherine is a 35-year member of the Beulah Homemakers Club, was the Royal
Neighbors of America recorder for 35 years and is a 30 year O.W.L. member. She
is an avid bridge player.

Herb was born at Dickey, ND, and grew up at Cleveland, ND. He came to Beulah in
1941 as an accountant for Liebelt Chevrolet. The years 1942-1945 were spent as a
ship builder for the Kaiser Company in Portland. Knife River Coal Mining Company
hired Herb in 1945 and the next 40 years were spent with K.R.C. in various
positions: chief clerk, superintendent, and manager of special projects.

        Catherine and Herb Scherbinske

        Val, H. Bruce, Patrick, Shanna Scherbinske

Herb has been very active in the community serving as a member of the Athletic

Ervin and Vi Schielke

Ervin Alvin Schielke was born the oldest child of Ludwig and Marie (Mehrer)
Schielke at Tuttle, N.D. on Oct. 19, 1935. Ervin graduated from Tuttle High
School in 1953. He served in the U.S. Navy from 1953 to 1957 aboard the U.S.S.
Seminole as a machinist mate and made three tours of the Far East. On Nov. 12,
1957, he began his 30-year employment with Montana Dakota Utilities Company at
the Heskett Station, Mandan, and was transferred to Lewis and Clark Station at
Sidney, Mont., May 1958. In August 1979, he was transferred to the Coyote
Station at Beulah where he is working as a performance technician in the
engineering department.

On Mother's Day May 11, 1958, Ervin married Viola Violet Kruckenberg at Tuttle,
N.D. "Vi" was born May 7, 1940, the second oldest child of Henry and Clara
(Unrath) Kruckenberg, at rural Beulah. Vi has four brothers and four sisters
including Dwight of Beulah. Vi attended first grade at a rural school east of
Hazen from 1946-47 when the family moved to Wing, where she was raised and
attended schools at Wing, Bismarck and Hibbing, Minn. Vi has graduated from
high school and has had some college courses.

        Vi and Ervin Schielke

Ervin and Vi are the parents of a daughter, Clarisa Marie, born on Easter
Sunday, April 14, 1963, at Sidney, Mont. She graduated from Beulah High School
in 1981, attended UND-Grand Forks and graduated from Wahpeton State School of
Science as an occupational therapy assistant. Clarisa is working at St. Luke's
Hospital in Boise, Idaho. Son Brian Douglas was born on their seventh wedding
anniversary, May 11, 1965, at Sidney, Mont. He graduated from Beulah High
School in 1983, attended Wahpeton State School of Science and is now employed
at Wahpeton.

Both are members of Zion Lutheran Church at Beulah and Germans from Russia
Heritage Society where Vi has served as secretary for two years, and is now
serving her second year as director at large. Ervin has just finished serving
as president of the local chapter Die Deutsche Stammhalter the past two years,
and Vi has served three and a half years as secretary.

Vi's great-grandparents, Gottlieb and Dorothea (Habelmann) Kruckenberg, came to
Mercer County in December 1888 before statehood, so her goal in life has been to
preserve and share her love of genealogy which she has been doing for 25 years.
Roxanne Salisbury and Vi have finished compiling Mercer County Cemeteries, a
project that they have been working on since 1980 and hope that it will be
published soon for preservation.

Marvin and Violet Schnaidt

Rudolph and Anna Schnaidt

Rudolph Schnaidt helped build the first church in Beulah - Zion Lutheran Church.

Rudolph was the son of George and Karolina (Burkhardt) Schnaidt. He was born on
Oct. 8, 1906, about 20 miles south of Beulah.

He started school three miles north of Beulah. He also attended school at
Eureka, SD, from 1921 to 1924. When his father died in December, 1924, he
returned to Beulah to help his mother with the farm.

On July 21, 1929, he married Anna Heth, the daughter of Wilhelm and Lydia
(Krueger) Heth. She was born on April 2, 1910, in the Expansion area north of
Hazen. She was educated in rural schools.

        Anna and Rudolph Scheidt

The Schnaidts lived on a farm southwest of Beulah for four months, then moved
to a farm five miles west of Beulah. Because of the damage of the drought and
grasshoppers to their crops, they left the farm in 1937 and moved into Beulah.

Rudolph started as a Star Route mail carrier in 1934. In addition to driving
the mail route, he clerked in grocery stores for nine years. He retired from
driving the Star Route on July 14, 1976, though he continued to serve as
treasurer for the Joachim Memorial Home.

The Schnaidts moved to Bismarck in September of 1979, because of Anna's ill
health. She passed away on March 1, 1980.

Rudolph still resides in Bismarck, participating in senior citizens'
activities, doing volunteer work at Medcenter One and singing in the choir at
Good Shepherd Lutheran Church.

The Schnaidts raised five children. Marvin, who lives at Beulah, was born on
Sept. 14, 1930; Reuben, who now lives in the Rugby-Devils Lake area, was born

14, 1935; Delmer was born on Sept. 15, 1940, and now lives in St. Paul, Minn.;
and Janet Richau, who now lives at Mandan, ND, was born on April 27, 1946.

Clarence and Leona Schneider

Clarence and Leona Schneider have been long-time residents of Beulah since they
arrived to work in the Beulah Drug Store. They were both born in Glen Ullin and
were well acquainted with each other before Leona's sojourn to Beulah. They were
married in Washington state and came here as a young family. Their apartment was
next door to the Beulah Drug Store so they identified with the business from
the start.

        The Schneider family: Clarence, Leona, Allen, Diane, Ione, Janet,
        Gary

Leona had relatives living here and Clarence was acquainted with Ted Herman, so
they found it easy to accept Ted's job offer. From then on he and Leona were a
real part of the store, although Leona's family commitments prevented her from
working full time.

Ted was fortunate in having such capable and trained help as Clarence, who was
trained in pharmacy during his three-year hitch in the service during WWII. His
training allowed him to fill and record certain prescriptions. Those returning
for the jubilee as well as numerous townspeople will remember the famous drug
store soda fountain. The specialty of the fountain was an original confection
called a "mud" that was mixed by hand. The drug store was a hang-out for the
students. Clarence says returning students still inquire about the "muds."

Renovation of the drug store saw the old-time marble top soda fountain moved to
Bismarck. What a treat for Leona and Clarence to sit on the other side and watch
someone else mix a mud. Through his 35 years at the drug store Clarence had
three different "bosses"--Ted and Jerome Herman and Dave Just.

The Schneiders bought their own home just north of the original brick school and
raised their family of five children. Ione (Frank) was born Aug. 23, 1942, at
Snoqualmie Falls, WA, and now resides with her family at West Fargo. Janet
(Osten) was born Aug. 24, 1945, at Bismarck and lives with her family at Lake
Crystal, MN; Father Gary, with the Confraternity of the Paulist Society, was
born in Beulah on Aug. 29, 1948 and now resides in Memphis, TN. Diane, born May
11, 1951 at Hazen, works with the Department of Interior in Ft. Collins, CO.
Allen was born Oct. 2, 1956 in Hazen. He and his wife live in Lakewood, CO.

Clarence and Leona preferred raising their children in a small-town atmosphere
but all but one have chosen to live in a large city. The children were involved
in the usual school activities and sports and were very talented musically,
taking lead roles in these programs. They also sang in the church choir. As a
family the Schneiders spent much time golfing together, and have been active
members of the Beulah Golf Club since 1946.

Clarence, born Dec. 19, 1916, is the son of Hugo (died 1965) and Anna Thieson
Schneider (died 1958). Clarence worked in retail sales at the Beulah Drug
Store, is a member of the Eagles, VFW, Chamber of Commerce and served on the
Beulah Park Board for seven years. He is a busy member of St. Joseph Church and
sang with the choir for over 30 years. He has done much volunteer work at St.
Joseph's, serving on the building committee and council and ministerial duties.

Leona, born Sept. 30, 1919, has been occupied with her role as mother and
homemaker. Her parents were Peter and Theresa (Tavis) Wilmes, deceased 1957 and
1985. In addition to community activities, she has been with the church choir
for over 30 years. She has been a constant and helpful member of the St. Anne
Altar Society and has held every office in the organization.

The Schneiders travel frequently and are able to spend time with their children
and grandchildren.

Edward and Rose Schulz

Edward and Rose Schulz were very successful farmers north of Beulah for many
years. They were also very active members of Zion Lutheran Church. Edward served
as county commissioner for many years and has served on the county welfare
board and the community nursing home board.

Edward Schulz was born July 1, 1906 on a farm south of Beulah and has farmed
west of Beulah and north of Beulah prior to moving to Beulah upon  retirement.
Ed's parents were John Schulz (died Nov. 21, 1954) and Juliana Koenig (died
June 10, 1923).

Rose (Klundt) Schulz was born Sept. 19, 1907 near Garrison. She also lived on
farms near Douglas and Expansion, ND. She lived on a farm north of Beulah prior
to her marriage to Edward. Rose's parents were William Klundt (died Jan. 11,
1953) and Elizabeth Losing (died Jan. 23, 1978).

The children born to Edward and Rose in Beulah are: Edgar W., born March 7,
1931; Eugene J., born March 7, 1931; Waldo P., born Sept. 2, 1932; Curtis I.,
born July 6, 1935; Ardella E., born March 19, 1937; Norlyn E., born March 5,
1944; and Gary L., born Feb. 1, 1946. In addition, Kermit and Dolliette Dietz
were raised by Edward and Rose Schulz.

Among the most significant changes they have seen were transportation,
communication, energy and medicine. Ed talks about the old wagon trail which led
to Beulah and crossing the Knife River without a bridge. The crossing was near
the area of the old Sheep Shed. Later east of Beulah was built the old Red
Bridge which became the route for the south farmers to do their trading in
Beulah and eventually, the Highway 49 Bridge was built and the highway was
rebuilt, graveled and paved, making it a major road to Beulah.

Improvement of roads from wagon trails to gravel roads and now many of them
being hard surfaced is a major change in the county. Ed recalls the horse-drawn
wagons and buggies and says a Sunday visit to the neighbors used to be quite a
trip while today you can take a car and go to another state or better yet, take
a plane and go to another country.

The convenience of electricity was probably the most beneficial change,
especially in rural America. "We used to burn coal in a cook stove which I dug
myself plus a potbellied stove in another room to stay warm. Now we have
electricity, electric heat, gas furnaces and all the conveniences of clean heat
only to find that people are going back to coal and dust and ashes, kinda back
where we started," Ed says.

"The telephone system is another very convenient and necessary communication
system to have. People would have laughed at you 50 years ago if you told them
that in 1989 you will be able to push 10 numbers on a dial and in seconds you
can talk to someone thousands of miles away. We are all very fortunate to have
available and enjoy longer life due to the vast improvement in the medical
field. If anyone had suggested some 75 years ago that we will be replacing a
heart, lung, kidneys etc., they would have quickly summoned the marshall and had
this guy put away because certainly there would have been something terribly
wrong with such a person.

There are many, many changes that have taken place. Very often we hear of the
good old days as being so good! There were some good things about those days,
such as a slower life style, but we would find it very hard to even think of
going back to those days. We enjoy television far too much to "give that up."

Beulah in the 1980's is different from the Beulah Joan and Jim first met.

Joan writes, "Much of the land upon which the north side of Beulah city limits
now rests was farmed by Jim, and before that, not only his father but his
grandfather. We've watched Beulah grow to our farm and on past it. At present
time, we live on the west side of Highway 49, still farming and raising cattle.
Yet we look out our window and directly to the east, across the highway, our
vista now includes motels, homes, apartments, and clinics - quite a contrast
from 15 years ago.

"And one interesting point: Our daughter, Debra, and her husband, Perry Sayler,
now live in the city limits but on land that four generations of her family
have farmed."

Ray and Elaine Schumaier

Ray Schumaier was born May 1, 1930, to Emanuel and Martha Schumaier. Emanuel
came to Garrison from south Russia in 1905. He grew up in rural Garrison and
came to Mercer County in 1926, where he started working in the underground
Beulah mine. He worked there until 1939 when he quit the mine and started
farming north of Beulah.

Ray's grandparents, Edward and Emma (Weigum) Kerner, were charter members of

Dave and Lori Schweigert

Dave and Lori Schweigert are considered new residents of Beulah, having moved to
their home in April, 1986. They were affiliated with local industries for some
years while residing in Bismarck as Dave worked for North American Coal and
Lori for Montana-Dakota Utilities. They both hold engineering degrees.

Jan. 1, 1982, marked a new venture when Dave received a transfer to the Coteau
Mine as a senior engineering technician. Their trailer house was moved to Hazen;
however, Lori continued her job but was busy looking for employment in Beulah.

In March, Kaiser Engineering Construction Company for G.P.G.A. offered her
employment as a junior electrical engineer technician. In November they sold
their trailer home and resided in a rental home in Zap until Jan. 1984 when the
urge for country living encouraged them to rent the Jake Becker homestead six
miles north of Zap. Following an enjoyable two years there the time came when
they felt they wanted their own place. They purchased their present home in
Beulah and moved in April 15, 1986.

Lori, a music lover, is a piano instructor and a member of the Music Teachers
National Association as well as the North Dakota Music Teachers Association.
Music is not her only pursuit as she has completed her training program and is
a volunteer squad member of the Mercer County Ambulance Service. She feels busy
being a homemaker and mother. Their daughter Shila was born in Bismarck, Dec.
6, 1984. She is a member of the Beulah Gymnastics Club.

The family enjoys everything associated with the outdoors. They spend their
free time hunting, fishing and boating. Love for action has inspired them to
enter the world of cross country skiing. They are very enthusiastic about this
sport, enjoying the outdoors, the exercise and the many delightful ski areas
close to town.

Dave is a member of the United Sportsman and both of them are certified Hunter
Safety instructors for the state of North Dakota. Their classes are preferably
small groups, or individuals from about 12 years old to adult. Their program
covers understanding, respect, and the procedures of how to use a gun safely
and wisely. They are there ready to help and instruct and inform the individual
concerning government regulations.

Dave and Lori have a unique interest that is also a rewarding hobby. They have a
piece of property south of Ft. Rice that they are developing into a wildlife
habitat, an area of natural surroundings and shelterbelts. It is a refuge for
an abundance of wildlife ranging from turkeys to deer.

Dave was born in Bismarck Dec. 2, 1952, the son of Emil and Louella Schweigert
who are both deceased, in 1970 and 1968, respectively. Lori's parents Douglas
and Arlene Beck are living in Minot where Lori was born Aug. 17, 1956. They are
members of Zion Lutheran Church and have joined various activity groups. Dave
and Lori say they enjoy Beulah very much and in the future hope to broaden their
friendships and acquaintances.

James and JeAnne Selby

Jim and JeAnne Selby met in 1969 while they were high school teachers on the
Stanton and Beulah facilities, respectively.

They were married on June 26, 1971, at Zion Lutheran Church, Beulah. They lived
in Stanton until 1978, where Jim was employed first as high school principal
and later as superintendent of the Stanton schools. JeAnne continued to teach
home economics at Beulah their first two years of marriage, commuting daily.

The Selbys moved to Beulah in July 1978, when Jim became a community
development representative for Basin Electric Cooperative. During 1986-87 he
served as a legislative assistant for Basin, and 1987 he transferred to the
member services department as an economic development and marketing
representative.

When the Selbys came to Beulah at the beginning of the construction phase of the
Basin and ANG projects in 1978, there were a few houses on the market. They were
among the many new families in town who built homes. Their house was built only
a block north of 7th St., at a site which was part of one of Jim Schumaier's
grain fields at the edge of town. JeAnne remembers 7th St. as the edge of town
in 1967, when she moved here as a single teacher.

The Selbys came to Beulah at a time in its history when many positive changes
were occurring as a result of energy impact. They watched the population climb
to an all-time high of 5,600 in 1983. They feel the community has been
fortunate in gaining many new skills and talents along with this influx of
people. They watched a new elementary school built only three doors to the west
of them. They also say many improvements in the school system, which resulted
in a North Central Association Accreditation for the Beulah schools.

During the early years, energy impact, Jim was involved in developing and
operating the Bachelor Quarters at the northern edge of town, which were used
as housing for temporary construction workers.

James Lloyd Selby was born on Dec. 15, 1941, at Sidney, Mont. He is the son of
Homer and Alice (Budka) Selby. He was raised on a farm in the Buford-Trenton
Irrigation project west of Williston. He is a business graduate of Minot State
College and received an MS degree in educational administration from North
Dakota State University in Fargo. He taught at McGregor, ND, prior to his move
to Stanton. He has served nine years in the ND National Guard.

He is married to the former JeAnne Mae (Mittelstedt) of Ashley, ND. The
daughter of Fred and Lenora (Miller) Mittelstedt, she was born at Eureka, SD,
on May 10, 1946. She is a home economics graduate of NDSU. She attended
graduate school at Iowa State University at Ames, and NDSU.

They have two children, Jennifer, 13, and Jason, 11, who were born at Bismarck.

Both Jim and JeAnne have been involved in their church and community through the
years. Jim has been a member of the Chamber of Commerce, Lions, Eagles, and
Beulah Municipal Golf Course, helping in planning and developing the golf
course. He has held various offices in these organizations. He also served on
the church council of Zion Lutheran Church.

JeAnne has taught very little since her children were born, so she has also
given many volunteer hours to her community. She has been quite involved in
Girl Scouting, serving as a troop leader, neighborhood chairman, trainer,
district delegate chairman, board member and council first vice-president. She
was awarded the Thanks Badge, the highest award given to an adult volunteer in
Girl Scouts. She belongs to the Crafty Corner Homemakers Club and has served as
Mercer County council president and NDEHC scholarship and cultural arts
chairwoman. She has been involved in ALCW and her church circle as well as
serving on various committees and projects at the church. She is a member of
the Beulah Woman's Club and Xi chapter of Delta Kappa Gamma, an educational
honorary for women educators. She is a charter member of the Beulah Lioness
Club. She has served as a trustee of the Mercer-McLean Library Board as well as
the first Beulah library board.

Jesse and Gertrude Smith

Jesse Smith was the son of Lulu and Fred Smith. He was born at Underwood, ND on
Feb. 18, 1907, and died of cancer on Dec. 26, 1978.

There were two other children in the Fred Smith family, Alice and Cecil: both
are deceased. Alice married and moved to Portland, OR. They had one son, and
seven daughters. Cecil married Atina Krieger. They had no children.

Jess's parents moved to Canada when he was around five years old. They moved
back to the United States when he was nine and settled at Wilton. They moved to
Beulah in the early 20's. Fred and Jesse both worked in the coal mine. During
the late 20's they held dances, roller skating and boxing matches at the Sheep
Shed. Jesse moved to Portland, OR. in 1930 and from Portland to Sunburst, MT.
He was inducted into the Army in 1939 and served in the South Pacific during
World War II. After being discharged he settled at Sidney, MT. He worked for
the Lalonde Hotel as bartender and owned and operated Sidney Monument Sales.

He married Gertrude Mitten on Sept. 19, 1955, at Savage, MT. Gertrude was one of
seven children born to Roy and Gertie (Stenehjem) Mitten. Gert grew up on a
farm in McKenzie County and attended rural school. She graduated from Sidney
High School, Sidney MT and attended college at Dickinson, ND. She worked for
many years as a secretary and bookkeeper at offices in Watford City, Williston,
Park River, ND and Sidney, MT. During World War II she worked at Reddig, CA and
Longview, WA. She returned to Sidney, MT in 1945.

Jess and Gert moved to Beulah in the fall of 1965, as Jesse's brother Cecil
passed away and Jess inherited the Greystone Hotel. In 1966 the Smiths
purchased the Schlitz Bar from Albert and Rufina Zeller. Jess operated the bar
and Gert the hotel until they retired.

Jess was a member of the Elks Club, the Legion and V.FW. Clubs, the Chamber of
Commerce and the Zap Sportsmans Club.

During her interim in Sidney, MT, Gert was a member of numerous organizations.
She was a member of the Pella Lutheran Church and the ALCW.

Since moving to Beulah she served one term on the city council, is a past
member of the Beulah Boosters and the Beulah Women's Club.

At the present time she is a member of Zion Lutheran Church, the ALCW and the
Sakakawea Art Association.

Jerald and Inez Sommer

The Sommershine Car Wash located along Highway 49 in west Beulah is owned by
Jerald and Inez Sommer. In addition to this business, they each have a
full-time job and are busy raising a family of four children.

Jerald Emil was born Nov. 27, 1943, at Hazen. He is the son of Emil and Alma
(Weigum) Sommer and his parents still reside at Hazen. Jerald came to Beulah in
1973 to work for North American Coal Company as a supply clerk. He participates
in various community activities and is a member of Beulah Eagles Club, the
Lions Club, the Chamber of Commerce and the Quarterback Club.

Inez was born April 26, 1946, at Richardton. Her father, Alvin Hermunstad, died
in 1950. Her mother, Margaret Fettig Hermunstad Schroeder, lives in Bismarck.
Inez is a member of the Beulah Lioness Club, the Merry Mrs. Homemakers and the
Beulah Woman's Club. Inez is a secretary at the Beulah elementary school.

The Sommers lived in several places before making a permanent move to Beulah
during the summer of 1973. They previously lived at Williston where son Ricky
Lee was born Sept. 26, 1967. Son Jody Jerald was born in Dickinson on July 17,
1966. The family then moved to Bismarck and lived there over six years. Both
daughters were born in Bismarck: Shonda Sue on Feb. 28, 1970, and Tamala Dee on
Feb. 18, 1974.

When Jerald and Inez moved to Beulah there were no available homes for rent and
few for sale, so they lived in a trailer house at the Scherbinske Trailer
Court. In the spring of 1974 they bought the John Bauer property, made some
improvements and lived there over two years. It was a wise investment because
in 1981 they built the Sommershine Car Wash on the house site. Development was
taking place in north Beulah and in the fall on 1976 the Sommers began building
one of the first three houses in the Century First Addition. They were able to
move into their new home in the winter of 1977. The former Schumaier wheat
field witnessed a building boom and was soon filled with other homes. The
Beulah elementary school was also built there.

The Sommer family has witnessed changes in Beulah during their 14 years of
residence. There was no place to buy gas or grocery items after closing hours
or on Sunday. They feel the changes have brought conveniences.

Henry Sr. and Rosina Spier

Henry Spier, Sr. was born Jan. 30, 1871, in Roumania where he met his wife,
Rosina Gunsch. She was born in 1875 and they married in 1897. In 1898 they came
to Tripp, SD, and in 1901 they came to Mercer County, settling at Zap. In 1938
they moved to Golden Valley for a few years before moving to Beulah.

They were parents of seven children: Joe, Dan, Fred, Helmuth, Henry Jr., Ida,
(Mrs. Henry Weil) and Rose, (Mrs. Sam Weidrich). Only Henry Jr. and Rose are
still living. Henry Spier, Sr. lived to the age of 98 and died March 17, 1969.
Rosina died May 28, 1958. Both are interred at the Zion Lutheran Cemetery at
Beulah.

Henry Spier, Jr. was born Nov. 30, 1913, six miles south of Zap, on his parents'
homestead. He married Frieda Mohl of Golden Valley, on Nov. 26, 1936. Frieda was
born Aug. 26, 1916, at Golden Valley, to Jacob and Elizabeth (Weidrich) Mohl.
Frieda came from a family of 12. Her brothers and sisters are: John, Ewald,
Jacob, Oswald, Clara, Hilda, Orlene, Marie, Rosie, Edna and Irene. After their
marriage they lived on his parents' farm and purchased the farm from his
parents in 1938 and actively farmed it until 1948.

In 1949 Henry, Jr. purchased a half interest in the Field Implement Company at
Beulah. In 1952 he sold his interest in the Field Implement Company to J.B.
Field, and acquired the Ford agency from Flemmer Sales and Service. In 1959 he
built the Spier Bowling Lanes in Beulah which he sold in about 1974 to Ervin
Mohl. They still own the Ford agency and it is Spier Sales and Service.

Henry and Frieda have three children and seven grandchildren: Orbadella Spier
has three children; Rene, Howell and Debbie, and lives in Bismarck. Murel Spier
has two children, Travis and Valerie. He lives in Beulah and helps his father
with the business. Diana Zimmerman has two children, Shannon and Shanna and
lives at Bismarck.

The Spiers are members of Zion Lutheran Church and the Beulah Eagles Club. They
have watched the village of Beulah grow from a horse and buggy era to a city of
power plants that is well known to all of the United States.

Clyde and Marie Stickney

Clyde LeGrant Stickney, the son of Cashus Stickney and Charlotte Rule Stickney,
was born in Hustler, WI, on Oct. 23, 1899. His brothers were Avery, Roy, and
Jesse; his sisters, Lenna Stickney Mattesen and Gertrude Stickney Johnson.

The family lived on a farm. Clyde attended a rural school from which he
received an eighth-grade diploma. He served in the United States Navy in World
War I from 1917-1919.

After his discharge from the Navy he came to North Dakota, where he was employed
at the coal mines in Beulah and Zap. In 1925, he became a Beulah rural mail
carrier, serving 25 years on the south route and 14 years on the north route.
In the summer, fall, and spring he drove a car. In the winter - in the early
days - he had an enclosed sleigh pulled by a team of horses. Halfway around the
route he would hitch up a fresh team of horses. His patrons were very good to
him. Many is the time they pulled him out of the mud or snow and helped him on
his way.

In the year 500, Herodotus, a Greek historian, penned the following words in
reference to the Persian postal system. They could be said of Clyde - "Neither
snow nor rain nor heat nor gloom of night stays these couriers from the swift
completion of their appointed rounds."

In addition to being a rural mail carrier, Clyde, together with Marie, owned and
operated a farm immediately adjacent to the west side of Beulah. In those years
the hill west of Beulah was known as Stickney Hill.

Clyde was a member of Zion Lutheran Church, the American Legion, and the Rural
Mail Carriers Association.

Clyde married Marie Opdahl at Stanton on June 13, 1922. Marie was born on Dec.
4, 1899, at Manfred, ND, the daughter of Peder and Christine Opdahl. The
youngest of four children, Marie had two sisters, Otilda Opdahl Dovre and Emma
Opdahl Aasand; and one brother, Edwin. She was raised and educated in rural
Manfred, although the family spent a short time in Canada.

She graduated from Valley City State Normal School and taught at the Grassy
Butte Rural School until 1921 when she moved to Hazen. She taught at the Hazen
Public School until her marriage. During World War II, she taught for a time in
the Antelope school district.

Marie was past president of the Beulah American Legion Auxiliary, past member of
the Zion Lutheran Church, a charter member and past president of the Mission
Circle of Zion Lutheran. She moved to Bismarck in 1965 following the death of
her husband in 1964. In Bismarck, she was a member of Good Shepherd Lutheran
Church and the National Association of Retired Employees.

During the years Marie raised her family, her creativity showed itself in her
sewing ability and other homemaking skills. While in Bismarck, she began
sketching and painting. Family and friends have many of her paintings in their
homes.

Marie passed away on Aug. 20, 1983 at the home of her daughter, Elaine, where
she had been living.

Clyde and Marie raised four children who were all born at Beulah and graduated
from Beulah High School.

Cleo was born on Dec. 22, 1923. She received a standard certificate from Valley
City State College in 1944 and a bachelor of science degree in education from
Minot in 1971. She has taught school in Spring Creek district of Beulah, Hazen
Public School, Conkling school district (rural Washburn), and the Washburn
Public School where she is now teaching second grade.

Cleo married Donald Nordquist of Washburn on June 6, 1948. Donald is  co-owner
of Nordquist Brothers, an implement and Ford dealership. During World War II he
served in the United States Army from 1941-1946. His active duty was in the
Pacific theatre of operations. He is a retired reserve officer in the Corps of
Engineers.

They have six children. Pamela, a graduate of Dickinson State College, is
married to Royal Lyson, who is senior district salesman for McCullough,
Division of Western Atlas International in Williston. Their three children are
Ryan, Natalie, and Brady. Donald, Bismarck, is married to Kathleen Bertie, a

Jim is parts manager for Nordquist Brothers in Washburn. Jennifer, a nurse, is

Cynthia has a bachelor of science degree in education from the University of

Carol was born on Dec. 29, 1927. She graduated from Wahpeton State School of
Science as a secretary. Before her marriage, she worked for Farmers Insurance
and the Veterans Administration in Fargo. She married Lawrence Schmidt of
Wahpeton on June 8, 1947. Lawrence served in World War II in the European and

While in Wahpeton, Lawrence was counter manager of the Auto Parts Company. The
