        The Art Tabert family

Arthur and Emma Tabert

Blue Grass was the home of Edward and Margaret (Mindt) Tabert when Arthur was
born Nov. 26, 1913. Arthur was only one when the family moved to Beulah and
purchased a dray line and livery stable, one of the town's earliest business
places, situated just north of the railroad tracks and a bit south of the
present Super Valu Store. The brisk business saw a decline as the cars and
trucks became more common. The livery stable was sold in 1925 and the family
moved to a farm north of Beulah where Art helped his father.

The era of the Dust Bowl was the 30s, and it became difficult to make a living
off the land. About this time Arthur married Emma, born Oct. 17, 1914, in
McKenzie County. Her parents were Edward and Bertha (Schuh) Schock. The
newlyweds made their home with Art's parents to help with the farming and give
financial assistance. Arthur secured a job working for the Knife River Coal
Mining Company.

Many people engaged in farming went to work in the coal mine as it was during
the Depression, and due to crop failures it was difficult to make a living.
Loading machines were introduced in the mine in 1934, which meant no jobs for
many of the miners.

Art worked at various jobs in the local garages until he became a part owner
with Fred Flemmer and managed the Corner Hardware Store. He disposed of his
share in this business and purchased the Variety Store on north Main Street
from George Kuch. After this business venture he was a car salesman for Spier
Sales where he also helped with the bookwork.

The Taberts bought a larger home just north of the downtown city playground,
where daughter Deane was married. There were five additional children in the
family: Larry, Marlene, Vernan, Richard and Jeanette.

Raising six children kept both parents very busy and the children saw little of
their father as the stores had long business hours. There was no such thing as
an eight-hour day as shops were open in the evenings and on Saturday until
midnight. Emma's days were long too, and she was busy caring for the children,
raising a garden and sewed all the clothes. City ordinances were not as strict
in earlier times and the Taberts were able to have chickens and a cow, too.
They raised pigs which they shipped out through the local stockyards. The yards
were in town east of the elevators.

Art and Emma moved to Mandan about 1962. Although Art did not have a formal
education in bookkeeping he had an aptitude for this work, so he found
employment with various automotive concerns keeping books and working in the
parts department. Later he carried on the same type of work when they lived in
Wyoming and Colorado.

The Taberts now live in Mandan, enjoying leisure time and the joy of friends,
children and grandchildren. They recall the earlier times in Beulah, and talk
about those rodeos that brought so many people to town. The grandstands were
full at all events.

The early fairs were also times to remember. The fairground was in the area
which is now southwest Beulah. A county fair held on the 4th of July, and large
crowd in attendance really impressed Art, as he said the town was so full of
people that the sidewalks were not wide enough.

Art's father died March 1, 1939, but his mother lived until Nov. 25, 1972.
Emma's mother passed away May 28, 1965, and her father died June 24, 1932.

Carl and Ragnhild Thelander

Since their arrival in Beulah in the early 1930s, Carl and Ragnhild Thelander
had a profound impact on the  community. Though they are both gone, their
influence lingers on Main Street as well as in numerous community organizations.

Son Charles now owns and operates the Ben Franklin Store for which his father
acquired the Ben Franklin franchise in 1954.

Carl was born in River Falls, Wisc., on Oct. 5, 1901, the son of Otto and Grace
Thelander. He was a graduate of River Falls State College. Carl had come to
Beulah from New Salem to open the Beulah RCU Store in 1932. In 1933 he married
Ragnhild Jelstrup, a New Salem school teacher. She was born in Greenbush, Minn.,
on Feb. 20, 1906, to Christian B. and Andrea Jelstrup. She was a home economics
major, graduating from the University of North Dakota, Grand Forks.

 They had two children. Nancy Andrea Susan was born on Dec. 5, 1941, at
Bismarck. She is a 1964 graduate of UND. She and her husband Brent Weiser,
originally of Hazen, are both music teachers, who make their home in Fargo. Son
Mark Allen Shropshire was born on Sept. 28, 1968, and Kimberly Charlotte Weiser
was born March 19, 1983.

The Thelanders' son, Charles Allen, was born Sept. 16, 1944, at Beulah. He is a
business administration graduate from Minot State College. He married Angela
Shramm, a Hazen native, while serving in the U.S. Army in 1967. He returned to
Beulah in 1972 to co-manage the store with his mother. Rags had assumed full
responsibility for the store when Carl died on Aug. 5, 1965.

Angie, a Bismarck Junior College graduate, has worked at the Beulah Post Office
for 11 years, accepting the appointment of postmaster on March 12, 1988. They
have one daughter, Carmen Andrea, who was born on Oct. 28, 1970.

The Thelander children, now with growing children of their own, have many
pleasant memories of the Beulah of their youth. Nancy and Charles fondly recall
riding the "Galloping Goose" to Mandan. This two-unit train made daily runs
into Mandan, stopping at every small town along the tracks to pick up cream
cans to take to Mandan. It transported other freight and mail, as well as
passengers.

Nancy and Charles grew up with the city's first water tower almost in their
back yard. They remember their back yard becoming solid ice when the water
tower would overflow in the winter. This seemed to occur at least twice every
winter!

The slough northwest of their house, which then was out of town, was a dandy
spot where the Thelander children could catch frogs. They would also tour the
slough on a home-made raft. This land of adventure is now the site of the Scott
Knodel and Marvin Schaper homes.

Carl and Rags Thelander were very involved in their community. Carl served as
president of the town board for eight years. He held continuous membership in
the Lions Club, Country Club, Athletic Club, Rodeo Association, Community Club
and Chamber of Commerce. He held numerous offices in these organizations.

Rags served three years on the Beulah school board and was a long-time member of
the Beulah Woman's Club, Mothers' Club (Extension Homemakers), Country Club and
Historical Society. Her favorite community project through the years was the
local library.

Charles and Angie have followed in his parents' footsteps, becoming actively
involved in the community also.

Charles has served as a member of the park board, Beulah Boosters, Chamber of
Commerce, Beulah Convention and Visitors' Bureau and the Beulah Municipal Golf
Course. He was a charter member of the Beulah Eagles Club as well as the Lions
Club.

Angie's main civic interests include the Woman's Club and Mothers' Club
(Extension Homemakers). She also is a board member of the Mercer-Oliver Health
Services, Beulah Library Board and the Parents' Advisory Committee (at the high
school).

James and Martha Thomson

James Thomson was born at Leal, ND in 1911. He graduated from Leal High School
and attended Jamestown College until the beginning of the Depression when he had
to quit to support the family. In 1941 he entered the Army and fought in the
European Theatre during World War II. He participated in the D-Day invasion of
Normandy, France and was wounded during the Allied breakthrough of the German
lines at St. Lo, France.

After his discharge in 1945, he came to Beulah where his sisters, Daisy (Mrs.
Cecil Davidson) and Esther (Mrs. Karl Schulz) were living at the time.

He was employed at the Beulah MDU power plant where he worked until his
retirement. He also farmed northwest of Hazen. In 1947 he married Martha Betz
Chute who had two children from a previous marriage, Darrell and Joyce (Mrs. Don
Zundel).

James and Martha had four children, Judith (Mrs. Raymond Knoell), Jane (Mrs.
William Swan), James G., and Peggy (Mrs. Cary Wolf).

        Thomson family Back row: James R., Darrell Chute, James G., Ray Knoel.
        Front row: Martha, Jane, Judy

Martha was born in 1918 and raised southeast of Beulah near Otter Creek on her
parents' homestead, where she lived until she was six. She contracted polio
during her first year of school. Her parents had to take Martha to Dr.
Mackerlin for treatments once a week. The treatments consisted of applying a
"good" smelling cream and shining a blue light on her back. That fall the
family moved to the Walter Stephens place and built a house there.

Times were hard. Her dad died in 1928. Martha's brother Ben worked at the mine
to help out the family. One special Christmas Martha remembers there was so much
snow that the family could not leave the farm for supplies or gifts. Christmas
Eve there was a raging blizzard and the family was huddled around the kitchen
stove for warmth. It seemed as if there would be no Christmas that year. Then,
a noise at the door! It was Ben arriving with special Christmas treats.

During the '30s Martha, her sister Edna, Ben and Ole, Glen, Hans and Charlotte
Tysver moved to the Badlands near Killdeer where land was available at 50 cents
an acre. They drove their cattle from south of Beulah and camped out for the
summer while trying to establish homesteads. At summer's end Martha, Edna, Ben,
Hans and Charlotte returned to the Beulah area. Glen and Ole remained at the
Tysver homestead near Killdeer.

In 1933 the Betz family moved their house from the Stephens place to Beulah.
During the Depression Martha worked for the NYA. She is presently employed by
the Beulah nursing home where she has worked for the past 22 years.

Martha is a world traveler. She has visited the Holy Land, Egypt, Italy, Japan,
Switzerland, some of the Caribbean Islands, Hawaii and Alaska, often traveling
with Ingrid Anderson.

Currently the status of the family of Martha and James Thomson is: James R.
died in 1976; Martha resides in Beulah; Darrell lives in Beulah; Joyce, a
housewife lives at 9 Mile Falls, WA; Judith, a teacher of science and history
in Hazen, lives on a farm northwest of Hazen; Jane assists her husband in his
missionary work with the Navigators; James G. resides in Beulah and works at
Coyote Station; Peggy, a fifth-grade teacher in Hazen, lives in the country
northwest of Hazen.

Gregory W. Thompson

Gregory W. Thompson has been living in Williston, ND, for eight years, but
still calls Beulah his home. "After all I was born near there, went to school
there, my family and a host of friends are still in that town. It has a warm
spot in my Irish heart."

        Gregory Thompson

Jess and Teresa (Cox) Thompson are Gregory's parents and he has a sister,
Susan, and a brother, Russell. Although the Thompsons lived in town they were
considered 'city' ranchers and farmers; thus Gregory became involved in
agriculture in action, helping out at the farm.

H.R. McKenzie was the county agent and he liked to see young people channel
their energy to worthwhile activities, so he encouraged membership in the 4-H
program. The Spring Creek 4-H Club was a spirited group with projects ranging
from photography to grains and cattle, with membership both rural and urban.
Gregory was especially interested in beef cattle and showed his stock at the
county and state level, gaining showmanship and 4-H key awards. He bought a
fine Arabian horse, and Smokey earned him numerous ribbons and awards at the
county and state fairs. He still owns some of his Arabians.

Gregory attended North Dakota State University, majoring in vocational
agriculture. He didn't plan on a teaching career, however; it was required that
he take student teaching. He said, "From then on I was 'hooked' on teaching.

His first teaching job was at Drake, ND, where he felt things went well for
him, his students and the school.

1980 saw a change for Gregory, as he became the vocational agriculture
instructor at Williston, which gave him an opportunity to teach in a more
expanded program. He encouraged the school to build a greenhouse which is an
asset to the city and his department. He feels good seeing his students respond
to the FFA program and they have received merit recognition in state and
national events. He has done extensive traveling to state and national meetings,
conventions and competitive events as advisor and counselor.

In 1981 he was voted Outstanding Young Vocational Educator for North Dakota at
the All-service Vocational Conference. He was also named to "Who's Who." Through
the influence of Diane Grosz, Gregory was nominated and elected president of the
North Dakota Vocational Association in 1983. He held subsequent offices and
served as a voting delegate to several national conventions, representing
agriculture distributive education as well as other vocational careers. He is
an NDSU supervisory teacher and is on the advisory committee for agriculture
curriculum development at the university.

Gregory enjoys down-hill skiing and his Arabians. He is active with his
professional and community-related organizations as well as political
activities. In his church he belongs to the K.C.'s, leadership in the RENEW
program, and the advisory council for youth enrichment and religion. He belongs
to the Big Brother organization.

Gregory feels proud of the learning progress, enthusiasm and achievements of his
students. He considers that a major part of his future.

        Jess and Teresa. 1987 Soil Conservation Achievement Winning Farm.

Jess E. and Teresa Thompson

Wayne Lubenow, a syndicate writer from Fargo, came to write a history about
Jess. He had heard about the Yankee Canadian airman and wanted to know what it
was all about. He wrote this story.

"Jess Thompson pages nostalgically through his World War II flying books and
photograph albums. What's more, he kept a day-to-day diary of more than four
years of sky war. Early in 1941 he came to Fargo to enlist in the Army Air
Corps. They had a full quota and he was told that he'd have to go into the
Coast Artillery. He wanted to fly so on Sept. 5, 1941, he went to Canada and
joined the Royal Canadian Air Force. He felt very disappointed that he was not
able to get into the Army Air Corps.

"Jess took pre-flight and flight training at Edmonton, Alberta. Then he was
sent to Saskatchewan to fly twin-engine Cessnas. Jess got his wings in the RCAF
and was sent to Nova Scotia where 15,000  soldiers and 2,000 airmen boarded the
Queen Elizabeth to Glasgow, Scotland. 'There was no convoy,' Jess says. 'The
Queen was a fast ship and we just zig-zagged across the Atlantic to avoid
German submarines.' He took instrument flight training in London and night and
weather flight training in Inverness, Scotland.

"He was an RCAF pilot, but Jess Thompson was an American first and foremost, so
in February 1942, he was allowed to transfer to the American Air Force.

" 'They checked me out in B-17s,' he says, 'and I hated it. It was like driving
a truck and I was used to flying smaller stuff.' Jess got transferred into a
B-26 squadron. The B-26, if you don't know, is a twin-engined attack bomber
called the Martin Marauder and Jess flew 72 combat missions in that airplane.
He flew some tough missions where the anti-aircraft flak was so heavy you could
have walked on it. He said his B-26 squadron had fairly low casualty losses as
they had good fighter escort planes.

"After the invasion of Europe, Jess and the B-26s were moved to airfields in
France so they could attack Germany. They used the same airfields they had been
bombing, and they were sure banged up. From the French airfields the B-26s
began pounding German missile site targets. They were the sites where the
Germans were launching their V-1 and V-2 rockets.

"After 72 combat missions, Jess was discharged in 1945. He came back to Beulah,
the town where he was born, with the Distinguished Flying Cross, with one
cluster, and the Air Medal with six clusters.

" 'I never thought of going anywhere but Beulah,' he says. 'This is my town and
I love it.' Jess likes to tell the story of how he got the very first new car
that came into Beulah after the war. "It was a 1946 Ford, and the dealer was
obliged to sell it to a serviceman and at the ceiling price. I paid $1,200 for
it."

"As the first veteran back to Beulah, Jess was offered a job with the Postal
Service as a rural mail carrier and he took it. The rural route didn't take
much time and flying was still in his blood so Jess bought a little plane, a
Piper Cub J-3, and began flying it around. Then he bought a quarter of land and
another plane and began giving flying lessons. Under the GI Bill, he was
allowed to start a flying school in Beulah. He also bought an old Navy Stearman
and did some aerial crop spraying.

"Jess quit flying 15 years ago, bought the Anderson Farm southeast of Beulah and
began a farm-ranch operation. He was instrumental in getting a Beulah airport,
which is located where his old flying school (Jess and Lie's Flying Service)
used to be, and he was chairman of the Beulah Airport Authority. He has also
been post commander of the local VFW, was chairman of the Selective Service
Board for 22 years, was president of the Beulah Chamber of Commerce and of the
city council, and the Sportsman Club.

"Now Jess Thompson takes things easy and his hobby is the farm and a little
traveling by commercial airlines. But ever so often he digs out his diary and
photographs and remembers when he was a Yank in the RCAF and those 72 missions
in his B-26 Marauder. And it's nice to remember."

The farm is called "The Whispering Pines," because the former owner, Mr.
Anderson, planted a fine grove of pine trees by hand. The Thompsons began
buying the farm in 1965. Running the farm and assisting with the children's 4-H
and F.F.A. projects kept everyone busy. They were active in programs of crops,
livestock and horsemanship, winning grand champion awards: Russ in crops and
beef and Greg with his beef and horsemanship. Together the family spent time on
canoe trips, sailing and tent camping.

Jess and Teresa join the British Commonwealth Air Force for their reunion at
Winnipeg and the 450th Bomb Squadron wherever they may happen to meet. It is a
pleasant time to renew acquaintances. The 450th met in Texas in 1987 and Jess
was able to go up in the B-26 Marauder--the only one that is in flying
condition today.

Teresa grew up on the Cox farm just a mile east of Beulah right on the banks of
the Knife River, a spot she dearly loves. The family called themselves "the
clan." Her parents, Christopher Cox and Mary (Molly) McGuire, were both Irish
people. There were four girls and four boys in the family.

Teresa worked at the Economy Hardware store and Jim's Cafe during the summer
months while she was earning her education degree. She taught school for a short
time. She worked in the Post Office while attending high school and when she
learned that the assistant postmaster was resigning, she wrote a qualifying
examination and began a postal career. During the years that the children were
small, Mrs. Goldade came and cared for the family. Teresa found time to join
various organizations and spent many years with the March of Dimes program, as
well as activities connected with St. Joseph Catholic Church, the Girl Scouts,
Cub Scouts and was assistant den mother. She was a member of OWL and bookkeeper
for the Jess and Lie Flying Service. She likes to hike and cross-country ski.

        Thompson family Standing: Terry, Susan, Gregory, Russell. Seated,
        Teresa, Jess

        David Hugh Thompson

Jess is the son of early homesteaders Manley and Isabelle (Henderson) Thompson.
While in school, Jess participated in all sports including Legion baseball, was
a life Scout and played with the Beulah drum and bugle corps. The Thompsons had
four children: David Hugh, Russell, Susan and Gregory. Russell and Darcy have
three children: Zachary, Jacob and Jessica. They operate the family farm
southeast of Beulah. Susan and her husband Terry Lutz live in Juneau, Alaska
with their children Andrew and Cassie. Susan is an accountant for Computer
Components. Gregory is a vocational agriculture instructor at Williston.

The Thompsons were the proud recipients of the 1987 Mercer County Soil
Conservation Achievement award in district five, an acknowledgment of
outstanding conservation practices.

        Manley and Bell Thompson

Manley Dow and Isabelle Thompson

Manley Dow Thompson and Isabelle Henderson were both children of early settler
families who came to Mercer County to establish homesteads. Manley, born in
Bethany, MO, was the son of Lorenzo Dow and Louisa Linville. The family of five
girls and four boys came to the area in 1908; a homestead was established south
of Beulah.

Isabelle, one of nine children, was the daughter of John and Elizabeth
(Zimmerman) Henderson. She was born at Ft. Rice, ND where her parents were in
the sheep business. They arrived from Nebraska in a covered wagon before the
turn of the century and moved westward to take advantage of homestead rights,
squatting on land where the Beulah park is now located. This home was a
combination of sod and dug-out, barely visible today. Henderson discovered coal
along the riverbank and used it for fuel.

It was soon discovered this was set-aside school land and not open to entry; he
then staked out his homestead on the present Myrtle Sailer farm north of the
airport. The barn he built is still standing. Bell's father hired a teacher and
built a small school for his children. Later Bell attended the academy at
Harvey. This ranch at one time had 160 head of cattle and 1200 sheep, and the
site where Beulah is now located was their hay meadow.

Bell remembered that she and her father walked and traveled by covered wagon as
they herded a flock of sheep to Glen Ullin with their dog. She was selected to
make the trip as she was a much better cook than her sisters. The money they
garnered from the sale of the sheep was spent on flour, sugar and other
groceries as well as shoes, clothing and yard goods which they brought back for
the family.

Manley and Isabelle were married at Stanton on June 12, 1916. She said her
brothers weren't in favor of this marriage, so they just eloped. It proved to
be a marriage of 66 years' duration. A special celebration was held on their
Golden Anniversary in 1966. Guests included 11 of the schoolmates who attended
country school with Isabelle.

Early employment for Manley was with the Northern Pacific railway; he manned the
pump station east of Beulah where the track curves between the hills and the
Knife River. The house was very close to the track and really shook when the
trains passed by. The locomotives of these trains were steam-powered engines;
they took on water and sometimes coal at this point. Manley used a hand-pumped
speeder to travel the rails to the depot.

He later farmed and ranched on his father's homestead and finally he moved a
house into Beulah in 1929 where they lived for the rest of their lives, just a
block off Main Street.

Just like everyone else in town they had their own chickens and had a well. They
were good gardeners and had apple trees, too. Mrs. Thompson's yard was a
profusion of flowers through the whole growing season. It was always known as
the place with the beautiful flowers, and many stopped just to enjoy the beauty.

Manley worked for the M.P. Moore Dray Line. The commodities used by the
townspeople were shipped here in box cars. The dray carried on a busy business,
unloading and making deliveries to the eight grocery, hardware, and general
merchandise stores. There were no big semi or Mack trucks at that time; in
fact, the first roads in some cases were mere trails. Sometimes the lumber for
a whole house arrived on the rails.

Manley decided to run for and was elected town constable. He held this office
for several terms, in which he did a thorough job of security and justice. The
kids around town soon had a "beware of Manley" attitude, but when his back was
turned they climbed the water tower anyway, something that really rankled him.
His job was not just walking the beat, he was also street and water
commissioner, which meant reading the water meters, grading the streets,
checking city wells and water pumps and the disposal system.

He kept law and order, checking traffic irregularities, the business places
after hours and kept an eye on the local bars. There was no drinking and
driving with Manley around--often the inebriated one would find himself
sleeping for a few hours in the city jail before getting his keys back . . . it
wasn't considered an arrest and no penalties attached. This tough cop didn't
bother with a gun either; his ever-ready billy club was a handy and dangerous
weapon. He later moved on to a job with better hours and pay, working for Knife
River Coal Mining Company in the underground mine, later working as security at
the office and tipple area until he retired in 1960.

Idleness was not in his blood, as he spent many hours in his yard and also
found time to help his son Jess with his farming operation and feed lot. Manley
died in 1982 at the age of 88. Seventy-five of those years were spent in
Beulah. Isabelle was here for 85 years. It is understandable that the Thompson
and Henderson name is legendary in this community. They are both buried at Rose
Hill Cemetery, a place they helped maintain through the years.

As a girl Bell was busy helping her mother, and sometimes helped herd the
sheep. As a wife and mother she was very committed to her family, took good
care of Manley and her four children as well as her grandson Gary Lauf. She
loved picnics and enjoyed preparing for those many outings. She was a very
organized and orderly person with a green thumb, and an excellent cook. No
wonder they had so many dinner guests.

She was raised in a Christian, conscientious family and found it distressing
not to have her church in Beulah. She worked with those of her faith and
finally there was a Seventh-day Adventist church near her home. Although this
was later in her life she devoted considerable time to her church, and the
people there were good to her.

In July 1984 while on a picnic with her church group she suffered a stroke, and
that gentle, patient lady died in September of 1985, just a short time prior to
her 95th birthday. At the age of 93 she could still live alone, care for
herself and tend to her own yard.

Jacob and Edna Unterseher

Jake Unterseher was born in Bessarabia, Lightentahl, Romania, and came to
America in 1909 at the age of three weeks. Fred and Magdelena (Holzworth)
Unterseher settled in Mannhaven, N.D., then later moved to Halliday and
Killdeer where his parents homesteaded. Jake's parents moved into Killdeer in
the 1940's, then Jake bought a homestead there.

Because there were only two quarters of land, Jake sold the homestead to Alfred
Schwalbe north of Killdeer and moved to Hazen in 1949 to farm his uncle Gottlieb
Unterseher's place. In 1954 Jake and Edna moved to south of Beulah where they
are still at the present time.

        The Unterseher family: Bonita, Allen, Jake, Marvin, Edna, Arvid,
        Luella, Marlene

Mrs. Jake (Edna) Unterseher's parents were Mr. and Mrs. Bernhard Kilber. She was
born at Mannhaven. Mr. Kilber was a native of South Russia, born Aug. 10, 1880.
He came to the U.S. in 1907 and settled in Mannhaven. He was married to Karolina
Weisenburger in 1909. Mr. Kilber was doing blacksmith work in Mannhaven until
1915 when he moved to Krem, N.D. and farmed there until 1930. Then they moved
to south of Hazen. In 1944 they moved to Hazen city. Mrs. Kilber died in 1949
at 58 years. Mr. Kilber lived in Jochim Memorial Home (Beulah nursing home). He
died at age 87 in 1967.

Jake and Edna went through hard times when they were married in 1934, but they
also had good years, many blessings, and raised six children. There was no
electricity until 1950; they carried coal and water, needed for the house. They
milked by hand for many years. They raised cattle, hogs and chickens.

They also used horses to farm until they could afford tractors and other farm
machinery. They now have only a few head of cattle, no horses, and no other
animals on account of their health--they are semi-retired.

They built a new home in 1968 where they no longer had to carry coal, wood and
water - their house is heated by electricity. Until a couple of years ago, when
the co-op was short on electricity they heated the basement with wood and coal
to help save the electricity. They do still heat with electricity.

We enjoy living in Beulah, have a good church to go to, Zion Lutheran. We have
good neighbors and a lot of friends far and near that we are very proud of.

Rev. Gordon and Rose Voegele

Gordon Voegele was born on Aug. 25, 1929, in the 'Glueckstahl area'
approximately 18 miles south of Beulah. He is the son of Donald E. and Emelia
Voegele, who yet reside in Hebron, N.D.

According to Rev. Voegele, the 'Glueckstahl area' was not an established
township but a community of farms owned by German-Russian immigrants who named
their new territory in honor of their home village in Europe. Rev. Voegele's
grandparents were Germans who emigrated from Russia in the early 1900s. Both
his father's parents and his mother's parents came to North Dakota and so it
was that his parents, Donald and Emelia, came to be born in America.

"My father's father, my grandfather Frederick Voegele, came to America in 1901.
He was German but he learned to speak Russian when he served in the Russian
army. My mother's father, my grandfather Jacob Sauter, came in 1910, learning
to speak Russian in the same manner as Frederick," says Rev. Voegele. "They
both came to Hebron, North Dakota, but it was Frederick who moved on to the
Glueckstahl area and that is where I was born."

He continues, "My youth was nothing exciting, but it has become very meaningful
to me especially now that I am older."

The reverend's speech carries still a hint of the sing-song lilt characteristic
of native German speakers. It is a lovely sound, once very common in this area
of the Midwest, a sort of lingering reminder of our ancestral beginnings. But
this particular visitation from the past was viewed as a hindrance by its
speakers, and probably would be yet if it had not all but disappeared. "It is a
matter of your perspective," says Rev. Voegele. "I used to get singled out in
college and found this very uncomfortable. They grabbed me right away and said,
'We are going to work on you!' And they did. I spent most afternoons with a
speech teacher to get rid of my accent. I am glad they did."

As with many of the Dakota-born, Rev. Voegele's memories are rural, those from
the farm, those of following the harrow with a horse, those of a strong work
ethic. "You were asked to do something and you didn't ask why, you just did
it," he explains. "There was no questioning, it just wasn't done. In some ways
this was a strength. When the Depression hit, I never heard my parents
complain. Of course, we lived on the farm and always had plenty to eat. My
parents got along with little, but they managed."

Other memories include attending a country church, a country school, with the
most vivid recollections centering around the Christmas celebration. Everything
having to do with the program was memorized - in the German. Rev. Voegele
recalls how his people, without that isolating device--the TV--would take time
out of their busy lives and visit each other in the evenings, just to play
games and talk. Comments the Reverend, "It was so much more simple then, but
everyone seemed to enjoy themselves."

Gordon Voegele left the area in 1952 to attend college at Dickinson State and
then seminary at Sioux Falls, S.D. It was then he met Rose Schneider, who was
to become his wife. She was born April 12, 1930, to Gottlieb (d. 1973) and Eva
(d. 1978) Schneider, in Hebron. Rose and Gordon were married in March of 1952.

"As pastor and family," says Rev. Voegele, "we have lived in South Dakota,
Kansas, Colorado and North Dakota." The birthplaces of the Voegeles' three
children reflect some of their travels. Kent was born Aug. 28, 1957, in Sioux
Falls, South Dakota, while both Kayla, born Jan. 23, 1967, and Kary, born April
28, 1968, were born in Wichita, Kan.

Rev. Voegele continues, "In 1979, we moved from Denver, Colo., to Beulah, where
I became pastor of the Immanuel Baptist Church." He considers it a tremendous
honor to be part of this body of Christ and also to have been involved in the
construction of the new sanctuary and education building.

Rose Voegele has since become employed in part-time work at the Beulah
Community Nursing Home.

"We returned to Beulah because these people are our kind of people. They are
kind and loving and have made our lives here very pleasant." There is a smile
in Rev. Voegele's voice as he refutes Thomas Wolfe--yes, you can go home again!

Jake and Sarah Voegele

Sarah Voegele came to Beulah in January of 1925 to visit her sister, Marie
Rumaire. "My first job was in the post office under Ted Scholz, postmaster,"
she writes. "There I met Jake Voegele who was working at Rose's Hardware store.
We were married in 1926, had a three-room home built by Jake Osteo and settled
down and lived in Beulah for 17 years with the exception of several years in
Grand Forks while Jake served on the first Highway Patrol in North Dakota."

During their stay in Beulah, they met many wonderful people and have fond
memories of all of them: Lambert and Alvira Rose (Rose Hardware), Dad Sovereign
(IGA Store), Dr. Rasmussen (their doctor), Dr. Jimmy Halbeisen (dentist), Billee
Vincent (restaurant), Irv Midermeyes (hardware), Marshalls and the Malaises
(lumberyard and theatre), Fred and Ann Gentz (banker), Fields (implement
dealer), Chilsons (funeral home), Lisa and Gottlieb Wohler (neighbors), Fred
Flemmer (neighbor), Lauce and John Unruh families (neighbors), John and Christ
Beekers, Grandma Reub (midwife), John Krause and family, Carl Sailer family,
Dr. Vinje, Norman Hastings, Clyde Stickney and Mr. Iverson (mail carriers), Mr.
Moore (drayman).

"This is just to mention a few. We wish them all well wherever their journeys
have taken them.

"Our 17 years in North Dakota were an uphill struggle with normal physical
setbacks, and a family of seven children when there was not much to work with,
and it was very discouraging at times. Compared to the drug, alcohol and
pornography in today's world, we were blessed in so many ways," Sarah writes.

"Jake passed away Jan. 10, 1962 of a heart attack. All seven of our children
are living and enjoy good health. We are able to have family get-togethers as
the children all live in Montana except Betty, who lives in Georgia. Marge,
Leland, Del and Jim live in Great Falls, Merlin in Helena and Vernon in
Bozeman."

"On our recent short trip to Beulah, it was interesting to see the progress in
the past several years," Sarah writes.

"Best wishes to all those good people who are pressing onward and upward."

Larry and Denise Walker

Larry and Denise Walker came to Beulah seeking employment at ANG (then GPGA) in
1983. The Walkers grew up in Missouri. Larry was born in Blackburn, MO to
Leonard C. and Fannie Mae (Campbell) Walker, on Jan. 26, 1947. He graduated
from high school in Marshall, MO, entered the Air Force in April 1966, and
spent the next six years, until April 1972, serving in the US Air Force.

Denise Eileen was born in Albuquerque, NM, June 4, 1955, to William L. and Helen
A. (Jacoby) Brame. When she was five the family moved to Denver, CO for a year
and then moved to Missouri. Denise is a radiology technologist. She attended
TennValley Community College and received her radiology technologist training
at St. Joseph Hospital in Kansas City, MO. Larry is a field technician at ANG.
They have two children: Nicholas Scott, born July 9, 1982, in Kansas City, MO
and Laura Megan, born July 17, 1985, in Bismarck. They are members of Concordia
Lutheran Church. Denise is active in the Lutheran Women's Missionary League and
Larry is a member of the Sunday school board. they enjoy softball, bowling,
soccer and belonging to the Gymnastics Club.

Denise writes, "Since we moved here in Sept. of 1983, we have grown to love
Beulah and the whole state of North Dakota, mainly because of the calm
lifestyle. After living in a large city it was different to be in a smaller
town. But when we return to our original hometown in Missouri and pass through
the fast pace of the big city we realize how much we prefer life here in
Beulah. We wish our families could be nearer to us and enjoy this life with us."

William Sr. and Magdalena Wallender

William Wallender, Sr. and Magdalena Schweigert were married on Dec. 12, 1906,
at Otter Creek, ND.

Bill was born in Russia in 1885, the son of Frederick Wallender and Paulina
(Buchmann) Wallender. He had moved to Beulah from Freeman, SD. Maggie was born
in 1883 and raised at Krem, ND, north of present-day Hazen. She was the
daughter of John Schweigert and Sophia (Miller) Schweigert.

        The William Wallender family

Through the next 16 years the Wallenders were blessed with seven children, all
born at Beulah. Hella was born on Oct. 13, 1907; Arthur was born Aug. 31, 1911;
Bill was born Oct. 28, 1913; Herbert was born June 27, 1915; Bertha was born
May 19, 1918; Alvina was born April 8, 1920; and Albert J. was born April 30,
1922.

The Wallenders homesteaded 12 miles south of Beulah on Section 28. They began
farming with three horses and a walking plow, which they used to tear up the
sod. Their first crop was solely planted into flax. With no fences in those
days, the horses roamed freely and were difficult to locate at times.

Using sod from the ends of furrows, they built their first one-room house in
1907. It measured 20 feet x 20 feet. They lived under the open sky the first
summer and slept under the wagon box when it rained. The sod house was finished
in the fall. It didn't have a wood floor in it for three years. When the floor
was installed, the walls and ceiling were also wallpapered - completely in New
Salem Journals (newspapers).

After ten years of farming, Bill decided to move to town and start a garage,
which was located at the site of the present-day Beulah Twin Cinema. The garage
burned down in 1918; without insurance to cover their losses, they were forced
to return to the homestead.

During the hard economic times of the 1920s and "Dirty Thirties," they found
they could not get ahead financially on the farm. In the fall of 1939 they sold
out and moved back into Beulah, where bill worked at MDU. He later worked for
Farmers Union Oil Company, which he had helped to organize in the 1930s. He
retired in 1957.

Bill passed away in 1963 and Maggie died in 1968.

Herman and Emma Walz

Daniel Walz, father of Herman, was born Dec. 21, 1870, in Halborn, South Russia.
He was four years old when he came with his folks to America. Daniel married
Wilhelmina Rapp in 1895 at Heilburn, S.D. They came to North Dakota in 1914 and
settled five miles north of Zap. Herman was born to them on July 12, 1899, at
Freeman, S.D. He went to Zap, N.D., in 1914 with his parents. Both parents died
there in the late 1930s. Daniel Walz died May 31, 1939, and Wilhelmina died
March 6, 1937. They both died at Zap.

Adam Weigum, father of Emma, was born May 2, 1878, in Crimea, South Russia. He
came to America in 1899 with his wife, Maria Becker, and one son. Emma was born
to them on Feb. 15, 1904, at Zap. Maria died in Oct. 1938, and Adam died in
November 1941, both at Zap.

Herman and Emma Walz bought a farm 16 miles northwest of Beulah after their
marriage on June 8, 1925, and lived on that farm and raised seven children
there. In 1960, they purchased a house in Beulah, but it wasn't until 1965 that
they retired and moved into that house. It is located on 300 Main Street.

Mrs. Walz remembers the terrible winter of 1949 and 1950. The farmers would all
wait to see if the mailman, Rudolph Schnaidt, could make it through. Then they
knew they could all make it to town if they needed to. Sometimes roads were so
bad, no one could travel. So the mail was packaged in bulk and carried in an
airplane by Jess Thompson, who would drop it at the schoolhouse. There, it was
sorted out to all the school children who would take it home.

Herman Walz was a school board member of the Slope School District #30 for many
years, a council member of St. John's Lutheran Church, Wittenberg and Zap, and a
member of the Farmers Union.

The original Walz family farm is carried on by son Duane, his wife, Karen, and
their four children.

Leon and Corrine and their son operate the former John Huber farm, which is
adjacent to the Herman Walz farm.

Mabel married Reuben Eisenbeis, and since their marriage in 1950, they have
lived on and farmed the John Eisenbeis farm 17 miles northwest of Beulah.

Ardella married Reuben Fischer and they now farm north of Zap after working at a
series of dam construction jobs which took them to South Dakota, Montana, and
Pick City.

Wilma married Walter Morast and they farm the former Ursus Morast place north of
Zap.

Betty married Gary Unruh and they now reside in Beulah. They lived in several
states when Gary was employed with the Boeing Co., working at missile sites. He
now works at Knife River Coal Mine, and Betty works at the Beulah public school.

Eunice married Vernon Christmann and they farm east of Center. Vernon is also
employed at the Great Plains Gasification Plant.

Together, Herman and Emma Walz have 19 grandchildren and 15 great-
grandchildren.

        George and Christinia (Hoffmann) Weigum

George and Christinia Weigum

George Weigum, son of Georg Michael and Elisabeth (Wiedrich) Weigum, was born
in Kronenthal, Crimea, Russia, on Dec. 8, 1852. (Georg Michael, known as
Jerigmichel in Kronenthal, was the son of Georg Weigum, immigrant to Kronental
from Stebbach, Baden, Germany. Elisabeth Wiedrich was the daughter of Peter and
Margaretha Wiedrich, immigrants to Kronenthal from Ludwigsburg, Wuertemberg,
Germany, and the younger sister of Michael Wiedrich, the forefather of the
Beulah and Mercer County Wiedrich families.)

Christinia Hoffmann was born to Paul and Elisabeth (Loeffler) Hoffmann on Oct.
24, 1853, also in Kronental. George and Christinia were married on June 7,
1874, in Kronental, where they were grain farmers and grape growers.

George's brothers and sisters were Maria (Christoph Modersitzki), Joseph
(Christina Weidner), Katharina (George Boeckel), Peter (Wilhelmina Boeckel,
Paulina Boeckel), Louisa (Wendelin Miller), John (Margaretha Breitenbuecher,
Sophia Moewes), Elisabeth (Nikolaus Hermes), and Philipp (Katharina Zeiszler).

Christinia's brothers and sisters were Joseph (Margaret Morast), Elisabeth
(Michael Hoffmann), Rosina (John Schroth) and Anton.

In October 1899, George and Christinia left Kronental for America. They traveled
across Russia to Hamburg, Germany, where they boarded the ship Augusta Victoria
and brought their surviving children by the Statue of Liberty, through Ellis
Island, N.Y., to farm about five miles north of present-day Beulah. Their
children were Peter (Mathilda Wolf), Margaret (John Friesz), Elisabeth (Jacob
Huber), John (Elizabeth Miller), Emma (Edward Kerner), Samuel (who at age nine
died during the voyage and was buried at sea), Edward (Sophia Achtenberg),
George (Louisa Koehler), and Alexander (Hertha Herman) . They were welcomed
here by George's younger brothers Peter, John and Philipp, who had earlier
settled in the Kronthal area. George and Christinia's farm was operated in
later years by their son Alex and in more recent times by their grandson Floyd.
Although their farm and most of the land once farmed by their sons Peter, John,
Edward and George is now a part of the gasification plant property and is no
longer farmed by the family, many of their relatives still farm here. Others of
their relatives still farm in Russia, but no longer in the Crimea, having been
deported to Kazakhstan about 1932. To this day, the Weigums in Europe and
America experience warm and happy visits with the Weigums in Russia.

Christinia was an exceptionally good cook. The German-Russian food she served is
still remembered by those who sat at her table. Although she was somewhat
temperamental and a rather strict parent, she was much beloved by her children
and remembered by them with great affection.

George, mild and gentle, idolized by his children, was a man of industry and
good will. He was exceedingly good-natured and he maintained his good humor
even in the most trying circumstances. He loved hunting, gardening and music.
His garden was off-limits to everyone. Only Christinia, by the strength of her
will, was able to go into his garden, but then only under his watchful presence.

George's music was enjoyed at "Hochzeit" dances and other festivities in Russia
and here at local barn dances. His pump organ is still in family use. It has
been written of George that his visits were much favored by friends and
relatives. He had licorice or halvah for the children and he "never saw" the
young men pilfer a supply of tobacco from his always-bulging tobacco pouch.

The adults were warmed by his widely acclaimed wine, usually brought in a wet
gunny sack. In America, his wine, nostalgically nicknamed "Der Krim" after
toasts to his birthplace, was made from grapes sent to him by his brothers,
Peter and John, who left here to grow grapes near Lodi, Calif.

In America, the Weigum family continued to speak in a beautiful and expressive
German dialect, as did other Germans from Russia in this area, rather than in
the artificial and affected "hoch-deutsch." When the Weigum family left the
Stebbach, Baden-Wuerttemberg, Germany, area for Russia in 1809, it is likely
they spoke in a Badenisch-Franconian dialect. However, after 90 years in Russia
living among Germans who spoke other dialects which influenced their own, their
speech ultimately included traces of Swabian, Pfalzisch, Alemannic, then some
Russisch, some Tatar and Turkish, and later a little English.

First generation children attended "English" schools and learned to read and
write English, but they spoke German at home and most were confirmed in German.
Although the language is slowly slipping away from the family as new
generations emerge, they celebrate their heritage through the enjoyment of
traditional German-Russian foods, pastries and sausage . . . awwer von dm Wein
"Der Krim" gebt's leider nimmi mehr.

In spite of being accustomed to an essentially good life in Russia and to the
mild climate of Crimea on the Black Sea, George and Christinia survived the
loss of their son during emigration, weathered the hardships of resettlement
and the climate of North Dakota to carve farms out of the prairie for
themselves and for their children.

Christinia died on July 3, 1918; George died on Jan. 3, 1921. They lie in Wolf's
Cemetery northeast of Beulah. George and Christinia professed Christianity and
were good parents, good farmers and good neighbors.

        George and Louisa (Koehler) Weigum

Back in 1949, the snowflakes really flew, according to Leona. She remembers when
the snow was so deep you had to dig out the horses. The roads were blocked from
January 6 until the first of April, when they could drive in with the truck.
Living on the farm meant there was always enough to eat. When they did go to
Beulah they used the horse and sled when nothing else moved, but there was a
time when the road had to be plowed before the horses could move. The Weils and
Fetches played a lot of canasta back then. The Fetches only lived down the road
about three-quarters of a mile.

Robert and Mary Wendel

Robert "Bob" Frank Wendel was born April 10, 1930, at South Heart to Clement and
Philomena (Cinder) Wendel. Bob came to Beulah in October 1964 to work as office
manager for Liebelt Chevrolet upon the recommendation of a friend, Wally
Wallender. They had worked together in Dickinson at Sax Motor Company and Wally
had moved back to Beulah to work for Liebelt. Bob had lived in South Heart and
worked in Dickinson and Belfield areas all his life except for the two years in
the army in 1951-52.

Bob writes, "When I came to Beulah in 1964 the city's population was roughly
1,200 and growing and when I was appointed city auditor in 1971 it was 1,344.
The south side of the city was sparsely populated and all of the property north
of Seventh Street was farm land. I remember, however, what it was like when I
drove bulk truck for Flamo Gas Company out of Dickinson and delivered propane
gas to our customers in the Beulah area, some of which were the Keogh Ranch,
Fred Flemmer residence, and the Corner Hardware Store which was located on the
comer where the Main Bar is located today. This was in 1949 and 1950. Propane
was pioneering in those days, and we had to drive over gravel roads to get here
from Highway 10. We experienced a very rough winter with very heavy snow that
year and highways were plowed to allow passage of single vehicle traffic in
many places. It was a must to carry a scoop shovel and a log chain, and it was
very common to pull vehicles out of the snow banks on Highways 49 and 31."

Bob was married in 1970 to Mary, daughter of Jacob and Elizabeth (Metz) Keller
of Dickinson. Mary was born April 6, 1939, at Dickinson. Their children are:
Frank, born July 24, 1959, and Betty Marie, born Dec. 22, 1962, both at
Richardton, N.D.

Bob's activities include: member of Saint Anthony, Dickinson; Veterans of
Foreign Wars, Disabled American Veterans, Quartermaster of VFW Herman Schmidt
Post 7759; 1970 and 1971, served with the Heavy Mortar Company--17th Regiment
--7th Army Division in Korea in 1951 and 1952. He is presently working at the
Beulah city hall as city auditor-accountant.

Mary is a homemaker and is a member of VFW Auxiliary, Tops Club, and a volunteer
helper at Beulah Community Nursing Home. She also enjoys ceramics.

        Fred and Emma Wolf and grandchildren

Andrew and Rose Wolf

In 1912 Andrew Wolf was two years old, his step-sister Helen, 8, and brother
Emil, 6, when his mother, Emma, and father, Fred, decided to venture from
Russia to America.

Considered well off in those days, they owned a beautiful wooden home in the
village of Garahout, located near Odessa, the capital of Russia. Wealth was
achieved through ownership of a flour mill generated by a large windmill.
Working 24 hours a day was not uncommon since the wind determined when the
wheat could be ground.

With the twin tensions of communism and war, the family, through the help of
United States agents, were able to schedule a trip to America. Leaving their
home and possessions behind was a small price to pay for freedom since history
shows staying would have been certain death.

Costing many thousands of dollars, they bought themselves aboard the second
floor of a steamship. Housing aboard the ship was restricted to three floors
with wealth determining the floor you could afford to stay on. The first floor
consisted of mainly the poor, the middle class on the second, and the top, or
third floor, was for the rich. Food and warmth were also equal to the floor you
stayed on. Though seasickness was quite common, the family enjoyed the 16-day
trip to America.

The children enjoyed the entertainment, especially the dancing, as well as the
round windows on the ship, which provided hours of gazing at the sea and the
jumping fish. Candy was occasionally tossed down from the rich to the children
on the lower floors. The scar on Helen's head still reminds her of her fall
aboard the ship. This is when Helen and the family were introduced to the
Band-Aid.

Upon arrival at Ellis Island, the Statue of Liberty was the first to welcome
people to the New World. Before any member of the ship was accepted into the
United States, each had to be examined for dangerous diseases. As the doctors
examined Emil, they feared he had one of those diseases because his eyes were
too red. With their diagnosis, the family was marked with chalk and ordered to
return to Russia. Once again the family had to arrange a trip to America
through United States agents. Through the necessary papers, they scheduled a
return trip through Germany and again had to pay the many thousands of dollars.

Around December 1912 the family arrived at Ellis Island for the second time.
They were allowed to stay and boarded a train for Hazen, N.D. The train came to
an end at a place called Expansion, believed to be north of Hazen along the
Missouri River. The next year would be spent with their uncle, who welcomed
them to North Dakota.

In the summer of 1914 they purchased a wagon, two horses (Lucy and Josy) and
various farming tools. Through the Homestead Act they acquired 160 acres of land
near Killdeer and in return had to live on it for five years to gain ownership.

For approximately one month the family lived beneath the wagon while the home
was being built. The home, roughly 60 feet by 24 feet, consisted of one room
divided into a sleeping and eating area. Twelve-inch squares of sod were cut
and laid together to make walls and to cover the logs to form the roof. A
mixture of mud and straw was then used to plaster the outside of the home.

Besides the two windows in the home, the two kerosene lamps provided the only
light for the family. The lamps were the responsibility of the women, whose job
was to fill and clean the lamps each day. The refrigeration system consisted of
a six-foot by eight-foot root cellar located inside the house. The root cellar
stored their many vegetables and acted as a refuge against dangerous weather.
The family was never cold, for even in the coldest weather the pot-belly stove
provided an adequate supply of heat.

Neighborhood hospitality and sharing were very important and quite common in
those days. The neighbors were very much appreciated when it came time to dig
the well. As the well was dug, a wood sleeve would be inserted to keep the
sides stable. Everyone was thankful that they hit water between 30 and 40 feet
deep. A simple hand crank and bucket were used to retrieve the water from the
well.

With fall approaching, a shelter had to be built for the horses and a winter's
supply of coal had to be brought home. The barn was simply a dugout cut into
the side of a hill with logs making the front and roof of the barn. The roof
was then covered with sod to provide warmth and stability to the shelter.
Finding coal in the Killdeer area was not difficult, but was time-consuming.
Wind erosion would expose the coal close to the surface, so it was just a
matter of finding the spots. The hard work was loading the wagon and having to
transport the coal from six or seven miles away.

No crops were planted their first year on the homestead with the house, barn,
well and winter preparations taking most of the family's time. When supplies
were needed, a trip had to be made to Dickinson some 35 miles away.

On these trips, the children would take turns going with Dad while Mother stayed
behind busy crocheting and knitting warm clothing for winter. Dickinson was
used as a grain exchange and a place to sell any small-game pelts acquired
through the year. The distance was too far to make very often, so supplies such
as coffee, flour, sugar and kerosene were picked up in great abundance. While
there, the mail was picked up and a treat for the children was not forgotten.

With fall came school. The one-room schoolhouse was located three miles from
home, or about an hour's walk. With weather permitting, school was attended but
not mandatory. Spelling, reading and arithmetic occupied the 9:00-3:30 school
day. When the winter snow was too deep, Dad would take the children with the
sleigh. After school meant doing chores, either by helping Dad outside, or
Mother inside.

Evenings were spent playing checkers, reading or doing homework with bedtime
around eight o'clock. Bathtime happened once a week with everyone sharing the
same tub of water, with no child being favored over the other.

Catalogues such as Montgomery Ward's, Sears and Roebuck, Chicago mail order and
even peach wrappers, all had more than one use at the Wolf household. If they
couldn't be found, they were usually located in the outhouse.

The following spring's crops were wheat, oats and flax, which were planted with
the aid of Lucy and Josy, who pulled the one-bottom plow. Mother was busy
planting a large garden of potatoes, pumpkins, watermelons, cabbage, carrots
and just about anything that could be grown in North Dakota. The watermelon was
pickled so to last through the winter, as was the cabbage made into sauerkraut.

Good health among the family was attributed to the shot of home brew each person
had each morning. Raisins, sugar, yeast and water were used in their still to
make the home brew. The still produced the 190-proof whiskey and was mixed
mainly with water for drinking. The home brew was stored in glass jars but
never sold, as it was against the law to make it in the first place.

With no way to refrigerate excess meat, the family hunted small game and
butchered ducks, geese and chickens for meat. Each fall the family butchered
two pigs that were made into sausage and smoked. The five cows the family owned
produced the milk, along with the butter and cheese the family made.

After the necessary five years on the land, the family decided it was time to
move. With the addition of two more children, the land and the house were not
sufficient to support a family of seven. Receiving $1,700 for the homestead,
the family moved north of Hazen and rented a larger farmstead.

In 1926 they purchased their first car, a used, black 1924 Model "T" touring
car, for $150. The car was used strictly for church and to go to town. At
first, the children were afraid to ride in the car because of the speed, but
soon came to enjoy the ride.

At the age of 17, Andrew became a hired man for neighboring farmers. In 1936 he
married Rose and moved to Quinn, S.D., working for the railroad for one year.
From there, they moved back to North Dakota where Andrew worked for the Lucky
Strike Mining Company of Zap, the Knife River Coal Company of Beulah, and as a
farmer south of Golden Valley. Together Andrew and Rose raised five children
and lost one child to a crippling disease at age six.

After many years of travel as a mechanic for a construction firm, the Wolfs
retired in 1975 and now reside in Beulah.

Dennis and Mary Margaret Wolf

Mary Margaret was born March 12, 1937, to Carl and Marguerite (McLaughlin)
Herman. She attended Beulah High School and Dickinson State and taught in
Wisconsin, Minnesota and North Dakota. On June 14, 1958, she and Dennis Wolf
were married at St. Joseph's Church at Beulah. Dennis attended Beulah High
School, University of North Dakota and the University School of Medicine in
Wisconsin. He is a practicing physician at the Rodgers and Gumper Clinic at
Dickinson.

        Dennis, Mary Margaret Wolf and family

They have three children: Karla (Mrs. Todd Lennick), Mike, a student at Bozeman,
MT and Kathy, a student at the National Business College at Rapid City. They
have two grandchildren: Megan and Tyler.

Donald J. Wolf

Donald J. Wolf is a Mercer County native who feels fortunate that Beulah has
developed the need for technical jobs such as his, which allows young people
looking for jobs to come home to Beulah for employment.

Wolf, the son of Emil and Hannah (Schopp) Wolf, was born Aug. 11, 1952.

While attending Beulah High School, he achieved the Eagle Scout Award with Boy
Scout Troop 19. He recalls those Scouting days with deep appreciation of the
special efforts of then-Scoutmaster Darold Benz.

After high school graduation, he attended Dickinson State College.

While serving in the United States Navy, he achieved the rank of Radarman Second
Class. He received the Vietnam Service Award while serving aboard the U.S.S.
Butte AE-27. He was awarded the Bronze Star for working with mine-sweeping in
Hai Phong, North Vietnam Harbor.

Wolf worked as a maintenance electrician at Coal Creek Station near Underwood
for five and one-half years; he is currently employed in the same capacity at
Antelope Valley Station.

Emil C. and Hannah Wolf

Emil was born Oct. 28, 1912, to Joseph and Selma Wolf at Hazen. He grew up on
the family farm and was educated in Hazen schools. Hannah was born Nov. 14,
1914, to Franz and Rose Schopp at Beulah. She grew up on the family farm and was
educated in the Beulah schools.

Emil worked for ND State Highway Dept. as maintenance foreman and retired in
1977. The Wolfs are members of Zion Lutheran Church where Emil served as church
deacon for 15 years and was also on the church council. He was also a Boy Scout
leader for several years during the time his sons were in Boy Scouts. Emil and
Hannah have three sons: Glenton, Walter and Donald. All three sons graduated
from Beulah High School and Dickinson State College.

        Emil Wolf family. Back row: Glenton and Walter. Seated: Emil, Donald
        and Hannah

Glenton and his wife Cheryl live at Grand Forks with their two sons, Curtis and
Chad. Glenton is a music instructor in one of the Grand Forks schools. Walter
and his wife, the former Sarah Huber, live at Center with their two daughters
Martina and Erica. Walter teaches high school mathematics, German and computer
courses in the Center school system.

Donald lives at Beulah. He is employed by Basin Electric at the Antelope Valley
Station.

Emil writes, "On the 4th of July in 1937, the town of Beulah was flooded. We
were in a saloon on Main Street where Sackman's Cleaners is now. We stood at
the bar in our bare feet drinking beer! Water covered the main floor. Chester
Haas was the bar owner."

Garvin Wayne Wolf

Garvin Wolf attended school in Beulah, graduating in 1953. During his high
school years he played the tuba in the Beulah band and was active in Zion
Luther League. Following graduation he taught country school south of Beulah
for one year. Prior to his death in 1955 he was a taxi driver in Mandan. ND.

        Herb Wolf family. Left to right: Carrie, Audrey, Lydia, Herbert,
        Geneis and Jerry

Herbert J. and Lydia Wolf

Herbert J. and Lydia (Miller) Wolf's ancestors came from South Russia and
homesteaded north of Hazen. Herb, the son of J. Jacob and Katherina (Morast)
Wolf, was born Nov. 24, 1906. Growing up, Herb enjoyed playing baseball,
hunting, swimming, ice skating and horseback riding. He attended country school
through the eighth grade.

On Jan. 3, 1929, Herb married Lydia H. Miller, the daughter of Sam and Marie
(Schuh) Miller. As a child Lydia remembers doing embroidery, tatting and sewing
clothes for her younger sisters and brothers.

After farming for several years the Wolfs moved to Montana and Herb worked on
the Fort Peck Dam. In 1937 they moved to Beulah where Herb was employed for 32
years with Montana-Dakota Utilities Company.

The Wolfs have five children:

Geneis Mildred, born Aug. 21, 1929, married Ruben Brunmeier; they have three
children.

Garvin Wayne, born Dec. 24, 1934, died July 17, 1955.

Jerry Dane, born Feb. 26, 1934, married Janice Porter; they have three children.

Audrey Mae, born Feb. 28, 1937, married Herbert Sasse; they have four children.

Caroline Lee (Carrie), born Jan. 3, 1942, married Myron Hafner; they have two
children.

Herb and Lydia are members of Zion Lutheran Church, Senior Citizens, the Beulah
Country Club, and Senior Citizens bowling.

Lydia is active in ALCW of Zion and served as president. She was in charge of
quilting for World Relief many times. Lydia also taught quilting to area
residents and continues to make quilts for all her children, grandchildren and
great-grandchildren. During the 1950s she sewed outfits for the Beulah
cheerleaders.

Herb spends the warm months playing golf. He also enjoys playing pool and making
wooden articles for members of his family.

The Wolfs live in Beulah.

Jerry and Jan Wolf

Jerry Dane Wolf (Feb. 26, 1934) is the son of Herb and Lydia Wolf. He attended
school in Beulah, where he was active in boxing. Jerry was in the Army and later
attended the University of North Dakota in Grand Forks and graduated from
medical school. Jerry is married to Janice (Jan) Porter (Dec. 31, 1938). Jan
grew up in Park River, ND, with her parents, Charles and Loraine Porter.

Jan is a registered nurse and active in the church.

The Wolfs live in Billings, Mont., where Jerry is a doctor of medicine
specializing in radiology.

They have three children:

Kimberly Renee Wolf (Feb. 19, 1960) lives in San Diego, Calif.

Michelle Loraine Wolf (Dec. 27, 1961) lives in San Francisco, Calif.

Gerald (Jerry) Herbert (Feb. 7, 1963) is a salesman for Snap-on-Tools. He is
married to Tara Bracey (Oct. 11, 1966), whose parents are Norris and Georgia
Bracey. Jerry and Tara live in the Los Angeles, Calif., area where Tara attends
college.

Armon and Peggy Wolff

Armon Wolff and Peggy Murray were married July 1, 1955. They live on the Wolff
ranch five and one-half miles southwest of Golden Valley. The ranch was
originally homesteaded by the Walker family and was called Willow Springs Farm.
This was the site of the Bronco Flat post office. Armon's parents, Mr. and
Mrs. Henry Wolff, purchased it in 1922.

        Armon and Peggy Wolff and family

Armon and Peggy have five children. Kathy married Blair Trout and they live in
Endiang, Alberta, Canada. They farm and are big game guides. Kathy and Blair
have three children, Teri, Jeff and Cody.

Patricia is married to Perry Fosse and lives in Filmore, Utah. She is employed
with the Bureau of Land Management. Pat and Perry have one son, Kole.

Tammy Sailer lives in Beulah and works at ANG. Tammy has one son, Jaye.

Scott is married to Sherry Voltz and they live on the ranch. Scott and Sherry
have one son, J.D.

Shane is married to Marsha Weisenberger and they live on the ranch. Shane and
Marsha have one daughter, Paula Jo.

Other than ranching, Armon went to auction school in 1964 and has been in the
auction business ever since. He is also a real estate broker and certified
appraiser.

        Henry Younker family. Back row: John, Fred, Lillian, Jack and Adam.
        Front row: Gust, Henry; Christina, Herbert

Fred H. and Gertrude Younker

Frederick Henry "Freddie" Younker was born Dec. 18, 1919, at Beulah, to Henry
and Christina (Neibauer) Younker. Freddie married Gertrude "Gertie" Sailer,
daughter of George and Regina (DeWald) Sailer. Gertie was born March 11, 1921,
on a farm north of Stanton.

        Fred Younker family: Gary, Gert, Fred, Pamela

        Robert Miller family: Brett, Pamela, Robert, Ryan

        Gary Younker family: Gary, Cheryl, Shawn, Mark

In his youth Freddie was a member of Boy Scout Troop No. 21 and was a member of
their drum and bugle marching band, of which Bert Webber was the troop leader.
Fred attended grade and high school in Beulah. In his sophomore year during
football practice, he sustained a serious hip injury which kept him out of
school the rest of the year. He was also a member of the Beulah Miner's
baseball team. Fred was quite a sports enthusiast and rarely missed a home game
of basketball, football or Junior Legion baseball games. Fred was employed from
1941-1944 by the Occident Elevator Co., under the management of Bernhard
Mahowald. From 1944 until his retirement in 1983, he worked for Knife River Coal
Company, retiring as foreman.

Gert grew up on a farm north of Hazen, but at the age of 16 became a resident of
Beulah. Gert writes that her most memorable days were the three years she spent
at Beulah High School. She worked as a sales clerk and dental assistant. They
were members of Zion Lutheran Church and Fred served a term as secretary on the
church council. He also served as trustee for the Beulah Eagles Club, of which
he was a member. Fred died July 30, 1985. They were parents of:

Gary Fred Younker, who was born Dec. 4, 1943, at Beulah. He married Cheryl
Harper, and they have two children: Shawn Renae, born May 6, 1966, at Bismarck,
and Mark Alan, born Dec. 11, 1968, at Bismarck.

Pamela Lynn Younker, born Dec. 2, 1948, at Beulah, married Robert Miller. They
have two sons: Brett Robert Miller, born Aug. 8, 1971, in Louisiana and Ryan
Michael Miller, born Feb. 4, 1977, at Bismarck.

Henry and Christina Younker

Henry Younker was born March 18, 1883, in the Crimea, Russia, to Henry and __
(Schopp) Younker. Henry married Christina Neibauer in Russia. Christina was born
Oct. 5, 1883, to John and __ (Doffee) Neibauer. Henry and Christina with their
daughter, Lydia, immigrated to the U.S. in 1910. They settled in Eureka, S.D.
In 1911 they moved to a farm 11 miles southwest of Beulah, and in 1915 they
moved into Beulah where they lived until their deaths. Henry was a farm laborer
and butcher. The Younkers were longtime custodians at Zion Lutheran Church when
it was the small German congregation. He was the bell ringer for the services
until his death in 1954. Christina was a homemaker and died April 21, 1958.
They were the parents of:

"Lydia" Lillian Heihn, born Oct. 9, 1909, at Crimea, Russia, died Oct. 16, 1982.

John Younker, born Feb. 9, 1912, at Beulah, died September, 1987.

Jacob "Jake" Younker, born October 1914, at Beulah, died 1964.

Adam "Whitey" Younker, born July 9, 1917, at Beulah, died August, 1982.

Fred "Freddie" Younker, born Dec. 18, 1918, at Beulah, died July 30, 1985.

Gustave "Gust" Younker, born Sept. 14, 1922, at Beulah, died April, 1966.

Herbert "Herb" Younker, born Jan. 18, 1924, at Beulah.

Kenneth and Cynthia Ziman

Kenneth Ziman was born Sept. 17, 1951 at St. Joseph's Hospital in Dickinson, ND.
He is the son of Edward and Mary (Erker) Ziman. He attended school and graduated
from Dodge High School in 1969. He attended one year of college at Dickinson
State College and then transferred to watch-making school in St. Paul, MN. He
worked four years as apprentice in Stadheim Jewelers in Albert Lea, MN.

        Ken, Cindy and Daniel Zieman

In 1977 Ken decided to move back to North Dakota and on March 21, 1977 in
Beulah he opened Ziman's Jewelry Store as a sole proprietorship.

On July 17, 1981 he married Cynthia Roshau, daughter of Richard and Marlene
(Binstock) Roshau, who own and operate Hazen Electric of Hazen. Cindy was born
at St. Joseph's Hospital in Dickinson and moved to Hazen along with her
parents, two sisters, and one brother. She attended school and graduated from
Hazen High School in 1978. She went one year to the University of Mary (then
Mary College) in Bismarck.

In September of 1980 she started working as a bookkeeper at Union State Bank in
Hazen, then transferred to a teller position until she had her baby and at that
time went part-time as a bookkeeper again, as she is still doing.

Their son, Daniel Kenneth Ziman, was born at Sakakawea Medical Center in Hazen
on Oct. 27, 1982. Daniel starts kindergarten in the fall of 1989.

Ken has taken an active interest in the growth and progress of his town. He has
been a Chamber of Commerce board member for two terms, president of the Beulah
Boosters and a member for 11 years, Lions member for seven years, park board
member for four years and starting another four-year term, a member of the
Trophy Takers Salmon Club, and is very active with the golf course, serving as
treasurer, vice president and board member. He was also involved in planning
the grass greens project.

Cindy has been active in Merry Mrs. Homemakers Club since 1983 and was treasurer
in 1985, a charter member of the Beulah Lioness Club, serving as secretary for
the club, is active in RENEW Group with their church, and is also a member of
Circle with the church.

They are members of the St. Joseph Catholic Church in Beulah.
